Finally beat the game and gotta say it's not as bad as people said, but I can see why they dislike it. First thing first, the only Tales game I played is Tales of Abyss on PS2, and I can't really speak much nor compare this game to the previous installments (e.g. Vesperia, Xillia), although I do have Symphonia on my library, I just haven't found the right time to play it yet (planning to play Berseria first, mainly because it's set in the same world as Zestiria, so hopefully the game is going to be on sale this summer).
Anyway, let's talk about this game. For my RPGs I often look to my holy trinity of perfection: challenging, rewarding, and emotionally impacting. It nails 2/3, the story had emotional value and great voice acting, yet the rewarding feeling for progress seems to not exist. Beating the story, and making progress in Zestiria feels like a chore list. While many RPGs use a list like side quest log, not all feel so drag. However, I can say the difficulty options in combat almost always give a great trade off for higher risk, higher reward and this game is no different. Boss fights are enjoyable and the combat was fantastic, up until you learn how to spec to spam calamity flare or maelstrom (cleans up mobs nicely). The progression of mystic artes is also enjoyable. And don't forget that soundtrack is definitely the highlight of this game, I spent quite some times listening to them and never got bored, also the Shrine Trials got me turning up the BGM and turning down everything else for the entire duration of the Trial. I love that it continues right into the battles while inside the shrines rather than switching out for more generic battle themes. Definitely up there along with Chrono Cross, Nier and Persona 3 in term of my favorite JRPG soundtrack all the time.
Also, the fact that none of the females in your party are involved with the main character romantically is such a breath of fresh air. Both females are very individualistic and following are the other supporting characters. They are all very interesting in different ways, little snippets of their characteristics revealed in the smallest areas and it makes them seem more realistic. There's no romance forced on you and where many players are frustrated that you can't romance the female characters, I'm very pleased that they kept to the realistic idea that they're amidst war and there are larger issues at hand.
With that said the time given to make the few side missions in the game worth doing was well noted. They do feel like mini episodic adventures. The area that falls flat, is that the time spent traveling or attempting to fast travel to complete these quests tends to ruin both the pacing of the game, and the cohesiveness of these stories. That, along with the convoluted  weapon/skill system brought this down to a 7.5/10 for me.
Gotta be honest, around 40 hours into the game, I started watching the anime and boy that first episode blew my mind. Ufotable really went out their way and I was holding my breath on the last 5 minutes of the episode. It's THAT good. I appreciated the direction they take with the anime too, and speaking of which, the random Berseria episode (I believe it was episode 5-6) is kinda unexpected but still interesting nonetheless. Violet is so much interesting and literally the exact opposite of Zestiria's MC. Hopefully they'll animate it one day, seeing Berseria has a pretty good sales record on Japan.

There's a lot of games out there that say: "We're bringing back the feeling of games you played from your childhood!" But most of them forget the little things that made these games so memorable. The thing is, in my humble opinion, when you play a hat in time, you're playing a game that, had it released in the era it was taking inspiration from, would have been able to stand tall with the greats of the platformer genre of the day.
Remember the scene from Ratatouille where the cynical critic eats the food and it transports him back to his childhood? That's kinda how this game was for me. It "Gets it". It gets why we loved the older games. The charm, the dark humor, the colorful characters both literally and figuratively, and the easter eggs that didn't need to be in the game but were anyway because you could tell the people behind it y'know,

While this game is sort of short, I'd say that for having like 1/7th the budget of yooka laylee they succeeded at what they set out to do with flying colors, and that was to make a game that paid respectful homage to the platformers we grew up with.
I'd highly recommend this game to anyone who likes platformers. It's not flawless, there are a few technical issues in the game like framedrops on alpine sky and sometimes graphics settings won't save, this game is still well worth your money as a lot of those things can be patched out and plus even the length issue will be remedied with steam workshop content that I'm sure the community is going to go wild with, or just at least recreate stuff from other platformers.

The story takes a dark turn, and after completing the game I wanted to know the legitimacy of the story.
I went in thinking this was based on a true story, and was excited in the beginning as this was the first "Interactive Documentary" that I'd ever heard of. It was exciting to play something that was familiar, but different in large ways.
If you are a Game Design student, or just someone looking for a game with a great story this worth getting.

If you enjoy RPGs, you may enjoy this game. As a learning tool, I'd say do yourself a favor and skip this game. Instead, get Learn Japanese To Survive! Katakana War, which is much more refined and a great learning tool. Hiragana Battle had me chugging potions left and right, with me unable to keep my characters alive through simple battles. I think this game should be skill based, where I do well in the game if I am learning the Hiragana characters. Instead, it is grind based, where I do well only if I sit through repetitive battles with Hiragana characters I've already mastered, levelling up my heroes to a point where they can actually endure the enemie's attacks. Zones are long, with poorly randomized enemies. For example, the same three Hiragana characters will show over and over in a zone, and it takes away from learning individual characters, instead optimizing learning a set of unrelated characters.
One of the most frustrating aspects of the game is the combat system. If I have four of my heroes attack one Hiragana character, and the third attack kills the Hiragana, the fourth character will send his named attack to a Hiragana that is still alive, which is the wrong name, ineffective and a wasted attack. There is no way to tell how many attacks a Hiragana character needs to take in order to die, so this problem happens over and over again. Again, Katakana War fixed this problem completely, which is why I don't recommend Hiragana Battle. I'd say use something like Duolingo or Ankiweb for learning Hiragana, and use Katakana War to learn Katakana. This game is just a waste of time because of the grinding that doesn't scale with my actual knowledge.

Stray Cat Crossing is a short, but intense tour into the rabbithole.
The story's start is pretty simple - you find the young girl called Cat wandering on the streets, and you offer her to take her back to his house - even giving your scarf to her not to catch a cold on your way. But you realize only after her entering the house that she still has your scarf, which is really dear to your heart, so you enter Cat's house to find her and ask her for your scarf.
While the short introduction also plays an important part in understanding the whole story, the real content of the game starts after entering the house.  On your left you see a blind girl, eyes covered with bandages, holding a camera, meekly asking you if she could take a photo of you...  and then you can pick your save slot :)  The game developers really cleverly implemented, and inserted the savepoint system in the game that it's actually a person, who appears at numerous spots during the game, always reflecting to your current actions - it's wonderfully immersive
After speaking to her, you see footprints on the ground, which lead deeper into the house.
The game consists of three different parts of the house, three chapters - each really different from the other ones, they build on the previous ones but there's a common thing in them - they are all has their own creepy characters, themes and actions that can send shivers down one's spine.  Each chapter gives you a clear goal, and you can reach it by completing smaller goals, sometimes puzzles.  The characters of the house had a similar feeling to me like in Silent Hill - they do have a strong resemblance to asian, or rather japanese horror-creatures, but what sets the macabre tone the best is that they are all clever, thinking - and has no real intention of hurting you. But, if it's possible, they won't let you go.
The game only has one point when you can die while you're just walking around, but it's more like an event, like a QTE is for a game - and it has a save point just before it, so it's safe to say that while saving is advised, it's not easy to get yourself killed. Which is nice, because you'll be able to spend more time exploring the house, and to see VCR-like short video-cuts appear, that unravels a little more about the story, while conveniently raising the creepy-factor a LOT.
I don't want to spoi the story, especially as the game is short, can be completed in three hours and it's really worth to be experienced rather than just told about. But as it can be guessed from the lack of combat, the game's story revolves around pretty serious matters, and it's elements presented through the game's symbols, with the whole story explained at the end. While the third, last chapter got pretty tedious compared to the first two, the game really did a great job by not making the story overly simplistic, and at the same the explanation was presented in a way that does not make the player feel stupid for not getting it during the game.
While the art style seemed a little at first (the characters are pretty big compared to the environment) the game did a perfect job at introducing, then gradually unfold and solve a story while making me feel intrested, weirded out, or at some points just staring onto the screen.  I've got the game from a bundle that cost maybe 1.5$ ; but I think if someone's looking for a more creepy-weird, than a scary horror and finds the art direction attractive, I can absolutely recommend the game even at full price.  It's done with RPGMaker but uses own art, has a great soundtrack and has a really nice story with a proper ending that's quite memorable.  It was a great experience for me.

Learning a new alphabet is difficult, and it needs you to do a lot of repetition. I've tried several ways to approach learning hiragana, just for the sake of entertainment and not as a serious endevour.
Learn Japanese To Survive had an actual good approach to this, integrating repeating a hiragana character over and over until it stuck by making it an integrated combat mechanic. The problem is, that they wanted to fit the Final Fantasy-esque combat ontop it so bad, that it makes the combat extremely boring. Combat is basically this: A Hiragana character can only be damaged by choosing the equivalent English sounding word/letter. Damaged, not killed. So this means, if you know the character, you have to click the same sound multiple times to kill it. So you think for ~2 seconds what the sound is, use ~6 seconds to plot it in (multiple times) and wait ~20 seconds for your choices to resolve. Repetition is key to learning a language, but instead you end up using the majority of the time just finding the sound and waiting for it to resolve.
If voice recognition is good enough, a better approach would be a voice-controlled Guitar Hero-like game where you could get past the thinking aspect and just get the letters out on reflex. Learn Japanese To Survive instead wastes time on waiting and the wrong kind of repetition.

It is kind of overwhelming when you get to learn a new language. Especially with such a complex language like Japanese.
I have just started playing/learning, and I am happy so far with this.
This game is more than just that, besides engaging into the story itself, it also serves it purpose without being too overwhelming with one thing at a time. Yes, there are free websites where you can learn Hiragana and such, but personally I need something to keep myself motivated into continuing on learning, and "Learn Japanese To Survive: Hiragana Battle" does that with the interactivity it offers, being a game made with RPG Maker. Plus said "free" websites usually start spitting complex words on you without even telling how is each letter/character pronounced.
One example, when I tried Livemocha, the first word they gave me was "Otokonohito" (man). How exactly is every word in "おとこのひと" pronounced?! Is it Kanji, Hiragana, Katakana?!
Instead, "Learn Japanese to Survive: Hiragana Battle" started with the basics, with a simple lesson on vowels; how are they pronounced, how are they written and such.
Like I mentioned, I'm just getting started myself, but so far I can say I rcommend this strongly to anyone that wants to learn Japanese from its basics.

For a cheap price, Jet Gunner is a decent run-'n-gun game in the veins of Contra and Megaman. Graphics are decent, but the music is very awful. Even some NES games have better soundtrack than Jet Gunner.
There are also several issues to be addressed. First of all, some obtainable weapon upgrades are straight downgrade to the normal shot. For example, the missile launcher as the most notorious one fires missiles that will either travel upwards or downwards, causing them to be uncontrollable. As such, it's pointless to even try to pick them up. Secondly, the game has cheap levels that rely too much on the jetpack. The later levels are very cheap in nature, having unpredictable spike and trap positioning. Most of the time your deaths will be caused by these cheap traps. Because of this, I feel that a checkpoint system to continue in the middle of the stage should be added to help new players. Lastly, not being able to shoot upwards is a big problem. You are forced to use the jetpack in order to shoot them.
Overall, the game isn't bad. It definitely passes as a budget 'Contra' or 'Megaman'. But it could be better if those issues are dealt with.

I'm really not sure how I'd rate this game.  Wait!  Let me start over!
I loved playing this game.  It was awesome.  And at a price of... free... it's well worth at least checking out.
That said, I honestly can't think of a price above free that would leave me feeling any affection for this game.  The art is... bare bones, the storytelling minimal, and the mechanics simple.  This is the type of thing that I could code in Ren'Py in a day or two, with minimal chance for review.  And yet, even with all that said, it's put together so well that I can't help but feel that this is actually a very professional piece of work.
And it passes my main test.  It was fun.  I didn't play it long.  The amount you see, around 1.3 hours, is the amount of time you need to complete it, and hunt down all remaining acheivements.  But during that time I had a great experience.
So... this... is my thumb up!

This platformer/puzzle game has a minimalistic black & white style that is rather absorbing.  There is not a music score playing through Limbo, but Limbo is better off for it.  Instead you're treated to atmospheric sounds that suits the graphical ambiance to the world.  The game is an extremely short one (only logged about 3 or 4 hours), but the imagery and what happens had left me pondering what this was all about.  The puzzles can be diabolical in some areas with some requiring some trial & error, logical leaps, and some precise timing.  But hey, that's part of the fun is overcoming the challenges.

For an early acces game, I find it already very enjoyable to play. I have not found any major bugs / flaws yet. It is true, the amount of items etc is still low, and the map is not that big. However there is a lot of things to do, and the survival is, very realistic. I greatly enjoyed foraging for food, scouting buildings etc and I look forward to this game being completed, and being bigger. I recommend this game to anyone who is into realistic survival games, but don't like fighting monsters / zombies all the time. Fight a wolf instead! After surviving for about 14 days I'd say 10/10 would play again.

Disturbed is a choose-your-own-adventure visual novel from Brad Moore. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
How many games do you get for free? There you go; pro number one for this game.
This game has 17 achievements and they couldn’t be easier to get. Just die. Die a lot and in various ways.
The atmosphere is great and the setting is most intriguing.
The Bad
It always pains me to complain about free games, because they’re free and I’m sure the developer put a lot of work into them. See the below section for me criticisms.
The Meh
The art in the game can be a little hit and miss, but, when it’s on point, it is really good.
The sounds, while good, are much to sparse.
I feel as though the setting is being held back from it’s full potential due to the simplistic nature of the game.
Verdict: Yea
It’s a free game. It’s a good game considering that it’s free. Look Disturbed up in the Steam Store if you have nothing better going on.

Deep at the bottom of the ocean is the city of Rapture. A city not for Gods or kings, A city for men.
Built to be a utopia for mankind's greatest thinkers to prosper.
The "world's best and brightest" were granted freedom of will and choice in Rapture, unrestrained by government, religion and similar established institutions. The results were amazing breakthroughs in robotics and genetics.
But On December 31, 1958, a massive working-class uprising, led by a man known only as Atlas occurred in upper-class locations in the city, This sparked a civil war in Rapture and marked the beginning of the end.
As the player you join the story after it has already concluded, left to wonder the ruins of this once great city, stalked by what's left of the survivors of the war, who due to genetic meddling are not quite human anymore.
The game has totally immersive environments that the developers clearly enjoyed creating, accompanied by an original and genuinely interesting story that unfolds before you.
With developers being far too willing to bypass story these days for the sake of throw away 'action' moments this game is an exception, Bioshock actually has strong literary references, with clear nods to books such as Logans run and George Orwell's 1984.

This is my first review so im glad I picked one of my favorite games to start off with (be warned its long, so if you want to skip to the end it sums up the review) . My hours don't do it justice but rest assured, I had this game for both PS3 and Xbox before buying it once again on Steam (Yes, I loved it that much, also theres no limit on units which is so much better than being capped on consoles). This game will never be RTS game that sets the bar for all other RTS style games, far from it, BUT, this is infact one of the best RTS games around nowadays.
Firstly, you get THREE campaigns for three different factions, each with a very unique style. GDI which is basically your standard army relying on highly advanced tech to destroy your enemies *cough* Mammoth tanks OP *cough* . Then there is NOD (All hail Kane!), arguabley the one that takes the most skill, as you are usually going to end up using stealth units or surprise kamikaze runs in order to halt your more advanced enemies. They may not pack the biggest punch, but they have a really mean defense system which is every turtles dream and every player who likes to steamroll's nightmare. Then there is Scrin, take the ships from Stargate Atlantis and Independence day, throw in some Tripods from War of the worlds and some menacing alien-infantry and you have one of the most OP factions in any RTS ever. All campaigns are great and all have replay value, and trust me, when the difficulty is on hard, you will need an act of god to save you for almost every mission. All and all, the campaigns are really good and all are essentially a tutorial in some way for Skirmish mode. Straight to the point, Skirmish mode is your standard Team Deathmatch, you can do anything between 1v1 to 4v4, or if you want to be a god do a 1v7.
Now lets talk about the cons. One of the biggest problems in the game is MASSING, in order words, spamming the same unit over and over cause you can't be bothered to use some real strategy and want to steam roll every skirmish or mission. Whether its creating a moving fortress of 20 Mammoth tanks, swarming the skies with 1000 (slight exageration) Venoms or just flat out crucifying everything in your path with some Scrin aircraft or tripods, if you want to mass, this is your game. However, there is an amazing array of different units with different abilities that the AI uses to its full potential and it takes quite a bit of skill to combat it, try to experiment with different units, massing isn't fun. Next con is the difficulty system. Easy is too easy, its a curbstomp and its the setting you'd use to teach your little sibling how to play. Medium/Normal is a step up but after a few games you should be fine although you can't 1v2 or 1v3 against Medium AI's. Then theres Hard/Brutal, whatever hate-induced state the developers were on when they made this setting, they wanted you to lose. Its nearly impossible to take down a Brutal opponent, it took myself and 2 other friends about 40 minutes to kill a Brutal enemy AI, its honestly that hard unless you mass/turtle. If you like a challenge, this is were you get one. I once did two Brutal AI vs myself and five mediums, after 10 minutes three of my allies were dead and we only won cause I turtled and spammed the super weapons.
Lastly the multiplayer servers are down, there is some fan-supported servers around but the official ones are down (♥♥♥♥ YOU EA).
So heres the summary, if you want a game for really good campaign and endless amounts of fun with Skirmishes, this is worth it. Avoid massing for a real challenge and use the Mothership to wipe out the whole map if you want to end the map with a bang, pun intended.

Any game that I complete should consider itself lucky. If I play through a game twice, it should feel honored. I have played through this game 4 times (on various platforms and non-steam versions). I consider the Bioshock franchise as my one of my favorites along with the Half-Life and Elder Scrolls franchises. The real star of the show here is Rapture. The city of Rapture is rich with detail and is very beautiful even though it is in ruins. Rapture was what made me keep going back to play Bioshock. In fact, before I was finished with my first playthrough, I decided that this game sucks and the only thing it had going for it was Rapture. The gamplay felt tired and clunky. I finished the game because I wanted to see more of Rapture. When I was done, I put the game back in its box and sold it on ebay. Months later my mind would return to Rapture and eventually, I bought it and played through it again. Sometimes the gameplay still feels clunky, but I've largely gotten used to it. I would give this game 9.5 stars out of 10.

I wouldn't say I'm a huge Tales expert, having only played Symphonia and every game preceding it. But Symphonia is the gold standard to which I hold this series, unfortunately probably due in part to nostalgia. Sure, it was generously peppered with cliches, like... well, every JRPG at this point (it was my first JRPG, so I did not recognize cliches yet), but it had a diverse cast of decently-written characters with compelling personality that played off of each other in interesting ways.
So why am I telling you about this on a Tales of Zestiria review? Because this game has NONE of it. I wanted to love this game. I wanted to be emotionally invested in these characters and their struggles. It even showed a bit of promise in the beginning. But, even after 30+ hours into the game, with an untold percentage of this time being spent in overly-long cutscenes and menus (thanks to trying to work with the bloated passive skills system), I could not feel myself being pulled into this game, because Sorey and company bored the soul out of me. I don't think I was even a third of the way through the game before I reached my breaking point.
Sorey, the central protagonist, is the ultimate in "Gary Stu" characterization. For the uninitiated, this is the male variant of "Mary Sue," a term that was created to describe poorly written characters who were overly ideal and beloved by their peers while lacking in any meaningful flaws. Sorey is unwaveringly and obnoxiously virtuous to the point that he barely seems human. This might be due in part to his "upbringing," to avoid giving away too much, but no matter the reason, I don't see anybody buying into this "paragon of absolute good" trope that Sorey embodies. His companions consist almost entirely of spry, smiley, upstanding young adults (the kind found all too often in JRPGs, to be fair), who are all as lacking in personality as he is, and rarely seem to butt heads with one another, since they're all busy being enamored with the smell of Sorey's farts. The (as far as I could tell) totally straightforward plot certainly didn't help matters either. It's safe to say nothing's really going to throw you for a loop.
With all this talk of non-gameplay issues, you might wonder how the combat actually holds up... well, it's decent at best, even if it eventually hits a plateau after which it doesn't change in any meaningful way. The character fusion system really breaks the balance though. If your characters seem kind of weak (which they are, horribly so), don't worry, just fuse a pair together to effectively remove most of the nuance and challenge. The free revives granted by this mechanic, as well as some characters' ability to revive after being switched out for a short amount of time, should leave you with nothing to fear. You'll probably only die if facing something strong enough to kill you in a matter of seconds. There's really no happy medium here. On a technical level, the combat doesn't even work that well. I'll try not to blame the 30FPS cap for not being able to keep up with my inputs, but trying to perform a directional arte and instead quickstepping is WAY more frustrating than it sounds. Also you have no camera control during fights (seriously, none), so, fighting in any kind of enclosed space will probably land your camera in the wall. Great foresight there.
There's not much else I can say about this game in technical terms, other than the FPS cap being unacceptable for a PC port, and the game crashing when you have 7.1 sound enabled is just embarrassing.
Unless you've made it your mission to play every Tales game in existence, you'll be fine just skipping this one.

The game wasn't actually *terrible*, but I'd have a hard time recommending it to a friend without a bunch of qualifiers.
Like most people have said, the art and music are pretty good. The art isn't quite my style, but it's obviously high quality. The music fits the atmosphere. That atmosphere is well-developed, too. The settings and characters add to the air of mystery throughout most of the game. One point of criticism here: the trailer is pretty misleading. Few of the animations in the trailer are actually used in-game in any way. While the game does have good art, the trailer makes it seem far more well-produced than it actually is.
Unfortunately, the gameplay and story are greatly lacking. If one of the two were lacking, it might be forgiven, but that's not the case. The gameplay is entirely puzzles, which would be fine if the puzzles were at all engaging. At best, the puzzles are insultingly linear and obvious. At worst, the puzzles are not only linear, but also employ moon logic to make you question if it's actually the solution to the puzzles. The areas are small and confined, and you can solve every puzzle in the game by running around and interacting with everything you see until the solution is effectively told to you. There is a chase sequence at one point, and it was well-executed, but it's the only segment of it's kind in the game. I see people complain about the last segment of the game in the attic. I can see how it might be frustrating if it were a difficult puzzle, but I figured out what I needed to do after the first reset. It was pretty quick after that. Also, the description on Steam is a bit misleading. "Challenging riddles and puzzles"? Not quite. "Test your wit to survive"? Failing to answer any of the "riddles" in the game doesn't affect you at all. You just get to try again. There are no consequences.
As for the story, there were definitely some good ideas here, they were just poorly executed and explained. I can appreciate leaving things up to the viewer/player, but this level of vagueness makes it seem less like it was intentional and more like the writer just wasn't sure what he was writing about. I figured out the "plot twist" less than halfway through the game, but admittedly, I was still strung along by the "mystery". That's in quotes because, apparently my idea of what the game's mystery was didn't match up with what the writer was thinking. About halfway through the game, I had pieced together most of the main character's backstory, and who many of the other characters actually were. But, I still had questions: what was going on in this place? Why were things so strange? For the few characters I didn't understand, where did they fit into this? Unfortunately, very few of those questions were answered were answered at all, and none of those answers left me with any sense of satisfaction. Right when I thought the game was just beginning, it ended and left me hanging.
Spoilers ahead:
Cat's backstory is fine and all, but where do characters like the grub/bug woman fit in? Why are there four wolves when we know the blind child has only one dog? Why are they being cursed by the "sphinx" from the story Cat's mother told her? Who is the toy maker? Why is there a ghost thing in the maze that teleports me to the start for some reason? This is just the tip of the iceberg. I suppose I may have just not have been paying attention, but if the house in the game is a memory, what are these things Cat is remembering? Is it all a hallucenation? Magic? Beyond that, how did Cat forget all this stuff in the first place? Does she have amnesia? And what's with that ending? Is it supposed to be another plot twist? A cliff-hanger? Like I said before, vague is one thing, and I love to interpret stories like this, but there's just nothing to go on here. There's nothing to analyze. It's just a bunch of stuff lumped together in a story for seemingly little reason. Even a little more flavor text on items in the world might have helped. More  things to explore on my own, instead of Cat telling me exactly what I'm looking at ("It's a light.", "It's a mirror.", "It's a plant.").
So, ultimately, I can't recommend this for most people. The art is good, the music is good, and if you're really interested in that, the game might be worth $3 just for the short and mildly interesting ride. Most people won't enjoy it, though, I don't think. If the game had cost me much more, I might be mad.

So I got outlast forever ago, and never made the time to really sit down and play it. I did so recently and was beyond impressed. This game never dissapointed me, and I would completely purchase this again. Heres Some pros and cons of this game,
Pros: Wonderful immersion. This game sucks you in and makes you feel like you are in mount massive the entire time.
The progress of the story is almost perfect, in the sence that it somehow only manages to become more and more scary as it goesn on. (I find a lot of horror games lose their spice as I play them)
Nice graphics. Nothing innovative but crisp enough to keep you in the moment.
It's challenging!! This game will challenge yu on any difficulty, without making you frustrated. The puzzles seem straightforward but always manage to trip you up along the way.
Interesting Map layout. The way that the map is layed out kind of tortures you in the sense that you are almost always looking at an exit you can't go out of for some reason. Also it has a creative way of taking you back to the same places you've been before. You don't really ever return to the exact same place you were before, but you will see rooms you've been in by looking out a window, or through a door frame that has rubble in front of it.
The story is also quite original. I won't say much about the plot but eben though "Asylum Horror Game" seems pretty cookie cutter, it manages to have a really interesting take on the whole thing. Play until the end of the game, and I'm sure you will be impressed.
Cons: Every now and then, the AI would bug out really hard, and remind you that you were playing a game. While this wasn't a common occurance, sometimes enemies bugging out would allow you to finish a puzzle in 20 seconds that would have taken you 20 minutes, therein ruining the challenge. Again, this didn't happen often.
The way that this game keeps you trapped in the asylum is the only part of the story I don't like. You are guided to an exit, that becomes unusable as soon as you get to it. This felt predictable.
This game also has a low replay value unless you want to go back and try to beat it on the harder difficulties. The story is set up to keep you in the dark for most of the game, and that is what makes so much of it scary, but when you play knowing what is going on, it loses some of it's creepyness. Also the game has class A jump scares that you are going to be expecting on the second playthrough.
TLDR: Outlast is my all time favourite horror game. Not for the faint of heart.

This game is worth every penny. Very refreshing, looks beautiful and genuinely unsettling. I especially loved the palette of colors used - it gives the game a very warm and welcoming feeling, kind of like a cosy rug in front of the fireplace, which makes it all the more jaunting when things get creepy. If you enjoy the kind of aesthetic evoked by the charming and bizarre world of Lewis Carroll, this is a fantastically modern take on a girl's journey down the rabbit hole, with it's own unique cast of colorful, uncanny characters and stream of riddles.
It should be noted that the game relies heavily on story and player interpretation. You'll be left with more questions than answers at the end and its biggest selling point is definitely its mystery. It is seamlessly atmospheric in that it is both magical and terrifying. The game-play can be quite basic and not always consistent, as you move from adrenaline inducing chase scenes to relaxed puzzle-solving, but Stray Cat Crossing is unwavering when it comes to the narrative, as with many RPG Maker games, and that should be the reason why you choose to play.

When a Mommy Contra and a Daddy Megaman love each other very, very much...
...you get a game that's just as hard as either of them, and just as rewarding. If you like the kind of difficulty that makes beating an early stage feel as satisfying as completing an entire other game, this one's for you.
TIPS:
- If you have a good combination of power-ups, try to make sure you don't die, as they may not be there next time - that's right, power-ups in this game are randomly generated!
- Personally, I found the spread gun, boomerang gun and the rockets to be the most effective primary weapons. For auxiliary fire, you'll want the rockets, beam weapon or the flamethrower.
- Each stage has three bosses. The middle one is always the hardest.
- If you can get past stage 2, it seems to get significantly more forgiving.
This game lays the foundation for a survival mechanic that is fun and not over the top. I'm looking forward to seeing the story mode.

Limbo really made me wish I was playing something else. It’s not even that the game’s idea is bad or that the controls or graphics suck. It’s just that I didn’t care about what was happening in the game. From the first few steps in the game I started to view it purely as a mechanical puzzle game because there was no connection to the player character what so ever. And that’s when the game started to get tedious. When you’re invested in a game you want to spend time in it. In the case of Limbo I just wanted to move on and at times the game just doesn’t let you. There are puzzles where you might have the right idea but because you make one wrong move in one part of the execution you fail and might think that it’s not the solution the game wants you to reach. It turns into try everything and then try again 50 more times and when you couldn’t care less it gets old fast. In a better puzzle game like Portal you can fail time after time but at least you know immediately if the thing you’re going to try might work. In Limbo you have to try another ten times just to be sure. The game has a neat graphical style and great controls going for it so in hands of a better designer it might’ve been a great little game.

(TLDR at bottom)
Move along, second rate mobile port game here. At least I hope it's a mobile port, that would at least give it some excuse.
First off, the game is called Unnyworld, but pronounced "YUNI" world. Not "UNNY" like "BUNNY". Small complaint, sure, but still just kinda...wtf.
Anyways, sadly that's the least of the game's problems. I don't know what's with all the positive reviews, as it seems they didn't get much into the actual gameplay.
It's pretty slow, with laggy, unresponsive controls. Sometimes even the mouse feels a bit off, and I would guess there's about a good 100-200ms delay between when you push a key, to when your character reacts. If they react at all, since sometimes it seems like your keyboard just cuts out for a bit. (Seems if I push too many keys at once)
Graphically.... it's a mobile game. Probably looks better on the tiny phone screen than it does on my PC.
Audio is not bad at least, though I'd really just like to disable the speaking characters.  I don't know if they're supposed to be speaking another real language or not, but it all sounds like gibberish and babyspeak to me, "cutified".
Gameplay itself was where I was really hoping the game would shine, as the concept here seemed like it would be interesting, but nope, rest assured they took an interesting concept and painted over it in all the typical mobile game shades. The character skills themselves are basically all the same on every character so far as I've seen.... they are basically just reskinned to look like a different element. Fireball, fire blast, fire shield, big fire bomb thing.... water ball, wave blast, water shield, big water bomb thing... you get the idea. Functionally, they seem to all be almost identical.
Next up: Ye olde mobile game "pay to speed up" gimmick. You start building stuff on your planet? Get ready for it to escalate super fast. 1m build times ->5m ->15m ->1 hour -> 6 hours... and so on. You can only build one thing at a time, so you either have to quit and go do something else, or pay to speed up the process. It's the same junk they pull in most 2nd rate mobile games to milk the players by not letting them actually DO what they want to do unless they pay or wait large amounts of time. I should also add, that I hit that 6 hour time limit after only a few minutes of building stuff/upgrading on my planet. It took VERY little time to escalate.
Don't even get me started on the strangely lined up quests (The game will sometimes give you quests that it already finished for you itself, also sometimes you get a quest to upgrade something, before you get the quest to build the thing you just upgraded.), and the "not great" translations ("You my hero!") etc.
I wanted to like the game going into it, I was really hoping for more; but this is just a mobile game trying to pass itself off as a PC game.
Frankly, games with that "nickle and dime" style pay structure where the alternative is to simply NOT PLAY THEIR GAME WHILE YOU WAIT, shouldn't get attention in the PC gaming market. This stuff is rampant and bad enough on mobile platforms already, and we have enough junk to deal with on PC (excessive DLCs, EA games that never finish, etc) without picking up another disease.
TLDR,
PROS:
-Graphics Are Cute
-Concept Idea -would have been- interesting
-At least it uses the keyboard
CONS:
-Graphics are mobile grade.
-Controls are unresponsive and slow
-Quests are messed up
-There's a lot of just reskinning going on here
-Mobile style "Pay to not wait"
-A whole lot of other less important stuff

Honestly, half the not recommend reviews are just plain stupid. The game is great and has no paywalls. New heroes? You can get them by playing the game! I know, shocking. And no - Just because you can't get something within 5 minutes doesn't mean it is bad.
Oh and the DLC you see that may turn you off from the game? Not a single one is what I would count as "True DLC", 2 of them are for people who wish to support the game (Defender & Starter pack) and the other ones? Skins or bag slots. They aren't making new content that you have to buy, they are selling skins. Stuff that the art team can make if they have no work to do.
And for anyone who mentions how the game is still in early access? Yes, cause y'know, games take time to make. Not every company has 100 workers or whatever and can produce a game out every second.
Can I recommend DD2? Yes, as my review says. I have yet to run into any problems so far - Not to say there aren't any. But early access is early access - You can't download/buy stuff like that and not expect bugs. Content doesn't come out super quick, but the devs also aren't silent like other devs. They may not post something every day, but they do keep us updated on stuff. DD2 gets my thumbs up.
P.S. For anyone who thinks you should get all the new heroes for free because you bought into the game, you are stupid. You got what you payed for.

I really wanted to like this game. The aesthetic looked really cool and the gameplay I saw looked awesome.
Honestly though, it's really underwhelming. I finished the story in like 2 hours, maybe less. It's very, very pretentious. I'll explain at the bottom if you care about spoilers in a 2-hour game.
The gameplay is alright, I guess. It gets very tedious, and it's often difficult to determine which bullets will actually hit you and which will not. I do somewhat enjoy the bullet travel time and having to calculate what you're going to hit, but some might dislike that.
My biggest gripe with the gameplay is that the 'not moving unless you are' is actually an outright lie. Everything is moving, just very, very slowly. To the point where you can be shot while you're thinking because bullets move rather quick. There's also no crouch, so if someone fires a shotgun at shoulder height, there's actually no way to dodge if you're a little close. The best way I found of moving, since actually moving and shooting advances time very quickly was to jump and hold space wherever I went. Everyone responds at a proper speed in this manner, giving you time and ability to properly dodge bullets which you absolutely can't do on the ground.
Cutting bullets in half with a katana also barely works. You can do one, maybe? But if someone has a machine gun or even a second person with a handgun behind them the swing time of the katana will guarantee you'll get hit by someone or something else.
The endless mode is broken, too. Unless you wait 1-3 seconds after dying to see the 'your score' screen, the game won't actually store your score which is really, really obnoxious.
The game actually feels kind of unfinished. I would've liked a more multidimensional story and more items--I understand the limitations of an indie team, but with what's in here doesn't feel like a $20 product. I have 6 hours clocked and I feel mostly done with the game. Maybe if I wanted to listen to a podcast I'd play, but if the selling point of the game is that it's a great time-waster while you're listening to a podcast, you're putting yourself in the same boat as free flash games.
The biggest problem of all, is the COMPLETE LACK OF MUSIC. Everything feels dead and extremely uninteresting. The most lively thing in the game is a minigame where you chop a tree--because it actually has MUSIC. The absolute silence save for a robotic voice screaming SUPER HOT SUPER HOT when you finish a level and watch the replay is atrociously obnoxious. And the GIGANTIC ♥♥♥♥ING TEXT covering ANY AND ALL REPLAYS is, AGAIN, very, VERY annoying. Also, how do you edit replays? How do you upload them? Neither really worked for me. And there's no way to just download them as a file.
TLDR;
The game is rather pretentious, boring, and one dimensional, and definitely not worth $20. There is no music through 90% of the above advertised game, there are a rather limited set of maps, the 'campaign' is extremely short, and everything after that is 'challenges' and 'endless mode' which are on largely the same set of maps. And, lastly, it's hard to tell when you'll get shot.
Game's got a little spirit though, I guess.
Spoilers:
I find the story very pretentious. For example, Spec Ops the Line handles the idea of 'stop playing, you're doing horrible violence' very very well. There's a decent story, and a lot of slow buildup to the twist. SUPERHOT basically tells you the twist in the first five minutes. And then it beats you over the head with it. You're told, basically from the start, to 'stop playing', in one form or another, and actually directly at the 1-hour mark, when the mysterious red text makes your proxy type 'I will not run SUPERHOT.exe again'. You can do that in a game that has a longer story. But when I paid $20 for your game LESS THAN AN HOUR AGO, the concept isn't that interesting, even if you tell me that the red people are real and 'bodies are disposable'.

I just finished playing BioShock (27 hours of game play for myself - a novice), a PC Video Game that came out a few years ago.  I must say that I thoroughly enjoyed the challenge of the game and while playing I was amazed at the techniques that the software engineers used.
The graphics, as well as the sound track  were astounding; they really were state-of-the-art for their day.  For me, I've been out of gaming for the lat 15 or so years and I was shocked at how far viideo gameing has come since last I played a game like this one.  For me, since I first  played game on my home PC (an Atari 800XL) back in 1983 (yep - 30  years of working with personal computers now), I remember the graphics on those first games were based on pixel mapping. - well the PC's then read in only 8 bytes at a time, were only 64KB and  didn't even have hard drives.  While today's graphics are based on advanced rendering, shadows, mirrors, and so much more.
Anway, Bioshock was an intriguing, haunting game, with a terrific soundrtack that included songs from the 1940's and 50's, as well as sound effects necesarily creepy when the time was warranted, .  And since it took place in an underwater City built in the 1940's (and destroyed in the late 1950's), it had an interesting Art Deco feel to it.
As for the Story itself - I'll leave off the telling - but you can look it up if you'd like.  Just know that it's more of a Science Fiction type, with a  terrifying  twist at the ver y end.
A true Classic not to be missed.

Amazing game, had a very good time playing it to 100% completion.
The movement mechanics and controls are extremely responsive and smooth. This is one of those platformers where it just feels good to move around in. The dive mechanic taken from Super Mario 64/Super Mario Sunshine is dope and I would even go as far as to say Hat in Time does the dive mechanic a lot better than Mario did. The distance and speed you gain from the dive is really satisfying, and pressing jump just as you land for an added speed boost is a great way to enable skilled players to play through the game quickly. The different kinds of hats that mix up the gameplay are a welcome addition to the game and the seamless way of switching between them through a radial menu is a much appreciated feature.
Now I know what you're thinking, we got a 3d platformer here, what's the camera like? Well I'm happy to say the camera was great for 95% of the experience. Making objects that could possibly block the camera transparent is quite simply, a genius idea while also incorporating a silhouette for hat kid when she is obscured by walls. The programmer knew that a good camera is super important for a 3d platformer and the effort has clearly been put in to make it the best it can be. You have manual control over the camera most of the time and if you know how to manually control a camera while moving around in a 3d platformer you aren't going to have any issues unless you really go out of your way to try and find them. The only times I got annoyed with the camera was in the very rare instances where the camera locked itself into a fixed position, but don't worry, these moments are very few and far between each other.
Levels or "chapters" as it's referred to in game are usually free roaming or completely linear depending on what mission you select, and both are fine. The first act alone I spent over an hour exploring the world and picking up every collectible I could find. The game really gives you the option to take it slow or plow through the levels at a fast pace. Watching speedruns of this game is gonna be great. Chapters 1, 2 and 3 were brilliant, especially chapter 2 and 3. Chapter 4 however was defintely the weaker of the bunch. The world was way too disconnected, loveable NPC's were nowhere to be seen and it got a little dull after a while, but not too dull to ruin the experience.
The characters and voice acting in this game range from really good, to, and I know this word is thrown around a lot, but cringe worthingly bad. A wonderful standout is the character "Snatcher" very easily the best character in the game for me. Well written, funny and an outstanding performance by the voice actor really bring the character to life. A bad example however is Mustache Kid. My god whenever this character opened her mouth I wanted to cover my ears. Extremely annoying, extends her words too much and really badly written. She just isn't a likeable character at all. I think she was supposed to
But overall just comes off as irritating.
Soundtrack was flawless, couldn't think of one track that I didn't like. A big variety of tracks is what makes it that much better, you've got your jumpy techno jams, smooth jazz, heavy metal boss fights and all sorts. The track "Moon Parade" has been stuck in my head for days.
Graphically the game is very appealing. The devs clearly had a vision of Nintendo Gamecube era games (Zelda Wind Waker, Super Mario Sunshine) and they wanted to emulate it and that's exactly what you get. Bright colours and inviting environments really fuel your mind with "ohh, what's over there?" thoughts and helps emphasise exploration.
I thought A Hat in Time was going to be a nice little distraction for me until Super Mario Odyssey came out, but it was much more than that. It was a memorable, fun experience that I will enjoy and come back to for a long time just like I have with Super Mario Sunshine and has very easily become one of my favourite games of 2017. I would highly recommend picking up A Hat in Time. I'm sure you won't regret it.

Right from the start, let me say that my positive rating comes with a caveat. If you are looking for a challenging puzzle game that becomes increasingly difficult and provides hours of entertainment, Mind Spheres is NOT for you. Save your time and money. However, if you want a simple, casual puzzle experience the will keep you busy for an hour or so, consider this game.
The object is to manipulate the playing field in a way that gets a ball from point A to point B. Seventy-five to 80% of the solutions are obvious right away. Approximately 15% will require to run the puzzle once, possibly twice to figure out the solution. The remaining 5% fall into one of the previous two categories, but require precise fine tuning of the playing field, resulting in you having to run the puzzle many times until you get it just right.
Overall, I fully completed the game in about 1 hour and 15 minutes, and there is no re-playability value. Please keep that in mind when considering purchasing this game.

After spending over 100 hours on this game, I have to say it's the best WWII multiplayer shooter I've ever played. The guns feel like they pack a punch when you fire them, you feel the danger and risk of being shot at (and suppressed), and teamwork amongst the 30+ players on each team matters more than you might think.
When I play this, I find myself almost constantly keeping my head down and eyes glued to the screen when I play-- it has that much of an impact on me. Getting the drop on an unsuspecting squad and unloading your Thompson-- Firing your mortar off in the distance corresponding with recon given by your commander and seeing the kills you got-- storming a bunker with a flamethrower-- keeping your head down and sprinting through machine gun fire-- engaging with 12+ commrades in a suicidal banzai charge against all odds-- These are all aspects of the game that bring such exhileration which is hard to come by in any other game, period. Scoring a string of even a few kills without reloading brings a stronger sense of satisfaction than any CoD killstreak.
The game looks great, runs great (depending on your machine, of course, but I find its not terribly taxing on modern rigs), and in particular, SOUNDS great. Gunfire and ricochet, artillery, shouts of motivation and agony all come together to create a visceral battlefield that feels remarkably intense. I recommend playing with a decent set of headphones, or really good speakers. You'll be able to hear where the heavy (and small) arms fire is landing, where enemy Japanese are charging from, footsteps, shots in the distance-- the sound design in Red Orchestra 2/Rising Storm is nothing but superb.
There's also a progression system that motivates you to keep playing, and gratifies you to see the results you get. These types of "unlocks" come in the form of weapon parts, recoil/steadiness/reload time/etc percentage raises, and more. These unlocks won't let you dominate the battlefield, so they're not game-breaking by any stretch of the term. This isn't necessarily a feature that's entirely unique to RO2, but it adds to the game and gives you a sense of fulfillment from your actions.
There's a reason Rising Storm won PC Gamer's 2013 GOTY award, and it's because its a unique experience you won't find anywhere else. I've recommended this game to a few shooter-enthusiast friends and now they're all hooked as well. All I can say is RO2/Rising Storm offers a type of experience I've yet to find in another multiplayer shooter, and I recommend it to anyone interested in Multiplayer, FPS's, World War II, simulation, or just looking for something unique. 5/5, 10/10, 3 thumbs up, I can't recommend this amazing game enough.

I will keep this short and sweet. This is probably one of the best survival game in my 400+ games library. I don't usually do reviews but TLD really deserves recognition.
Like all survival games, your character is faced with limited resources and challenging environment. To survive, you have to make a certain decisions like risk hunting for food with the wolves or hide somewhere to fish and hope you can make enough food to make the effort worthwhile. Certain resoures are finited and once they run out then you're pretty much at the end of the game - you die. However, most people die because of things like wolves, wounds and diseases rather than running out of finite resources.
This game is tough for new players. It's exceedingly hard on normal mode when you have little to no clue of where to go or what to do. As you start gaining real survival expericences, then you will be able to survive longer.
Overall, this is a great survival game with minimal frills and gimmicks. It's straight forward and you have a lot of freedom to do what you want while you actually have little if you try to survival.

Dungeon defenders 2 is a tower defense game where you build towers and defend against an army of orcs. There are multiple maps to play and new maps are being added. The game is grindy and you'll need to farm for gear alot if you want to progress into the higher difficulty, if you're into grinding then this game will be for you.
There are 6 classes (7 really soon) monk, squire, apprentice, huntress, abyss lord and EV2.
is more of an utility having spells which heals players near him or crowd control enemies, 1 aura which can heal and the other which can buff defenses damage (and health if you have a sphere for it) he has a lightning aura that can damage enemies and can stun them too if they are drenched in water and there's the anti-air tower which should be obvious at what it does. Shoots air targets.
Is  a tank which can be built as dps thanks to the new weapon, he has a shield to tank hits and has 3 abilities which are, a damaging spell, a taunt and a stun. His defenses are the basic ones he has a cannon tower, barricade, ballista and a training dummy. People should really focus the squire for his barricade because it has alot of health and just saves games for everyone or go dps if you got someone to build walls for you already.
This guy like the squire has similliar defenses. a flameburst tower, barricade, frostbite tower and earthshatter tower. His spells are a tornado, arcane volley which hits enemies that been marked by you, and a mana bomb where the apprentice explodes nearby enemies dealing huge damage. People usually focus him for frostbite towers but he can be built as dps aswell.
If you're new to the game, this is going to be your best dps class. almost all her towers are about damage. her ablities are concussive arrow, oil flask which slows enemies and can be used as a combo with her third ability Piercing shot which fires a fire phoenix damaging enemies and making them on fire if they're covered in oil.
Her defenses which are, explosive trap, a geyser trap which launches enemies into the air drenching them in water, Blaze ballon and a poison dart tower.
Now to get the 2 classes you will need to get defender medals which are earned from playing the game, doing daily quests or weekly quests. They are totally free and can be earned in 1-2 weeks. Or you can buy them for gems and support the developers. They cost 10k defenders medals (12k for 2 weeks after release). Now people are saying the game is going the "microtransaction way" is just dumb, because that's not where they are going. You can buy costumes and heroes (which you can still earn for free) that's it. They aren't selling some premium weapons which offer bonus stats and are going to help you in your journey. Now let's continue with the 2 classes
This guy can be built in 3 ways. Towers, dps or walls ( focusing on your barricade). He has 3 abilities, 1 which buffs any tower of his. His abilities are as follows, abyss stones, knight of the abyss, direct command.
His defenses are orc blockade, skeletal ramster, bone archers and the colossus. If you're going to focus on towers then your best bet would be bone archers as they deal the most damage. Command and Conquer 3: Tiberium Wars is a real-time strategy game that was developed and published by Electronic Arts mostly due to the acquisition of Westwood Studios by EA and Westwood's closure back in 2003. This game continues the Tiberian Sun story arc and is a direct sequel to Tiberian Sun & its expansion Tiberian Sun: Firestorm.
Following the franchise tradition, this title follows the story of the almost never ending conflict between the Global Defense Initiative (GDI) and an international paramilitary / militant religious organization called the Brotherhood of Nod. Unlike its predecessors however, this game introduces a new faction in an effort by EA to add more gameplay diversity. The new faction is known as the Scrin.
+ The game has good art style and graphics: (Both of which aged really well specially since this game was released back in 2008.)
+ Very good Sound design and unit voice acting.
+ Quality live action cinematic played by very well known Hollywood stars and the ever iconic Joseph D. Kucan as “Kane.”
+ Lengthy Campaign for each of the factions (about 20 hours if you play them in the Very Hard difficulty setting)
+ Great story that is interwoven with each faction (meaning that each faction “wins” in their own right)
+ New Faction that is fun to play and comes with an unlockable Campaign once you finish both GDI and NOD campaigns.
+ Old factions (GDI and NOD) has been revamped with new units and playstyles without deviating from their respective origin stories.
+ Fast paced and intense action.
+ Lore heavy with story continuity from the old games.
+ Fun and challenging missions during the campaign.
+ Revamped game mechanics such as squad based infantry, super unit capture etc.
- No online multiplayer due to GameSpy shutdown:
- Some unit pathfinding quirks
- Some balance issues (specially with the super units)
- Relatively small maps
- Limited tech-tree options and build orders
- Campaign strategic options has no real effect
- Random difficulty spikes between the campaign missions
+/- Mission objectives are immediately marked in the map thus depriving the player of map exploration. A.K.A. spoon feeding the player enemy locations.

There's a lot of games out there that say: "We're bringing back the feeling of games you played from your childhood!" But most of them forget the little things that made these games so memorable. The thing is, in my humble opinion, when you play a hat in time, you're playing a game that, had it released in the era it was taking inspiration from, would have been able to stand tall with the greats of the platformer genre of the day.
Remember the scene from Ratatouille where the cynical critic eats the food and it transports him back to his childhood? That's kinda how this game was for me. It "Gets it". It gets why we loved the older games. The charm, the dark humor, the colorful characters both literally and figuratively, and the easter eggs that didn't need to be in the game but were anyway because you could tell the people behind it y'know,

While this game is sort of short, I'd say that for having like 1/7th the budget of yooka laylee they succeeded at what they set out to do with flying colors, and that was to make a game that paid respectful homage to the platformers we grew up with.
I'd highly recommend this game to anyone who likes platformers. It's not flawless, there are a few technical issues in the game like framedrops on alpine sky and sometimes graphics settings won't save, this game is still well worth your money as a lot of those things can be patched out and plus even the length issue will be remedied with steam workshop content that I'm sure the community is going to go wild with, or just at least recreate stuff from other platformers.

"SUPERHOT IS THE MOST INNOVATIVE SHOOTER I'VE PLAYED IN YEARS!  Join me now!"
SuperHot is a FPS time manipulation game where time only moves when you move.  The objective is simple, kill all the red guys and live until the next round.  This makes each level feel more like a puzzle than a twitch shooter.  The game play is incredibly addictive and fun, the game runs smooth and has fluid controls.
The downfall of this game is in two areas.  The campaign is arguably too short being roughly completed by most people in 2 hours.  The other downside is the cost of admission.  For some people 20-25 dollars for a 2 hour campaign isn't a justifiable purchase.  The developer did include trial missions/challenge arenas that will keep you coming back for more, including an Endless Mode.  I personally feel the cost of this game isn't all that bad, especially with the inclusion of those modes.  The story was pretty good at screwing with your head and is definitely best played in the dark.  It's definitely something one needs to experience themselves rather than watching someone else play it.
I do recommend this game and do not regret purchasing one bit. If you're still unsure after reading this review then head on over to:

To start off I would like to say I recomend this game fully to anyone and everyone who enjoys a game that pushes their limits to be unique. Sometimes it works, other times it doesn't. SUPERHOT nailed it.
The game overall is based around its gameplay, and more specifically its gameplay mechanics. Time only moves when you move. You use this to your advantage to plan out the fight and make intricate dodges or shots. Honestly this mechanic IS the game, so if you're looking for groundbreaking multiplayer experiance or story you're not going to be satisfyed with SUPERHOT.
That being said, I think most every game should get this game as it is unique and very enjoyable. I can already tell I will be spending many hours on this game trying to get perfect runs, testing my limits and challenging myself. It has amazing replayablity and is well worth the price.
Overall Rating 8/10
Story - 4/10
As I said before this game was not based off of story. However it does have some inside of it that drew me in to some degree. It kept things mildly intresting though it wasn't what made me keep booting up the game after leaving for work in the morning.
Game play - 9/10
I am really hesitant to give this game a full 10 for its gameplay. The only two things that are holding it back is two very small things that most probably don't care about. This game has no ability to run, keeping your movement at a crawl when you are trying to move around a map. Most of the time this plays into your favor, other times it can be a slight annoyance. The other thing is the inability to crouch, which would give you the ability to dodge more attacks and help with the overall game in my oppion. Either way the gameplay of SUPERHOT is phenominal and the mechaincs of it are amazing. Like i said before, this game is built around its gameplay.
Replayability - 8/10
This game will pull you back to it undoubtably. You feel like a badass and want to get that run perfect and feel a sense of satisfaction when you do. I personally found myself up much later than I usually am just becasuse I was so engrossed in the game. The next day at work it was on my mine frequently and I found myself booting it up as soon as I got home.
Style - 9/10
I am weird and judge a game highly by how it looks. If something is ugly I am not going to spend more than a few minutes looking at it, and thats only if it's an intresting ugly. Superhot is a minimalistic art style that plays extreamly well into its gameplay and its performance. I would be suprised to find a computer that couldn't run this and have it look good. The game's art style is simple, yet functional and elegant.
Depth - ?/10
Unfortunatly I cannot say as to how deep this game will go with its progression system. While it is already very good and offers quite a few rewards for completeing certian challenges or getting so far in endless ect. There has been hints are more to come. Right now I would give it a 6/10 just because it seems like there is only small modifications to gameplay and new maps. However there is no really unique enemies or weapons to experiment with, which isn't terrible, thoguh it would add another layer to the game to make it more intresting.
Anyways those are my thoghts on SUPERHOT. I would recomend this game to anyone in a heartbeat, so if you're still reading this review, scroll up, click add to cart, and buy the game already!

Play it at night with headphones if you can.....I couldn't.

is a relaxing puzzle game where the player is tasked with manipulating the level in order to allow a marble to navigate itself to the end goal. There are a number of different platforms that can alter the path the marble will take and that bounce the marble around obstacles. I found that most of the levels were quite easy to beat, where most can be completed with only one try. I really appreciate that restarting the level also does not reset the placement of its obstacles.
As for what I don't like: there's a severe lack of information when I'm met with new mechanics. Each platform is basically the same shape and size, the only way to differentiate them is by their colour (other than some pyramid looking things that behave the same way as the basic platforms, I don't know why they exist other than to confuse). There's no visual indication for what each platform does so it's often impossible to know how to plan a level before trialling it. I also feel that the soundtrack, which mostly comprises of a softly played piano, does not fit the tone or theme of the game.
There are a number of issues in
regarding the overly sensitive rotation of platforms. There's a random "sorry" fail-state that pops up for no discernible reason even when my marble is still in motion. I have also discovered an unintended bug where holding the mouse down to rotate platforms will also begin to rotate any other platform if I continue to drag the cursor over them, it really should be locked to a single platform at a time as this can quickly ruin the layout of a course.

I sometimes wish there was a neutral option for Steam Reviews, because while I certiantly didn't dislike my time with Stray Cat Crossing, it's ending third, specifically the part in the theatre, leaves an awful taste in your mouth.
Anyway, Stray Cat Crossing is a surreal horror RPG maker game, like Ib, Ao Oni, and many other before it. Stray Cat Crossing has a lot more polish than most of those. the pixel art graphics themselves are almost worth the admission price, and the music is also great. The story is definatley above average for a RPG maker romp, telling a sad tale of jealousy and domestic neglect.
Unfortunatley, not as much love and care was put into the gameplay. Stray Cat Crossing relies on several "tricks" to add artificial length to what otherwise would have been a single sitting game. The most infamous is the theatre section, which I talked about at the start, but it runs through the whole game. Actions (such as rotating a bridge) take ten times as long as they should. An early chase sequence requires you to sit through the same 30 second cutscene every time you retry (And you will die A LOT at that part). A part involving carrying objects slows you down to an absolute slow as hell crawl. All of this builds up, and what started as minor annoyance eventually blossoms into resentment. It feels like the game is wasting your time, and thats never a good feeling.
Overall, Stay Cat Crossing left me feeling kind of mad, but I can't say I disliked it's macabre world.
Wait for a sale, if possible.

Unnyworld is a strange online game where you're trying to combine weird parts of multiple games into one component.
Gameplaywise, there are 3 main components, the advertised MOBA where you run and gun, running your little planet farmville and invasions.
In part one, you control a hero that comes with 5 skills. Each skill is activated by the mouse and some are activated by a click and drag. There is a left click common attack, a drag-a-straight-line attack, an inverted-V shield, a long range V attack and a right click ultimate. Every single hero is the same. Get this, in order to learn your hero skills, you have to collect skill pieces and then pay to level them up.
In part two, you build and upgrade a town hall, build and upgrade ships and build and upgrade a whole list of other stuff, just like Farmville. It's a wonder how they even got support for this game.
In part three, you get to use your hero to raid other players' planets and get resources out of them. Wooooooopie do. If you run of ship energy, you can't invade anyone unless you pay for more energy.
Conclusion, skip this cash grab piece of junk.The pay to win system is truly in your face. They want you to buy Gems, Unnycoins and Acquvium, with Acquvium being the grindable currency. Do you have $50 USD for 17,000 Gems?
Note: Unnyworld is made by Unnyhog, a Russian company, their investors (Flat6Labs, TwoFour54, YC) mentors (Yannick Theler of Ubisoft Abu Dhabi, Vince Ghossoub of Falafel Games, Michael Seibel and Justin Kan of YC) and the Unnyhog’s team, which is located at Park Rotana Complex, TwoFour54, Abu Dhabi, UAE. It used to be located at Naberezhnaya Gazovikov, 3, 4 Ukhta,  169300, Russia.

Right so here is the thing. I DID enjoy this game. Don't get me wrong, it isn't anything majorly exciting or anything like that. It's just a nice casual little game with some not too strenuous puzzles. You can blaze through most of the puzzles in a single try bar a couple of them which honestly were more annoying than fun. Which can be seen as a flaw actually, some of the puzzles just being too annoying to want to do. The visuals weren't painful to look at and the music was relatively interesting, all in all what you want if you just want a small game to unwind with. That being said...it did have some issues.
So here are the major cons.
Despite my RAM being plentiful for this game it would constantly crash not only the game (coming up with some total BS system memory low message) but on some occasions the whole computer, forcing a restart to be done. This is made even more frustrating given I haven't played it for much time at all and yet it happened multiple times.
Second, for some questionable reason on the screen where you manipulate objects on many occasions the screen would go completely white. It would revert upon hitting space to get the ball rolling but...well what's the point if the white screen stops me being able to move stuff around? I did manage to win a couple of levels with that though (which reinforces just how easy some of the puzzles were if you don't even have to change anything). But even so the only way I could stop that happening was quitting and restarting the game...and then hoping I could go through as many levels as possible before it happened again.
Third. Now this was also really annoying. There were times when the game would just randomly decide you had failed a mission at random intervals and bring up the "restart?" screen. The ball was still moving and actually hadn't even come close to stopping on many occasions that this happened on. Once my ball was in mid air coming down onto the end goal and it just randomly decided I had failed and blurred out the screen. Now I probably don't have to explain how f'ing annoying THAT was.
So while I liked it and I do recommend it if anyone is just looking for a bit of relaxating gameplay...I would definitely like to advise the developer to look into these issues because it did get to the point where I was about to quit and uninstall the game. So if you (developer person) can have a little look into some of these matters to make the game better for everyone, I'm sure it would be appreciated.

What an absolute blast. This feels as if Taito and Sunsoft had gotten together and made a game that was a mix between Batman: Return of the Joker and Air Fortress. For anyone who doesn't get that, Jet Gunner feels and plays like a solid late 80's NES game.
What's refreshing to me was how the gameplay reminded me of a great Sunsoft title, but the bumpers between levels reminded me of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Electrobrain or Taxan game. In that regard, Jet Gunner feels genuinely NES and not just retro for retro's sake.
The video presents it to be a frenetic shooter, but it's actually much slower paced, and I like that. The core element of the gameplay, the jet pack, worked well and added nice platforming challenges. The weapon types were varied, and constantly changed throughout the game, even in the same stages if you had to replay an area over due to a death. This kept the game feeling fresh and active throughout.
For the price, this a steal. The presentation is solid and the gameplay offers about an hour worth of oldschool entertainment. Totally worth it.
