Amazing game, had a very good time playing it to 100% completion.
The movement mechanics and controls are extremely responsive and smooth. This is one of those platformers where it just feels good to move around in. The dive mechanic taken from Super Mario 64/Super Mario Sunshine is dope and I would even go as far as to say Hat in Time does the dive mechanic a lot better than Mario did. The distance and speed you gain from the dive is really satisfying, and pressing jump just as you land for an added speed boost is a great way to enable skilled players to play through the game quickly. The different kinds of hats that mix up the gameplay are a welcome addition to the game and the seamless way of switching between them through a radial menu is a much appreciated feature.
Now I know what you're thinking, we got a 3d platformer here, what's the camera like? Well I'm happy to say the camera was great for 95% of the experience. Making objects that could possibly block the camera transparent is quite simply, a genius idea while also incorporating a silhouette for hat kid when she is obscured by walls. The programmer knew that a good camera is super important for a 3d platformer and the effort has clearly been put in to make it the best it can be. You have manual control over the camera most of the time and if you know how to manually control a camera while moving around in a 3d platformer you aren't going to have any issues unless you really go out of your way to try and find them. The only times I got annoyed with the camera was in the very rare instances where the camera locked itself into a fixed position, but don't worry, these moments are very few and far between each other.
Levels or "chapters" as it's referred to in game are usually free roaming or completely linear depending on what mission you select, and both are fine. The first act alone I spent over an hour exploring the world and picking up every collectible I could find. The game really gives you the option to take it slow or plow through the levels at a fast pace. Watching speedruns of this game is gonna be great. Chapters 1, 2 and 3 were brilliant, especially chapter 2 and 3. Chapter 4 however was defintely the weaker of the bunch. The world was way too disconnected, loveable NPC's were nowhere to be seen and it got a little dull after a while, but not too dull to ruin the experience.
The characters and voice acting in this game range from really good, to, and I know this word is thrown around a lot, but cringe worthingly bad. A wonderful standout is the character "Snatcher" very easily the best character in the game for me. Well written, funny and an outstanding performance by the voice actor really bring the character to life. A bad example however is Mustache Kid. My god whenever this character opened her mouth I wanted to cover my ears. Extremely annoying, extends her words too much and really badly written. She just isn't a likeable character at all. I think she was supposed to
But overall just comes off as irritating.
Soundtrack was flawless, couldn't think of one track that I didn't like. A big variety of tracks is what makes it that much better, you've got your jumpy techno jams, smooth jazz, heavy metal boss fights and all sorts. The track "Moon Parade" has been stuck in my head for days.
Graphically the game is very appealing. The devs clearly had a vision of Nintendo Gamecube era games (Zelda Wind Waker, Super Mario Sunshine) and they wanted to emulate it and that's exactly what you get. Bright colours and inviting environments really fuel your mind with "ohh, what's over there?" thoughts and helps emphasise exploration.
I thought A Hat in Time was going to be a nice little distraction for me until Super Mario Odyssey came out, but it was much more than that. It was a memorable, fun experience that I will enjoy and come back to for a long time just like I have with Super Mario Sunshine and has very easily become one of my favourite games of 2017. I would highly recommend picking up A Hat in Time. I'm sure you won't regret it.

My favorite game setup?
60 laps on the short speed track with 23 other cars using an XBOX 360 controller on maxed settings.
From start to finish, the races are nothing short of pure carnage & adrenaline.
The wrecks are incredible. Too many "shock & awe" moments to name.
By the time we get mid-race, there are crushed, flamming, and smoking metal corpses littering the track; literally.
The track itself has come apart in areas due to crashing into its walls.
Safety tires and tire marks litter the speedway.
Fenders, wheels, glass, doors, hoods, and all sorts of debris litter the speedway.
The race track eventually turns into a minefield.
And when I'm speeding through it, I get this warm fuzzy feeling inside.
It's like 1975 Rollerball meets 1985 Mad Max.

And it looks GLORIOUS! :)
Setting up your opponents at the right time to have them careen into these junk piles is a vision to behold.
The pure glee of pulling off these maneuvers is something I can't explain. You have to experience it yourself!
And we still haven't talked about the racing!
The cars handle in lifelike manners considering the context.
Different cars handle speed, turns, braking, collisions and power differently. You WILL feel the weight of your car in your hands. Despite its damage gimmick, Wreckfest is a very good racing sim. It's not arcady like Flatout (Bugbear's other developments). It's more on the side of a sim. So you wanna win the race by RACING, not pushing a boost button.
Moreover, all this wouldn't even work if the graphics and physics weren't so superbly done.
You can run this game at defualt graphics and have an amazing visual and gameplay experience.
At the detected default setting, the game runs perfectly fine and looks amazing!
The force feedback (FFB) on the controller is spot on.
As far as content goes, you have access to several cars, tracks, and events.
You can set the races to suit you.
There is enough here to keep you busy for a while.
You have online races to mess with too. But the offline AI is pretty damn good; especially for an early access game. It offers an awesome amount of challenges.
This is worth $10 and 2 hours of your time. It's an experience you won't forget.

Okay, so I've had the same review for Five Nights at Freddy's for a while now, and I wanted to change it as it was getting old in my mind, and it didn't really make sense to me after a while.
First of all, let me get this out of the way...
And no, I'm not a FNaF Fanboy. I prefer games like Portal, Garry's Mod and Terraria more. I just find it a bit annoying when people judge a game by its community. Especially when it's singleplayer.
Anyways, onto the review.
Five Nights at Freddy's is a short, fun, indie horror game made by Scott Cawthon that takes place in 'Freddy Fazbears Pizzaria'.  You're the security guard who pulled the short straw and works the nightshift, however. You must survive an entire week in the pizzaria, wiether you need the pay or you're forced to stay. Seems simple, right? Well, not exactly. There are 4 animatronics that are progreammed to entertain the children in the daytime. Well, what about the nightime? There are no children to entertain, so the workers set the animatronics to freeroam at night, so that their servos don't lock up and they won't be broken for the next day. Why the animatronics aren't always set to a freeroaming mode might seem obvious to you, but there's a bigger reason than just "They're killer robots. They come and try to kill me every single night." There was an incident placed in the year 1987, at a previous Freddy Fazbears Pizzaria resulting in someone's frontal lobe being bit off by an animatronic, although unknown to the player which one. This incident is simply known as "The Bite of '87".
With the first in the series, your goal is to survive until 6 AM, for a week. You are sitting in an office with entrances on both sides, both of which have a light button and a door button. Your goal is to survive until 6 AM, for a week. Both buttons on either side are toggleable, which is great, as when they're on, they drain your power supply, of which you have a limited amount of. When the power goes out, both the lights and doors deactivate, leaving the doors open and the lights off, which leaves you vulnerable to the several animatronics in the pizzaria, Freddy, Bonnie, Chica, and Foxy, designed after a bear, bunny, chicken and fox respectively. If you run out of power, as said before, your lights and doors won't work, and Freddy will appear in the left doorway playing a tune that sounds like it's being played out of a music box. Eventually, the tune will end, most likely being cut short, and the very dim light allowing you to still see your desk will darken, leaving you in a pitch-black office. After that, at a random time, Freddy will pop up and kill you, unless you're lucky enough for the time to roll over to 6:00 AM. While the power is still on, Bonnie, Chica and Foxy can attack, and Freddy can still move around and attack, although not in the way he does when the power's out. Bonnie and Chica just generically move around the facility, while Foxy can charge at your door when you either give him too much or too little attention, although that will only delay him. Foxy's charge is inevitable, and will almost always happen at least once on the later nights.
Five Nights at Freddy's is a neat, small game that can be played on most computers (MOST, not all) and can provide a couple hours of something to do. The animatronics aren't programmed in a way that you can just memorize which animatronic attacks when, which is something that can add some replayability, although not much. I will still support this game and reccomend it however.
Thank you for taking time out of your day to read my review! I hope that you understand why I recommend it, and if you're one of those people who hate FNaF because of the community, maybe I changed your mind? Although unlikely, it could be possible. Have a good day!

"Ya like Jazz?"
Is the question I want to start off with.  Cuphead is a RUTHLESS platformer that goes back to the days when platforming skills were all you needed in the gaming world (i.e. Mario, Mega Man, etc.).  You make a mistake?  You'll be punished for it.  One little slip up means your continuation or your death.  With it's 1930s-esque cartoon style and swing/ragtime music to boot (even recorded using techniques or in the vein of 30s-40s music), Cuphead is a game you don't want to miss.
Pros:
+ the game is VERY fluid in everything it does
+ graphically the most unique game I'd ever seen
+ controls are tight and responsive
+ upgrades that you can buy and equip for your own personal playstyle
+ bosses are challenging and unforgiving
+/- the platforming areas allow you to collect gold BUT you can only go back to collect pieces you missed
+ upgrades are inexpensive, meaning you can easily rack them up
+ drop in/out co-oop (haven't tested this yet but that's how I assume it works)
+ GORGEOUS music; they nailed the style of 30s rag and swing music.  (If you don't like the actual *sound* of the music [it sounds fuzzy and that's the point; recorded music of that era usually did])
+ cartoon-esque "way way" VO which is an incredibly nice detail to add in for some characters
+ unique parry technique for pink objects
+A "simple or regular" mode for bosses for those who don't want to be ♥♥♥♥ed up the♥♥♥♥♥by bosses!
Cons:
- some may find the graphics options... minimal.  But for a game like this there really wouldn't need to be any (NOT a big issue for me at all, though)
- if you collect all the gold during a "run and gun" level, you can't go back to farm it (not much of a deal breaker but again it could be for some)
1930/1930: would play ridiculously challenging platformer again.  Ya like jazz?

On the surface Five Nights at Freddy's doesn't seem like that scary of a game, and it actually isn't... that is, until you're properly immersed.
I've beaten night five, and it was genuinely challenging to manage everything at once.
You have a limited amount of power of which you can spend on looking through the cameras, flicking the door lights on/off, and locking the door.  It makes you manage when you look around, and how often you do it.
You can't sit with your eyes glued to the cameras because it'll drain your power just as fast as keeping a door closed.  Speaking of which, I love how all of the devices consume the same power, so there's no inherent punishment for locking down the door, and it just creates a better game flow in my opinion.
True fear is created by the feeling of helplessness, and that's something FNaF gets really right.
What really makes the game frightening for me is the suspense.  Not of the monsters themselves, I don't find them particularily scary.  What really gets to you is that at any moment you could slip up and blow the game in a second.  You have to keep your guard up the whole time, because at no time during the game are you safe.  The feeling of insecurity, the atmosphere, the apprehension.  Those are what makes the game frightening.
Positive.
+Great atmosphere / sound effects.
+Gameplay makes for intense and frightening moments.
+It's not flashy and over the top to ruin the atmosphere.
+Challenging enough that you'll get frustrated, but not in an angry 'ragequit' way.
+Freddy.  Possibly the scariest animatronic in the game, soley because when he jumps out and frightens me, I'm only half sure he's going to do it, or not expecting it at all.

-Graphics.  I'm not expecting it to be a triple A masterpiece, but I'd appreciate the ability to alter the resolution.  It looks crappy on my screen and is a little jarring going from my native of (1680*1050) to the game itself of (1024*768).  It doesn't ruin or detract from the experience in a major way, but it's annoying to me.
-Predictable Jump Scares.  Most of the jump scares become predictable really quick, and act more as a 'Dang it I screwed up.' and creates less of a 'pee my pants in fright' reaction.

First off, I'm not a big fan of the 'Hardcore' Hard games like Dark Souls. Games that are head-bangingly difficult from the get-go are a no-go for me. Cuphead avoids this for me. It IS hard. It WILL grind you down. But it doesn't pick you up and deliberately push you down again in the mud, wondering where to go next time, because there isn't an obvious path for you to take. Dark Souls does that, and I dislike that for it.
Cuphead, on the other hand, is a GOOD kind of difficult, where you will die but say "Oh, I could do that next time," instead of get frustrated. The hints you pick up as you play and learn the attacks of the enemies, the layouts of the level, even the parryslap thing it makes it so you improve. And eventually, you can take down even the toughest foes you were struggling with before.
It's easy to struggle in this game, but not hard to push past those points. It's a GOOD difficult game, and I absolutely applaud MDHR for that.
P.S. I can't be bothered to learn the real names of the bosses, so I just make them up as I go along, Blue Blob Bill being a prime example.

So I was pretty excited to pick this game up after having played the demo what seems like ages ago.  So now having beaten the game let's get to the pros and cons of Stray Cat Crossing.
Cons:
- This one might be more of a Windows 10 issue, but this game crashes a lot.  If you press two buttons on the joypad at once, if you accidentally press a non-bound button on your joypad, if you attempt to combine items and so on.  Basically if you give it an excuse to crash it most certainly will.  Fortunately the frequency of save-points is an effective stopgap.
- The lack of volume control.  The volume levels of the music tracks are all over the place and you have no in-game way to adjust the volume.  Some tracks are still deafening at minimum volume settings on my headphones and others need to be turned up to be heard.
- The game is short, like really short.  You can pretty much subtract a half hour of play-time from having to re-do things before I got OCD about saving.  It feels like you've got three quarters of a game here with the semi-final act missing.  Now while I'm sure the creators of the game intended to leave things vague to add to the surrealness of the experience; I feel like it left a lot of characters under-developed.
But with that said there are some real positives to the game:
+ The music is good stuff, volume levels aside.  It's got the creepy minimalist vibe to it; which enhances the experience.
+ There is some great surreal imagery here.  I played this ony my Twitch stream and there were a lot of instances where what I saw caused me to just stop talking mid-sentence to wrap my head around things.  I want to keep my review spoiler free, so it's hard to go into detail, but nothing is quite as it seems in this game.
+ The art itself in the game is great.  I think the game strives to have it's own sense of style while still delivering a 16 bit retro feel to it.
So the bottom line is that you are basically getting 3/4ths of a good game; but when you factor in the price of the game you're really getting some decent bang for your buck.

In short:
As it is right now, I did enjoy "Banished" for a few hours but that's about it. It's very simplistic and unrealistic. The overall concept is great, but nothing new. It has full 3D graphics and you can rotate seamlessly the view 360 degree, though that's really not even necessary and in the end is more a gimmick. Same with tilting up / down and zooming in / out. Overall, Banished is beautiful, yet VERY simplistic in terms of game mechanics, AI and UI. Beautiful graphics (well, they're not mind-blowing) alone don't make a good product, that's what most devs forget. I rather have more simplistic graphics, but much more sophistication and complexity in a game (AKA "Factorio" or "Prison Architect").
Because of that, in the end I just can't recommend to get it (unless it's on sale and you don't care about the things I point out below), I got it on sale for $5 and might hop into it at some point again for some casual entertainment, but for something challenging that I can really get into, I rather load up Factorio or Prison Architect.
So, if you're interested, here are (some of) the issues I have with it:
1.Not enough stats output (graphs) - for example, how efficient is someone at their work? Or at least, how efficient is a work-space? Is demand met with supply? It's common sense that you've got those graphs, to effectively manage people (whether that's in a business or colonists trying to establish a town or an established city).
2. Too much micro-management due to "flawed" AI...
2.a. For example, you have a storage barn with food in it. You build another one so you can relocate to another area (there's no way you can do that in the first year, you have to settle, even just temporarily, at that location!) and want to move everything from the previous one to the new one. So you give a demolish order to the old one so that everything is moved over to the new one as soon as that one's built (or even if you wait until it's built, doesn't matter). Yet, as soon as you give the demolish order, everything in it, food, tools, ... will become unavailable to those people. Until it's transferred to the new storage barn and put in there.  Which results in the people starving to the point of dying. Makes perfect sense, right?
2.b. Those people don't seem like virtual versions of humans, but rather robots that look like and have the needs of humans. If I'd be starving, I'd refuse first of all to go long distances to some remote place, knowing that I'd starve on the way there or back; secondly, I'd eat at least a little bit, to the point that I won't starve; third of all, the devs obviously never heard of jerky / dried fruits and veggies!? Why aren't those people taking some food and water along. I mean, come on, that's common sense.
2.c. In RL nobody goes mining / hunting / exploring w/o even the smallest of a backpack. Or goes to work without taking food along (unless you have a cafeteria at your job), even if it's close-by - instead, in Banished, every time someone gets hungry, they walk all the way to their living quarters to eat. Do you know anyone who doesn't work from home and does that? That's very rare to happen, even in a settlement like that where people don't have a 8-5 job but sometimes have to work from 5 in the morning until 8 at night or whenever the sun goes down, to get as much work done during daylight (I know somewhat from personal experience, and I know people who have done that kind of work and told me about how rough it is and what they had to do).
2.d. The "wildlife" (well, there's only one kind, which are deer)... where should I start... For once, they're running all over the place, through your settlement(s), eating right next to where you mine / build / ...; not to mention there's only one kind - the aforementioned deer. No rabbits or other smaller animals. There are also no predators (bears, wolves, ...) in Banished.
3. I'm also not fond of (because it creates a disconnect from reality) how time has been implemented... basically, your settles have babies, raise their children, they become eventually old enough to work and then at some point they die due to old age (or before then, due to accidents). All good stuff.  Also, it implements seasons and each of the four are further divided by three (early, mid and late). However, your "banished" people age rapidly within a year. I haven't paid full attention but I think it takes about three in-game years for people to go through their full life cycle. I understand that you can't obviously play the game in real-time, but all this could've still been implemented much better.
4. In connection to what I just mentioned in 3. regarding time, this also becomes very obvious when building structures or harvesting resources (actually that's another point but I'll just say it here - you have 3 resources for building, that's it: wood logs, stone and metal - not even different types of metals; and two types of fuel, which is fire wood from cut up wood logs, and coal)... it can take a whole month to build a wooden house (one part of a season), yet it takes about the same time to create a fully functional mine.
5. The UI and font both do not scale with your screen resolution, same goes for the location placement of the windows. Also, they don't "snap" to each other's borders. Again, it's usable, but just the way everything is implemented, is just very simplistic.

Simply awesome: TLD is one of those games that sucks you in the minute you start playing it. Of course, that is if you are into these type of games. What type is it you ask? Well, it's some kind of first person perspective, survival, PvE, looting/scavenging & crafting kinda game, all wrapped up in sandbox glory. Be warned though: you WILL die. You will die because 1) you froze up, wandering too long and losing track of where you are because a snowstorm suddenly took you off-guard, or 2) you didn't see the damn wolf coming at ya from behind, or 3) you were not smart enough to know you can melt the snow and boil the water from it, or 4) you thought you had superman abilities and broke your leg jumping from too high, or 5) you thought a bear could be killed with a rabbit snare (try a rifle...if you can find one that is), or 6) thought you could hide behind a tree after your snare kill tentative ultimately failed....
Graphically speaking, it's nothing too special, considering Ultra settings at 1080p seems to make my R9 270x work so hard, but it's got its charm and reminds me of Telltales's Walking Dead games. The sound department does an extremely great job at making you feel you're not in a Club Med resort... combined with the visual cues (you can see yourself breathe), you'll probably get chills even if you're playing while bathing in a hot tub.
Soooo... the sandbox mode (the only mode available for now) and its great potential, albeit being somewhat repetitious, makes you wish for the upcoming story mode that will, at least, provide much more incentive to play further other than just the Loot to Survive/Survive to Loot kinda thing.
But, this game is still thumbs up for me and I'd recommend it to anyone who is even remotely interested in survival games. For the price, you can't go wrong. Especially if you can find it on sale.

Mind Spheres is a puzzle game where you need to move a marble from one end of a track to another, by manipulating elements in the track to get the ball where it need to go.  I got it from a Indiegala giveaway, and have found it pretty fun so far, so I thought I'd throw in my two cents.
First, this game is pretty casual.  Its music is very relaxing, and its puzzles are relatively easy compared to most Steam puzzle games (*coughEnglishCountryTunecough*).  Also, it doesn't have a lot of mechanics, though it does build on the few it has (This game takes the "less is more" approach to its mechanics, which is good).
If you're looking for a tough challenge, you won't find one here.  If you're a puzzle game veteran who wants a long game to sink your teeth into, you also might not like this one; I tore through about half of the game's puzzles in around 20 minutes, and completed it in ~1 hour.  But if you want a relaxing puzzle game, or if it's your first time venturing into the puzzle game genre, Mind Spheres easy to recommend.
This is a physics game, and the physics are relatively sound (I really don't understand why the game has a space background, as the puzzles are pretty grounded in gravity).  Three flaws, however: (1) I've had to restart a level multiple times because I put my platform JUST A PIXEL TOO HIGH and the marble got stuck on it (which is super frustrating.  This even happened because A PART OF THE LEVEL was sticking out and made my marble stop.  Really?!), (2) the lack of zoom in this game or any way to rotate the camera does not help, and (3) the triangle-bouncy-thing makes the marble bounce *way* too high, so it's nigh inpossible to see where it'll come down.  It's also a tad irritating that you have to restart the whole level when you make just one mistake, but then again the levels are so short, it's not too big a deal (not as big as it might be in other games, anyway).
This game also chooses the "learn by doing" approach of teaching new mechanics: it just puts in new platforms in as you go, and lets you see what they do.  I think it works, mainly because the levels introducing them are short enough that you can just try again if something unexpected happens.  And I definitely prefer it over a boring tutorial.
Mind Spheres also has Steam trading cards, so.  There's that, if you're a trading card fan like me.  It also has quite a few achievements, all which are unlocked naturally as you progress.
All in all, this is a pretty neat game, a casual physics puzzler with some good fun to be had.  I'd totally recommend it if you want a light, relaxing experience.
(Also, personally, I would LOVE a level editor to create and share my own puzzles--the simple mechanics and maps just begs for a level editor.  PLEASE, Microblast Games?)

I quite enjoyed Jet Gunner.
First off, it's not the most original game in the world.  But it's also not meant to be.  I see a lot of references in reviews to Mega Man and Contra, but it doesn't remind me of those games at all.  No, the inspiration for this seems to be more rooted in the Natsume NES games of old, games like Shatterhand and Shadow of the Ninja, although with more emphasis on projectile weaponry.  But the inclusion of said projectile weaponry doesn't turn it into a run-and-gun, although it does shift the focus a bit.  It's faster-paced than the two aforementioned games, but not meant to be as blazing as Contra.  It's an interesting middle ground...
...that's even more interesting with the inclusion of the jetpack.  It allows for some interesting platforming challenges, and the physics with the 'pack feel quite nice.
Most of the game does a good job of aping the NES look, although the between-level cutscenes look pretty terrible to me.  The rest of it is just fine.  There's nothing really offensive about the audio, either.
Really, it's a nice snack of a game, inspired by games from a simpler time, and I definitely recommend it if you enjoyed a lot of the Natsume and Sunsoft platformers from the NES era.
With the amount of time I've spent, it's been immersively the best learning from any game, but could use a few ways to speed up the learning process.

Second, the campsign itself had little thought put into it. The missions consist of multiplayer maps which have been repurposed for singleplayer gameplay. The flow of multiplayer doesn't translate well into singleplayer at all, especially with the horrid AI. Defence missions are particularly difficult. This all leads to the campaign feeling like a chore to complete. Stick with the multiplayer, which is excellent.

Tales of Zestiria was my first Tales of game, now I also own Tales of Symphonia, but I shall review Zestiria. possible spoiler towards the end, please be aware and read at own risk, if you love discovering things yourself!
Personally, I really enjoy the game a lot and there is a lot to take in at first and it overwhelmed me, so I started off on simple to learn the game and learn the battle system etc. The characters are funny or relatable, although  I do not feel that Sorey goes through much of a character development so far, despite him being the main person, being the sheperd and all. I personally feel that there's more emotion and growth in the people around him.
I love the environments and that in battle or walking through places gives you skits and or there will be a little conversation come up in lower left telling you about the place or about certain monsters, love this element.
The little tutorial tool tips you find on monoliths seem like a lot to take in, I usually learn by doing and prefer it this way, but I would say if there was a con, this is definitely one of them along with the skillsheet/fusion system, which after 35 hours I finally started to understand just by doing it myself and fooling around with it.
The tooltip to help you out in battle which on controller is RB is crucial, I discovered that it is very important to pay attention to it during battle to help you out!
Also love the enemy book, it tells you what they are and the characters tell you how to deal with them or give handy tips in a note underneath.
For some people who don't know this there is a story synopsis element in the same menu as the enemy book, in case you forgot or just want to read up on the story if anything is unclear.
LOVE the artwork and many monsters look unique and act unique, definitely love the way the game plays. It feels smooth and it's fun and interactive, it's not just button mashing, be strategic with your skills (martial artes/hidden/seraphic) and your blast gauge usage or who you armatize with! This aspect makes it more challenging to play the game.
The story so far, well let's say it really opens up later on! and there a lot of funny story elements, I personally think the story is worth playing this game for! :)
I love the fact that there are boss like monsters on each map! gives me something to hunt and I find that element pretty cool!
Love the alternative colors to outfits! won't mention color schemes as people may want to find out themselves.
I find that certain "glamour" items you find are extremely funny and make the characters a bit more customized, superb element!
The other human character that is in your party basically functions as your quest tracker and will give you hints and tips about your quests and locations.
Definitely a fun game despite people saying it's not a great story, it's still a fun JRPG to play and invest time in, it's a game I'd recommend people to play.
There's a lot of stuff to do in the game and I don't want to make this review bigger than it already is, so if you want to find out more, I'd recommend buying it on a sale on steam.
**possible spoiler**Lots of skits play when you visit an inn, this also includes certain story elements from certain seraphim in your party, this was unclear to me and thus I missed a few things so far already, but this makes me excited to play again on a harder difficulty!

This is the first game of the Tales series I started playing, I came with no exceptions but left with a lot of positive impressions.
When I first saw the game I felt quite biased, on the one hand the "anime" style of the game looked kinda old and not that great, when compared to the Witcher 3 for example, on the other hand it is quite unique in it's art style and it fits the way of the game very nicely. As I progressed in the game I noticed just how fitting the graphics were to the game, it had Anime cutscenes which were really enjoyable and overall I think having an other art style would have made the game much worse.
The world and characters seems really diverse, I like how you interact with all your party members and during your journey they start to develop into a full fledged party that started as strangers and quickly became quite like a family. One of the things I enjoyed was that every party member interacted with you in their own way. Found a new enemy? One of the party members might tell you how strange it looks and makes a lot of remarks about it, another time another party member is excited to see something much different that they haven't seen before. It makes it so that you really feel like you are traveling with people and not with just npcs.
Now the combat is decent I guess, it's just enough to not get boring and the more you progress, the better the feeling for combat becomes, however it is not the forte of the series. It is fun to play and have different combos but other games have a much better combat system which feels a lot more dynamic than it does in this game. I don't say it's not fun but it kinda feels a bit unpolished and clunky.
So, would I recommend the game?
If you enjoy storytelling and traveling with party members who are very lifelike then very well yes, I can recommend you this game. On the other Hand, if you don't enjoy a combat system that isn't that exciting and if you don't really like the graphics, then go ahead buy it and try it. If you don't like it, then refund it but I tell you to atleast give it a try before you flick around to other games, because this game deserves it.

A lovely, quaint village building sim. Everything's a bit smaller scale and more focused on sustainability rather than endless growth than is common with games in the genre. While this means that there's less variety in what you can do, it also makes everything feel a lot more immediate, predictable and manageable. The more "zoomed-in" scope of Banished's simulation makes it a much more relaxed, measured game to play than traditional city builders, which can feel overwhelming to the point of being stressful just with how much Stuff there is.
A big plus on the technical side: all the text and GUI can be scaled (though the "GUI scale" slider currently works in reverse), to the point where Banished is actually playable on a TV from the couch. This is a *massive* rarity in simulation games, and much appreciated.

This game is just too hard; people will say it's not unfair, but there are plenty of undodgeable spots in Cuphead Bosses. So unfortunately, unless you're really into hard games, even though it is an amazing game, I simply can't recommend it. Onto the review, I suppose.
God, how long has it been, 3 years? Yes, 3 years. I first saw its article in GameInformer alongside the likes of Shovel Knight and other amazing indie games. Cons
- Difficulty. Extreme difficulty, and undodgeable spots in bosses and levels. They exist.
- Dean Takahashi
Glitches
- When you die during a boss transition, the match continues without you.
- Custom keyboard binds should be displayed as they're set, for example if I set Z to K, then in

Simply awesome: TLD is one of those games that sucks you in the minute you start playing it. Of course, that is if you are into these type of games. What type is it you ask? Well, it's some kind of first person perspective, survival, PvE, looting/scavenging & crafting kinda game, all wrapped up in sandbox glory. Be warned though: you WILL die. You will die because 1) you froze up, wandering too long and losing track of where you are because a snowstorm suddenly took you off-guard, or 2) you didn't see the damn wolf coming at ya from behind, or 3) you were not smart enough to know you can melt the snow and boil the water from it, or 4) you thought you had superman abilities and broke your leg jumping from too high, or 5) you thought a bear could be killed with a rabbit snare (try a rifle...if you can find one that is), or 6) thought you could hide behind a tree after your snare kill tentative ultimately failed....
Graphically speaking, it's nothing too special, considering Ultra settings at 1080p seems to make my R9 270x work so hard, but it's got its charm and reminds me of Telltales's Walking Dead games. The sound department does an extremely great job at making you feel you're not in a Club Med resort... combined with the visual cues (you can see yourself breathe), you'll probably get chills even if you're playing while bathing in a hot tub.
Soooo... the sandbox mode (the only mode available for now) and its great potential, albeit being somewhat repetitious, makes you wish for the upcoming story mode that will, at least, provide much more incentive to play further other than just the Loot to Survive/Survive to Loot kinda thing.
But, this game is still thumbs up for me and I'd recommend it to anyone who is even remotely interested in survival games. For the price, you can't go wrong. Especially if you can find it on sale.

Command and Conquer 3: Tiberium wars is one of my favorite games of my childhood and still continues on 8 years later into my adulthood. Being the first and best RTS games I ever played (originally I played it on Xbox 360 first as the demo when it came out and later the full copy). Here is why it's awesome.
The Single Player Campaign (SPOILERS):
This game has some fun RTS gameplay and a awesome story that has continued the Tiberium universe in this epic story from the GDI, NOD and Scrin sides. The story culminates into one arch with Kane's goal of Ascension, GDI's goal of stopping tiberium and the new faction the Scrin to take tiberium from Earth. As you play, you get high-quality cut-scenes. EA did a very good job of putting a good budget for the cut-scenes qualities and actors. Notable actors that play in the stories characters are Michael Ironside as Jack Granger, Jennifer Morrison as Kirce James and of course Joe Kucan as Kane. The high-production quality of the cut-scene alone is a damn good reason to play the campaign. The missions on the other hand though are...FANTASTIC! Great missions both challenging and interesting in their own ways. Most of them can be beat though through simple strategies (such as spam), others are very hard and require tactics and strategies to complete the objective. The intel you get throughout the campaign is quite fun to collect and read (you get the intel through completing the missions main and bonus objectives). Other notable things about the campaign that I enjoy is the small "Establishing Video Uplink" in-game cutscenes in the top right-hand corner uplink feel like you're actually being talked to while you prepare for battle. Ultimately outside of the great acting, lore and missions the game has a unique universe that makes it great for the players as you shape it as you play through this fun and amazing campaign.
Skirmish and Multiplayer:
The skirmish and multiplayer for this game is quite fun. This is the 2nd primary reason you should get this game. Battling against enemy AI's is quite fun when you are alone and then going to multiplayer to survive against a brutal AI with friends is VERY fun. Battling against each-other is very enjoyable and requires skills either out-tech your opponent quickly (if you are GDI) or out-maneuver them through stealth and hit and run tactics as NOD. For the Scrin, simple air spam. (xD) The games can last for around 30 minutes to a hour at most depending on the AI you are going against or player. Other things to note is the lack of official servers for Tiberium Wars, I suggest using evolve or C&C Online if you plan to play with friends or regular players. Overall, its a great time to slug it out and annihilate each other in a war to end all wars game.
Maps, Graphics and Performance:
This games map designs and graphics blend beautifully to make a wonderful looking tiberium-infested world. From battling in Egypt to Small Town USA, their are many maps types and many ways you can use these maps to your advantage for your faction. On maps you will notice Tech buildings. The different type of tech buildings are...
-Tiberium spike Provides an initial bonus and then a constant stream of funds.
-Mutant hovel Allows recruiting of Mutant Marauders.
-Expansion Point Provides additional ground control.
-Subway Hub Provides control over Subway entrances.
-Subway Entrance Allow infantry to transfer between entrances.
-Tiberium silo Provides a one-time bonus to the first player who captures it.
-Reinforcement bay Provides reinforcements.(Campaign only)
-EMP control center Allows the launch of an Electromagnetic Pulse at regular intervals.
As such straight from the cnc.wiki, the tech buildings allow a side to get a advantage over the other with these buildings using a engineer. They are pretty straight forward as the descriptions say above. But to continue with the graphics, the game looks fantastic. Maxing out all the settings and looking at the eye candy that comes aftward while building your base or leveling someone else's' is quite beautiful. The fidelity and visuals make the game look very wonderful compared to its previous title (Tiberium Sun) and allow the player to have visually stimulating good time. Performance wise, this game runs pretty good. 30 frame cap can be a issue for some, but it rarely dips below that while in-game as battles are usually short and decisive. If you have a decent computer (with at least 8 gigs of ram, a GTX750 or a AMD R7, you will be fine). If you have a gaming computer, prepare for max graphic and no lag. (Outside of that stupid frame cap)
Mods:
The modding community has kept this game alive and well for many years since its release. With mods that bring back old Tiberium Sun units and Structures or do crazy stuff with Chuck Norris, you will enjoy playing the mods made by the Community.
But to be more specific, I will list the categories and links to the mods I most enjoy and you should check out!

What I really enjoy about this Modding community is the amount of successful and awesome total conversation mods that bring back many old units from previous games and make them better with the newer engine. I also enjoy the mods that bring in other universes to the engine.
My favorite of all of those has to be Tiberium Essence (Sorry Chuck) as it brings some wonderful units and buildings from Tiberian Sun. The mod also does well of improving some of the Units such as the Mammoth Mk2, as its Rocket Pods and Gun turret now actually function and are effective in battle. Also a upgrade on it allows either duel grande launcher turret (to kill enemy infantry in buildings more effectively or clear buildings of enemy infantry) or a Anti-Aircraft duel-railgun turret for shooting down most aircraft with ease. I also been following the mod for years and it has a wonderful developer, community and always more content on the way! The next update will contain The forgotten Faction (Also sorry Forgotten Mod).
To get off my box now on my favorite mod, please check out all those mods their, to install a mod and get it to work on steam, make sure you create a Mod folder in Command and Conquer 3 Tiberium Wars folder that should be found in My Documents (You should also see another folder called replays, if you see that, your in the right place). Make sure [Mods] is spelled exactly like that without the brackets.
After you make the mod folder, throw the mod into the Mods folder (make sure you have winrar to extract the mod, most mods use a rar file) and then go to your steam library.
Right click on Command and Conquer 3 Tiberium Wars in your Steam Library, click Properties, make sure your in the GENERAL tab and click on Set Launch Options. You should see a box come up with a blank text box. Type in the text box [-ui] (without brackets). (DASH_SPACE_LOWERCASEUI)
Now the Game browser will appear! Select a mod & play!
Overall, Command and Conquer 3: Tiberium Wars is a great game. Fantastic single player campaigns, great skirmish and multiplayer modes, wonderful maps, graphics and good performance. I Highly recommended it if you are a true RTS fan and honestly, this is the last best Command and Conquer game (including Kane's Wrath).

What it is:  Addictive fun, fast, easy to learn WW2 "hex and counter" turn based wargame.
So I was hesitant to purchase this game as had its origins as an iOs game .  I chatted a bit with one of the devs online and wfound out this was not a straight port but a rework.  For 10 bucks, I figured what the heck.  I am very happy I gave it a shot.
What it has:  A very well done UI, quite easy to understand and friendly.  Nice graphics.  When I started in the tutorial I was reminded of the classic Panzer/Allied General games.  The tutorials are very well done and teach you everything you need to know to play well.
A ton of content comes with the game.  Over 9 separate campaigns, each with multiple missions.  3 levels of AI make the challenge customizable for all player levels.  If you are a wargames expert and want a human opponent, there is a 2 player hotseat mode with 10+ scenarios as well.
The game play is fast, clean and easy to understand.  Your units can move and attack (think soldiers and tanks firing on the move) wuth a reduction in their combat effectivness.  Cover and terrain are very important for protection and line of sight as the map is shrouded (fog of war).
Overall impressions:  I really like this game!  I started it up and when I looked up, 2 hours had gone by and I was still having a great time.  One of the first games in a long time that I was disappointed when life interferred and I had to stop playing.
Do yourself a favor, get this gem of a game.  I know the devs are working on a American Civil War game as well and I am really looking forward to that one as well.

A Hat in Time is one of those special games, the kind that just plays so well that every moment spent in the game is a joy. Inspired by 3D platformers like Super Mario Sunshine and Banjo-Kazooie, A Hat in Time absolutely nails gameplay. Hat Kid is fun to play as, and few games can make the simple act of moving feel so damn good.
That isn't to say the game is without it's issues. Many models in the game seem to have no collision, and it can be very distracting when you jump through something instead of bouncing off or landing on it. There are also some odd tonal and gameplay shifts which not everyone will like. On the other hand, the gameplay shifts are few and far between and help to add some variety to the varios missions.
The game has five main parts, each of which take place in varied locations. Each part emphasizes different aspects of the game -- Dead Bird Studio is fairly linear and full of setpieces, while the Subcon Forest has tons of areas to explore that you never visit in the main missions.
The game took me roughly 12 hours to complete, which mainly consisted of beating the main levels. Doing all the time rifts and finding every collectible adds a few more hours of solid entertainment, but after that there isn't much left to draw you back in the game. That said, every minute I've spent playing A Hat in Time has been incredibly enjoyable, and the workshop support coming soon will definitely get me to come back to the game.

I am currently in the middle of my second playthrough of the game (on Hard, don't have the time to deal with Chaos) and I can wholeheartedly recommened this game to fans of the Tales series. To general RPG fans or people who have never touched a Tales game however you might want to look elsewhere and I will explain why in greater detail when I discuss game mechanics. Steams character limit stopped me before I could get halfway so I'll condense this review.
1: Graphics: 6/10. Graphics don't break a game for me but some of the poor enemy graphics in addition to rigid walking and game engine cutscene animations degrade the score of this rather unimportant catagory. However the video style cutscenes are awesome and the PC options are pretty good actually.
2. Sound Design and Soundtrack: 9/10. Poor sound design in engine cutscenes are the only thing holding this catagory back. Get you the OST, now. Battle and dungeon themes are varied and engaging and boss music is chillingly beautiful. On par with Witcher 3 honestly.
Gameplay Mechanics: 7/10. Where my review was cut short, could write an essay on the good and bad. The good: Battle is fluid , challening and exciting, aramtization is very fun. Support talents are intuitive and mostly useful. Lord of the land are hit and miss and mostly useful post game or for backtracking since you get them late in areas. Item fusion is a god awful mess and a♥♥♥♥♥♥system. If you have the patience for it the it lends to some very broken combinations that make intense and chaos difficulties a joke. The fusion system is what should drive away casual fans.
Story and Characters: 6/10. Didn't even get here before steam cut me off. The story is a bit generic though it touched my feels multiple times. The term I would use is "Engaing and underwhelming". A couple characters are pretty shallow and boring, a couple are pretty cool, and a couple are just incredible. A mixed bag of unfilled potential honestly.
Overall 7.5/10 as a Tales game, 6/10 as casual RPG. I personally loved the game and can recommend it over Tales of Graces F and Xillia 2, around on Par with Xilla 1, not nearly as good as Vesperia or Symponia. I have yet to play Beseria so I can't compare them which is a shame because Beseria is a prequel to this. Don't start your Tales series here. If you have an Xbox 360 start with Vesperia, otherwise grab a PS3 and start with Graces or Xillia. Symphonia on PC isn't a bad choice to start out either. A genreal RPG fan should stay away from this one until they play a different Tales gam IMO.

Edit: I've changed my review to not recommend this game. I haven't changed anything I wrote in the review.
================
The story isn't interesting, it’s cliché.
But the battles are really fun. If you're good enough at the game, I think you can beat level 80 enemies at level 1 because you can always dodge attacks with sidesteps. There's a new mechanic called SC that you use up when you do any action. It regenerates by itself and replaces TP. I feel that the battle system is a lot more complicated than other Tales games I've played. Throughout the game, you find monoliths that slowly teach you more and more about the battle system. There's a lot of cool things you can do, like reducing art casting time by using it in the middle of a combo, but I didn't really need to use a lot of those mechanics. I'm sure I would if I was on a higher difficulty level. In every area and optional dungeon, there's an optional boss. It's a good challenge.
There's a new mechanic with your equipment that allows for stat boosts and stuff depending on what you equip and what skills that equipment has. You can also fuse equipment to get the skills you want on the weapons you want. You could make some godlike armor if you wanted to.
There's a bunch of sidequests to do too. And it isn't like Tales of the Abyss where you have no way to track your sidequests. Your party members will keep track of all the sidequests you're on and give you some hints on where to go to get new ones sometimes.
The graphics look good. Normally, the game is capped at 30fps. It didn't really bother me at all, but if it does then there's a mod you can easily install to fix that problem.
The dialogue is good most of the time, but sometimes cringy. The skits are funny, as the usually are with Tales games. It’s all voiced, which is cool. You can choose Japanese or English. I liked all the party members except the main character. His always nice and positive personality made me angry sometimes.
The music is good.
You probably want to have a controller for this. It is playable without one, but this is a PS3 game port, so it's designed for a controller. I used an Xbox controller.
There's some tedious running around sometimes. In the other two Tales games I've played, the player is given an easy way to get around the world sometime in the game. In this game, that never happens. The only way to get around quickly is to spend your gald to teleport between save points. It costs around 5% of your gald, I think. But walking around isn't that bad.

Fun litle educational game. The Hiragaana lessons were solid, and the battles were a fun way to memorize them. The actual RPG gameplay, however, could have been much better.
I never felt like I was in any serious danger throughout the game. At the very beginning there were times when a party member got down to around half health or so, but they were very easily brought up to full health and I got through every level without ever once despairing that I may have to back out and try again.
After only a minimal amount of grinding to level up and purchase the most updated equipment, I could handle every level without any fear whatsoever. The party handled almost every encounter in one turn, before the Hiragana warriors even had a chance to strike. On the occasions when a battle required two turns and allowed the enemy to hit back, they either missed completely or did 0 damage. Only very rarely did they roll high and do something like 12 damage, which was negligible.
The magic system is a joke. The characters have an M.Attack parameter, which is strange because there are no magic attacks. There's a spell to give all characters a boost to defense, which is useless when the characters almost never get hit. There's a spell to give a boost to attack, which is also useless since every character except Misaki will usually kill an enemy in one hit. There's a revive spell if a party member dies... which will never happen. There are spells for removing conditions on party members, but even in the cases where a chracter is hit with an attack that imposes a condition, the enemy can still usually be taken out without having to deal with that.
The heal spells can be useful at rare occasions, usually at the beginning of the game. You can stock up on potions that do a lot of the same things as the spells, but you'll almost never need them.
There are two main stages in the game. In the first stage, you're in your home country. In the second stage, you chase the enemies to Japan. After you've bought all the most updated equipment in each stage, money becomes essentially useless.
I accidentally stole a NPC's entire life savings by looking into a potted plant. It was only 2 gold. Made me feel kind of bad, but the game wouldn't let me give it back.
There was very little effort put into the game's story. I know it's an educational game, but it would have been nice if there was some effort to make it feel like the story wasn't just an excuse for learning. When you're directed to a new level, the directions are like, "In order to continue our lessons, you must go to such-and-such village" - why not even put some minimal effort into it and say something like, "We've got a tip that weird stuff is happening in such-and-such village, we need to go chek it out!"
I know that's a small thing, but attention to details like that would have made the game feel more like a game.
The menu system was bulky and awkward. They could have very easily fit more hiragana options on one screen without the need to scroll. The way general options were set up was also very inefficient, often requiring a lot of back tracking and fiddling around to do what you want to do.
Overall, though, I'd recommend this game because it teaches Hiragana well, and the RPG gameplay, while imperfect, was game-like enough that it distracted my mind from the tedium of studying.

A big plus on the technical side: all the text and GUI can be scaled (though the "GUI scale" slider currently works in reverse), to the point where Banished is actually playable on a TV from the couch. This is a *massive* rarity in simulation games, and much appreciated.

This is one of the better RPG Maker games I've played.

-Good, consistent visual style.
-Great soundtrack and atmosphere.

Cons:
-Early on there's a lot of video cuts that are supposed to be scary. They're kind of jarring and don't really fit with the game and aren't particularly scary.
-The plot doesn't progress organically. It makes an abrupt jump from creepy 2spooky4u to generic "solve the mystery" style adventure game. First of all: I like the general idea of this game quite a lot. combining fun and learning is always the best way to teach and hiragana battle does pretty much precisely that. it is the balance of the two that is worrying me though.
frankly: the odd thing about hiragana battle is - at least in my opinion -  that the learning part is much more fun than the gaming part.
yes, fighting the hiragana symbols by giving correct answers is a nice way to learn by repetition, but the rpg-part is at times too difficult and tedious. you never know how much health an enemy has- there are no hp-indicators. will one attack suffise or will you need more? will one strike instakill and the next attack on the same symbol be wasted? you just never know. initiative is unnerving and you often end up with half your team being hit or inconvenienced by effects like poisoning, sleep or paralysis, before you even had the chance to do some damage or counter the effects of the last round. you should constantly save the game because there is permadeath that throws you back to your last manual save and with battles as unpredictable as the ones in this game, the grim reaper always seems to lurk around the corner. one streak of badluck and your entire fellowship gets buggered with a fishfork. while the general controls are relatively intuitive and generally alright, inventory management and equipping are quite cumbersome.
these are things you will have to put up with between lessons. learning the symbols, vocabulary and writing is way more satisfying than going out into a ruinous labyrinth, fighting two battles and then having to head back to your base village to heal  and revive your little party over and over again. but then i am not a very rpg-o-phile person and others might be quite happy to endure all that.
if you are stictly looking for a japanese-learning program, have no experience with old rpgs and no patience, keep away from this game. if you like to play oldschool rpgs like the early final fantasys and on top of that learn some basic japanese, then this will be perfect for you. i do hope they refine the next title and make the game part less disruptive and more adaptable to the players preferences.

Goes over the Hirigana and some words, other people have taken issue with the fact that some of the words taught are usually spelled with Katakana but as the game serves to teach you the Hirigana I don't really mind this. Just don't worry too much about remembering the 'spelling' of the words being taught.
In terms of actual gameplay, it's a very simplistic jRPG style game, you can attack, guard, use items, cast defensive/buff spells and buy new equipment etc. Now to be clear, I hate old school turn based jRPGs, even classics like FF7/8 and Lost Odyssey eventually wore thin for me before I got to see the ending, but mercifully this game requires very little grinding in order to gear and level up your team to the point where they're fairly powerful (mine were about lvl 32 by completion on an ~12 hour playthrough, aided by the bonus levels gained through completing side quests). In fact the joy of it was I liked grinding because it was helping reinforce the Hirigana I was learning.
I will echo some of the other reviews by saying that you do begin to see patterns of enemy formations rather than having to identify 3/4 random enemies each time, but this didn't diminish the value of the practice too much for me.
Finally I will say that this is not the first time I have learnt the Hirigana, the first being a few years ago, so a completely fresh learner may have a slightly different experience. I was also supplementing the game with Heisig's Remember the Kana (or was it the other way round) which is vastly quicker but much less fun than playing through this short game! All in all worth the very low cost for a fun way of learning/reinforcing the Hirigana and perfect for a long weekend/quiet evening.

Wanted to like this game. Has good old school NES gameplay. Pretty short, and levels aren't that interesting. Cool upgrades. What did it is the mechanics and platforming, which were too amateur-ish. The jump and falling are super jerky. When you jump up in the air or let off the jetpack, you fall way too quickly and just jerk down. When you boost up you jerk up high into the air. It is not smooth or intuitive at all. When you get hit there is the dumb mechanic of you are stunned and fall back a decent amount, which just makes platforming frustrating and not fun. You get 3 lives to complete 6 levels, and there are a few 1-ups and a few healths scattered in there. If you die on the final stage you have to do it all over again. This isn't bad initially. Then there is the hitboxes, which are spotty. Enemies fire at you immediately when they get on screen and before you can see or react to them, meaning you get hit when there is nothing you can do about it. The bottom of the screen is terrible. It registers you dying when only a bit of your foot touches it. This makes no sense because many time on the final stages you are expected to fly under things, and with the jerky unintuitive dropping and flying there is no way you might not graze the screen, but in this game thats an instant death and restart the level. The poor flying also doesn't work when they want you going in between top and bottom spikes, and you can't just hold it and keep it. The instant deaths from the bottom of the screen, poor jetpack mechanics, annoying enemies attacking before you see them, repeated 6 levels with 3 lives, and getting knocked back, all make this game poor by NES standards. Games back then usually had more polish. 4.5/10

Growing up around the Mario platformers of the late 90s and early 2000s (and recent with the Galaxy series and upcoming Odyssey), there's a special place in me for these types of games, and A Hat in Time reminds me of the classic Mario platformers.  The five different worlds are all each unique, including a "traditional" world, a movie studio (which then forks into 2 other level types), a horror/ghost world (with one of the more terrifying levels I have seen, which REALLY changed the tone of the game), a free-roam world, and then the final world which felt somewhat like a Bowser level from the Mario series.
Unlike Yooka-Laylee, each "act" in a world provides a basic idea of what the theme of each time piece is (such as "train rush", indicating that there will be a timed event on a train level).  With Yooka-Laylee, I felt as if I was just thrown into a large level, and somehow had to go around and find each pagie, which felt tedious, especially when you may have not had everything required to accomplish the goal. This was not the case in A Hat in Time.
There is a vast soundtrack to the game (78 tracks), proving a unique audio experience to each level and event that fits the level's atmosphere well.  If you appreciate the music as well as I did, buying the soundtrack DLC is a no-brainer; having the MP3s to listen to whenever is a nice touch to have.
The main issue I had in the end was the length of the game.  There are only 40 time pieces in the entire game (only 25 needed to complete the full story), and I was able to complete the game with 100% completion in about 17 hours.  Having more worlds (and therefore more time pieces) would have been nice.

This is really... it puts me at a loss for words. After the terrible disappointment that Yooka-Laylee was, I, well, I never even thought of this game. I found about its existence back in 2014 from a video from YouTuber brutalmoose, who was reviewing a very early build of the game. Looked cool but there wasn't much to go off of. Then, it sort of vanished as far as I was aware, and I NEVER heard any news or anything about it. But fast forward to early 2017, and suddenly the game has a presence again, with astoundingly good social media PR that did wonders at spreading the game, and here we are.
A Hat in Time is easily my favorite game this year, with BOTW in second place now... though I admit that Super Mario Odyssey will likely take AHiT's place, don't take that the wrong way! A Hat in Time is an amazing 3D platformer that everyone, fans of the genre or not, should give a try! I'm not much of an in-depth reviewer, but I can say this: It's just... amazingly well crafted, with great dialogue and voice acting to boot; and 4 intricate worlds that Yooka-Laylee wishes it could have. The difference here is that they're worlds that you WANT to explore. Every part of them has a purpose and things to collect, things to do in them. Not just extra world space for the sake of making it bigger; huge worlds does not instantly = good. And the game is also getting TWO more worlds as free DLC later down the line! Like, I really don't even WANT to go more in depth, honestly... 30 dollars is a crime for this game. I would drop the full $60 *easily* for A Hat in Time.
Please do yourself a favor. Get the game. Get overloaded on cuteness. And enjoy everything the game has to offer.

First 20 mins: "Ok, this is different in a good way."
Next 20 mins: "Still paying attention. I'm interested in this Coda fellow."
Next 30 mins: "Ok, ok... seriously guys, when the ♥♥♥♥ did I start playing, 'Pink Floyd: The Wall: The Video Game'"??
Last 20 mins (after the "big reveal"): "Wow, I can't believe a game went from interesting and relatable to someone just whining. This isn't even a game, more like a way for someone to get paid for their therapy session."
In the end, this is something different. Some may like it, some won't. I am hard pressed to call it a "game" in terms of the way most people would think of one. Maaayyybe you could say it's a kind of narrated walking simulator.
I think the trailer is a bit misleading. You see a little of it right away, but you'll quickly learn that's the case as the narrator focuses on HIS thoughts/experiences with the person in question. What is the use in "playing the games" if you yourself don't draw any conclusions about them since you're railroaded by the narrator's thoughts? Even if, the game isn't really about that. Once the "big reveal" or "twist" comes you'll realize it was
, So, if it's all true and Coda's a real person (which I don't believe) then it all comes off a little pretentious.
In the end it's not good, but it is an experience. It's about 90 mins, so you will waste as much time on this as a bad movie if you end up disliking it. If you're on the fence just know:
It's not exactly like the trailer suggests.
The twist ruins it (IMO).
The "game(s)" only serve to push the narration along. So much so that sometimes you're just standing around waiting.
I found it to be more of an interactive therapy session...errrr...movie.
I paid $7.99. Do I regret it? Yes. But I waited 18 days to play it, so yeah. Had I paid 1.00 in a Humble bundle, I would have felt better about it.

I bought the game on sale about a year ago and it was a fun game, but there wasn't a lot of variations with the races. It is still early access, but I think it is worth the money. I've certainly put in enough hours to enjoy the game.

In the two weeks since the June 30th major patch, there have been numerous improvements that make the early reviews out of date already.

Rarely do you see a game with a world as rich as this. Bioshock tackles complex political philosophy right from the opening scene, using it as a backdrop to set the stage for the depths of human depravity.
It doesn't use the low-hanging fruit of communism or fascism, either - such a backdrop would have worked, but instead the writers chose the popular but digitally underrepresented philosophy of Objectivism, Ayn Rand's claim to fame. It's often difficult to disagree with the villains of the game as they espouse their sensible, rational views of free markets, even as you gun down twisted shadows of humans corrupted by the sinful excesses of those markets.
Bioshock boldly addresses the constant struggle the free world has between the desire for distributive justice and the stance for individual liberty. I don't think I've ever seen a game as brave as this succeed so well. It says a great deal about the talent of the writers to offer up a controversial philosophy without becoming preachy either way.

Goes over the Hirigana and some words, other people have taken issue with the fact that some of the words taught are usually spelled with Katakana but as the game serves to teach you the Hirigana I don't really mind this. Just don't worry too much about remembering the 'spelling' of the words being taught.
In terms of actual gameplay, it's a very simplistic jRPG style game, you can attack, guard, use items, cast defensive/buff spells and buy new equipment etc. Now to be clear, I hate old school turn based jRPGs, even classics like FF7/8 and Lost Odyssey eventually wore thin for me before I got to see the ending, but mercifully this game requires very little grinding in order to gear and level up your team to the point where they're fairly powerful (mine were about lvl 32 by completion on an ~12 hour playthrough, aided by the bonus levels gained through completing side quests). In fact the joy of it was I liked grinding because it was helping reinforce the Hirigana I was learning.
I will echo some of the other reviews by saying that you do begin to see patterns of enemy formations rather than having to identify 3/4 random enemies each time, but this didn't diminish the value of the practice too much for me.
Finally I will say that this is not the first time I have learnt the Hirigana, the first being a few years ago, so a completely fresh learner may have a slightly different experience. This is a very good game for learning the Japanese language. It took me 21 hours to complete the game, which is long than most people who reviewed this game, because the game suggests you write everything in a notebook but instead I wrote every little detail in the Notes application on my iPhone and iPad using both Japanese keyboards which are included in the Settings application.
I made two different pages in the Notes application which look a bit like grids because on one page I wrote the hiragana letters in one column, how to pronounce them in the next column, then the same hiragana letters with dakuten marks (") or handakuten marks (o) in the next column and below those columns I wrote grammar particles such as は, が, を, ヘ, の and ですwhich mean words like the, to, of, a, is and after learning all the hiragana letters this game also shows you how sentences, phrases or question are set up using these particles all of which I wrote down in Notes as well. The other page in my Notes application shows all the Japanese words I learnt throughout this game in hiragana letters one column, then in romaji (Latin/English letters) in the next column and then the English translation in the final column. If you have an iPhone or iPad or other smart device which you can easily access Japanese keyboards on I suggest writing down every little detail in a grid or table on an application like Notes the same as I have done.
I am looking forward to playing the sequel Learn Japanese To Survive! Katakana War which I have also bought recently and am going to start now. If you want to learn kanji characters there is currently no game in this series for them but after I learnt all the hiragana letters from this game I decided to buy a Japanese language manga volume (specifically volume 1 of 君の名は/Kimi no na wa/Your Name) and it nearly all has hiragana letters or kanji characters and next to each kanji character it shows you how to write it in hiragana letters too so I can just translate everything I don't know yet online by using hiragana letters and learn kanji characters at the same time (which I also write down in my Notes application) so this game was very useful for helping me read my manga too. If you can find a Japanese manga volume like mine with hiragana letters next to kanji characters I think it would be very useful after learning all the hiragana letters from this game to learn kanji too while waiting for a speculated sequel in the Learn Japanese to Survive for kanji characters.

I got this game because it was on sale and I was curious about how good it would be. I love educational games, I feel like I have a ton of experience with them, and I considered Japanese an unlearnable subject for me, something that could only be learned with a really good educational game.
Turns out this is an AMAZING educational game! After just the first set of characters, the simple vowels, I looked back on my notes and realized what I had done. I've written Japanese characters. Me! I did that! And I look at them and I understand their meaning! THIS IS INCREDIBLY EXCITING TO ME :D :D :D
Now I've learned many characters and a few words and I'm starting to feel overwhelmed, but I won't stop being amazed at how much I've changed. I understand basically how Japanese works now, and I can hear the individual syllables in the words whereas before I heard nothing but gibberish! That's a huge accomplishment imo! My way of thinking has been irreversibly changed. And I don't think Japanese is that hard anymore. Well, not hiragana anyway xD There's still katakana and kanji to learn but those are entirely different subjects and games (and only this one and katakana are available right now). I'll probably pick up those sequels at some point because wow this style is effective!
I'm not looking to be fluent or able to understand/hold a conversation with this. I'm just learning it casually, for fun. But even if I forget all the words I learn and how to read the characters, this breakthrough in my mind made it worth it. :D IM SO PROUD OF MYSELF!!!!!!!
When the game
my mind was blown. That's when I knew this was working, I've learned something. I'll never forget it. It was a moment of epiphany and enlightenment and overwhelming joy - the joy of discovery, of learning something new by figuring it out on my own. Something I've been sorely missing for a long time. That's the best way to learn, and that's what this game encourages. Sure it tells you to memorize all these characters and words and stuff, of course there needs to be memorization. But it doesn't feel so in-your-face and pressuring. It lets you do things in your own time, repeating as much as you need and just overall being gentle with the process. And it helps that it's an rpg with random battles where you have to attack with the correct meaning of the symbols, so it gives you the necessary repetition for memorizing but in a fun way.
The music, especially during lessons, is very soothing and relaxing. It helps to keep you stress free while you're trying to learn something as new and strange as Japanese. In fact, I find this game very relaxing as a whole mostly because of the music. I like to practice drawing the hiragana with a brush and ink along with the lesson music just to relax.
I strongly recommend the game, especially if you want to learn Japanese but, like me, considered it too difficult or time consuming. Or if you want to have fun learning a new subject, it's good for that too since it is an educational game. :D

Simply awesome: TLD is one of those games that sucks you in the minute you start playing it. Of course, that is if you are into these type of games. What type is it you ask? Well, it's some kind of first person perspective, survival, PvE, looting/scavenging & crafting kinda game, all wrapped up in sandbox glory. Be warned though: you WILL die. You will die because 1) you froze up, wandering too long and losing track of where you are because a snowstorm suddenly took you off-guard, or 2) you didn't see the damn wolf coming at ya from behind, or 3) you were not smart enough to know you can melt the snow and boil the water from it, or 4) you thought you had superman abilities and broke your leg jumping from too high, or 5) you thought a bear could be killed with a rabbit snare (try a rifle...if you can find one that is), or 6) thought you could hide behind a tree after your snare kill tentative ultimately failed....
Graphically speaking, it's nothing too special, considering Ultra settings at 1080p seems to make my R9 270x work so hard, but it's got its charm and reminds me of Telltales's Walking Dead games. The sound department does an extremely great job at making you feel you're not in a Club Med resort... combined with the visual cues (you can see yourself breathe), you'll probably get chills even if you're playing while bathing in a hot tub.
Soooo... the sandbox mode (the only mode available for now) and its great potential, albeit being somewhat repetitious, makes you wish for the upcoming story mode that will, at least, provide much more incentive to play further other than just the Loot to Survive/Survive to Loot kinda thing.
But, this game is still thumbs up for me and I'd recommend it to anyone who is even remotely interested in survival games. For the price, you can't go wrong. Especially if you can find it on sale.

Cuphead is a
perfect game.  Gorgeous, highly creative art, amazing soundtrack, easy to pick up but hard as nails to complete...it's one of the best games I've played this year.  It's absolutely infuriating at times, but no moreso than the retro games it's inspired by, and all your failures just make your successes all the more powerful.
Every time I thought "THIS IS IMPOSSIBLE" I tried and tried again until I could feel the rhythm of each level, learning to play the controller like a musical instrument.  When I finally completed the last boss, I stood up, threw my fists straight up in the air, and gave a euphoric, triumphant "
".  What a game.  And all this for a measly 20 bucks.
If I
to make one critique?  The overworld could have been more interesting.  It was mostly static with NPCs that weren't very memorable.  Nothing really to do in it, with few secrets to be found.  It mostly just served as a means to select your level, but it could have been more.  It could have had some mini activities to give you a little downtime and change up the pace before you rushed headfirst into the next punishing level.
That's pretty much it.
There have been a hell of a lot of great titles this year, but I hope Cuphead receives all the awards it deserves.  It is a masterpiece in its genre and will be enjoyed for many years to come.
