I bought this game because Yahtzee of Zero Punctuation said good things about it, which happens to about two games per year. It's not normally my kind of game, but I'm impressed nonetheless.
First impressions: It's essentially Assassin's Creed, but with guns. Real guns, not the ancinet bayonets from AC3. Also, a world map that is, in Yahtzee's words, "Willy-shrivellingly huge". And he's right; the world map is over 1000 square kilometers.
EDIT: Second impressions: I still claim that Just Cause 2 is Assassin's Creed with 20th century technology. Definitely not 21st; you're on a romp in a communist island nation, so they're a few decades behind the world superpowers. Still, everything you can find in later Assassin's Creed games, you can find here. Maybe with a bit less assassination, but everything else is here.
Wanna climb buildings, or, hell, anything? You got it; rather than climb like a ninja, you can climb Zelda-style with a super-long-range hookshot that can grab literally anything. Speaking of the hookshot, it seems to be one of the main features of this game. It's got loads of uses; in addition to being a reason to never need stairs, you can use it to yank enemies off of ledges to kill them, yank enemies on the ground to stun them, yank yourself to a vehicle to hijack it, or just speed around all over without ever needing to walk.
Also in the name of "Modern Assassin's Creed", there's the massive array of collectibles. Something like 2700 item pickups and some comprable number of government objects to blow up. Then there's all the side missions. Ballpark estimate, there's somewhere around 100. At least, if you count all the races. Which are about half of that total. And honestly, the plane races that ask you to fly stupidly close to things that aren't air could have been removed from the game with no real consequence...
At the end of the day, however, Just Cause 2 is one of the few games that's doing things right. It's so open-ended that it's not so much a sandbox as it is a desert. And frankly, that's what we need from games; open-ended objectives. Essentially, there's a difference between "Use the BFG to destroy the thing" and "Destroy the thing"; the latter leaves me with options, and Just Cause 2 consists almost entirely of the latter. It's fun, it's addicting, and it only really cares
stuff gets blown up, not

The other fact of it only taking me 2 hours to beat the entire thing (including getting every bit of dialogue in the play) kind of supports that need that the game finishes up a little too fast for its own good. It would have been nice to spend some more time in places that might have needed it. Ending doesn't really give me that feeling of "it's over" or that it was about to be over or that everything is all set in the end (connections of characters etc. remains foggy but maybe intentionally).
This being said I was gotten a lot. It was great gets of me, a funny way of saying it, and this game really worked well with some tropes and not so much tropes (I'm referring to the way the play works which I think is a little flawed but altogether an interesting way of using time travel - I don't know how many roses I ended up with but I kept collecting them) of RPG games, kind of alluding to something like Misao or y'know, a lot of 'those types' of games. Would like to see more from the people who made it - obviously the sprites are great and probably its most appealing feature. There's more to it that works pace-wise for the first half so well (my thoughts are that later it's a little less done well, but still ok) that really make everything come together.

First off, let me start off by saying that this game is SHORT. I beat it in around 50 minutes, and as far as I know, there isn't any branching paths or hidden levels or anything of the sort, which is fine, but I'd like a reason to replay it, because it is a fun game while it lasts.
It's definitely a difficult playthough, and in certain spots the game can seem a bit unfair, giving the player very very little time to react to what it going on. There also is a problem with flying and shooting at the same time. You can't hold down the fly button and shoot buttons simultaneously. The character won't shoot. I don't know if this is a problem, or a design choice, either way it still bothered me some
Graphics - 8/10
The graphics for the game aren't bad, but they are lacking in some areas. At times, I found myself mistaking background tiles for foreground platforms, only to find that when I tried to land on it, I went straight through and fell to my death. This is especially prevelant in the airship stage. The sprite work is all done pretty well and the animations fit the era this game is emulating very well. The color choices for the stages is also pretty well done.
Sound - 9/10
The music and sound effects for this game are perfect. They fit the setting perfectly, and sound like they are coming straight out of an NES. The tracks for the game aren't entirely memorable, but they aren't terrible either. They work, and that's all that matters.
Gameplay - 9/10
This game is HARD in some sections. And then in the very next section, it will be a cake walk. I know this is a pretty subjective thing to say, but the over all balance of the game's difficulty is a mixed bag. Some of the later bosses were complete push overs. I had absolutely zero problems defeating the final boss of the game. Infact, when I beat the boss, I fully expected to see it transform into something else and begin a second phase of the final boss. It was just too easy.  Then again, the stage before it was brutal and full of situations that seem a bit unfair, especially the area with all the spikes and lasers. A warning pops up on the screen for a split second, only to disappear as a massive laser comes ripping through the center of the screen. The first time it happened I died and didn't even know why. There is also an extreme problem with enemies that fire so rapidly that you can't get in front of them to shoot them, or they fire the second they appear on screen. Majorly frustrating. Don't take this all the wrong way, I had a lot of fun playing this game, I just feel that there could have been some balancing done to make this an even more enjoyable experience. There are a bunch of different weapon upgrades, and sub weapons too. The jet mechanic is often used in clever situations. I really liked the section in the airship stage where the giant fans take away your ability to fly. Very nice change of pace.
Story - -/10
There really isn't a whole lot of a story to this game, but as it's emulating the classic 8-bit style games of old, I'm not really too concerned about it. I didn't enjoy the game anyless because it was missing an enthralling tail to go along with it.
Overall - 8.6/10
I would definitely recommend this game to anyone that loves retro-styled games, and especially to people that love traditional platformers, which there are few of on Steam.

It's nice when there's a game released which tries something completely different. I played the prototype a while ago and was sold on the concept almost instantly.
Story mode (while short) does do a reasonably good job at setting the tone of the experience. If you fall in love with the story, would definately recommend hunting down those secrets then visiting ggroups.exe to gain more of an understanding of what's happening.
If you're more into just killing red dudes, you can unlock endless mode after completing the story. Success in this mode is rewarded with new areas and endless mode challenges which will keep you playing for hours. Alternatively, there's a challenge mode which will have you replaying story levels with different rules which alter the entire way you think about facing encounters.
Killstagram is also a pretty cool feature, allowing users to share their best moments in the game. If you want to step up your Killstagram game, you should look in ggroups.exe for some tips. I have had a few problems uploading full length clips to Killstagram, but that may just be an issue with my own internet connection.
If you're unsure as to whether or not you'd enjoy the game, definately check out the prototype first. If the mechanics in that don't sell you, the game probably isn't for you.

This is my 1st Tales Games and i bought it at 75% discount because i was unsure to buy Berseria at Full Price. Zestiria conviced me and i have just bought Berseria! :) - Zestiria is the perfect example that you can make a funny story with generic characters. But what made me enjoy 46 hours of gameplay here is the game itself wich is GENIUS, not the story. I will explain:
As a game Zestiria is ADDICTIVE because is FUN TO PLAY, the gameplay itself is the MAIN REASON i kept playing this. I am buying a game, i prefer the gameplay to be funny and adictive and that is exactly what i got. Even trying a boss fight over and over again was fun! Because the combat system is wisely fun and addictive! (You can make 20+ different moves with 1 character alone) I had to repeat an (optional) boss fight like 7 times and i DID NOT GET BORED. What kind of game does that? Zestiria does... :)
The music is the 2nd best feature because it makes you enjoy parts like "trials" (some kind of dungeons) that in other JRPGs are boring, but in Zestiria they wisely added exciting/fantasy/danceable music in those "trials" - that small gesture made me enjoy it. The Soundtrack is memorable.
The characters are mainly generic and of course you can easily forget what the story was about, except: the final parts - the final 10% of the game is hella great!
This game is not worth $50, it's worth $20 or less -  if you want to spend $50 then buy Berseria. Why do i recomend Zestiria? Because as a RPG it's FUN, and i want to have FUN with a game. Also, because this was an experiment to evaluate Berseria at full price ($50) and Zestiria conviced me, Berseria is 10x times better! (Edit: Also, Berseria is a PREQUEL to Zestiria so playing both games is an excelent experience! I am at 50% Berseria i am enjoying so much so far... the link between games is wisely done!)

I'll admit, I wasn't really planning on getting this game; I actually haven't heard of this title before, but Eric and Dan told me to purchase it since it's had some nice devs and a work-in-progress history--
Let's just say that I haven't regretted playing this for one minute. It's a Gamecube loveletter nobody asked for, but it somehow achieves at grasping the nostalgia of great titles like Super Mario Sunshine. In some cases, this actually better represents Banjo-Kazooie better than Yooka-Laylee in some perspectives.
A Hat in Time started out as a one-man project. It soon evolved into a small team that wanted $30k to make the game (at one point, they doubted themselves and lowered it to $20k). After their initial goal, they soon raised over $250k to make the game with tons of bonuses coming in the future.
The music is also fantastic. I feel like every track fits in with each level and objective perfectly. I was blown away just by the sheer loading screen, and it just got better from there on out.
My only complaint would be the short-ish length (there's even a speedrun timer built into the game). If you really wanted to complete this game quickly, it's possible, but since it's had so much support on Kickstarter, the devs have promised more content: 2 new worlds, online multiplayer co-op, and they even put mod support despite being very busy with the game's recent launch (I'm very thankful I'm able to mod-play Trucy Wright).
I've heard nothing but great things about this game; the only """legit""" complaint I've heard from Gamespot is that it has "too much voice-acting" which 1.) you can turn off and 2.) there's an upgrade where you can make the characters mumble in a nonsense fashion like in the original Banjo-Kazooie.
I can tell the devs were very supportive of users that purchased this game. They honestly deserve every penny their way.
I am not disappointed, and if you were to purchase this game, neither would you.

This game is Early Access. Not a finished product.
This game is Pre-Alpha. Not beta. Not alpha. Pre-Alpha.
What that means is that some updates will be a step forward in some areas and a step back in others.
That means that this game is very sparse on content and polish.
That means that, for now, updates are going to be infrequent because they're mostly working on the game engine and physics engine and things like that. Frequent updates at this point would just mean buggy, glitchy updates. Once Pre-Alpha is over and the game moves into Alpha, then content updates (new cars, tracks, etc) will become more frequent.
This is Bugbear, who brought us some of my favorite racing games of all time. The game is already very fun with an already very functional multiplayer. It's still miles off of resembling its finished state, but I have faith that, in a year or so, this game is going to be spectacular, if given the proper time and funding. Which is why I purchased this game so early in development.
The only reason to purchase this right now is to support the development of this game. Buying this game and then criticizing it or refunding it for being incomplete is completely against the idea of Early Access and just hurts this game's chances of ever becoming something amazing.

I like it:  Simple, yet challenging.  I hold strategy/management/build-em-up games to a higher standard than I do combat-centric games, because it's easier for them to get boring if they're not well balanced.  This meets my high bar.
Banished could certainly use more depth & content before it's stamped 'complete', but the production quality is clearly there, as is the framework for the needed depth.  Most of what the game needs in order to be complete is already there in-part, it just needs fleshing out.
I applaud the developer for making the game difficult; a learning experience requiring you to think critically about interactions between seasons/climate conditions, your geographical advantages/disadvantages, and the way you've assigned your settlers.

I've always been a big fan of survival games, ever since way back in 2002 when I was playing the isometric desert island game Schiffbruch. I was thrilled with Minecraft game out, and not long after that, we had games like DayZ. By the time DayZ became popular, the market was flooded with survival games of various quality (usually of poor quality, see War Z). They also almost always contain zombies, and to me, the whole zombie thing is overdone and unoriginal.
When I look for a survival game, I look for a quality game where the devs actually care about the players and improving the game more and more over time. I look for a game that isn't rage-inducingly difficult, but not too easy and would get boring within a short period of time. Another important aspect of a survival game for me is the quality of its single player mode. I almost never, ever play online for various reasons (bandits, cheats, hackers, mods who don't seem to care). So the single player side of a game is very important for me. Unfortunately, a lot of survival games these days put the majority of the emphasis on the multiplayer experience, if they even design a single player mode.
The Long Dark is one such game that meets almost all of my qualifications for a survival game I would enjoy. It's unique, plays well, is challenging but not too easy, and is a completely single player experience. Your enemies aren't zombies in this one, but are instead hostile wildlife such as wolves, and even nature itself. You'll be going around trying to keep warm while also satiating your hunger and thirst levels, all the while being ever diligent to look out for wolves, which will mess you up big time if they get ahold of you. Something I like about the game is that it doesn't hold your hand, and doesn't put emphasis on combat. There's only one weapon right now, a hunting rifle, and good luck finding that. Even if you DO find one, ammo is very scarce, so you'll be either finding ways to avoid wolves, scare them off using flares, or making every bullet you have count.
My only complaints are as follows:
- The limited weaponry. It's fine to not focus on combat, but if I run out of flares, I'm pretty much screwed if a wolf comes out of nowhere and attacks me. I'm especially screwed if I don't have any bandages. It'd be great if there was at least some way to fend off a wolf without being taken down by one first, such as using the hatchet offensively, or using the knife during the quick time event with the wolf. Perhaps even bows and arrows would be great. Such things wouldn't put significantly more emphasis on the combat, but would help balance things out.
- Speaking of wolves, holy crap. Even when I'm extra careful and on the look out, I almost never see a wolf until it's too late. It's like they just pop up out of nowhere, and can spot you from a mile away unless you're carefully sneaking. I won't complain about how every wolf is always hostile, since I understand the devs wanting to put that in the game, but some minor variations would be nice. Maybe one out of every ten wolves or so won't immediately attack you, or will run away or something.
That's all I have for now. If you want a true single-player survival game that challenges your wits and resolve and perfects you through trial and struggle, get The Long Dark. It's currently in Alpha but there's every reason to believe the devs are constantly working on improving the game. So, if you have any suggestions, feel free to throw them at the devs.

Oftentimes a player enters a game and immediately notices the music--How it influences the way they play, encouraging them to jump in a lake of acid or hide in a nearby corner while a giant monster roams about sounding horribly constipated. Or, sometimes, a complete lack of it, of music or any atmosphere aside from the sounds of physics at work; And, occasionally, even that much is absent. The Long Dark...is a perfect blend of these themes. When you're desperately sprinting over brittle snow in the midst of a howling snowstorm from ravenous wolves, you might expect, as a gamer, horror or action music. Not this game. With the wind as loud as it is and the sound of your own breath like a foghorn, you dont know you're wolf bait until the furry bugger is pinning you to the snow, ripping your guts out to the tune of howling gales and shards of ice that sing as they bury themselves into your skin. It FEELS real, to the point where I shrieked when first attacked, and didnt stop screaming until the 'You've been killed" screen popped up a few seconds later. It's that fast, that brutal, that horrifically sudden--This is it, no turning back, start over and try again. But, asides from the start over part, that's how it is. And it is beautiful in how it does it, in portraying just how fragile we are to the whims of nature, in how just one change in the weather--A drop in temp by five degrees, for example--can end you as fast as a bullet would. I fondly remember Fluffy, that one wolf in the dam area, whom attacked out of the creaking shadows of my storm lantern almost silently--and then it was snarling, screaming, cursing, stabbing, and a bloody carcass beside me a split second later. I was bleeding, concussed, left hand sprained and couldnt see anything...I paused the game, got up, and turned every light in the house on, and then continued. This game masters the use of atmosphere, of when to use and not use lighting, sound, even just a simple shadow or play of the light to draw our eye and give us a friggin heart attack. In short: The Long Dark masters the use of atmosphere, suspense, and the fragility of the human condition versus Nature itself. I full recommend buying this game, if for nothing else than just the feel of it, the ecperience you get. Well, those of you with a heart condition...Ha! Good luck--You'll need it.

I'll put this out there right now- I LOVE this game. It's one of the more unique games I've played in quite a long time. Most of the complaints I see about this game revolve around the short campaign. Yes, it is short. It took me a bit under two hours to complete. However, that is not where the meat of the game lies. Where this game excels is in its delightfully hidden secrets, its punishing endless mode, and its, well, challenging, challenge modes.
SUPERHOT's gameplay is sublime. I've never really experienced anything like it. The time slow mechanic makes you feel simultaneously powerful, and fragile, as you know even one bullet can kill. Weaving in and among bullets, slicing them or shooting them out of the air, never gets old for me. Rushing an enemy, slicing his bullets out of the air before decapitating him, just makes you feel so awesome, especially when slicing them out of the air.
In terms of bugs and performance, I've encountered none. SUPERHOT runs at a rock-steady 60fps for me, and I've experienced very few bugs, although that may be because the devs fixed many in their day-one patch.
I do have a few issues with the game. I do wish the story mode had had a bit more to it, admittedly, and I wish there were more endless levels. Hopefully, the developers can integrate a map editor sometime later. One final quibble I have is that I wish that "real time" was a bit faster.
When you start looking for secrets, it becomes apparent just how much effort the developers put into these levels, as these secrets are hidden in the most conveluted of places, and encourage you to try to "break the level" so to speak. The endless modes are endless fun, just a pure expression of SUPERHOT's fantastic time-slowing gameplay, which is the real star of the show, not the story. The story was fun, and a good frame for the mechanics, but again, it is not the highlight. In addition to the main game and endless/challenge modes, this game also has many extras and secrets to find around its menu screen, from a fun little woodcutting game, to a forest fire simulator with ascii trees, to an .exe I still haven't figured out yet. While the story is short, the secrets and the extra modes will keep me playing SUPERHOT for  quite a long time to come.
Overall, if you are here for a long story mode, leave. But, if you are interested in a fantastic game with superb mechanics and many, many hours of challenging gameplay, SUPERHOT is for you. If not now, then next steam sale.

First off, this game is absolutely different from Dungeon Defenders 1. This isn't to say that it's a bad game, just don't go into it thinking you can pull the same stunts as the last game. You are not going to be afk farming in this game. You will be out on the battlefield holding down the fort and defending with all of you character abilities. Every original character feels really balanced and has a few roles they can fill. Gear hunting is great because there's actual game-changing abilities on the gear that can dictate how you are going to be playing the character. There's more game modes and difficulty options that can keep you entertained and on your toes. Also, they Devs really put an emphasis on "use more than one character or else you will fail". Like I said, you won't be sitting here building with a mage and afking wave after wave. In this game, it just isn't good enough. You need to find your combos and create/build characters that synergize. Have one character throwing oil while your mage is igniting them with his flame towers and stuff like that. It's a good twist. Not to mention there's no more stupid helicopters flying in and dropping ogres from random places on the map, or spiders that drop down from the sky out of nowhere to sabotage your builds. All in all, this is a solid game and I can definitely say it's a step in the right direction. Worth playing, hands down.
My only real complaint is the strength of the DLC characters. The summoner and EV2 just don't belong in this game at the power they're currently at. The summoner is a step above all of the original 4 in terms of straight dps output. It takes a lot for others to compete with his tower strength and utility. However, EV2 is just absurd. Without gear and using one ability, EV2 can solo campaign mode on normal at lvl 13. Then she can solo nightmare 3 at lvl 30. At level 50 with around 300 gear score, EV2 is easily putting out about 300k dps. A hunter with straight hero dmg and ability power is only pumping out around 50k, but it requires double the gear score. That being said, EV2 is reaching levels of damage that SHOULD NOT be attainable in this game! SHE NEEDS AN IMMEDIATE NERF. Proton beams allow her to sit on the crystal and shoot halfway across the map and clear lanes with ease. Levels that should be challenging are just turned into minor inconveniences with her on your squad. A Hat in Time is a 3D platforming collect-a-thon that evokes memories of games like Mario Sunshine, whilst also being able to assert an identity all of its own. The game is spread across just four main levels, but each of these is split into numerous lengthy acts and shorter side challenges. The focus of the game is very much old-school platforming, with little emphasis on combat or overarching plot (though each level has its own contained story to contextualise the platforming challenges).
I think that A Hat in Time is a charming, wonderful game that absolutely deserves to be considered alongside the greats like Mario and Spyro (PS1-era spyro, anyway :P). If you have any interest in platformers, you owe it to yourself to give this game a try. No problems I have with the game are significant enough to actually impact my enjoyment of it, and when it is good, it is simply excellent.

With 200+ hours on this account for this game; I'll make it quicker than I want it to be and I'll be providing a TL;DR at the bottom.
This game is beautiful. No, not just because of the graphics since that does not make a game great. I'll admit that being made in 2007: the graphics do hold very well to this very day. I'm talking about how the game feels to play, how much lore that you can unfold in this game and a very important point I will bring up later on.
The game itself is very easy to pick up and learn the basics such as what units do what, what your base does and many other things. As you progress through the story; you'll meet bonus objectives that you can complete for a different medal at the end (great for you completionists). The campaigns can have some very challenging moments for newer players but it will make you do what you're supposed to do: Come up with a strategy to win.
Notice that I said campaigns. You can play the GDI (Global Defense Initiative), NOD campaign and a short Scrin campaign. The last being unlocked once you have completed both of the other two campaigns.
This game supports free building (allowing you to build almost anywhere on the map except impassable terrain), there is no unit limit and there is some decent to good balance in this game.
Now, onto that point I mentioned earlier: It's the community. The C&C community has been part of me throughout my childhood and still is. People have constantly pushed out custom maps that have gamemodes for them such as No money, Art of Defense and Comp stomp. Command and Conquer Generals was my introduction to the community but not the series and I'm glad to see how much it has flourished.
If you wish to play this game online: Look into C&C Online. It's a community project that provides players to connect to their servers to play online so you can play with your friends or strangers. Downloading and installing custom maps is incredibly easy to do and can provide you more enjoyment in this game.
Now, here's another important piece of the community: Mods. There are tonnes of them that bring things from the older games or whatever the team behind the mod wanted. I've played dozens upon dozens of mods and because of that; this game has continued to be something I love to play and relax with.
TL;DR: I love this game and if you're wondering that if it is worth your time and money; I hope you do pick this amazing game up. This game has good replayability with custom maps and mods that you can find via Google.
Needless to say that this C&C fan will be giving this game a 10/10.

Limbo is a very relaxing puzzle adventure that should take you less than 4 hours to complete. It's a fine example of what I would call a worthy Indie title to play.
Despite the art work being nothing more than a silhouette, there is a lot of body language in the animations. There's also a lot of camera zooming in/out/panning smoothly and some nice background shadows all of which when combined create a peaceful yet creepy atmosphere. The creepy mood is also reflected within the music ambience and sound effects.
There is a bit of some ragdoll-like physics, but thankfully this doesn't take complete control over the gameplay (or I would go nuts). I think what I like the most is that throughout the game, there are some pretty crafty puzzles. Maybe throughout the game you'll encounter about four puzzles that might make you scratch your head for about 20 mins each, but not long enough to get you frustrated. The rest of the puzzles are easy but not made to make you feel like a fool. My rule of thumb is, if you seem to get stuck, always head backwards to find something to bypass the obstacle ahead.
Limbo is the perfect title for this game as well. Story-wise it's like you're living in a nightmare. There are some things going on. 1/3 of the game is like a spider chasing you. 1/3 feels like you walked into land owned by a nasty tribe. 1/3 is like a saw mill filled with so many death traps. Death seems to be a common occurrence and theme within this game.
As a kid, I never liked games where you are chased by an invincible enemy or unstoppable force. And the only direction you can travel is forward. I dunno, maybe I got traumatized as a kid when the planet Zebes blew up in Super Metroid and you had to run away from the lava. In Limbo, the unstoppable force happens to be the big♥♥♥♥♥spider! But it's not so hard and doesn't happen frequently. So that's still alright.
Unfortunately just like Hotline Miami, for some reason my Steam Achievements aren't being saved. I've had the "The End - Where Credit Is Due" achievement pop up for example, but it hasn't been recorded/saved to my profile. This is more of a Steam problem I would say.
All in all, I would recommend this game if you can get it on discount.

I fell in love with the dungeon defenders franchise with the first game.. It was a wonderful mix of genres and I just loved it.
Then in came Eternity, which had some improvements, but also made the game a bit less fun, due to the lack of local co-op (don't know if that was changed at a later date, but when I played, there was none).
Then in came Dungeon Defenders II, and I was excited.. Bought it as soon as I had the money for it and I liked it.. I liked it a lot.. Just like many other reviews have mentioned before, you got some premium money (gems) when you bought the game when it first came to early access, and back then there was no talks about any other uses for gems aside from costumes & more inventory space. So I spent my gems and kept playing..
Then there wasn't enough new content to keep me interested, felt like updates came far too seldom..
Then I heard that there'd be a new character coming, the abyss lord.. and I got all excited about the game again..
Started my game up & tried making a new character aaaand then I noticed that the character costs gems.. or "hero medals"..
That just broke my heart. The game series that I had loved and spent hundreds upon hundreds of hours playing, was just turning in to an early access f2p moneygrabber..
If you liked the original dungeon defenders, go play that instead. Or if you want to try this one, don't waste your money on it. I'm out 20€, and what I got to show for that, is a couple of outfits for my characters.. or I could've gotten a character unlocked, if I'd saved my gems for a year and a half.
It's unfortunate, but this game series got ruined with the switch to a free to play model.. sure.. It's free to play, unless you want to get a new character & not have to grind for day after day to get your hero medals to unlock said characters with.

Finally, a love letter that the GameCube deserves. A Hat in Time isn't ashamed of its roots as you'll probably see some direct inspirations. That being said, this game isn't a Frankenstein monster of Nintendo games and has its own original ideas that provide a whole experience for those who aren't nostalgic for the GameCube.
With Super Mario Sunshine's creative platforming, LOZ: Windwaker's energetic art style and Paper Mario TYD's charming comedic tone, A Hat in Time is a joy to play through.
It's not without its drawbacks though. The difficulty is usually interesting but safe. The platforming is never really challenging and the bosses can be annoying at times. The structure of the worlds can feel a bit restrictive at times as you can only collect a timepiece (star/jiggy equivalent) in its respective level. Disappointedly, the level design, for the most part, is linear. Also, the $30 price tag for 10-20 hours might be asking too much for some.
However, the positives absolutely steal the spotlight from the negatives.  While the difficulty of the platforming may not reach the height of classicly difficult games, it's never boring. Hat Kid is flat out fun to control. Double jumping, wall climbing, and diving to land tight jumps is satisfying. The different hats also grant unique ways tackle both platforming and combat. The worlds can be restrictive but they're always fun and diverse. The cartoonish colorful art style makes the worlds pop and compliment their unique gameplay arcs. While the experience is short, you can tell that the developers put a lot of effort and a world of heart into this game. It is rare to see that much endearing charm put into a game.
I'd recommend this game to people who love the GameCube or Colectathons. Even anyone who wants a charming experience might want to give it a look. A Hat in Time will make you smile.

Wreckfest is phenomenal. While in pre-alpha, it already plays better than 80 percent of full releases (or all Ubisoft games) and hits a chord with all of us who were brought up playing games like Ridge Racer and Burnout. Personally, the soft body physics this game presents are the type I always wanted in those video games, but they were heavily limited by the medium on which they were presented (N64, for example). So the games foundation is fantastic, it hits home with a slightly nostalgic feeling, it plays mostly fantastic (~80-100 FPS at 1440p on a single GTX 980) and it can only go up from here. It's for this reason Wreckfest is some of the most fun I've had on PC, which is saying something, since Wreckfest's sole premise is to crash into other players at high speeds - something you'd never do in real life (I hope).
However, the true icing on the cake is simply that the developers are very passionate about this game. When a dev is all about player experience and is willing to listen to community feedback to perfect a game, there's nothing I want more than their success. It's for this reason Bugbear is definitely in my goodbooks, and I'll be interested in all of their future endeavours.
Developers like Bugbear are great examples of why I came to PC, and I couldn't recommend Wreckfest enough.

Recently, I have been mulling over horror games made in RPG Maker. So when it was brought to me attention that there was an intriguing new title known as Stray Cat Crossing, I had to give it a look over. And while it is far from a complete horror experience, it is an exceptional case of RPG Maker horror done right. A signpost of sorts to guide the way.

Indie devs Jurlo and JetPackGone have created a wonderful, beautiful, creepy little game in Stray Cat Crossing. It goes in the right direction, but never quite reaches its destination.
After the first few minutes of Stray Cat Crossing, I was hooked. It grabs the player with some astoundingly pretty presentation. The graphics are reminiscent of GameBoy Advance-era 2D pixel art—charming if sparing animated brightly colored sprites set upon creative backdrops. The world of Stray Cat Crossing is bizarre and fascinating, a fantastical mixture of Silent Hill and Alice in Wonderland. It features creepy anthropomorphic creatures, Japanese Noh masks, freaky babies and theatrical interludes. The horror isn’t outright—the emphasis is placed more upon weirdness and subtle uncanniness. Jurlo’s music manages to bring calm and fright to the atmosphere, laying as it does somewhere between Akira Yamaoka and Yasunori Mitsuda.
Stray Cat Crossing places nearly all of its strength into its presentation and atmosphere, and boy does it ever perform this well. Beautiful graphics and sound-work, effective art direction and a flurry of inspirations that come together as something wholly unique. These facets make it worth the price of admission.
Unfortunately, this does not make the whole game. Not everyone places so much value on the presentation. The regrettable flipside of Stray Cat Crossing comes from its two greatest weaknesses: Un-engaging gameplay and a lazily vague plot.
The gameplay, by itself, is serviceable. Definitely a flaw, but not altogether bad. It simply suffers from never feeling cohesive. One doesn’t get the sense that there was much design philosophy behind the gameplay. There are occasional inventory puzzles. There is one chase sequence involving light platforming. There are some dialogue puzzles. Yet none of this ever seems to come together—they feel like challenge added for the sake of having a sense of gameplay, rather than the game organically developing its play.
I’m reminded of the Charnel House Trilogy, which the developer Ashton Raze has admitted did not lend itself well to gameplay. But the devs at Owl Cave Games managed to accept that and work around the game’s inherent shortcomings, doing what they could to make it engaging as a game despite not having much by way of challenge. Stray Cat Crossing‘s gameplay feels like a sequence of arbitrary puzzles—some challenging, others not so much—that in the grand scheme just don’t match the rest of the game. They may be filtered over with the game’s atmosphere (filling a fountain in a dark garden with the right amount of water in order to save a giant bug, only to inadvertently lead that bug to be eaten), but they don’t feel like they fit. Puzzles in Stray Cat Crossing are always obstacles. They simply never feel like progress.
In addition to this, some of the puzzles are just plain bad. The horrendously repetitive final act involves exchanging various items with people in order to gain the script to a play, allowing the play to finish and the game the move forward. Only one must perform the previous scenes of the play multiple times in order to speak to the correct people and obtain the right items. It is essentially one large, monotonous fetch quest, quite unwelcome at any point in a game but especially right at the end.
Then we come to the story. Now, Stray Cat Crossing‘s story is by no means bad. In fact there is a lot to like about it. It touches on themes of childhood, jealousy, loss and regret. But its way of being told really distances the player from these themes, leaving them with neither a solid narrative nor a sympathetic character to connect to. Rather we get a quirky cast of one-dimensional creatures and a few curious but ultimately nondescript humans.
The vague story in indie games has been bugging me for a while now. Perhaps popularized by Limbo, one of the few to actually perform it right, a great deal of indie games have been turning to player interpretation narratives. In only a few isolated cases is the vagueness ever a complement to the overall game. Limbo, for instance, works because it never makes any attempt to really tell a complex story—it only asks that the player experience this weird German expressionist-inspired journey. Another example, Lone Survivor, meanwhile gets a pass because it is a conscious experimentation in dream logic. Stray Cat Crossing doesn’t have these excuses. The execution of the story, as a result, comes off as lazily constructed—a nonlinear sequence of events assembled as a means to set the aforementioned great atmosphere together. They could have combined much more smoothly, but this lack of synchronicity between them causes the story to simply drag the atmosphere down.
Thus we have the three pillars of Stray Cat Crossing—atmosphere, gameplay, narrative—and only one is stable. These pillars rely on each other to hold the game up, but Stray Cat Crossing put all its weight on one. And while it doesn’t quite cause the whole game to collapse, the strain definitely pushes the overall experience down a bit.
I like a lot about Stray Cat Crossing, don’t get me wrong. It just doesn’t hold up as a game on its own. If Jurlo and JetPackGone were to team up again for something more cohesively designed, that would be absolutely worth checking out.

I fell in love with the dungeon defenders franchise with the first game.. It was a wonderful mix of genres and I just loved it.
Then in came Eternity, which had some improvements, but also made the game a bit less fun, due to the lack of local co-op (don't know if that was changed at a later date, but when I played, there was none).
Then in came Dungeon Defenders II, and I was excited.. Bought it as soon as I had the money for it and I liked it.. I liked it a lot.. Just like many other reviews have mentioned before, you got some premium money (gems) when you bought the game when it first came to early access, and back then there was no talks about any other uses for gems aside from costumes & more inventory space. So I spent my gems and kept playing..
Then there wasn't enough new content to keep me interested, felt like updates came far too seldom..
Then I heard that there'd be a new character coming, the abyss lord.. and I got all excited about the game again..
Started my game up & tried making a new character aaaand then I noticed that the character costs gems.. or "hero medals"..
That just broke my heart. The game series that I had loved and spent hundreds upon hundreds of hours playing, was just turning in to an early access f2p moneygrabber..
If you liked the original dungeon defenders, go play that instead. Or if you want to try this one, don't waste your money on it. I'm out 20€, and what I got to show for that, is a couple of outfits for my characters.. or I could've gotten a character unlocked, if I'd saved my gems for a year and a half.
It's unfortunate, but this game series got ruined with the switch to a free to play model.. sure.. It's free to play, unless you want to get a new character & not have to grind for day after day to get your hero medals to unlock said characters with.

I stuck with this game for over a year and during that time I was very active on the steam forums. After 600+ hours of play, I became very familiar with the direction of the game and how the devs operate.
It's a grind, and that's all there is to it.
The game changed many times to just add more grind and RNG. It's impressively worse than it was when it was when it started early access.
Much like all awful F2P, the devs don't really care if the game is fun, they just want you to be stuck grinding.
Note: I could go into much more detail (and have done so before), but I'll try to keep it short because otherwise it'd excessively too long for anyone to read.
The devs don't prioritize fixing the game.
Bugs can linger around for months or years. There's even things that are clearly broken that they'll stubbornly label as "Working as intended" to not deal with it.
The main reason I gave up on this game is because the devs have no respect for the time the players put into the game.
A certain update (campaign revamp update) denied a bonus to veteran players with no real excuse. And a later update (trials update) flat out removed items that the players paid for with their ingame currency. Said currency was not refunded, and instead you were given a really uneven compensation with a worthless inferior currency.
Both were situations that could had been VERY easily solved with very few lines of SQL. So we have to conclude they did this intentionally.
They don't care.
Probably to prevent cheating, the game runs on the server. Your client merely sends instructions to the server.
Like many other games that run like this, it's not good. You're at the mercy of the server's connection (which aren't great), making you slide around all over the place and into ravines.
At some point I had developed an aversion to moving because I felt that if I did I would die, that's how bad it'd get.
On Xmas 2016, they introduced a new enemy by surprise: a siege roller. This enemy wasn't invincible, but was riddled with bugs and caused a ton of issues.
They put that into the game, and went on vacation the next day. Not that it matters because once they got back, they still didn't fix it til 2+ months later.
On another update, the devs made poison dart towers (PDTs) extremely overpowered. a week or 2 later, they nerfed them, but they still remained the most powerful defense in the entire game, trivializing every map/difficulty for over 8 months.
This was reported in playtesting, and several times on the bug report site (the poison from PDTs would stack twice for some reason), and they just let it ride like that.
"working as intended".
First few hours playing this game are fun, I'm not even going to deny that, but you will quickly enter the unreasonable grind. I'm not talking about a month of grinding, not even 2, I'm talking half a year to even get anywhere.
I can't stress enough that the game is about the grind.
I'm not saying a game can't be fun if you have to grind anything, I'm saying that

A Hat in Time is a 3D platforming collect-a-thon that evokes memories of games like Mario Sunshine, whilst also being able to assert an identity all of its own. The game is spread across just four main levels, but each of these is split into numerous lengthy acts and shorter side challenges. The focus of the game is very much old-school platforming, with little emphasis on combat or overarching plot (though each level has its own contained story to contextualise the platforming challenges).
I think that A Hat in Time is a charming, wonderful game that absolutely deserves to be considered alongside the greats like Mario and Spyro (PS1-era spyro, anyway :P). If you have any interest in platformers, you owe it to yourself to give this game a try. No problems I have with the game are significant enough to actually impact my enjoyment of it, and when it is good, it is simply excellent.

A fantastic game that I would highly recommend to practically everyone; I was smiling through many parts of this game thanks to its designs, music, and varying gameplay. It's not super technical, the graphics aren't the best and the platforming controls can be frustrating at times, especially when trying to make certain jumps and not all the music is good; some of its wears after a while. While the graphics aren't the greatest, they don't need to be; this game does very well with its designs to the point that I'd say they might even be timeless and hold up years later, which in my opinion is much better than trying to display thousands of different shades of brown. The game has five worlds, but each one plays very differently from the last, quality over quantity. The story is also quite good, never bothering to sit the player down and explain everything to you, rather you are left to your own devices and can figure stuff out on your own, it left me with a sense of wonder about the locations in the game. I managed to complete the game in 13 hours, but I enjoyed every hour of it and wish there was more, but that's what a good game does: leaves you wanting more.

This is a psychological art piece.  If you enjoy reviewing games, or talking about what games mean, you may enjoy this.  This is not a funny game.  I believe the main point is to make you feel a certain way, and then have a twist to make you feel some other thing.  Somewhat like a psychological-thriller movie, but more like listening to critics explain a completely red canvas in an art museum.  If you're looking for that kind of experince, you should get this game.
If you will be offended that there are only two hours of content, then you should not get this game.  (You should stop going to the movies too.)  But even though I don't enjoy the feeling this game left me to consider, I appreciate that this game exists.  Art doesn't need to make you feel happy, but just feel something.  And therefore I believe it does deserve the $10 I paid for it.
Why did I not enjoy this game, but still recommend it?  Because I thought the narrator was too pretentious.  And I didn't enjoy the ending because I felt cheated.  But I do enjoy reading people analyzing this game in the same way that the narrator analyazes the games within the game.  And I'd love more games like this to exist than clones of Minecraft, Bejeweled, or another zombie game.

Nightshade is, without question or doubt, my favorite game in this genre. Over the past year, I think I've played the bulk of the (localized) big hitters of otome: Amnesia, Hakuoki, a host of other Idea Factory / Otomate offerings on Vita (Norn9, Code Realize, Period Cube, Collar Malice, Bad Apple Wars, etc). I've played indie projects-- Cinderella Phenomenon, Cinders, Rose of Winter, Hustle Cat, Hatoful Boyfriend. Many I liked; some I loathed (Ozmafia!, lookin' at you). Nightshade, in my opinion, stands apart from them all, particularly for its well-developed and motivated characters, intelligently supported (if still unapologetically soapy) plot, lovely, lovely art, and inoffensive, even pleasant, sound design.
More detail:
To start, I really appreciate the protagonist, Enju. By necessity, the player character in the majority of romantic visual novels is a cypher best, if not solely, described as a Nice Girl. She wishes to avoid making waves, she wants to please everyone, she's shy but loves her friends: she is a perfectly normal, extremely contrived, HGTV nondescript beige intended for any player to step into and feel more or less at home. Moreover, to work through setting up the story's exposition, she must be oddly unfamiliar with the world she inhabits, unable to fend for herself (not to say incompetent, but...), and generally know as little as possible about anything. This narrative ignorance is even more crucial in the context of the character's relationships: to maximize the story's romantic arc, she must be in some conflict with the object of her affection, and since she's a Nice Girl, that restriction means conflict must usually come from her exaggerated modesty and shyness, and/or the gentleman's being Not Nice. Suffice to say: there's a narrative reason for all the bouts of convenient amnesia in these games, and there's likewise a reason for those tsundere lads that make Mr. Fitzwilliam Darcy look like a sweet social butterfly.
Enju is unquestionably a Nice Girl. But here's the thing that Nightshade does best, in part because I rarely see it done anywhere else: while Enju bears a superficial resemblance to her sisters in the genre, unlike many of them, she is a well-developed character with reasoned basis for those traits. Instead of incompetent, she is inexperienced; instead of merely ignorant, she is sheltered; instead of vague helplessness, she is tripped up by her own insecurities. That might sound like splitting hairs, until you are asked to find the trait relatable-- I'd argue that there's hope for a strong arc in a flawed character that is inexperienced, sheltered, and insecure, thrust into a harsh world beyond their ken; an incompetent, ignorant, and helpless character has a more bleak outlook, and I would consider them less "flawed" than flat and underdeveloped. Enju feels like a person, and if her starting point is inauspicious, she has a good distance to travel on her journey in character as much as geography.
This extends to every part of the writing, character and narrative both. No one in this game is perfect. The best shinobi of all time isn't going to have the best social skills; the cleverest flirt isn't going to be right in each assessment; that childhood friend that sets out to protect you from anything and everything bad is really doing you a disservice. This isn't a game that relies on a deus ex machina to save the day (mostly), and it doesn't assume that romance is summarized by a nice kiss at the end of a story-long misunderstanding: these characters have to get to know one another, develop trust, and we, the player, have to care about it.
To that end, the story is easy to follow, and everyone has a full motive when they take an action. There's no weird technology from the future that's really the past, no vampires, no magical girls, no amnesia. There's death in this game, and it has heft and consequences,
. Depending on who Enju is running with, tragedy may well lace even an otherwise officially "happy" ending. But none of the drama feels like it's just for show here, to me: when you take the characters given-- flawed individuals with histories that extend beyond the start of the game and desires that exist outside of their pants-- and put them into the narrative, what follows are the consequences of specific personalities, with different motives, morality, values, and abilities, tested in specific ways. No route is wrong, no route is ‘golden’. Some routes, friends die; in some, the bad guy gets away.
In sum: Nightshade is that rare, special otome that is complex in a good way, with a layered but tidy plot and well developed characters, not excluding the player character. The romance and the plot are balanced and pleasantly nuanced. It isn't the greatest love story ever told, but I'd gladly argue it's the best I've found in this medium.

Where to begin, where to begin... If only I had a guide for where to begin to describe this game.
I watched my friend play this game the other day, and saw him sit, riveted to his seat, as he stared blankly at this oh so simple game. As he pulled off his headphones, he simply shook his head and told me to get the game.
After it finished downloading, I sat down and began. It started out as a simple game, with Davey yet again weaving his subtle gaming magic into the dialogue.
Little could I have known how deeply into my very soul these threads were being woven.
The game took but a mere 84 minutes to complete, looking at all the content held within.
But the game took a toll on my poor, suceptible heart. As I followed in my friend's path, and removed my headphones, I sat, weeping, in my chair. The Beginner's Guide brought into questioning every friendship, relationship, and familiial tie I have ever known, and shattered me to my core.
On the simple topic of mechanics, it is a simple puzzle game, and by simple I mean it in the most literal sense of the word. You're truly playing this game for the experience, similar to playing the Stanley parable.
Davey remains one of my favorite game designers, ever since his beautiful work on the Stanley Parable, and this game just goes to show that it's the simple things in life that hit us the hardest.
P.S. Davey, I would like an apology for making me cry for a solid ten-twenty minutes.

Bioshock could rightfully be considered a piece of art and an excellent game at the same time. The game's graphical style is much more colorful than other would-be horror games. Fits it like a glove, really. And Jack, while mute for most of the game, is an enjoyable character to play, even though he doesn't have that much of a personality. On the gameplay side, it's all gone bananas, with setting people on fire with a flick of your fingers, or playing tennis with grenades and Telekinesis. While this may sound crazy in theory, the game takes itself seriously, and succeeds in creating a pressing athmosphere, thanks to the primary element of the game, which is water.  It creates this feeling of isolation and loneliness, as you are one of the few sane humans remaining in the underwater 1950s-inspired dystopia, Rapture. There's quite a bit of psychology to the game, as well, mainly idealism, or so I heard. Really though, you don't need to think that deep in order to enjoy this masterpiece. Challenging, beautiful and rewarding. You'd be doing yourself one heck of a favor by buying it.

The story is a bit atypical of an otoge- bittersweet, and backed by war and monarchy. Even for some of the routes, the events through the happy ending could make a grown man cry. Usually, an otoge would also have quite a predictable storyline, and in this case, there were some elements that were expected, but there were also so many twists that just slapped me across the face with no warning what so ever. At the same time, looking back, those twists were tied together nicely with the premise before.
There were, however, flaws in the composition of the story. The pace sometimes felt a bit too fast, or sometimes it felt like they were including unecessary scenes (honestly, there was way to much time spent on exagerating how the MC is a nice, merciful human). The characters (ahem- apart from Enju-) are well developed and extremely human. I honestly would pay for a DLC or sth with Kyara and Ieyasu as playable routes. Banished is a very fun, relaxing game to play in your spare time. In this game, you build an settlement for people and you have to manage resources and construct buildings to advance the progression of building a city. Citizens will become hungry if there is no food, so food is one of the main prioirities to keep a steady flow of. Then, the popluation. People die of old age in the game which can lead to you having no populaiton within your town. Tools also play a major part in the game. The are used by the citizens to collect resources and construct buildings so a blacksmith is another top priority. It can get very cold during the winter, so the citizens will need firewood to keep them warm. Woodcutters are required in order to make firewood to keep the citizens warm. Personaly, I haven't experienced any deaths from Hypothermia so I can't tell you how long you have until a citizen passes out. Education. You can also manage education within your village, although this isn't one of the top priorities, but educated citizens perform their jobs better than uneducated citizens.
Overall, this is a good game. However, it may require you to invest some of your time to fully understand the game and how to grow from 5 families to 500 families.

Minutes after I installed the game, recalling a game called "A Dark Room" and thinking that this game might be simmilar, I opened the game and immediately got sucked in by the simple and yet creative art style and dark atomsphere of the game.
In this story, as written in the description, you will assume the role of a farmer that is a rather average man trying to make his living out of his farm which has become the victim of a plague that attacked the land. From this point, what happenes is completely up to you. You will be have to choose what to do from the very beggining.
You'll probably die though, more than once, but it's all worth it.
Another thing that adds to the atmosphere of the game is the minimal sound effects. While you can't say that this game is loud or that it has an amazing soundtrack you can definitely say that the sounds effects give from time to time a chilling sensation.
There are two things that have bothered me, though: The UI- which isnt too complicated to use but could be more convenient- and the font of the text in the game- something which is really not a deal breaker but just felt a bit too casual to me.
However, these disadvantages take very little away from the thrilling expirence that this short game offers you for no price at all.
One last thing I'd like to point out is that a person could play this game even if he can't read as there is an option for a self-voicing mode. :D

Very promising game, very well polished for the Early Access, active developer, exciting direction.
Things that I liked:
- Very thorough survival system based on basic caloric needs, harvesting materials, staying warm, etc.
- Rich and detailed world, stylized graphics but very good visual direction.
- Characters are voiced by awesome Mark Meer and Jennifer Hale. That alone is worth an upvote.
- It's incredibly fun to explore, move from place to place, discover new locations, loot and scavenge while trying to stay alive.
- Very high quality for Early Access alpha. I haven't encountered any obvious bugs yet, all the systems work, there's a variety of items, areas and activities.
Things that I hope to see improved:
- More logical crafting. You don't need a crafting table to attach a line to a hook. You don't need to look for guts to use as a rope when you have three pairs of extra shoelaces.
- More early game direction. Early game relies too much on knowing map and having good luck with item spawns. It's almost impossible to survive without knowing right away where to go.
- Save system. Right now game forces all players into "hardcore" mode where your save gets deleted when you die. I feel like it should be an option rather than a requirement, especially considering how easy it is to simply create backup saves out of game.
- Wolves feel like placeholder. Struggle mechanic doesn't feel like it fits in the game, wolves don't behave like wolves, it feels like they are used purely as a game mechanism to discourage exploration. There's something about the dark allure, twisted characters, and poetical sense of realisation that will completely entrance you as you play. I'll keep this review short and sweet, as not to give too much away, for I believe its the  mystery that truly immerses you into this world. If you're a fan of the darker works of Tim Burton, Hideo Kojima, Neil Gaiman or Studio Ghibli, then I hope you'll take my word in faith and purchase this game without reading too much about it.
It was a game I played from start to finish- that rare feeling of wanting to play it all at once, though you know you shouldn't or it will all be over too soon (and I'll admit I got no sleep last night because of it). The graphics are beautiful, the art pulls inspiration from all corners of the world, the music is perfect and it has a glistening array of eccentric characters.
That's not to say it's not without fault. Admittedly I struggled for great lengths of time on some of the puzzles, and even had to look to walkthroughts. At one point it got very repetitive, but honestly I can only say that added to my immersion, a true sense of desperation as you get trapped in this house of horrors.
On the surface it's polished, well written and exciting, though it truly is a three dimensional game (metaphorically, pardon the pun) its exploration of the darker side of the human psyche left me wanting to play it again from a new perspective.
I can only say- for £1.99 this game is a complete steal. I'm awestruck.

There's a surprising number of RPG Maker horror games, if you've never looked. Most ditch the RPG trappings entirely in favor of a minimalist retro-2D walking simulator style, and most of those tend to be boring or poorly designed. But every once in awhile you'll find a gem in the pile, and Stray Cat Crossing is one of those gems.
Your lovingly-rendered character happens across a small girl wandering the road at night. The girl, Cat, runs off with your treasured scarf and you follow her all the way home like the worst sort of creeper just to get it back. Don't feel bad, though, because her house is full of all kinds of nightmare beings. SCC is a surreal adventure game through symbolic realms of guilt and loss, expressed in a magnificently detailed and colorful art style. Characters are memorable, environments are vivid, and the atmosphere is excellent.
The sound design is on point as well, but the real stand-outs are the bizarre video clips the game hits you with periodically. Every once in awhile, you'll be interrupted by a short scene that looks cut from the VHS tape in The Ring. These sequences are incredibly jarring and effective. I am not a fan of jumpscares in the least, but these felt well thought-out and earned. They add immeasurably to the atmosphere and help hint at future story beats, as well.
The story itself is quite good, managing to dabble heavily in symbolism and moralizing without falling into the traps other games often do. There's nothing forced or heavy-handed about the plot developments, and you tend to catch up with things as your tight-lipped protagonist does. The one place the game stumbles is in the puzzles, which start off strong and clever but end on some sour notes. The final sequence is honestly quite clever as well, but in a way that's not actually very fun to get through. It comes at the very end, though, so at that point there's no reason not to power through for the satisfying finale.
You'll finish the game in two hours or so, which is perfectly fine considering the price. They're a tense and emotional two hours that would be worth experiencing just for the cast and atmosphere. Luckily, the whole game pulls together to form something I can whole-heartedly recommend.

First of all, Tales of Zestiria is not a 'bad' game. As you can see from the generally positive reviews here on Steam, it's definitely possible that you might enjoy it. But as both an avid JRPG and Tales fan, there were just too many things I didn't like about it, things which disappointed me and made it a mediocre experience at best. And a lot of wasted potential.
Let's talk about the good parts first, though, like the battle system. Probably being Zestiria's highlight, it feels smooth, engaging and has tons of visual effects going on - it's fun. Tales never seems to fail on that.
The soundtrack often gets a lot of praise, but I don't think it's that great. Especially the music during the shepherd trials often gets mentioned, and yes, those tracks sound awesome, but there's a strangely big quality gap between them and the rest.
The characters are a mixed bag, but generally most of them are likable and have at least some personality. Character development is another story though.
And that's about everything positive for Tales of Zestiria I can think of. Now, there are a few big issues I have with this game and they all intertwine in the end.
- The story. I don't usually say such things, but in my opinion it's just plain bad. It could have been an intriguing plot about politics, religion, how the figure of the shepherd fits into this world and gets drawn into the schemes of powerful people, and how great a burden all of it must be for a young man like Sorey. Now, Zestiria TRIES at all these things several times, but fails miserably. In the end, it's nothing more than "I want to travel the world and defeat evil", but even that would be okay, IF Sorey had any character development. But that's not the case. Basically, his personality can be broken done into two sentences: "I want to help everyone, no matter how stupid or illogical it may be!" and "I couldn't help / protect anyone!" - Seriously, that's how he acts in the beginning, that's how he acts after thirty hours of adventuring. An incredibly boring protagonist for an incredibly boring plot. They wasted so much potential here, it's unbelievable.
- The map / dungeon design. While the overworld areas are too big, empty and ugly, the dungeons are always laid out like a maze. If there are any puzzles, they're either very simple or just annoying. The discovery points are a cool idea, but there's far too few of them to actually make the lifeless landscape any more interesting. That aside, after some hours not even searching for treasure chests feels motivating anymore, since there's simply too much junk in them. Big part of this problem originates from the...
- Item Crafting System. This is, besides the story, the second huge problem I have with Zestiria. So, what you can basically do is fuse items of the same name together, which creates a stronger version of that item with better stats probably new skills. There are lots of different skills that, combined with each other, can strengthen or create effects. Sounds cool. On the paper, that is.
Because in the end, this system does only two things: First, it annoys and probably confuses 'normal' players, who don't want to read skill spreadsheets to actually understand what's going on, especially since the game does a bad job explaining about it. Second, it's just demotivating to see and find the same equipment over and over again. Even more so once you realize that even a +10 weapon probably has worse (damage) stats than a new one you can buy in the next town. And, at least on normal difficulty, the upgraded weapons' buffs never matter. So, why even bother? Why search for loot if 90% of the time it's just unrewarding? .. Why explore anything in the first place?
Honestly, I can't think of any good reason to play Tales of Zestiria. It's just an incredibly boring and generic game. The story, the maps, even the items. If it wasn't for the battle system, I would've quit after a few hours, but I kept going on and hoped it might become more interesting. Well, it didn't. I think every Tales game of the past years is better than this one. But as I said in the beginning, many people seem to have enjoyed Zestiria, and all of this is just my opinion. But I believe it is fair to say that if you're looking for an all-around well-made JRPG ... you should probably look somewhere else.

This was my first Tales game- and honestly I'm not too impressed. I am mixed though.
Graphics:
- I'm shocked to see that this was a 2015 release-date game. There is an odd mix of decent modeling/textures, and then downright awful 'you had the polycount to fix that' and 'that is one stretched texture there my guy'.
-I loved the ability to dress my characters in stupid clothes. The official Shepard Dress code was the ten gallon hat and shades. Hilarious- but I saw that clipping. And it was. Distracting.
-Repetitive/Boring environments. Fields. A river. Up a mountain. The coolest moment for me so far was the museum.  Is there better? I dunno- only played 17ish hours.
Gameplay:
-Made the wrong decision of buying PC port, the controls are the balls for both keyboard and controller (DS4)
- Combat was also balls, and because of the above, was reduced to a lot of button mashing with occational directional arrow pressing. Frustrating, and even after I thought I had it, I'd get wiped by a boss. (Alt. I just suck.)
Charm:
- Considering this game is part combat part story, its already falling half-short. As for its story, I'd say it was the only thing keeping me playing.
- Cliche hero story, cliche hero characters. So much it hurt, and I loved it. Even if the tropes were borderline annoying, it softened you to the characters. Sometimes you wanted hug'em, other times, throttle them.
- That opening set me up. It was way more intense and dramatic than what I felt. Where was my 'public beginning to shun Sorey' like his fire friend said? Is it further in? God dammit. It just felt too perfect. Not enough conflict for our protagonist aside from his 'I don't wanna hurt people' spiel which. Spoiler, happens anyway. Did we get inner turmoil? Not within 17ish hours aside from a one line 'I'm conflicted'.
- The set-up of being a badass sword Shepard who could fuse with my friends got my inner weeb goin. Feed the beast. But I still felt distant from the characters and story. I wish you could choose the outcome more- maybe wane a bit from the path of perfect hero.
All in all, its not a bad game but its not a good one either. If you are buying for PC like I did, wait for the sale. Its story and characters, unfortunatly, are forgettable. After playing it twice, I haven't bothered to play again since. I'm sure it gets better and that it has its positive ratings for a good reason, however, even its promise of long gameplay and team-dressup didn't weigh this Tales in my favor.

PC port runs like a dream (even well optimized for weaker computers), with the nice touch of a chromatic aberration slider (though this is one of the few games I think works well with CA, as it does fit the aesthetic of an analog TV or a VHS well, but it's nice to have the option to change the intensity/turn it off). The style of the game just oozes quality, with beautiful hand-drawn animation, catchy music that fits the 1930s era cartoon style the game emulates. The game chooses to run at 60fps, a creative liberty which does make the animation all at once not quite fit the aesthetic but also looks gorgeous with the added frames in motion and greatly helps the fluid gameplay.
It's challenging, but fair. The mechanics are completely solid and responsive, as well as the threats are well telegraphed, which helps that you never really feel it's the controls which make you die rather than your ability. The bosses are creative, memorable, and fun (all with multiple stages) and often are somewhat tasks of dealing with multiple threats at once. There's some platforming run-and-gun levels, and it may take some people used to Mario and the like to un-teach themselves to not jump on enemies heads, but those who were fans of Contra, Gunstar Heroes, etc., should immediately feel at home.
Seriously, this is a quality video game that perfectly encapsulates the addicting 'one more go' mentality, and the style, charm, solid mechanics, and fairness in the challenge all make it so instead of frustrating it often is addictingly fun. It truly feels like they hit the nail on the head to accomplish everything they wanted to with this title, and I fully recommend it.

This was an easy buy for me based on how much I loved The Stanley Parable.
While The Stanley Parable was a game about games, The Beginner's Guide is an art about art. As such, it's fundamentally less interactive, far more pretentious, and ultimately less interesting.
It develops and opens up as you play, and there is character development (surprinsingly). There are interesting ideas and themes present. I'm sure I'll spend some time thinking about it later. But despite being moody and emotional, it fails to connect because the player is an observer, not a participant in anything of consequence.
It's not terrible, it's not long, and it's not expensive, so if you're interested in moody naval gazing, it's worth playing through. But if you're not seriously into overtly meta ruminations on the nature of expression, you're not going to find anything great.
It was a positive surprise!

Finally, a love letter that the GameCube deserves. A Hat in Time isn't ashamed of its roots as you'll probably see some direct inspirations. That being said, this game isn't a Frankenstein monster of Nintendo games and has its own original ideas that provide a whole experience for those who aren't nostalgic for the GameCube.
With Super Mario Sunshine's creative platforming, LOZ: Windwaker's energetic art style and Paper Mario TYD's charming comedic tone, A Hat in Time is a joy to play through.
It's not without its drawbacks though. The difficulty is usually interesting but safe. The platforming is never really challenging and the bosses can be annoying at times. The structure of the worlds can feel a bit restrictive at times as you can only collect a timepiece (star/jiggy equivalent) in its respective level. Disappointedly, the level design, for the most part, is linear. Also, the $30 price tag for 10-20 hours might be asking too much for some.
However, the positives absolutely steal the spotlight from the negatives.  While the difficulty of the platforming may not reach the height of classicly difficult games, it's never boring. Hat Kid is flat out fun to control. Double jumping, wall climbing, and diving to land tight jumps is satisfying. The different hats also grant unique ways tackle both platforming and combat. The worlds can be restrictive but they're always fun and diverse. The cartoonish colorful art style makes the worlds pop and compliment their unique gameplay arcs. While the experience is short, you can tell that the developers put a lot of effort and a world of heart into this game. It is rare to see that much endearing charm put into a game.
I'd recommend this game to people who love the GameCube or Colectathons. Even anyone who wants a charming experience might want to give it a look. A Hat in Time will make you smile.

​Where to start...
Firstly, I think it has to be said that 'The Beginner's Guide' is not a game. And you would be mistaken to think that it's 'not a game' just like 'The Stanley's Parable'. On that game you have choices and decisions. The Beginner's Guide does not have any of that. It is purely narrative, and the 'gameplay' is purely linear.
What I would say, is that this is actually an Experience. An interative one for sure, but an experience using visual and narative aid. In fact, this would make a great VR experience as you can relax and take on the sight. It's almost like a documentary that you, as the player, can get involved in although you cannot change your path nor the outcome.
As for the content...
I had a hard time finishing it even though it doesn't last very long. And since it is a narrative only game, there is no replay value. I think I had a hard time finishing it because the topic discussed is very depressing. Where else The Stanley's Parable is full of humour and joy, The Beginner's Guide is more thoughtful, melancholy, and filled with sadness.
I'm not entirely sure what the game is trying to say, what thoughts it's suppose to evoke, or whether it even had a message or any meaning what so ever. Especially if the narrative is not based on reality, and that it might not be true.
I would have a hard time recommending this game even though I loved The Stanley's Parable. It's not a game, so the player must prepare for that. It's thought provoking, but it lacks integrity and strength in what it is trying to say, if anything at all. It's not clever nor is it anything new. There is nothing for you to find out, nothing for you to really solve, nothing is hidden. It just doesn't really connect with me, and if anyone can relate to the game - maybe that says more about me and it does about them.
In the end, it just left me kind of empty...
