Personal ramblings:
I can’t get this game out of my head.
I’m listening to the OST non-stop and I can’t stop thinking about it.
It’s really, truly, one of the best otome games out there.
And I’m not just talking in terms of plot or characters. I’m talking in terms of everything. The combination of everything together was simply divine.
I didn’t think it would hit be in the feels - both happy and sad - as much as it has, but it surpassed it all.
This game has been on my Steam wishlist for a while until a few days ago when I decided to play it on a whim.
I’m so glad I did because it took my breathe away.
This game is a Japanese PSvita game that is now available in both English and Japanese on Steam.
I HIGHLY recommend you play it.
The common route may be a bit slow-paced, but trust me. Once you get into the individual routes you’re in for the shock - and happiness - of your life.
I’m going to break it into categories to try to make some more sense about how fantastic this game is.
So… whether you’ve played it or not, I hope you enjoy (:
The Plot:
The story follows our heroine, Enju (name can be changed but otherwise will be voiced) - born in the union between two clans. Being the leader’s daughter, she’s the princess of her village. But she’s also a shinobi (Ninja). Or at least, she desperately wants to be.
There’s nothing Enju wants more than prove her worth to her village.
When our story begins, she finally gets her chance. She, along with a few of her friends, are to be set on a mission in the city of Kyo.
But things are not what they seem. And something terrible hides in the shadows.
Who will Enju become? And who will she choose to go on this journey with her?
The common route starts slow and steady with a few action-scenes in between. It consists on 4 chapters. The choices you make during those times will decide which guy you’ll end up with.
The individual routes are fast-paced and very… shocking. You’ll laugh, you’ll cry, you’ll love, you’ll feel. For everyone in this game.
I suggest you save the game in the beginning of each new chapter, as well as Quick save whenever presented with a choice in case you haven’t chosen the “right” one and want to go back to change it.
You’ll know you made the “right” choice when you see glowing flowers in front of your chosen character.
In the common route, the character you earn most affection (flowers) with is the one you’ll end up with.
The plot of this game sounds easy-enough, but trust me when I say you will not… see what’s coming.
Prepare yourselves.
The Characters:
Hanzo: The strongest shinobi of his time. Believes in following the mission, no matter what. Is harsh, yet kind. Is serious, yet boyish. Gives you space to grow into yourself, yet is there whenever you need him.
My thoughts: Hnazo was the best route of this game. And one of the best characters I’ve ever seen in otome games.
I had a feeling he was going to be a good one, I just had no idea he was going to blow me away.
They are, simply put, the best for each other. In so many ways.
Kuroyuki: The childhood friend you haven’t seen in 8 years. He’s a tease, he’s funny, he’s forward, he’s endearing. But is he the same boy you used to know? And what exactly happened to him during those 8 long years?
My thoughts: Kuroyuki’s route was… pretty dark. In terms of character-development and romance. That being said - I ended up falling for him (probably against my better judgment).
i can’t say anything more here due to spoilers, but… just know you may experience annoyance, anger, but warm and fuzzy feelings at the end.
Playing him after Hanzo may cause you to think “what the hell is wrong with you, Protagonist?!” since the protagonist acts differently in each route - but especially between Hanzo and Kuroyuki’s route.
That being said, bear with it. It’s worth it (at least to me it was).
Goro: a flirtatious stranger you meet when you get to the city of Kyo. He’s always there to help, give advice, and make you smile.
My thoughts: While Goro isn’t my usual type of otome guy, I found the lightheartedness of his route to be refreshing, much needed, and sweet.
I would actually suggest playing him last if you wish you leave the game on the lightest of notes.
I found his route to be a solid one and quite enjoyable (:
Chojiro: Your cousin and teacher. He’s the one who taught you everything you know about being a shinobi. Much like Hanzo, he believes the way of the shinobi is finishing the mission no matter what, or die trying.
My thoughts: Chojiro’s route was a good one, but could have been better. I found it to be lacking - but mostly overwhelming - in many ways.
It’s… dark. Unlike with Kuroyuki, Chojiro’s route is dark in terms of plot. Prepare yourselves with some tissues.
Gekkamaru: Your second childhood friend. The one who’s been with you all this time. He’s your bodyguard, your shield, and your protector. And he’s always there when you need him - and even when you don’t. He’s the only one who goes above and beyond for you - even when it’s not his own route.
My thoughts: At first, I didn’t think I was going to like Gekkamaru’s route. He was way over-protective, as well as not my usual otome guy type. But. It took me one time seeing him in the other routes to know I was going to like him. And I was not mistaken. This guy is the only one that’s always there for the protagonist - no matter what. In every… single… route.
I ended up loving Gekkamru very much so (!). He’s definitely one of the best routes of this game, and his route answers - and deals with - the most questions.
Recommended play-through (in terms of spoilers), would be: Hanzo - Goro - Kuroyuki - Chojiro - Gekkamaru.
Of course, you can switch up between Hanzo and Goro as well as between Chojiro and Gekkamaru.
Or, you can play the game however you like - although I actually suggest playing Chojiro and Gekkamaru routes last.
Personally, I played the game like this: Hanzo - Kuroyuki - Goro - Chojiro - Gekkamaru.
So it’s really up to you (:
I ended up loving them like this (from most favorite): Hanzo - Kuroyuki - Gekkamaru - Goro - Chojiro.
The Protagonist:
Enju was, without a doubt (and yes, I’m probably using this phrase a lot lately, sorry), one of the best things about this game. And I can’t say I’ve said this often about an otome game protagonists.
She was at her very best in Hanzo’s route, but in every route she always showed us that fighting spirit of hers - the will to live and fight.
And I couldn’t help but love her for that.
She was obviously very mentally strong, but she was also physically capable of fighting - she just never knew she had it in her.
What I admire most about a protagonist is their fighting spirit. Be in mentally, physically, or both, the will of the protagonist can do wonders to a game.
Another thing: in otome games, it’s important to remember you can’t just develop the romance-able characters, you have to develop the protagonist throughout the game, too. Which is something i found lacking in many games, but not in Nightshade. Not at all.
So… WELL DONE.
You went above and beyond for this protagonist. You made her the kind of protagonist I was proud to play as a character, and not just for the romance-able ones.
When I think of this game, I end up not thinking about the guys - although I do - but of Enju (:
The Art:
The art… was… divine.
The scenery was breathtaking.
Every time I saw it I had to take it in for a few moments.
It was so beautiful, it felt so magical yet so real, that I could literally see myself walking these paths, breathing that air, and missing a time I was never part of.
For the rest of the review:

I cannot recommend this game enough. The art is absolutely gorgeous at first glance and I found myself eagerly returning to play just for that reason alone.
The reason I like Nightshade so much is because the main 5 routes are not the only thing that it has going for them. Sure, I cried over the beautifully written main characters, but the side characters, Kyara, Ennosuke and Kasumi are nothing to turn your nose up at. They have a large part in making me bawl my eyes out almost every route.
Surprisingly enough, I like the MC that you play as too; quite a lot. She has a reputation of being a quiet, but dedicated clan member - the daughter of the clan leader - and one of her things that I was instantly drawn to, is that she feels like she owes her clan absolutely everything, just for supporting her. Further in, it becomes apparent that she feels frustrated when she becomes a liability and will do just about anything to be useful. Depending on what route you choose, she can become a confident, assertive shinobi, or an uncertain, reliant on everyone person.
Speaking of which, the story is superb! Kudos to the writing team for thinking of something a little more imaginative than just your plain old 'she's a traitor, kill her'. I won't give too much away, but depending on the route that you choose early on, impacts which of the two stories are used (this will make sense after you play all the routes).
And the story...
There is no lack of content. Seriously. My first session which involved 1 and a half routes, was 915 minutes long. I kid you not. I played this beautiful game for the entire day because I just couldn't rip myself away from it. The music, the SFX, the characters and story THEY ARE ALL AT THE BEST QUALITY.
I didn't think that a VN would ever be able to pull off an intense fight scene, but thanks to the actual stakes of the fight, coupled with an MC WHO ACTUALLY FIGHTS WELL, I found myself enjoying the quicker paced scenes more than I thought I would. As another reviewer said before me THIS GAME MAKES STATIC ART INTERESTING. The use of the space was utilized to its utmost best.
Pacing is good. The art. I've already gone off about it once, but I have never taken so many screenshots in a game before - and sometimes it was just of the same character with a different pose, or against a different background. Teita is a genius. I'll say this, if this game ever gets adapted into an anime, it would be worth the watch just for the art alone.
Bonus content awaits you after finishing one ending of a route which is very, VERY nice. Should I mention that you can choose which of the voice actors narrates the main menu? Because that's a thing.
Speaking of voice actors, THEY ARE SHINING GEMS. I could listen to their voices forever (shoutout to Kuroyuki's VA).
In conclusion, if you are a fan of otome games - perhaps Hakuouki in particular - then absolutely get Nightshade. I too, was a little 'is it REALLY worth it' over the slightly higher price compared to other titles, but I am completely and utterly satisfied with the product that I received, and I know I'll be playing this for many more tear-filled hours, long after I've received all the endings. You might play for the game, but you return for the characters.

Think of it as flashcards with a plot. It's a campy, light hearted, and simple plot but it's still there for texture. If you're trying to learn Hiragana, this will definately help recogize the characters. As far as learning how to speak Japanese, well, I'm pretty sure that's not really the primary focus, but you might pick up a couple vocabulary words along the way. I've learned a couple words, but mostly this is about Hiragana.
What we have here is a simple twist to a classic style of turn based, RPG combat system where you have to answer the characters name/sound in order to damage them. Characters being introduced to the player/student are pretty much just stronger monsters, meaning you are going to have choose the correct name/sound of the same character more frequently in order to deplete all their HP. This means if you need a refresher on characters that don't show up in later dungeons, you can go back to earlier dungeons and one shot some of the weaker enemies, but only after you rediscover its sound/name. It's a pretty clever dynamic that loans itself quite well to its medium.
There seems to be a good mix enemy encounters, but a lot of the same arrangements of enemies repeat while others not so much. Having a limited vocabulary in Japanese, this is a bit of a concern for me.
The frequency of different characters appearing in the random battles may of may not be in response to how often one might see them in everyday Japanese conversation. For example, the letter 'E' is the most frequently used letter in our language. I'm not sure what the most commonly used Hiragana character is in the Japanese language. Hopefully, whatever it is is appearing the most frequently in the Japanese language is also appearing the most frequently in the random battles of the game. Is this a drawback? Ambiguously.
One thing you might want to do playing through this game is focus more on buying good armor. Not that the monsters are particulary difficult, but I find it helps you learn to not kill the Hiragana Warriors too quickly. Like I said, the combat system very much feels like using flash cards, and being able to use the same cards sooner, rather than later can be a big help for you. Omoshiroi, ne?
Ultimately, I think I'm getting my moneys worth here. It's an inexpensive game that can help you out quite a bit. It's not going to build a massive hype train, but it's definately one of the more fun ways of learning the lettering system of another language. I paid seven bucks for it, got 8 hours out of it, learned a couple things, and I still have more hours of gameplay to put into it. I looked at some of the other reviews, showing some people managed to get 13 hours and even 16 hours out of this for only $7. Sounds like a good deal to me.
It's just one dollar. You got nothing to lose.

After meeting a lost girl named Cat you give her your scarf and make sure she reaches home safely: once you get there you realize you forgot to ask to have your scarf back though. You try and get inside to quickly look for her and get your belongings but the house is empty, weird footprints go towards a door and you start to experience strange visions.
Stray Cat Crossing is an RPG maker horror game featuring lots of surreal imagery, dialogues and characters, a cryptic story and some puzzles in between.
-the pixel graphics look simple, but are quite detailed and manage to render the various areas and characters quite well
-great sound design, the various noises are appropriately creepy
-very good soundtrack
-great atmosphere, the various levels you move through and creatures you meet look as something straight out of a bad nightmare
-the story is never fully revealed, but what's there is pretty interesting and touching
-powerful ending
-the whole plot might be a bit too murky and cryptic for its own good, while some'll appreciate the amount of conjecture this brings others might be disappointed at only having hints regarding what truly happened
-puzzles are either easily solved or can feel a bit awkward, requiring some trial and error until you realize what you need to do, they're never truly challenging or satisfying to be honest
-a chase scene during ACT I is truly frustrating, requiring you to quickly run side-to-side while jumping over holes with little room for error: too bad the controls simply aren't good enough for what's required and this quickly becomes a tiring and frustrating section
-Act III requires repetition to solve the final puzzle and get everything you need, think of it as something out of Groundhog Day: while the premise is interesting there's too much repetition involved, and the same lines over and over, to mantain a decent momentum. If you make a mistake in the sequence then things will be even worse as you're forced to retry over and over
-a couple of exit points from areas can easily be overlooked, leaving you stuck until you find them
-pretty short,I was done in about 2 hours
Stray Cat Crossing is a somewhat difficult game to review to be honest, I feel it sports a great atmosphere and a quite engaging story backed by gameplay that's somewhat dull or uninteresting in comparison: while Act I was genuinely creepy and enjoyable Act II and III felt like a step backwards in terms of gameplay with puzzles that ended up more annoying than anything else.
If you can endure the somewhat lacking gameplay the story is truly good though, there's lots of surreal imagery, half-hidden truths, metaphors and disconcerting implications that easily pull the game into the realm of psychological horror: what truly happened is left unclear though and you can find lots of theories in the Discussion area.
The aforementioned story, ambience and imagery are why I'm giving it a thumbs up since they made the game a decent experience overall: do consider the various pros and cons mentioned above before deciding if this game can be good for you though.

This game is reminds me of Standed 2 with better graphics. It also reminds me of Stranded Deep although not as far along.
I do believe this game has potential.
There are aspects that I like about it that I feel make it better than Stranded Deep, although in this early stage, not many.
I never understood why in most survival games, access to water is so incredibly limited. I understand that water is very important for life to thrive, so to me, it makes sense that at least one island should have a water source, (a lake, a rive, a creek, a spring). Most survival games make you work hard for and worry about water. I am guessing that it is because they lack the ability/imagination to make it challenging without doing so.
Lost in Nature, (LIN), places at least one water rock on the island. This doesn't make thing a whole lot easier, because, (at least on the island I spawned in on), the island is quite large. So at times you might race to get back to a water source.
I only encountered one bug, and unfortunately, it was a game-breaker for me.
In this game, you have to deal with losing your mind. Keeping your sanity is important, just as it would be in real life if you were standed alone on an island.
I cannot say I really understand why night means you loose so much sanity. I would think that if you were stuck on an island, that, by the time night falls, one would be so tired from all the work needing to be done that they would pass out.
I could imagine that, during this time in which you are sleeping, that you would not rest very well, and having just been ship wrecked, probably would be plagued by nightmares for at least a few days.
In LIN, you fight (in)sanity with fire.
The problem is, this only seems to work if you are dry and the whether is good. I lost my sanity in a storm. I was under my shelter, with a fire in front of me. I was soaked.
I expected that, while standing in front of the fire, that my sanity would increase. It did not. I thought, ok, maybe i have to dry off first. I dried off, and my sanity did not increase. My vitality kept dropping, even though I was dry, under shelter, and next to a fire, and was well fed.
Eventually, I died due to this. So it seems to me, that night creates x amount of insanity, and the storm must muliply it. But the shelter, or how well fed and watered you are does not act as a multiplier, and the fire isn't enough of a multiplier to stop the combined insanity brought on by both the night and the storm combined.
Two frustrating things,1. there is a torch in the game, but I could not build it as it requires coal. I could not get any coal, cause that requires a kiln to be made. I cannot make the kiln, cause it requires ashes, (not sure what the logic is behind that), But I cannot figure out how I am supposed to get ashes. I dont see any in the fireplace to collect.
So what is the point of putting something in the game, if it cant be built, or is not yet functioning? Is that supposed to excite us? Sorry, More frustrated by that than excited. Make it buildable and funtioning, then I'll be excited.
Overall, I  think the game has as much, (or almost as much), potential as Standed Deep. So far it seems to be less about island hopping, which depending upon your view, makes it better or worse.
At this point, being an (very) early access game, there is little to do. I littereally feel as though I did eveything there is to do so far, in one hour. After that hour, it just get food and wood for fire, cook food and night, rinse, repeat.
I will keep playing this game to see where the devolper takes it.
Graphically, the game looks very good.
Playabilty, again, being in early developement, is very limited.
This is a list of things I would like to see brought in to the game
Other ways to fight off (in)sanity.
More early stage craftables.
Coal nodes and/or veins.
More creatures. Smaller ones to start, ones you might expect to find on most islands, like rats, squirrels, rabbits maybe.
A simple or primitive knive to skin/fillet/gut above small creatures.
Skins could be turned into water skins, fillets (should be obvious, lol), and guts/sinew could be turned into cordage and fishing twine and bait for crabs and fish.
Some basic clothes made from palm leaves and string.
A basic spear, even a fishing spear would be nice.
The coconuts say in their tool-tip that you might be able to get more than liquid and "meat" from them with further processing. I'm guessing that there are plans to process the coconut to get fiber from it to make strings.
Let us retrieve ash from the fireplace.
If any of these things are already implemented, tell us how then, because it seems to be in some no intuitive way at this point.

​Where to start...
Firstly, I think it has to be said that 'The Beginner's Guide' is not a game. And you would be mistaken to think that it's 'not a game' just like 'The Stanley's Parable'. On that game you have choices and decisions. The Beginner's Guide does not have any of that. It is purely narrative, and the 'gameplay' is purely linear.
What I would say, is that this is actually an Experience. An interative one for sure, but an experience using visual and narative aid. In fact, this would make a great VR experience as you can relax and take on the sight. It's almost like a documentary that you, as the player, can get involved in although you cannot change your path nor the outcome.
As for the content...
I had a hard time finishing it even though it doesn't last very long. And since it is a narrative only game, there is no replay value. I think I had a hard time finishing it because the topic discussed is very depressing. Where else The Stanley's Parable is full of humour and joy, The Beginner's Guide is more thoughtful, melancholy, and filled with sadness.
I'm not entirely sure what the game is trying to say, what thoughts it's suppose to evoke, or whether it even had a message or any meaning what so ever. Especially if the narrative is not based on reality, and that it might not be true.
I would have a hard time recommending this game even though I loved The Stanley's Parable. It's not a game, so the player must prepare for that. It's thought provoking, but it lacks integrity and strength in what it is trying to say, if anything at all. It's not clever nor is it anything new. There is nothing for you to find out, nothing for you to really solve, nothing is hidden. It just doesn't really connect with me, and if anyone can relate to the game - maybe that says more about me and it does about them.
In the end, it just left me kind of empty...

Finally, a love letter that the GameCube deserves. A Hat in Time isn't ashamed of its roots as you'll probably see some direct inspirations. That being said, this game isn't a Frankenstein monster of Nintendo games and has its own original ideas that provide a whole experience for those who aren't nostalgic for the GameCube.
With Super Mario Sunshine's creative platforming, LOZ: Windwaker's energetic art style and Paper Mario TYD's charming comedic tone, A Hat in Time is a joy to play through.
It's not without its drawbacks though. The difficulty is usually interesting but safe. The platforming is never really challenging and the bosses can be annoying at times. The structure of the worlds can feel a bit restrictive at times as you can only collect a timepiece (star/jiggy equivalent) in its respective level. Disappointedly, the level design, for the most part, is linear. Also, the $30 price tag for 10-20 hours might be asking too much for some.
However, the positives absolutely steal the spotlight from the negatives.  While the difficulty of the platforming may not reach the height of classicly difficult games, it's never boring. Hat Kid is flat out fun to control. Double jumping, wall climbing, and diving to land tight jumps is satisfying. The different hats also grant unique ways tackle both platforming and combat. The worlds can be restrictive but they're always fun and diverse. The cartoonish colorful art style makes the worlds pop and compliment their unique gameplay arcs. While the experience is short, you can tell that the developers put a lot of effort and a world of heart into this game. It is rare to see that much endearing charm put into a game.
I'd recommend this game to people who love the GameCube or Colectathons. Even anyone who wants a charming experience might want to give it a look. A Hat in Time will make you smile.

To start, I've only done 2 routes, but I was wildly impressed with this on the first, so I'm ready to write this review.
Pros:
-Art is good
-Music is good and mood-setting
-They somehow figured out how to make action scenes action-y with STATIC ART.
-Protag has a personality! She has goals and fears like she's a person or something! She got a few "non-responses" as I call them but generally had thoughtful dialogue and internal monologue.
-This game is QUOTABLE. Like, things were said I will actually remember cause it was so COOL (in spoiler just to be safe):

-Hands down, this game has the best translation I've ever seen in a VN. They did a great job.
-When other reviews said I'd cry, I didn't believe them. Guys, my heart broke over characters that weren't even romanceable. And that was a GOOD ending. It hurt so good.
-This game actually makes use of themes, instead of just trying to put together a situation for romance things to happen. I'm not going to say the story is great literature, but I did actually get invested. There are lessons for all the characters to learn. Yes, ALL, not just the protag. The "bad" ending is when those lessons aren't learned. The characters themselves are surprisingly well-rounded. Just...not the villains.
-One of my pet peeves is when sexual assault on behalf of the LI is presented as romantic. So far, this has not been a problem, and the game actively steers away from it. Also, protag has a meaningful friendship with the men she's not romancing, and other women in the story too.
-LIs vaguely fit into the common "type" tropes you see, but they were more dynamic than that.
-Basically everything good the other reviews say about the protag's development are entirely accurate.
Cons
-You may have to exercise your suspension of disbelief.
-Villains are bad. Not just evil, but objectively one-dimensional.
-Could do with a few more CGs, could do with some slightly better ones. They are adequate.
-Very few choices to make, maybe just over 1 per chapter. Didn't really bother me, though, because I generally agreed with the choices and liked reading how they unfolded.
Recap: EVERY NON-ENGLISH VN SHOULD USE THESE TRANSLATORS; They did the protag and friendship stuff super right; I felt real feelings for stupid fake people, like, 3 layers of tragedy. 11/10, give me more ninja tragedies.
P.S. Don't listen to other reviews, Hanzo is not the best route (though it was very good). Chojiro is the best route. All the feels, guys. All the feels.

This is an overall great game, and you can tell it was made with love! The controls are very concise and most issues with platforming have to do with your own abilities. There are many hats which give special powers and abilities that shake things up in gameplay, though I will say there are some hats *cough* ice hat *cough* that are really underutilized. There is one hat that really opens up the game and it can create (kind of, they already exist so it kind is like phasing) platforms. It is a really cutesy game with delightful visuals and colorful dialogue. It can be pretty funny, I would say my favorite character would be the owl train conductor who speaks with a really exagerated scottish accent and is pretty self centered. Everything is either about his "beautiful train" or the bird movie awards with him.
Another thing I absolutely love is the way hatgirl can be customized. She can have the colors of her clothes and hair changed to your liking (you have to unlock them though) and can utilize badges which further your own abilities. Hatgirl you can change the way hatgirl plays and I think that it is pretty neat!
There are some negatives and in particular I have some issues with the glitches in the game. Sometimes you fall off a ledge and teleport or things don't seem to quite match up. Fortunately it isn't as bad as it seems and is still definitely playable. From what I understand this game is the developer's (Gears for Breakfast) first one so these glitches are to be expected. It is also rather short and can be finished within a couple hours. Replayability is expanded with a few hidden collectibles, secret levels, and "relics".
I hear there may be dlc and steam workshop support so I can only expect the game to improve over time! I expect great things from Gears for Breakfast in the future.
Overall I give it 8.5/10

Disturbed is a fairly short visual novel that takes on a slight horror atmosphere. You play as a farmer in a decaying land that is cursed by a spreading plague which is wiping out not only crops, but livestock as well. You will need to proceed through the story, solve a few small puzzles, and return the land to its once inhabitable form. The title uses the Ren'py Engine, which is the current standard for most visual novel games, so if you've played any previously the interface will be familiar to you.
I'm going to say right off the bat that the story here is lacking pretty severely; there's nothing interesting or fun about being a depressed farmer who wants to restore the fertility of his land. With that being said, where Disturbed really excels is its dark atmosphere, morose mood, and raw graphics. All of the scenes are hand drawn in black and white, and honestly they look completely untouched by Photoshop or other image editing software; rather they look like they went straight from the paper to the scanner, in to the game. Another fun thing to do in this title is to find out all of the ways that you can possibly die, and there are about a dozen different ways.
Another lacking feature here is the audio. You can play for minutes at a time without hearing anything whatsoever, and music is virtually nonexistent. The only sounds are the ones that indicate when you're on a death screen, and effects such as doors shutting or keys jingling. Even just a slight dark ambient soundtrack would suffice, it certainly wouldn't take away from the corroded atmosphere of the game; in fact, it would enhance it. Most players get mind-numbingly bored without any background audio to listen to. There are also quite a few spelling and grammatical errors throughout the dialogue, but some of these have been patched out.
So you may be wondering why I'm recommending Disturbed even though I listed off more cons than pros. Simply put, the game has an impenetrable depressive atmosphere that should be experienced by any horror and black metal fans. It's also easy to tell that a lot of time and passion went in to drawing all of the scenes, and there are quite a lot of them. Disturbed is best saved for a rainy fall day, when you have an hour or two to kill (or to be killed).

If you are a fan of fairly straight forward city building games, Banished is for you. You start a town using the resources provided to you from the beginning, unless you're a sadist and chose to start with nil, and slowly branch out and grow your humble burg into a city proper. The creators chose to give you free reign in how and in what manner to build your growing village with all structures available from the beginning, the only stipulation being the materials required to construct them. Over time you get to see your villagers wither and die of old age, and their offspring become the new generation of farmhands or brewers keeping your town well fed and well inebriated.
Pros:
-All buildings accessible from the get go.
-Fairly Intuitive menu system
-Scenery and buildings designs vary, so you dont have a town with 20 of the same house stacked next to each other.
-Procedurally generated maps make each game different.
-Can share map seeds if you or a friend find one you like.
-Great city builder for the price, even better on sale.
Cons:
-STEEP learning curve, if you arent prepared, winter will kill you.
-Pathing can be hard to work around if your resources are far between.
-Hard to know the moment you made the fatal flaw that doomed your village to starvation, in order to load.
-(In a small way) There are only so many buildings you can create, and so many resources to collect that once you have  a few of each and a stable food vs. demand, there isnt much more to do without any quests or goals besides the steam achievements.
-Your girlfriend is better at this than you.
8/10 if I had to give it a number rating.

With the wiki page doing a better job explaining the basics of the long dark I went through and slowly began to find my way through this world. Its harsh and punishing but it has a nice 'lonely' feeling that you just dont  get these days. In 99% of survival games you have to watch your back in case some titwank wants to shoot you and steal your beans. But not here. In the long dark you are 100% alone and other then the wolves waiting around every corner its you versus nature.
The art style is very borderlandsy and I like that. Its in a realm of its own and it really takes the first hour or so to appreciate it. The gameplay is fun though, with the calorie burn the way it is, it becomes a bit repetitive after a while which is my only gripe. In a lot of good survival games after the intial sprint for supplies you start to feel a little comfortable. Now i would have no problem having this comfortability taken from me within reason. but you find me to fat big eating 10 fish a day just to stay mildly full..You have all these supplies saved up but if you cant go outside for a single day you'll end up using them all as you burn almost 700 calories sleeping for 11 hours..The long dark makes sleep a real threat which makes no sense provided you do it in the right place..
But finally its the little things that make this game worth purchasing, The weather effects are incredible, the interactivity between the wildlife is glorious to watch and just being able to do something as simple as retrace your own footprints because youre walking in the snow is something even a lot of AAA games appear to miss out on. I only wish that perhaps there was a bit more of an explanation and that you didnt burn calories like youre permenatly on a treadmill..

Ninja Blade is a goofy action game made by From Software. It has a ridiculously stupid story line and even stupider gameplay.
At no point does this game take itself seriously which is very much a point in the games favor, because there's simply no way anyone else could have. The dialogue, story and cutscenes are an idiotic, brainless bit of B-Movie fun. But sadly, that's where the good parts of this game come to an end.
Ninja Blade might have a funny and entertaining story, but the gameplay is a sloppy, unpolished mess. Hit detection is infuriatingly imprecise, character animations are hilariously terrible, (to the point where, during normal gameplay, characters look like badly made action figures being tossed around instead of properly animated characters) and the combat is mindless, button mashy nonsense which has any and all possible sense of flow absolutely destroyed by CONSTANT QUICK TIME EVENTS. I'm not kidding when I say that if you cut out all the time spent mashing buttons for QTEs in this game, you'd be left with probably about half the play time.
Aside from the combat there are also sections with required platforming, with typical "Ninja" actions such as wall running and triangle jumps. These might be fun if the player character (don't even remember his name) didn't control like hot garbage. The way he moves around and navigates the environments when you're attempting these actions is bafflingly janky; he'll snap to walls and surfaces you don't want him to, he'll get stuck in corners and jitter in place until you can waggle him free, he'll grab onto non existent ledges frequently leaving him hanging onto thin air, etc. It's almost hilarious how poorly done this part of the game in particular is done. If it had stayed a simple mindless hack and slash, then it probably wouldn't have been as bad, but the horrendous platforming garbage REALLY kills it. Prince of Persia this game is NOT.
On top of that, there are constant bugs too. This is a poorly done port of an aggressively mediocre game. If you want to play a good Ninja action game, seriously just go grab a copy of Ninja Gaiden Black. It's dirt cheap these days and is also backwards compatible with Xbox One now, and still a damn good game.
As for Ninja Blade, spend your money elsewhere. Skip the boring, janky gameplay and just watch the cutscenes on YouTube.

All right, listen. Maybe you've been playing Call of Duty for many years and have grown accustomed to its semi-real run-and-gun, or the way a sniper folds in and out of the scope.  Maybe you're a Battlefield person, opting for a more real, team-oriented experience. Maybe you are neither of these, or maybe you're both.
It really doesn't matter. This is a must-play FPS.
You might say, "World War Two? Seen it." Please, do not say that about this game.  I would say that it is because of this timeframe that Red Orchestra 2 feels and plays like the most in-your-face multiplayer war experience you can find.  You are immersed in fighting to defend your homeland or strike back upon those who would do said homeland harm.  Even if the direct immersion into the patriotism of the game don't immediately hit you, the ever-constant danger of death will push you onward.
The shooting mechanics are not hard to grasp; the class and weapons system may seem a bit convoluted at first, and the difficulty of finding an ideal server in this tightly-knit community might put you off at first.  However, once you're in, you cannot simply go back.  This is a masterwork of war gaming, and I applaud Tripwire Interactive for their work on this title.

I have been waiting for this game to come out ever since the release of their original demo. I must have played those few levels over and over for probably a total of hours so you can imagine my excitement when they got greenlit and set up a Kickstarter. I followed them through all that time until finally it came to their point of release.
Superhot is a game about using time to your advantage. The more you move the faster time moves. If you're standing still it is to the point of almost being stopped. You can watch the bullets slowly fly past you (Or into you). If you're shooting or moving around quickly it speeds up to around real time depending on how you're moving. This allows you to get out of situations with multiple enemies that may seem impossible considering you have no health and die in one hit. It also allows for amazing looking replays when sped up to real time.
The game has a scheme of three colours, red for the enemies, black for weapons and white for the environment. However it couldn't work better with the game. It makes it easy to pick out enemies and weapons around the area whilst still being able to create an environment. The enemies are made of glass which provides a satisfying shatter sound and visual upon killing them. There is no blood or gore just broken glass. The weapons also shatter upon impact should you throw them at a wall or enemy. The whole thing creates a style that seems crystalline and pristine whilst also creating an air of fragility.
The campaign is short, only around 2-3 hours long, but it couldn't have been made better. Each level is a different environment with a different setup of enemies. Some of the levels put you in immediate danger, forcing you to figure out tactics through trial and error but an instant restart system negates any annoyance that may cause. The whole campaign is underlined by a story which breeds intrigue as well as adds an unsettling feeling to it all.
Superhot is exactly the game I hoped for ever since playing the demo. The mechanics are smooth and the whole thing is visually appealing. The levels are inventive and the story solid and well done despite almost not being essential. However the $24.99 USD price tag ($35.07 AUD) for a 2-3 hour long campaign may seem a bit much. I would recommend waiting for a sale that's somewhere around 50% off and picking it up then. There are challenge and endless modes which are exactly what they sound like but they still don't really provide enough for what they're asking. Despite the cost I enjoyed playing this game immensely and would highly recommend it to anyone who wishes they could take their time with first person shooters.

Alright so I've played through the entire game and collected all 40 time pieces because I like to do that with collect-a-thons and this is what I got to say.
Here are the good things.
The Controls for the most part are clean and responsive such as jumping, diving and attacking. I'll get into the specific moves that don't work in the negative section of this review. Jumping and diving is a lot of fun and I love the jump cancel maneuver as it gives you the precise control you need to stop on a platform.
The levels are really well done and they clash elements together into one whole world like in the 3rd level you have a forest to go through. When you jump across a gap in a bridge, you come across a wintery biome with icicles and a glacier to go through. Then there is an area with trees for houses and an area where you have to cross over a swamp, making them feel like multiple levels rather than just one level which helps forget the fact that this game only has four worlds and one small, final world. The 4th world introduces free roam into the mix but it basically just allows you to get a time piece in any order and not leave the world instead of being tied to one scenario each time piece.
The Scenarios themselves are fun to play. The best one is the second world where you must help either the owls or the penguins to win the award on their movies. You help the owls by starring in a western train ride where you must become a detective and solve a crime of a murder, then the second act has you try stopping a bomb from destroying the train. Then you have the Penguins where you must gain popularity for the movie by walking to the penguins and then the second act has you leading a parade of... owls. Well the Penguin acts aren't very fun but the Train Western is where it's at and it's a blast trying to swing away from the detaching train and solve a crime by avoiding the crow's site who have the train on lock down.
There are time rifts you can jump into when you find them that remind me of Super Mario Sunshine's obstacle courses. They implement elements from the part of the level you choose like the bird parade and the green/purple platforms to use your mask on. These platform levels are fun for the most part when it's not dicking you out with those ducktale-hair crows that push you back off the platforms. There are also purple time-rifts that use the level aesthetics you enter them from, and are based on the memories of the enemies that have been hit by the Time pieces. There are also page collectables that reveal the origins of how those worlds happened before Hat Kid's influence.
This game has Steam workshop support via opting for Beta and will get a full release soon which will help people come back to this game and people have already started making levels like Whomp's Fortress, the first level of Yo! Noid 2 and brought back Beta Hero from... the beta of Hat in Time. The game will also get 2 DLC levels in the future which will further sweeten the deal.
Time to get to the bad parts
Wall running is very annoying to deal, especially when you are trying to get off a wall of a narrow path. You cannot just move away from the wall to get off from it and if you try to jump and move away from the wall parrelell to you, it won't work and Hat Kid will wall run again, making you go further upwards when all you want to do is get off the GOD DAMN WALL! Then there are time where you accidentally wallrun on a wall that doesn't lead you anywhere like in the warehouse part of the 2nd World. You can press the R trigger to stop wall running but even this doesn't help when you are against narrow walls. The Wall running isn't even all that useful in general and is a confusing addition to hat kid's moveset when you can already Double jump. The game could have not had wall running at all and it would have made the game control better.
The homing attack is incredibly unreliable. Even if you are at the right height, sometimes the homing attack just won't work. You'll be pressing that X button and Hat kid just drops to the ground and does nothing which is very noticeable in the first boss fight of the game where you are ENCOURAGED to do a homing attack! I feel that the developers didn't want people to be overly reliant on the attack so they made it cumbersome on purpose but again the game encourages you to do a homing attack to defeat the Mafia enemies since it does a lot more damage than just jumping on top of their heads so it feels more like a punishment to be told how to defeat the enemies.
The boss fights are a mixed bag. The 1st Boss is well designed and fairly challenging which is good. Then you get to the 2nd boss and everything just falls flat on it's face. The problem with this boss is a mix of cheap attacks and a dialogue scene in the middle of the fight that happens everytme you die from the boss. The 3rd boss ends abruptly after it just throws♥♥♥♥♥♥at you from all sides. The Final boss is okay but there was one time where I was holding an explosive fruit at 1 health and died when a cutscene was playing which was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
The Hats feel more like a nuisance rather than an addition to your moveset because they don't really have any other effects than what they're intended to do. The Sprint hat is the one you will most likely use for the whole game because it makes you run faster and allows you to make longer jumps while allowing you to dive. The Brewing hat allows you to blow up boxes. It can also kill enemies but it's attack start up time is too slow to be an effective weapon that you'll already have killed them with your umbrella and once you've collected all the badges, it is essentially useless because the Pons will be useless. The Ice Cap is only useful for taking it's spring pads and nothing else. The Mask allows you to reveal green platforms and remove purple platforms which is only required for a few sections in the 3rd World and the Twilight gate in the 4th world. The Time Stop hat is only required for one time piece in Mafia town but is a big help for the Final Boss.
It feels like the abilities could have been better implemented by being an addition to Hat Kid's movesets rather than being split up into different hats. This is something that Yooka Laylee does better.
Badges are also in this game where you can use them to make life a little easier for yourself. You only get to equip one at a time at first but you can eventually buy pins to get a maximum of three badges at a time. However the problem is that one of these badges which is the hookshot badge is required to be used for almost every level. This is confusing because I got the idea that Badges were merely handy perks so to have a Badge that is required to get through the game nullifies the slot upgrade. I don't understand why this function couldn't be added to the umbrella from the start as there really isn't any excuse for this.
Overall
The game is good but just wait for a price drop for the moment or wait for the DLC levels to come out or when the game's Steam Workshop becomes more bustling with stages. As whether this or Yooka Laylee is better, I'd say Yooka Laylee has better controls and better use of abilities than a Hat in Time while A Hat in Time has a better replayability factor and better level design than Yooka Laylee. Since I like platforming collect-a-thons, I give this game my recommendation.

If you are a fan of fairly straight forward city building games, Banished is for you. You start a town using the resources provided to you from the beginning, unless you're a sadist and chose to start with nil, and slowly branch out and grow your humble burg into a city proper. The creators chose to give you free reign in how and in what manner to build your growing village with all structures available from the beginning, the only stipulation being the materials required to construct them. Over time you get to see your villagers wither and die of old age, and their offspring become the new generation of farmhands or brewers keeping your town well fed and well inebriated.
Pros:
-All buildings accessible from the get go.
-Fairly Intuitive menu system
-Scenery and buildings designs vary, so you dont have a town with 20 of the same house stacked next to each other.
-Procedurally generated maps make each game different.
-Can share map seeds if you or a friend find one you like.
-Great city builder for the price, even better on sale.
Cons:
-STEEP learning curve, if you arent prepared, winter will kill you.
-Pathing can be hard to work around if your resources are far between.
-Hard to know the moment you made the fatal flaw that doomed your village to starvation, in order to load.
-(In a small way) There are only so many buildings you can create, and so many resources to collect that once you have  a few of each and a stable food vs. demand, there isnt much more to do without any quests or goals besides the steam achievements.
-Your girlfriend is better at this than you.
8/10 if I had to give it a number rating.

The sound effects  are great, from the disturbing noises resonating through the dark hallways, or the sound of the horrible rainstorm outside, it is always immersive. Banished is a simulation game similar to the likes of SimCity, Cities, and Tropico.  It is a small village simulation game, in which you essentially run a village in medieval times.  You start with a set amount of citizens, and from there, you must assign them roles, hunter, gatherer, blacksmith, farmer, fisherman, etc...  But for some of these professions, you must have the right building for the citizens to perform their assignments, for example, a blacksmith will do nothing (or possibly you won't be able to even assign anyone as a blacksmith), if you haven't got a Blacksmithing shop built.  On that same note, fisherman require a fishing dock, farmers require farmland, and so on.
You can have your citizens go into the surrounding areas and gather wood from trees, rocks, iron or so on and store them in your own stockpile, set areas for controlled woodcutting, then have someone to cut the wood into firewood for the homes, build new homes and larger homes for more and more people, and ensure your people are warm enough and have enough food to make it through the winter season.
The game has nice graphics, nothing amazing though, with a great set of sound effects and music, and really nice mechanics.  It's a bit hard to get into at first because of everything there is do to maintain and control, but it's fun once you get the hang of it.
My only real complaint is how difficult the game seems to be even on the easiest difficulty, but that isn't all the games fault.
I recommend this game for anyone who enjoys these kinds of simulation games, and is up for a challenge.

It's not a bad game, still, i find myself unwilling to suggest it to others.
It is basically a Middle Ages Sim City completely focused on city building, and this is its strongest point, but also its greates weakness. Ok, you create a city, manage to feed some people, and keep them warm. Now what? Nothing, really. Continuing the game makes it more complex and add more levels of variability (in particular, the most challenging point of the game are the sudden drops of population due to starbation, cold, or, if you have done your homework right, old age), but that's all.
It's quite similar to Stronghold for the setup, but without the quests, and with a less precise forecasting system (for example...will my 10k units of food be enough for my population of 100 people? funny thing, little shift in the population number may cause a general starvation).
In the end, it doesn't feel very balanced, and it still, in my opinion, lacks an "adventure" mode, with some smaller objectives. Mods make the game better, but not that much.
Suggested only to hardcore fans of Sim City and medieval settings.

If you don't ready anything else in this review, please read this:
Absolutely, 100%, without a doubt, Do not buy this game! Even at 10 dollars, this price is too steep.
Ninja Blade is an excellent example of when you take a poorly made game and then turn it into a poor PC port. A sloppy, bwildering, mess of a game.
If that doesn't turn you away, I'll be more specific.
If you hate quick time events, stay far away. This game is full of them, and I mean constantly. I am bold enough to say that 50% of this game is played out in quick time events rather than player driven gameplay. It's so hilarious that I start chuckling when I exited one quick time event, got control of my character for a few seconds and then went into another long chain of quick time events, hah, it's like the developers didn't even care.
Character control is passable at best. During what little combat there is (when you're not in a QTE) hitting enemies feels great! Unfortunately,that's only about 10% of the game. This game incorporates an unhealthy portion of platforming and wall running. This is by far the most infuriating and unsatisfying mechanic of the game. The controls simply fail at this objective. Often I found that was about a 50/50 chance that my character would cling to the wall, if not, I had to reinitiate collision with the wall, hoping that this time it would work. This wouldn't be awful if it didn't put you into timed chases scenes that demand you can quick attach, jump, and detach from surfaces.
Boss battles are pretty lame. They feel like long drawn out button mashing sessions instead of intense battles. In fact, the bosses don't actually do that much damage to you, but they do often possess a great deal of health and find way to remain invulnerable almost as to try and win using attrition.
Those are just a few major gripes that arose from my thankfully short experience with Ninja Blade...
Oh, I almost forgot to mention, on top of it being a below average game, it's an awful port on top of it all! While I didn't experiencing the same game breaking crashes so many other users did, I often found that I could not actually exit the game. It would just hang and I would have to forcibly close it.
In addition, I found that my character would sometimes go into what appears to be a climbing annimation for no ascertainable reason and would then fall through the floor. Bizarre.
Oh, well, I did find one aspect of the game that I found enjoyable. Despite the lack of detail everywhere else in the game, the developer put in an extensive color editor for character's costume. You can customize just about every part of the protagonists outfit, making all sorts of neat looking ninja suits. What a shame I will never see any of the cool costumes I made in action, because I refuse to play this game for another minute.
I'm not sure what else to say. Please don't give this developer any money for making this. It's terrible.

I woke up in a clearing, just ice and snow around me. A few rocks here and there. I walked up a hill to get my barings to be met with a spectacular view of the surise. That's when some of the snow collapsed and I fell about 4-5 metres and sprained my ancle as a result. It didn't seem like a big deal at the time. I limped my way over some more hills then found a hut with an energy bar in it. I hadn't eaten in so long so it felt good to have something in my stomach. I continued on my way. Still limping since I didn't have the first aid to heal myself and I needed to find some supplies before I stopped for the night.
I then found myself in a blizzard. The wind was beating down on me as I limped toward more endless snow. Each time I saw a rock I pictured it as a hut and got a glimps of hope only to see it as it truely was. A mirrage, the illusion of savior.
I was getting cold, real cold when I finally found my way out of the blizzard and to a small clearing when I could make out an old train track and a building in the distance. That's when I heard it. A slight grumble of a wolfs breath. I looked around slowly, feeling around my pockets for a knife I had found early that day. But I was too slow, everything went slow when I saw the wolf pounce towards me. All I could think about was how funny it was that I had survived a fall from a cliff, starvation, dehydration, getting stuck in a blizzard with no fire wood. I survived it all only to die here when my salvation was in sight.
The wolf burried its teeth in my neck and for once since all of this happened I was finally warm. My blood felt like a hot shower as it covered my body. The wolf jumped off me and I rolled over. Tryign to stand. Red blood tainting the beauty of the plain white snow.
My vision was blurry then it all when black. No more hunger, no more cold. Just warmth.
I did all of that surrounded by some of the most beautiful art I've seen in a game for a very long time. 10/10 would bang.

Note: I don't highly discourage you to buy this game, as most people will like it. However, ToZ is a poor iteration of the Tales formula and I wouldn't recommend this to any Tales fans.
:::
I've always liked Tales games. I played Symphonia just a few years ago and felt it aged well. Zestiria is terrible and I regret buying it. Yes, I finished the game, but that's because I'm a perfectionist, even obsessing about no deaths in Boss fights (actually impossible unless you are Buddha of infinite patience).
The fact is, a week or so after initial release, many video game stores in Japan were refusing to take in copies of Zestiria (second-hand resellers). This tells you how much most of Japan hated this game.
In the middle of grinding this game to a finish, I think I've awoken to my inner masochist. I kept telling myself I hate this game, but at that point the sun was already rising... I ask myself why do I keep playing then? The answer was my sexuality: I was a pansexual masochistic Transport Helicopter.
This game is a revolutionary BDSM JRPG. There are no BDSM themes, but the game does whip you to this depressing submission you begrudgingly accept: the fact that this Tales game is a poo.
:::
What this game boils down to is F2P-like grinding system mixed with Graces f-Lite combat - something like Tales of Borderlands. The story is too flawed, unbelieveable or predictable at times to really keep you excited, and the best part about this game is actually the Japanese drama surrounding it to be honest.
(note: all in-game terms have been simplified, i.e. Seraphim (天族) to spirits)
--
Combat gets very dull and repetitive, especially on higher levels where casting huge AoE spells and farming good item 'traits' become key to survival. On lower levels, the combat drags on because of the lack of variety. So you're stuck between a boringly easy mode, and a frustratingly stupid mode.
Don't get me wrong, Hard is 'hard', but it's not hard in the way DMC3 and 4 were hard but rewarding games.
The friendly AI, in all levels, is absolute buttocks. This was never explained in the game, but the equipped Title of each character actually affects its AI significantly more than the Strategy menu you use to finetune your AI's moves, and even then the AI is still horrendous, doing risky attacks in front of a boss that OHKO's you if you don't block every single time. The worst part is that I'm obsessed with having everyone alive at the end of a battle, and the AI will never defend well, even if you equip defensive titles.
If you go on Youtube and find the guy that ran through Zestiria fighting only bosses and no mobs at all, you'll see that he's stacked his item traits very well (creating 'Union' effects), and most of the boss fights consist of having the AI completely shut down offensively (Defense command), and basically playing 1v1 against the boss. I will tell you right now that will be the most challenging thing you will do in this game: patiently whittling down the damage sponge boss until you die of high blood pressure (See: Friendly AI)
There is still a plethora of things that♥♥♥♥♥♥me off about the AI, but explaining that will take too much time.
I always play Tales of games on Hard and I will say babysitting in this game is the hardest, not in terms of fun challenge, but in terms of making sure your useless melee weapon AI partner doesn't constantly try to off themselves. The spirits all have long range spells, but your human partner is human deadwood - no, human refuse.
At the end of the day, most boss fights are fought with all the AI sitting back, and me controlling 1 or 2 characters to spam at the boss.
--
Character levels aren't as important in this game. It's better to get decent gear for that level than it is to get 5 levels.
Grinding is a pain in the big red bum. The all-important item traits you need are randomly-generated for every weapon drop or weapon seller in town, UNLESS you unlock a feature which significantly raises the droprate of the TRAIT in question for any one specific region (changeable). This means you have to grind again (only in that area) if you want better weapons.
You also can't move weapon traits to different level of weapons. So if you have all the best traits on a lvl 10 weapon, it's stuck there forever (with exceptions).
This section also ignores the stupidly unnecessary 'complexity' of 'Weapon Fusing' and item trait 'Unions', which add nothing to the game but min-maxing MMORPG/Borderlands style. At first it was confusing, after I completely understood how it worked (in-game tutorials on this are sparse and unclear), it was annoying.
The in-battle 'Character Fusion' feature where two characters combine into one with better stats is also an 'eh' addition to the game.
The new 'open world' element of the game is a novel idea, but most of the open world feels lifeless and unexciting. You will definitely not come to this game for open-world immersion.
The story is lacklustre, which only makes the plotholes even more annoying.
The characters are bland. This is subjective, but Sorey is one of the weakest Tales MC ever. If you watch anime a lot, the most efficient way I can explain this is: Sorey is the ultimate fun-guy Kimura Ryouhei hero protagonist, with little character development. Other subplots could have been more interesting such as the ones with Alisha and the other spirits.
--
The drama though, is top notch.
There are no other Tales games in its history that has garnered so much drama. I have no idea who really came up with the stupid parts of Zestiria, but BanNam staff screwed it up in PR.
See the tumblr blog translation of the drama around this for more. If you can read Japanese, enjoy it over at the dedicated wiki for Zestiria drama.
RIP BabaP.

This game is an amazing nood to games like Super Mario Sunshine, Banjo and Kazooie, and Mario 64. With WindWaker style graphics, an AMAZING soundtrack, cute charactors (Most of the time *shudders*) and wonderful level design. This game is one that makes me remember why I loved platformers in the first place. This game is packed FULL of charm. I havent felt this attacted to a game in a long time. Dungeon Defenders 2 is a fun free to play game, with the option to "pay to get ahead". While at first glance when in game it may seem like new characters are inaccessible, that's a short term examination of the game. If every game only took two or three days, even a week to get everything in the game, you would stop playing. To start with everyone gets 4 character slots (assuming the player wants one of each class). Each character levels up when in your deck (4 hero slots, oh look less grind work) meaning when you start off and create one of each character (or whatever config you like) your first 4 heroes will reach maximum level at the same time. Simple beginnings no? After this comes getting good gear by playing endgame maps (working your way up the nightmare ladder). While you play however, you are also completing dailies, weeklies (monthlies will probably come back in a bit) and gaining defender medals. These medals can be used to unlock new characters (12000 the first two weeks for new heroes, 10000 afterwards, may eventually change) purchase special boosters (like pet love), keys (for the non paid costume and seasonal costume chests), character slots (2000 each) or eggs. While characters might sound pricy, if you like the game you will easily play long enough to quickly obtain them and then be left wondering "what do i spend it on next?" Overall, it's not the most polished or perfect game, but its damn good fun and they are working hard to make it not a product or service, but an experience that will entertain and spread enjoyment. They are aiming for 120 heroes, 12 down and 2 in the works that we are aware of and 2 gender swapped heroes that possess a few things different than the originals. Every other week seems to be a release or event of some sort, not including special medal boosting weekends. This is my overview and recommendation of the game, hope it helps sway you in favour.

I want to start by saying that for the most part I really did enjoy Nightshade. It’s a little tragic for an otome, but the artwork and characters are stunningly beautiful and it's a very well polished game overall - which isn't really surprising given the price. The voice acting is extensive and very emotionally impactful; it really adds to the quality of the experience and if you have yet to try a game that's fully voiced (in Japanese FYI) you should definitely give it a go.
After reading a few reviews however, I couldn't find too many that really address how dissatisfying the game can be, so despite the thumbs up here I go.
The story can be quite tragic, and when done properly it was very bittersweet, but more often than not I found it to be a bit jarring and at odds with the romantic character arcs. For example, the MC might have just witnessed
and then moments later gets giddy and embarrassed because her crush held her hand?
The routes share a couple of interesting twists but when you boil it all down that's pretty much it. Most of the game is spent
All in all I can't say that's something that woud ever deter me from enjoying an otome game - I'd be lying if I said I'm here for the plot - but lumped together with a couple of other niggles makes it all a bit of a naggle (mixed experience).
The protagonist is a bit floppy and does very little herself. I understand the need to be rescued every now and then, but when it’s done constantly by not just the love interest, but every single guy around (and always out of nowhere), it gets very old fast. She's a bit like a sack of flour that's just thrown around and hoisted over people's shoulders all the time. If she manages to
why can’t she pull her head out of her♥♥♥♥♥and intervene, or even, god forbid, win, when people she cares about are threatened?
Throughout the game it’s emphasised that Enju has less experience than some of the others and that she must be protected etc. In fact, this is probably her defining characteristic and the writers seem to have bent backwards trying to create excuses for why she can't do something herself when other outcomes would just make more sense. There seems to have been more effort put into Enju's intense phobia of having a spine than anything else in the game. This leaves her with very little impact on the world around her, especially for someone so central to the politics and schemes of the era. She should essentially be making some of these important decisions but she ends up spectating and then dressing wounds more than anything else (you’ll quickly find out for yourself that I’m really not exaggerating).
No one buys an otome game expecting a highly realistic historical narrative, but when setting out any good story there should at least be some consistency in world building and characterisation.
In almost all the routes, Enju has a lot of incentive to figure things out for herself or take action, but for a spy/assassin she’s shockingly dim and naïve, and it really irritated me to see that potential go to waste. I know it's pretty much the norm, but it would have been so satisfying to see a story crafted around someone capable and intelligent, filled with intrigue and espionage, without resorting to the classic born-yesterday-MC you find in every game. Her passive nature also makes almost every interaction feel one-sided or even kind of demeaning, which, barring a small niche demographic, can be very uncomfortable to read as a player.
Generally speaking, the characters are sweet and often likeable, especially the MC as she puts herself above others and it manages to come off as genuine thoughtfulness without being too irritating. As a protagonist, I thought her design and background were quite unique and it's nice to at least be an actual shinobi instead of the usual princess or bystander. A number of the scenes the characters all have together are funny and set up emotional attachments for the player, but the dialogue does feel a little padded out sometimes. There was a lot of exposition and occasionally the more dramatic scenes were very repetitive or lasted far longer than they needed to. Conversations often go in circles and everyone keeps saying the same thing over and over in different ways - not for dramatic effect but just... because? Not to mention a lot of the "mysteries" are not very mysterious at all and I'm pretty sure a 7 year old with a decent grasp of logic would be able to understand everything before the MC does. I'm not sure if this is all done under the assumption that teenage girls will somehow not be able to handle a more complicated narrative, or if the developers are just sticking to the "delayed-reactions-are-easier-than-plots" otome gold standard, but it does come off as a little insulting sometimes.

New family went in, BUT, they did not get any food either since some blasted women, whos houses were FULL of freaking food, were always picking the remaining food from the storage right before the new family could get any. The father of that family went to the fisher, got a crate full of fish, and transported it, .... not to his house where his family was starving, NO to the storage, .... and guess what ... that darn hag with a house full of food went there again and picked up the freaking fish, and brought it to her house. While starving father was occupied transporting some other stuff.
Father of the starving family went back to the fisher and got a new crate full of fish. On the way back he finaly died of starvation, with the crate of fish still in his hands ... which kinda serves him right for being so god damn stupid.
Like eat the freaking fish you are holding in your hand, YES EVEN RAW would be better than dying of starvation!
With now 2 families dead (because of general AI stupidty), production was slowing down drastically. And even more so when I noticed that most people were not working anymore. They were standing at the house where the two families had died and guess what ... they were mourning! MOURNING OVER THEIR NEIGHBOURS THEY GREEDILY LET STARVE TO DEATH by stockpilling all the remaining food into their own houses, which were already full of food. Oh the irony! And now they even singed their own suicide note by stopping work for mourning. Okay I should have build a graveyard, but this behaviour is ridiculously exaggerated, and basically a death sentence to the whole village. Stoped playing right there out of frustation for the lack of control and idiotic game logic.
I usualy love sim games like this, I also like challenging hard games, but this game is not hard because of a believable, smart, or complex system. No this game is hard because its AI is so darn dumb and utterly incompetend in keeping themselfs alive. Its like a village full of Lemmings. This is whats causing all those "spirals of death" this game is so well known off.
Worst AI simulation I have ever experienced in a sim game. People who call this a feature are just wrong, "You were not producing enough food!" Ok fine, but if overproducing food is the only way of compensating stupid AI behaviour to prevent unstopable spirals of death, then this is REALY BAD GAMEDESIGN. And don't come up with "But this game was made by only one person!" so what? So is Rimworld, which is by far a better game, with a lot smarter AI, ingame depth, events, more control and a lot more long term content than Banished. And its also hard and challenging, but this time for the right reasons.

Too scary to play. I could only play it for a few minutes.
Joking of course, I always play Outlast offline, I recommend playing it offline, and also recommend that you wear headphones. This was hands down the best horror game i have ever played. It was actually terrifying, unlike most horror games. In the game you play as a journalist who got a tip email from a whistleblower working in Mount Massive Asylum, the email informs the journalist of strange things happening in the asylum and asks for help. The game starts out at the gates outside of the Asylum. The atmosphere is very unnerving from the very start. The sound effects  are great, from the disturbing noises resonating through the dark hallways, or the sound of the horrible rainstorm outside, it is always immersive. I wont spoil any of the story, but it keeps the tension level high all the way to the last second of the game. The scariest aspect the game is the fact that you dont ever get any weapons, you are forced to hide when enemies are nearby, or run. You are a very fragile character who can be easily killed. When i first learned you dont get weapons I thought, screw this game, I want to kill something. But after my first encounter with an enemy I was hooked. Theres nothing quite like roaming the halls of an old, dark , seemingly abandon Asylum unarmed. Outwit you enemy to survive. An actual realistic approach to Survival Horror. Even if you arent a fan of horror games, you should definately try this game. Its quite different from anything i have ever played.

I purchased this game in April 2016 and run it on Windows 10.
The game requirements are not high and you can play decent
at 60 FPS on older configurations (AMD 7750).
The game is a Ninja Gaiden clone infected with QTE all over the
place - you can not even finish a combo without being annoyed
by QTE.
The game is broken: you can not save your progress. At least
with the current version on steam. Also the game is sometimes
complaining that the right memory slot is not selected and
some texts are directly from the console version.
What kind of memory slots and cards shall I use on the PC?
This is rediculos. Also, the game says that your save game
is successfuly complted. When you try to load it, you spawn
directly after the INTRO sequence from the beginning of
the game at lavel 1.
It is not so bad. You can pick the game for casual play and
play it through. It is not hard. Executing basic commands
will not invoke QTE. But any kind of combo attempt will
fire the QTE imediately.
The enemies are very stupid and can easily be killed.
But - not everything is so easy. The enemies use
cheap tricks, when surrounded by 3, they wait for
you to attack one and then another one will jump
into you and damage you for sure.
Boss fights are nice but get repeditive. You just have
to repeat one and the same thing over and over
again. Killing a boss is epic. The feeling is nice.
The game mechanics are somewhat funny. Some
moves like wall run use an additional key for no
reason. In ninja gaiden if you run against wall
and jump on it, it becomes a wall run. Here you
have to hold the RT for the wall run.
You can play the game with the mouse. I find this
very nice. A lot of movie sequences use the game
engine with a far too strong blur filter.
Don't bother with the story. It has some flips but
everything feels so cheap.
If you could at least save and restore properly,
it would be a nice alternative weekend game.
For sure in 2016, this is not worth the $10.

I recommend this to anyone who likes those types of games. It's great 2-3 hours of intriguing story and very memorable experience.

(I'll keep updating this review now and then until the game is finished.)
This is what I mean when I say "survival". You are dropped in the middle of nowhere (and if you are unlucky - in the middle of a snow storm... in the middle of the night) with no idea of where to go or what to do. And even when you know where to go (I'm getting good at making my way around the first map without getting too lost too often) and what to do the game can still easily kill you.
There are several things to overcome. Though the wolves are a deadly nuisance they can be avoided. I would say that in the early and mid-game, the weather is your main antagonist. The wind will wear down your clothes, snow storms will trap you in odd locations for days, the thick and sudden fog will make you walk around in circles untill you freeze or starve to death (I've done this. "Hello, Deadfall Area... for the fourth time. I think I'll try another direction now."). In the long game (which I've never really reached) I would guess that resource management is key.
Greed also kills me more frequently than I would like to admit. ("Just one more piece of meat/hide/gut. I really need it (would like to have it) and it's not that cold/dark. I'm sure the wolves won't be back for a while.") *Sigh*
