This game is very well done. I would recommend. I generally play TE-Realism (territory-realism) so cannot speak for much else, so I will focus on what I know.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Disclaimer-I wrote this the day the Troop Transport and etc. patch came out so I cannot talk for the new game mode nor have I encountered how the transports affected the gameplay (though I doubt this will change my review at all).~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Now onwards:
First off, I would not recomend this game for a drop-in drop-out team-deathmatch style play. The real beauty in this game lies in it's tactical layout that is fully fleshed in the territory game mode, which has a chain of command from Lt. to Sgt. to Riflemen(or whatever you are playing as) with players taking each role as able. Platoon to squad to individual in other words.
In order to succeed in this game, teamwork is one-hundred percent essential. If you want to be an mg, you are going to need someone to give you ammo when you run dry and to protect your six. If you want to be a sniper, you have to pay attention to what your team is calling out, and to prioritize the correct targets (do you hit the enemy sniper, team leader, or engineer?).
Realism mode is exactly how it sounds. bullet pen. and deviation happens, getting shot in the leg slows you down, and if you don't patch your wounds you will bleed out and die (if you aren't killed outright already). AT rifles can't penetrate the SLOPED front armor, and the ppsh is a *ahem* on the recoil aspect.
Only three complaints: sometimes people join a match only to mess with others (via chat, TKs, etc.) This is not that big a problem, and if such a person arrives it is an easy procss to kick said individual. Secondly, the roles can be taken very quickly and sometimes matches are just bad (usually for the russians because the russians seem to never have good teamwork). With some patience and perseverence this can be over-come however. Finally, and my main complaint, people often drop out of matches when they are over. While this is not a bad thing per se, usually if a team gets absolutely wiped during a match almost invariably 50% of the team throws out some form of pessimistic "this team sucks/what noobs/I hate my team" and quits the server. Invariably this only furthers the disparity in the teams, as one side slowly accrues vets who are have a lot of experience that day on the server working together while the other is constantly rotating new people who have base teamwork.
These problems are entirely player-based and as such are no fault on the game itself, and I 100% recomend this to whoever reads this.
It CAN be said that this game is extremely hard, both in the beginning and later on. I was there, dying sixty times a match, never getting a kill, etc. At level 60+ now I can honestly say, it is just experience. Like in a real war the greenies do poorly at first, so it is here. Just keep trying, find good people to play with, and learn from the vets and you should do fine. It IS a hard game, and it IS worth the trials you might face every once in a while.
EDIT: Troop Transports and whatnot did not affect the game in any negative way at all. While sometimes people cheese them and block doors to objectives, or use the mg as a mounted gun this only adds more to the realism of the game: people build barricades to defend themselves, and more mgs seems like a great idea. Plus, you can throw grenades over the transports. Both teams get transports if transports are on a map. While I do believe the Soviet is faster, the germans have a better gun and can carry more (i believe). All in all, still a most excellent game.

"Quck Time Event - The Game"
This needs to be said right off the bat.  The game is chock full of Action Commands and Quick Time Events.  They are everywhere.  90% of the cutscenes will be Quick Time Events.  Every boss fight will have at least 5, if not more.  If you despise QTE's with every fiber of your being, this game is not for you.  But there is good news!  This game doesn't go all Resident Evil and make you watch 10 minutes of cutscenes beforehand or throw a game over at you if you screw up.  Rather, the game just pulls a Prince of Persia: Sands of Time bit and simply rewinds the QTE back a few seconds.  The prompts rarely change, so if you miss something, you can do it again very quickly instead of waiting forever to get it right.
In a nutshell, the gameplay is action/platformer.  You will be wall running, jumping, and swinging through levels while slicing up zombies and other monstrosities through Japan as it's taken over by some kind of virus.  Ken (The protaganist) is basically Ryu from Ninja Gaiden, slicing everything into 1/8ths.  You get three weapons, a standard sword, a heavy sword for armored enemies, and daggers on strings (think sword-chucks) to clear swarms of easy enemies.
The story isn't anything special, but it thrives on being absurd.  At one point you will land a broken airplace on a highway, and then pull it to a stop.  By yourself.  You will also smash a giant spider with a wrecking ball.  It's all in good fun.
As was stated, QTE's make up a huge chunk of the game, so it tries to keep them non-punishing.  Nothing bad happens when you fail, it just rewinds a bit.  There's a score system in place which includes how many times you failed QTE's in a chapter, but you have a fail a lot (like 100's of times) for it to make a dent in the rating system.
If you like watching a super ninja slice, dice, smash, and destroy everything that Resident Evil came up with first, all the while running down skyscrapers, then this game is perfect for you.

Zestiria is a pretty straightforward Jrpg - Grab your party and travel the world to better understand its fate and to learn more about the stories of the members who travel along with you.
The story is overall simple and clear, being somewhat predictable in some points, but the context and the characters give shine to it, enriching and making it interesting enough to grab your attention.
The combat system introduces mechanics very different from the other games of the series - like armatization, where you fuse two characters together, and the locking of some characters unabling you take them off your party - however just like the many other Tales Of games, the battle system keeps its core: lots of hack n' slash while you try to order the party members around you and make sure they're properly equipped. The combat, along with the equipement system, are not perfect and may feel cluncky before you get used to it, but it isn't something that should ruin the overall fun experience.
The graphics, despite being rather dated, fit well into the mood of the game, and still looks beautiful enough for players to feel comfortable when playing.
This isn't the best Tales Of game for sure, both story-wise and combat-wise, nonetheless it is a great game for those who enjoy a good Jrpg. Fans of the series will surely have a good time playing it, and many who never had contact with this series seem to find Zestiria really enjoyable, so it might be a good introduction into the Tales Of universe.

It's a fun gameplay concept, a good marriage of puzzle and shooter, and the art style is pretty and functional. But there's just not enough levels, or content to warrant the current price ($25), I beat the "story" in about an hour. And while there is an endless challenge mode, I got bored with that after the first round. Wait until the price drops.

(Note; I've played this game for over 250hrs outside of Steam)
It's no Tiberian Sun, but it's by no means bad. It's certainly not as horrendous as C&C4 by any stretch, but it could also have been better.
I do however have some gripes with this game that I need to mention.
- The game varies from the typical image I felt fit GDI and Nod quite well, making Nod more of a religious fanatical force, and GDI more a modern-day military, which sadly seems to be an attempt at mirroring the whole 'middle eastern conflict' that even today stretches on.
- The technology seems to have dumbed down; after the Second Tiberium War, a load of units (Titans, Subterannean units, etc) were decommissioned. Most of them are rectified in the expansion, but they were iconic to their factions and logical tech paths for them to have taken; removing them seems rather silly.
- The atmosphere is lacking in comparison to its predecessor, Tiberian Sun; the tiberium wastelands sorely lack the same sort of apocalyptic feel that was present in TibSun.
- The storyline of CABAL from TibSun: Firestorm seems as though it was completely ditched, which is a little sad.
Overall, though, the gameplay is very much solid and even to this day works well. I would recommend it, especially with the Kane's Wrath expansion, and I give it an 8.5/10.

Whether or not you like
will rest heavily on what you want out of it. I found that it didn't have what I was looking for in terms of combat and the quality of writing, but that may not be true for you. As this review focuses on criticism, I recommend reading a positive review to see what people liked.
*
While many enemies have specific vulnerabilities and resistances to encourage using one character over another, the fact is that it just doesn't much matter most of the time what you do. The game has a mechanic called "armitization" in which the main character and a "seraph" partner merge into one combatant with increased powers. You can armitize and literally mash the attack buttons and win most fights. Battle very quickly becomes tedious when you realize that careful strategy fares only slightly better than a casual attention to simple using the correct seraph to armitize with for a particular fight.
*
While I enjoy a deep combat system as much as anyone, ToZ has a bizarre and convoluted paper-rock-scissors system of "mytic artes", "seraphic artes", and standard attacks that occur in such rapid succession as to make actual strategic decisions impossible. Without going into detail, it
be a tactical decision which to use, but timing makes it impossible. Imagine your opponent throwing rock, so you play paper, but paper is slow, so by the time the paper comes down, the opponent has switched to scissors every time. This goes along with the above in the sense that there is really no decision to be made, and you can play virtually at random and do as well as you would with careful planning.
*
ToZ's characters have a tendancy to babble on and on about trifles in vague terms that seem designed to fill space, sometimes extending for
at a time. Most of it reads like it was written by someone who was paid by the word and wanted to get as much out of the arrangement as possible. Most of this dialogue does nothing to develop the characters or advance the story, and are just casual ramblings about the environment. Worse, the language is reminiscent of a second-grade level novella. The lines are simplistic and cloying. This may not bother younger players, but I couldn't stomach it. I found myself simply skipping through
of lines of filler dialogue, and I do not exaggerate.

It's everything I've ever wanted in a 3D platformer! The amazing platforming, the amazing level design (Loved the Murder on the Owl Express, that was absolutely brilliant, and the I could see the reference to a murder of crows. Very clever.), the quirky and likable characters, (The mafia guys and the Snatcher immediately come to mind as awesome supporting characters.) the clever humor, the awesome abilities you learn throughout the game (The scooter is amazing and adorable!), incredible soundtrack, and on top of all that, it's cute as heck! I cannot wait to see more of A Hat in Time! This game definitely deserves more attention than it's getting!

This game has some of the best controls I've seen in recent years. Doing simple platforming with Hat Kid feels extremely rewarding because of how good the movement is. That, coupled with the extremely creative and varied level design, makes this game have some of the best gameplay I've seen. While it is true that it is a short game, it's an incredibly entertaining experience that will charm you with its humor, characters, and crazy missions throughout. The music and atmosphere are nothing short of incredible, and those two alone might keep me coming back to replay this game.
My only critique of this game is that it lacks a bit of polish. I don't have the most powerful PC, but it is still quite good, and I still experienced some severe frame drops in a few spots in the game (even at lowest settings). On top of that, there were some weird animation bugs and clipping happening in a few spots.
Regardless, these are just minor complaints in a fantastic game otherwise. Easily glides to my top 5 games this year (which is impressive considering how stacked this year has been).
My score would overall be 9.5/10.
If you are even mildly considering this game, go for it. The developers definitely deserve every sale they get.

Yes it's slightly shorter than most games of this kind, but it has SUCH UNBRIDLED CHARM! Hat Kid is THE most adorable character in any game ever. Your hat abilities are definitely tons of fun, but true mastery of the game is being able to swap between the correct hats quickly, which is not to say that this game is hard. By and large, the game is crazy easy, but it's so colorful and delightful that you just won't be able to stop your sense of childlike wonder and awe. The humor is bizarre and brilliant, and doesn't rely almost at all on fourth wall breaking (glares in the direction of a certain recent platformer).
The only real downside I can see is that it is somewhat short, but not debilitatingly so. The music, the visuals, the mostly easygoing gameplay, the creativity, the originality, the memorability, the voice acting... all of it is absolutely incredible. 9.5-10/10. Yes, it's just that good.

Creepy.  Moody.  Atmospheric.  All those cool buzzwords.  The art direction is extremely minimalistic, and it works very well at conveying the bleakness of the world the main character is traversing.  The story is also very bare bones, but it's really all that's needed, and it leaves a lot of what's going on up to the imagination of the player.
The puzzles are for the most part simplistic, but deceptively so in a devilishly diabolical way.  It's a combination that works extremely well, and it left me feeling both super dumb for not being able to figure some of them out quicker and super smart for finally getting it right all at the same time.
About the only thing I found really frustrating about the game was actually my own fault.  I went into it intentionally entirely blind to what kind of game it was, so I had this - in hindsight, extremely foolish - preconception that it was a more or less straightforward platformer and that death was a bad thing.  It wasn't until about a third of the way in that I suddenly made the realization that not only is it a puzzle platformer with more emphasis on the puzzle part than the platforms, but that death is a central core mechanic and sometimes the only way you can figure out how certain of the puzzles work.  After I got that through my thick skull, I was able to relax and enjoy the game more on its own terms.
Beautiful, engaging brain-teaser that I enjoyed solving even as it was making me pull my hair out.  Definitely recommended for both the brilliant puzzles and the wonderfully dark esthetic.

Nightshade is a game that I simultaneously enjoy and dislike.  That may seem like a difficult task to pull off, but it's possible.  Now, I admit, the artwork is absolutely gorgeous and the voice acting phenomenal. BUT... those two things can't carry a story, and that's where Nightshade falters.  Plot issues aside, the characters are where the game truly shines and is what kept me interested  beyond my first play through.
Let me get straight to gushing about the game's characters.  While I wasn't in love with each and every one of the obtainable love interests right off the bat, most were interesting and likeable enough for me to seek out the resolution to their individual storylines.  Yes, all of the standard character tropes are present, and although Nightshade doesn't break any boundaries when it comes to its romances, it does them well.  And honestly, that's all I'm really looking for out of these games, well-written romances.  Of course, while some of the guys are more appealing than others (Goemon and Hanzo), there's at least one that will have you completely smitten by the end, maybe two.
When it comes to artwork, the game is stunning.  The character sprites are not only amazingly detailed but feature emotive facial movements that lip sync to the dialogue.  Although this isn't the first time a VN has accomplished the feat, it's always appreciated and certainly helps bring the characters to life.  Nightshade's CGs are some of the best in the genre and are not only beautifully drawn but emotionally poignant, wonderfully emphasizing the more dramatic scenes in the story.  The dialogue and voice work are also top notch with fluid writing and believable acting.  Seiyus generally do not make or break a game for me; if they're bad or distracting, I simply turn them off, no big deal.  I do admit they're really good here, and it helped immerse me in the times I felt my immersion beginning to wane.
Unfortunately, where Nightshade stumbles is in the plot department.  Granted, I've read worse otome stories, much worse, but there is WAY too much repetition in the sequence of events that follows the common route chapters.  Sure, there are some minor changes in details, but for the most part Enju spends a good portion of the game traveling through the forest evading capture by the same 3-4 shinobi clans.  It isn't until the final chapters that things change enough to rekindle my interest, but it's just not enough to keep me engaged past the 3rd character route.  By my 4th and 5th play through I had shut off my brain's story "receptors" and was merely hoping the relationship between Enju and her beau would quickly move beyond hand holding.  And no, I'm not expecting anything saucier than some light kissing, but when that's all I have to look forward to?  Well, just kiss already, dangit!!!  That said, there are plenty of feels to be had and a few enticingly steamy situations that had me begging for more.  The build-up of the romantic tension was handled splendidly in just about every route and is reason enough to play through them all.
Sadly, the abundance of feels wasn't enough to leave a bigger impression on me. I really thought I'd walk away from the game with a stronger attachment for it than I have.  As a lover of pathos and angst, there's certainly enough here you'd think I'd be in heaven, but I feel kinda...meh.  Don't get me wrong, Goemon is worth the price of admission alone (seriously, if anyone claims to hate his character, FIGHT ME). I just wish there were more weight to the story, and maybe that's a result of not relating to Enju more.  Whatever the case, I feel a little empty now thinking how this beautiful game didn't quite live up to my lofty expectations.  Perhaps someday I'll come back and play it again without those same expectations holding me down.  Still, I recommend it if you enjoy otoge at all; even with its shortcomings, it's better than most of the current offerings on Steam.

When it comes to learning a language, you have to take measures, tests, and do your best to drill all that info into your brain. It's not easy, especially if you forget easily.
Learn Japanese To Survive! Hiragana Battle is one of those multi-genre games that, with the separate gamemodes by themselves, are very bland and unimaginative. But together, it's a fantastic game that can teach you how to read Hiragana in 10 hours.
The learning part is simple. You learn a letter, learn the writing of it, and the pronunciation. Rinse and repeat for the next letter. By itself, it gets the job done, but there's a guarantee that you will remember some, but most likely not everything.
The JRPG part is nothing special either. You have to translate the Hiragana warriors to kill them. By itself, it's very bland and generic, and has the feel of a old NES RPG, with it's simple mechanics and no auto-targeting system.
But together, it's a fantastic contraption. The JRPG part REALLY drills the letters into your brain, as you need to remember to keep going with the game. The lessons are well thought out, and it's a really fun game to play.
The few critiques I can give is that reviewing lessons is easy, but there should've been previous Hiragana in later areas so you don't forget any of it, and the story and characters are sorta just there.
But it's not about the characters, it's about learning. I give this game a 8/10 for being a really good teaching tool and a pretty fun albeit simple JRPG.

As game, it's fairly bland. I could list a lot of things that could be improved.

However judging this as just another RPG game would be doing it a disservice because that's obviously not what the developers were focused on. It's a tool for teaching hiragana, with a game layer to make it more interesting.
And it works quite well.
I do have some words of caution for potential buyers and possibilities for improvements for the developer's next games.
1) The game teaches you mostly to read hiragana characters. There are a few words and sentences thrown in there aswell, but don't expect it to be enough to hold a full conversation or read any manga (except maybe those aimed at children?)
2) The game does teach you how to write the characters, but it has no mechanics to reinforce it. Unless you actively work on writing the letters yourself, you're likely to only recognize the letters when shown, and not to actually be able to write them. A writing mechanic could greatly improve this (though you'd probably need a tablet to use that effectively).
3) The game could do with some more repetition. The characters you learn are usually only shown in one particular area. Once you're past that area, you may not come across them ever again untill the last dungeon. This makes it very likely you'll forget at least some of them. Introducing words in battle sooner or a new game + mode where every character can be found in battle in every area might help here.
That said, the game does a much better job in teaching a foreign language than I've ever seen in schools, even if it's only a starting point. Definitely try this if you're interested in either japanese language or educational games.

Good idea, needs more balancing.
The developers toot their own horn about realism and the fragility of human nature, but a huge part of the endgame challenge in this game is bad game balance. There are essentially two phases to this game. When you first start, you scramble around looking for basic necessities and establishing some kind of stability. Phase two is when the nearby supplies run out and you must start hunting and crafting to survive. Phase one is super fun, phase two (the way it's implemented in Feb of 2015) is horrible. You will die for stupid reasons, and you will hate the game for it.
Stupid reason 1) The rifle in this game is impossible to use. Apparently at one point every shot was an instant kill, which made the game too easy, so now every shot is an instant miss. I'm not really joking. Bullets seem to miss consistently at anything past spitting range. If you do get a lucky shot, your target will take off like an olympic runner across the map leaving a helpful blood trail. If you manage to track it down, expect to shoot it two or three more times before it finally drops. Eventually these animals will die on their own from blood loss, but that never helped me. It seems like lucky headshots at close range will kill something instantly, but out of about 30 shots I've taken since I got this game, that only happened once.
The rifle in the game is a .30-06. In real hunting, the primary way to kill an deer is to destroy their heart, which should kill them nearly instantly. If you're lucky enough to shoot the head it's possible to kill an anmial that way, but very unlikely because their skulls are thick and their brains are small. A proper shot to the vital (heart) area might not kill them instantly, but will cause massive trauma and bleeding to death in minutes, not this olympic sprinter crap.
The most effective way to use the rifle is to get close enough to a wolf that it runs at you, shoot it once, and then finish it off in the wolf attack minigame. Stupidly unrealistic and dangerous. This penalizes you for using actual survival knowledge.
Stupid Death 2) You will inevitably die because you are never given notices or warnings about your changing conditions. The basic mechanic in this game is managing your warmth, thirst, fatigue and hunger (in that order). These qualities degrade constantly, and you must stay on top of each to avoid dying. Normally, checking your survival stats frequently (tab button) is enough to keep you on top of your situation, so that even if you die, you know why you're dying. However, some activities advance the game time (things like sleeping, cooking, and crafting), which degrades these survival stats very quickly, since they compress hours of game time into seconds of playing time. If you're not careful, your character will literally work themselves to death, giving you no opportunity to intervene in preventable deaths.
Once I very nearly died from dehydration while working on a wolfskin coat. I had lots of food and water on my person, and all of my needs were satisfied, so I keyed up eight hours of crafting work. Once finished I was more than 2/3rds dead from dehydration. That was annoying but not tragic. More aggrivating was the time when I wanted to harvest a full deer. I had good warmth to start, but while harvesting a storm kicked up and the temperature plummeted. When I finished I was freezing with 7% condition left, which gave me a wonderful minute of panic searching before I died. My well developed character died with a fully stocked and warm safehouse just over the ridge, because they worked right up to the point of death.
What makes a survival game fun is managing risk and making informed risk vs. reward decisions. Like I said at the top- this game works wonderfully in the first phase. Which way do I go? Does this area look dangerous? Is it worth it to run past that wolf or should I save my flare and take the long way around? That feeling breaks down in a big way once you want to set up a base camp. Maybe this is, in part, an inherent limitation of the current sandbox mode, and I will absolutely love the eventual story mode. Unfortunately, it feels to me like all of my late game deaths are entirely due to the game design and not the consequences of my own decisions, which is why I can't reccomend the game in it's current form.

I've been watching Superhot pretty closely ever since the demo they released back in 2013. I'm not sure how the dev time was so long, but I'm happy to say the final product has met my expectations very well, and that's without any extra updates or features added after launch (if there are any pls say yes devs)
So what is Superhot? It's like... a very fast-paced shooter based entirely around playing slowly. Sounds strange at first, and that's exactly what Superhot is. I feel the best way sell how good this game is, is by telling you firsthand instead of trying to describe it.
To put it bluntly, Superhot is probably the only game that lets you jump around the corner of an office cubicle in slow motion, then launch a katana from your hand while sailing through the air to pierce two people straight through the chest and literally turn them into a f'king kebab.
Superhot is probably the only game where I can kill a large group of heavily armed enemies just by throwing bottles and glasses at them.
Superhot is probably the only game where I can throw my weapon at somebody to make them drop their weapon, then sail through the air, grab their weapon in slow motion, fly directly out a nearby window, turn in a full 180 and then fire back at the person I stole the weapon from while sailing out a window to my death.
Superhot allows for so much freedom in how you play. Whether you sit back and slowly and methodically kite each enemy towards you while you whittle them down slowly, or you go cartwheeling through a big maze of bullets defending yourself with random clutter items left on the floor and impaling everyone with a katana, it's pretty strategic. Each level pits you against a certain amount of "Red Dudes", who you fight. You can use whatever you want to in order to defeat them, and it's that freedom to dive around the room, dodging bullets in slow motion that makes Superhot so hectic and fun.
It's also got a story, and quite a trippy one at that. The main game only lasts about 2 hours, which is hardly worth the 20 euro price tag, but Superhot also comes with two other modes, both of which are filled with extra content. So far, I'm over 10 hours into the game and still nowhere near bored, and keep in mind, I'm only playing this at 20 frames. If I can play a fast paced game that requires a high framerate at 20 frames and it keeps drawing me back into it every time I try to do something more productive, you can assume the game is addictive.
The only cons of Superhot are the hit detection. Man, the hit detection. For a game that requires such surgical precision, it's surprisingly bad. I can't seemingly fit between two bullets, even though the gap between them is definitely big enough. I throw a katana at someone but it goes right through them. I throw a clutter item at someone to stun them and it just bounces off them without having any effect. The hit detection needs an improvment.
Other than that, the spawn points on Endless mode are very messy. When an enemy spawns, they'll go through a short "fade-in" animation. The problem is, you can't see them during the animation but they can still fire at you. To add to this, enemies can spawn directly behind you, and there's nothing worse than losing a killstreak because someone suddenly appeared behind you with no warning, and then just filled your back with lead.
Other than those two small gripes, the game is perfect for anyone who enjoys bullet time, shooters and fast-paced, hectic gameplay.

After getting this game for free in a Giveaway, I had decided to give it a go to blow some time.
Overall, the game has pretty solid mechanics but suffers from a poor sense of level design and player direction/teaching.
In the very first screen of the game, I found myself having to scramble to find out the controls while I was already taking damage from an enemy with a quick projectile. Once I managed to defeat that enemy, I spent a bit of time jumping around and getting a hold of everything, only to be attacked by more enemies (some of which were in the air) that were spawning from the right.
Once I started progressing through the level, I noticed immediately that any enemy that fired a projectile had no tell or warning of it's attack, and the enemies' projectiles were too fast to react to. On top of this, enemies will fire at you the moment they appear on screen, resulting in many points of damage that are near-impossible to avoid without knowing it's location.
Another thing I found was that despite how many enemies you defeat on your way across the level, enemies will continue to spawn from behind. Often times when I needed to back away from a swarm of enemies to collect myself, I found myself confronted by a similar bunch of enemies in the same area I cleared not 5 seconds prior.
The powerups in the game are fun but their powerlevel is varied immensely. Anything that fires slow prevents you from attacking the projectile-shooting robots before they hit you, and anything without a range or spread will leave you unprotected against at least one or two of the enemies on screen at any time. The color coding itself seems fairly backwards as well, as the pickups that change the gun that shoots orange bullets is blue, and the pickups that change blue bullets is orange. I understand that this is supposed to match the character and the side-kick's color schemes, but it caused issues when I'd accidently overwrite a good weapon. Another point of interest with powerups, is that the same shot type has different symbols depending on if it's for the main character or the side-kick.
Other than that, most level design issues stem from enemy placement (covering entire platforms, being placed in spots that will probably get you shot if you try to attack, spawning behind you) and the initial difficulty level in the first levels.
Overall, I feel like the game can be really good if the developer just tweaked the enemies a bit (give them a small warning animation before they shoot at the player) and looked at the difficulty curve of the early game. Making some weapons better would most likely be beneficial to the player, but it's not a requirement. I still reccommend playing this game if you are looking for an NES styled nostalgia trip, just don't expect it to be fair all the way through.

Command & Conquer 3 is the Sequel to 1999's Tiberian Sun, which in turn is the sequel to the classic Command & Conquer from 1995. EA Los Angeles had lived up to expectations with this game.
C&C 3 is the first game in the franchise to use squad-based gameplay. Tiberium (the resource) is abundant and can be easily found on the map and can easily be told how valuable it is, as Blue Tiberium is more valuable than the common Green Tiberium.
Even though using the same game engine as the previous game, Command & Conquer Generals, the game looks drastically different. The dark dystopian theme fits the game so well, showing that both of the main factions are fighting for there life. The units are made so that it is easy to tell which side they are one, as GDI units are more Gold and metallic, while Nod units are usually black and matted.
Even though the game does try something new, it does not lose the 'Command & Conquer' Style, unlike the next game in the series... (I'm looking at you, C&C4...)

Pros:
- Fun and tight gameplay evoking the likes of Contra, Power Blade, and -- bizarrely yet awesomely -- Kirby (due to the innovative jetpack mechanic)
- Truly excellent graphics and sound design, with a feel that reminds one in particular of some of the finest Sunsoft games of the NES era
- That wonderful balance between being challenging enough to hold interest but nowhere near the obnoxious over-difficulty most modern "retro" games are rife with
Cons:
- Sadly, the music doesn't compare to most decent NES games' OSTs, and is unfittingly quite poor in comparison to the rest of the game's quality.  So many fantastic Famitracker musicians out there could have been hired to create a wonderfully composed and fitting soundtrack for this game; I don't really know what happened here, but it's very disappointing.
- The game's over with extremely quickly, even compared to NES games of very modest length, perhaps partly due to how rarely you'll die and be forced to memorize the stage and boss patterns as perfectly as most such games.  It might be worth it to crank up the difficulty even on your first playthrough if you're an experienced retro gamer for this reason.
- Cutscenes are completely pointless even for a guy like me who generally enjoys them; simply slapping sprites that are weirdly ugly compared to the rest of the game of your player character and his boss and having them spout one or two very basic lines doesn't really have a place.  Either go for Ninja Gaiden-style quality, Clash at Demonhead-style humor or just don't bother.
Overall, though, the fun factor and quality of *most* of the game is high enough that this title is absolutely worth the price tag for any oldschool action/platformer/run-and-gun fan.

Before I review this game, let me explain the history between me and the "Tales of" series:
Tales of Symphonia has been my favorite game since playing it on the gamecube. Yes I also have a review of this on Steam, feel free to read it too. Yes, I loved Symphonia more than Final Fantasy VII, or any other JRPG I have ever played.
Then I played Symphonia: Dawn of the New World, It was so bad, with a plot so terrible that I could not manage worse if I tried, and with such a self-contradicting story that I actually blocked memory of playing it until Ityped some of the words below and came back up to type this in right here. I must remove myself from the topic of this game, or else I will rant on forever.
Then I played Tales of the Abyss, and although they improved the battle movement controls, its story was an incoherent mess where instead of naming the element of magic they would refer to every element as a numbered "Phonon" tier, and to top it all of the story was kinda poor beyond that.
Then, I played Tales of Xillia, and it had what is perhaps the greatest battle system I have ever played in an Action/JRPG. It was great until in the last few hours of play, when the plot tries to make drama by making the hero characters protect the anti-magic NAZI villains for a faint hope at what could only be a false and temporary peace. The turn of events was so stupid, that I barely could play through any of Xillia 2 before I gave up on it.
I briefly tried Tales of Vesperia, but didn't get far... I had lost hope.
Then, I prepurchase Tales of Zestiria on Steam. At first, things were looking up. The world felt soft and sweet. The protagonist was an optimist in a pessimist's world, which remided me much of Symphonia's Lloyd and his optimism in that pessimistic world. This feeling did not last long.
I quickly realized the gameplay was crap. First thing I noticed was how the camera is always centered right behind your player character. This is a major issue, as it makes it nigh-impossible to figure out how close you are to the enemy you are fighting.
To make matters even worse, they added that stupid thing where your protagonist fuses with one of the spirit allies. You might say "It cannot be that bad" or "It was like the Limit Breaks from Final Fantasy which you loved", but these are not true. First, they are bad because they remove one character temporarily from play. This means that if you need to use a specific fusion to increase your chances of winning and that character happens to be your healer, you have probably already lost. Second, Limit Breaks, Overdrives, and Trances are not required to win in Final Fantasy and you can do fine without using them, but the fusions are definitely necessary. Some bosses just cannot be beaten without exploiting their elemental weakness via the proper fusion.
Furthermore, I never have had to really grind in a Tales of game until now, because the Action elements allowed you to supplement your low level with skill and a liitle luck until now.
Lastly, the combos and blocking in this game felt wrong. As of writing this review, I have long since dropped this game, so I cannot remember excactly what it was. It may have been the controls or even related to the terrible camera, but I do recall having a terrible time with attacks and blocks.
I gave up not too far into the game. It was shortly after that one character leaves the party and you leave the first major city. People who have played this game might criticize me for reviewing this with only a short while played, and I cannot necessarily fault them for that. Even so, I really can't recommend this game.

Classy, cool gun-fu has been seen before in games (The Specialists HL mod springs to mind). Bullet time has been seen before in games (hello Max Payne). Stylish oversaturated minimalistic graphics have been seen before in games (not everyone at once scream Mirror's Edge please). However Superhot seems to be the first that mixes it all together in an very effective way and adds a special fourth wall breaking sauce over it with croutons of a deeper meta story mixed in.
Excellent game.
However, not counting endless mode and the challenges, it is a *very* short game. Thirtyfour levels in three hours and only a few of those levels pose a real challenge. The game, however cool and stylish it is, however good the gameplay is, is just too damned short and easy at the price it's selling.
I would recommend waiting for a spring/easter/christmas/humble bundle/save the whales sale, for a tenner (in UKP/EUR/USD) I would highly recommend it, but at launch price the admission fee to the coolness is too high.
Still, recommended.

If you're looking for a decent otome game with some really nice art, would definitely recommend this game. All in all the story is pretty meh. Nothing too outstanding and nothing too out of the box. The art is fantastic though. Great quality all around, no weird poses. They really put a lot of work into the artwork for this VN and it's probably the best aspect of the game (to me at least).
I would also like to applaud the animation for the fight sequences. It's nothing extravagant, but just having the characters move around the screen instead of reading blocks and blocks of text was a huge + for me. It was a big help when trying to visualize what was going on.
The game kept me interested for at least a few routes. After that the main plot, apart from the romance, was a snooze fest. It's also a bit confusing, because they use different plots and motivations for different routes. It kinda screwed up what I had originally thought was going to be a coherent overarching story. I really hate it when they do this. Because of this there is no real "correct order" to play the routes in. Though if you're really wanting to go by some sort of list I'd recommend doing Goemon -> Chojiro -> Hanzo -> Kuroyuki -> Gekkamaru.
Now in terms of romance...
I had the most beef with Chojiro's route. You spend half of his route pining for him instead of spending time with him. Ugh. He got cucked more than Gekkamaru, and Gekkamaru is the childhood friend archetype. What is this. AUGH, by the time you finally get to be in the same room as him I was already done with his route. Sorry. I did finish it, but nothing in that route could save my interest at that point.
Gekkamaru, on the other hand, had a pretty decent route overall. I was surprised cause his archetype usually ends up being the normal one. The control. The one you get out of the way cause everyone else will have a more interesting route. But I found his to be the most balanced route. Good from start to finish. 8/10 would maybe go through again.
His brother though...what a doozy. Drama from beginning to end. If you like that whole angsty spice, then you'll love Kuroyuki to bits. Not to say there aren't sweet moments, but I'm not into stockholm syndrome story. It's a big turn-off. He's a cute kid with a sad past, that's all I really have to say about his route.
I saved Goemon and Hanzo for last because I love the stoic and playboy types.
Goemon was...ok. I was a bit disappointed, guess I expected too much. His was route was far from being bad, I just felt there were a lot of missed opportunities. It's also the "everyone lives happily ever after" route so after playing every route where SOMEONE DIES I just...it was way too lighthearted to end with. I regret playing his route last lol.
Hanzo, on the other hand, was refreshing. Mainly because the mc doesn't act like a wimpy little girl even though she can obviously fight as a ninja too?? She talks a lot about wanting to prove she isn't a liability in the first few chapters, but she acts like a martyr in 4 out of 5 routes??? Can you tell I was really bothered by it? Cause I was. IT WAS SO NICE to see her stand up to fight instead of standing up to DIE for once. The romance was good. I didn't have any strong thoughts towards it. Oh, and his last cg was the most disappointing CG I have had the privilege to witness in this VN.
Some of the translations miss their mark, but what can you do. It's not terrible to the point where things are overlooked, so don't worry too much about it.
I'd order the routes (imo):
1. Hanzo
2. Gekkamaru
3. Goemon
4. Kuroyuki
5. Chojiro
1 being the best overall, 5 being the worst overall.
This ranking is also influenced by my preferences, so take it with a grain of salt.

"Ya like Jazz?"
Is the question I want to start off with.  Cuphead is a RUTHLESS platformer that goes back to the days when platforming skills were all you needed in the gaming world (i.e. Mario, Mega Man, etc.).  You make a mistake?  You'll be punished for it.  One little slip up means your continuation or your death.  With it's 1930s-esque cartoon style and swing/ragtime music to boot (even recorded using techniques or in the vein of 30s-40s music), Cuphead is a game you don't want to miss.
Pros:
+ the game is VERY fluid in everything it does
+ graphically the most unique game I'd ever seen
+ controls are tight and responsive
+ upgrades that you can buy and equip for your own personal playstyle
+ bosses are challenging and unforgiving
+/- the platforming areas allow you to collect gold BUT you can only go back to collect pieces you missed
+ upgrades are inexpensive, meaning you can easily rack them up
+ drop in/out co-oop (haven't tested this yet but that's how I assume it works)
+ GORGEOUS music; they nailed the style of 30s rag and swing music.  (If you don't like the actual *sound* of the music [it sounds fuzzy and that's the point; recorded music of that era usually did])
+ cartoon-esque "way way" VO which is an incredibly nice detail to add in for some characters
+ unique parry technique for pink objects
+A "simple or regular" mode for bosses for those who don't want to be ♥♥♥♥ed up the♥♥♥♥♥by bosses!
Cons:
- some may find the graphics options... minimal.  But for a game like this there really wouldn't need to be any (NOT a big issue for me at all, though)
- if you collect all the gold during a "run and gun" level, you can't go back to farm it (not much of a deal breaker but again it could be for some)
1930/1930: would play ridiculously challenging platformer again.  Ya like jazz?

First off, I'm not a big fan of the 'Hardcore' Hard games like Dark Souls. Games that are head-bangingly difficult from the get-go are a no-go for me. Cuphead avoids this for me. It IS hard. It WILL grind you down. But it doesn't pick you up and deliberately push you down again in the mud, wondering where to go next time, because there isn't an obvious path for you to take. Dark Souls does that, and I dislike that for it.
Cuphead, on the other hand, is a GOOD kind of difficult, where you will die but say "Oh, I could do that next time," instead of get frustrated. The hints you pick up as you play and learn the attacks of the enemies, the layouts of the level, even the parryslap thing it makes it so you improve. And eventually, you can take down even the toughest foes you were struggling with before.
It's easy to struggle in this game, but not hard to push past those points. It's a GOOD difficult game, and I absolutely applaud MDHR for that.
P.S. I can't be bothered to learn the real names of the bosses, so I just make them up as I go along, Blue Blob Bill being a prime example.

The Good:
Great replay value
Lots of diverse items to use throughout the playthrough
4 Character Classes to choose from; Warrior/Rogue/Huntress/Mage
8 Specialty Sub-classes/Masteries; Gladiator/Berserker for Warrior, Battlemage/Warlock for Mage, Freerunner/Assassin for Rogue and Sniper/Warden for Huntress
Scroll of Wipe Out = Tactical Shop Robbery
The Bad:
Durability System; can be systematically abused by the AI even when you conserve items to help prevent this
No Save, even a soft interval save at bosses, 1 run or your done
Some items I feel need to be tweaked a little for balance; Huntress Ranged weapon for instance
Ankh, while seemingly attractive, mostly punishes you for being used, especially in later levels where its needed most
The Ugly:
-Conserve your upgrade scroll when not using them! I cannot stress this enough, which means every time you run into a fire you run risk of burning them up & until you can buy (or rob) the Scroll Holder from the shopkeeper. Later levels will quickly have you fumbling with broken weapons that don't work well on monsters even if you are the same experience level they are, you invested a ton of resources into a great weapon/armor, don't waste it now!
-Soft Interval saves at Bosses would be nice, not required as some I have talked to argued it would make the game TOO easy.
-The Ankh should really let you recover some/all items from your previous corpse if you get resurrected by it, getting killed at level 22 then having 0 items at that point means either essentially killing yourself (as you now likely have no means of combatting durability loss in items or healing or eating) or starting over. Either way, back to the main menu.
-Huntress Ranged Boomerang should not drop from your inventory if your are resurrected from the Ankh either, I know typically only equipped items make it through a resurrection, but since you can have a melee weapon & still use the boomerang (the main featured weapon for Huntress I remind) why must it be forever gone also? Its not like I can find another one on my way down....
-Scroll of Wipe Out, one of the few things that I feel are OP because it can be abused also but unlike other items this actually works in your favor & most times you need that to balance some of the other issues I mentioned. I keep my SWO for shopkeeper levels, I sell all my useless crap to the shopkeeper then BAM! Killed all the monsters on that level currently(for a hefty XP boost) & rid myself of a no-good, overcharging shopkeeper and help myself to all his wonderful (and now free!) items, including the healing potions & expensive bags they want you to buy. Shopkeepers here like that reminded me of Ripley in the movie Aliens; "You know Burke I don't know what species is worse, you don't see them screwing each other over for a damned percentage". Who the bloody hell tries to profit from the depths of a monster ridden hole anyhow? But I digress.....
Overall: Great & entertaining but nothing legendary, especially in the graphics department, don't look for shiny graphic 'oh wow' moments here. I played this mostly on my phone before buying it here on Steam during the Holiday Sale for $3. I think normally its $5, but still well worth it
If there was ever a game that was worth waiting 87 years for...this is it.

Really beautiful art from the amazing Teita with some really interesting visual effects thrown in to go with your visual story. The battle scenes are really cool. The backgrounds are lovely but after 2-3 routes you will notice the recycled art. For me this did not detract from anything at all. Another fully voiced (minus the heroine) game with some top quality acting from some favorite voice talent. Your ears will thank you for playing. Each voice is really matched perfectly to the characters. The music fit well and I really enjoyed it. I wish I had gotten the OST bundle but I plan to buy the soundtrack anyway later.
The story itself is beautiful but often it gets rather tragic. These period warrior pieces tend to be on the sad side more often then not and Nightshade is no different. Saying that, the romance is well done and builds slowly over the course of each story. They did a great job of trying to keep it in the realm of believable. Sometimes I got really frustrated at the heroine's inability to decide if she is shy or not. There was also quite a lot more overlap/repeat in the stories of each route then I would have liked but at that point its just being picky. The story itself is good with a few interesting twists per route.
Each route seems to only have 2 ends (good and bad). I wish there would have been more endings and/or more dialogue choices for each one. That could be a matter of preference though. I like when the story makes me feel like I have an impact on it. Otherwise, I really enjoyed it and there was no shortage of swooning thats for sure! Two thumbs up from this player :)  I would not at all mind seeing a part 2 to this one with a continuation of their stories or some sort of epilogue of their happy ever afters.
The menu/ui is pretty standard fare for a VN. Skip goes -really- fast but theres some options in the menu to customize that.  Auto mode is nice to sit back and enjoy. Theres also the standard gallery and a memory section to re-play chapters. Nothing to exciting. If you don't set the character name in the extra menu then all memories will default to 'Enju'.  You can also set the menu's character voice in the settings which is a nice little addition.
Unrelated to the game itself but a personal gripe of mine... I really wish more companies would release some of the merchandise our way when they localize these titles! Theres so much they put out but its so impossible to find as we often don't get translations at all or until years later and have to scour auction sites.

It was July 7th, 2011.
While investigating reports of unlawful weapons trafficking, peacekeeping forces encountered an unclassified carnivorous species occupying a small village in Northern Africa. These rabid creatures were easily provoked and resistant to conventional attack. Eight specimens were encountered in the region now referred to as "Ground:ALPHA"... Only four were successfully contained for study. Victims of the attack were quarantined at a research facility nearby. These victims displayed signs of internal liquefaction and accelerated necrosis, similar to symptoms of other flesh-eating viruses native to that region.
But it wasn't a viral outbreak. It was a parasitic infestation. A previously unidentified species of hook worm was found beneath the skin of the Ground: ALPHA specimens. These parasites, we call them "Alpha-worms", laid dozens of eggs inside their hosts, which in turn produced numerous larvae. These larvae penetrated the bloodstream and triggered a variety of genetic failures. However, unlike most genetic failures, these symptoms were not fatal. Instead, infested victims were larger, stronger… and driven by hunger. Using the research gained from the Ground: ALPHA specimens, a team of some special individuals were assembled. Minor outbreaks occurred over the next few years, but elite squad quickly put them down. Which brings us to the current situation in Tokyo...

It's the most innovative shooter i've played in years. No joke. If Hotline Miami was a first-person shooter, this game would be it. The game throws you in every kind of action movie scenario from jumping into buildings full of bad guys or having a good old fashion bar shootout. The controls are very responsive and all the mechanics work as intended. You will easily spend a few hours being sucked into it.
That said though the story mode is incredibly short only being 2-3 hours in length, a shame really when you consider the $25 price tag. Another gripe I have is the lack of weapons. There's only a pistol, shotgun, and an assault rifle for the guns, while melee consists of just a katana, baseball bat, and a lead pipe.
Nonetheless, it was very well made game that kept me entertained from beginning to the end and there was hardly a dull moment. I hope that the devs will address the game's length through perhaps a more fleshed out sequel, or at the very least a free expansion.

This is a game that cannot make up its mind what it wants to be.  It manages to have the worst combination of elements from a sim racer and an arcade racer, resulting in a game that does neither element well.  All of the vehicles handle as though none of the developers have driven a car in real life; cars seems to always exhibit copious amounts of understeer or spin wildly out of control the instant you have the audacity to touch the brake.  My pickup truck handles better than these “things” that the game lets you control – I hesitate to call them cars.
Technically, the game is a pure fright.  My aging, but still by no means humble, gaming laptop was largely unable to run this game with the graphical configurations above the lowest possible setting, resulting in a game that actually manages to look and run worse than the original FlatOut.  Let that sink in for a minute – a ten year old game manages to look prettier and run better than a game made in
!  After cutting the in-game resolution in half and disabling as many graphical options as possible, I finally had what looked like a worthy contender for Best N64 Game of 1998.
The damage modeling is a joke.  Parts fly off cars and the frames bend up to a certain degree, but at the end of the day, the cars handle like rigid bodies and have a damage model to match.  If you want spectacular crashes, go play BeamNG.Drive.  The cars handle like actual cars – and that’s considering BeamNG’s fairly simcadey car handling to begin with – the game isn’t utterly impossible to run, and the damage modeling makes an utter mockery of Next Car Game.
As a final insult, it turns out purchasing this game through the developer’s website was the worst idea I’ve had in a long time.  It turns out that Valve will not refund games purchased outside their store, even though the game
.  There’s no DRM free version, no alternate digital portal that the game could have been purchased through; even though the game is a Steam exclusive, I’ve essentially been soaked for
.  Needless to say, it’ll be a while before I throw extra money at a developer – especially Bugbear.

If you are open to it, this game can make you look at games, art, and people a little bit more closely than you did before. To say anything more revealing about it would ruin your fun.

The Good:
Great replay value
Lots of diverse items to use throughout the playthrough
4 Character Classes to choose from; Warrior/Rogue/Huntress/Mage
8 Specialty Sub-classes/Masteries; Gladiator/Berserker for Warrior, Battlemage/Warlock for Mage, Freerunner/Assassin for Rogue and Sniper/Warden for Huntress
Scroll of Wipe Out = Tactical Shop Robbery
The Bad:
Durability System; can be systematically abused by the AI even when you conserve items to help prevent this
No Save, even a soft interval save at bosses, 1 run or your done
Some items I feel need to be tweaked a little for balance; Huntress Ranged weapon for instance
Ankh, while seemingly attractive, mostly punishes you for being used, especially in later levels where its needed most
The Ugly:
-Conserve your upgrade scroll when not using them! I cannot stress this enough, which means every time you run into a fire you run risk of burning them up & until you can buy (or rob) the Scroll Holder from the shopkeeper. Later levels will quickly have you fumbling with broken weapons that don't work well on monsters even if you are the same experience level they are, you invested a ton of resources into a great weapon/armor, don't waste it now!
-Soft Interval saves at Bosses would be nice, not required as some I have talked to argued it would make the game TOO easy.
-The Ankh should really let you recover some/all items from your previous corpse if you get resurrected by it, getting killed at level 22 then having 0 items at that point means either essentially killing yourself (as you now likely have no means of combatting durability loss in items or healing or eating) or starting over. Either way, back to the main menu.
-Huntress Ranged Boomerang should not drop from your inventory if your are resurrected from the Ankh either, I know typically only equipped items make it through a resurrection, but since you can have a melee weapon & still use the boomerang (the main featured weapon for Huntress I remind) why must it be forever gone also? Its not like I can find another one on my way down....
-Scroll of Wipe Out, one of the few things that I feel are OP because it can be abused also but unlike other items this actually works in your favor & most times you need that to balance some of the other issues I mentioned. I keep my SWO for shopkeeper levels, I sell all my useless crap to the shopkeeper then BAM! Killed all the monsters on that level currently(for a hefty XP boost) & rid myself of a no-good, overcharging shopkeeper and help myself to all his wonderful (and now free!) items, including the healing potions & expensive bags they want you to buy. Shopkeepers here like that reminded me of Ripley in the movie Aliens; "You know Burke I don't know what species is worse, you don't see them screwing each other over for a damned percentage". Who the bloody hell tries to profit from the depths of a monster ridden hole anyhow? But I digress.....
Overall: Great & entertaining but nothing legendary, especially in the graphics department, don't look for shiny graphic 'oh wow' moments here. I played this mostly on my phone before buying it here on Steam during the Holiday Sale for $3. I think normally its $5, but still well worth it

This is my first "Tales of" game that I've played, as I'm more of a Final Fantsy fan. I bought this game expecting about 40 to 60 hours, and was surprised by how long it took to play through. I did all of the sidequests available on the first playthrough, and was definitely not expecting 100+ hours. Not sure if that's a normal timeframe for a Tales game, but again, FF games can be done in 40 to 60 hours. I won't lie, it did start to feel somewhat tedious the longer it went on.
I really don't understand all the hate this game received. Yeah, it does have some flaws, but for me, none of them are deal breakers. The battle system can be repetitive if you choose to make it that way, but the same can be said for every action RPG I've ever played.  The story is one of the most cliche I've seen in a really long time, but I found it charming and it gave me precisely what I wanted. The characters were engaging and interesting throughout the game.
Again, the game isn't perfect. Locked at 30 FPS sucks (unless you use the community patch). But still, I'd recommend this game for sure.

Jet Gunner is a side-scrolling platformer with a late-era NES aesthetic that wildly succeeds in emulating the most frustrating and archaic elements of that era.
Enemies that fire immediately as they appear on screen, usually while you are mid-jump. Weapon powerups that have strange arcs that prevent them from hitting enemies directly in front of you. Massive knock-back. Vertical stages in which the bottom of the screen instantly kills you. Bullet-sponge enemies that necessitate a large life bar, resulting in a sloppy, inelegant play experience in which you can't finesse your way through a level but must rather brute-force your way through like a rabid speedrunner taking damage-- just to make it through a level, not to shave time.
These flaws could be overlooked or even appreciated as period-specific quirks if the visual and audio design of the game were more memorable, but they're just aren't. It succeeds at being a hard-as-nails NES game but that isn't really enough as unless you've played the entire NES library, there are probably dozens of better designed *actual NES* games that you could play and enjoy instead as well as better retro pastiche games on Steam.
That said, it still felt pretty ♥♥♥♥ing good to beat it.

I've got kind of my own little steam game based retro console going on my alienware. If it were a real console, I couldn't be happier with the launch line up, and Jet Gunner rounds things out so nicely with amazing run and gun platformer action - the first of its kind that really feels like an NES game but with none of the things that make going back to that console sometimes a little disappointing. Jet Gunner has the pallet and graphics you remember, but the controls are way more air tight and the whole experince is just smooth as silk. It really says something about this game when it saves your progress so you can continue from the last level you played but I always choose to play from the begining anyway because the experince is just so much fun. This may be the best purchase I've made on steam so far. I could give this game a simple but controversial three word review, and I mean this sincerely: "Better than contra." This game isn't just reminecent of the NES era, its what we all thought NES gaming should have been but so rarely was. With some distance between us and that wonder console now we can finally craft games that emulates its unique style but corrects all its limitations to bring a simple, addictive, and blissful gaming experince and Jet Gunner shows them how its done. Plus a hardcore a challanges mode to keep you coming back to master the game (and unlike many games, this one is actually fun to pursue mastery of) long after you've beaten it standard.  I really hope other retro style game developers are taking notes on this title but even more than that, I need Jet Gunner 2 to be a thing in my life.
The Beginner's Guide is probably the best proof of this media has finally come of age.

Overview:
Hiragana Battle is an interesting look at how a videogame could be used to educate someone on a subject beyond small bits of information or factoids. The game does a decent job at teaching Hiragana, thought it lacks in other areas.
The game attempts to teach the player the Hiragana form of Japanese writing, which is said by the game to be the most basic form of Japanese writing and that almost all forms of sentences can be written from it.
Gameplay:
The gameplay teaches Hiragana by presenting you with lessons and then adding the content of the lesson into battles. The battles play out in normal JRPG style, but the enemies are Hiragana characters you have learned. In order to damage them you must know what they mean.
The gameplay is by no means complex. The combat is simple, and most of the gameplay aspects follow suit. However this isn’t that big of a deal; Hiragana Battle is a game about learning Hiragana, not about tactical turn based combat.
Story:
The overarching story is pretty cliché. Wizard wants power. Wizard tries to get power. Heroes decide to kill wizard. So on. So forth. Perfectly acceptable seeing what the actual goal was.
The characters aren’t very engaging.  I found myself forgetting their names not seconds after I met them.  That’s fine though; the characters are intended to ease the pain of learning a whole other language, not to grip you with a harrowing tale of wizard fighting.
I came to observe the game from a designer perspective and to have some fun learning something new. Some philosophical meaning behind the story would fog up the real point of the game. The point is to learn Hiragana. Everything else is servile to that end.
Education:
I can’t speak on the accuracy of what I’m learning. This is the first time I have ever heard of the term Hiragana; much less that Hiragana is one of three writing styles in Japan. I have to take it on faith that these people know what they are doing. I hope that my faith is well placed, which by the majority of reviews it seems it is.
Before I delve in, you need a pen and paper, no joke. Unless you plan to communicate with a single Hiragana vowel, at the risk of sounding like a caveman emerging from Mount Fuji, you might want to write this stuff down. Class in session!
The developers made it pretty hard to screw up learning Hiragana. They give you the sound of the letter or phrase, the English equivalent, an animation on how to write it with the exact order of the strokes, and they give you a study-guide that you can fall back on if you are a bit rusty or don’t remember something. They got their bases covered which adds credibility and makes it far easier to learn.
This being said, the game does ask that you actually study Hiragana on your own time. This is the only way you’re going to learn this stuff. Yes, you can make a cheat sheet and just look off that, but that negates the whole game. If you want a story driven JRPG, I respectfully point you to the Final Fantasy series. Hiragana Battle is a JRPG, but in reality it is a game about learning Hiragana, so if you are looking for story and gameplay alone Hiragana Battle might not fill that gap.
I am a tad bit dubious as to what extent can you actually take what they teach you. I consider this as an introduction to the language, but I’m not really in the position to say. As I stated earlier this is my most basic exposure to this stuff.
In Total:
The game does what it sets out to do. Teach people Hiragana. Not only does it succeed, it got positive reception too. Hard to get positive reviews when making a game that teaches anything, much less something as complex and as vast as a language.
I would recommend this game to anyone who want to give a well-executed educational game a try, people who want to try and learn Hiragana, and most of all, game developers. Yes, game developers. A lot can be learned from this game in terms of teaching through gamification, and I would love to see a wave of awesome educational games that I can have fun playing while also expanding my mind (even if it’s just a bit).
I would give Hiragana Battle a 7/10. The details of the lessons really shine through when learning Hiragana. The story and combat leaves something to be desired, but is more than adequate to keep the player entertained while they learn.

Banished is a game where you have, in the start, group of people. You build a village and try to keep them all safe, warm and fed. Game is really beautiful, made with heart and complex enough to keep you busy from hour to hour. Or busy is actually wrong word. You see, even in the fastest mode, everything happens in it's own steady, slow pace. You see them birth, raise, play, study, work and die. Actually, they may die in birth already and kill their mother at the same time. And moreover, only a few will die of old age. Disasters, accidents, sickness, starvation, freezing... There's so many ways to die prematurely.
Usually they will starve to death at some point. Or freeze. Problem is that you have only very limited control about what they do. You plan what they build and where. Then you can decide what they do (in general) or what they are supposed to do but you can't order them. There's quite many profession but every single one settler is precious so the balance is hair thin. You have to have enough specialist to produce raw materials and food plus maybe teacher and/or physician/herbalist but all the time you ought to have enough labourers to do everything else. Like carrying materials from place to place, gathering resources and so on. And once in a while there's good to be someone to build new things. At some point your carefully planned structure will fall and people will die. You see how it all starts, you know how to prevent catastrophe but there's absolutely nothing you can do to it. If there's no game to hunt or they don't catch a fish it's tough luck and slow death to all. Farmers, on the other hand do produce food well but it will be in only at autumn and meanwhile those farmers are off from every other work.
It's frustrating, heartbreaking and annoying to see your little people run around and starving and freezing to death one by one, leaving behind only few struggling survivors. It's also fascinating, hypnotizing and fun. I deeply recommend this if you like macromanagement, hard challenges and you're not afraid to fail, time after time.

Just finished this game after about 3 hours so here's my review.
What initially drew me in to this title was the whole presentation of it and the name: Stray Cat Crossing sounds eerie, cats have been often associated with witchcraft or some sort of evil messegers or messagers of the dead, so I half expected what this game was going to be about. Of course, I was surprised who the actual "cat" was and how the real cat had such a trivial role. By saying that, I don't mean it in a bad way.
The soundtrack is definitely the best part of the game, it's very atmospheric and I would really be able to listen to it when I'm in need of some good instrumentals. I also very much loved the mini-animated clips when the screen would randomly turn to static; the first time it creeped the hell out of me lol; but they're very artistic.
This is a rpg mostly focused on gathering "pieces" that make off the overall story and so, most part of the game is going to be focused on puzzles. I personally am a very big fan of these types of rpgs and this one was not a disappointment in that particular area. I had fun trying to solve the puzzles and I didn't find them particularly brain wrecking, so don't worry. Just take a bit of time and you'll manage to solve them on your own.
I have to also praise the writing when it comes to the dialogues/monologues between the twins. They were, to say the least, fantastic! It really reminded me of TweedleDee and TweedleDum of Alice in Wonderland. Maybe there was a refference there, though I don't know. XD I would be able to relate this game with Alice in Wonderland for some elements, mostly because on some parts it's quite "unique" and "twisted". But don't expect a girl in a blue dress and a white rabbit. That you won't get. It's more of a "feeling".
The thing that I'm disappointed in though, is the ending and the revelation of what truly happened. I can't exactly say why; maybe on one side I found it a bit "trivial" and "too simple". There wasn't any big revelation in the ending, just didn't have enough impact to care about it properly. And it was kind of annoying to repeat the same scene at the end for like 5 times without able to at least skip on the already read text.
But overall I still recommend it. 3$ is not much, and it deserves them.
Other games like this one that I would like to recommend if anybody's interested are: Ib, Mad Father, Witch's House and the Crooked Man.
To be honest if you're getting started on pcs dont buy this game, great for experienced gamers.

After two hours I can say with absolute certainty that this is by far the best, and most interesting, foreign language 'class' I've taken. I did Latin and German back in middle school and high school, al those classes really did was let me know that I have something of an aptitude for languages. However, this is the first time I've had to learn a whole new set of characters, German and Latin both use the Roman Alphabet that English uses, so it was a simple matter of learning spelling, pronunciation, and meaning. This integrates both the spoken and written language into one seamless leasson. You learn what the character looks like, how to properly draw it, the sound, or syllable, it represents, and how to properly pronounce it, all in one easy to understand package.
My one caveat is this. When you take notes, pay attention to the dialogue box for the easiest way to draw the chacter, then watch teh animation to learn the proper stroke order. The animation assumes that you're using a caligraphy pen, and often looks very different from how the character is commonly written, diffent even from what is shown in the dialogue boxes.
Overall, I would say that this is an excellent method for teaching any subject, turn it into a game that rewards study, repitition, and persistence. I would recomend this to anyone who has ever had even a passing interest in learning Japanese, and I wish the creators would make more like this. Advanced Japanese, Mandarin, German, Italian, French, Russian, and more besides. If the creators of this are able to create another learning game like this, I would likely buy it without hesitation.
