Good idea, needs more balancing.
The developers toot their own horn about realism and the fragility of human nature, but a huge part of the endgame challenge in this game is bad game balance. There are essentially two phases to this game. When you first start, you scramble around looking for basic necessities and establishing some kind of stability. Phase two is when the nearby supplies run out and you must start hunting and crafting to survive. Phase one is super fun, phase two (the way it's implemented in Feb of 2015) is horrible. You will die for stupid reasons, and you will hate the game for it.
Stupid reason 1) The rifle in this game is impossible to use. Apparently at one point every shot was an instant kill, which made the game too easy, so now every shot is an instant miss. I'm not really joking. Bullets seem to miss consistently at anything past spitting range. If you do get a lucky shot, your target will take off like an olympic runner across the map leaving a helpful blood trail. If you manage to track it down, expect to shoot it two or three more times before it finally drops. Eventually these animals will die on their own from blood loss, but that never helped me. It seems like lucky headshots at close range will kill something instantly, but out of about 30 shots I've taken since I got this game, that only happened once.
The rifle in the game is a .30-06. In real hunting, the primary way to kill an deer is to destroy their heart, which should kill them nearly instantly. If you're lucky enough to shoot the head it's possible to kill an anmial that way, but very unlikely because their skulls are thick and their brains are small. A proper shot to the vital (heart) area might not kill them instantly, but will cause massive trauma and bleeding to death in minutes, not this olympic sprinter crap.
The most effective way to use the rifle is to get close enough to a wolf that it runs at you, shoot it once, and then finish it off in the wolf attack minigame. Stupidly unrealistic and dangerous. This penalizes you for using actual survival knowledge.
Stupid Death 2) You will inevitably die because you are never given notices or warnings about your changing conditions. The basic mechanic in this game is managing your warmth, thirst, fatigue and hunger (in that order). These qualities degrade constantly, and you must stay on top of each to avoid dying. Normally, checking your survival stats frequently (tab button) is enough to keep you on top of your situation, so that even if you die, you know why you're dying. However, some activities advance the game time (things like sleeping, cooking, and crafting), which degrades these survival stats very quickly, since they compress hours of game time into seconds of playing time. If you're not careful, your character will literally work themselves to death, giving you no opportunity to intervene in preventable deaths.
Once I very nearly died from dehydration while working on a wolfskin coat. I had lots of food and water on my person, and all of my needs were satisfied, so I keyed up eight hours of crafting work. Once finished I was more than 2/3rds dead from dehydration. That was annoying but not tragic. More aggrivating was the time when I wanted to harvest a full deer. I had good warmth to start, but while harvesting a storm kicked up and the temperature plummeted. When I finished I was freezing with 7% condition left, which gave me a wonderful minute of panic searching before I died. My well developed character died with a fully stocked and warm safehouse just over the ridge, because they worked right up to the point of death.
What makes a survival game fun is managing risk and making informed risk vs. reward decisions. Like I said at the top- this game works wonderfully in the first phase. Which way do I go? Does this area look dangerous? Is it worth it to run past that wolf or should I save my flare and take the long way around? That feeling breaks down in a big way once you want to set up a base camp. Maybe this is, in part, an inherent limitation of the current sandbox mode, and I will absolutely love the eventual story mode. Unfortunately, it feels to me like all of my late game deaths are entirely due to the game design and not the consequences of my own decisions, which is why I can't reccomend the game in it's current form.

Not your typical horror RPG game, Stray Cat Crossing is more of a Through the Looking Glass style tale about a girl named Cat and the disturbing world that surrounds the house that she has gone into while making off (unknowingly) with your scarf. Why you need this scarf so much and just why this house seems to hold so many nightmares within is soon explained in three parts.
Admittedly, I was waiting for Stray Cat Crossing since greenlight and now that it's out (and cheap) I was happy to play it. You'll be able to play this in one sitting. At the most, you'll do three hours if you're getting stuck. You probably won't.
There's no real combat in this game other than fleeing from a few monsters. Most of the time you'll be scratching your head over some moderate brain benders, but nothing is really too tricky in this game. The hardest puzzle is the red larvae passwords and that shouldn't be too hard if you listen to the other hints from the larva and try to draw connections to the storyline in that area. You'll figure it out eventually, I promise.
This game is unusually storyline-rich. There's less gore and less emphasis on the jumpscares (they are there, however, but tend to pop up only in relevance to what you're doing) and more on figuring out Cat's story. I find that some RPG horror games can overdo it on the scaring you out of your skin aspect. This game seeks to disturb you and keeps you involved by introducing these figures in Cat's life. You're immediately shown that Cat feels guilty over something, but why? What is wrong with this tiny little girl and why are you chasing her through this nightmare house that Tim Burton might rent for a summer vacation?
The music is rather beautiful in the game. I was disappointed to not hear the trailer music anywhere (I'll live!), but every level was delightful. Leaving the game on pause for a quick break wasn't a nightmare. I can see (and hear) the effort. The jumpscare cutscenes are animated very well and while not something that certainly scared me, but made me feel uncomfortable and with an impending sense of doom. I preferred that over screaming in horror. I loved the design of the characters and how other-worldly they felt. While the main character was the only "normal" person there, supposedly, they also had a special look to them as well, which made me feel like there was something more.
Now that I've lavished praise, let me talk about my dislikes of the game. I was reduced to only using the arrow keys. A mild annoyance and once I was able to sprint, I didn't complain as much. It gave me a reason to rest my hands across the keyboard. However, after only using the jump function for one part of the game, it was relatively useless. I would have loved to see it again after I had mastered it. (Because that is one angry fetus monster and he did eat me a few times!)
Since I'm a handicapped gamer and I often make reference to it, there is quite a bit of flashing graphics in this game. Do not, by any means, play this game if you are prone to seizures. This game may cause severe migraines. Please take a break and do not play straight through. Otherwise, it wasn't too awful. It's not so much a negative as I was neutral on it. This game has probably the best atmosphere of any RPG maker game I've ever played. The visuals are so much better than Ib or Witch's House or really any of those games; SCC has a beautiful art style that perfectly fits the dreamlike quality of the game, and the soundtrack is absolutely stunning. It is at times reminiscient of movie scores by Atticus Ross and Trent Reznor (Gone Girl, The Social Network, Girl with the Dragon Tattoo), eerie and discordant, and at times creepy carnival music—an appreciated cliché.
It's not a particularly scary game after you complete the first "stage," but it does maintain a very unsettling atmosphere the entire time. You even feel, in the best way possible, faintly unsettled after the ending.
What I really enjoy about SSC is that it doesn't hold your hand through the puzzles. Often when I play RPG maker games it feels like I'm just constantly being spoon-fed instructions, and it takes away from the actual fun of the gameplay. Of course, there is the opposite problem of not being given any direction and subsequently becoming really lost, but SCC's puzzles were never so difficult as to frustrate me and detract from the immersion. Instead, you feel satisfied for solving something on your own in a reasonable amount of time.
The story itself wasn't anything incredible; by around halfway through the game, I felt like I already (mostly) knew what was going on. However, the game's symbolism of that story is awesome. I plan on going back and playing it a second time just so I can fully appreciate the rich imagery, as well as little details hidden in book titles and whatnot.
Although the characters weren't particularly compelling, esp. the main character, I didn't mind at all. SCC felt like playing a work of art; it didn't need a 3D main character to make the game interesting. The visuals, gameplay and symbolism were more than enough to make SCC an enjoyable experience.
TL;DR - Great game. Amazing atmosphere and music. Rich symbolism and imagery. Good, smart gameplay. Worth it!

My grandson Isaac convinced me buy this wonder of a game around 4 or 11 years ago, and for that I always thank him! This game has been a blast from start to finish, all 98.3 hours of it! The graphics are encapsulating, and the gameplay is fierce and puts me on my toes like I was young again, but not too intense for an old fart like me to get startled! I remember my first match, as an Italian MOTD had graciously coated my screen along with the blaring of Lil Jon's
hit from 2003 gracing my tiring speakers, I tell you, if it had 4 legs, that was the third broken one!
As soon as I rushed to put on my glasses to actually see what in tarnation I was actually looking at, I caught a glimpse of what appeared to be a soldier in what looked like a parka embillished in artic camo whizzing by my screen at a breakneck speed, leaving behind only a fading red trail. Not too long later, I heard a deafening gunshot, followed up by a deep, monstrous voice yelling "M-M-M-MONSTER KILL" as it faded out, with the distinct echoes of the word "kill" being lost to the echoes of time, I had come to accept what my son had initiated me into. He was going to kill me by means of heart attack, all for my inheritance money.
Not too long after, I too was sucked into the battlefield. I remember it clearly, there we all were, standing completely still like pieces on a chestboard. I slowly crane my neck to the right to see amongst these brutes, there was a cartoon lady with blue hair with earphones on, completely disproportionate to human anatomy. It was a surprise alright, but it was a breath of fresh air. I had hoped the cold, murky military theme weren't to coat the entire game, and my wishes were granted. However, I have never seen that girl again, and I do not know why.
As I finally began moving, I noticed my account balance of 16,000 U.S. dollars. "Wow," I thought, "why don't I just run off with this?" but back then, I wasn't aware you needed to purchase weapons with that money. Although, in my defense, why would a Special Air Service agent (British elite military unit) purchase his own weapons in a different currency than his own country, in Israel of all places?
This was my first fault, and it was the cause of my first punishment. Many voices began to ring in my ear, all foreign, but the delivery, the anguish, the anger lead me to think in the end, they were all calling for my head. It had briefly brought me back to the war. I felt like a deserter, and I sure as hell was treated like one, within 4 seconds, a vote for my removal from battle came up onto the screen, and it lasted as fast as a virgin. I was out of there, once again looking at the two soldiers on the main menu as they stand there for all eternity.
At around 80 hours in I had finally gotten the hang of things. It turns out the B button is the Buy button, and as my arsenal imrpoved, so did I. Although I still haven't a clue on what my comrades are saying, I can only imagine it's the stark contrast of the outraged colloquy amongst foreign tongues comparitive to a conversation from The Sims that I had originally experienced. But alas, it only makes my battles more realistic.
And so, on that night I murdered my grandson with a knife.

The game is creepy, heart-pounding, but suprisingly fun.  Give this game a shot!

This game is still on early access, so expect some bugs and glitches here and there, but the devs update the game every month or so. There are still a lot of features in the game which cannot be used, this is obviously going to be part of an update in the future (I hope).
For an early access game this already shows promising graphics and other visual effects even though there isn't much "graphics" options in the starting menu, I was honestly surprised by this.
In its current state, the devs still has some way to go to improve the gameplay, the AI's in the races are pretty tough to beat, the weather system barely changes how the cars actually accelerate and handle. But despite all that the gameplay is very smooth (If minimum requirements are met).
Almost getting a perfect score here, only if the devs added some music while playing the game instead of just hearing your car all the time, I know this is more of a personal preference, but I think it needs music for the extra touch.
With all the aspects in place the devs still need to add extra features I mentioned and the missing features in the game for a better overall experience. For it's current state its going nicely, I wish the progress to make this game better improves in the upcoming future.
For it's current features and settings, its not worth the price they are asking, starting at £22.99 for the base game and £29.99 for the deluxe edition its very expensive to start with. But like all early access games, the price will speak for itself after the whole game is finally finished. As for its current state I cannot give a score higher than 5.
Overall, this game has a great potential of being an awesome game, I can't wait to see what it will look like when everything is all finished ;3

When I first saw that game on Greenlight I just couldn't wait untill release.
Then the game was released and so it bringed me a little bit of a dissapointment.
PROS
+ Graphisc: These retro style graphics are just like taken from the best 90' games. Both the background and characters animations will make you feel like playing your old good NES once again. 9/10
+ Soundtrack: Same for soundtrack. Perfectly suits the game, however it could contain a little bit more of tracks. Using same one for all 25 challenge stages was a bit annoying. 7/10
CONS
- Gameplay: The weakest aspect of a game. The thing that made 90's games special was their playability. This game have none. You can use only 2 buttons: fire and jump. Maybe it's same like in old NES games but when I launched it for a very first time I was suprised that I can't even aim my weapon up or down. You can only fire your weapon left or right - thats all, and with certain gun combinations it makes so hard to hit the enemies that are close to you. The physics are weak, main character is slow and the knockback is really annoying. 2/10
- Main story: The game has no story. Go to the space base, kill the Mother Brain -> profit. In fact you don't need a story for an arcade game, but...
The levels (all 5 of theme, what makes game very short) are very unbalanced. You are dashing through very easy stage to face the hard boss. The further you are, the bosses are easier. Just like the devs run out of ideas for them. I was tryharding to beat first one but killed last 2 (including the final boss) for a very first try. The final "F" level is nothing more than a boss rush when you just have to face all bosses again one by one without dying to reach the motherbrain. In fact, I had more fun playing extra challange mode levels than a main campaign. 3/10
- Level desing: As I said, the first stages are bit easy but still fun to play. There is almost no difference in difficulty between stages 1 and 4. However, the fifth one is hard as ****. But not in a challenging way. It rather reminded me IWBTG series, where everything was covered by spikes and traps and the only way to beat the level was repeating it again and again untill remebering locations of every single enemy and trap. 4/10
Summing up, if that game was released like 20 year ago, it would be just fine. But for now, it's definitely not worth its price and I would not recommend buying it. I hope it would change in a future as a game would be still develeoped.
But if you only want to bring some good, nestalgic memories back - go ahead and try it ;)

Conclusions: Solid game worth every dollar spent.

It's been years since a piece of art so fundamentally affected me as this has. It's about our loneliness and need to create. It's about how viewing a piece of art changes it miles from what the creator had intended. How we project our flaws and insecurities on the people around us, and hurt the people closest to us trying to fix the problems we see in them. It's about how creation for someone other than yourself can destroy the joy that creation of something brings. On what it means to be human and seeking connection.About how we see other people as having achieved some perfection we have not, some "wholeness", and not realizing that they have their own struggles, their own fears, their own unfulfilled dreams....
It was so deeply human, so deeply personal, and it was the reflection of the creation from my own personal insecurities, hopes, and my dreams that it's impossible to really describe.
I have no problem saying I was brought close to tears a number of times. There was no "story" in the classical sense. There was no ending. There was the experience of trying to understand someone, and then realizing you may have had no idea who they were.
I can't describe what the game was...it's impossible...and it would probably mean something different to you. But, seriously, you need to experience this.

This game was a pleasant surprise. I don’t know about everyone else who played this game, but… were someone else other than me shocked by how impressive the story was written and programmed? If it’s not the writing, it’s the moving of characters, voice acting and music that grips you into the story. I need more.
This game can truly be considered one of the top “must have” Otome games on steam.
There are so few of them on steam, but for the past 2 - 3 years, we have seen a slow and steady increase. And with a game as good as this, getting an English translation, will hopefully encourage other companies to import more games to people who can’t read Japanese all that well (and I mean to Steam, not PSvita/Mobile).
Also… a fair warning if you’re planning to buy this: This game is very addictive. I never imagined I would ever say this about an Otome, but it’s true. With such a story, I found myself reading away for hours in one day. All because I wanted to know everything about the story.
Hanzo > Chojiro > Goemon > Kuroyuki/Gekkamaru
+A long Otome game (we need more of these on steam!!)
+Very intense and emotional story. The story also split into 2 different ones, depending on which route you’re going for. Not only that, but each route had their own personal charm to them, so it would never feel repetitive whenever you decided to start on a new route.
+Strong female MC (heroine).
+Beautiful art style and CGs (< for the most part).
+Great OST and sound effects.
+Very good and solid voice acting
(However some of the Japanese voice acting isn’t 100% translated compared to what’s written on English. Some words are either changed or left out, but in the end, it pretty much means the same thing as what’s written on English – it’s just me being a little picky.)
+The characters say your name if you chose to name yourself the default name the game gives you, “Enju Ueno”. I recommend using “Enju” while playing – it makes you more immersed into the story IMO.
+Extra bonus scenarios when finishing a route.
+Achievements.
~Not an
‘text log’ button. I found it purely by accident when I scrolled up with my mouse wheel while on a route. Once you are on that log though: It’s well formatted, you can replay voice-clips, and you can even jump back to a previous moment to re-experience the dialogue/a battle (I was pretty impressed by that to be honest).
-Some of the CGs were bad, or I just couldn’t relate to while reading the text and looking at the picture. The anatomy on some images were weird…
.
This was most likely due to the perspective that some CGs were drawn in. During those moments though, it was actually hard to see the true emotions of the characters, and thought that the character sprites did a better job displaying their emotions.
-Minor annoyances such as: a few punctuation errors in text, general text errors such as: default name shows in text when you have actually chosen to call yourself something else + Japanese signs, an annoying white flash when quick saving, and rare occasions of having a visual bug where MC’s sprite/other character sprites/text box would flicker for a second.

As much as I'm a complete sucker for these throwback projects, Jet Gunner has some issues -- some quirks, some poor design -- that make it hard to recommend.
Some of the weapons are extremely specialized. A short-range flamethrower won't help if your target is far away. A gun that shoots two projectiles diagonally isn't much help when you're trying to hit a target across a gap. Specific-use weapons can be cool, but Jet Gunner seems to randomize which ones are placed in its levels. I would struggle against a boss with one weapon, and then completely murder him the next time around, because the game handed me a more effective gun at random.
You can get little robot buds that fight with you, like in Shatterhand. Man, I love Shatterhand. Again though, they're all over the place when it comes to usefulness, and the robot types available seem to be randomized. I know Shatterhand had a few dud robot designs, but at least you could plan ahead and choose the kind of robot you got.
Your character has a bit of acceleration/deceleration when moving. One recurring nitpick I have is that when you change direction, you don't
until all of the momentum from the old direction is gone. It's hard to explain in text, but: running right, jump right, tap left to shoot at something in the air -- you haven't
left. This can get pretty annoying during boss fights.
You have a jetpack that lets you float in the air for a short period, but you can't shoot while thrusting. A good number of enemies and bosses are placed high above the ground, and you need to stay in the air to actually hit them,
The "old action sidescroller" is a simple formula, but it requires some attention to detail to make something that really clicks. I like the overall idea for this game, but I feel the execution falls a bit short.

Really wish I hadn't played Hanzo's route first because it honestly made me reluctant to move on to the other routes.  What I loved the most about his route was the progression of their relationship and their characterizations were reasonably well done. I'm a sucker for the brooding/ workaholic/actions-speak-louder-than-words type of male characters so maybe that's why I loved Hanzo's route as much as I did. Hanzo's role isn't just to be MC's romantic interest but also as a mentor. I thought his treatment of her (In consideration of his age, his occupation, and his initial motivations) was reasonable and it didn't venture into Hanzo deviating into a completely different character in the end just so we can have our fan service.
I was very worried that the MC would devolve into a 2 dimensional character whose only purpose is to be the damsel in distress so that the romantic interest can play the knight in shining armor. Obviously, there are some moments when the MC will have to be rescued but the story is developed well enough to where you feel actual anxiety instead of exasperation. She actually uses her ninja skills, fights, and trains so she can be better. Imagine that. I also love me some angst and this one definitely delivered it in spades. The price is so worth it even with just Hanzo. Nevertheless, I soldiered on and tried Chojiro's and Goemon's routes.
Didn't mean to fan girl so much over Hanzo, but...uh...yeah. Definitely play his route. You won't regret it.
Overall, this game has A+ voice acting, music and art. The supporting characters are pretty good (with the exception of Kasumi specially in Chojiro's route). If I had one bad thing to say about the game, it's that the overarching plot doesn't really change too much regardless of which route you take but I guess it makes up for it by giving you a different dilemma depending on which romantic interest you're with.
I definitely recommend this to anyone looking for a good Otome game!

Okay, fine, I'll recommend it. But I gotta be honest: it's just because it mixes two completely different items to an interesting result. These being a classic JRPG setting, and learning Hiragana. There's probably a more-than-average overlap between those who want both. I mean...I thought those crazy symbols were to hard to ever learn, but it provided an excellent entry for me.
The sad truth is, however, that neither of these elements can carry the end result by themself.
-I'm not much of a JRPG player, but this really is as generic as it gets. This game is made with RPG maker, and it shows. The storyline, the (attempt at) sidequests, the characters, sound and music...they're bland at best and shallow at worst. Fights are literally nothing but naming hiragana characters at infinitum. The levels you pass through are set up to be mazelike to increase your random encounters. Sidequests are (until now) nothing more than "hey...here are a few Japanese words! You now have some extra experience. :) ".
-at first I liked the teachings of the characters, and assumed this to be hard. However, it quickly turns out that it only uses repetition in order for you to actually learn the stuff. There are no mnemonic hints or visual tricks for memorization (hint: get the "dr. Moku's Hiragana & Katakana" app, and use it for about half an hour...it'll make all the battles in this game a chore). Worse: as your vocabulary grows, so does your list of attacks. I stopped playing at a point where I could instantly identify the enemies but couldn't be bothered to scroll down the nearly endless list of options. Dakuten should've been a submenu option, or we should've just be able to use our keyboard to type the sounds, but alas...here as well, things are better on an app (like "hiragana - learn Japanese". Aside from quizzing and fast typing, this also quizzes your ability to write hiragana).
I can't deny that this game is more addicting than it should (I easily played two extra hours after determining that I would learn better on the mentioned apps), and has more charm than its technical shortcomings may indicate. As such, a thumbs up. After all, it doesn't matter how hard I can try to rationalize why the game isn't good if it has this huge a "one more dungeon" kind of feeling (and unlike most other games, you actually DO get something useful out of it :D ).

I didn't know about this game before it had come out, much to my shame, but as soon as I saw the trailer I fell in love with the game. The colorful visuals, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic soundtrack, the return to the almost non-existent 3D collect-a-thon. I was ready to sink my teeth into this adorable game and suck everything it had to offer, but then I played it.
I realize I am going to get a lot of negativity because of my review, but I really feel like I should warn people like myself who are in love with old-school platformers and collect-a-thons. Beware, this game, while deceptively cute has many problems.
The game isn't bad. At times it's great even. Most of the times, however, the flaws almost ruin the experience.
The game has beautiful visuals. The cute main character is adorable and the game never stops placing her in cute situations. The same can be said for the rest of the games visuals. The enemies and the levels look great as well. The graphics were one of the things that made me buy this game so hastily. I guess I am a sucker for cartoony visuals.
The soundtrack. Oh my god, the soundtrack. It's just divine. I absolutely love every single track I have heard ever since I frist launched the game. The tunes are catchy and fit in perfectly with whichever scenario the game throws at you.
The voice acting is also nice. The cast consists of great voice actors who really try their best to stay memorable. It's great that many of the characters also have different accents.
The game also doesn't lack in the creativity department. One mintue you will be leaping from rooftops in Mafia town and the next you will be running throug a train on a movie set. The game never seems to stop surprising us with it's colorful and interesting locations.
Unfortunately, this is where the pros end and the cons begin.
The controls are OK, they are not perfect but they work as best as they could considering the engine the game was made in. Unreal Engine just isn't a great choice to make such a game but, to the developers' credit, they did make it as best as they could, which I can respect.
However, this brings us to my biggest problem with the game. When I saw the trailer, I immediately thought of Banjo Kazooie, Yooka Laylee and Super Mario 64. A 3D collect-a-thon. And sure enough, that is what the game wants you to belive it is.
The main goal of the game is to collect 40 collectables. As I mentioned before, I love games where the main objective is to collect things, so I was very surprised that the very first world, Mafia Town, was so big, vast, beautiful and yet, there was little point in exploring it.
The case is the same with all other levels. They are begging to be filled with collectables, things to do, side-quests and activities, yet they all have one goal, which can sometimes be completed in less than 5 minutes.
You have hourglasses, which are your main objectives and once you collect one, the level ends. Scattered around the level are marbles, which act as a currency. You use these marbles to buy badges. Scattered around are also yarn balls which are used to make hats.
While it seems like a lot, only the hourglasses are important. The rest of the things are just kinda, there. For instance, the yarn balls are needed to make hats which give you powers, that you need. I never counted but I would say that there are about 20-30 yarn balls on each level. The sad thing is, you only need about 3-5 of them to build most of your hats and collecting the rest just gives you extra yarn, which feels a bit dissapointing.
During my first few hours, I was collecting everything and in the end, I felt like I had only wasted time because only the Hourglasses mattered. So, quite honestly, this game isn't really a collecta-a-thon, but a 3D platformer and there is nothing wrong with a 3D platformer, provided it's done well, and it isn't, at least in my opinion.
Like I said before, the controls are as best as they could be on the engine the game was based on. This makes the controls great for exploring but not so great for platforming. The main character moves like her feet are made of butter. She zips everywhere really fast and the jumping controls are sometimes too... jumpy. Often at times, I was able to find an easier, chepear way to get to my destination just by exploiting the flowyness of the controls. There were sections that required me to use power-ups I din't have to get over long gaps, but I was able to do it with a well timed running jump followed with a dash. It doesn't sound so bad, but when you notice that the game wants to be restrictive and yet you find a way around it, your immersion starts to fade.
This is especially noticable during the middle of the game, where the game becomes much more linear and the platforming takes a bigger focus. There are sections made much harder than they look simply because of the controls.
Climbing a large three in word 3 was much harder than it should have been because of the controls.
I want to mention that the controls work the same way as they do in Yooka Laylee. In Yooka Laylee, such controls weren't the problem because the majority of the game didn't have tight platforming like A Hat in Time has, thus I couldn't complain about them, even if they were flowy just like they are here.
Another thing that bothered me more than it should have were the boss fights. The bosses aren't hard. They all have predicatble patterns just like in most games of this type. They are memorable and fun to do, but they take way too long. One boss fight can go on for around 10 minutes because of how much hits they can take.Seriously, it's ridiculous. I found myself shouting at the screen going "How is this boss still not dead?" after hitting several bosses over 20 times and yet they just kept getting up and getting more powerful.
The badges you collect range from useless to essential. The hook-shot badge, for example, is essential for progressing through the game while the one-hit-death badge just makes the game harder. Unfortunately, most of them fall in the latter category and feel like a wasted opportunity.
The game, only has a couple of power ups, which seems dissapointing. I really thought that the game would have more. The power ups come in form of hats, which look cute and are an interesting way of showing which power up you currently have equiped. Out of all of them, I only ever seemed to use the speed power up, just to get through the levels faster. The rest of them were just context sensitive.
As far game optimization is concerned I don't have too many complaints. I experienced some frame-rate dips (one time, the character wentinto an elevator and the game froze and continued to run at 2 fps, but it continued running fine afterwards) and there were no game crashes. I am surprised that the game has a bunch of graphical options but not an option to redifine keys (still, nothing a patch can't fix).
The game is also short. With only 40 levels (some of which can be done in less than 10 minutes) and only 4 words, it feels very short. Especially when you consider the price.
My biggest issue with this game is the praise it is getting. While this game does deserve some of the praise it is getting, nobody should be able to say that it's better than Yooka Laylee, beacause it simply isn't. Don't get me wrong, Yooka-Laylee wasn't perfect and it had problems but so does this game. Let's at least be fair and acknowledge that "A hat in time" has just as many, if not more, problms just like Yooka-Laylee.
That's my review of this game. It's not bad, but it's not great either. Honestly, if you are in the mood for a 3D platformer, you could do so much worse than this one. If you can handle the loose controls and aren't too bothered by collecatbles (or their lack off) you might just find a somewhat exciting adventure.
But for the price I paid (28 euros), this game is simply NOT WORTH IT. For HALF that price, the game is worth it.
Fantastic story, unique gameplay, great visuals, buy this game NOW.

AVOID THIS GAME!!!!
For starters this game uses Quick Time Events which isn't a bad thing, the issue is the the sheer amount of QTE's. Segments that should be cutscene turn out to be a boat load of QTE (quick time event) sequences which if you progress through the game quickly will happen sometimes every 5 minutes or less. Or if you want to you can QTE every single enemy with no sucsse. If you are using a controller the Quick Time Event prompt fades in giving you less time to react where the keyboard prompt is an immediate thing. All around it feels like quick time events were something that was just tacked on at the last moment and it doesn't really fit. But don't despair, the QTE's have a difficulty setting; if you don't want to put up with them you can set it to the lowest setting and watch it as the cutscene it should be although the prompt will still pop up like you are still gonna give it a go.
As for the story you will be completely lost as to what's going on unless you watch the prologue in the extras or on the store page. Gameplay wise it feels like its trying to be 3 different games in 1 and fails horribly.
1. The setting feels like its trying to be the Shinobi reboot for PS2 with the whole modern urban Tokyo ninja thing.
2. Your character looks like Ryu from Ninja Gaiden and tries to be just as cool and fails at it.
3. The combat system feels like it was based around not your first weapon but your second that feels a lot more natural for some reason and happens to be dual wield sword but it makes you use this super slow broad sword through MOST of the game. The upgrade system mimics that of God of War as well as some of the attacks that you unlock via upgrading. The Quick Time Events mimic God of War in the way of being activated in the same ways. Aside from the games it tries to be there are also poorly incorporated turret segments that completely break the flow of the game. There are moments that also happen quite often where you will have to go through your weapons just to continue through the game. And again this wouldn't be and issues if i was done less often but its over used. The gameplay looks and feels very broken as if the cosmetic things where more important the having a solid foundation for the cosmetic items to be built upon. Most of the main issues with this game could have easily been patched out after its release to PC.
Graphically this game looks sub-par for its era at max settings and you will have to keep going back into the settings in order to have a descent frame rate due to the game insisting that your frame rate does not exceed 30 fps. Mind you this is a port to PC after debuting on Xbox 360 five months before. There is obvious clipping and at times the audio will just cut out, so if your not using subtitles you have no idea what's being said. The game could use more than it's fair share of optimization, because I get better framerate in crytek games with loads of particle effects with better framerates.
Overall this game does not feel like it was made to be on PC at all and it needed another few months of development in order to work out its serious bugs or at least a patch to correct them after release. Only worth the cash it you want to see how not to make a game.

Let me start by being completely honest, I have had a great time playing Banished but suspect I don't play it very well as I haven't gotten any achievements for it yet.  >.>
Banished is a brutal city simulator where you start with practically nothing in a colonial-esque setting and must help the townspeople by instructing them what buildings to build, where to work, and generally micromanage them from a godlike perspective as you often do in city sims.
Pros:
1)  Fun to play and watch, you'll want to put it on fast forward, but watching the people go about thier business is fun and fascinating.
2)  Very immersive with lots of resources and things to manage.
3)  A wide variety of buildings with a wide range of benefits mean you're constantly building something.
4)   Seasonal changes mean you'll watch as winter settles in and fades into spring and summer, foliage doesn't change for autumn which doesn't detract from the game but would be a nice addition.  However I bet someone's already made a mod for that.  (If there isn't one and there's a modder reading this...  Here's an idea for you!)
Cons:
1)  When things go wrong, they go wrong fast.  You might have one family marked as starving one minute, but the next it could be all of them.
2)  Resource allocation is critical, super critical, super super super critical.  If you run out of something restock it immediately or your productions will quickly grind to a halt.
3)  Citizens actually age faster than the calendar suggests.  What I mean is your city may be in Autumn 5 (meaning the season is autumn and your city has existed for five years) with a 14 year old farmer, but by Autumn 6 the same  farmer is several years older instead of just one...  This makes population planning a bit complicated.
The Overview:
As I said, I don't claim to be good at Banished but despite that I find it an enjoyable challenge.  The graphics are pretty good, and the quaint buildings have a picturesque charm that will quickly grow on you.  You'll soon get swept into the hustle and bustle and enjoy watching everyone get to work builing your vision, which is also their means for survival.
The name of the game here is balance.  People are a resource, they grow old and eventually die, so you'll want a stable population that grows at a modest rate (there is a display that tells you the number of people in the village, but not their average age or anything like that which would be helpful...) but if your village is growing too fast you won't be able to produce enough food.  If you have a lot of houses you'll need more firewood, if you want more firewood you need more logs, but you need enough logs to cover the houses you're building etc. etc.  This is a city manager that is a tricky balancing act involving gathering resources, keeping the people happy and healthy, and expanding.
For an indie project this is a solid title with lots of replay value (at least for me since I'm often starting over >.>) that rewards the meticulous and methodical planners who are comfortable tracking and anticipating the needs of the people to an almost excrutiating level of accuracy.  While this review may seem a little frightening I encourage you to try it, it's a good bang for the buck and a nice challenge that you'll quickly become engrossed in.  There are plenty of mods available that tweak things like resources per harvest that might make the game easier but I've yet to install them.

I would like to give it a neutral review, as the it has both many pro and many cons, and I can see why people would both like and dislike this game. But ultimately the craftsmanship and care is what makes me give the game a positive review.
On the pro side; The pixel art is superb, easily the best I've seen in an RPGmaker game, it has a lot of detail in everything, and it makes the unique and surreal designs comes to life. The atmospheric soundtrack makes it even better. The story was well done. The first act was great, it had both solid puzzles, suspense/horror elements and introduce the player to the world and its surreal nature pretty effectively.
Now on to the downsides. This game pretty short, clocking in around 2 hours long. Another big issue is that while the first act is great, the second and third act are drug down by some tedious puzzles that are on the unintitutive side and require a bit too much trial and error or repetition to complete and ultimately detract from the experience. The horror and suspense elements are also gone after the first act as well. Lastly, aside from the introduction sequence, the first act was released for free as a pre-release teaser/demo, so the best part of the game is free and was played by many people (such as myself) months before the game was finished.
That being said, the skills of the developers certainly have some well honed talent, I sincerely hope they take the criticisms to heart and make more games with that in mind. I look forward to what they will make next.

Stray Cat Crossing is one of the better indie RPG Maker-style games I've played in a while. The game looks lovely - the visuals are surreal and unique. It's clear the game is drawing heavily from Alice In Wonderland, but it doesn't simply directly reference its source material by having rabbits and whatnot. Instead, it feels more like an original setting, with its Japanese influenced art and cartoonish character designs. The dialogue is also great, giving you just enough information about the setting and story. The gameplay has more variety than what I was expecting - one puzzle in the middle of the game was particularly interesting. I liked that the game tried to make sure that the puzzles were intuitive through gameplay, without much specific info-dump-like dialogue. This breaks down at the end - the final puzzles are tedious and require a lot of fetch quests and rewatching cutscenes over and over and over without the ability to skip through them or speed up dialogue. It really took away from the rest of the game and I almost didn't recommend this game over it. However, the story and the rest of the puzzles are strong enough that the game is worthwhile. I'd recommend picking it up if you want to enjoy a short story through gameplay.

Ignore my hours. I had this game on disk since it first came out, and honestly, its had more time put into it than any of my other strategy games put together.
When Westwood still existed the C&C series always were wonderful to play - There was just that touch of polish and care which went into their games that you didn't quite get with others, even right down to the little animations of the commandos lighting a cigerrette and chucking it aside, quoting one of their infamous lines with a chuckle. So for 2D units  you were commanding quite a colourful and unique army.
However when C&C3 came along... Oohh boy, that jump into 3D. It brought fresh life to the series!
... too bad it was the last 'good' game beyond Red Alert 3 after that. EA had washed everything 'Westwood' down the drain.
As always the three factions are almost brilliantly balanced; They each have strengths and flaws which play a triangular role against one another, with similar but unique powers and tech trees. While they can be infamous for certain reasons - Scrin with their hordes of alien ships for example - there is no reason why a player cannot use either GDI or NOD to the same extent and counter it.
From the previous two games the missions are also once again varied, can last you a while, and the AI can be dubious when you're unprepared (if not a little clumsy here or there) which means you can get quite a few hours out of Skirmish mode.
-- Edit --
Unfortunately however these days the game's multiplayer has all but dissolved. I think there is still a small community and you might still be able to play matches, though its rare and you're going to have to go out and find it. Despite this I still enjoy playing the game and its Kanes Wrath expansion as a time waster and fond memory of the good times I had with it.
--
Like I said. Sad to see its the last 'good' game of the series.

I don't really see the point of this "trials" update. You still have to make multiple of the same type of character just to specialize and minmax for DPS and each individual tower with this whole new "ascension" infinite leveling thing (why exactly is hero crit chance and damage under "utility," the same tree as some tower upgrades, rather than "offense?"). The only difference now is that we have to re-farm for everything since the update ♥♥♥♥ed up the stats on all the gear we had. The new system looks nicer and more sleek but overall still seems pointless when we're still essentially doing all the same things, just wasting more time, because there are more things to farm for and lower droprates now.
Along with that, "Chaos" difficulty replacing Nightmare is horribly done. The new enemies are nice, but the actual difficulty of anything past Chaos I is absolutely ridiculous. I'm an old veteran of the game with several heroes who had full NM4 and iPWR 750 items (essentially endgame gear for anyone who doesn't know), but you can't even tell how strong individual items are anymore since the iPWR rating seems to be removed, and I'm struggling to do ANYTHING anymore, even with my old gear, with the cluster♥♥♥♥ of enemy types that can't be countered all at once. The only difficulties I can play and complete anymore give gear that's LESS powerful than what I had several months ago when I last played.
I think I preferred Nightmare over Chaos difficulty. Yeah, it might've been more artificial difficulty than anything, but at least there weren't spams of so-called "counter" enemies that didn't actually counter strategies, but actually only countered specific towers, mainly those of the 4 free heroes, which are already generally weak anyways, which then forces you to buy or farm for the heroes that have to be "earned." This game is giving me pay-to-win vibes now on top of everything, and I don't like it.
TL;DR you have to farm all over again and do it more often and for more things but you can't because droprates are down and difficulty is too high.
But hey, on the bright side, not everything is dependent on gear now, since some effects have been split off into shards and the Ascension system rather than additional passives on equipment, which goes well with the new lower drop rate and makes it feel a lot more rewarding and meaningful when higher gear rarities do finally drop. That's a big, coincidental step in the right direction.
P.S. Trendy, fix your ♥♥♥♥♥♥ netcoding already. My friends and I are all tired of rubberbanding into instant death pits twice per wave just because we're not directly connected to the same network your servers are running on.

The person that made this doens't fully understand how to make a run-'n'-gun style of game but does seem to understand the components that WOULD make a good one. Honestly, it makes for a rather dull experience overall.  Let's start from the beginning so we can get an idea of what's wrong with it:
1) Enemy placement - Enemies are often placed in areas that aren't well thought out (or perhaps they are, but for the wrong reasons). You'll find yourself tapping the controller or keyboard to move forward rather than have your character move at a constant rate for fear of an enemy popping up on the very edge of the screen and immediately firing. While this isn't terrible if you are into that sort of thing, I like to play my run-'n'-gun style of games where I'm actually RUNNING and GUNNING, not stutter stepping and jumping.
2) Weapons - Good lord are the things generally useless. A bullet spray that shoots in a random barrage of bullets? Why not just make it the ever classic spread from Contra? In this, the bullets might miss smaller targets generally, and require me to maneuver in bizarre fashions to maximize the damage from an enemy.
A misslie launcher? Sounds amazing, except it's not because the missiles generally have this nasty tendency to fly upwards after a few moments of being shot so they always seem to skirt *around* the enemies rather than at them! If that wasn't bad enough, the missiles are incredibly slow as well. Lame.
Boomerangs? Okay, these actually aren't that bad, but it WOULD be better if you could switch between them and your standard gun.
I could go on and on about them, but let's just say that most of them are a noticeable downgrade from your standard shot. This is absolutely not good at all. Sure, you can have weapons that are better at moments, but having them be worst in almost any conceivable situation is absolutely unacceptable.
I especially love how the drops are random, so until you actually remember the symbols for your power-ups, you'll never actually be able to know which ones are actually useful or not (just skip most of them). Even worse is that some of them are a "partner" powerup, so there's no reason to not have those guys even if they have limited ammo and most aren't particularly helpful.
The Jet idea is pretty nifty but I feel like it's not utilized very well. Let's take the first mini-boss for instance, using your jet dodges every single attack it has, and even in hardcore mode, by the time it's actually ready to charge its next attack, your jet meter has already filled back up to the top again and can be used to dodge. I'm not saying remove the jet, but the enemies should have more attacks since the game knows that you will ALWAYS have the jetpack.
Lastly, I absolutely hate how the vast majority of the enemies are over your character's head but you cannot shoot up. That's not how you design something. Yes, I get that the jet pack is there to let you level out with the enemies, but it's excessive from as early as state 1, area 1-1. The helicopters should most definitely have a method of being shot at if you run underneath them outside of running backwards to shoot it (which causes enemies behind you to respawn), or running passed it; this makes it even more pointless to fight as it's no longer an obstacle.
All and all, it's not the most wretched game I've played-- it's not even really bad, it's just... Not good. In any real way.
Why was my review so long? I don't know, maybe it's a message to the developer so he can make a better game. I feel like if he made "Jet Gunner 2" and got rid of the above problems, the game might be pretty good.

I didn't know about this game before it had come out, much to my shame, but as soon as I saw the trailer I fell in love with the game. The colorful visuals, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic soundtrack, the return to the almost non-existent 3D collect-a-thon. I was ready to sink my teeth into this adorable game and suck everything it had to offer, but then I played it.
I realize I am going to get a lot of negativity because of my review, but I really feel like I should warn people like myself who are in love with old-school platformers and collect-a-thons. Beware, this game, while deceptively cute has many problems.
The game isn't bad. At times it's great even. Most of the times, however, the flaws almost ruin the experience.
The game has beautiful visuals. The cute main character is adorable and the game never stops placing her in cute situations. The same can be said for the rest of the games visuals. The enemies and the levels look great as well. The graphics were one of the things that made me buy this game so hastily. I guess I am a sucker for cartoony visuals.
The soundtrack. Oh my god, the soundtrack. It's just divine. I absolutely love every single track I have heard ever since I frist launched the game. The tunes are catchy and fit in perfectly with whichever scenario the game throws at you.
The voice acting is also nice. The cast consists of great voice actors who really try their best to stay memorable. It's great that many of the characters also have different accents.
The game also doesn't lack in the creativity department. One mintue you will be leaping from rooftops in Mafia town and the next you will be running throug a train on a movie set. The game never seems to stop surprising us with it's colorful and interesting locations.
Unfortunately, this is where the pros end and the cons begin.
The controls are OK, they are not perfect but they work as best as they could considering the engine the game was made in. Unreal Engine just isn't a great choice to make such a game but, to the developers' credit, they did make it as best as they could, which I can respect.
However, this brings us to my biggest problem with the game. When I saw the trailer, I immediately thought of Banjo Kazooie, Yooka Laylee and Super Mario 64. A 3D collect-a-thon. And sure enough, that is what the game wants you to belive it is.
The main goal of the game is to collect 40 collectables. As I mentioned before, I love games where the main objective is to collect things, so I was very surprised that the very first world, Mafia Town, was so big, vast, beautiful and yet, there was little point in exploring it.
The case is the same with all other levels. They are begging to be filled with collectables, things to do, side-quests and activities, yet they all have one goal, which can sometimes be completed in less than 5 minutes.
You have hourglasses, which are your main objectives and once you collect one, the level ends. Scattered around the level are marbles, which act as a currency. You use these marbles to buy badges. Scattered around are also yarn balls which are used to make hats.
While it seems like a lot, only the hourglasses are important. The rest of the things are just kinda, there. For instance, the yarn balls are needed to make hats which give you powers, that you need. I never counted but I would say that there are about 20-30 yarn balls on each level. The sad thing is, you only need about 3-5 of them to build most of your hats and collecting the rest just gives you extra yarn, which feels a bit dissapointing.
During my first few hours, I was collecting everything and in the end, I felt like I had only wasted time because only the Hourglasses mattered. So, quite honestly, this game isn't really a collecta-a-thon, but a 3D platformer and there is nothing wrong with a 3D platformer, provided it's done well, and it isn't, at least in my opinion.
Like I said before, the controls are as best as they could be on the engine the game was based on. This makes the controls great for exploring but not so great for platforming. The main character moves like her feet are made of butter. She zips everywhere really fast and the jumping controls are sometimes too... jumpy. Often at times, I was able to find an easier, chepear way to get to my destination just by exploiting the flowyness of the controls. There were sections that required me to use power-ups I din't have to get over long gaps, but I was able to do it with a well timed running jump followed with a dash. It doesn't sound so bad, but when you notice that the game wants to be restrictive and yet you find a way around it, your immersion starts to fade.
This is especially noticable during the middle of the game, where the game becomes much more linear and the platforming takes a bigger focus. There are sections made much harder than they look simply because of the controls.
Climbing a large three in word 3 was much harder than it should have been because of the controls.
I want to mention that the controls work the same way as they do in Yooka Laylee. In Yooka Laylee, such controls weren't the problem because the majority of the game didn't have tight platforming like A Hat in Time has, thus I couldn't complain about them, even if they were flowy just like they are here.
Another thing that bothered me more than it should have were the boss fights. The bosses aren't hard. They all have predicatble patterns just like in most games of this type. They are memorable and fun to do, but they take way too long. One boss fight can go on for around 10 minutes because of how much hits they can take.Seriously, it's ridiculous. I found myself shouting at the screen going "How is this boss still not dead?" after hitting several bosses over 20 times and yet they just kept getting up and getting more powerful.
The badges you collect range from useless to essential. The hook-shot badge, for example, is essential for progressing through the game while the one-hit-death badge just makes the game harder. Unfortunately, most of them fall in the latter category and feel like a wasted opportunity.
The game, only has a couple of power ups, which seems dissapointing. I really thought that the game would have more. The power ups come in form of hats, which look cute and are an interesting way of showing which power up you currently have equiped. Out of all of them, I only ever seemed to use the speed power up, just to get through the levels faster. The rest of them were just context sensitive.
As far game optimization is concerned I don't have too many complaints. I experienced some frame-rate dips (one time, the character wentinto an elevator and the game froze and continued to run at 2 fps, but it continued running fine afterwards) and there were no game crashes. I am surprised that the game has a bunch of graphical options but not an option to redifine keys (still, nothing a patch can't fix).
The game is also short. With only 40 levels (some of which can be done in less than 10 minutes) and only 4 words, it feels very short. Especially when you consider the price.
My biggest issue with this game is the praise it is getting. While this game does deserve some of the praise it is getting, nobody should be able to say that it's better than Yooka Laylee, beacause it simply isn't. Don't get me wrong, Yooka-Laylee wasn't perfect and it had problems but so does this game. Let's at least be fair and acknowledge that "A hat in time" has just as many, if not more, problms just like Yooka-Laylee.
That's my review of this game. It's not bad, but it's not great either. Honestly, if you are in the mood for a 3D platformer, you could do so much worse than this one. If you can handle the loose controls and aren't too bothered by collecatbles (or their lack off) you might just find a somewhat exciting adventure.
But for the price I paid (28 euros), this game is simply NOT WORTH IT. For HALF that price, the game is worth it.

I say that I don't regret shelling out some of my savings just to play this VN, spend a whole day completing Hanzo's route, and doing his route over again until I realized that there are still other routes available to pursue. And then after playing all the good endings, I played Hanzo's route again because I'll never get tired of the slow burn of a romance, the positive character change that happened with Enju, as well as with Hanzo, the drama and the struggle at the near end, and the satisfying ending that came with it. And no, I don't care if he's actually
, because I'd still bang him nonetheless. If this VN will ever have an anime and they're going to use Hanzo's route....Gah, who am I kidding? Gekkamaru is considered to be the main guy here! But still, I'm going to throw my money at the screen just to see this happen.
Overall, Nightshade is a pretty solid VN. The MC is not as flat and irritating as I expected in visual novel heroines, the LI's are all interesting (I'm biased towards Hanzo but Kuroyuki and Goemon's story are also good as well) and the side characters have their own quirks as well. I just wish there was an Ieyasu route in this game, something that focuses more on the political intrigue instead of all the routes become "a runaway ninja" story.
Gekkamaru and Kuroyuki's routes have the biggest twists in the story so better save them for later if you don't want to get spoiled (and possibly depressed throughout your playthrough). What I just don't like with Gekka is that he is just your ever faithful, Captain America-level of perfect, loyal protector from start to finish.
. Ultimately, Gekkamaru's and Chojiro's routes left a bad taste in my mouth
but because of how the major plot twist turned out which actually deflated the whole conflict which made me say "Wait, so that's it?" instead of anticipating what's going to happen next upon the revelation of the surprise.
Kuroyuki's route is interesting because you'll see the other side of him. A bit of yandere-ish and stockholm syndrome-ish at the start, but trust me, the will get better further through the story as you see Enju and Kuroyuki's relationship develop into something healthier (with the help of their friends who made them come to their senses).
Choujiro's route is a mixture of depressing and WTF?! and I haven't even played his bad ending yet (what's the worst thing that could happen in this route?). But I guess I'm not too interested in him because for me, Hanzo is the only perfect shinobi. <3
Goemon's story is the most lighthearted among the five guys and should be done whenever you are feeling heavy after playing the other routes. You'll, of course, know the story behind the ninja-turned-thief but that's just the icing on the cake. The true gem comes from the character interactions in this route. Just a tad disappointed that there's no further "action" (if you know what I mean ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°) ) from our friendly local libertine.
The art for this VN is great, although there are still CG's where it seems "off." The action scenes are made more exciting by the sprites clashing or through forced perspective between the characters. It's also fun seeing that the MC's sprite also gets included with the other characters in the conversations. It makes the character to be immersed in the story as well.
The music may become a hit or miss depending on one's taste in music but there's nothing too jarring that it will distract you from reading. The OP and ED especially makes me want to wish that this VN will get an animation deal someday.
So TL;DR,
. It may look pricey but it's worth every cent and every minute you play this. It will lead you to a roller coaster of feelings and its variety of characters and side characters will get you hooked in this story.
Now I must go and do another run with Hanzo's story..

Hiragana Battle has the honor of being my first Steam Review.  That said, this title is well worth full price, I bought it on a whim during a sale.  It teachers you the Hiragana alphabet while being a very enjoyable RPG.  However, I will say you should treat this title as a supplement instead of an end all be all, just as anything else you would when you are learning something new.
Hiragana Battle does exactly what it promises and then some.  I learned and committed the alphabet to memory through light grinding and a few online resources.  The explanations for how to write the characters, while not too involved, were more than enough for me to follow and understand.  As you play, the game provides you with plenty of vocabulary, and even touches on sentence structure.  I don't claim to be fluent, but I did spot a few inconsistencies with my other learning resources, but for the most part everything agreed with whatever I researched.
The story itself is no Witcher, but a nostalgic callback to simpler JRPGs in the vein of say, Dragon Quest.  Simplistic turn based combat and spells are in your arsenal, though not at all required to complete the game.  Boss battles are not difficult at all, but then again I grinded a bit during each area to make sure I knew what characters were what before moving on.  It's a learning game first after all.
I want to give a special note to the soundtrack, it definitely helped the light slog because the songs are all very good.  I can't think of one that I didn't like.
All in all, if you want to learn Japanese, or at least begin to, this is a great place to start.  You still have to study, you still have to set aside time, and you still have to commit, but at least here you'll enjoy yourself while you learn.  A must have for aspiring language learners.

4/10 - TOO PUNISHING TO BE FUN
This game has one problem, and that is it doesn't know the difference between "challenging" gameplay and "punishing" gameplay. "Challenging" gameplay allows the user to make a choice and react, which this game doesn't give you much of a chance to do. Whenever an enemy enters the screen he immediately fires his weapon, giving you no time to react because the shot has hit you before the enemy is fully visible. Also if you land on the same platform as an enemy he will immediately fire, once again not giving you a chance to react to it. It's not challenging, it's flat out unfair.
I started my first playthrough on Hardcore Mode because i wanted a really solid challenge but was unable to even get past the first level due to having no indication of when an enmy will fire his high velocity lasers at me. Hardcore Mode doesn't allow you to collect extra lives or health pickups and you take double damage, so trying to get through the very long levels having only 3 lives is nothing short of impossible.
This game looked cool but it's just way too punishing to the point where it's not fun and i feel i don't have control over a situations outcome. The dev needs to analyze retro games to see the difference between challenge and punishment. A good start would be adding a visual indication that the enemy is about to fire his weapon, that way the player has the chance to react and will only have himself to blame if they aren't fast enough. I'll always appreciate an atempt to bring back challenging retro games, but this just doesn't do it right.

On the other hand the gameplay itself, due to being limited by the RPG Maker rules, and also due to being strictly reduced to puzzle solving, did not keep me interested as much as I thought I would be after watching the trailer.
The puzzles can be very tedious. These are the kind of puzzles I always hated in similar games, since they purposely prolong the gameplay by giving away only tiny hints, while the player must often traverse the scenes multiple times to find the solution. Be prepared to be annoyed after a while, especially during the event in the attic.
The horror element in this game is also pretty much nonexistent unless you are very easily frightened. Maybe my expectations were beyond what one should expect from a RPG Maker game, I don't know.
Even without taking its overall shortness into account, what I do know howewer is, that despite its semi-interesting story, good artwork and soundtrack I was not entertained, shocked or mystified by this game at all, and I wouldn't recommend it to other people despite it's low price tag.
If you are into puzzle solving, mysterious and/or macabre stories, that Pan's Labyrinth/ twisted Alice in Wonderland feeling, I would strongly recommend getting "Fran Bow", another adventure game recently released on Steam.
I played that game before this one, maybe that is why it left me utterly unimpressed, depite the interesting premise.

Outlast is one of the best survival horror games I have ever played! The atmosphere is genuinely creepy, with great ambient effects to really draw out the effect on the player. I would recommend getting this game (maybe not the DLC). This game is also VERY graphic, so expect that if you plan to pick up this game. Guts and gore EVERYWHERE and there is some male nudity (minor in the main game and significant in the DLC).
If I had to nitpick, I would say that the character models could have used some more detail as most of them aren't super detailed and the scarring looks a bit simple. That isn't to say that all the character models are this way, just the average "patient", if you will.
The DLC is a big question when it comes to this game. I think the developers did a pretty ok job with it, but it uses many of the same elements (scare types, etc) as the main game. As the DLC is a prequel to the main game, I found that the main game lost some of its zing after playing the DLC. There are also some glitches in the DLC where two main baddies are spawned, a few of the jump scares are not exactly done super well, among a few other minor things. The DLC also has some really great things about it as the "Gluskin" enemy is pretty creepy I really really enjoyed how the story was filled out by playing the guy who originally leaked information to miles upshur (your character in the main game).
In the end I highly recommend getting this game; however, it doesn't really have much replayability and the main game is about 2-2.5 hours in length. The DLC adds about an hour or so, which still ends up leaving the game pretty short. Ultimately, you are likely going to be playing this game once and then maybe whipping it out to scare your friends once in a blue moon. My advice is to pick it up while it's cheap, as it really is worth it.

I should start with saying that The Long Dark is Alpha done right:
Launch with a stable engine, a few hours of playable content, enough to make an enjoyable first impression.
Keep a regular dev log, do major content launches every couple months, bug fix constantly.
Bask in the adoring light of a raptured fan base.

The Long Dark is lovely, it is brutal, and it ain't done kicking my butt yet.

To be honest, the first time I heard about The Long Dark I was sold. I loved the idea of a survival game set in the remote Canadian wilderness. I bought TLD the day it came out on Steam Early Access
I've been involved with a few Early Access games on Steam so I know about the general process: you buy a game in "Alpha", watch the dev blog closely, and hope that devs remain committed to the gameas much as you do. I've been impressed with TLD; plenty of updates and communication with the community.
The game itself is awesome: I love the raw "you vs the environment" survival setting. I've never seen anything like it. Most survival games have a "hook": zombies, sharks, cannibals. TLD is all about you vs the environment. Sure, there are wolves, but the primary enemy is the cold, harsh environment you find yourself in.
I can't wait until Hinterland releases the storyline of TLD. If done well they can really take the survival genre to new heights.

TBG is a really beautiful game, and especially relatable to me. I've been making 'games' like Coda about once a year or so for about 4 years. The entire story of Coda reflects myself, my depression, and my lack of creative energy to keep creating games.
I've always felt the same way as Davey thought Coda felt. I started making games to impress a girl. My first crush, actually. Ever since then, I've wanted to join a game company. But that desire has tapered off over time, and I don't know if I want to anymore. I kept making games because of a feeling of obligation, like I should make them for other people. Or only make things that people might like.
I never made anything for myself. I felt as though I needed to make things in order to improve my skill so that one day I could be a video game developer.
It was a horrible experience. I once thought about ending my life because I was feeling so mentally exhausted.
And the games were never good enough. I always thought they were ugly, or boring. But I never showed them to anyone anyway, so I could never actually know if they were bad.
I still make games sometimes, but not very often these days.
Overall, this is the most relatable game I've played in my life, and it made me think about a lot of things.
It's definetely worth the money.

even if the characters aren't the best ever written, i'm still having fun with them.
it's anime, not the witcher. if you don't take it too seriously, you can even find yourself chuckling at yourself, as you sway along to the amazing soundtrack, or as you listen to the cute (and over the top) japanese voice acting.
in short: if you're expecting "the next big rpg", then this isn't it.
but if you enjoy traditional jrpgs with anime tropes, something relaxing and not too demanding, a world you feel like you already know a little and that you can disappear into for a while, then this might be the game for you.
maybe don't pay full price for it, though, if you're not certain.

TL;DR Nightshade is the equivalent of an AAA game in the otome world, and absolutely worth its price.
First for an overview.
Nightshade is a visual novel on what it means to be a shinobi in the Sengoku era of Japan, during a time of tentative balance teering on the brink of change. The main character (I strongly recommend keeping the canon name Enju since the other characters will actually say her name) is a girl who is determined to give back to her shinobi village, and finds herself way in over her head in a conspiracy.
There are five routes the story can take, each involving a romance between Enju and a specific shinobi man. Each route is the perfect length IMO, not too long and not too short. In total, the game should probably take between 18 to 30 hours depending on the speed of your reading. There are a total of five routes--2 of which are angsty, 2 of which are hopeful, and a third in-between (slightly more on the hopeful side though).
Pros:
-The historical Sengoku era and shinobi aesthetic is very cool even for someone who knows basically nothing about the historical figures (but was inspired to look them up more after finishing the game.).
-Writing across the board is high quality, with each route taking their own spin on the game's overarching theme--what in the life of a shinobi is truly worth living/fighting/dying for. Suspense and tension are very nicely maintained. The stories know when to be serious and when to be playful, so this consistency in tone is reassuring. Some plot threads are picked up and then dropped, but that is pretty natural to any visual novel with multiple diverging routes and in this game it never occurs on a truly bothersome scale. Overall it's extremely easy to immerse yourself in the story IMO.
-Character development can be absolutely superb in some routes. The side characters are great fun to have around and also ripe for drama of their own. I can say that in every route, the main characters change in a believably human way with consistent motivations and goals.
-Voice acting is stellar. They shelled out for the VAs, and it shows. Every main character has a perfectly fitting voice. You can even choose which character's voice you want to hear when you're navigating the main menu! I do wish Enju herself was voiced, but oh well.
-Visuals are generally beautiful. The portraits are gorgeous, the backgrounds are lush. Teita's art style fits this game perfectly. Even the fight scenes are somehow very captivating despite the typical visual novel limitations (can only be written with portraits blinking around, clashing noises, etc.)
-Soundtrack is good overall. There was one screeching guitar track I disliked during action scenes, but that was the only one of its ilk, while there is a particular dramatic action track I absolutely loved.
Possible cons? Your mileage will vary on whether these are negative or even positive.
-Story only has a single very fundamental premise. Of note, there is one /giant/ branching point early in the story that divvies out the five routes into two branches. The plots and reveals of the two branches are fundamentally different. However, there are two routes in the same branch that have quite similar stories, so if you do one your suspense during the other will be significantly decreased.
-Some routes get more closure in terms of the overarching story than others. However, I can say that every route does achieve closure. Often the routes that didn't get that "overarching story closure" often received far more satisfying "individual journey closure," so it's not a strictly bad thing.
-Just like every otome game (nay, every visual novel) in existence, some character archetypes will naturally appeal to you more than others. As a result, most people find themselves with one or two favorite routes that they want to reread over and over. Those one or two routes alone could justify the entire price of the game :P On the other hand, this means most people also find themselves with one or two routes that are unappealing.
-UI can be a bit clunky, but it's tolerable and very much usable. It has the much appreciated industry standard options of Quick Save/Load, see the previous script, jump back to an earlier scene, etc.
Other notes:
-There were text readability issues for the first few days, but it has been fixed. I can safely say that right now the text is perfectly comfortable to read.
One last word, don't let looks deceive you--Hanzo is the cutest boy in the cast.
