Jet Gunner is a side scrolling run and gun shooter that utilizes a jet pack for more high flying platforming and combat. While this mechanic is interesting, and I am a fan of arcade style run and gun shooters, I feel the execution here is a bit subpar.
The jet pack works in that after jumping, you can press or hold the button as many times as you want to ascend while fuel holds out. The way fuel is handled though is perhaps my biggest complaint about the mechanic itself. Instead of having a set amount you can rise per jump, you have a fuel meter which slowly recharges when not jet packing. What this essentially means is that before or after many jumps, you'll have to sit still and wait for the meter to finish recharging before you can go again. While it's not terriblye noticeable most of the time (it recharges quickly), it still cramps the games fast paced run and gun action a bit, and makes the jetpacks use feel a bit more limited and restrained than it should be (in my opinion).
Beyond the jetpack system, there's also a weapon system in which you can stock a standard weapon and a floating satelite (with limited use), mixing and matching the two. However some of the weapons vary in usefulness a bit too much. The worst offenders being a flame thrower with far too short range, a gun that shoots directly above and below you but not in front, an incredibly slow moving wide shot, and a missle launcher with pitiful speed and an annoying randomized aim. I can appreciate the attempt at variety in the weapons, but a few too many of them harm you more than anything. In fact, pretty much everything that's not a standard straight shot is pretty awful.
The level design doesn't make good use of the jetpack consistently enough. Occaisionally, there are interesting acrobatic manuevers, but these are a bit too far and few between. For the most part, the jetpack is just used to jump over slightly lengthier bottomless pits or other such hazards that could just have easily been solved with a more traditional double jump. Beyond jetpack use, the level design  is not particularly interesting, with fairly standard run and jump layouts for about half of the game. Enemy design is a bit weak, mostly consisting of standard foes who simply shoot at you before dying, forcing a single duck or jump whilst being too static to force any kind of improvisation or quick reflex once memorized.
Boss design varies. A few bosses (the first one, for example) offer great design with a mix of strategy, reflexes (thanks to some slightly random attack patterns), and a need to use your jetpack well. But like the stages, some of them are a bit uneven, with a few snoozer fights numbering equally against the genuinely fun ones.
The game also has occaisional flaws and cheap moments in level and boss design that makes the whole experience feel a bit unpolished and poorly play tested. Examples:
-On stage 1, you stand on a small moving platform over a bottomless pit, and pass under a block that prevents you from jumping. On a nearby wall, an enemy climbs up and down the wall and fires when you enter within range. If you're lucky, it won't pass by while you're under the block, or at least will fire at a height where you can duck, otherwise damage will be unavoidable if it happens to pass by at a crouching level.
-On stage 2, a miniboss has a pattern in which it fires a random spray of slow moving bullets, followed up by an unreactable (I think) slew of fast and random cannon balls that are only consistently dodged by staying directly underneath the cannon. If you get bad rng on the slow moving bullets, you can get a wall of bullets that forcibly prevents you from getting to the safe zone, and results in unavoidable damage.
-On stage 4, a platform moves when you jump on it, with ceiling fans that prevent you from jet packing. If you get knocked back onto the previous ledge (or jump back there for safety in avoiding an incoming enemy) you will be completely incapable of reaching the platform and will have to suicide in order to get it to respawn
-etc.
Overall not a bad game, but a very simple memorizer with a few standout moments and a few flaws holding it back. The gimmick is neat but stirkes me more as something with potential that's not fully realized here. If you really enjoy the genre, you may enjoy this, but I'd personally recommend something more masterful like Bleed first.

Probably the most fun and engaging 3D platformer I've ever played. Controls are good, environments are very well designed and platforming is good. Every level feels like it's asking you to do something different (the chapters even moreso), and all of those different things are all quite engaging. The art, music and sound design are all excellent. The main character is adorable, and the other characters are all great fun and do a lot to keep the new experiences coming.
Difficulty is a bit on the low side so most players should be able to beat it. Individual challenges are sometimes fairly hard, and you certainly won't be sleeping through it, but the game's excessively forgiving if you fall or die. And while the bosses are creative and have some nasty attacks I believe the game starts throwing extra hearts at you after ~3 deaths so you won't get stuck. But this isn't a game you play to test yourself, it's a game you play to have fun and experience everything.

Stray Cat Crossing is a nice little narrative adventure. There isn't much in the way of challange to it but that's alright. The core of the gameplay can be summed up as bumping from point A to point B, interacting with something or someone in order to advance the story. There are several puzzles thrown in to spice things up a bit, which is certainly a welcome decision. Everything is pretty straightforward, though, so there is little chance to get stuck for more than a couple of minutes at the same point. The single exception to this could be a small but very unforgiving action sequence (which I sincerely hope is tonned down at some point).
The story is intriguing, though the game never really takes the time to explain some details and lets the player imagination fill the gaps. The music is great and adds a lot to the ambience. The art is nice too and has a lot of personality. The backgrounds can get a bit repetitive, but they are populated with big, detailed props which really help to ease that feeling. All these elements feel well integrated with nice shadowing arround them and simple lighting effects livening things up a bit. The sound effects are maybe a bit lacking, with very simple PSG-like samples played to give feedback about things like locked doors.
As for the tone of the game, it certainly fits the horror label in the beginning. But this aspect is progressively downplayed and the final act pretty much drops it completly. If you come expecting a traditional horror experience you may feel disapointed.
All in all, I really enjoyed this title and found it's release price very fitting. My compliments to the developers.

Bioshock delivers a strong story and unique environment wtih its survival horror RPG and FPS mix. Jack goes to an underwater city named Rapture after a plane crash and is immersed in the dystopia, derangement, and power struggle of the city. The game has philosophical ideas from the two antagonists along with a morality choice by saving or harvesting the Little Sisters. Gameplay is similar to System Shock, which is Bioshock's spiritual successor. There is shooter action along with shops, hacking, exploration, plasmids, crafting, and upgrades. Players start initially weak but can gain more strength from collecting items. This blends nicely with the atmosphere of the game, a steampunk underwater city. The style looks like the 60s but with technology and horror elements to show the ruin of the city. As the game is set underwater, the water effects are pretty good. The music played ranges from actual licensed music from the 60s and past to a orchestrated score for creepy or serious moods.

Graphics:
- Nice comic-style with a lot of bright colors, resulting in a very "warm/lovely" atmosphere
- A lot of variation in maps for example old dungeons, green fields, gigantic sewers, burning cities, spooky forests or a throne room and there is much more! New maps are constantly added, each with their own layout and theming.
- The characters are designed with a lot of love for details and they all look very different from each other. You can also buy skins with ingame currency to give you a bit more variation.
-> Overall one of the biggest pros for me are the graphics. I could stare hours into the beautiful landscapes and also write hours about it ;)
Balance/Bugs/Ingame Currency
-> Trendy constantly adds new content to the game, so they can have all features they want as quickly as possible, but this also results in a lot of bugs. The worst bugs get fixed quickly. The balance issues are not that bad in early stages of the game, but in the endgame there are only a few viable towers/characters. I´m sure the balance will get fixed, since most of the old characters will get reworked soon to be as good as the new ones. The ingame currency is fine. You can get some skins and additional inventory slots with it, but nothing that would give you an advantage in the game.
Gameplay:
- A lot of variation in maps, difficulties, items and characters. You can even equip spheres to boost your character to the max. or take a pet to help you in battle
- Tons of enemies, each with their own strengths and some with special abilitiess
- The normal gamemode is nice and balanced and will take you a good amount of time to reach the last difficulties.
- The second gamemode is named "onslaught" and is basically an endless mode. The gamemode is fun but does not provide good rewards at the end. I´m sure they will make some work on this gamemode soon.
- The third and last gamemode is named "incursion" and is a much harder version of the map you choose. The gamemode is very challenging and is okey so far. But they currently work on adding a different task for each map and a unique reward if you win. There is already one map with this concept and i´m very happy with it.
- Daily missions/monthly missions have good rewards and are well done.
- Characters all have their own playstyle and look.
I could write on for hours, because there is so much more to talk about, but i wanted to keep it short and just give you an idea of the current state of the game!
Result:
-> The fantastic graphics, love to details and the variety of characters, pets, enemies and maps, make this one of my favorite games. I spent over 440 hours on this game so far and don´t regret anything. The Trendy team is friendly and listens to the community. Constant patches with new characters, challenges, maps and much more keep the game interesting and fun. Just keep in mind that the game is in development and still contains some bugs and balance issues, but overall I can totally recommend you to test it out yourself, you won´t regret it!!

To be honest, the first time I heard about The Long Dark I was sold. I loved the idea of a survival game set in the remote Canadian wilderness. I bought TLD the day it came out on Steam Early Access
I've been involved with a few Early Access games on Steam so I know about the general process: you buy a game in "Alpha", watch the dev blog closely, and hope that devs remain committed to the gameas much as you do. I've been impressed with TLD; plenty of updates and communication with the community.
The game itself is awesome: I love the raw "you vs the environment" survival setting. I've never seen anything like it. Most survival games have a "hook": zombies, sharks, cannibals. TLD is all about you vs the environment. Sure, there are wolves, but the primary enemy is the cold, harsh environment you find yourself in.
I can't wait until Hinterland releases the storyline of TLD. If done well they can really take the survival genre to new heights.
Highly recommended. 10/10 would get eaten by a wolf again :)

The combat isn't the best and takes a fair bit of getting used to mainly because the default setting does most of it automatically so it's initially hard to understand why you are attempting to do certain moves but actually doing different ones. You can attempt to counter this by turning off all automated combat for your main character but then you will probably die a lot before you figure it all out.
And that's my only real criticism of this game because the storyline and dialogue are of an extremely high level. The parts that are meant to be funny are witty and often laugh out loud funny, those that are meant to be serious or poignant are, and dramatic moments tend to be suitably dramatic. This latter is helped by the fact that the musical score is as diverse as it is accomplished and cutscenes are of a very high quality. If you are the type of person who prizes a rich story and high production values above gameplay mechanics then this is certainly for you. And even if you are not then you may still find this to be a good game if you take the time to learn the combat with zero AI assistance. A sharp contrast to Tales of Symphonia which I bought on sale a while back and quickly refunded.
*edit* the more I play this the more I realise that the combat is, in fact, NOT bad but that it just has a steep learning curve. The adventure is epic and the scripting is a lot better than 99% of JRPGs and 90% of all rpgs.  Overall score 90%. I love it.

Playing this game has been a fantastic experience. I've always wanted to learn a second language, namely Japanese, but when it came to youtube or document-based tutorials, I just couldn't get engaged. It seemed futile, but on a whim (and during the Christmas sale) I found this unassuming little gem for just over a dollar. What could I possibly gain from buying it?
I've only been playing for three days now, but within that time, I've learned 25 different Hiragana characters, can say at least 10 sentences and I know some handy greetings. For example, I didn't actually know 'karaoke' was Japanese, and there's even a language system known as Katakana that's specifically for representing foreign words. I'm currently on lesson 3 but it's already given me a ton to process.
You need the temperament and attitude of wanting to learn Japanese. Of course, there's a game underneath and it totally services what it was built for, but "Learn Japanese To Survive! Hiragana Battle" is really a thiny-veiled second language course and that's how it needs to be treated. I was surprised when the game asked to take notes, but believe me, this is an extremely essential part of the game and you'll want to write down every single thing it says, including practicing how to write the characters, memorizing them and any other memetic trick or habit you can think of. Writing down vowels in Hiragana for the first time was pretty difficult, but after doing it a lot, it became really easy; it's clear that learning this stuff is designed to rewire your brain, and you're not gonna get that unless you actually write these things down. It'll be even worse when you're actually fighting against the "Hiragana warriors" because you're guaranteed to forget some of this stuff.
Playing this game taught me that I don't really learn well unless I'm in some kind of classroom environment. Cherry picking things off of Youtube or random tutorial sites is bound to fail me because, unlike this game, it lacks the necessary components of learning, which is feeling engaged, interested, focused and rewarded. I dunno if any of you are like this or not, but if you are, I highly recommend picking this up, whether it's on sale or not.

A lovely otome that managed to positively surprise me. One of the best thus far on Steam. Absolutely recommended!
The sprites and CGs are gorgeous. The soundtrack, which I usually mute in VNs, didn't bother me and fit each scene pretty well (I had also mistakenly bought the OST bundle instead of the game as standalone, so I felt almost obliged to give it a go orz). The voice acting was stellar and each voice fit the characters extremely well. I blushed several times, courtesy of Goemon and Kuroyuki dulcet tones. The fight scenes, despite the limitations that a VN format brings, were not dull thanks to perspective changes on sprites and a great use of transitions. I was so impressed I needed to praise them, this production value is a breath of fresh air.
The first 4 chapters form the common route, and there are 13 chapters in total. I'm a fast reader, in 20 hours I managed to read all the good ends, force skip to get the bad ends and get all memoirs (those were hellish to get orz) to get 100% completion.
There is no description of the love interests on the store page, so I'll write a line or two about each guy and his route:
My recommended order would be Goemon > Hanzo > Kuroyuki > Gekkamaru = Chojiro. Goemon's route is the most positive. In Hanzo's the angst becomes more serious. Kuroyuki's route serves as a grand finale of the three and the beginning of the true angst™. Gekkamaru's and Chojiro's should definitely be last, with Chojiro's route being a big hit or miss due to the POV switching/his absence for a big portion of it.
The only pet peeve I had, call me petty because of it, was that kisses/hugs were as far as physical things went. I was expecting at least a little bit of intimacy to go with the mature themes. The lack of it becomes unbelievable
Idk there were several moments when I felt that the intimacy was forced away from the plot (possibly because of rating?). Maybe I'm old, maybe I've been reading too many Dogenzaka smut mobage ports. Maybe I'm hoping for a 18+ fandisk. Who knows :P again, minor pet peeve.
Quality of life suggestions from
: if you keep Enju as the MC name, it will be voiced when the other characters call you by name (instead of generic nicknames)! In the settings you can change the speed of auto read and skip. You can also change the character in charge of all the little voicelines in the menu (I set it to random to have some variety).
: one of the best otomes on Steam, great cast, there's angst™

It's a fun, fast paced and challenging game that's like a mix of Megaman and Contra on crack! It has lots of enemies that respawn if you backtrack, lots of powerups which can significantly alter the behaviour of your weapon and you even come equipped with a jetpack. Powerups are also randomized so you can't beat the game strictly by trial and error making skill and reflexes key. The presentation is absolutely spot on right down to the segmented health/energy bars and achieves the retro 8-bit style perfectly -- it looks, sounds and plays just like an NES game. The sprites are large and easy to distinguish and they explode into colorful 8-bit pieces!
My only issue with the game is that the controls aren't as tight as I would like them to be. Sometimes when I try to move in the opposite direction it doesn't register particulary if I do it too quickly. Furthermore you can't remap the controls and the only controller it supports is the 360 gamepad, and it's not very playable with it because the controls are significantly delayed however the developer is working on fixing it. The options currently don't save either and be warned: This game is ***VERY LOUD*** when you first load it up.
But all in all, it's a great game that does what it sets out to do very well. It took me an hour just to beat the first stage and there's 6 in total. So make no mistake it is hard, especially unforgiving in hardcore mode. If that's what you're looking for, then for the price you really can't wrong with this.

Outlast is a game where you play as a reporter, who gets contacted by an unknown user who tells him about the horrors that is happening in an asylum. So far that seems pretty normal for a horror game, but as you progres you find out that it was a retakaning on the MKULTRA experiments of sleep depravation and experiments of the sort made on patients of the asylum, the plot thickens as you go on and discover what happens.
There are great unforgetable moments on the game, the story is not too expansive besides the notes that you find, there are little "cheap" jumpscares, but most rely on thick ambiance and paranoia of the player.
The graphics and production values are nothing but amazing for an indie developer, they are top noch and could be easly compared to a triple A title with water physics, SSAO, great lightning effects, great sound (pherhaps  one of the best I have seen), and while the game is a bit short it is a scary expirience throughout the entirity of its gameplay (3-5 hours) keeping you on your toes most of the time.
There are just a few complains. There arent any real puzzles and the game does get a bit repetitive , but this are minor and is definetly worth the value of admitance.
Great game, cant wait for the sequel to come along! :D

I highly recommend this game. Very well-worth its price. This is my very first playthrough with Kuroyuki but man, this game just blows me away. Now, I'll proceed with the pros and cons.
Pros:
+High-quality voice acting. Delicious ear candy.
+Beautiful graphics and animation.
+ Gripping and riveting story. The story takes you on an emotional roller coaster ride (and I like it!) You are able to put yourself in your character's shoes and directly feel what she feels. I love how this game can keep you in your seat and be entertained. The story seems pretty long but I don't dread spending more time to unlock other character routes. In fact, I'm looking forward to them!
+ Relationship bar. It's a nice feature to see your romantic progress with each leading man.
+ The heroine isn't annoying at all. I was initially expecting the typical and usual irritating, damsel-in-distress, no spine heroine you usually find in other visual novels but I was proven wrong. She can actually hold her own and has a mind of her own. The heroine is easily relatable.
Neutral:
There are a very few typos and grammatical errors but you can easily brush them off (unless you easily get offended by grammatical errors and typos) since they don't affect the storyline in any way. No biggie.
Cons:
- Sometimes the music doesn't really suit the current situation and the music can be quite repetetive.
- Some parts of the storyline has a bit of a slow progression but it's totally bearable.
- I just found it a tad annoying that my character kept on saying "Kuroyuki" almost every time she's speechless or while she's listening to Kuroyuki speak. If I had a dollar for every time she did that, I'd be sleeping on a huge futon of dollars by now.
- No Tokugawa route. :(
This game is really difficult to put down because it's addictive to play. Personally, I couldn't seem to get enough of the story. Even if it's already early in the morning, I found myself clicking away so I can find out more about the story. If you love visual novels, historical fiction, handsome men, and Japan, then this game is totally for you! Please buy the game and support the devs. The devs deserve support for all their hardwork for bringing us this beautiful, spared-no-expense game.

I finished the game in around nine hours or so, including restarting after dying many times.  I really like games where I haven't played all the content in 40 hours in and I'm still entertained.
On a final note: This not a survival game, This is a horror game.  Not horror survival.  Just horror.  It actually doesn't have really any of the elements of a good survival game, unless camera batteries are gonna be the end all be all to your existence in an apocalypse.

I came across Stray Cat Crossing (no pun intended) while scanning the greenlight community, and idk why but the title design pulled me in; I proceeded to watch the trailer, to which my inner weeaboo was satisfied (animated trailer and that music, it was like watching a JRock MV), so I gave the demo a try. The Alice in Wonderland vibe I got from the game hooked me for good and I was definitely interested in the final product upon release. This purchase did not leave me disappointed.
You start off as an unamed girl merely being a decent human being to a lost child named Cat by escorting her home, and when you reach your destination you're pulled into a house of mysterious creatures and settings as you discover just who Cat is. Now, I'm not familiar with games made from RPG maker - though I have heard some negative things - but in my opinion this is one of the better ones. The pixel art is indeed gorgeous and well done (the cutscenes served their purpose well too), and the puzzles were a perfect balance of "Oh, I know this," and "Hmm, gotta actually think." It's not really horror in the traditional sense of inducing fear, but I suppose one could see some of the creatures and actions as disturbing. The soundtrack was hauntingly perfect and set the mood for everywhere the protagonist traveled, and as the plot unfolded before my eyes I was surprised in a bittersweet way.
The only gripes I had with this game is the keyboard layout and steam overlay. Although the controls are few and simple (up, down, left, right to move, enter/space to interact, shift to run, and A to jump), there was only the one scene where jump was introduced that I had trouble with. It felt awkward using shift and A at the same time and I wish I could've changed the jump command from A to space, but I managed through the scene. As for the steam overlay it's nonexistent, and while it's not necessarily a bad thing, it would've been nice to know that attempting to screenshot via F12 would actually bring me back to the menu screen and I hadn't saved for a while.
All in all, I could totally see this game extended a bit since I was left with a few questions, but for $2.99 and roughly 2 hours of gameplay I definitely recommend Stray Cat Crossing. It's a short but good one.

Jack goes to an underwater city named Rapture after a plane crash and is immersed in the dystopia, derangement, and power struggle of the city. The game has philosophical ideas from the two antagonists along with a morality choice by saving or harvesting the Little Sisters. Gameplay is similar to System Shock, which is Bioshock's spiritual successor. There is shooter action along with shops, hacking, exploration, plasmids, crafting, and upgrades. Players start initially weak but can gain more strength from collecting items. This blends nicely with the atmosphere of the game, a steampunk underwater city. The style looks like the 60s but with technology and horror elements to show the ruin of the city. As the game is set underwater, the water effects are pretty good. The music played ranges from actual licensed music from the 60s and past to a orchestrated score for creepy or serious moods.

I enjoyed playing Outlast. I recommend it to everyone who likes a story-driven suspense and horror game ...
The story is actually quite good. During most part of the game (also in the DLC) it does not develop much. You are in something "simply too big for you" and your are
fleeing for your life ... But the end offers quite some surprise and making this thing "bigger", stepping up speed and context.
First you need to get used to the gameplay, because you only have to options: hide or run away, usually combined. So there is not defense, no attack, not fight ... no ordinary gameplay. Once you get used to it (i.e. you know what the game expects you to do ...), it looses some of its suspense. Basically you know how to solve the situation. Still, it is entertaining, because to some major this games lives from its story and atmosphere as a helpless man being caught in something just "too big".
The "shocking moments" in the game is almost never subtle and in general not "surprising". But they choreographed, scripted and timed very well and always make you twitch. So: well done! In the Whistleblower-DLC there are some more subtle sections, with faint sounds moving through the fog around you ... also rather classical, but: well done!
Basically graphics and sound are fine, serving the game well. There are only 2 issues:
First, the volume in the dialouges is sometimes too low. You might miss some messages ...
Second, the engine lacks indirect lighting. Very often you move into some completey dark hallway, just to realise that bedind a bend there is a light source ... that should actually indirectly cast some low illumination into the hallway.
Do not miss the Whistleblower-DLC. It does not add new gameplay features. But it turns the story further, nicely interacts with the main game ... and might even point to some coming Outlast 2 ...

Banished is a small scale city building game with survival elements.
You take command (I use that term loosely) of a small group of travellers that have been (SURPRISE) banished from their homeland, and you create a place for them to live and grow.
There is a large variety of building paths and factors to take into consideration, and the world generation keeps restarts interesting (though you can retain seeds if you found a world that you enjoyed building on).
I need to stress that I am not good at this game, and I found that many things are resolved through trial and error. Persistence is king here, and is justly rewarded. Similarly, logical thinking (my people are hungry, therefore I need to prioritise production of food, or look for a new source) and common sense (perhaps I should have made sure the well I made was actually accessible so as to fight the fire that just destroyed my entire town) are also important.
There is a strong community online that is willing to help shed (geddit) light on ideas, processes and common mistakes and it can help immeasurably should you choose to take advantage of it. I went in as blind as I could, and it is consequently a challenging and rewarding game, with a healthy dose of utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t on the side.
The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t can come in many forms. For me, it was a fire early into my second year that swept through my primarily wooden settlement. Could this have been averted? Yes, and that is knowledge I will take with me into future playthroughs. Another kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t I stumbled across in one of my longer lived settlements is famine. Famine isn't fun.
Graphically, the game isn't the most stunning piece of software you can find but the visuals do the trick and, coupled with the beautiful score, are strangely serene. It's a good game to play if you're a bit stressed as it's easy to play at a slow pace (game speed tool is included) and just get lost in the environment.
Seasonal effects are serviceable and easily identified, and there are countless markers to let you know precisely what it is you're doing wrong.
I have had some spectacular issues with AI, such as dying of starvation despite having a house inventory full of berries and venison and potatoes and the like and just generally being useless, but these aren't as common as they feel when you stumble across them.
There is workshop support, but I am yet to experiment with it.
I enjoy Banished, and while it is a cruel mistress sometimes (you can turn disasters off if that's your thing), it is also a thoroughly enjoyable game and I can't wait to lose another settlement to a fire because I forgot build a well.
They stopped development. If they put another bit of work into it it could be a great game.

I think with over 760 hours qualifiies me to write a honest review.  Do I like the game...  hmm..  I said I played the game for over 760 hours, what you thinK?
Let's start with the con's:
1.  The game is easy to play for a few game years, but difficult to master growing a large civilation.
2.  It is easy to make mistakes that requires many game years to discover, which unfortunately ends in disaster.
3.  There is a serious flaw in the the way the population model works which is what you end up spending most the game trying to accommodate.
4.  There are also a couple flaws in the game engine.  For exampe some food sources are better than others that don't make sense realistically.  It is just the way the developer coded it and you will just have to research what they are (outside of the game).
The pro's of the game:
1.  The fact the game is not easy drives you to want to replay the game "one more time" because you just figured something out.
2.  The game has an excellent balance between simulation with the populous doing their thing and being a game that can be continually micro-managed by zoning new buildings.
3.  The game doesn't have a technology tree or deep "you must build this first" requirements.  The game just naturally seems to follow "Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs".  For example, who has time to build and gather resources for fancy clothes if they must first gather food before the entire population dies.
4.  The game is completely open-ended, allowing you to do whatever you want (including wiping everybody out).
5.  There are in-game achievements for those that like the challenge.
This game is a lot of fun. I look forward to more updates...

There are many assets that provide a great audiovisual experience. The graphical effects and sounds are perfectly implemented to set the mood and theme of a World War II simulation, grabbing the player's full attention in immersive and tense scenarios. All of the official maps are also beautifully crafted, with much attention to detail, including good quality textures and tactical environments. Since this is a multiplayer only game, that is where it all starts falling apart. Firstly, the developers opted to use the archaic, erroneous, and intrusive PunkBuster anti-cheat service in the game. Not only is it extremely innacurate and unreliable, it also requires its own separate installation onto your system; which means it will force itself to run in the background, in addition to the game client. Secondly, the server browser and in-game pings differ by at least 30 or 40, every time. In other words, the ping being shown in the server browser is always at least 30 or 40 lower than what it actually is in-game. This is a problem that has been reported in both the Steam and official game forums for a long while, without any response by the developers. Thirdly, even though there is an average of 1276 concurrent players in the last 30 days at the time of this writing, finding a populated server with a tolerable ping is not easy. The few servers available with a playable ping (100 or less) have the low artificial intelligence bots taking place of the absent human players, which brings down the game's fun factor to an unbearably low level. In addition to the lack of active servers, when there are people playing on a full server, many player pings are in the 200s, and some in the 300s. What could have been a great, engrossing, realistic experience ends up being marred by all of its technical online problems. While one may find adequate multiplayer conditions to play the game properly from time to time, I have found that this happens very rarely. What you will find are high ping servers with a small human population and a high bot population, with the occasional populated high ping server with human players whose pings are well into the 100s, 200s, and even 300s. A multiplayer only game should never be played in those conditions. If you are able to find a good server with people playing, there are many fun and fulfilling hours to be had. Too bad these ideal conditions are few and far between.

In short, if you're just looking into learning the basics of the Japanese language, this is a surprisingly fantastic starting point. It made education surprisingly fun, at least for the first while, after which it became somewhat monotonous mechanically, but remained a solid learning resource nonetheless. It also encourages pretty decent study habits, which, admittedly, many people seem to lack. I'd highly recommend it so long as you fulfill one simple criteria:
You have to want to actually learn.
Simply put, learning a language or well.. anything takes a lot of time. You can certainly learn to understand each individual hiragana and to sound out words with what this game provides, but you have to be willing to put forth the effort. Writing things down when the lessons prompt you to is practically a must for anything to progress in a timely matter. The educational structure of this game presents you with 5 hiragana each time, starting with your basic vowels and leading into consonants and modifiers (dakuten) and the like. It's paced well enough that you can get a solid grip on the 5 most recent hiragana that you were shown before having more characters forced upon you. If you want to practice, you can always traditionally grind mobs in certain areas corresponding to the hiragana set you're looking to practice.
As far as the actual game's mechanics outside of the basic education it provides, it's mediocre at best. The story is expectedly cliché, the characters are your standard affair for mediocre RPGMaker-esque games, and the writing is most definitely nothing to write home about. If you're buying this for the actual gameplay, you're looking at the wrong game. This is solely a means to educate you with progressing through the game being your incentive. It's effectively chasing a carrot on a stick, you just have to want the carrot.
The controls are fairly standard affair but are pretty clunky if you opt to use mouse only, but that's really my only gripe regarding functionality.
All in all, for someone looking to learn hiragana who thinks the concept of incentivized learning in an RPG format is appealing, by all means, you don't want to pass this up. Especially when it's on sale, as it often goes as low as two dollars.

Even though this is a new game, as soon as I started it up I was immediately hit with wave after wave of nostalgia for hours on end.
A Hat In Time is a 3D platformer that takes very heavy inspiration from the 3D super mario games as well as having nods to banjo kazooie. The game follows the aptly named Hat Kid as she searches for her ship's lost power supply on an alien planet so that she can return home from... somewhere to...somewhere. It isn't ever actually explained. The game's gimmicks are hats that grant different abilities when worn, offering things like increased movement speed and different attacks, along with badges that add new abilites or enhance old ones.
I'll list the game's pros first, then cons.
First off, the graphics. The game is beautifully stylized, especially when running on uncapped frames, really making you feel as if you've travelled back to the gamecube days. From haunted forests to seaside cities, the game offers the perfect mix of old and new. The level of care that went into the visuals can be truly impressive sometimes, even to the point where nearly every mission has its own unique artwork on the loading screen before it. The sound design is excellent too, with punchy, fitting effects for everything from smacking an enemy to simply running around.
Each Level is completely distinct, standing in stark contrast to one another and adding amazing variety to a somewhat shorter game. You'll traipse through movie sets, coastal towns, haunted woods and more to retrieve the time pieces, which then extend the areas by adding bonus levels whose entrances are hidden somewhere in the overworld to find. Even more interestingly, during certain bonus levels you can hunt for pictures during each stage. Collecting every one unlocks an expositional slideshow a la psychonauts, telling the stories of certain charcters you meet on your journey.
(A godsend for a game with such a thin plotline) (also, prepare for feels)
The voice acting is (for the most part) really good for an indie game, with some characters sounding better than some characters in big AAA games. (Looking at you, Mass Effect: Andromeda.) And since a good 90% of all dialogue in the game is spoken, having bad acting could have crippled its humor by forcing players to skip through it.
The game has a ton of wit sewn into everything, with self aware humor and tongue-in-cheek laughs galour, with some simple stuff mixed in as well to keep everyone giggling all throughout with very few jokes that fall flat. Also kudos to the devs for making a horror sequence in a cute 3D platformer that actually manages to be quite terrifying.
And the MUSIC. Amazing, one of the best game soundtracks I've ever heard. Every song fits the situation perfectly and occasionally had me standing still for a few minutes or replaying missions just to hear every note.
Now for The gameplay.
Simply put, this game is DAMN fun to play.
The controls for every facet of gameplay are near flawless, while feeling familiar to anyone who have played the 3D mario games. (Especially with the dive move that looks and feels eerily similar to that of a certain plumber.) Platforming also has the the right amount of weight, striking a perfect balance for every precarious platform you'll jump accross.
Next, the main character is friggin' adorable. Whether making faces at the mafia or running around posing for pictures, to skipping along as she leads a parade, Hat Kid is sure to make you smile whenever she's on screen from her sheer cuteness. (So no false advertising in that regard) She even shows a more sarcastic and jaded side in some of her musings and character interactions, which makes her all the more endearing. You know you've designed a good character when they can scream "Down with the mafia!" and start beating people to death with an umbrella and still have it be adorable.
Now the cons.
If you're looking for a gripping story, you won't find one here. Like the games before it, this game doesn't just put narrative in the back seat to gameplay, it hits narrative with a shovel, ties it up and stuffs it in the trunk, having very little story other than "You see that shiny thing? Go grab it!" While this does keep it in ranks with games like mario in this regard, it's a shame that the story wasn't more flushed out, as not only did it have potential, but let's be honest, thin narrative gets old after 30 years. Also, if you peer between the cracks, you can see they were trying a bit too hard to be the next undertale,
The side characters are flat and simple, but they do their purpose well and have good acting, so I can give them a pass in that regard. (Except for mustache girl, whose teeth marks you can see all over the scenery) But unfortunately, Hat Kid is a kind of character that I cannot excuse after they've been around this long: A silent protagonist. That means that her only communication during cutscenes are nods and facial expressions and in normal conversations, she just stands there with a dumb look on her face, robbing her of a ton of potential character. And the thing is, she speaks full sentences during gameplay, has a journal you can read, and even narrates the game's steam trading cards, so there's no excuse for this trope to be continuing in a non-rpg game.
Some animations in places look awful, with such notable examples as characters that open their mouths to speak during cutscenes, keeping them open all throughout, and then flail around like they're having a stroke, as well as Hat Kid's facial features looking like stickers stuck to a blank face. I know it's supposed to be stylized, but at one point she stuck her tongue out in a cutscene and it looked as if she just slapped some red tape down her face.
While the gameplay is near flawless, there are some poor desisions that keep it from being so. Games that take staple abilities such as a magnet effect for picking up drops or negating fall damage in a game about jumping and falling and making them unlockable abilites that take up slots to equip are unneccesarily complicating things. At the very least, if you're going to make the abilites unlockable, make it so you can equip them all rather than a maximum of 3 at a time. Also, while the platforming itself is tight and fluid, wall jumping can be tedious. When wall jumping, your movement is locked in place with you being unable to jump away in any direction other than dead straight, which can lead to some frustrating deaths and time-consuming falls.
Also, bugs. obviously with indie games the devs can't spend nearly as much on playtesting as larger companies, but that being said, the game is still full of game breaking stuck-spots, especially in Mafia Town. Spots in the environment you can end up in accidentally that stick you in place are frustrating to deal with, and while most of these spots can be escaped by wiggling and button mashing, some lock you in for good, forcing you to quit back to the hub and abandon all your progress on your current mission and start over.
Alright, time to recap, (puns intended)
The Pros:
+tight, fun, responsive gameplay
+amazing level design
+good amount of content for the price
+near perfect soundtrack
+quirky side chars
+adorable main char
+stylized graphics
+constant nostalgia rush
Cons:
-gameplay needlessly complicated at times
-mustache girl's scenery chewing
-silent protagonist
-some ugly animations
-thin, cheesy story
I give A Hat In Time a 9/10, as it sets the bar high for modern 3D platformers and indie games in general with very few significant slip ups. You've earned yourselves a fan, Gears for Breakfast, Keep at it!

Some people say that this is the worst "Tales of" game but it is my first game of the series and I love it.
The story is epic while also being lighthearted at the same time. It may be difficult to understand the basic of combat or skills at first, but when you do, the game is a blast. Combat is in real-time just like Final Fantasy XV. Managing SC points (stamina / mana), defending and dodging, and casting buffs/debuffs are keys to victory. Experimenting with fusing is very enjoyable which reminds me a lot of Atelier game series. The world is a semi-open-world not unlike Dragon Age Inquisition with many large areas that you can go anywhere you want. One thing that surprises me the most is that there are no quests! There are only the story missions and side-story missions, so no fetch quests to be found in this game (I'm not sure but it's been 30 hours now and no fetch quests yet). You play Ueno Enju, a young Japanese woman who is a novice shinobi, caught in the middle of peacetime politics and government espionage. Nightshade is a gripping story set in the Sengoku Era, very loosely based off of the years after Nobunaga Oda's death. You will come across original and fictionalized historical characters and, depending on who you choose, your heart will soar or be crushed—or both! Besides the main character (MC), this visual novel is fully voiced and the art is a stunning interpretation of the period.
(I will mostly be referring to Hanzo's route here) Sometimes I'd look at Enju in awe because of her love for her friends and her ability to adapt. While admirable, she was the typical naive, porcelain skin, young woman that is seen too often in Japanese VN's. I also wish she weren't so docile and self-deprecating (though I understand it is a result of her environment) but I love who she becomes. Another thing I am grateful to the writers for is that some of the love interests (LI) never blame her for horrific things that happen. For example, Gekkamaru and Hanzo understood that situations were out of her control and explicitly said it was the other party's fault. Oftentimes in VN's, the LI would get irrationally upset and blame the MC, saying it could have been avoided but that never happened. I loved it.
At the beginning, sometimes I wanted Kyara to be the protagonist or to have her own route (still do). Kyara is confident, down to earth, funny, vulnerable, non-apologetic, and there's just a lot to love about her. There were missed opportunities to open up for more political intrigue and action sequences. In addition to Kyara, the game would have also benefited with a route for Ieyasu, mostly because of what I found during my brief research of the Nobunaga Oda (yay, tangential learning!). Ieyasu was a historical figure who, as a child, was a hostage of Nobunaga's clan and eventually grew to be one of his strongest allies. Again, missed opportunity.
The overall story is intriguing but doesn't branch very far. Every route is linear, whether you choose dialogue for the good or bad ending. Besides the finale, the same thing will always happen each route but the MC's characterization and development may vary. If you were like me and wanted to go down Hanzo's route first, it is nearly impossible to get it without restarting multiple times or following a guide. Even if you chose neutral options for other characters, simply picking the wrong area to visit will ensure you don't unlock his route (or your desired path). I'm not expecting Bioware-level decision making but having to choose places to visit with no indication of which route it benefited dragged things out; it's an inconvenient storytelling mechanic if you want a specific path.
The voice acting is phenomenal. I don't mind that Enju doesn't have a voice. It allows the player to place themselves into her shoes more easily. I also suggest using the MC's name instead of customizing it because the characters actually say her name aloud. Plus, it's odd to have dialogue suddenly cut off, especially during heated moments. Another mechanic that was completely unknown to me until recently is, if you have a mousewheel, you can scroll up to review and rewind back to a dialogue you might have missed. Lastly, some of the audio was recycled which broke immersion because it'd make me laugh. It's funny hearing the same kissing clip multiple times. It can be easily overlooked though!
There were times when the narrative and characters fell into overused VN tropes but it can be endearing for the novelty. If you can power through that, I'd say this is a win just for the production quality alone. There are still some bugs but the developers are always patching and they've been very responsive to the community which is terrific. People may also appreciate a diagram of the keyboard/mouse mechanics; hopefully it will be added! From the historical revisionism (particularly Hanzo and Goemon), to the visuals, the soundtrack and acting—you'll find yourself in love, in awe, in tears. Despite its shortcomings, you'll be entertained for hours on end and Nightshade may even re-ignite your love of shinobi legends like it did for me. TL;DR: Play for Hanzo only.

I really have no idea what to say about this game, but I will try my best.
---I like everything medieval so the setting and atmosphere was appealing. I think it did a fair job conveying it.
---The sound track throughout the game nicely coincides with the atmosphere. I did not tend to like the opening theme song, but, in hindsight, it works anyway despite it.
---The artwork was well done and for once most/all the characters are dressed stylish instead of sad and pathetic (I am especially looking at you Amnesia memories).
---Most of the time there is only one dialogue option in each chapter and I personally did not see how one option could change the flow of the story THAT much . The characters do not seem to act much differently and quickly continue on the story without "seeming" to have make much change in their behavior or the story (with the exception of the endings). If the floral symbol gains color this is how you know you said the right thing, but the other options are not necessarily bad either.
---The MC is generally likeable, but I personally found her flat as a character. I am not sure whether this is because she is the only character unvoiced or (more likely) how most otome MC's tend to go with the flow of the story and just happen to lack character because of it.
---consistencies was fairly consistent between routes with some minor instances suggesting otherwise. Example:
---It was interesting to have the characters fight battles. Most of the time you just see flashes of what can only be called as sword slashes across the screen. It would have been cooler, though probably more expensive, to have a short video of the fights. I started thinking of watching anime fight scenes like those from SAO.
---I think I generally made all the points I could to nick pick at this game. Just because I did, do not let it completely sway you from this game. I write the bad to give a complete and honest review as unbiased as possible. This being said, it is one of the better Otome games out there on Steam. I have played Amnesia Memories, Ozmafia, and the ones from Cheritz though I didn't like the Cheritz ones (sorry over there) and I feel I have more experience reviewing Otome games now. I suppose I should change my opinion on some of the others, but probably won't since that is how I felt at the time.
Nightshade is pretty good and you can tell there was some time and love spent on it. I love everything medieval and the atmosphere felt authentic and the romance (though I hated the sound effect of the kissing...ugh...no thanks, silence please) it was not over the top. (thank god.)
Yes I would recommend it to Otome lovers and I believe most will be generally pleased. I guess I should add I am very happy adding this game to my collection. I am not sure if it is my absolute favorite since there are a couple I really like, but I would put it up there. I am not sure which of my favorites is my favorite.

Probably the most fun and engaging 3D platformer I've ever played. Controls are good, environments are very well designed and platforming is good. Every level feels like it's asking you to do something different (the chapters even moreso), and all of those different things are all quite engaging. The art, music and sound design are all excellent. The main character is adorable, and the other characters are all great fun and do a lot to keep the new experiences coming.
Difficulty is a bit on the low side so most players should be able to beat it. Individual challenges are sometimes fairly hard, and you certainly won't be sleeping through it, but the game's excessively forgiving if you fall or die. And while the bosses are creative and have some nasty attacks I believe the game starts throwing extra hearts at you after ~3 deaths so you won't get stuck. But this isn't a game you play to test yourself, it's a game you play to have fun and experience everything.

The spiritual successor to System Shock, this game from Ken Levine, and 2K games from all over, uses Unreal Engine 3 so well that Unreal Tournament 3 cries. It's a lot like System Shock 2 only it's steam-punk intstead of cyber-punk, and instead of being in space, you're underwater. There's a lot of verious religion in this game, ranging from Rapture to Adam and Eve.
You will use magic spells -- or "plasmids" -- a pipe wrench, and various firearms of the period -- revolver, tommy gun, pump shotgun, etc -- to kill your enemies. You have a few different types of enemies, most common are "splicers" which are the people of Rapture, gone insane from the power of Adam and Eve and Plasmids. Then you have the different types of Big Daddies that protect the Little Sisters, that splicers are always after because Little Sisters use needles to obtain Adam from corpses. If you get too close to the Little Sister or you attack the Big Daddy, you've got a tough fight on your hands. But the battle will be well worth it, because there's power in it for you if you survive, and you can choose to save the Little Sister, or turn her into a slug and obtain more power. Your decision of what to do with Little Sisters will give you one of two endings. You can even use your camera to snap photos of enemies and increase your damage against them.
A solid FPS inspired by various first-person shooting/role-playing games like Deus Ex and System Shock, this game has a great story, solid controls, and a good use of the Unreal Engine for its time. However, there is a serious problem with framerate at times, but not the actual framerate, just the frames per second of characters a certain distance away. It's very odd but the game will make up for it in numerous ways and you will be intrigued from start to finish.
+ The world and lore
+ Cast of characters
+ Good shooting mechanics
+ Plasmids
+ The bond between Big Daddies and Little Sisters
+ The twist at the end
+ Two endings
+ Boss fights
+ Secret areas with great stuff
+ Weapons
+ Using plasmids to melt ice, put out fires, or electrocute water
+ Camera to increase power against enemies is a smart mechanic that works well
+ I CAN SHOOT FREAKING BEES FROM MY ARMS

- Not a terrible, but not a great PC port
- Hacking minigame
- Some areas that are seriously too shiny

After logging hundreds of hours of play on my KindleFire with Pixel Dungeon, I am not disappointed with the Steam version at all.  I never got the Windows version but was happy to throw payment to the devs for the Steam version for the past fun I had with the game.
The graphics are charming and look great even for pixel characters, if you have been with this for awhile you know the extra efforts put into little things like backround, lighting and etc over the bunch of updates it had since being created.  Now it's the norm "rougelike" and permadeath that will leave you tearing your hair out most times, but still drawing you back for more.  Having great armor and weapons but dying of hunger is a common thing,  or having lardders of food and getting beat to hell by the monsters.  The number of times I have died to a gnoll on the 2nd level is almost uninstall worthy.
For those of you from the early PC days, and I don't mean Starcraft or Diablo, but C64 days of yore and where most games were permadeath (unless you pulled the disk out of the drive after you died quick enough or created another character disc) there was a shining creation of a game called Sword of Fargoal.  Pixel could be the direct great, great grandson of Fargoal, both share many traits and each their own also, which when I found Pixel I was brought back to those great days and fell in love with the game.
The game is easy to learn and can be played for hours or a few quick minutes with auto save when you quit.  Classes play different as a difficulty system somewhat with added bonuses for each class.  Pretty much click where you want to go, click to pick up, click to attack/throw/use item etc, very nice for a sit back and relax game.  Potions and scrolls have to be identified or fingers crossed used to find out what they do, sometimes with horrible results.
I know there are plenty of reviews on this game allready with gameplay and pros vs cons but for me it is a rekindling of my great years playing PC games which were designed to be hard and have days or months of playing time with no internet faq or walkthrough to help you with the game.  This is a great game period, worth the $5, for me yes and a review if it's worth the money, very much so.  Buy it and enjoy.

Survival-Crafting Alpha releases seem to be a dime-a-dozen on Steam lately, so does The Long Dark stand itself apart?
(TL;DR? We talk about the game and all of its features and shortcomings HERE on Steampunks) (Coming soon)
Though the story mode is the main feature promised once the game exits Early Access, we’re given a taste of the scenario that lands you in the game’s events. You’re a solo bush pilot, navigating his or her way over the Great White North when a geomagnetic disaster devastates the landscape, enrages the wildlife, and knocks your plane out of the sky. It’s a simple but effective setup that pits you in the classic man vs. wild conflict in a terrain so compelling that we’re honestly surprised we haven’t seen more often in the genre. There hasn’t been much to go on, but it’s obvious that the episodic narrative on the horizon will be a warm welcome. For now, there’s a lot of satisfaction to be found in creating your own stories of survival in Sandbox Mode.
There are distinct exploration styles that players can adapt and combine in order to forge their path. Most are likely to spend the bulk of their early playtime scavenging through abandoned settlements for food and supplies while simultaneously beholding the sights and sounds. This type of point-and-click-while-smelling-the-roses playstyle is very reminiscent of Gone Home, though here players are piecing together what objects are most valuable to their longevity rather than uncovering a core narrative. The potential for that type of story progression to fuse into the existing gameplay is certainly viable once the game is complete.
Hunting and fishing become available once you’ve persevered long enough and found the materials necessary, though sometimes this can occur from simple luck of the draw. The game places higher emphasis on discovering treasures and keeping the key items in your inventory in top repair after you’ve found them, rather than gathering loads of materials and crafting towards better equipment over time. That isn’t to say there aren’t craftables, but for now these remain as mostly clothing items to keep you warm, rather than tools such as improved firearms, hunting knives, or hatchets. As it stands in the current build, these tools need to be found in the randomly generated mix of items spread throughout the map. It’s once these items are collected that the game starts to really switch gears, and will become the preferred playstyle for most. Explorers eventually become well equipped with a hunting rifle, fishing tackle, flares, and other necessities. There’s a certain pride to experience in building yourself up to be a self-sufficient hunter. Evolving from vulnerability and feeding off scraps to feeling like a legitimate threat to the wild carries a big payoff. Most of all, it quickly becomes the most likely way to keep your stomach filled.
The game measures your survival in almost every imaginable way. Hunger, thirst, cold, and fatigue can all be observed from the in-game quick menu, and are rapidly and appropriately impacted by your decisions. A separate calorie counter keeps track of the energy left in your body, meaning you can intake low-nutrition food items to spike your blood-sugar, but these won’t hold you over for the long haul. Unsafe water sources need to be disinfected through the use of collected additive pellets or boiling, or their consumption comes with the risk of infection. First aid supplies can be found and created in order to tend to these ailments and keep up your condition, complete with medication, bandages, antiseptic, and painkillers. Your warmth is affected by the quality of the clothing articles you find and their condition, meaning you’ll be rewarded with being able to spend more time in the great outdoors once you find and sew up some proper winter gear. This becomes vital since actions such as fishing and foraging for wood are time-lapsed, with the effects taking place on your person after the fact.
When these features all come together, keeping every part of your well-being in check derives a legitimate sense of desperation. Almost every action you take is based on the necessity of the situation. It’s a real accomplishment for an Alpha development, and it manages to do so without a single zombie. Other than the need for a graphical user interface regarding your player’s clothing, the only problem we found in all of this was the somewhat ghastly strength of the game’s only aggressive mob, the wolves. More often than not you’ll find your play-through at the mercy of their jaws, even if that’s only because you had to make a risky move to go find more supplies. They’re the dreaded creatures that they should be given the context, but it still feels disappointing to have a good run come to a sudden conclusion from a blindside attack. The non-optional permanent death may sour some to the experience, especially in this respect, but it feels necessary in creating the true survival immersion that these other features go so far to create. Separate difficulty settings allow for play with more or less punishing hazards, giving you the freedom to choose if you want more of an adventure experience.
The finely crafted exploration extends its way into the game’s artwork as well. The visuals are unmistakably Canadian in a way that has to be seen in order to be given proper justice. The distinct palette combined with the carefully placed polygonal edges and etched shapes make you feel like you’re exploring a genuine piece of Inuit artwork. Fine tunings like the rhythmic puff of breath in front of your face or the feel of your stride stiffen as you enter thicker snow constantly remind you of the harsh nature of the surrounding climate. Daylight casts through the windows of the cabins in which you seek refuge, revealing specks of dust flickering in the sun. Some of these dwellings even proudly carry their national flag above their front door. The attention to details like these help cement the feeling that you’re stranded in the real Canadian north instead of a powdered sandbox filled with things to keep you busy. Some individual textures themselves may not exactly amaze anyone, especially the graphic-savvy, but they still make for endearing log cabin interiors, and beautifully ominous outdoor scenes. Animations with many objects leave a lot to the imagination, mostly due to the lack of hands or any viewable body part. Certain interactions such as lighting fires and reloading rifles could really benefit from this extra attention, but omissions like these can be forgiven due to its Early Access status.
The choice of music implementation is scarce and careful. Sparse atmospheric tones are brought in occasionally as you stomp around or discover a new locale, highlighting the experience. When the entire recipe is brought together it can make for some remarkable cinematic endeavors despite not yet having any real narrative backbone.
The Long Dark is certainly a refreshing treat after a recent sea of mediocrity overtaking the survival/crafting genre. As this brand of game continues to grow, we can only hope that more titles take inspiration from this piece and create finely-honed experiences of realism that remain faithful to existing real-world culture.

This review takes into consideration that this isn't just a video game for sale, but moreso the ability to directly fund a video game project that piques my interest.
As it stands, there are three available "maps" which are all connected (you aren't limited to which map you wish to explore).  The "goal" is to survive for as long as you can.  You'll probably get bored after you've looted everything of interest, but the real goal is for you to experience the concept of game play, and offer up constructive criticism to the developement team.
You can craft, you can loot, you can fish, you can hunt animals, you can explore.  The ambience is spot on, worthy of turning the lights off and turning your speakers up.
There are 3 difficulties currently, which mostly affects the wildlife (harmless, violent, don't stop running).  Playing the "casual" setting will actually keep the wildlife away, so this will force you to rely solely upon looted goods (there's plenty) or fishing to stay alive.
The graphics are reminiscent of cel shading, but you find that they don't quite matter after awhile, and the atmosphere is only enhanced, if anything.  This also makes the game easier to handle for your PC, and gives the devs a little more time to focus on actual content.
Keep in mind it's basically a living demo, and I think you'll be please.

There are many assets that provide a great audiovisual experience. The graphical effects and sounds are perfectly implemented to set the mood and theme of a World War II simulation, grabbing the player's full attention in immersive and tense scenarios. All of the official maps are also beautifully crafted, with much attention to detail, including good quality textures and tactical environments. Since this is a multiplayer only game, that is where it all starts falling apart. Firstly, the developers opted to use the archaic, erroneous, and intrusive PunkBuster anti-cheat service in the game. Not only is it extremely innacurate and unreliable, it also requires its own separate installation onto your system; which means it will force itself to run in the background, in addition to the game client. Secondly, the server browser and in-game pings differ by at least 30 or 40, every time. In other words, the ping being shown in the server browser is always at least 30 or 40 lower than what it actually is in-game. This is a problem that has been reported in both the Steam and official game forums for a long while, without any response by the developers. Thirdly, even though there is an average of 1276 concurrent players in the last 30 days at the time of this writing, finding a populated server with a tolerable ping is not easy. The few servers available with a playable ping (100 or less) have the low artificial intelligence bots taking place of the absent human players, which brings down the game's fun factor to an unbearably low level. In addition to the lack of active servers, when there are people playing on a full server, many player pings are in the 200s, and some in the 300s. What could have been a great, engrossing, realistic experience ends up being marred by all of its technical online problems. While one may find adequate multiplayer conditions to play the game properly from time to time, I have found that this happens very rarely. What you will find are high ping servers with a small human population and a high bot population, with the occasional populated high ping server with human players whose pings are well into the 100s, 200s, and even 300s. A multiplayer only game should never be played in those conditions. If you are able to find a good server with people playing, there are many fun and fulfilling hours to be had. Too bad these ideal conditions are few and far between.

Decent game. My only complaints are:
EA completeley changed the atmosphere of the game. It went from post-apocalyptic, dramatic and gloomy with some heavy science-fiction elements, to Modern Warfare as an RTS game with aliens. They completely got rid of a lot of aspects that made Tiberian Sun such an atmospheric game, such as map-wide ion storms, tiberium mutants (while they still exist canonically they only rarely make appearances), and NOD was dumbed down greatly in the sense that their technology now sucks pretty badly and their numbers/strength are fairly laughable.
You can't have a singleplayer skirmish without the AI spamming grenadiers/black hand/buzzers. Those are the only infantry units that the game's AI will make and it makes it extremely frustrating to employ infantry of your own because those three types of troops clear garrisons and kill infantry instantly.
The scrin are OP - it's mostly a matter of how you fight them but considering they get fighters that don't need to re-arm and gunships and frigates and all that and the NOD and GDI only have fighters and some light AA, it's not really fun to go up against them unless you know exactly what you're doing.
-Another thing about the Scrin is that all or most of their units get shields. It's like playing against the protoss in Starcraft all over again.
Another thing is that defenses suck (unless you play with the old Tiberium Essence mod) - there's no walls and turrets are pretty weak.
All in all I'd give it a 7/10 because I loved the previous C&C games and EA did a good job of continuing the story for the Tiberium series, but it is lacking in some areas that could have been executed better.

The year is 2045. World is almost completelly infested with a strange, green substance, called Tiberium. It is evolving.
On Earth, there are those, who want to get rid of this thing. And also those, who can claim it, worship it, and use it, maybe for greater good. These two sides can not go side by side. Thus - they are at an apocalyptic war across the entire planet !

I still remmember how long I waited, together with my brother, to get this one in hand. I was 17 years old when it came out - and our poor old PC (2.4GHz Celeron - ONE core, 0.75GB RAM DDR2, and 0.5GB graphic card) can run it only on the lowest settings. Some people say that this is the worst "Tales of" game but it is my first game of the series and I love it.
The story is epic while also being lighthearted at the same time. It may be difficult to understand the basic of combat or skills at first, but when you do, the game is a blast. Combat is in real-time just like Final Fantasy XV. Managing SC points (stamina / mana), defending and dodging, and casting buffs/debuffs are keys to victory. Experimenting with fusing is very enjoyable which reminds me a lot of Atelier game series. The world is a semi-open-world not unlike Dragon Age Inquisition with many large areas that you can go anywhere you want. One thing that surprises me the most is that there are no quests! There are only the story missions and side-story missions, so no fetch quests to be found in this game (I'm not sure but it's been 30 hours now and no fetch quests yet). Every mission is part of the story that helps you feel more engaged in the plot. No more wondering what you were doing before starting a long list of side quests like in other games.
In short, it has been a while that I encounter a game like this. I love open-world and RPG games in fantasy setting and this game delivers. If you are interested in this game and decide to buy it, give it a chance by playing for a couple of hours before judging. Give it some time and you may love it like I do.
