Pros:
* Immersive world of ninjas and samurai, based on a real historical time period (End of Sengoku Era)
* Refreshing storyline, and captures your interest from first impressions within the early chapters
* Conflict between the ninja clans within an overarching political war created a more complex plot
* Great world-building, and detailed background on the universe of Nightshade
* A lot of unique ninjutsu incorporated into the game, which made it more exciting and authentic with the ninja theme
* Tale of adventure, self-discovery, self-worth, familial loyalty and love
* Writing and execution of the storyline was a strong point of the game
Cons:
* Main linear storyline is prevalent in all the routes (common route is the same for all characters)
* Game branch diverges into two linear story paths.
* Although there are alternate events and different endings for all the characters, the core events of the storyline are repetitive. This makes the game become rapidly stale by around the third or fourth playthrough.
* Events that would once invoke surprise or shock became predictable due to the linear storyline.
* The character routes are not fully disconnected from one another, and they all build from the same premise.
* No true/canon ending.
Recommended Route Order: Goemon → Hanzo → Kuroyuki → Gekkamaru → Chojiro (storyline makes the most logical sense and greater spoilers throughout the Koga ninja trio routes)
Pros:
* Captivating cast with fun and interesting relationship dynamics with one another
* 5 obtainable bachelors; each with different and unique personalities
* Interesting character pasts and twists
* Delves into the thematic concept of what it means to be a Shinobi, and sense of duty conflicted by morals and beliefs
* Crafted stronger attachments to the characters, due to the multi-faceted dimensions of their personalities due to the tragedy of their pasts
Cons:
* Ieyasu Tokugawa is not an obtainable character, which is a huge waste of his lovely seiyuu and character design.
* Needed more diversity in the character roles
* They're all ninja, whereas including Ieyasu Tokugawa would have created a significantly more refreshing and multi-dimensional storyline in comparison to the current cast.
* Would have made a unique path with a different perspective to the current storyline rather than running as a fugitive in every route
* Would have liked epilogue endings for the characters with bonus CG for a more wholesome conclusion for the character stories.
Pros:
* Highlight of the game
* Surprising number of character sprites in the game that are illustrated and voiced
* Beautiful character designs (especially for Enju's outfit and colour motif).
* Backgrounds especially well done, they look like a water colour painting.
* Nice character sprite poses, especially their fighting stance, ninja outfits and unique weaponry
* Teita is the same artist for Norn9 by Idea Factory
Cons:
* Artist is a little inconsistent with hands/body poses in some CGs, but it's a negligible point that can easily be overlooked.
* Side profiles were noticeably the most awkward in CGs
* Small discrepancy in quality between character sprites and the CGs within the game
Pros:
* Lovely music and OST
* Enjoyed the battle theme
* Experienced and famous character cast, and emulated their personalities very well.
* Similar voice actors to the Hakuoki series, will instantly recognise their characters and voices.
* For example: Hattori Hanzo (VA: 津田 健次郎 Tsuda Kenjiro | Yu Gi Oh as Seto Kaiba, Hakuouki series as Chikage Kazama)
* Goemon Ishikawa (VA: 緑川 光 Midorikawa Hikaru | Fate/Zero as Lancer, Starry Sky series as Yoh Tomoe, Fire Emblem series as Marth and Haven't You Heard? I'm Sakamoto as Sakamoto)
* Chojiro Momochi (VA: 鳥海 浩輔 Toriumi Kōsuke | Naruto series as Inuzuka Kiba, Hakuouki series as Saito Hajime)
Cons:
* None

Pros:
* Includes all basic functions such as save slot, skip, quick load/save and CG Gallery.
* Nicely designed UI
* Nice extra effects such as leaves falling, sakura blossoms scattering and rain animation.
* Character animations such as blinking and mouth moving when speaking were included.
* Flowers appear on screen hovering over the bachelor whom you earned affection points with.
* Memories tab allows you to replay chapters of your character route, and unlocks bonus events upon completion of route.
* Had very clean fighting animations, definitely made the game a pleasure to play as the action unfolded
* Variety of bachelor voices to choose from for the system dialogue
Cons:
* First day release had text spacing issues. The team did fix after a couple of hours, but for a delayed release of 4-5 months after the original release date, you do not expect for these issues to still occur.
* Text font choice could have been much better and clearer to read.
* Had trouble initially adjusting the text speed because it kept setting text speed to 99% rather than 100%. As a result, text did not appear all at once and took some fiddling around with to work. This is a problem I have never encountered before.
* Ease of use of the UI is average, and is on the clunky side.
* Would have liked to see scene recollection included, rather than only being able to play the specific chapters of the character routes.
* Jump button would have been useful (for skipping to the next decision) especially during the common route.
* Solid game
* Heavily inspired by Hakuoki. Athough Nightshade has it’s own fair share of suffering and tragedy, it overall was nowhere near as dark and painful.
* Had more light-hearted moments and genuinely happy endings rather than the bittersweet ones in Hakuoki.
* Main highlight: beautiful artwork, stellar voice acting and great music.
* First playthrough = 8hrs, subsequent playthroughs were 3-5 hrs per character. Total Game Time: 20-30hrs, which is fairly short.
* The linear storyline and lack of character role diversity really took away from the overall feel of the game. It definitely lost its momentum and surprise factor by around the third playthrough, as it essentially only followed one of two linear game branches that both revolved around the same concept
* Enju's character development did not feel as fleshed out or as well-developed in the other routes in comparison to Hanzo's story.
* Not having Ieyasu Tokugawa as a character was a huge waste of potential for both storyline and character development
* Would have liked to see a true ending/canon ending route.
* Captivating character cast
* System could have been greatly improved
* Nonetheless, it is very enjoyable and one of the better otome games on the market
* Would recommend
OVERALL RATING: 3.5/5

You get to play as a female ninja during the Sengoku period in Japan. Like most visual novels/otome games, your choices will determine what happens in the game. There are 5 different routes with a common route that branches off later on. The story itself doesn't change much from route to route, mostly just which guy you end up with, so a lot of parts may feel a bit repetitive.
The concept of the story isn't new in any way but it is believable and it's written very well. The characters are also believable and they feel very realistic, all of them being very different from each other. I do however feel like some characters received more love than others, and a couple of routes are really bittersweet in comparison to the others, even in the good endings. My personal favorite is Hanzo, because his route is one of the most mature romance stories I've ever read in the otome genre.
The surroundings and visuals in the game are well done too. The fact that some people, events and places are historically correct helps a lot with the illusion of realism. The voice acting, the art and the immersion just makes everything perfect. I also think that the music that was used is good, and it's used during appropriate moments to convey feelings.
I didn't encounter any game-breaking bugs, only some minor spelling mistakes. The game is very solid and it's a must-play for anyone who likes visual novels and otome.

There's hints that something more depressing has happened in the subtext, but for all intents and purposes you are navigating an unfriendly world with no no motivation other than to survive and continue moving forward.
The real appeal of Limbo is in level design. Using a surprisingly versatile drab grayscale color scheme, a wonderful illusion of depth, ominous, ambient music, and clever puzzle design,
If you want a short, imaginative puzzle platformer, Limbo is great. Just be prepared to die terrible deaths over, and over, and over again.

It's fun, but there is so much bullsh*t from the attack system and item drops that you pretty much will kill yourself in the first 4 levels. There are better dungeon crawlers out there although for a turn-based one it does things pretty well. My three major gripes with it are the Hunger System, Attack System and the Item System.
Hunger is bull, it's hard enough keeping your health up but having to go out of your way to search a level that may or may not have any food on it is stupid, either remove the system or reduce the frequency of its occurences because the Item System isn't helping either.
The Item System is interesting, the fact that with Potions, Armour and Weapons you don't know what will happen until you try it is cool, I really like that feature and find it a bit humourous when I drink a potion not thinking to just throw it first and then self-igniting myself. The issue with this system is that the items are rare and sparce, you may go through an entire level and pick up maybe 2-3 items (excluding Dew Drops and Seeds but they're not that useful). Also I often find that it's only after I reach level 3 usually that I actually have a new Sword and Armour, it's annoying that it's that far down and the enemies can do near identical damage to you which makes it a real pain when you just need a Healing Potion or some better armour but you can't get to it because you keep getting killed before you can find any, because the items are so rare in this game.
The last one, and I swear to eveyone's based god, the most crippling one to this game, the attack system. The attack system is absolute crap, you will miss more times than you will hit, while your enemies will hit nearly all the time. I can understand with an enemy like the Wraith, as its a ghost that it's hard to hit but when I start at full health with a Healing Potion and can't hit this guy once before dying, that's too far and the Wraith don't even do that much damage so it was a good 12-20 hits. The other thing is that enemies are almost random with the amount of damage they do, I've fought rats that'll deal 1 and 2 damage and I was thinking that I was going to kill it and then it deals a 5 and I'm dead, seriously, the second level introduces this enemy, I can't remember the name for but looks like a squirrel-sort of and it deals a consecutive 3-4 damage almost all the time where I'm luck to land a 6 on them. It's such a pain getting killed by a single creature and it's so annoying when the only thing it says above the enemy is evaded, evaded, evaded, dodged, dodged, evaded. It's painful to watch something like that happen.
So if you want a game that'll kill you within 4 levels with no more than 30 enemies get this game, but if your looking for a genuinly fun and enjoyable Dungeon Crawler where each venture is very different, then keep looking because this game is relentless.

A Hat In Time harkens back to the era of classic n64 collect-a-thons. The game starts you off in a hub world and you use time pieces you collect throughout the various levels to unlock new areas. A Hat In Time has 5 worlds: mafia town, battle of the birds, subcon forest, alpine skyline, and time's end. These worlds have multiple acts that take place in the same stages but with slight alterations. This design choice reminds me of super mario sunshine and mario sunshine is a very apt comparison to A Hat In Time.
The most important aspect of a collect-a-thon platformer is by far good controls and a good camera. A Hat In Time has wicked slick and tight controls. Precise jumps are easy to land and when you get accustomed to your jump distances the game rewards fast, technical movement. Each of the levels feel like they have super clean movement flow when you run, jump, dive, dive-cancel, and wall jump through them. The camera is also stellar for the most part and the options menu even has camera distance preferences you can set. I never changed the camera settings because I thought they were fine but you may get more enjoyment out of tweaking the camera. A hat in time nails it's controls and it feels great to play.
The levels in a hat in time are generally really good. I think battle of the birds is the weakest segment platforming wise because the levels are too linear and too boxed in. This setup works great in one level of battle of the birds but the rest of the act is pretty underwhelming. Boss fights are hit and miss. None of the boss fights are hard or even challenging, but some are definitely more fun than others.
The sound is great. the music is pretty good.
On to the bad,
the game has some technical issues. I experienced a crash right before I landed the final hit on the first boss(Chef Mafia.) I noticed the water in mafia town would sometimes just freak out for no reason. Also I got stuck inside one of chef mafia's attacks and I couldn't take damage and I couldn't get out so I had to restart the whole level. luckily boss levels are usually short so at least it didn't take awhile to get back but it was annoying.
Overall, A Hat In Time is an 8.5/10 game. the experience is great and I 100%-ed the game but I can't gelp but feel like the design of battle of the birds was a little underwhelming and the technical issues dampened the experience for me a little. Overall this game is worth your time if you like collect-a-thons.

Survival-Crafting Alpha releases seem to be a dime-a-dozen on Steam lately, so does The Long Dark stand itself apart?
(TL;DR? We talk about the game and all of its features and shortcomings HERE on Steampunks) (Coming soon)
Though the story mode is the main feature promised once the game exits Early Access, we’re given a taste of the scenario that lands you in the game’s events. You’re a solo bush pilot, navigating his or her way over the Great White North when a geomagnetic disaster devastates the landscape, enrages the wildlife, and knocks your plane out of the sky. It’s a simple but effective setup that pits you in the classic man vs. wild conflict in a terrain so compelling that we’re honestly surprised we haven’t seen more often in the genre. There hasn’t been much to go on, but it’s obvious that the episodic narrative on the horizon will be a warm welcome. For now, there’s a lot of satisfaction to be found in creating your own stories of survival in Sandbox Mode.
There are distinct exploration styles that players can adapt and combine in order to forge their path. Most are likely to spend the bulk of their early playtime scavenging through abandoned settlements for food and supplies while simultaneously beholding the sights and sounds. This type of point-and-click-while-smelling-the-roses playstyle is very reminiscent of Gone Home, though here players are piecing together what objects are most valuable to their longevity rather than uncovering a core narrative. The potential for that type of story progression to fuse into the existing gameplay is certainly viable once the game is complete.
Hunting and fishing become available once you’ve persevered long enough and found the materials necessary, though sometimes this can occur from simple luck of the draw. The game places higher emphasis on discovering treasures and keeping the key items in your inventory in top repair after you’ve found them, rather than gathering loads of materials and crafting towards better equipment over time. That isn’t to say there aren’t craftables, but for now these remain as mostly clothing items to keep you warm, rather than tools such as improved firearms, hunting knives, or hatchets. As it stands in the current build, these tools need to be found in the randomly generated mix of items spread throughout the map. It’s once these items are collected that the game starts to really switch gears, and will become the preferred playstyle for most. Explorers eventually become well equipped with a hunting rifle, fishing tackle, flares, and other necessities. There’s a certain pride to experience in building yourself up to be a self-sufficient hunter. Evolving from vulnerability and feeding off scraps to feeling like a legitimate threat to the wild carries a big payoff. Most of all, it quickly becomes the most likely way to keep your stomach filled.
The game measures your survival in almost every imaginable way. Hunger, thirst, cold, and fatigue can all be observed from the in-game quick menu, and are rapidly and appropriately impacted by your decisions. A separate calorie counter keeps track of the energy left in your body, meaning you can intake low-nutrition food items to spike your blood-sugar, but these won’t hold you over for the long haul. Unsafe water sources need to be disinfected through the use of collected additive pellets or boiling, or their consumption comes with the risk of infection. First aid supplies can be found and created in order to tend to these ailments and keep up your condition, complete with medication, bandages, antiseptic, and painkillers. Your warmth is affected by the quality of the clothing articles you find and their condition, meaning you’ll be rewarded with being able to spend more time in the great outdoors once you find and sew up some proper winter gear. This becomes vital since actions such as fishing and foraging for wood are time-lapsed, with the effects taking place on your person after the fact.
When these features all come together, keeping every part of your well-being in check derives a legitimate sense of desperation. Almost every action you take is based on the necessity of the situation. It’s a real accomplishment for an Alpha development, and it manages to do so without a single zombie. Other than the need for a graphical user interface regarding your player’s clothing, the only problem we found in all of this was the somewhat ghastly strength of the game’s only aggressive mob, the wolves. More often than not you’ll find your play-through at the mercy of their jaws, even if that’s only because you had to make a risky move to go find more supplies. They’re the dreaded creatures that they should be given the context, but it still feels disappointing to have a good run come to a sudden conclusion from a blindside attack. The non-optional permanent death may sour some to the experience, especially in this respect, but it feels necessary in creating the true survival immersion that these other features go so far to create. Separate difficulty settings allow for play with more or less punishing hazards, giving you the freedom to choose if you want more of an adventure experience.
The finely crafted exploration extends its way into the game’s artwork as well. The visuals are unmistakably Canadian in a way that has to be seen in order to be given proper justice. The distinct palette combined with the carefully placed polygonal edges and etched shapes make you feel like you’re exploring a genuine piece of Inuit artwork. Fine tunings like the rhythmic puff of breath in front of your face or the feel of your stride stiffen as you enter thicker snow constantly remind you of the harsh nature of the surrounding climate. Daylight casts through the windows of the cabins in which you seek refuge, revealing specks of dust flickering in the sun. Some of these dwellings even proudly carry their national flag above their front door. The attention to details like these help cement the feeling that you’re stranded in the real Canadian north instead of a powdered sandbox filled with things to keep you busy. Some individual textures themselves may not exactly amaze anyone, especially the graphic-savvy, but they still make for endearing log cabin interiors, and beautifully ominous outdoor scenes. Animations with many objects leave a lot to the imagination, mostly due to the lack of hands or any viewable body part. Certain interactions such as lighting fires and reloading rifles could really benefit from this extra attention, but omissions like these can be forgiven due to its Early Access status.
The choice of music implementation is scarce and careful. Sparse atmospheric tones are brought in occasionally as you stomp around or discover a new locale, highlighting the experience. When the entire recipe is brought together it can make for some remarkable cinematic endeavors despite not yet having any real narrative backbone.
The Long Dark is certainly a refreshing treat after a recent sea of mediocrity overtaking the survival/crafting genre. As this brand of game continues to grow, we can only hope that more titles take inspiration from this piece and create finely-honed experiences of realism that remain faithful to existing real-world culture.
SCORE : 8.8/10

But first timers are probably asking, what kinda game is this?
1. It's hardcore-mode. Unless you have a special item (which I've never acquired until the first shop), when you die, you die, no second chance.
2. Almost entirely randomly generated. The rooms change, and the items/potions also change - what was a health potion last playthrough might be a Toxic Gas potion this time around!
3. The art style is pixelated, and very cute IMO.
4. The combat is simple turn based hack-n-slash, point-n-click, but don't let that stop you from trying it. It's still a very challenging game.
5. Watch out for hidden traps and doors! Use the search function to search nearby blocks, or "cells".

While I do miss the Mario triple jump -- which I think should have been added -- I still think the freedom of movement and diversity of approaches to all situations make this game immensely fun to replay and speedrun.
I think some Rifts / Artifacts could use a little bit of polishing in regards to conveyance: The purple rift in Subcon Forest stumped me for quite a while and for no good reason, in my opinion.
The game is wonderfully well optimized, running incredibly well even on my mid-low-end laptop. It plays awesome at minimum settings and it looks absolutely beautiful at max.
The only thing I should say that I didn't like is that Moustache Girl doesn't really pop up very often in the story at all. If she had more speaking roles or showed up to be a nuissance more often, it would really go a long way toward making her a cool little rival. As it stands, it kinda feels like she just shows up, is implied to be important to the plot, and then shows up again at the end for no reason. Of course, this game's story is not very important since its mechanics, visuals, polish and overall fun factor really do carry it, but regardless of that, if Moustache Girl had seen some more involvement, the game would be that little bit more superior.
If you like cute as heck characters and if you enjoy enthralling platformers and miss the old days of Mario Sunshine, Banjo Kazooie, Super Mario 64 and even a little bit of Spyro, grab this pronto. You really don't need to question that anymore.

When I found out you needed Unity Pro to actually do anything with this - -all of my progress had to go into the trash and I had to start over completely.
The only saving grace was that I made my own assets and imported them into the game.
Pros
- It's a wonderful terrain editor. It did everything I wanted with ease.
- The developers were extremely helpful and nice.
- It greatly simplified something you can do in Unity. I mean wow.  Essentially building a huge detailed landscap in unity would take 3 hours to a couple of days - In Game Factory, you can churn out quality, non repetitive and unique landscapes in an hour once you know the tools.
Cons
- Newbie trap. Why is it that all the decent software have some sort of catch that turns it into crappy software?
- It's like shareware with export/save disabled, even after you paid for the full version.
- You can't export objects with your map unless you made it or imported it from outside the game.  This includes the trees in the editor. Don't get too attached to them because they won't go with your project.
When I was working on my project, this wasn't a problem but for others I can see how this is a tremendous setback.
- You need Unity Pro to get the best out of it. At the time, when I was actively using this program -  Unity Pro did not have the subscription model they do now. It was a flat fee and out of the question.
If you want to screw around, sure grab it when it's on sale and have fun.
If you want to actually build something, break out that wallet.
If you're a poor game dev, then look elsewhere - do not let the price point trick you if you're unable to afford other software.

At 170+ hours recorded in this game, I feel like I can finally have some ground to review it.
- Coming from DD1 on the PS3, a game that required a bit of coordination in multiplayer to keep making steps, I lost the satisfaction of progression from campaign to NM modes pretty fast. In a span of 2 hours one evening, my friends and I jumped 300+ points in iPwr. That feeling of accomplishment one gets from finally cracking a code in a game was lost.
- At times, trying to get gear in this game is a bit painful for someone trying to "min-max". Example, I'm building a Waller Squire. This requires the use of "Hearty Blockade" secondary stats. Since the game doesn't use a loot table found in a lot of other games with bosses, it comes down to RNG. Even worse though, is the hoops the RNG jumps through to decide what gear you get.
You can carry 4 heroes in your deck at a time (starting at level 50), so there's a 25% chance for gear to drop for one character. And then there's the number of gear slots possible to drop (7 for squire). AND THEN there is the numerous sub-types and secondary stats that can be applied to a piece of gear. It is almost inevitable that (or so it seems) that gear not used by your class type will drop everytime. It can be painful.
- As this game is in Alpha, the devs seem to be actively calling for community participation in helping mold it. It is for this reason that the game constantly feels fresh when a patch comes out. New characters, mobs and incursions keep me looking forward to logging in.
- I put "good" in quotes because it is a subjective term. When my and my buddies play, there is never a compliant about the constructs of the game ruining our experience together. Sure, as with all games, bugs happen, but for us, it isn't because of server instability. It's hard to imagine this game is in Alpha for as polished as connectivity and stability is concerned. Even playing with PuGs, it doesnt get so bad.
- For a game with "min-max" depth, and ability/stat checks through out levels, it's nice to see the "fun" in a game still, in a world where some franchises are taking themselves too seriously. The sounds effects and voices from characters, the jokes and personalities from tavern folks, and the puns. It's a cute little game that is enjoyable even when I'm sitting here AFKing from an Onslaught writing this review. :)

I grew up with Simcity and the like, so any kind of city simulation game usually catches my eye.  My favorite part of Simcity was disaster prep and recovery, cutting of non-essential parts of the city so the core can survive, cutting a fire wall path to spare a cherished downtown, etc.  Banished has those elements, and does so in a calming atmosphere.  Instead of dealing with thousands and millions, you're dealing with dozens to hundreds, each citizen getting a job.  If you want to survive the winter, you're resource gathering for expansions dwindles, if a plague blows through, prepare to shut down entire industries so the village doesn't freeze to death.  Long-term success will mean short-term sacrifice; prepare to feel the hurt when that baby boom only means 25% of your village is in school and only sucking resources.
There are so few games that present a scenario where everything you've built can be destroyed, where you lose so bad that the only thing to save it is to scrap it, learn something from the disaster, and start over.  This is one of those games, and there really is a satisfying feeling to watching your city team with life- just make sure you have enough doctors and wells to help some of your people survive the inevitable doom.

Pixel Privateers is a side-scrolling "shooter" of sorts. You have a party of explorers flying around in a ship, and you land from time to time to explore a planet. Usually you're required to collect a certain amount of something, or scan the walls, or something else equally meaningless/tedious. Sometimes you're required to fight a boss. The bosses and enemies in general have interesting visual design, and it's one of the highlights of the title. A playthrough involves collecting certain "essences" from 4-5 bosses to stabilize a portal to your home world. Between these boss fights, you seem to land on randomly-generated planets with the aforementioned objectives. Sometimes, your ship will be invaded and you'll fight there as well. A band is constantly playing on your ship with ridiculous music that never failed to make myself and my co-op partner chuckle.
The thing that struck me about Pixel Privateers is that it gets everything right BUT the gameplay. There are plenty of other games that have great gameplay, but then there are other annoyances to deal with, but this one is the opposite. You have a lot of customization options in terms of your party and its composition.
There are class items that you can use to change the class of one of your characters (there are 5 classes altogether), and there are actually different variants of these. So one "Marine" class item might grant a different ability than another. Additionally, there are countless different guns or melee weapons, armor, and helmets that can be equipped based on what you're attempting to do with each character. Your characters also level up and gain attribute points to distribute, as well as the ability to equip items of a higher level. As you explore worlds you collect foreign objects that can be researched. As you research these items, you gain research points that can be spent on abilities for your characters. You can create "matter" out of items you don't need, and use this to clone copies of your characters or different items you like. Lastly, you need enough fuel to fly around the galaxy, but this is easy to come by. This all sounds complicated, but it's really quite simple. However, it is very very time consuming. After every mission, my co-op partner and I probably spent about 5 minutes assigning attribute points, digging through gear, and selecting research projects.
This would be fine if the core gameplay was engaging, but it just isn't. Gameplay, for us, involved selecting all of our characters and clicking on one enemy after another to be attacked. The characters would move where they needed to in order to attack, and attack as often as possible until the enemy was defeated. Icons would appear above the heads of our characters and above the enemies that could be used to activate special abilities of our characters (a buff or especially damaging shot), but these appeared and disappeared so quickly that I would often miss the opportunity to use the ability, and just as often I wasn't sure quite what I had clicked on. Most of the battles went fine, though occasionally one of our characters would die and need to be respawned. The was frustrating, because we never felt very "in control" of what was happening on screen.
The game might benefit from a feature that allows your characters to "auto-equip" the best equipment for their class, or to "auto-select" attribute points to reduce time between missions. However, what would most benefit it, in my opinion, would be to make the combat turn-based. In this way, a player could see the potential of each class and make the most of the abilities that are granted by the research.
I didn't have an awful time with Pixel Privateers and finished a playthrough, but I just can't recommend it without feeling an engagement with its core gameplay.

Tales of Zestiria is, overall, a good game.
The graphics for the game are stunning. Animated cutscenes look clean, the worlds are expansive and breath-taking to look at, and all the characters in the game are very detailed and well-animated. Definitely a high point in the series when it comes to looks. Soundtrack sounds very nice as well and are beautiful works all by themselves.
It uses a combat system that similar to Tales of Graces ƒ. The game rewards you for dodging at the right times and for attacking with elemental weaknesses. Unlike Graces, where you are encouraged to chain attacks to keep the enemy staggered, Zestiria makes you take a more defensive approach. You'll find yourself guarding very often in order to ward off attacks that would otherwise decimate you. Personally, I don't feel completely satisfied with this combat system, as it sometimes amounts to just button mashing in regular encounters, but boss fights are very fun to play and are a nice spike in difficulty.
Speaking of difficulty, the game seems to balance out the different modes in a different manner than previous games. Rather than increasing the stats of enemies, your EXP gain is instead lowered in exchange for other perks (increased money and grade). This change can put you into situations where you're matched against enemies that are far over your levels depending on the difficulty, which can create unfair gameplay when faced against strong enough enemies.
The interactions betweens characters are also amusing, though I felt they weren't exactly the best cast Tales has to offer. Most of them don't develop past a certain point and are largely static once their role ends. Though this may lead to some bland character development, it does create a well-established party dynamic that the skits and story can take full effect of.
The story is quite clear-cut black-and-white, which isn't a bad thing. You're basically on a quest to quell evil, and there's not much outside of that. Definitely not really up to Tales standards, which serves to deconstruct cliches, but it's a good story in its own right.
I'd recommend this game for anyone who is an open-minded Tales fan or someone who wants to get into the Tales franchise.

Tales Of fans, feel free to skip this review. Odds are you've already bought and played it anyway; if you haven't, well, you'll probably enjoy it despite its myriad flaws.
It might seem odd not recommending a game I've dumped 60+ hours into (at time of writing), but a) I wanted to give the game its due before reviewing it, and b) I'm a massive ♥♥♥♥♥ for Tales games. As a Tales fan, I'm willing to forgive quite a lot, but Zestiria has so much going against it that it's impossible to just look past it all.
First off, the world, story, and characters are all shallow and dull. It's your typical high fantasy "big monster threatens peace" scenario, complete with chosen youth and everything. The politics are dreadfully simple; everything is black and white, with cartoonishly evil villains and protagonists who are naive to the point of it being painful. There are a couple weak attempts at moral ambiguity, but all just makes for some melodramatic and corny scenes. The characters can all be boiled down to a single personality trait and motivation with absolutely no variance. Seraphs- semi-divine beings who are worshipped by the humans of the world and play a major part in the story- make absolutely no sense. Many people don't believe in them, as they are invisible to most, but they're not incorporeal or anything; they could literally just pick up a rock and wave it around in front of someone to prove their existence. It's not like it's even a matter of faith or anything, either- it's just something that has apparently never occurred to any seraph in the history of this world.
The world itself is boring not only from an expositional standpoint, but a visual one as well. While most of the overworld is passable, the dungeons are all practically identical. Not only are their "puzzles" all the same, every dungeon that shares a type (i.e. ruins, forest, cave, etc.) have the same wall and floor textures. This becomes a problem when you're trying to clear out the monsters in those areas, as there are no visual cues besides lighting differences to tell you the difference between each dungeon. Seriously, there's nothing even in them besides monsters; they're just bare hallways leading to big open rooms. The only exceptions to this are the Shepherd's Trial dungeons and the final area (which is fantastic).
Combat plays much like Tales of Graces, where you combo into different attacks by pressing different directions on the left stick. You're also able to fuse with the seraphs in your party, granting you access to new movesets, elemental damage types, and an expanded health pool. It's very satisfying once you get the hang of it... until you get to the later parts of the game. Eventually, it becomes necessary to inflict power hits on enemies (bosses in particular) in order to deal any significant damage to them, but once you learn which moves stagger each type of enemy, it becomes extremely easy to exploit. After the first boss encounter that requires you to use that tactic, monsters rarely pose a threat to you anymore. Even if things start to get rough, Sorey and Mikleo's fusion is obscenely overpowered, allowing you to roll right over anything that might have otherwise posed a threat.
The skill system is pretty daunting at first, but I got a fair amount of enjoyment out of it. Skills (which, to clarify, are not the special moves you use in battle, but are buffs to your characters) are tied to equipment and laid out on a grid, allowing you to form rows, columns, and stacks to further increase their power and unlock bonus skills. I had a surprising amount of fun plotting out my gear and which bonus skills I was going to use on each party member, but I ran into a brick wall when trying to get the gear I needed. Actually acquiring equipment with specific skills is an immense grind that, no joke, would have added a couple dozen more hours to my playtime. It's a huge, unnecessary slog that should have been much less tedious.
I did enjoy parts of my time with Tales of Zestiria, but not nearly enough to recommend it to anyone who's not already a Tales fanatic. If you're looking for a good entry into the series, go get Symphonia; it's also on Steam, and even with its generally cheesy dialog, it's much, much better. If you're looking for a pulp fantasy anime game, then you'll probably enjoy Zestiria; if you expect anything more out of it, though, you'll be sorely disappointed.
Edit: also, the script blows, the English voice acting is atrocious (thankfully there's dual audio or this would have been unbearable), and it's poorly translated. Playing in Japanese, I frequently noticed thath the subtitles didn't match up at all with what the characters were saying. Some jokes and puns obviously had to be changed, as they wouldn't make any sense in English, but there were a lot of lines that changed the tone of what a character was saying drastically. Edna and Rose are particularly bad for this. I guess the counterpoint to this is that not even a better translation could save this dumpster fire of a story, so it doesn't really matter anyway.
Edit Again: Tales of Berseria retroactively fixes a lot of the story issues with this game. If you play Zestiria, you should absolutely play Berseria afterwards (which is a much better game anyway).

I'm not much of an FPS player, but I really enjoyed this single player game.
The story-line, in a nutshell, is about a software pirate whos life gets turned upside down after download something that at first glance seems to be a game. Playing this game, this...virtual environment... becomes more and more addictive.
Like I said, this is a first person shooter, and it really is nothing more than that. But it focuses on that little nugget unlike any other game. Imagine a game where you are in a constant bullet time mode; Where the speed of the game is determined solely by you mouse moving or keyboard input. You are the one that decides the pace of the action, by combining melee and ranged combat, switching between the 2 in a split second.
As much as this game looks and feels like an FPS, the strategy you employ and your ability to switch strategies whilst retaining your situational awareness will prove an interesting experience to say the least.
If I had to compare this to other games, the ones that come to mind are Ronin, Max Payne and The Matrix, with a twist of The Stanley Parable.
It looks good, although don't expect too much texture and model detail; It serves a purpose and it serves it well, and like most games that put mechanics ahead of graphical quality one shouldn't expect too much. I really love what they did with the menu system though ;-)
There are some problems I have noticed in similar games though. For instance, you have the ability to throw an (empty) gun or melee weapon at your enemy to stagger or even kill them, but I found myself in situations where I saw my katana fly through my enemy without doing either, as if they didn't have a body (collision detection problems). In other situations my weapon would bounce off into some random direction, again without affecting them. Enemies firing their weapons AFTER you've punched it out of their hands, killing you by 'magically' spawning bullets out of thin air, weapons falling apart in mid-air because invisible wall (collision detection, once again).
Nothing game-breaking, but annoying at times. The game is actually nicely split in small levels and that makes up more than enough from my perspective. This kind of fine collision detection, which seems to be the cause of the majority of these problems plagued Ronin as well and I'll take it as a symptom of the genre.
All in all I highly recommend giving this addictive and unique shooter a try. Although, I must admit the price of 20 Euro's may be a bit steep for most.

A Hat In Time harkens back to the era of classic n64 collect-a-thons. The game starts you off in a hub world and you use time pieces you collect throughout the various levels to unlock new areas. A Hat In Time has 5 worlds: mafia town, battle of the birds, subcon forest, alpine skyline, and time's end. These worlds have multiple acts that take place in the same stages but with slight alterations. This design choice reminds me of super mario sunshine and mario sunshine is a very apt comparison to A Hat In Time.
The most important aspect of a collect-a-thon platformer is by far good controls and a good camera. A Hat In Time has wicked slick and tight controls. Precise jumps are easy to land and when you get accustomed to your jump distances the game rewards fast, technical movement. Each of the levels feel like they have super clean movement flow when you run, jump, dive, dive-cancel, and wall jump through them. The camera is also stellar for the most part and the options menu even has camera distance preferences you can set. I never changed the camera settings because I thought they were fine but you may get more enjoyment out of tweaking the camera. A hat in time nails it's controls and it feels great to play.
The levels in a hat in time are generally really good. I think battle of the birds is the weakest segment platforming wise because the levels are too linear and too boxed in. This setup works great in one level of battle of the birds but the rest of the act is pretty underwhelming. Boss fights are hit and miss. None of the boss fights are hard or even challenging, but some are definitely more fun than others.
The sound is great. the music is pretty good.
On to the bad,
the game has some technical issues. I experienced a crash right before I landed the final hit on the first boss(Chef Mafia.) I noticed the water in mafia town would sometimes just freak out for no reason. Also I got stuck inside one of chef mafia's attacks and I couldn't take damage and I couldn't get out so I had to restart the whole level. luckily boss levels are usually short so at least it didn't take awhile to get back but it was annoying.
Overall, A Hat In Time is an 8.5/10 game. the experience is great and I 100%-ed the game but I can't gelp but feel like the design of battle of the birds was a little underwhelming and the technical issues dampened the experience for me a little. Overall this game is worth your time if you like collect-a-thons.

This is probably my favourite game of 2017.
The addition of the badges goes a long way to making each playstyle matter but I did find myself only ever using the same three.
The voice-over babble badge should have been an option in the settings menu. It's silly to have to forego a badge slot just for that. I do understand the developer wanted to value the voice-actors they've paid to have but options should always be "free", so to speak. There is no sense in having mechanical implications in this case.
While I do miss the Mario triple jump -- which I think should have been added -- I still think the freedom of movement and diversity of approaches to all situations make this game immensely fun to replay and speedrun.
I think some Rifts / Artifacts could use a little bit of polishing in regards to conveyance: The purple rift in Subcon Forest stumped me for quite a while and for no good reason, in my opinion.
The game is wonderfully well optimized, running incredibly well even on my mid-low-end laptop. It plays awesome at minimum settings and it looks absolutely beautiful at max.
The only thing I should say that I didn't like is that Moustache Girl doesn't really pop up very often in the story at all. If she had more speaking roles or showed up to be a nuissance more often, it would really go a long way toward making her a cool little rival. As it stands, it kinda feels like she just shows up, is implied to be important to the plot, and then shows up again at the end for no reason. Of course, this game's story is not very important since its mechanics, visuals, polish and overall fun factor really do carry it, but regardless of that, if Moustache Girl had seen some more involvement, the game would be that little bit more superior.
If you like cute as heck characters and if you enjoy enthralling platformers and miss the old days of Mario Sunshine, Banjo Kazooie, Super Mario 64 and even a little bit of Spyro, grab this pronto. You really don't need to question that anymore.

I used to think it was excellent but upon replaying it I am not so sure it needed a third game because this game is maybe a low 7/10. Besides, we all know how that went with JC3. After hearing about all the horrific problems the 3rd game has I decided to install this and play it agaain and it just isn't as bad♥♥♥♥♥as I thought it once was. To prevent the game from crashing you want to remember to turn off bokeh filter and decals. As many different times as I have reinstalled it over the years I don't remember that and it is a pain to have to remember to google it. Besides that though the game is, for me at least, pretty technically sound.
Driving controls are god awful. When you press A or D to steer left or right even a slight tap forces your car wildly in that direction. I spend most of the time driving slamming into oncoming traffic, accidentally killing pedestrians, or careening offroad out of control because driving controls suck so bad.
You constantly run out of ammo and grenades and getting more is hard since there are hardly any ammo boxes around. They are too expensive to keep having air dropped, and getting them off dead enemies is impossible if you are low on ammo because any stray guys near the dead ones will mow you down in seconds. So it's a game based 100% around a destruction score to advance the story line and you can run out of ammo easily. If you time it right though you can get ammo from dead guys if you can manage to clear them out before you run up to loot one, but often that is a pipe dream since they usually don't stop flooding in at you.
On the other hand the game, even today, still looks beautiful and has some of the best looking destruction effects I have ever seen in a game. If you are the type of person that likes to mess around in free roam or use mods then you will like this game a lot. I am not much for sandboxing so I like to usually stick to the game's main story and side missions.
Another downfall of the game is that there really isn't much variety: find a base, blow it up to increase your destruction meter, sometimes do escort missions, and thats basically the whole game. Although a♥♥♥♥♥♥load of fun for some time, it does get very repetitive after a while.
I would still easily give it a high 6.9/10, maybe even a 7 or a little higher. Very well made and from what I hear is superior to JC3 both in gameplay and technically.

This is only a recommendation for 6DOF Descent style game fans that don't have anything else to play.
The game is very rough around the edges. The story is very bare bones and only fleshed out through bad radio communications sounding voice acting. The characters are forgettable. The gameplay can be OK once you get the hang of it but there is a high learning curve made all the worse by not hand holding the player on the first level and throwing them too deep in way over their head. I'm a veteran of playing Descent and the first level was like starting on one of the later levels in Descent in terms of difficulty but with limited fuel and resources!
Here's what you must do when playing this game in order to get over that awful learning curve.
1. Go over your control mappings and make sure you are comfortable with them. Expect to die while doing this.
2. Make sure you can easily slide left and right go forward and backward and boost.
3. Especially make sure you know where your GPS button is. Mine was mapped to 'T' and I think that's the default. You will use it a lot. It will sometimes get confused.
4. Rely on your escorts. They are invincible. You are extra squishy. In the early stages, particularly stage 1 get behind them. Use them as shields. Let them take out the baddies.
5. Resources matter a lot! Pay attention to the HUD indicating close by resources. The most annoying ones to manage are Oxygen and Fuel. When you are out of fuel you can still move but you have a lot of inertia. When you are out of oxygen your pilot will die. When you get perforated by gunfire you will leak oxygen.
6. Money is annoying. The best equipment will probably not be something you can afford. Ever. Make sure you get good enough weapons and stick with the machine gun and a missile launcher. Everything beyond that is expensive, not worth it and not readily available in ammo boxes.
7. Do not get distracted by mining. Yes the environment is fully destructible. Yes you can drill all the way through whatever you want. Yes you can sell that stuff and get more cash. BUT.... it's slow and time consuming. Selling stuff doesn't net you that much money. And worst of all: you will run out of fuel and oxygen while mining and then you might be forced to purchase fuel and or oxygen and there goes all the money you just made mining raw materials. Only mine when you need to as an objective or as a way to circumvent walls/fences that you can't break or to get through doors. Be careful when circumventing doors you can get into places that will get you lost. Usually doors can be opened by hacking the right monitor.
8. Radioactive plutonium and solar flares will take down your pilot's health fairly fast. Avoid solar flares. Be careful around plutonium.
9. If you can't find your stuff check the inventory of your ship. I thought I lost all my stuff when I had to drop it for the knights and then went back to my ship without picking it all up and then I didn't have my drill and extractor for the next task. Found them in the ship inventory just before I was about to rage quit.
The story is forgettable and incomplete with a big "To be continued". At the very end
. Most annoyingly, after getting an ingame "Campaign Complete" pop up the player is left with a confusing GPS track that leads you back to your ship after going past it and back to it. Once in your ship you can revisit anywhere in the solar system.... including places that were never a part of the story at all. No game credits or feeling of completion. Why is there a space Hippie peace sign space station? Why is there New Mecca that's largely empty with no resources? These empty areas should have just been cut.
I'm pretty sure the achievements are nearly totally broken as I only earned 1 and then none of the other supposedly unmissable campaign progression ones despite finishing the story.
This was an ambitious take on Interplay's old Descent. They did some things right and a lot of things wrong as the story is forgettable. The architecture/maps are overly complex, confusingly laid out, poorly lit, and graphically dingy looking. Textures are reused far too much. Most of the characters are horrible semi-racist caricatures. The Fourth Reich (Space Nazis) are actually helpful to you and not bad guys (why aren't the space nazis the bad guys? Come on!). Nothing ever comes of when you uncover a space concentration camp (though I had stopped caring about the story at that point so I might have missed it).
Bottom line: Horrible game but it scratches the 6DOF Descent itch well enough that if you're a fan of the genre you'll put up with all the flaws and maybe enjoy the gameplay but for the love of God ignore the story it's really bad.

This game makes the players understand that they have to work in a co-operative, co-ordinative and communicative way in order to have the upper hand. Bioshock , as a series (including it's predecessors System Shock), remains a beacon or light and hope in a dark time for First Person Shooting of the Horror Genre.
It expertly melds true FPS gameplay with extremely tense fighting scenarios, regardless of the difficulty selected. The plasmid abilities like lightning, fire, etc. far from gimmicky, add to the combat allowing the player a plethora of choices available to dispatch their opponents. And that's a good thing too, because in true horror game fashion, ammo and items are not always openly available.
Which brings me to my final point: Exploration is rewarded with rare items, upgrades and ammo types, but also scares and combat. This is where Bioshock and its sequel excel. Even though the goals are somewhat linear, the levels are all big and open to much exploration. Add to that mixture a steampunk retro 50s themed dystopia at the bottom of the ocean, constantly regenerating enemies, and a rich storyline = FPS Must Own List

Now, this title piqued my attention when it was first unveiled. Visually stunning, vibrant and greased. And so, the immersion began.
Where to begin? Clunky CQC, uncomfortable movement / sprint mechanic , odd camera angles. Let it be twitchy NPCs,
Antagonist invasion system puts the titular villain in the role of the hunted. Why? Because matchmaking. Being a Lvl 0 I expected to be evenly matched with newcomers, but no - I was pit against Lvl 4 - Lvl 17 group that left NO chances for me to make a stand. Being an antagonist has no advantages whatsoever. Especially with a stalking Harec / Sniper on the opposing team. Because player name looms on top of the antagonist and the all-seeing eagle-eye quickly discerns the villain from the crowd and puts him down. Players characters out specifically for you, in groups. And if you run into the two or more of them, there's no possibility for a victory. The broken movement/cover system and melee hooking put you down in a matter of seconds.
If that PvP aspect would've been an avoidable / optional part of the PvE story, but no... It is essential to getting new weapons. You need to be a specific and usually highly-invested rank to get them. However the progression system has been made so that you have to grind time-consuming missions over and over to reach your desired rank. And if you lose - you're gradually pulled down.
My experience has been downright stressful and that's not what I expected from an action-adventure title.

That said, the community is largely friendly and helpful to newcomers who mind themselves and the game. Graphics are acceptable, basic Unreal 3 quality, though the sound effects are exceptional. I highly suggest purchasing Rising Storm, as it includes the complete RO2 multiplayer suite, while RO2 only gives you access to the bare minimum of Rising Storm features.

I'm
glad this game exists. Both to be enjoyed on its own merits, and so that when I complain about Yooka-Laylee and people retort with "well, what did you expect", I can point to
Playtonic's lukewarm showing was enough to make people start questioning whether the 3D collectathon platformer genre really was so fundamentally overwrought in design that it could only truly have been successful in the 90's, but thanks to this we finally have proof positive to the contrary.
The worlds are actually populated with well written characters who feel like they belong in their respective environments. There's a reasonable population of fodder enemies who aren't a chore to engage with, and pickups that draw your eye to unexplored areas. There are unique setpieces all over the place that flow naturally with the game design rather than sticking out like a sore thumb. Worlds are large without feeling barren. The platforming is quite snappy and precise (even while sprinting, and you don't need to worry about a dumb stamina meter). It's just plain
On top of this, there's a crazy amount of modding support, and the promise of co-op and two MORE worlds in free future updates!
There are minor issues like lack of control remapping, a better-yet-imperfect camera system, and getting stuck on odd bits of geometry. Some of the voice acting grates a little bit. I can sympathize with the people who followed this through its alpha stages and lament the content that ended up on the cutting room floor; some of that stuff sounded pretty awesome. Perhaps most gratingly, objective markers will lead you by the nose to some places that you'll want to find for yourself. Yet with exactly the same number of worlds as Yooka-Laylee had, Hat in Time manages to be ten times more engaging, demonstrates much more competence and creativity with its design, and has singlehandedly given hope for the revival of this genre.
Get it now, get it on sale, or just silently appreciate it in passing -- A Hat in Time is a game of
and I applaud it for that.

TL;DR  "A great introduction edutainment game for learning Japanese."
Probably the best edutainment game designed to teach you Japanese, so far as I'm aware. Unfortunately it only goes so far. One might think they are only learning Hiragana though & I can at least say there is a fair amount of grammer & vocabulary that is taught as well. They have already announced another game for katakana, so I'm hopeful they will be able to move on to some kanji for something more around my level.
The battle game challenge is a bit intense if you don't grind as it intends you to do since each battle is mini review. I didn't die once in this game, but there were many times when it was close. In fact, pretty much every encounter was me being close to death with each turn. And since many things had higher speed with my first encounters with them, they would get some hard hits in regardless of my own skill. I think the balance would work better if there were 3 characters, but each took more around 1/3rd damage instead of a full 1/2+ if one were a bit underleveled.
You're allowed to run at 100% success rate with no penalty. I think I like this, but of course with my preferences these days it wouldn't be a problem if the encounters were visible before doing an encounter and there were ways to avoid the enemies. I'm not sure these devs are skilled or financially independent enough to go through with all that anyways. As it stands with random encounters, having an easy escape tool is good enough for a learning tool, I suppose.
The story is mildly comedic, which I think is a fine approach. I think it was kind of a lost opportunity though much of the story's events being all too brief. They could have fleshed out the characters, setting & added funnier jokes in some of the text & events that feel more like filler. Granted a game like this is designed to be padded, but it feels they didn't pad it out with much other than the battles and all the 'puzzles' that basically give the run around.
It's still a solid study tool sans actual writing. It asks you to practice writing each new character, do what it says to help you remember. It is because of it being a reliable tool for learning that I recommend this for all beginners of Japanese!

Driving controls are god awful. When you press A or D to steer left or right even a slight tap forces your car wildly in that direction. I spend most of the time driving slamming into oncoming traffic, accidentally killing pedestrians, or careening offroad out of control because driving controls suck so bad.
You constantly run out of ammo and grenades and getting more is hard since there are hardly any ammo boxes around. They are too expensive to keep having air dropped, and getting them off dead enemies is impossible if you are low on ammo because any stray guys near the dead ones will mow you down in seconds. So it's a game based 100% around a destruction score to advance the story line and you can run out of ammo easily. If you time it right though you can get ammo from dead guys if you can manage to clear them out before you run up to loot one, but often that is a pipe dream since they usually don't stop flooding in at you.
On the other hand the game, even today, still looks beautiful and has some of the best looking destruction effects I have ever seen in a game. If you are the type of person that likes to mess around in free roam or use mods then you will like this game a lot. I am not much for sandboxing so I like to usually stick to the game's main story and side missions.
Another downfall of the game is that there really isn't much variety: find a base, blow it up to increase your destruction meter, sometimes do escort missions, and thats basically the whole game. Although a♥♥♥♥♥♥load of fun for some time, it does get very repetitive after a while.
I would still easily give it a high 6.9/10, maybe even a 7 or a little higher. Very well made and from what I hear is superior to JC3 both in gameplay and technically.

A Kickstarter revival game with a Jontron cameo that's actually good.
The aesthetic of the game is very bubbly and cute from the soundtrack, to the design of the levels, to the little cute flourishes Hatgirl does.
The design of the spaceship hub is very soft and comfortable, it reminds me of that old live-action McDonald's tv show, or Bill Nye, or Sesame Street, where you were willing to suspend your disbelief and believe that a felt-covered world exists where grown people live in pillow forts. The game has a sort of childish innocence about it, looking at the world without cynicism. You could plop your kid in front of this game and they'd LOVE it, BUT it still has jokes for adults. My favorites are about "ethical consumption under capitalism" and some wanna-be writer's failing marriage.
The game is fun, I beat it in about 14 hours with a controller (39 hourglasses), though on the whole it's pretty easy. The hardest parts are where the game locks the camera and it disorients and works against you. The camera angles aren't janky and are manageable, which put me off of Pyschonauts. There are a couple camera issues, and most of the difficulty actually comes from the jarring difference between locked and unlocked camera.
The game controls and performs pretty smoothly most of the time, though there was some stuttering and buggy hitboxes during some of the boss battles, especially the Mafia don. Also there are times when it's hard to tell the trajectory of a jump due to weird depth perception. This is most apparent in the Forest level (AND THAT ♥♥♥♥ING BIG TREE).
Th.e level design is decent, each of the worlds you can access from the hub have their own "thing" so each level doesn't get repetitive. The later levels start to get really large and spread-out, like the forest and Alpine Heights get pretty confusing to navigate.
The soundtrack by Grant Kirkhope is AMAZING. All in all, this game is well worth the money, and fun for all ages.
Someone's definitely going to make Hatgirl rule 34 though.

If you played Pixel Piracy you'd know this is a monumental step forward for the developer's. This game is amazing in comparison and truely shows what I think they wanted to do all along. About the only thing I miss would be the ability to actually build my ship. If they'd allow us to fully craft our spaceship then this game would be perfect. Overall the gameplay is stellar if you like grinding. Go to a planet, clear it out, cycle through loot, level your guys and repeat. There is a storyline which I have yet to finish and the bosses do have some strategy to them such as moving your entire party out of a pre-marked nuke zone. I'll give a breakdown on the pros and cons that I've experienced thus far:
Pros:
+Great gameplay, feels very smooth and fluent in combat
+Stat point upgrades to distribute for each character.
+Random loot with random stats for days. Finding those perfect stats could keep you looking for ages
+Class customization based on equipped tool and each class has multiple tool types that grant different abilities.
+Don't want to use a tool, that's fine you can dual-wield and still pump out damage.
+Pump up the difficulty for each planet by adding levels to enemies, which in turn grant a bonus to loot rolls.
+Music is decent, but I generally have it turned way down.
+There is a skill tree of sorts that is pretty in-depth allowing you to really pump up a specific class/tool if you wish.
+Request missions to always have an active mission up on planets that you haven't explored yet. Sure you could clear out the planet without a mission, but the missions give great EXP and even more rewards to keep you moving.
+Outfit customization for each character with even more random loot. Each character can even have their own pet.
Cons:
-Maps can get very repetative. Land on the planet and clear each section until you've wiped out the entire thing, repeat.
-Random encounters that require you to fight on your airship can get tedious if you haven't invested in defense and if your ship is HUGE. These can happen randomly as you travel from planet to planet. Although this can also be made easier through the skill tree.
-No customization of airship aside from the freedom to place "rooms" in the designated free areas of your ship. I'd like to be able to fully build my ship like you could in Pixel Piracy.
Overall this game has been very well worth it to me. I'm still very addicted after 27 hours in and I got it on sale during the summer sale 2017. Even if it wasn't on sale I'd still say it is worth the pricetag. I look forward to the updates that are still coming for this game.
EDIT: I've read some reviews stating that this game is just boring with the mechanic of just let my guys go in and fight until you win. This does seem to be true if you leave the planets on the normal +0 difficulty, but if you bump it up to even +1 enemy levels it can require a more tactical pause and strategize approach, and it goes up to +7 which I haven't even attempted yet because +1 is already a huge difference in difficulty.
The game gets incredibly boring, very quickly. I can't recommend it.

But let's be serious here, FNAF is one of the most scariest games I have ever played. Oh and believe me when I say I played 100's EVEN 1000's of different horror games. I thought "this looks boring....NEXT" but as I'm glad I contiuned to watch more I realize how truly scary it was. Oh god....when I played it for myself I had nightmares for 2 straight weeks.
Now let's talk about the concept of this game. Well, it's unique and very simple. All you do is feel isolated in a room, check the cameras so often, use the lights and doors on either side. That's basically it. You may say "OH DATS SOUNDS SO BORING UGRH!" But as you see and hear these creepy animantronics getting closer to you. You have no choice but to wet your pants. But...since the concept is so good, devs are trying to steal Scott's idea. What amazes me is, just pictures put together with a very simple concept can make a game truly terrifiying.
FNAF 2 has been greenlit. I'm indeed looking forward to the game. I love the new animantronics. I love the new room that you are now isolated in. I love the brand new mechanic, which is you can put a mask on to fool the old animantronics. But since the new animantronics have better technology, they can see you as a human unlike the old and slighty broken animantronics. But the thing that worries me the most is that FNAF 2 will get boring and won't be scary after about 1 hour like FNAF. I still find FNAF slighty scary but not as scary when I first played it. So if FNAF 2 manages to keep you on the edge of your sit at all times, then we will be wetting more pants.  But I am really looking forward to FNAF 2. I played it on PS4 until it reached a point so bad, that I downloaded it here just to leave a review.
Just to start with something positive: Character design, models, and general art direction looks fantastic. The game LOOKS beautiful and instantly drew me in.
Now, who likes playing a mission for 20+ minutes, just to win it and get zero rewards!? It's the best, right? When selecting  between 4 reward choices with 4 players, I thought it would work like Warframe's Relic system, where multiple people can choose the same reward.... But no.
Not only do you have to choose between gold, character progression points, faction progression points, or  new weapon blueprints at the reward screen (instead of partaking in all of these basic reward types, like another game I mentioned), but if someone else wants the same thing you picked, the game will randomly decide who gets that. The other player(s) get ZERO rewards, even though one of those other rewards I mentioned goes unclaimed.
So even when you win, you can end up completely wasting your time!
Other issues that I could let slide are the cheezy 1-hit kill grabs, the awkward shakey zooming camerawork and editing during cutscenes that makes it hard to see the art and models, and the fact that the free campaign doesn't even let you play as the character Lycus unless you play Antagonist (also good luck finding a game as Antagonist on PS4, unsure if it's the same here), which means there is zero possibility of progressing him until you buy a campaign.
I could forgive all of the minor problems and buy some DLC if progression wasn't possibly the dumbest system I have ever seen in my gaming life. I don't know if Dev's read these based on the slew of mixed reviews, but possibly check out how Warframe's relic rewards work, as that would go a lot further than possibly cheating you out of all rewards after winning a game. Slow progression sucks, but it's better than no progression.
And FWIW, I could not seem to connect to the server when trying to play on Steam.

(*** I am a game developer, but I'd recommend this to anybody.)

Sandbox
Sandbox mode has a good balance in what you can and cannot predict. Things rarely spawn in the same place twice, including you! The game has some challenging setbacks for you that most open world games are friendly on. No quick access map, going to inventory or mini menus does NOT pause the game, and it only has one way to save. Save by sleeping. If you die, you can't return to a previous save; only when you are still alive can you load back.
Good times are sleeping a week straight in the Home Trapper's Homestead. Bad times are being frozen, bleeding, starving and thirsty at night. Plenty of ways to die, but the most common is by an aggressive wolf. If you read the fine print in the beginning, they state that they aren't going for a realistic approach to the wolves, which explains a lot for their behaviour..but personally I wish they had a more reasonable transition from Pilgrim (Easy mode, no wolf attacks), to Voyeuger (Medium, wolves attack). I have yet to try out stalker mode, and I will wait for further progress in combat/defense updates.
Currently, not many ways to continue once you run out of ammo, supplies, and working tools. Hopefully, they add more things to build. More traps, tools, and clothing. Let us use the bones, make spears and a bow/arrow, have expandable navigation tools. etc. Maybe some exotic game to hunt. Put a whale in Coastal Highway, and a tough bear in Mystery Lake.
My favorite feature by far is the connection of the maps. If you start in Mystery Lake, follow the train tracks to the tunnel, and you'll end up at the top of the road in Coastal Highway. I guess that is the only alternative once you run out of things..damn that's cool!

UPDATE: So Superhot has some problems
Problem 1: In the latest patch they changed the movement speed to what feels almost 2x as fast as it used to be. This makes basic movement and dodging much more difficult and way less satisfying in general. Enemies can now move much more within even a brief key tap. This can be somewhat avoided by using a controller (since you can push the thumbstick forward a tiny amount to move slowly.
Problem 2: What's even worse is that it feels like they increased the time that passes when you turn. In the old version you could do a quick 360 to get some situational awareness and plan your next move, even while being attacked. Now turning even 90 degrees is enough time for a guy to shoot you from halfway across the map it seems. Suspect a guy is behind you? Turning around is enough time for him to kill you, and ignoring him means he will kill you. Tough luck.
The combination of these two changes (mistakes, honestly) ruins the flow of the game. It's more difficult, and while difficult does not = bad it also makes the game less fun, which IS bad. It feels like the only way to get a high score in the endless mode anymore is to hunker down somewhere where the enemies can only come at you from one direction and can't see you until they are close. That's right, they turned a game about acrobatics, style, strategy, and movement into a game about ...camping. Superhot was supposed to be DIFFERENT from normal shooters, and now it just feels more like them, and not in a good way.
Let me show you what I mean:
This first clip was captured by me before the changes
This second clip was also captured by me, on the exact same level, after the changes
See the difference? Running around like in the first clip just isn't possible anymore, or is at least much more difficult to pull off. The amount of time it takes to do anything now, even simply looking around to understand what you're dealing with, is too much time.
Now, I'm not gonna lie: That second clip was still pretty fun.
And that's the thing. After all this, I still can't dislike this game. The 12+ hours I put into it before this patch got me more than my money's worth, and other than these two changes the game is unchanged.
But it isn't as fun as it used to be.
At the moment, I still recommend the game. The idea is fresh, the art fits perfectly, the story is great, the map designs are varied, the challenge modes change the game in neat ways, and the endless mode is a fun way to casually game while listening to a podcast. If you're a new player you probably won't even have any problems with the new changes since you don't know what it was like before.
But for me, THE MOST INNOVATIVE SHOOTER I'VE PLAYED IN YEARS was the old Superhot, not this new one, and I hope they change it back.
