I have to admit. I've known about "Tales of" series for quite a long time but have never bothered trying as I've always been a Final Fantasy fan and playing another RPG felt like treason!
Decided to buy this game when it was on sale during Christmas and I have to say it's worth every cent. It has been quite some since an RPG have hooked me this much.
Please note that I have not yet completed the game, so my review is based on I've played so far.
Characters are well designed and story is great, although I'd enjoy some more depth to it (I love RPGs that you have to play more than once to fully understand the plot, such as Final Fantasy VII). I like how each character has its own personality and how that is reflected in an humurous way throughout the game.
Gameplay is enjoyable, albeit linear, but again, pretty much every RPG I've played in the past 5-10 years or so have been like this. If you come from other RPGs series, such as Final Fantasy (especially up to 10), the battle system is one of the main differences. It's different, and takes some time getting used to, but still a lot of fun. It has more action and you just dont punch in actions on a menu. The upside is that you have lot more fun, and the battles feel much more natural; The downside of this approach is that it's a lot harder to be strategic (you can't just sit at the action selection menu thinking what you should do).
Regarding the technical details: Visual wise, the graphics look very good. It doesn't aim to be realistic (pretty obvious), but they are very well polished and detailed and add alot to the overall game atmosphere. The OST is good, witb the songs helping wrap the player with the plot, but I haven't got a song stuck in my head for days as some other RPGs have done. The controls are very intuitive and feel right, although I notice that sometimes the controls get a bit messed when I'm trying to use specific artes (using the left analogue stick) and it thinks I want to move, but other than that, they are comfortable.
Overall I'm quaite satisfied with this game and I would recomend it to everyone looking for a an enjoyable RPG.
I'm now looking forward to play Berseria, having pre-ordered it. Meanwhile I'll be completing this one and trying Symphonia, which according to many, seems to be the best in the series so far.
Good job Namco!

A Kickstarter revival game with a Jontron cameo that's actually good.
The aesthetic of the game is very bubbly and cute from the soundtrack, to the design of the levels, to the little cute flourishes Hatgirl does.
The design of the spaceship hub is very soft and comfortable, it reminds me of that old live-action McDonald's tv show, or Bill Nye, or Sesame Street, where you were willing to suspend your disbelief and believe that a felt-covered world exists where grown people live in pillow forts. The game has a sort of childish innocence about it, looking at the world without cynicism. You could plop your kid in front of this game and they'd LOVE it, BUT it still has jokes for adults. My favorites are about "ethical consumption under capitalism" and some wanna-be writer's failing marriage.
The game is fun, I beat it in about 14 hours with a controller (39 hourglasses), though on the whole it's pretty easy. The hardest parts are where the game locks the camera and it disorients and works against you. The camera angles aren't janky and are manageable, which put me off of Pyschonauts. There are a couple camera issues, and most of the difficulty actually comes from the jarring difference between locked and unlocked camera.
The game controls and performs pretty smoothly most of the time, though there was some stuttering and buggy hitboxes during some of the boss battles, especially the Mafia don. Also there are times when it's hard to tell the trajectory of a jump due to weird depth perception. This is most apparent in the Forest level (AND THAT ♥♥♥♥ING BIG TREE).
Th.e level design is decent, each of the worlds you can access from the hub have their own "thing" so each level doesn't get repetitive. The later levels start to get really large and spread-out, like the forest and Alpine Heights get pretty confusing to navigate.
The soundtrack by Grant Kirkhope is AMAZING. All in all, this game is well worth the money, and fun for all ages.
Someone's definitely going to make Hatgirl rule 34 though.

This game's main story maybe only about 2 hours or so long, but it is worth it beyond your wildest dreams! Let's get this out of the way first: the pricing is a little steep. If this game went of about £10 or so, it would be just right, but even so, the game is utterly brilliant and beautiful that you probably won't care. SUPERHOT's main game mechanic allows you to control time; in a sense. There is no button to pause it or anything like that, but it's only when you move that time does as well. This allows for amazing crazy fights, plus all of the combined fighting equipment, ranging from pistols and shotguns, to crowbars and bats; even everyday obejcts like TVs, pool balls and power drills. Of course, there had to be a katana, which you can slice bullets in half with by the way.
The game's plot and overall story is short but sweet. After you have taken the couple of hours to complete it, endless levels and challenges are unlocked, which are the best part of SUPERHOT. There are lots of different main menu easter eggs and extras that are somewhat fun to browse through. but they are merely a distraction.
If you want it in simple terms, here:
Pros:
-Beautiful game in both gameplay and art design
-Original and awesome game mechanics
-Addicting and exhilirating
Cons:
-Somewhat steep on pricing for what's in the game so it is recommended you get it on sale if you are unsure about it
Overall, brilliant and magical; a strange homage to Martix styled fighting and Quentin Tarantino paced action.

Learn Japanese to Survive - Hiragana Battle is one of the more unique games in terms of idea and creativity. The whole concept of creating a JRPG where you have to continually learn and master Hiragana is very original.
The story isn't anything revolutionary. An evil wizard and his Hiragana warriors destroys your hometown, and you then set out on a journey to defeat him by learning Hiragana yourself. It's cliche and it doesn't set the game apart at all, but it does give an explaination to why you're learning Hiragana.
The characters and dialogue isn't too special either. There are some attempts to give the characters a personality and some attempts at humor, but it all blends into one and another.
The gameplay reflects the idea of learning Hiragana, by having to use the skill which corresponds to the Hiragana character in order to damage it. It's easy and simple, and it works well in the early part of the game. Later on, when you learn more Hiragan, you end up with a list of over 50 skills. It gets more complex in terms of the Hiragana you have to keep track of, but there isn't much progression in the gameplay itself. The list of skills end up becoming one big mess which is tedious to scroll through, and it's pretty much about using the correct skill over and over again.
With a great game concept like this, I really wish the developer would have dragged all the creativity further to strenghten the gameplay. It would have done so much to see some progression in the gameplay, by for example having to chain different answers together to defeat words for example.
I also found the equipment and levels to be unneccessary. The game would have worked just as great if every Hiragana character was killed by one correct answer, and by only damaging the player if the wrong answer is given. The game pulls in these unneccessary JRPG elements which doesn't add anything to the game, and it hurts the gameplay.
The graphicsis pretty much like what you expect from most RPG Maker games. It's not bad, but it doesn't set the game apart or give it an individual artistic look. The audio mostly consists of some generic background music, as well as sound effects of pronounciation of Hiragana characters and words.
For $2.99 (on sale), I got a very creative game concept with mediocre execution, as well as learning Hiragana. I would love to see similiar games (Katakana Battle, for example), which takes the same concept and push it even further by refining the gameplay and artistic identity, because I feel like Hiragana battle is mostly a rough concept sent through the RPG Maker factory at this point. I still recommend it if you're interested in learning Hiragana though.

The concept is there.  I believe there is a large and growing niche market for a solid program.
However, the UI is not intuitive.  (I've used Magic Set Editor and even delved into the scripting along with an archaic out of published system called Card Designer.)  The icons greatly lack in variety.  For example, no icon for dice.  The ability to create unique cards such as rounded frames around artwork, multi-colored borders, etc. is not there.  Then there are the bugs: such as it auto adding a star when clicking icon, and for some reason, refusing to let you change it, and even refusing to pull up the editing board, unless the program is shut down and restarted.
Again, I really want to like this program.  But, and it's with sadness I write this, I have designed better cards in a word template I created myself (and I am terrible at graphic design).  Maybe with time, they will make a finished product.  But, as of right now, this product feels like it is an alpha state.
Sorry designers.  I know you are working hard, and I will gladly keep my purchase and change my review when I come back when it's ready.  I would think that might be a year or two though.

Running this program, I was met with a clunky, unintuitive UI.  Could I learn over time how to use this smoothly? Big issue number two was when I went to import the first image onto my first card-- the program crashed!  (Mind you, I'm not using a netbook or weak pc-- I'm running a gaming rig with a GTX 1080).  Then when I was able to actually upload an image, I could find no way to resize it other than "fit", "fit width", or "fit height".  No option to manually change the size, and the steam documentation page made no mention of it.
Then I went to add text to a card-- no matter what font, size, color, etc I picked, all the text look blurry both in the program and when exported.
I have filed for a refund because at this time I don't want this headache.  This program has potential.... but as it is now, at $18 on sale, I cannot recommend it, especially with free programs out there that work better with far less frustration.

I bought Card Creator about six months ago in June, and if there's one thing I could praise it for, it would be its simplicity. Card Creator did, in fact, make designing cards for my games relatively quick and painless! I did feel a little...limited, however, and that would be its downside. However, Pixelatto has been working hard to improve the versatility of Card Creator; and, in recent weeks, it has shown. When they made the initial addition of the blueprints system, I was discouraged because it looked really complicated and, above all else, they only allowed textboxes to be one line of text (unless I'm mistaken?). Every card I could think of for my games required at least more than one line of text, if not separate lines of text. But I came back just today, and I guess I was imagining things, because it's so much better now!
Card Creator feels a lot more dynamic and versatile. I still honestly feel that it's a bit over-priced, but that could just be me and my sad, nonexistent income talking. Anyway, I wanted to say that, for what it's supposed to do, Card Creator does its job and does it WELL. I'm a tabletop game designer myself, and I need cards made quickly and cheaply, but nicely. I could use index cards and a pen, but I think Card Creator is the better, more professional route. Might not be as fast as writing five words on a tiny slip of paper, but the difference in quality speaks for itself! I wouldn't say that it's absolutely perfect, but I'm definitely giving it a "thumbs-up" recommendation because, how could I not? Like I said, it does its job and does it well. It's also much, much better than index cards!
If nothing else, Card Creator is perfect for compatibility with another tabletop program, Tabletop Simulator, which I also have and enjoy very much. If you're an upstart game designer and you don't have the money (or maybe skills) for something like Photoshop, Card Creator is definitely for you! It certainly was a good choice for me!

Playtest with this software, fool around with your mechanics, and then take it to photoshop or another high-end software to produce the final product.
For the price, this is a great tool that, most importantly, will save you time over the long journey of playtesting.

This game is a tremendous amount of fun. It's a fairly simple, straightforward shmup. The major twist gameplay-wise is the "VulFighter" system that changes your attack pattern in one of four ways - if you elect to even combine with any of the VulFighters at all, of course. Each one gives you a new bullet pattern and one-use "Omega Weapon" to fire back at wave upon wave of enemies with, from the wide-firing Needle Kaiser to the highly-damaging but close-range Drill Kaiser, and they each feel just different enough to be able to have a favorite - and to feel terrible if you take enough damage for your VulFighters to be knocked out of commission for the rest of your run.
The story is a great homage to classic Super Robot shows like Mazinger Z and is pretty fun, but as much as I like it, it really isn't anything to write home about. But then again, who plays Shmups for their story?
The game is a solid 9/10 if you're a fan of giant robots, shoot-em-ups, or both.

I have this game on Origin with 335 hours prior to purchasing on Steam.
is a worthy addition to the C&C franchise. It runs well and is generally bug-free — though a few irritating bugs
present, such as: sometimes, while in a skirmish game against an AI, stealth is useless. Their units follow your stealthed units around as if the unit was visible.
The game butchered the 'tiberian' canon somewhat from the previous games. Originally, 'Tiberium' used to be some sort of organism; a plant that crystalizes minerals from the ground and emits poisonous gases. This entity was sent to the earth by the Scrin to transform Earth into a planet suitable for them. In this game, they completely changed the chemical composition of the entity. Instead of an alive plant-like organism, 'tiberium' is now a crystal that acts like some sort of lifeless radiative substance sent to Earth to crystalize the entire planet for mineral harvestation.
Aside from the canon, the storyline is... okay. It's not great, but if stories aren't your
it's passable. If you're joining the series without prior C&C experience, the story is not really that interesting.
As an RTS title, I would say it is disappointing. Work has gone into balancing and unit design, and generally works, but as a balance system alone, it is pathetic. In order to win, you need less strategy and more tank-rushing. Infantry are almost useless and aircraft aren't far behind.
A good point of consideration is the availability of mods, however. There are some mods that add desperately-needed balancing changes to make the game require an actual brain. There are also mods that boost the total hours you are going to get out of this title by converting the game to fit with unique themes, such as: Dune II, Cold War era, modern warfare, etc.
I would recommend this game
if you have been introduced to the C&C series prior to the release of this title. If were looking at it purely as an RTS, it does okay. You might want to pass it up if your standards are somewhat high. Otherwise, I suggest giving it a try. I love the game.

If you are looking for a end-game or a story, look elsewhere.  This is a ...well, middle-ages village sim?   Think a very simple Dwarf Fortress.  Or a coplex Sim-Ants?  You start out with a small number of fasting living humans (they age five years for every one game year).  Because they are very shy they refuse to mate in front of their parents - in other words two adults of mating age need a house all their own.  So a vanilla game will be you mostly making houses when not collecting resources (food, logs, stone) to build other buildings.  The people need fuel in winter, food all the time, and are most effective when educated and when equiped with steel tools.
In some ways you are trying to find a balance between producing new babies and keeping the adults alive long enough to get some work out of them.  They die swiftly so after a period it is likely you don't really worry about individuals as much as numbers.
I use mods - one for example makes the populace age one year for one year.  It slows the game down a tad as it could take 20 years before your town is big enough to even need a trading post - by then most vanilla games had hundreds of individuals.  And mines which can give you iron or coal at the cost of killing off adults almost weekly, are just not worth making till you have the numbers to keep them open.  In other words, the populace is no longer just a mass of unnamed ants but people.  It changes the game for me, making it more interesting and harder, in some ways.  It also means you get to know the populace more then in vanilla.
You CAN get a story out of it - the populace all have names, can get ill or unhappy (some will kill themselves when too depressed) - and so on.  Like Dwarf Fortress or any other open-ended game you get out of it what you put in.

This was my first Tales game and I honestly did not know what to expect besides it being a JRPG.
Rating: 7/10
Pros: Story, Character Interactions, Length
Cons: Combat System, Fusion System, Grinding
This game was great - I almost enjoyed myself from the beginning to the end. Almost. The games story was interesting enough to keep me wanting to continue but by far the best thing out of this was the character interactions. Rarely do I find in-game dialogue or events hilarious, this is one of the few games I found myself laughing hard or wanting to see more side-dialogue, going out of my way to find certain points just to trigger them. The characters are the strength of this anime game and they are really the best thing about it.
Its combat system is.. interesting. Its fun, when you get used to it and even better when you start to gain more moves. Its based off a system of strengths and weaknesses. Some enemies are weak against certain elements, so using said elements will add onto a damage multiplier which can unleash incredible amounts of damage. The opposite is also true, using an element that the monster is strong against - can either do reduce damage or just send that damage right back at you. This is actually the part of the game that let me down the most because its incredibly frustrating - especially when the enemies are spell casters. The combat system relies on being able to trigger status elements (stunned, burned) but doesnt really tell you how - besides spamming a move - which you cant spam because you have to do moves in a certain order. This creates a point where you either get obliterated or just have to grind your way through.
The fusion system is by far the most confusing - it was only near the end I realised what I was actually supposed to do and by that point, I was far more weaker than I should have been at that point. Wasting my money and time, fusing useless things because I just didn't know any better. You have to either look at forums or google just what fusions are best and how combining certain items give you more skills.
The game is also long - you will get your hours worth in this game and thats not a bad thing. I actually wished there was more dialogue between the characters that I could find and some of the side stories are interesting.
Overall, the game was real fun but let down by its confusing fusion system and combat system. I do recommend this game but be prepared to be frustrated by its mechanics.

You can choose exactly where everything goes, and you really have to think about the lay-out and planning of your town to make it as effeciant and seamless as possible.
I've been playing this since before all the workshop mods, and even then it was a great game. But now with the inclusion of user-created and dev created mods it's just a work of art. The crafting ladders are now massive, and you can happily run a small village or expand into a heavy working production town. You can choose to lay out your houses in beautiful hamlets, or build big and close together for the real medievil city feel.
As you can see from my hours, which don't include the 150+ that for some reason vanished when I transferred my account some time ago, I have played this and loved every second of it. Taking your small band of villagers from a group of 20 to a booming town of 500 is amazing but challenging and it really keeps you on your toes for foward planning.
Oh, and we can't forget the naming system. Probably the best thing about the entire game!

I will start by saying the game its self if good but there are for sure some points i can agree on with others, the short to this review is, it's worth playing if you enjoy the tales series/the anime this game has had adapted to it but as a first time player, you might want to try others like Xillia first.
So the good first, i will sum these up together to keep it simple.
The characters are loveable, i always find in tales games there is someone you hate, i like all characters in this game for their own reason but best off the humans (who play a big role in your party) are great in their own ways, from Sorleys some what dim-witted all be it innocent and noble view of the world to Alisha's cute and innocent side followed with a side of bad♥♥♥♥♥more laid back Rose, they are all great, but even the Seraphim are all likeable.
The games story line is good and offers the user some fun in battles with fusion of humans and seraphin, this enables multiple combos to exploit enemies weakness and helps in boss battles on harder modes.
Whilst i could go into the other elements i enjoyed like support talents (creating snacks on the move, quicker movement speed collecting gald ect) i feel these are minor trickets as apposed to what makes a game good which is story and characters.
So the bad? Well i love tales series but this has a few problems which bug me. First it the battles systems, weapons and equipment now features 'fusion', this is standard in "OTHER" RPG (especially MMO) but not so much tales, it is combining the same equipment to create higher + versions offering enhanced stats and then advancing it further at +10. This feature failed due to it made grinding annoying as you was always after equipment, there was less variety of weapons and such in game as it felt like it expected you to fuse over get new stuff and the games explanations felt lacking, the systems is explained in the skits which take place, sadly unless you sit in the inn buying food to see all of these, they are spread out through the game (well they are anyway) so by the time you see them all, you have worked it out for yourself and probably ruined some good gear, also the game never explains 'sealed' gear, it touches on it only to have Lailah cut off and in short tell you to figure it out yourself... thanks. This systems really wasn't enjoyable.
The camera was bad as well, in the free world it is fine but in battles you would sometimes have the cam spaz out or you would just dissapear due to being near walls or other obsticles, this doesn't help as battles take place exactly where you stand, this is common in games but the point is, if you are in a small corridor with enclosed walls, yeah, you wont see much in the battle, just bash buttons. I find you can dissapear as well when dodging, with the correct skills active you can hold your guard button and use analouge (or keyboard equal) to quickly sidestep or front/backstep, this is great in battle, just when you use it to flee back to get some distance, if you other party members aren't close by it cuts you off cam... like why the one im playing?
Artes.. oh god. I love mages, infact i loved playing as Elise in the Xillia games, her dark artes combined with heals was fun. This game is lacking so much here, first, you don't learn like any artes... at all. Most characters will learn 5 chains of artes which are just upgrades to previous ones, this leaves no variety as you ironcally have 5 buttons to set them to. Charactes using magic suffer a lot here though, ignoring their artes seem to be quite weak there is some big issues, first, they are destined to have to have their low level artes set and use the games function to chain into high artes as the artes cast times are surreal. Next, magic is lacking, like Elise and Rowan in Xillia was full on mages, here everyone (er Seraphin) just have bits, i think Edna is more focused on magic but still lacking, she is the closest to a healer with her healing circle skills which take forever to cast and kind of suck, Elise had lots of fun heals and could attack all as well. This game makes artes(magic) feel pointless, they are weak, time consuming and all around not worth it, but the worse it this next point, it is hard to execute even the quickest artes, I go to cast a low level spell and im always interuppted, why? because enemies only target spell users, Xillia offered skills to give interuption rates reduced which would help prevent this, sadly, here you only can 'resist' interuption by certain attacks from enemies which speed up cast time, but this feel weak to compensate as mentioned all enemies target whoever is casting. I can beat enemies down to a pulp and they just walk past me (rose) and Sorely (CPU) to target Edna, is also makes her strategy of 'fight from afar' useless, it doesn't help she seems to randomly just run in even with good sp.
One more battle issue is humans are essential, other games you gain huge parties and choose your favourites to fight, in this Sorley can't leave the party (how lame, i have nothing against him but in Xillia i wasn't forced to have Jude, i hated him and would of hated to have him stuck with me) but equally you must have Rose or Alisha, now i love these two and always play Rose (or Edna) so don't mind but it feels so restrictive. Also, should you not have a human, you only can have 1 Seraphin, they are attached to humans so it's 1 human = 1 seraphim (2 ppl party), 2 humans = 4 player pt. One last gripe here is, Alisha leaves you early on and you don't have her join you until the end of the game, i didn't enjoy playing as her though did like cpu to do that, but i still liked having her around, even if it was for her cute smile.
Finally the big issue i have next is you have to run around as Sorley, tales normally let you change who you play, i wanted to run around as Edna or Rose please, if you don't play Sorley in battles, it takes time to get into running around as Sorley to starting as Rose in combat.
I know that looks negative but the game is actually fun, it is just easier to write about the bad than good at times, the game does still hold up well and is a good play through, slap the difficulty up right away and the game will take ages to beat offering great play time, just don't ruin it with the dlc offering items such as x2 exp or gald.
I would recommend the game to tales players who whilst i can't say will love some changes (such as battles) will probably love the story and characters (Seriously, Sorey is great, Mikileo is adorable, Edna is the best, Rose is out of this world brilliant, Alisha is cute as can be, Lilah has her own comical charm and i wont touch on the cool as can be win spirits for spoiler reasons) and thus appreciate the game. New players might enjoy these elements as well, well you might more so as you don't hold expectations like veterans, but if you find these elements a let down, don't think all tales games are the same. As a whole, still a great game, just the battles need looking at and they need to fix Artes usage, i love magic users on all games and going from bad♥♥♥♥♥dark spells/heals of Elise to no variation of any kind with anyone felt kind of sad.
PS: DLC Alisha story is worth the extra game time, costumes, i would get one set if you want them (the games defaults aren't bad though) and not more, there isn't much need for them as you will likely find a favourite and only use them, i like the idolmaster ones as i do love Idolmaster the anime and the music change).

An extremely middle of the road title as far as entries in the Tales series go.
Bland environments; bland non-evolving charicatures rather than interesting characters; and a plot that for the most part is bland, predictible and so cliché it actually does the 'visit all four elemental temples'-trope. Even the musical score, which otherwise is top-notch in Tales games, is bland with only one or two memorable tracks.
Gameplay-wise, most of your time will be spent battling enemies in real-time, with 3 AI controlled partners. The AI partners can be tuned to give precedence to certain type of combat actions; to maintain HP at certain levels; to attack from a particular preferred range; etc. and in addition can be given direct commands to prioritize attack or defense and to spread out and engage all opponents or to focus on whomever the human-controlled character is engaging.
Sounds good in theory, but in practice it results in the AI having two modus operandi:
The AI dies. A
.
The hard part of boss battles is not beating the actual boss. It's keeping your AI partners alive so you don't end up with an atrocious battle grade.
Oh right; all battles are graded. And each KO subtracts from the grade number you earn. Finishing a battle with a status ailment halves it as well. (And there's no easily castable cure-all-ailments spell like in previous Tales series.)
Grade mostly does two things:
Firstly, it ties into the quality of equipment drops, which you need for decent skills, which we'll get to in a moment.
Secondly, it is fed to the governing guardian; the Lord of the Land, of whatever area of the world you were fighting in, to level them up and unlock bonuses. Getting the useful high-level bonuses takes a
time that way. Luckily, you can offer item bribes to level them as well. And it's actually faster to flat out ignore everything until the end-game and then abuse the massive amounts of money you can get dropped from battles to buy high-grade healing items and force-feed your Lords to the highest level.
Equipment drops are randomized and dictated by grade. Each piece of equipment can have up to four skills attached to it, which are used to buff up your character. (Raw stat bonuses; elemental resistances or attack bonuses; better aptitude at fighting certain types of opponents; etc.)
Making any kind of meaningful use out of this system requires aligning activated skills in rows, columns or stacks to unlock the much more substantial bonus skills. (Awesome stuff like +80% to inflict a status ailment; +20% max HP; +20 to all base stats; etc.)
Getting the proper gear means you need to spend a
time (seeing a pattern there?) farming for the right drops and 'fusing' them to mutate skills together in such a way that you end up with the set you want. Ofcourse, the game doesn't give you any easy means to look up "if I have gear with skill X, which skill Y do I need to fuse with it to get skill Z that I actually want?" You're expected to figure out the system behind it and do the math yourself.
When you finally have your skills arranged, you can start the entire process over when you get gear with better base stats, or you can continue on fusing the older gear together: each fusion ever so slightly improves an item's base stats.
Ofcourse; the type of gear that drops from enemies and is sold from shops is partially bound to your experience level, so eventually that gear will
.
Thankfully all that lunacy can be largely avoided when playing at lower difficulty levels, which are almost laughably easy, save for the frustration of bosses knocking out your party members. (But then again; at that point a good grade for a decent equipment drop with good skills stops mattering as well.)
However, if you want to get the most out of the game and want to try your hands at the higher difficulty levels on a second playthrough, the equipment/skill system will frustrate you to no end.
The PC port is locked to 30 FPS, though it can be modded to 60 FPS via the TZFix runtime-patcher/injector graciously supplied by community-member Kaldaien. It's not perfect, but gets a very decent 90% passing mark and can be disabled in troublesome scenes. (Next to that it automatically disables in a few scenes which completely break when run in 60 FPS.)
TZFix is also needed to fix audio-related issues that you may experience. In particular when you use 7.1 USB headsets or have your audio quality configured for anything above 44.1KHz in Windows. (The game crashes without.)
Without TZFix the game has no mip maps for textures. This degrades performance and when looking at materials that have equilaterally spaced lines far in the distance, you get some downright atrocious stair-stepping effects. (Most visible when looking at the Pendrago castle walls from a distance. A central location you'll be visiting quite a few times during the game.)
Controls can be freely switched between keyboard+mouse and game controller and everything can be rebound. However,  when rebinding certain actions, there are menus which may break down. So it's best to stay with the defaults.
The game can be run windowed, borderless and fullscreen. Fullscreen comes recommended because it is the best way to avoid problems with the extremely flaky frame-limiter / frame-pacer that can cause the game to feel quite jerky. TZFix also injects a different solution for this, which works a heck of a lot better.
Next to all the things TZFix can fix, there are some it cannot. Some players experience a nasty visual bug where the polygons that make up the hair and/or face of a character can glitch and fly outward in large; jagged; completely screen-obscuring 'starbursts'. This may happen semi-randomly anywhere in the game, though there are a few key locations (looking up the stairs from the corner staircase in Ladylake; the T-junction leading to the Great Tree in Marlind; looking along the main street of Lastonbell) where it triggers fairly consistently.
These are very obvious, very immersion-breaking and in many cases ruin key story cutscenes.
Neither developer nor publisher has commented on this bug; there is no patch available that fixes the problem; and there is no demo available to verify whether you'll get this bug or not. You will need to purchase the game, blast through the introductory zones to make it to Ladylake in under two hours and then attempt to trigger the bug at the first location where it triggers somewhat reliably. You'll need to try a few times to have any kind of confidence whether you're affected by the issue or not.
Only at bargain prices.
The actual gameplay is frustrating and the plot and characters are truly one-dimensional.
The game's sole worth is in having more backstory knowledge for the soon-to-be-released prequel Tales of Berseria, which is shaping up to be a much better game.
The fact that a community-mod is necessary to fix a lot of issues with the game is inexcusable and certainly should not result in you paying the publisher a full triple-A free. On top of that, there's a fair risk of running into the previously mentioned 'starburst' graphics glitch when you're already well passed the 2 hours refund mark for Steam, leaving you with a rather expensive turd to stare at.
Also; if you live in the EU and have a PS4 available, get the PS4 version of the game instead.
It's virtually the same, but where the Steam/PC version continues to be sold at a 49,99 EUR price, the PlayStation Store has the PSN/PS4 version at 29,99 EUR, saving you 40%.

As I crouched behind a low outcropping of rock to shield myself from the fury of the blizzard that was at that moment screaming in my ears, my thoughts turned briefly to the chain of events that had brought me here. It started when I saw that rifle, leaning casually up against the wall of one of the cabins. My prayers had been answered, perhaps I was saved after all. But not because of the gun itself. It was just a means to an end, you see. The gun would free me from the wolf pack that seemed to have claimed the railroad tracks as their territory and penned me in here. See, It's not the big things that will save you -- it's never the big things. It's the little things. What I needed, to save myself, was a little thing indeed. A sewing kit.
My clothes were rapidly becoming rags. I needed to do something about it. If you've never been here, you might dismiss this as a cosmetic issue. It's not, it's a matter of life and death. The cold outside was becoming increasingly bone-chilling as my clothes began failing to protect me. My scavenging expeditions were getting shorter and more desperate. If I did not do something soon, I would freeze, or starve, whichever I ended up neglecting most while I attempting to fulfill the other need. So I gathered as much of my remaining supplies as I could, got a good night's sleep, and set out at dawn for another cabin I had seen in my earlier travels, hoping that perhaps there I would find my sewing kit. It's funny, you know. So much of survival relies on hope. It doesn't matter how often you find your hopes dashed, you must continue to hope. You must always grasp any hope you see, no matter how slim it may seem. Once you lose hope, it's just a matter of time before the end comes.
The trip to the cabin was uneventful, as far as these things go. The rifle did indeed make short work of the wolves, and as the sun climbed, I began to feel slightly less frigid. But when I got to the cabin, I did not find what I was looking for. The sewing kit continued to elude me. Luck had definitely not completely abandoned me though, as I found a thick, warm, and almost brand-new coat to replace my tattered one. This was a huge triumph and would be more than enough to keep me going. For now.
In the late afternoon, as I was about halfway home, the weather turned. I trudged onwards despite the cold and the decreasing visibility. With my new coat, I hoped I could bear it long enough that it would pass. But eventually my coat alone could not protect me as the temperature continued to plummet, the winds began to howl and with visibility approaching zero one of my most primal fears was being realized, I could not continue, I could not even see. I had to stop and try to keep warm. I was trapped in a blizzard, without shelter and far from home, as night approached. I had thought I was experienced, but nothing I had experienced so far had prepared me for this. I found a rock ledge to hide behind and built myself a small fire out of scraps I had in my pack, and hoped, desperately hoped the blizzard would soon abate and give me a chance to sprint home to safety before nightfall or before exhaustion claims me.
And that is how I found myself sitting here, with so much time to think about my situation. So quickly my triumph has turned to terror, but I must stay calm and keep my wits about me. As the evening drags on, I pull my precious coffee grounds out of the pack and brew some coffee over the fire to help fight the sleep deprivation, but the blizzard just keeps getting ever more violent. If I were to fall asleep out here, unable to tend my fire, I know with absolute certainty that I would end up as a meal for a wolf.
Finally, with night rapidly closing in and the blizzard still refusing to let up, I decide to cling to my one last, desperate hope. Heating up one last hot cup of coffee to help keep me warm, I abandon my makeshift shelter and charge headlong into the wall of shrieking snow. I try desperately to maintain my direction, but I somehow end up running into a dead end canyon. Retracing my quickly fading steps, I try to guess where I made the wrong turn. I seem to guess correctly, as I eventually stumble across the railroad tracks, which is ultimately my salvation as they pass close enough to the cabin that I stand a good chance of finding it before I freeze.
At last I see it, my cabin. I don't know whose cabin it was before, but it's fair to say it's mine now. I am unbelievably fortunate to have found it, and just as fortunate to have made it there without seeing a single wolf. I killed some earlier in the day, but there are always more. I'm certain that if I had seen one, my death would have followed shortly afterwards. Even if I had killed it, or fought it off, the melee likely would've left me too wounded to survive the remainder of my journey home, my health is precarious as it is. Without any visibility to aim, I am forced to confront the sudden and remarkable uselessness of my not-so-all-powerful rifle. I cannot see the wolves, but I have no doubt they have seen me. I am not attacked, though. Perhaps they are not hungry. Or perhaps they too are sheltering from the storm. It doesn't matter, I am home. In a cruel irony, moments after I step inside, gasping for breath and shivering for warmth, the blizzard's howling begins to fade. As I stumble towards my bed, I can see moonlight start peeking in the windows. I am frozen, exhausted, and half-delirious from stress and pain. But I have a new coat, and I survived another day. More challenges await tomorrow; I still need a sewing kit. But I survived today. And for now, that's enough.
10/10 would nearly freeze to death in a blizzard again.

This game is just about flawless. You're given a really unique, cool, but easy to understand concept, and the game just goes with it. You make a hectic, spur-of-the-moment action scene, but you're doing it so deliberately, and the game rewards you for planning, being fast, and playing smart rather than pure mechanical skill. Tight controls, satisfying AI, good level design, the graphic design and user interfaces are unique and really work. The story is the type that can only be told within a video game, and for a game about killing red dudes it's actually pretty good, especially because it has tiny amounts of narrative and dialogue. Plus the challenges and endless modes are where you'll get a lot of mileage from.
It's a game I haven't really seen since Hotline Miami. Here is a level full of dudes and weapons, you and the dudes die in one hit, go nuts. You have a similar action flow (knock Dude 1 down, steal his gun, shoot Dude 2, throw gun to stun Dude 3, steal Dude 3's katana, chop up Dude 1 before he even stood up, throw katana at Dude 3, hotswitch into Dude 3, grab katana midair, impale Dude 4 with aimed katana throw), but unlike Hotline Miami the game makes it feel so natural, planned out, and deliberate until you watch the last minute-and-a-half of action compressed into ten real-time seconds of straight up dude killin'. It's good, it's really good, it feels satisfying to pull off, and it looks impressive too. Most of your deaths and failures are preventable with proper time/resource management, not like Hotline Miami where your deaths are funky hitreg or not being able to see a gunman a mile away.
I can easily see this game on a bunch of GOTY lists, but at $25 I don't think it's worth it. At least, not for everyone. If this game was $10-15 I'd heartily recommend it, but when there are other titles on Steam that are just as (if not more) innovative and unique, for half the price, and with more content. The gameplay's solid like you wouldn't believe, but I beat the campaign in an hour and a half, and the challenge/endless modes are just alterations on levels in the campaign. Only one enemy type, 3 guns, 2 types of melees, so far no promises on adding extra content, developer or usermade. Can the gameplay support the price? I think so, but I don't think most people can agree.
I suggest buying it on sale. At worst, you can buy the game, beat the campaign, and refund it and still be ~20 minutes under the time requirement to return it.

I purchased a copy of Space Engineers and was pretty stoked that it came with this. Starting the game up, I was greeted with a reasonably pretty game based around a solid concept and horrible writing which over the course of a few hours play, completely falls on its face and becomes pants-on-head ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Gameplay-wise, the controls feel solid. Sorting out your weapons can take some getting used to. When switching ammo types, the games reminds you of the controls you set for different weapons. If you're near a minable resource, it'll remind you of your controls again (though it will only remind you of keyboard controls). But that's really the only positive point.
Even on Normal, a few missions in you'll start seeing some flaws that will likely end up killing you and forcing you to put it down. Endlessly respawning enemies are very commonplace. If the game tells you to do something, it wants you to do it now, and you can explore later. Even where there is no objective (see the map, Gates of Hell), you'll find enemies respawn anyway, and in some cases, a couple of seconds after you kill them. A few other negative points include:
- If you travel to a new area and it gives you a quest, you cannot leave until it's completed. It rarely offers you any reason for what you need to do.
- Different merchants have different market values, for seemingly no reason.
- Achievements (for some people) don't trigger.
- No indication how much damage you're taking.
- Allies only spawn sometimes, and only in some areas.
-
- Rewards for completing the "31 epic missions" are... well, not a thing. You get another mission. Thanks.
- Marcus' script is terrible, and makes him look like an idiot.
- I didn't see any mining upgrades, and I couldn't figure out hacking upgrades.
- No unique hacking minigame.
Overall, this game isn't worth $9.99USD (price at time of writing). It lacks personality, and looks like another Greenlight product that overpromised and oversold what it wanted to do, but it has a couple of redeeming qualities. However, if it's a space trading/pirating sim you're looking for, best look somewhere else. Buy it if it's 75% off or more.

Fantastic city builder game. I grew up playing SimCity excessively, and this game is a very unique twist on the city builder genre. Rather than merely being about proper management, it's done with a survival aspect.
At first the mechanics are a little bit hard to get, so my first few towns failed quite quickly, but once you get the idea, the game flows very nicely. You can't just expand, and hope for the best, because there won't be enough food or firewood for everyone, so eventually people start dying off by the dozens. You need to create food stores, and expand in a way that will bring more food into your barns. In addition to food and firewood (warmth), you need to watch out for clothing, building materials, education, health, happiness, tools, and even make sure your population is eating a proper diet. It's a good system that provides both challenge and enjoyment.
The only problem is that the game is a bit simplistic after a while. You actually get to the point where 1/4 of your population are just lounging around, because there's nothing for them to do, because your town is so awesome. The achievements give the game some nice challenges, which will help prolong your gameplay. Also, the modding community is quite active, so there is a lot of extra content which will make the gameplay last even longer.

As a fan of Gatchaman!, Voltron, Tekkaman Blade, and Robotech I had an absolute blast with this game. As a matter of fact, when I watched the trailer for it, I had to double check online to make sure this wasn't an adaptation of a more obscure series. The creators get mad points for that.
So, at its core, Vulkaiser is a horizontal bullet hell shooter. Coolio. In keeping with its theme of retro anime mecha, your core mech is equipped with a standard, but weak, vulcan cannon. A charge meter at the bottom of the screen constantly fills up as you shoot: activating it fires off a more powerful shot. In addition to your core mech there are four other parts to the Vulkaiser that you can combine with during each stage, each with its own unique weapon. A cluster of missiles, a close-range drill, a weak but screen-filling spread shot, and a wide electric attack. The idea of mixing and matching your mech on the fly reminds me of an older NES shooter, Mag Max, although Vulkaiser is more fleshed out.
With all of its various mech parts and special weapon gauges, is Vulkaiser worth playing? Yes. I was able to beat the game in my first attempt without dying. I came close by the end, and two of my partners had to bail a la Starfox, but it was doable. But what's cool are the multiple levels of diffculty. Too easy your first playthrough? Crank it up a level. I can see myself coming back to this in the future to try out the harder diffuculties.
Is Vulkaiser the best shooter I've ever played? No. But it's certainly fun and what it lacks in depth in makes up for in style. Totally worth a buy if you're a fan of the genre or of classic mecha anime. Rick Hunter would be proud.

The developers appear to have made a pretty involved implementation of an Elite / Freelancer style game here, with mining, equipment hacking and terrain alteration. However, they promptly make an utter hash of it by starting their - extremely complicated - game in media res, with alarms and explosions and characters screaming at the player. There's a reason why Freelancer starts its player in a calm spot and introduces its game mechanics one at a time. Miner Wars 2081 completely missed that concept. This flaw culminates in characters screaming at you while you are trying to read tutorial pop-ups.
Miner Wars 2081 tries to have a combat oriented campaign but sabotages itself in several ways. The combat design is atrocious and the missions devolve into "please now fly at a turret which will kill you in 0.5 seconds and is already pointing at you". The level designs heavily punish attempting to do anything amusing or sneaky to go around or sneak up on enemies. For no apparent reason, there isn't a quicksave / quickload feature, only unmarked autosave checkpoints, so the game becomes tedious and painful if you get stuck at some obstacle, having to repeat the same actions over and over again to get back to where you can try again. As I crouched behind a low outcropping of rock to shield myself from the fury of the blizzard that was at that moment screaming in my ears, my thoughts turned briefly to the chain of events that had brought me here. It started when I saw that rifle, leaning casually up against the wall of one of the cabins. My prayers had been answered, perhaps I was saved after all. But not because of the gun itself. It was just a means to an end, you see. The gun would free me from the wolf pack that seemed to have claimed the railroad tracks as their territory and penned me in here. See, It's not the big things that will save you -- it's never the big things. It's the little things. What I needed, to save myself, was a little thing indeed. A sewing kit.
My clothes were rapidly becoming rags. I needed to do something about it. If you've never been here, you might dismiss this as a cosmetic issue. It's not, it's a matter of life and death. The cold outside was becoming increasingly bone-chilling as my clothes began failing to protect me. My scavenging expeditions were getting shorter and more desperate. If I did not do something soon, I would freeze, or starve, whichever I ended up neglecting most while I attempting to fulfill the other need. So I gathered as much of my remaining supplies as I could, got a good night's sleep, and set out at dawn for another cabin I had seen in my earlier travels, hoping that perhaps there I would find my sewing kit. It's funny, you know. So much of survival relies on hope. It doesn't matter how often you find your hopes dashed, you must continue to hope. You must always grasp any hope you see, no matter how slim it may seem. Once you lose hope, it's just a matter of time before the end comes.
The trip to the cabin was uneventful, as far as these things go. The rifle did indeed make short work of the wolves, and as the sun climbed, I began to feel slightly less frigid. But when I got to the cabin, I did not find what I was looking for. The sewing kit continued to elude me. Luck had definitely not completely abandoned me though, as I found a thick, warm, and almost brand-new coat to replace my tattered one. This was a huge triumph and would be more than enough to keep me going. For now.
In the late afternoon, as I was about halfway home, the weather turned. I trudged onwards despite the cold and the decreasing visibility. With my new coat, I hoped I could bear it long enough that it would pass. But eventually my coat alone could not protect me as the temperature continued to plummet, the winds began to howl and with visibility approaching zero one of my most primal fears was being realized, I could not continue, I could not even see. I had to stop and try to keep warm. I was trapped in a blizzard, without shelter and far from home, as night approached. I had thought I was experienced, but nothing I had experienced so far had prepared me for this. I found a rock ledge to hide behind and built myself a small fire out of scraps I had in my pack, and hoped, desperately hoped the blizzard would soon abate and give me a chance to sprint home to safety before nightfall or before exhaustion claims me.
And that is how I found myself sitting here, with so much time to think about my situation. So quickly my triumph has turned to terror, but I must stay calm and keep my wits about me. As the evening drags on, I pull my precious coffee grounds out of the pack and brew some coffee over the fire to help fight the sleep deprivation, but the blizzard just keeps getting ever more violent. If I were to fall asleep out here, unable to tend my fire, I know with absolute certainty that I would end up as a meal for a wolf.
Finally, with night rapidly closing in and the blizzard still refusing to let up, I decide to cling to my one last, desperate hope. Heating up one last hot cup of coffee to help keep me warm, I abandon my makeshift shelter and charge headlong into the wall of shrieking snow. I try desperately to maintain my direction, but I somehow end up running into a dead end canyon. Retracing my quickly fading steps, I try to guess where I made the wrong turn. I seem to guess correctly, as I eventually stumble across the railroad tracks, which is ultimately my salvation as they pass close enough to the cabin that I stand a good chance of finding it before I freeze.
At last I see it, my cabin. I don't know whose cabin it was before, but it's fair to say it's mine now. I am unbelievably fortunate to have found it, and just as fortunate to have made it there without seeing a single wolf. I killed some earlier in the day, but there are always more. I'm certain that if I had seen one, my death would have followed shortly afterwards. Even if I had killed it, or fought it off, the melee likely would've left me too wounded to survive the remainder of my journey home, my health is precarious as it is. Without any visibility to aim, I am forced to confront the sudden and remarkable uselessness of my not-so-all-powerful rifle. I cannot see the wolves, but I have no doubt they have seen me. I am not attacked, though. Perhaps they are not hungry. Or perhaps they too are sheltering from the storm. It doesn't matter, I am home. In a cruel irony, moments after I step inside, gasping for breath and shivering for warmth, the blizzard's howling begins to fade. As I stumble towards my bed, I can see moonlight start peeking in the windows. I am frozen, exhausted, and half-delirious from stress and pain. But I have a new coat, and I survived another day. More challenges await tomorrow; I still need a sewing kit. But I survived today. And for now, that's enough.
10/10 would nearly freeze to death in a blizzard again.

I'd maybe even recommend it as a generic RPG for people new to the genre. But this game shows that the people that worked on this installment are set on taking it in a new direction. And this causes me a bit of worry. Not because it can't work (like taking the series in a 3d direction, it 'can' work and maybe the next installment in the series will polish the combat system for a 3d environment and do it right), but because in this case it didn't work nearly as well as it could have. And after all; 'tales of' is quite a name to live up to.
As a long-time fan of the 'tales of' series since the snes era (though I'll admit I missed a game or two later down the line), I found zestiria to be a bit of a disappointment. My main complaint so far wasn't the story or the characters (though it didn't quite have the same epic feel as some of the older games' settings), but certain aspects of the actual gameplay.
Namely:
- Transformation gimmick (and a new resource linked to it that is separate from HP and SP) that seems a bit forced. It has some utility to be sure (the transformations provide a nice attack boost) and you can use the resource for other things as well. But it's basically just one more thing you need to keep an eye on and manage, while it doesn't really feel like it adds anything substantial to the game.
- Revamping the combat system to full 3d, instead of the tried and true 2d setup which allowed for a much more tactical approach in terms of setting up different formations, isolating enemies, protecting allies and the like. Not that I have anything against 3d, but the new combat system that resulted from the switch didn't really feel fluid and intuitive enough to justify that trade-off.
- Changing melee skills to standard attacks (which still cost SP, making SP act more like a stamina), and adding some weird form of magic for the main character which he can combo off. To act as a replacement for the melee skills the 'tales of' games used to have.
- The revamped equipment system, which on higher difficulties highly encourages some farming. Not that I mind a bit of grinding but an actual need for it should never be all that prevalent in a well paced RPG as long as you clean house in whatever area you travel through. And you certainly should be able to get by on equipment you buy/find in areas where you buy/find them despite the difficulty, without needing to merge gear with gear with gear to upgrade them. So this too is more or less a new gimmick that adds very little to the game, complicating matters more than it helps.
Just play a few hours of zestiria so you get an idea of how the game works, then go back and play let's say phantasia (PSX remake if you really want an example of a 'tales of' game done right in just about every single way). If these two games were food, one would be a fabulous five course dinner fit for a king, while by comparison the other is basically comfort food. It's not really bad and it leaves you full, sure, but it doesn't quite satisfy.
Long story short; play if new to 'tales of', and then move on to older installments. But be wary if you're a long-time 'tales of' fan and expect the triple A experience the series is usually known for.
But hey, that's just my 2 cents, different strokes for different folks. ;)

I've grown very bored with the way survival games usually tend to steer these days, they're too easy and most of the time they poorly simulate things like hunger, weather and injury. I'm not saying that the long dark does all these things amazingly well, but there is a very intense immersion going on in this game.
You are utterly alone, you're cold, starving and afraid (and rightly so since the wolves are, or at least if you choose to play it difficult, a very real danger). You have to weigh different options, making sure you eat just enough to make your food last, make your water last. Perhaps you need to wait for a blizzard to pass, but you're starving, so you risk freezing to death, scavenging the nearby fishing-cabins for supplies. You find a couple of cans of beans and some water in a toilet, but you're tired, and frozen, and you can't get back to a house with a bed without collapsing in the snow.. so you wait.. shivering, hoping that mother nature gives you a second chance. Outside, the wolves howl.. prowling.. waiting for you to make a mistake.
This is a solid survival game, a really immersive experience.
Unless you're an experienced tactician, it will challenge you, and my best guess is that you will love it :)

I was very discouraged to get Tales of Zestria because of strong negative opinions of the community. Luckily the game was very cheap on sale and it turned out to be awesome. I was prepared to install gamefix mod but haven't really bothered... Though I might at some point try to see if I can get the game working on Linux using the mod, but at this point I am too enthralled with the game to start spending time with Wine and system settings.
This is only my second Tales game; the first one was Symphonia. What stroke me in Symphonia was depth of the gameplay where only minority of the gameplay mechanics were required to beat the game (the game could have probably have been beaten with auto battle!). Tales of Zestria takes this complexity of the mechanics a few notch higher and the ammount of details in mechanics resembles more very elaborate boardgame than a videogame. Fights in Zestria have been more fun than in any other jrpg and there are quite some I've played.
The plot in Zestria is the usual "regret is turning people (and animals) into monsters, you have to save the world" thing. But hey! This is a jrpg, you weren't expecting anything more. The thing in writing is that it focuses quite much on comedy aspect which sets it apart from other jrpg. Also much effort has been spent animating character movement. Characters do so much more than the obligatory sword swinging. The writing and movement animation makes characters very vivid and lively. This is something very different from for example Hyperdimension Neptunia games where cute characters joke all the time but remain as persons shallow shells. The vivaciusness of Zestria characters has obviously been a major focus and it is achieved. Every character in Zestria is a real person or atleast their japanese versions are. Quite much of the stuff works only in japanese but the english translation of the script is a decent job altough much is lost in translation. Lost joke here and there isn't very major and Miyu Matsuki talking weird stuff doesn't necessarily need to be translated to be funny.

As of the current revision (27. Aug 2017) this program feels like it is in early alpha. You can make cards with a decent amount of flexibility, and the results are suprisingly useful. But there are quirks and bugs that make the program incredibly tedious to use, and you will encounter some hard limitations you cannot sidestep at all.
For example; If you load a card set from the main menu, you do not load it with any of the customized look & feel you spent the latter hour to perfect. These has to be loaded separately. Oh you did not save those separately earlier you say? Though luck.
For example: If you export your cards as a PDF, the process will FAIL if you did it already. To resolve this, you must go into your save folder and delete all the previously exported data, carefully avoiding to delete the card data or separately-saved-styles residing in the same folder in the process.
For example: I really wish I could have put some smaller font on the flavour section of the card. Flavour text that take up 80% of the card real estate is annoying, and I ended up having to cut it as a result. I don't mind if the users have to strain their eyes to read that part.
Issues like this aside, I have great faith in the concept. It certainly meets a niche, and saved me from spending the weekend playing with HTML to make cards that wouldn't have looked half as good. I feel the money might be worth it at some point. But right now I feel the asking price is a bit steep compared to how many quirks you have to dodge. Hopefully that will improve.

This game is just about flawless. You're given a really unique, cool, but easy to understand concept, and the game just goes with it. You make a hectic, spur-of-the-moment action scene, but you're doing it so deliberately, and the game rewards you for planning, being fast, and playing smart rather than pure mechanical skill. Tight controls, satisfying AI, good level design, the graphic design and user interfaces are unique and really work. The story is the type that can only be told within a video game, and for a game about killing red dudes it's actually pretty good, especially because it has tiny amounts of narrative and dialogue. Plus the challenges and endless modes are where you'll get a lot of mileage from.
It's a game I haven't really seen since Hotline Miami. Here is a level full of dudes and weapons, you and the dudes die in one hit, go nuts. You have a similar action flow (knock Dude 1 down, steal his gun, shoot Dude 2, throw gun to stun Dude 3, steal Dude 3's katana, chop up Dude 1 before he even stood up, throw katana at Dude 3, hotswitch into Dude 3, grab katana midair, impale Dude 4 with aimed katana throw), but unlike Hotline Miami the game makes it feel so natural, planned out, and deliberate until you watch the last minute-and-a-half of action compressed into ten real-time seconds of straight up dude killin'. It's good, it's really good, it feels satisfying to pull off, and it looks impressive too. Most of your deaths and failures are preventable with proper time/resource management, not like Hotline Miami where your deaths are funky hitreg or not being able to see a gunman a mile away.
I can easily see this game on a bunch of GOTY lists, but at $25 I don't think it's worth it. At least, not for everyone. If this game was $10-15 I'd heartily recommend it, but when there are other titles on Steam that are just as (if not more) innovative and unique, for half the price, and with more content. The gameplay's solid like you wouldn't believe, but I beat the campaign in an hour and a half, and the challenge/endless modes are just alterations on levels in the campaign. Only one enemy type, 3 guns, 2 types of melees, so far no promises on adding extra content, developer or usermade. Can the gameplay support the price? I think so, but I don't think most people can agree.
I suggest buying it on sale. At worst, you can buy the game, beat the campaign, and refund it and still be ~20 minutes under the time requirement to return it.

So, overall this game is pretty great.
The gameplay is solid, the controls are good (MUCH better with a gamepad) and the 70s mecha anime aesthetics are spot on and really capture what they're going for.
And then there's the stuff that's not so great.
Resolution: The resolution in this game is set and can not be changed. I get they did this to make it seem more "authentic" along the lines of the non-widescreen anime of the 20th century, but having it stuck at a constant 400x600 makes it look ugly, gives less space to see projectiles, and causes the steam overlay to act weird, making achievements and notifications take up nearly a quarter of the screen. Also there is no pause button.
Content: While I did enjoy this game I felt like it was kinda lacking in content. For five dollars you get 5 levels and varying difficulty modes. This can get stale quickly and unless you enjoy repeating the same levels over and over, trying to get new high scores or complete different difficulties you may find yourself bored very quickly.
However, if you can look past these small flaws this game is very enjoyable and is a great time waster. Would recommend to mecha fans and anyone with some extra funds in their steam wallets.

When playing the long dark I noticed some pros and some cons. The devs obviously put a lot of time into this game cause it looks beatiful and runs well on my toaster of a laptop.
Now the Pros of this game are:
1.Being completely underpowered (If you aren't well equipped then you are going to die from one wolf)
2.A atmosphere that really sucks you in and doesn't let go
3.Weather conditions that make you either try to make a fire ASAP, or make you have to run from the pack of wolves that you just realized are following you.
4. A looting system that makes every item feel like an achievement.
5. Combat items (Yes even melee) are hard to find expect heart pounding sneaking
6.There is loot even outside drawers and cabinets so you have to look through the enviroment
7. Sleeping has its advantages and it's disadvantages (Say you want to sleep to morning and it's 9:00PM then you would be thirsty and hungry when you wake up)
8. Crafting is diverse (Say you want to repair a tear in your shirt,you would need cotton and something to sew with.)
9. Active devs and a pretty great community
Now here are something to take into consideration:
1.Wolves are everywhere, instead of focusing on this beatiful lake, nope gotta make sure that wolf doesn't get too close.
2. Defensive items are very spefic (I just found something made of metal now I can fight!... All it does is help me open stuff?)
3. Game is hard to get into, but in the end is worth it.
4. No multiplayer at the moment (Most likely will be added in)
All in all, I think I would rate The Long Dark at the moment 8.5/10. Not the best game ever, but hey! It's up there!

Listen, you got to know what you're getting into here.
It's early access, so there's that.  It's not finished.  But it does seem to have frequent updates.
All you've got for now is sandbox mode [in case you skipped the actual page, where it says this].  There's two areas as of the time of this writing, one which you must find in-game to unlock [and that's cool.  Gives purpose to the exploration].
tl;dr - If you like exploring, making your own stories, being scared of wolves and feeling oppressed by a gorgeous yet hostile environment, then you will love this game.  If you like your run-of-the-mill, craft-crazy, build-your-base type of survival game, then keep on moving.  This isn't the game for you.
-------------------------------------
This is not your copy-paste survival game.  Crafting is limited, it's more realistic in the scope of it, as it is stuff that the average seasoned camper would know how to make.  THERE IS NO BUILDING IN THIS GAME.  You don't build anything.  The focus is on exploration with survival thrown in as the main mechanic.  I'm pretty sure this is to cater to the story mode that will be released much later down the line and is supposed to be the main game mode.  It is clear the intention isn't for you to find a nice spot and make it your home.  The main goal is to keep going.  You scavange buildings, maybe stay for a while to cook some food, warm yourself up and rest, and boil some water, then you move on.
There is quite a lot to explore.  But this is not a randomly generated map, it is always the same, so after a while you will know where every building is.  Supplies you will find in said buildings change though.  Then there are the wolves... your one and only antagonist.  Wolves will kill you.  There are ways to scare them off, and you can kill them if you get lucky and find the rifle [and ammo for said rifle].  But most of the time you will be running for your life, hoping you make it to a building you can load into to escape.
IF you don't want to deal with wolves, there is a game mode that makes them not attack you.  I would suggest goin in that way to get used to the game mechanics first.  Survival is the main focus of this game.  Dynamic weather is your true worst enemy, as well as your hunger/stamina [measured by calories], hydration, evading hypothermia, and resting.  Most things you do/consume will affect multiple things.  For example, a hot meal will warm you up along with easing hunger.  Resting in a warm bed in a building will warm you up as well and make you rested, but you burn calories, so don't sleep for too long.
You have to plan, you have to think about what youre doing and when, and you have to hope you find what you need to survive.  You need wood for a fire?  Better hope you can find some laying about.  You can't chop down a tree and take it.  You have to rely on what you can find laying about.  Your character is incapable of ripping furniture to bits and using that wood for a fire.  Again, this comes from the fact the game wants you to keep moving and not hunker down in one place forever.
I recommend this game because it is good at what it does.  That being said, know what you're getting into!  Go on youtube, watch some people playing it, there are tons of lets plays on there.  Just watch one for a few minutes and you'll get the idea of the pace of the game [slow.  The pace is slow].
The art style is pretty, the UI is clean, I've yet to face any bugs [not saying there isn't any, just saying I haven't found any yet].  It feels a bit bare-bones at the moment, but that's because the main event [story mode] isn't there yet.

As an avid level designer always seeking the most effective way of creating various types of landscapes, I can say that after just a few hours of testing this product, I am amazed at it's power and simplicity it brings to it's target audience. While the program itself is being worked on, it goes to show that with each update, both major and minor flaws are looked at and patched, with continuous updates across all the products AGF has to offer.
The developers themselves are some of the most engaging and polite people I have ever had the pleasure of speaking to. When I had an issue with understanding how importing/exporting in the Constructor worked, I receieved a reply e-mail within
of sending it out, at 3am! The fact they take their time and carefully check on these kinds of things gives me great confidence in what will come in the future of this product.
If you purchase this product expecting to make the next Skyrim, or the next FarCry, you are setting your expectations far too high. This is an environment and asset tool used to make medium to moderately high detailed landscapes and assets, and for a heck of a steal! You get over 100 assets to play with, and the Constructor tool allows you to mix and match those "pieces" to make something entirely of your own. The combinations and possibilities are fair considering what you are paying for.
I have spent hours upon hours researching the Unity marketplace and if you want something AAA quality, you're going to pay AAA price. The fact that AGF have gone from their first type of business model, to the various split packages, shows that they want this program to be accessible for all aspiring game developers on a budget.
Honestly, I find it unfair that the people at AGF have gone to great lengths to do what they do and be so negatively critisized for not making something "of Industry Standard". This is a work in progress that is being developed (at the time of this writing) on top of all the other things they have to offer! Go browse the Unity store, look for everything you want, and do the math. Exactly. Until you have the budget to make that happen, this tool can provide useful for building up prototypes to fund your projects, or even make something personal for your own enjoyment.
Overall, I highly recommend this product. The people at AGF are wonderful and will help you when you really need it, offering insight on literally any question you have personally!
+ Easy to use when sculpting landscapes
+ Asset builder (a.k.a Constructor) with 100's of combinations for your own custom assets
+ Pre-built landscapes to get you started
+ Medium to Moderately High quality assets and textures
+ Engaging and very helpful development team, always willing to assist
- Standard Interface is a bit of a pain to get used to unless customized
- Depending on resolution, sometimes sculpting terrain can be lagged
- Community references and sources are limited (information wise)
- Import feature can, at times, be a bit overwhelming in Unity (time, memory usage, loading, etc)
- Some bugs get overlooked when they are key to fixing problems (in my opinion)
8/10

This is not a game maker.
It can be used to design and test some assets and locations before exporting them into a game engine but you cannot, for example, create characters, plots, menus, skills, missions, etc. The name is therefore misleading.
It is a cool idea and the guys who make it look really genuine but it fails for the following reasons: the user interface is HORRIBLE - you have a three tier menu to get to select an item, the camera moves on it own, there is basically NO DOCUMENTATION at all. You will have to trawl through youtube and forums to find basic instructions. The only official information is some tutorial videos which themselves make it clear that they are "quick and dirty". The Steam manual is a joke, it's a two-page PDF with some patch notes.
In my opinion this software is useless for an experienced game maker and incomprehensible and unusable for a newbie. I think there is a niche for people who want to test out whiteboxing scenes befor exporting but that isn't what the name of the game implies and I'm not convinced you couldn't achieve your ends better in Unity.

So, since I have played 2+ hours on the software I thought I would write a review.
It's an awesome software where you can create cards in any shape and style you want.
Pros:
1. You can customize your card with any color, aspect, text, etc. you want.
2. You can customly put in how big you want your cards to be when they print.
3. You can select the quality of the cards (1x, 2x, 3x, and 4x).
Cons:
1. When you print them out, you would may want glossy printing paper or card, which could be more expensive than the software itself.
2. Cutting the cards can be a pain in the neck if you don't have a paper cutting board.
3. It doesn't have a big selection of icons, so you may need to make your own.
So basically you need some materials to cut and print the cards. If you want make a big collection of cards, and you don't have a paper cutting board or any kind of sharp scissors, you may want to go and buy that before you get the game.
Overall, I would rate the game a 7/10.
