It's hard to say no, but eh. It's F2P, I bought into it in early access and it was better then. It's not really P2W because there's no competition. However, as is becoming the new thing in games, you can spend real money to speed up the grind process to get better items faster. Which incentivizes the dev's to stretch the grind process from rewarding to dying of old age before you make any real progress. Which isn't horrible, if you enjoy the Dungeon Defenders gameplay. It's kind of a 3rd person tower building defense game. Now, like a most TD games, eventually the game gets stupidly hard. You get so many pathways and your defensive power is so limited that failure is certain, so it's kind of broken at that point. And all players share a build point pool, having more players does NOT increase this pool. This sucks for two reasons. First and most importantly, most people who play this are morons. They don't know how tower defense works at all and I'm guessing they don't speak english, because a lot of the time you talk to people they don't even respond, they just keep walking around blowing build points on useless towers in dumb@ss locations. They clearly have no idea how the map plays and most likely don't understand how the game works in general. 2nd - this means that these idiots eat up that build pool, so build phase becomes a mad dash of trying to throw down a few useful defense structures before the idiots eat it up with towers/walls that are facing the wrong way, are easily destroyed/vulnerable, are easily bypassed because enemies don't even walk there, etc. It really is bad, and what's most confusing is, these people obviously are capable of using a computer, I don't know how you can be intelligent to download Steam, insert your credit card info, buy this game, launch it, choose a class and yet then be virtually non-functional as a human being in the game and not even be capable of grasping the basic concepts such as defend key defensive points or focus defensive structures at choke points where multiple paths meet. Yet, they manage to be clueless as to everything about the game. So that's harsh, because it's a Co-Op game. That OR everyone once in awhile you run across a 'master', these guys are the extreme opposite of the other kind, though way more rare. These guys don't need you, in some cases they don't even want you, why they bothered to do a public match instead of play private it confusing. They know exactly what's going on, but they're going to chew up all the build points for themselves instantly. All you will get to do is run around and attack things with your character, granted you'll get loot and money, but you get more xp when your towers kill stuff and you won't get to place a single one with these guys. At least though I understand them, cause that's my next step, recommending that IF you try this out, to become the 'master' type. Learn how the game works, learn every level well enough that you can play it entirley on your own. Then when you get idiots who don't know how to play (some don't even know how to place towers, which is actually helpful if they're that stupid) as long as you can build a solid defense they can hop about like idiots and all having more players does is increase the loot quality. Items and money seem to be exclusive to the players, so you don't have to worry about other players running around and picking up all the money and loot, what you see in the world isn't what they see and hence they can't loot steal. However build resources (green magic) is NOT exclusive to players and whoever picks them up first gets them. That can be annoying, especially with players who don't build.
Past the players you have the money mongering. So yeah, you can spend money to get better loot, essentially proof they know they stretched the grind beyond the point of being rewarding and making it tedious to make you willing to spend money just to make it end. They also locked the classes and their cosmetics up. Now cosmetics I'm used to, and a few of them are pretty cool. There are nearly a dozen classes though and I honestly don't know how many you get when you're a free player. Again, I bought into this before it was F2P, so when it went F2P they gave me a bunch of in game currency, free back pack slots and some cosmetics of my choosing. I have four classes, luckily the only four I"m interested in, but all the classes are rather interesting so I can see someone wanting them all. Also, I said backpacks, yes you have limited inventory and it can be a pain to go through the inventory. If I had fewer back packs than I do, it would be more annoying. Good news though, XP is shared between your characters! The character you play as gains XP much faster than your unused characters but hey, it's nice. Also inventory is shared between characters, so if you get a nice sword for your knight, no tedious mailing items between characters or banking it between them, with the press of an "F" key (F1-F4) you instantly change characters and can equip the item.
Honestly, over all, it's a pretty fun game. Though I put probably triple the hours into the first game, I also had a friend to play that with and I have no one to play this with. The drag is, cosmetics are pretty awesome, which I don't usually say about games, and if I could grind for them I would, but they are real money only which sucks because getting 'gear' just isn't worth the work. The further into the game you go the more vicious the levels become to the point of near impossible, so I just play the first five levels over and over, they're wonderfully desgined and while challenging don't present so many pathways that the level can't be managed. Since it is free, hey give it a shot, it actually is a pretty good 3rd person action TD hybrid game. Just beware that the devs obviously decided they were more interested in micro transactions that just making a good game, which is true for virtually all F2P titles I suppose, so you'll run into design choices that pressure you to spend money to avoid almost punishing game mechanics.

There's little to no story. I guess you can keep using the same one of four units over and over for each stage JUST to see what they say, but other than that the story is super simple and 70's esque. Its a fun nostalgia fest.
As for the gameplay, it was challenging. If you are new to shmups, easy will feel like "hard mode".
It involves using 4 unique power ups: drill, thunder, rocket, and needle. Each one with their own strengths, weaknesses, uber moves, and "mini uber", which is activated by letting go of the fire button when the "charge" is filled up. The way the shooting has a charge meter adds a nice rhythm to the shooting, with each unique charge filling up once every 3 seconds or so. Its a nice unique way to add a small gameplay dimension to the shooting instead of the usual "hold down fire and aim the ship".
Is this game a masterpiece? Heavens no. Is this game worth the price, ESPECIALLY on sale? Definately.

You can't quite pause the game, change resolution (watch out for the huge Steam popups in the corner) or reconfigure the controls, but if you can get past those annoyances, you're in for a treat.

Expect the level of ludicrous bullet hell to climb exponentially on the higher difficulties. Fun, but indubitably with its frustrating moments.

Superhot is a game basically about trickshooting and making "cinematic" fights, you're going to find yourself doing things like shooting someone next to you, then because your next shot isn't up yet you throw the gun at the person shooting at you so they drop their gun so you can shoot them with their own gun, because that is surprisingly faster. And when it does it's job at making you feel cool it does it REALLY WELL.
However, the game doesn't support it's instant death very well in terms of giving you enough information. Turning around to check your surroundings for people causes time to speed up and likely kill you in later levels where there's around 5 people attacking you at once, and there's no indicators other than where you're looking as to where enemies are going to be.
Now dying isn't usually a problem in that many video games, but SUPERHOT is not your average video game, SUPERHOT thrives off of having flowing gameplay, and anything whatsoever breaking that flow turns it's incredibly fun gameplay into a quick slog of a game that you just want to get to the next level and really hate restarting over and over.
One of the biggest problems is the assault rifle in the game. The Assault Rifle allows enemies to turn the game into a bullet hell that must be carefully navigated, instead of the early games "do what you think is coolest" gameplay the massive amounts of bullets makes you walk on eggshells trying not to be cool, but to just survive.
In short: SUPERHOT turns from a game about being cool, into a game about being pixel perfect just to avoid dying, you will die over and over again trying to figure out just what the hell you are supposed to be doing and it stops being fun.

If you didn't buy this in last month's AMAZING deal from a certain sight *mumble-mumble*, you might agree with some of the people who review this software line as a money-grab.  Check out the store page in detail, and you'll wonder why they don't just give everythig to you for the base-software price, right???
However for each DLC pack, there are new royalty free assets, new setups for game genre building/testing, and some have new tools for streamlining design using different methods.  These all took more time and work for the developer to finalize, and he might not be in the wrong asking for payment for the content.   New features cost more money for people who already bought the software?  I believe that is the concept in any add-on DLC.
I did indeed get this and many of its DLC at a steep discount-  so if this does peek your interest, I advise to look around for a deal on it.  Earlier this year, I'd seen the base AGFPRO on sale for about 5 dollars, on three seperate retailers, on different weeks of software sales.  So, take the people who complain about having to pay premium for other people's work with a grain of salt.  If you want to see what it's about, there are videos explaining the features and UI online you can watch for free.
Personally, I find it a designer's time-saver.  I haven't actually exported anything yet, as I'm still feeling out the interface, so I can't personally vouch for how well all features work;  but the expedited world/scene creation is preferrable.  Matt McDonald (and family) have put bounds of work into creating a seamless game-world design tool.  They also personally run support, which makes them super-busy, but since they do make themselves available, it's admirable IMO.
Original assets can be imported, custom textures can be used, and there are quite few cool things you can do with them in the standalone AGF engine.
If you want to work on this quality-level, without the pricetag on the full package, you should get Blender and Unity 5 Personal (those are both very powerful and free, and useful with or without AGFpro), and learn how to make 3d environments using them; but I feel this tool's well worth the dinero, expediting the building of environment and basic game-mechanics which would take many more hours and headaches to accomplish (especially if you aren't a schooled and seasoned game designer).
Now, I don't care for some of the DLC packs, but only because I feel personally about using mass-produced free assets and game-mechanics.   That doesn't mean they're bad-- and the developer did put a seperate allotment of time and focus on building them for add-on content.  If you want to benifit from them, you have to buy them.
I do think it's well worth the price for AGFpro PREMIUM, since the point here is to design a beautiful, yet un-finished game world, complete with scenes/stages, and set up basic features like lighting, day-night cycles, parallax textures; then export them for use in building a polished current-gen game in the Unity3D 5 engine.
After looking at the add-ons for Unity, from many various coders and publishers, I think AGFpro PREMIUM is not really over-priced at all for what it can do.
Of course,  that's coming from a guy who got this at a mind-blowing, STEAL of a price! ;)
To conclude; PLEASE understand I'm not saying that this is the BE-ALL/END-ALL of game design tools.  It is very easy to run into moments where you're probably wishing for features, and you absolutely can suggest them to the dev team, although their main focus is creating more expansions for now, since the 3.0 update.
It can tend to be constrictive for game design since game and story features are built-in and can't be tweaked beyond what options are made available.  However, that's what makes this tool unique; to set up a project that can be used to build onto and polish using other tools and the Unity 5 engine (AGFP Premium), I definitely must recommend it.

Banished is one of those little gems that looks flawless until you get it under a microscope.  Don’t get me wrong here, I really like Banished, but there are a few things they could have done to make it even better.  I'll also explain my negative recommendation towards the end.
My first, and probably biggest, nitpick is the fact that your entire village is just that, one village.  You have to build within those limits or you’ll quickly find yourself loosing villagers until you have none left.  The first few times I played I tried to go for a little bit of realism in my construction.  I placed city structures in the city, with houses here and there.  Then I went off into the country, placed farms and a few houses there.  I also did the same thing for lumber and fishing industries.  Then I started noticing peasants dying on me.  The chief complaint was starvation, when I had a building full of food.  Well, it turns out that the farmers would bring all of their food into the storage building and take nothing for their houses by the farms.  In addition, the houses by the farms weren’t even populated by the farmers working there, they were populated by other random townsfolk.  This led to my population traveling great distances just to do the most minor tasks as the housing I provided wasn’t being used as intended.  As a result, the entire population died.  There was no AI saying anything like, “Maybe I should live close to where I work”.  Nothing saying, “I’m hungry, maybe I should eat some food from my farm instead of delivering all of it to the storage building”.  It was like they were all robots with the basic of intelligence.  Need a home?  Find a vacant one and use it, doesn’t matter where it is.  Hungry?  You can't eat anything until someone brings food to your home.  It was just… Disappointing.
Now, what they did get right is the rather large and complex nature of cities.  Virtually every building is useful and required if you want to get the most out of your villagers.  Take the school, it directly impacts the working efficiency of those who’ve attended it.  Clothing, required to help your villagers survive the cold winters.  Medicine, required to deal with any illnesses.  Even the various farms and food producers have their usefulness.  It’s beneficial to have many sources of food, as random effects can affect them at any time and a food shortage can quickly lead to starvation.  This makes city design and management extremely important.  Growing your village quickly can be as disasterous as not growing it fast enough.  There's a very strict balance you have to maintain or you'll quickly find your villagers dying off.  It's quite the challenge, and that's why I love it.
The only true thing this game is missing is the addition of Multiplayer.  This is an excellent RTS city building game with enormous maps and it’s rather disappointing that you can’t openly share the experience.  Even if you wanted it to remain as a non-combat experience it would have been fantastic.  You could have established regular trade routes, had diplomatic relations with other players, and even lent aid to another player’s village if they were in trouble.  Of course, adding in city walls and militia to execute raids wouldn’t have damaged the experience either.
The biggest reason I can't recommend this game is because it just feels unfinished.  The premise is that you’re settlers who have been banished.  As your city prospers you never again hear from those who banished you.  They never check on you, or attack you, and you can’t gloat to them about how successful you are.  There’s a disconnect in every game that makes you suddenly and abruptly ask yourself, “Ok, now what?”  It’s like reaching the final chapter of a really good book and finding out it doesn’t exist.  Growing your village is all there is.  There’s nothing more.  Your goal is to see how high your population can get, which is great if your game is called SimCity, but it really doesn’t feel right for Banished.
The missing multiplayer, brought together with the lack of any kind of outside threat (and defense from said threat) just makes this game feel unfinished.  I really enjoyed it back in the days when updates were frequent and we still hoped for more content, but I wouldn’t recommend it today.

This game is a failure simulator, and that's awesome. This experience is going to harden your skills as a player. You're going to learn about life.
1. Don't rush. You're going to want to start building a bigger farm,wider pasture, schoolhouse, market, chapel - and then suddenly your current farm is going to get a disease and all the tools are going to break. Half of your population will starve. There won't be anyone left to cut firewood. Take it slow.
2. It can't be perfect, and you're probably going to have some regrets. The way this game works, you'll probably spend several years with all of your people in a rowhouse. That's how it goes. You'll probably also lose several people to old age before you really get going, and they'll probably die in the summer. That's life, don't mourn the past.
3. Think. Don't just set things up and click the fast button. There's plenty in here that you'll miss. Maybe you should harvest at 60%, the weather is getting cold . . .
4. Nothing lasts forever. You've got venison, milk, blueberries, thick coats, mountains of firewood - you're eatin' nectar. But then the tornado hits. The children die. The gatherer's hut is destroyed. It'll take almost a year to get built up again after a disaster, and who will do the work? Enjoy the good times.
I'm going to go kiss my wife now. Buy this game.

As a way to learn Hiragana, it's fun and I feel pretty effective. I am not a fan of rpg maker games nor the battle system this one has (it becomes repetitive and boring soon), but the system works for learning Hiragana - turn based battles give you time to think and recall what each letter is, grindy nature of it ensures you get to see letters again and again (and there's always escape option if you want to skip the battle for whatever reason). You can always revisit the lessons and the penalty of not getting Hiraganas right the first time around in the battle is not big, so it's not super pressured either which I like.
I didn't expect to see any words introduced, so it was a pleasent surprise that the game has bonus word lessons (words are not revised in battles) and some small side quests which introduce around 3-5 new words (like greetings, or today/tomorrow/yesterday, or few nature words, etc.) and they give a nice break from all the battling.
Recommending, it's great for its purpose which is teaching Hiragana in engaging way.

All of the assets and the engine support ultrawide resolution, but unless you hex edit the executable it just takes standard 1080 and stretches it. If you're looking for the video game representation of any MIcheal Bay action flick, this is it. The graphics are stellar even by today's standards, the combat is a bit lacking, but the level of destruction and amount of exploration you can do is staggering.
The world of Just Cause 2 is beautiful, vast, and full of variety. While other games have superior combat and driving in the same genre (Like the Saints Row series), what makes this game is the exploration and subsequent destruction of the world as you come across it. I can grapple onto a car, drive it off a bridge, and then parachute onto a boat all the while not even noticing the explosions.
While the sense of exploration and destruction make the game amazing to play through, the game may as well not have a story, with most of the missions involving things you would be doing on your own anyway or just outright boring missions entirely.
If you enjoy open world games that have a ton of exploration, get this game. If you're looking for a story driven world with at least decent combat, look elsewhere.

The build of this application is stable.
Would I recommend this software to other indie game designers for prototype creation?
-No, not at its current state.
Would I recommend this software to other indie game designers for production layout?
-No.  It's a very basic application.
Granted the UX is slick, minimalistic and pleasing to the eyes.  It's just not flexible enough to create any card you want.  It pretty much sticks to the format of how Magic the Gathering cards are laid out.  You can adjust sliders to manipulate the size of each part of the card.  However, you cannot manipulate the orientation or (on the build I was testing) the alpha of them either.  And for some reason they use aspect ratio when determining the size of the card.  That confuses me, like the devs haven't done anything in the card making industry before.  It should be either standard sizes like Poker, mini-poker, tarot, etc.  Or at least give a unit of measurement on the sliders either in centimeter or inches.
It says you can import your own artwork, but only into main object designated for artwork.  There are areas all over the card where you can place icons, but those icons must be chosen from a set of predefined icons.  You cannot import your own icons.
At launch the PDF export was bugged, but thankfully the dev was quick to patch this back into operation.  The dev's seem like nice people, and are what seems to be always watching and answering the discussion threads on this project.  So, I'll give them props there.  Excellent job on communication.
As it stands, I would rank this application as an early access release, like version 0.8-beta not a 1.0 release candidate.  I understand that they have a lengthy list of things they want to add, and maybe once those come into being it will be worth the $20 price.  But I cannot recommend this application to anyone other than people just wanting to make cards for fun.

A sidescrolling SHMUP in the vein of 1970's SUPER ROBOT mecha anime. WITH YELLOW SUBTITLES!
It's pretty gawd-dammed perfect as far as what it sets out to do. You shoot all of the the things while bombastic music plays in the background facing a recurring miniboss and so many enemies that are obvious references to the tatsunoko era of anime. It's very self-aware and pretty glorious.
Best of all, there's actually some interesting design choices for the genre, so you'll actually find a different gameplay experience here. Namely in the health system. Rather than being a 1HP hero, you have a fairly meaty health bar, but it carries over from stage to stage and only gets some repairs between stages. Moreover, your co-pilot partners who act as your powerups also have their own, much smaller, health bars and just like in Star Fox they can get KO'd for good if you're too careless through the short 30 minute campaign.
Plus, rather than a whole bunch of bombs in a stage like most shoot 'em ups, you only get one OMEGA BOMB per stage to use when the going gets tough, so strategic deployment of both your team mates and when you pull out your super move is actually fairly critical.
And it's all executed flawlessly. Literally the only complaint I have is that the video used to sell the game with the sung VULKAISER themesong isn't actually in the game. If it was it'd be 110% perfect!
As it is, I'll just settle for 100% perfect.
Go, Go, VULKAISER! Destroy them with your super electricity!

1995... A game named Command and Conquer appeared... and paved the way for an entire genre. It's a name that many RTS veterans should be familiar with. The franchise had its ups and downs throughout the years. 2007, the long awaited sequel of Command and Conquer Tiberian Sun appears. Has it passed the test? Let's see...
Visually, the game is downright gorgeous, even for today's standards. You can tell at first glance, whether the map is situated in a still pristine Blue zone, a conflict-torn Yellow zone or in an almost unearthly Red zone. The units are also well designed and their appearance alone tells something about the respective faction. Topped off with non-excessive and neat special effects, the visuals give a good impression.
Gameplaywise, the game has undergone major changes. Instead of one single build queue, where the amount of respective facilities only determined production speed, now each production facility has its own queue, and units have gained special abilities. These changes were not wellcomed by all fans of the franchise, but I'll allow myself to use a proverb: "I don't know if it's going to be good, but if it is to become better, it must change". Other than that, the "hard-counter" unit-system has finally reached a desireable level, unlike in previous titles, pretty much every unit can be put to a good use and has its weak points. Not every change is good though. The gameplay is kind of too fast-paced compared to its precedetors, and that signifficantly weakened the efficiency of commando-infiltrations, which were the brandmark of this franchise. Command and Conquer 3 lets you deploy a countermeasure in a matter of seconds, leaving little to no room for a classic commando rampage, which was possibly the most fun thing Command and Conquer could offer. That aside, the gameplay gets way more than a passing grade.
The audio: The first thing C&C fans will notice that the OST simply doesn't have the same magic as the ones composed by Frank Klepacki. Just thinking of "March to doom" playing as you scrape together leftovers of your army in late-game for a final desperate attempt to win sends chills down my spine. Still, the soundtrack is by no means bad. The sound effects are seamlessly implemented, and is good and bad at the same time. Remember how your hands started sweating when you hear the ominous thundering sound of the allied Cruiser's cannons in Red Alert? It was the sound saying: "say goodbye to your base". On the other hand, with the sound effects not standing out too much, you can keep being fully focused on the events on the battlefield and can clearly make out the very important and helpful announcements of your EVA unit, pointing out upcoming danger.
Despite all the flaws pointed out, Command and Conquer 3 Tiberian Wars is a very enjoyable game and I recommend it to both newcommers and veterans.
Verdict: 8.5/10

This game is a failure simulator, and that's awesome. This experience is going to harden your skills as a player. You're going to learn about life.
1. Don't rush. You're going to want to start building a bigger farm,wider pasture, schoolhouse, market, chapel - and then suddenly your current farm is going to get a disease and all the tools are going to break. Half of your population will starve. There won't be anyone left to cut firewood. Take it slow.
2. It can't be perfect, and you're probably going to have some regrets. The way this game works, you'll probably spend several years with all of your people in a rowhouse. That's how it goes. You'll probably also lose several people to old age before you really get going, and they'll probably die in the summer. That's life, don't mourn the past.
3. Think. Don't just set things up and click the fast button. There's plenty in here that you'll miss. Maybe you should harvest at 60%, the weather is getting cold . . .
4. Nothing lasts forever. You've got venison, milk, blueberries, thick coats, mountains of firewood - you're eatin' nectar. But then the tornado hits. The children die. The gatherer's hut is destroyed. It'll take almost a year to get built up again after a disaster, and who will do the work? Enjoy the good times.
I'm going to go kiss my wife now. Buy this game.

With only one pack and 1 free mission available to play currently, this potentially great game simply suffers from having almost no content. Two things that I could see fixing this immediately as story packs are released would be a horde mode with increasing rewards as you live longer, and some sort of competitive pvp mode with at least 6 maps.
Additional changes needed in my opinion could be a different look at the free to play model. Giving free players the option to matchmake into any mission they don't own just without choice of where they go, offering reduced rewards. Reduce cost of new characters with in game currency. This because it wants to be a multiplayer game, but with the titan 3rd person fps warframe that already has its foot in the door. I don't see why people would spend money on this when they can play warframe completely free and spend their 10-40 dollars elsewhere.
Overall the game has a long way to go to be worth the time and money commitment the devs are requesting. I would like this game to go to bigger and better and places because I honestly want to want this game. Raiders of the Broken Planet  just currently isn't all there.

This game isn't exactly your average type of game, even if you categorize it after a full run.  It's not your usual type of psychologhical game where the setting would either be horror or mind blowing concepts. Funnly enough, it's simple yet complex.
It starts with an introduction to the game. The narrator is constatly there guiding you and giving his interpretation over the games. I said games because this is a collection of games made by a certain individ that once knew the developer of this ... collection. So everything seems normal, and suddenly the presentation starts taking a deep and dark twist. The narrator tells us certain aspects about games, the process with which they're made and also his interpretations over what the developer might have thought or felt while making those games.
As much as I've understood, The developer was doing game purely as a hobby and didn't like to show the to the public because either he didn't consider them complete work or he wasn't making them to be shown to the public. Then one day at some game jam, this guy(the narrator) shows up and shows interest in the games that this developer makes. They keep contact with eachother and they become friends.
(From this point I'll reffer to the Narrator as Dave and the Developer as Coda)
After Coda gave Dave his creations,  for unknown reasons, Dave starts questioning if the games made by Coda and gave to him reflected Coda's emotional/mental status. These two would often get into an arguement about the status of the games as they're not exactly playable and accessible and why are they made if so. At a certain point in their friendship, Dave starts conflicting with Coda's wishes and he shows his games to the public, and they really liked the game and Dave felt good about it, but for Coda? For Coda it started to become bother some because what was once his hobby became more like a responsability and as a result he started being more and more inactive through the process.
Dave became needy of those games so he would have what to show to the public for the good words they would offer but Coda lost his escape from maybe a difficult time, which was making games. After a few years Coda made a last game in which he wanted to tell to Dave what he felt and probably what he wanted to tell him for a long while. Getting there tho, it's the most difficult part. The game was basicly impossible to complete without being modified, but I think that Coda knew that Dave would do that. And so he did. after you've passed those parts Coda wrote a letter to Dave in which besides telling him his thoughts, he also stopped any kind of connection that they had. Thus leaving Dave in the dark but  not without an answer.
The game is deep, it can easily touch a sensible point but I think that the game presents an undeniable truth about people: The people that get addicted to others will in the end make other's life hard to bear with. I personally recommend the game, not for what it is, but for what it represents.

I really want to give this game a good review.
I believe it has a very good physics engine, very accurately modeling the effects of driving 80 mph on a dirt road. There are some questionable things that happen sometimes at the edge of control, but all in all, quite a reasonable approximation. The sound is also very good, particularly the sound of your engine in the cabin, and reflecting off barriers as you drive by. You can tell where AI drivers hit the gas, and where they lift. You can hear crumpling sheet metal, and grinding steel against concrete in accidents. The shock absorbers are modeled to be less than perfect on the american cars ( bouncy ) and stiff on foreign cars. The american cars feel real in that they respond to input in realistic ways. There's body roll, there's slip, there's inertia, there's tire howl. The hood can get bent so much you can barely see over it. The guy you're trying to push off the road resists your efforts, and counters. You can go over bumps fast enough to catch air, and lose control. You can run into a stack of tires, sending them flying. Generally, you can continue to drive your car LONG after it would be realistically damaged beyond use. I've barreled down racetracks with so much damage to the front of the car, that the drivers side front wheel sat about where the oil pan does.
The AI is pretty good at racing in front of you, but behind you, their priority is disabling you. This make for a very frustrating race unless you can get in front and maintain 1st place, or get behind and maintain last place. The AI drivers are dumb enough to be funny, in that you can tell their intentions to push the closest guy to them into the wall, and keeping guys behind them from passing. As others have said, during the course of a race, car pieces/parts will LITTER the course to the point of absurdity.
But the main thing is... this simulation is FUN. it might not be finished, it might be very coarse, and quirky, but it's a blast. I don't think it's worth the price, it should be $10. A lot of work went into what we have now, and that is fair. I've had a lot of fun racing against the AI, as well as simply turning off all the other cars and just screaming down a road as fast as I can go. I'd like to see updates to the modification options, and maybe some different cars, paint jobs, and tracks, but its fun as is.
To be clear, I would recommend this to others if it were:
1. Finished
2. Cheaper
or
3. Updated more frequently
Best $1 I have ever spent.

TL;DR: Buy this game. Seriously. If you've ever loved 3D platformers, you will love this game.
The long review:
I can't remember when the last time a game made me feel like a kid again. I seriously got a punch of nostalgia, like I was sitting in front of my gamecube booting up super mario sunshine for the first time. This game was worth every cent, and I will buy /ANY/ DLC that comes out in a heartbeat.
The four worlds mix up gameplay in such creative formulas- If you think every level is just hopping around trying to collect items, you will be pleasantly surprised to find out there is so much more than that. From popularity contests, murder mysteries, boss fights, and a god DAMN stealth horror level (seriously, that was terrifying), this game mixes up the classic "hop and collect" formula in so many delightful ways. The level design is creative and the artistic direction is beautiful, seriously, the first time you go into Alpine Skyline your breath will be taken away- And it's not just for show, hopping through the gorgeous level is just as delightful.
The music suits each and every level perfectly, and the way the music's instruments smoothly transition as you switch areas without changing the tune is delightful. Some of the most impactful audio moments for me was in the memory-rift levels, where every time you complete a section a new instrument is added to the tune. It actually made me feel nostalgic for the level, even though I had just been in it minutes ago.
And jesus christ, this game is funny. The voice actors all have unique tinges to their voice to carry out their hilarious lines. The characters are all super lovable, the one that stands out to me is the Ghost... Guy, you'll know him when you see him, and all the Mafia men. Applause to the VAs, you guys did a wonderful job.
There were quite a few small issues, such as the quality of the character models of the two girls being a little awkward, some bugs here and there (a few frustrated me such as my hits not registering to bosses, but it's nothing unplayable), and those GOD DAMN BAND OWLS THAT FOLLOW YOU AND SMACK INTO YOU FHJDSLFS, but they don't impact the experience in any severe way (but you will notice them.)
Anyway, consider me a new huge fan of Gears for Breakfast. I've seriously already begged my friends to buy this game, and if you've made it this far in my review, please pretend I'm begging you to buy it too. Support this studio. This indie game proves to be just as fun as 3D platformers produced by massive companies like Nintendo- And that's amazing. I can't wait to see the 2DLC worlds and any future games!!

***Please note this review was upon the very initial release***
In the world of card design, there are 2 reasons to create cards: The first is that you want to create cards for an existing game, either to rework existing cards, or to add or supplement what was officially published for your own home rules. The second reason is to design your own game.
In the world of card design, there are 2 types of people who create cards: The first is the serious gamer/designer, who wants cards of high fidelity regarding an existing property or to create something that is uniquely theirs, that could be trademarked or copyrighted. The second is the casual/new gamer/designer who doesn't care about fidelity and simply needs the mechanic the card infers.
Card Creator serves absolutely none of the four possibilities of overlap on this punnet square, and seems to have been developed in the absence of the above information and does not deserve your money. I'll explain why.
SERIOUS GAME DESIGNER
Let us say, you are a serious designer. You want to add cards to existing games, either tabletop ones such as Dominion, Sentinels of the Multiverse, Legendary, Dead of Winter, Agricola, Robinson Crusoe etc. or LCG/TCGs such as the Pathfinder Adventure card game, Magic: The Gathering, Star Realms or Yu-Gi-Oh. Fidelity is not something Card Creator can offer in any of these contexts. Here's why.
SYMBOLS:
Many of these games are combat based and require things like attack, defence and health. There are symbols you can put in, but the variety without the specificity to the context of many fantasy tropes is disconcerting. There is no simple sword or shield, though there are various weapon icons or armour based ones.
In the case of TCGs, rarity is an integral component. Yet this program offers no way to change the colour of the symbols used to delineate common, uncommon or rare.
Additionally, the symbols may only be placed in specific circles on the inside of the card art, and not anywhere else on the card, such as underneath certain values in the top/bottom right/left of the card or next to the sub-heading of the card underneath the art, such as where the Magic: The Gathering symbol resides.
ART:
Many games have full bleed art without the text boxes, but still with text. This program cannot do that. It cannot recreate those full art MtG cards. Additionally, the art can only be placed in the one spot relative to certain other elements of the template. While you can remove the top title box and instead have the title underneath the art, you cannot move the description to the top of the card with the art below. The art must also be in a square box. While you can round the edges of the text boxes, not so with the art box. You cannot place a border around the art beyond a set square. Oh and did you want a border design for your card? No. Too bad.
You want to colour code your cards? Well, you can't have different text boxes different colours. All text boxes must have the same colour as each other. You want something other than a solid colour, perhaps a gradient or even a texture? Nope. Doesn't exist.
TEXT:
You have one font. That's it. You cannot bold, italicise, underline, strikethrough, or align left/center/right. You cannot change the size of the font. Basic functions of any program that uses text simply do not exist here. What if your card doesn't have a picture, but simply text in different ways? Well, you can have 3 paragraphs technically, but you cannot separate those paragraphs with lines, or other more interesting designs. It is all one big, square, solid colour, block of text.
SIZING:
There are two preset sizes of Standard and Mini. This of course covers every card size present in games today. While yes you can manually adjust the heigh measurement, it is unclear how this impacts the dimensions of the card, as you can only change 1 dimension. Not 2. You cannot accurately be sure if you have made a Tarot-sized card. or a square card. Speaking of sizing, you cannot adjust the horizontality or verticality of the card easily. There is technically a setting for this, but it is not clearly defined what the output then looks like or how it measures. It also applies to the entire set, which is not a bad thing per se, as you can always just create a second set for different cards. But still.
The fact is, for serious game designers, there is too much functionality not included in this program, or not enough content like symbols. There is no Steam workshop so no chance to upload new templates, or fonts or symbols, or anything else anyone would want to include on their card. If you're serious about designing, you will use Photoshop for the unlimited customisability which this program cannot even approach.
CASUAL GAME DESIGNER
So what if you're a casual designer and you want a quick and easy-mock up? Maybe you want to just do the pre-alpha for a new game you designed, or you want to add cards to Dominion, or Race for the Galaxy, or Shadows Over Camelot without a care for how the card looks? And you don't have the time or money to use photoshop? Well, I would ask if you'd rather pay $15-20 for this program, or $0 for something which does the same job.
MAGIC SET EDITOR
If you haven't heard of this program, look at it and try to use it before this one. I don't work on or for the people who designed that in any way, and I don't receive any money from them. But if you only need mock ups, then MSE is free and can do that. Sure, there is perhaps slightly less adjustment you can do, as you have to use a pre-made template. However, even on their website, the base package comes with a few dozen templates which all have more unique feeling that what can be designed in this program. Did I mention it was free?
CONCLUSION
I want to like this program. There is definitely a niche for an accessible, customisable card creator. But this program is not it. If you're serious about design, you'll use photoshop. If you're casual, why spend the money at all and not just use Magic Set Editor, Strange Eons, or a web-based card creator like
or
I really want to like this program, but it has no real audience. And the audience it will capture, it will only capture because of a lack of awareness of what else is out there which also fulfills their need. Card Creator has all the feel of a v0.1 release. It feels like all of these Early Access titles that are charging money, that have some content and basic functionality. But this program simply doesn't deliver.
Shame on the developer for releasing a program that has this little functionality for this sort of price. It may be all well and good to say "we are currently working on many of the features you have concerns about" but if you're saying that, then you weren't smart enough to realise they would be concerns in the first place.
Use something else.

this is the first review ive written on steam so forgive me if i get off topic.
i love the dd games. but sadly i never got to experience dd1 on pc (i played on the 360) so i cant compare that aspect because anyone can tell you its like two different games on console vs pc. however just judging dd2 as it is i have to say that it  is an awesome game. i love that it is a grind fest for gear ,the fact that you can run a map 100 times and get different gear every time is great to me. but ppl are complaining that it takes to long to get the good gear that they want.i have just one thing to say to those ppl,grind more. i think that the grinding is what makes the game fun. what would be  the point of playing a game that gave you the best gear to start. would there even be a reason after that to keep playing.
now onto the ppl who say that the game has gone p2w, i still dont get how they think that. so there are at this point two new charecters, ok well you can buy them ( ill admit i did but in a way i see it as promoting future content) or you can play and earn them. " but it takes to long to earn the medals to buy them". i see regular updates saying when the heroes will launch and its usually quite a bit in advance. so my advice to you is stockpile. when they say that a new hero is coming thats the time to start grinding and playing to get those meddals so that you can afford that hero.
now onto the difficulty. yes i admittedly am having trouble getting a good foothold into nm4. and for this some will say see its to hard while others will just say i suck. either way i dont care. yes it is quite a gap (and yes i mostly solo my games) but guess what. its a trial and error process. find out what works and what doesnt to advance further. if youre gear isnt good enough then play a level ,kill what you can,get what loot you can,and lose. odds are after a while of this process you should be able to get at least something that will help you with the process.yes it can take awhile and yes it can get frusterating, but thats how you can see if you truly want to advance,or if you just want to hang back. no one is forcing you to do any of this.
yes i realise this is more of a strategy/rant but its my way of helping ppl understand how i feel about this game and how i play. so yeah i love dd2. i love the grinding. the insane difficulty.the fact that you can buy or earn new characters. to me its just a fantastic game that will only get better as time goes by.

Good concept, but extremely short. The main story runs about 1.5h, and has 34 missions/maps. After completion, you unlock 13 challenge modes (katana only, speedrun, etc) with ~25 missions each (reusing maps), and an endless mode in order to increase potential playtime.
The enemy spawning can seem unfair at times, as enemies can shoot while spawning in, and spawns can be triggered on enemy "Wave" deaths. If you happen to be near a spawn, and looking away (as you just killed the last enemy in the previous wave), it's possible that an enemy can spawn in and kill you before you are able to turn around. Enemies and bullets are textured the same, so if an enemy fires directly at the camera, many times it's difficult to see the bullet/trail (especially important in melee only challenges).
Some minor issues with melee weapon hit detection, as multiple times I've had the melee attack 'this attack will hit' texture appear on an enemy, but my attack misses, probably due to enemy movement. I've also had times where I throw a katana at an enemy, and it sticks in the wall behind them (the katana is visibly through them, but does no damage as it is in the wall). I have also had a couple issues with thrown objects falling out of the world (which effectively ends a katana only challenge).
Some achievements are also currently bugged. While booting this again to check challenge count, I was awarded an achievement for beating the "red times" (set 'high scores' to beat) on every speedrun mission, after only completing 6/25 levels.
Overall, I like the game and idea, but it needs additional polishing and much more content in order to be worth the full $22 they're asking. I would say it is worth picking up when the price is significantly reduced (50+% or so? depends on how far you want your money to go).
Also, please take the "It's the most innovative shooter I've played in years" phrase that is being parroted around reviews and forums with a HUGE grain of salt. It's a viral marketing phrase that the game explicitly tells you to use. People that enjoyed the game are likely to use it as a novelty, without realizing that to an unknowing potential buyer, it's being taken as full truth.

Yeah... I don't know about you folks, but I don't play games I don't like. Especially not for that fuggin' long.

But seriously, I really enjoy this game, even made a Youtube video review/thoughts on style thing for it. I see a lot of people commenting how they don't like that it's so short, but this wasn't ever really a story-mode style game. The idea and the gameplay is what everyone was interested in. Depending how good you are, you can finish the story anywhere between 1 - 3 hours, and the story is pretty interesting I might add. All in all, I really enjoy this game, the gameplay is unique and fun, while the story isn't incredibly long, you can replay everything in a ton of different ways.
If you're not up for paying $25 for something that doesn't give you enough story content (or content in general), then I'd suggest just waiting for a sale, it's worth it.

After over 100 hours of playing it is definitely time that I write a review for this game.
I bought Banished on a whim during the summer sales, I played lots of Sim City 2000 during my childhood and I was after another game like that but of course at the time Cities Skylines was out of my budget, so after a bit of YouTube research I added this to my games collection.
When I started my first village I was completely lost, in fact my first four or five villages were complete failures. This game had a lot to balance up, a constant battle for resources that I always seemed to lose, it was very frustrating at first and I almost abandoned the game with about five hours playtime. I took to YouTube again and learnt the basics of making it through winter and keeping up with farming and eventually I made it past the usual three year mark and got a village that was actually growing and moving forward. With the town in full swing I was able to expand further and further, making smaller communities that would join with marketplaces and eventually with trading ports to bring animals, all leading up to the town hall which is great for prediciting resource consumption, housing needs and allowing the entry of nomads.
At this point I was spending almost entire days just tending to my village, I built a huge bridge spanning across a lake to connect up two distant communities and made both self reliant, with each year adding more houses, schools, forester lodges and so on. The problem is that if you don't maintain just one element of your village, the collapse is VERY sudden. One year my sheep got sick and this affected the whole herd, meaning I had to kill them all; in tern this meant that my tailor couldn't make the highest quality coats and since I didn't change the settings to a lower material, I had no coats stockpiled for winter, leading to many of my villagers freezing to death.
My newest village is going strong with around 280 citizens but everything lies in the balance, the further you get the more you have to keep track of, but it feels very rewarding to make it through a year without someone starving to death. I have to juggle my farmers around so that once a harvest is finished they are then pushed into the mines and quarries to retrieve resources until spring comes again, if I forget to change that option in time then that causes a huge drop in my food production, so yeah you need to stay on top of everything. My screen is usually covered with all my building objectives that need to be filled and the town hall stats that will show where to put my labourers.
That all being said, Banished isn't going to be a game you will return to every week, I could play for days on end at first but now its a bit intimidating returning to my town, that could be because of the stress of it all. The music can get quite repetitive but overall I did really enjoy the soundtrack, very appropriate for the theme of the game, but when you hear the music on start up everytime it can just get you out of the mood of playing, i'd put a playlist of your own on standby if you're going to play for more than two or so hours. I have been lucky to avoid most of the in game disasters unlike other players but that can be toggled to your preference. I agree with some players that there could have been a few more build options on top of what there is, more types of housing is something I would have enjoyed, but i've been playing without any mods so far and haven't felt the need (yet) to go in search for them.
Once you get your first successful town, the game is very cosy and its great to have the different map seeds with flat land or valleys to spice things up. You are going to need patience at first that is for sure, look up guides if you get caught in the lag of the first few years and that will help move things forward. The art style is quite detailed for such a small game and the camera feature that lets you cut back and forth to far apart settlements is so useful, in fact many of the shortcuts available make management of the game a lot less stressful as you go along.
Banished is a game I would definitely recommend to anyone I know. While it has difficulty options available to you, I would say this game is for people in that middle zone with it being a bit challenging for casual players and maybe lacking that complexity a more hardcore simulator player would prefer. Go watch some videos and add it to your wishlist!

Overall it makes a good first impression. Hand drawn sprites and backgrounds combined with soothing music are the perfect way to start a short break. As for the concept: The game seems to promote a SF novel, so I guess it contributed to some degree.
Well, that was short enough. So now the cons:
You move your air balloon sideways by horizontally separated zones, which have different wind directions and/or forces. The problem is that even the strongest wind accelerates you very slowly. But you know what? Those aren't the reasons why I don't recommend
.

I know this game has been reviewed a bunch, but I'd like to share my take on ol' Freddy and his crew. I've played a good number of scary games, but none have made me feel as helpless and paranoid as Five Nights at Freddys. When you start playing and watch the animitronics move around, it's one of the most intense experiences you can go through. Just sitting there, unable to move, and the fear of a robot animal sneaking in at any second to kill you, the fear filling yu with each second. Every time you look at the time, it feels like your chances of survival slip every more quickly as you realize it hasn't even been an hour since you last checked that clock. No other game has made me feel like turning on all my lights and huddling in a corner like this one. Now, this doesn't make it perfect. One of the big flaws for this game is the repetitive atmosphere. If you sit there for a few hours and play this, the fear just dies, because you figure out when your threatened and when you need to use that valuable power. And the big rule in horror games is that when you lose the atmosphere, you lose the player. With this in mind, I still enjoyed this game. If you want to capture what it's like to be near helpless while a bunch of murderous robots are stalking you, buy this game!

Okay now that that is out of the way, as most other people say, don't read anything and just buy and play this game. But you're still reading this aren't you? You don't listen to instructions. You go your own way, forge your own path, and end up deciding things on your own. Well that's fine too. I'll try not to spoil anything about the game, but I'm going to give my personal account anyway.
I'd bought this game on a whim because I'm one of those people the message of the game pertains to, someone who's interested in game design, but aren't sure where it may take them in life. I bought it a few days back while it was still under the just released price, and knew I wanted to play it through in one sitting, so I found the time, and started playing this at about 1:30 AM as I was bored and needed something I could do before bed, and ended just before 3 AM, which is where I'm now writing this review, because it deserves it, and I'm probably not going to sleep any time soon thanks to this thought-provoking nonsense.
The game itself plays fine with WASD and a mouse, like you'd expect. It's made in Source Engine, just like Stanley Parable, and Counter Strike. But it's not really a "Game". It's more like an interactive movie, and it goes on to discuss games as a whole, a community, a person, a thought. I can't delve too much into it without giving it away, but I played it through to the end. And, well, I'm glad I did. It deffinitely stands out, and with as much attention as it's getting, it will probably be here for a while longer, with more questions than answers.
At the end, I'm left puzzled, and my thoughts range from all over the place, to nowhere at all. I'm not sure what to think of this game, but I'm pretty sure I'll be thinking about things from this game for a while to come. It sets a pretty deep message, tells an interesting story, and does an all right job getting it's point across. I thought I could lay down and go to sleep, but instead I had to write this review just to vent out some of my odd feelings about this game. You don't "Enjoy" this 'game'. It's not "Fun" to play. But it is impactful, and bloody brilliant coming from the guy who made The Stanley Parable. The man is a genius for making two different and unique game experiences, and after playing both, I'm just flabberghasted no one's thought of this stuff before. It makes me believe that people CAN come up with new ideas, uniuqe, and not just borrowing ideas, making sequels or spin-offs. (Ironic, considering what this game is actually about). And here I am, I'm left with nothing but mixed feelings and thoughts, and that, in itself, makes The Beginner's Guide a win for me.
So, if you're thinking you might want to get The Beginner's Guide to understand what people are talking about, then just get it. Just don't go in expecting "The Stanley Parable 2." Because this goes in a completely opposite direction, and should be considered it's own identity. Sure, there may be video walkthroughts. For $10, your mileage may vary. But playing it is the best way to find out what it's all about.

TL;DR: Buy this game. Seriously. If you've ever loved 3D platformers, you will love this game.
The long review:
I can't remember when the last time a game made me feel like a kid again. I seriously got a punch of nostalgia, like I was sitting in front of my gamecube booting up super mario sunshine for the first time. This game was worth every cent, and I will buy /ANY/ DLC that comes out in a heartbeat.
The four worlds mix up gameplay in such creative formulas- If you think every level is just hopping around trying to collect items, you will be pleasantly surprised to find out there is so much more than that. From popularity contests, murder mysteries, boss fights, and a god DAMN stealth horror level (seriously, that was terrifying), this game mixes up the classic "hop and collect" formula in so many delightful ways. The level design is creative and the artistic direction is beautiful, seriously, the first time you go into Alpine Skyline your breath will be taken away- And it's not just for show, hopping through the gorgeous level is just as delightful.
The music suits each and every level perfectly, and the way the music's instruments smoothly transition as you switch areas without changing the tune is delightful. Some of the most impactful audio moments for me was in the memory-rift levels, where every time you complete a section a new instrument is added to the tune. It actually made me feel nostalgic for the level, even though I had just been in it minutes ago.
And jesus christ, this game is funny. The voice actors all have unique tinges to their voice to carry out their hilarious lines. The characters are all super lovable, the one that stands out to me is the Ghost... Guy, you'll know him when you see him, and all the Mafia men. Applause to the VAs, you guys did a wonderful job.
There were quite a few small issues, such as the quality of the character models of the two girls being a little awkward, some bugs here and there (a few frustrated me such as my hits not registering to bosses, but it's nothing unplayable), and those GOD DAMN BAND OWLS THAT FOLLOW YOU AND SMACK INTO YOU FHJDSLFS, but they don't impact the experience in any severe way (but you will notice them.)
Anyway, consider me a new huge fan of Gears for Breakfast. I've seriously already begged my friends to buy this game, and if you've made it this far in my review, please pretend I'm begging you to buy it too. Support this studio. This indie game proves to be just as fun as 3D platformers produced by massive companies like Nintendo- And that's amazing. I can't wait to see the 2DLC worlds and any future games!!

I'll make this unusually quick. As a game, this is really bad. The story is some nonsense about a Japanese mage invading the world, or whatever. Who cares. The controls are simple, the graphics bad, the sound bad and so on. If you want a good JRPG, this isn't it.
What this is, however, is a great way to get an introduction in Japanese. That mage I mentioned has a whole army of, uh, letters at his disposal, and the only way to beat them is to match the Japanese letters with the English ones. For instance, if the symbol for "ka" pops up, you need to pick "Answer", then select what you (think) the letter means. If you pick "ka", the enemy takes damage. If you pick anything else, the enemy won't. While this sound simple, keep in mind they usually attack in groups of two or three, and they really like to vary things around. So even if you are on your third "lesson" with the latest five symbols, you will still find the first symbols in the random battles you encounter. But this means that for once, grinding is a lot of fun. You are constantly getting symbols thrown you that you haven't seen in a while, so you really need to learn what they mean to proceed. (that's one reason why the game suggests you keep a notebook. Don't use it a a cheat-sheet (you won't learn anything that way), but it can be quite handy as reference.)
Now here's the best part: When I started this, I didn't have a clue about what each symbol was. It's just a lot of nonsense to me. But after ony two hours of playing, I have a pretty decent understanding what 15 of these symbols mean, and many of them can "transform" into other symbols by adding a " at the end. So the more you play, the more you learn. Of course, it's not like you're going to be fluid in Japanese after playing this game. Not by a long shot. But the game WILL teach you enough to give you a good starting point. Once you've mastered the basics by playing this game, you can move on to more advanced stuff. Read Japanese comic books. Play your favorite game with Japenese texts. Visit a Japnese forum.
So to make the mandatory too long, didn't read:
As a game, it's terrible.
As a way to learn Japanese, it's fun, cheap and pretty darn good. Don't get this if you want a good game, but DO get this if you are interested in learning Japanese. Especially if you are like me, and have tried and failed all sorts of boring text-books etc.

I didn't really enjoy Satazius that much yet i really enjoyed Gigantic Army so when Supercharged Robot VULKAISER hit steam i had some interest in it but i never got around buying/playing it but now that i finally decided to give it a chance i'm more than impressed.
The presentation is fantastic, It's just like a semi-cheesy japanese Sentai, It even has those big yellow subtitles which i found amazing, the music is great and the characters and art are very appealing.
The gameplay is really fun, You pilot the Vulkaiser robot which by itself it has a regular forward shot that when charged releases a Rocket Punch attack, it's really cool that it charges as you shoot, so you don't actually have to stop shooting at any point, You just let go of the button when the gauge is full to use your "Special" attack.
That's pretty cool and all but the best part is that you get 4 secondary pilots with smaller ships that pop up at certain parts of the stages so you can "Combine" with them, This adds a secondary shot on top of your regular shot as well as changing your special attack completely and giving you a unique smart bomb depending on which pilot/ship you combine with, Smart bombs refill whenever you combine with a new pilot so it's a great resource to your arsenal which you aren't punished at all for using.
You have a long lifebar which takes around 13~ (Give or take) hits which gets refilled a little between stages which makes the game very lenient when it comes to difficulty, also, each pilot has their own lifebar so switching them out after you take damage is something to consider, If their ship blows up during a run it can't be repaired anymore and you have to start over to get them back, this is a great way to make you switch out ships if you are constantly taking damage, but of course, if you don't take damage you don't actually have to ever switch out if unless you want to due to strategical advantage, given that each combination has their unique shot types and special attacks.
After getting the 1CC in Normal difficulty (There's 4 difficulties total) I can safely say Supercharged Robot VULKAISER is a great game worth playing, the enemy variation is great, the constant DARIUS homages are fantastic and c'mon this game has giant Robots shooting at stuff and there's so much stuff going on in every stage, how are you gonna say this game is not the jam? :)

Mankind is well and truly doomed for certain this time! Invaders from another dimension in another galaxy have arrived to take over, control, as well as enslave Earth! You, the most heroic man of all time and space, must pilot the Supercharged Robot VULKAISER in order to save existence itself from the greatest threat that could possibly be imagined in forever! Whether you grew up with Voltron, know your Ultramans from your Jet Jaguars, or just enjoy quality 2D shooters, there's something for you in this game.
This is a horizontally-scrolling shooter, but it's more of a danmaku than Gradius or R-Type. Even though I've been using the word "danmaku" for over a decade, I only just now looked it up. Apparently it means "barrage", and that definitely applies to VULKAISER. The alien armada doesn't mess around, as they'll throw battalion after battalion at you until your health meter is depleted. Yep, this is a shmup with health, and it can even be restored in-between stages. However, you only get one life and no continues. So yeah, you have just one chance to save the world, better make the most of it.
So how do you handle this situation? With a barrage of your own. The VULKAISER isn't all that effective by itself though. Over the course of each stage you can combine powers with your four best buddies. This results in increased firepower, different weapons, and screen-clearing Omega attacks. The option to swap partners presents itself at various points in the game. Sometimes you'll want a particular weapon for the next area, or the health of your current ally is running low. Yep, everyone has health meters. If they're wiped out, there's nothing you can do for them. Hopefully you can honor their sacrifice by saving the world. This lends a touch of resource management to an otherwise simplistic game.
Each of the six stages offers a good mix of smaller "popcorn" enemies, larger battleships, and a handful of mid-sized cronies. As with any other barrage shooter, you have a hitbox that's much smaller than your actual robot. It's rather odd to get used to, even for someone genre-savvy like myself. You'll adjust to it over-time, and the first two difficulties aren't too bad when it comes to throwing bullets around. The sixth and final stage does present a rather sizable jump in difficulty. In my last play-through on the normal setting, I barely eked out a win, even though I went into it with full health. For the most part though, you're going to be crushing loads of enemies with lots of firepower. It's very satisfying. The 70s aesthetics and music have their appeal as well, though admittedly it's lost on me since I never watched Giant Robot shows (Aside from Robotech but that's more Space Opera).
With play-throughs lasting just under 20 minutes, this game is on the short side. Much of the replay value is going to come from improving upon high-scores and attempting the harder difficulties. VULKAISER isn't a content-rich game, but neither are most 2D shooters. All that really matters is if a shmup delivers on the fundamentals, and I think this one does. The stages are fairly designed, the bosses are well-done, the controls are solid, and everything functions as it should. Also, I believe the shorter than average length works to this game's benefit. The action is tightly-paced and doesn't suffer from any wasted time.
I highly recommend giving Supercharged Robot VULKAISER a look.

This is the Second Tales game I played while the other being Tales of Vesperia which to me was a good game. This game; however, doesn't really add up to it. I haven't finished the game and honestly I really don't want too.
Combat gameplay.
Honestly the controls and gameplay of the game is really messy with bad camera angles such as when facing a foe and the camera goes right up to the wall of a building. Also the multiplayer concept of this game is jsut a sham by not explaining how to set up the split screen but also that the combat system doesn't really fit with two players. The combat system has characters sharing different aspects of an element and thus that an enemy can be weak against that element. Also the combat system has the idea of combining characters to use more powerful blast against foes that are weak to a certain element; however, this is where the flaw lies. Usually I would combined to have a advantage over an enemy while my friend has to combine into something and really can't do a whole lot of damage.
Story
Honestly the story to me was kind of exciting in the begining but then it becomes the whole idea about being the good guy and vanquishing the villian. There really isn't a lot of plot twists in the game which makes the plot very standard and being cliche. Characters to me seem to be very standard and like able with their personalities and their conversations which made them really good characters. These characters also have the same like goal that they want to save the world from the dark lord (except for two) which makes the conversation between them really boring and predictable due to the pattern of speech.
Overall:
If you are trying a Tales game for the first time then I would suggest buying a different Tales game for a console since I heard that the other tales game on steam have a lot of problems. This game has a lot of problems with the combat and to the rather simple plot which didn't really motivate the player to continue the main story but rather force them. I will say that it has the same aspect of other tales games but it just seems rather rushed at the begining with no tutorial feature at all to help you with these features.

Get ready to drop a bunch of time in this game because it is pretty fun.  Although there are a few game decisions that make me scratch my head...it still doesn't take away from the overall.
Here's the good:
Gameplay is simple and easy to understand.  After the Tutorial mission you'll be ready to rock.
I personally recommend that you stick this on the hardcore mode even for your first playthough.  Sure you won't be able to use cloning but if you put this on normal mode and enable cloning, it makes the missions less intense.
Loads of different loot and lots of fun possibilities such as having a % chance to summon a drone out to attack and Heal group when reloading.
Maps and missions are all procedurally generated and the direction of corridors are always going to be different.
Lots of nasty and nice surprises awaits.  You never know what the next room may bring as it could be a trap with loads of enemies or a room that will have a bunch of chests with fistfuls of money.
Here's the bad:
Your guys don't auto attack ... EVER.  Even if they are getting roflstomped. If you don't have your guy selected and you clicking on the bad guy to attack, he will stand there and get hit until he dies.  I understand that perhaps they shouldn't be shooting but IMO if they are getting hit, please shoot back!!
If your inventory is full and goes to a 3rd or 4th storage and then you purchase a new ship.  You get to keep your storage room to build over to the next one, but it will be completely empty.  All of the stuff that was in it will disappear!
If you are somehow acquire a new guy on a mission that makes your maximum go over the cap, you can't move until you disentegrate somebody.
All said and done, pick up this game.  You won't regret it.

First review I've ever done for a game.
It was good.

Video Review:
But seriously, I really enjoy this game, even made a Youtube video review/thoughts on style thing for it. I see a lot of people commenting how they don't like that it's so short, but this wasn't ever really a story-mode style game. The idea and the gameplay is what everyone was interested in. So they really fleshed that out.
Depending how good you are, you can finish the story anywhere between 1 - 3 hours, and the story is pretty interesting I might add. But the thing with this game is how much you can replay it, in so many different ways. Just talking about the challenges (which are ways you can play the story, such as a katana-only mode) it adds several hours of gameplay that's new and fresh. You can only play with katanas, or only punching people, or all these different challenge modes. It really adds a lot to the game. Then there's the endless mode, which I thing is pretty cool. It's the gameplay, the thing everyone wanted, just pure game. There are several maps (6 - 8?) and you unlock them by playing more. It's just pure gameplay.
All in all, I really enjoy this game, the gameplay is unique and fun, while the story isn't incredibly long, you can replay everything in a ton of different ways.
If you're not up for paying $25 for something that doesn't give you enough story content (or content in general), then I'd suggest just waiting for a sale, it's worth it.
