[TL;DR - ENG: The game is finally as much fun as it was back in early 2015 before the notorious June update, and is slowly but surely coming together thanks to publisher intervention. Updates are promised to come more frequently, and Bugbear could so far deliver the promise more or less. If you're looking for spectacular banger racing with a nice tactical touch on derbying, I strongly recommend to get the game. It's shaping up to be indeed a spiritual successor of FlatOut, as originally promised.]
[TL;DR - HUN: A játék végre ismét ugyanolyan szórakoztató, mint a hírhedt 2015 júniusi frissítés előtt volt, és lassan de biztosan végre összeérik, köszönhetően a kiadói közbelépésnek. A csapat gyakoribb frissítéseket is ígér, amit eddig úgy-ahogy tartani is tudtak. Ha látványos kontaktversenyzésre vágysz némi taktikus derbizéssel, akkor erősen ajánlom a beszerzését. Úgy tűnik, tényleg a FlatOut szellemi örököse lesz végül a játék, ahogy eredetileg ígérték.]
LONG - ENG:
This is the second time that I update my review on Wreckfest, but this time I'm doing it gladly, as the game improved a lot since my last review. Following the wreckfest of updates that were released during 2015 (pun intended), Bugbear got the game's original concept back on track by the end of 2016, and keeps enhancing the game ever since. As of the time of writing this update (July 2017), Wreckfest is again a great destruction racer with a light simcade physics, and a driving model which also works well with a keyboard (with assists turned on). WIP levels and cars are slowly but surely finished/enhanced, and new tracks + vehicles are also occassionally thrown into the mix.
The devs finally also started implementing gameplay enhancements that are expected to come fully to fruition with the career mode still in the works. Car customization and tuning is expected to offer richer opportunities, while the new car armor system will add an extra "strategic" layer to preparing for races: purchasable armor elements will offer extra protection against crashes, but their weight will understandably impact driving performance, forcing players to either find a balance between armor and performance, or build the car according to their playstyle. There are lots of opportunities in this system - I'm curious how it will turn out eventually.
While the car assembly segment has been greatly enhanced as such, Bugbear thankfully also streamlined the Garage mechanic by removing the unintuitive (and gameplay-wise, counter-intuitive) part wear and degradation system. Repairs between races are therefore now part of the past, which is great news: if you prefer agressive racing, you don't have to worry about part wear and tear anymore.
Tech-wise, the game is a mixed bag. Graphics are not bad, but after five years of development, it's frankly outdated. Cars look neat, the environment is generally OK, but overall there is nothing great in the visual department, save for the crashes and car deformation. The game can also use some optimization as well, but that will take place before release, as far as I know. The game is much poorer in the audio department: engine and crash sounds are OK, but ambient sounds are non-existent and the music library also contains one single bland rock instrumental. Here's hoping that with THQ Nordic stepping in as publisher, they may afford to license some rock tracks as was the case with FlatOut and Empire Interactive.
So the game is very entertaining, and finally coming together well, it seems... But after four years of early access availability, it should be.
LONG - HUN:
Másodjára frissítem már a Wreckfest értékelésemet, de ezúttal örömmel teszem, a játék ugyanis sokat javult az előző értékelésem óta. A 2015-ös katasztrofális frissítések után a Bugbearnek 2016 végére sikerült rendberaknia a játékot, ami azóta is bővül és fejlődik. E sorok írásakor (2017 július) a Wreckfest végre ismét egy szórakoztató destruction racer, aminek a fizikája kellemes lájtos árkád-szimulátor keverék, vezetési modellje pedig billentyűzettel is jól kezelhető (ha minden assist be van nyomva). A fejlesztés alatt álló pályák és autók minden frissítéssel fejlődnek, és általában újabbakat is kapunk az egyes update-ekkel.
Fontosabb viszont, hogy a csapat végre nekiállt a játékmenetet bővítő elemek lefejlesztésének, amik elvileg a szólókarrier bekerülésével csúcsosodnak majd ki. Az autók testreszabhatósága és tuningja gazdagabb lesz, mellettük pedig páncélzatot is szerelhetünk majd a verdákra, ami extra védelmet nyújt, de negatívan hat majd a menetteljesítményre. A játékosoknak így van meg kell találniuk az egyensúlyt a két vonal között, vagy a játékstílusuknak megfelelően páncélozottabb vagy gyorsabb kocsikat tudnak építeni. Kellemes taktikai lehetőségek rejlenek ebben a vonalban, kíváncsi vagyok mit hoznak majd ki belőle.
A Bugbear emellett viszont karcsúsított is az autómenedzsment vonalon: az új frissítéssel végre eltávolította a teljesen felesleges, és a derbis játékmenetnek is ellene dolgozó alkatrészjavítási vonalat. Személy szerint ennek az újdonságnak örülök a legjobban, így végre az agresszívebb játékosoknak sem kell aggódnia az alkatrészromlás miatt, bátran lehet zúzni, max. a jó helyezést bukjuk, nem a verdát. :)
Technikai téren a játék elég vegyes képet mutat. A játék nem csúnya, de öt év fejlesztés után kissé elavultnak fest. A verdák dögösek, a környezet elmegy, de a grafika az ütközéseket és a törésmodellt leszámítva nem kiemelkedő, és híján van az optimalizációnak - ez mondjuk elvileg a megjelenés felé még javulni fog az ígéretek szerint. Audiotéren a játék sokkal gyengébb: a motorhangok és ütközéseffektek jók, de környezeti hanghatások szinte egyáltalán nincsenek, és a zenei könyvtár is egyetlen semmilyen rockszámból áll. Hátha a THQ Nordic licencelni tud majd pár jobb rockszámot, ahogy a FlatOut-ok esetén is megejtette az Empire Interactive.
Összességében, a játék nagyon élvezetes, és végre úgy tűnik, lassan összeáll - de ennek négy év early access után éppen ideje is volt már.

Been squeezing some about 6-10 hours a day to play this. Not bad, but definitely not a favorite.
After putting at least 22 hours into ToZ, I can safely say the following:
- The battle system takes a while to adapt to, especially while playing with keyboard and mouse. I supposed it's a lot easier playing with a game controller, but that's irrelevant. It took me a while, more than 14 hours of gameplay, to finally get the hang of all the battle strategies. For example, I wasn't able to determine which element of seraph I was expecting while randomly pressing 1,2,3,4. It took some bit of "trial and error" to finally grasp which number each seraph is tied to. It's somehow very disheartening to say that you can't change the key bindings for this, so if you're bent on wanting to enjoy the game, you have to do some reading and experimentation on your own, by that I mean, referring back to the in-game tips, which I aren't too sure how many people actually do.
- The controls are choppy. At some point it's easy to make combos, while most times, the game doesn't respond that much... smoothly. Why aren't ESC and right-click mouse the same thing? I often find myself getting stuck because I couldn't exit the menu.
- I'm not impressed by the fact that we're limited to only two playable characters in battle, Switching between the two playable characters is an absolute pain. (I hate the controls)
- Lack of directions. I get that sometimes having too much spoon-feeding in a game spoils all the fun, but come on, a clue or two wouldn't hurt to keep the MAIN story going! For example, I'm currently stuck at finding the remaining two trials. Like where should I be heading next? I'm all for open-world but I don't like the idea of getting my♥♥♥♥♥whipped within a span of a minute by some high-level monsters in some unknown field / ruin because I wasn't all that prepared to fight them. The game gives more than enough clues to side quests but almost very very little for the main story. Sometimes you may find yourself struggling to figure out what exactly you're supposed to do. Your traveling companion / squire can only provide you with that much information.
- Titles: God Knows What Purpose They Served - same question that went through my head while playing Tales of Xillia, but that's another story for another time. Have I tried switching titles? I don't see a reason to. I stuck to the same one that was intiially equipped on each character because why would I want to dumb down their stats by equipping a new title? It makes no bloody sense! Actually, it would have been very useful if more stats are added each time the title proficiency goes up.
- Equipments: It ain't too bad. Just that the idea of Fusing Items don't quite sit well with me. Couple that with getting equipments of the same ... name at various levels. I would expect to get better equips, not going backwards.
- See that strange looking creature that looks very much different from the rest? There's always one of these in every field. The game provides little to no information on them and you would only know the truth the hard way when you thought that it would be cool to battle one of them. NOPE. AVOID AT ALL COSTS, until you think you're strong enough... then again, how could you be so sure?
I would still recommend this game to others, but only if you have tried playing other Tales games, most preferably Tales of Graces f, because that one is my absolute favorite. Otherwise, this would be a pain to go through with. Despite my many disappointments with the game, I still find it a joy to indulge in, because it provides a different gameplay experience (may or may not be a good one, but that's all relative). There are many flaws but there are also some parts of it that one can get used to after some experimentation. I still don't like the character switch during battles. I think that's my number one pet peeve at the moment.

Overall, even if you're new to Tales franchise, Zestiria is worth to buy. Heck it even get me hooked on other Tales game now.

First off, this game is absolutely awesome!
While I can't go into any detail on the story without spoiling something, it takes you on quite the wild ride. It's also expertly paced and not a single minute went by where I felt like I was slogging through filler content.
The gameplay is solid and innovative and revolves around the core mechanic of time slowing down when you don't move. In practice, the game plays like a puzzle shooter, where you start unarmed and have to figure out ways to avoid being slaughtered, gain weapons and kill all the red dudes. It's quite simple and there are often numerous ways to improvise and solve the "puzzles". You'll seldom have only one viable option.
Unfortunately, it's very light on content and the story is over in about two hours. Sure, you can play the game forever in endless mode or do challenges, but as far as
content goes, I don't feel it's enough to warrant the price tag. If it ever receives more content or about a 20 % price drop, I'll bump my rating up a notch, but until then I'd wait for a sale unless you absolutely can't wait to experience the game (and I wouldn't blame you for that).

This game is a great tool to kickstart learning Japanese.
I have tried to learn Japanese several times before with different methods, but I've never been able to stick with it. Most recently, I tried the Rosetta Stone software, but it's 'immersive' teaching style left me very frustrated. With Japanese being so different to english, I wasn't able to figure out much of what was being presented, and gave up quickly.
Then I found Hiragana Battle. I flew through the game in a weekend, and gathered up the motivation to give Rosetta Stone another try. This time it went much easier. Having a basic understanding of what the language is built out of, and being able to sound out the written portions made the initial lessons much less overwhelming. Hiragana Battle also threw in a few grammer tips (like how は is often used to denote the subject) which made a world of difference in my understanding.
Pros:
Characters are presented in well organized groups, makes remembering them easier
Well paced, new groups of characters are presented quickly enough to prevent boredom, but far enough apart that the old groups are sure to stick.
Interesting enough gameplay to keep engaged, assuming you like JRPG style party management
Cons:
Lacking enemy group variety.
No long-term practice. If you don't start using your new knowledge of Hiragana for something it will fade quickly.
Hiragana Battle made it much easier for me to start learning Japanese with Rosetta Stone, and I believe it would work just as well as an addition to any other learning method.

Game hub says I get to travel the world but it truly felt like, I've only been travelling throughout the country of Hyland and Rolance and that's about it. I could say it would pass as a continent however I dare to say, THIS IS NOT THE WHOLE WORLD OF ZESTIRIA.
At some point of your journey, you will meet wind seraphims which would little by little, albeit rather vaguely, tell our young Shepherd Sorey and young Seraphim Mikleo, how huge the world is but what do you get? 2 Kingdoms fighting each other and you're stuck between them. To add a bit of spice to that, there's a big baddy bearded kitty causing all of these.
What happened to the summons? What happened to exploring ruins/dungeons which leads you to cool boss fights which rewards you awesome equipment or something else for your effort? Our two beloved dorks, Sorey and Mikleo's passion is exploration so why is this not the main focus or at least feature of the game?
. This is not the same Tales of that a normal fan would expect of.
I have loads more to complain and no doubt, I certainly can write paragraphs, pages even, for each point but I'm not even going to bother writing those. I'm just going to list 2 of the major pain of my life while playing this game and tell you why I despise them so.
Keep in mind, these are just 2 points. There are more to cover but I'm going to stop here. I cannot lie, I have also enjoyed playing the game but most of the time, I have not because of the reasons aforementioned.
SO! If you're planning to get this game and you want to get into Tales of franchise, I suggest NOT to start with this game. I'll repeat it again, this is by far, the worst Tales of game I've ever played considering the fact I have 100% cleared every single one. However, if you're a Tales of fan and is curious whether to get this game or not, consider my words above and if you're all okay with that then sure, go for it. It's going to be a LONG ride.
I am so glad that I'm done with this game. Hopefully, Berseria, although set in the same ' world ', wouldn't be as terrible as this abomination and sorry excuse for a Tales of game.

If you're a fan of the Command & Conquer series, three small words are bound to get you excited: Kane is back. Indeed, so are a good number of beloved series hallmarks, like a huge amount of full-motion video and intense strategic combat. But Tiberium Wars is a lot more than just lip service to franchise enthusiasts, and you don't need the rose-hued glasses of nostalgia to appreciate its polish and intensity. It's simply a superb game that's fun and exciting to play both online and off.
The missions themselves are incredibly varied and involve a lot more than destroying an enemy base or defending a particular structure. You'll have to do these things, of course, but you have both primary and secondary objectives to complete, which include using engineers to capture certain buildings, amassing beam cannons to take out defenses, or teaming up with your sworn enemy to defend against alien attack. You'll be doing it all in a variety of real-world theaters, such as Washington, DC, downtown Sydney, and the eerily dry Amazon basin. The near-future take on familiar locales makes the intense battles feel even more thrilling, because the settings are recognizable and meaningful.
That's not to say the combat isn't gripping on its own. If you're usually content to turtle up in real-time strategy games, you're in for a surprise: Battles are intense and focused, and they give you little time to prepare. Like any RTS, you still need to build up resources, but it's a quick process of plopping down a bunch of tiberium refineries and power generators and finding the action, because if you don't, the action will quickly find you. Once you get past the first two acts of each campaign, you'll discover that Tiberium Wars' artificial intelligence is aggressive and resourceful, and it will take advantage of your strategic flaws. Don't expect to put your trust in one or two favored units, because even the most powerful units have noticeable weaknesses.
It's a rusher's paradise, but you shouldn't take it to mean that technological advancement and thoughtful strategy don't have their places. You won't need to deal with long, complex tech trees, and it makes Tiberium Wars feel somewhat limited in this aspect next to advancement-focused strategy games like Supreme Commander. However, you do have multiple powers and upgrades to earn by building various structures. The powers run the gamut from GDI's powerful ion strike to Nod's vapor bomb, and they fit each faction perfectly. As you use units they level up, making them more effective in battle, and in some cases you improve units by more unconventional means. For example, you can use a Nod warmech to destroy your own flame tank, and the mech will then spew fire in addition to its own native attack.
How differently each faction plays is impressive, especially with the new Scrin faction added to the mix. GDI units tend to be straightforward and powerful, and a huge force of mammoth tanks and juggernauts is a challenge to counter. Nod relies on sneakiness and smart use of unique abilities, and a small force of stealth tanks and viper bombers can cripple an enemy's economy. But playing as the Scrin is Tiberium Wars' greatest delight and challenge, since the alien faction is so different from the others. Your first encounters with the Scrin in the campaign are breathtaking, since even low-level units like buzzers look interesting and intimidating. In fact, the most threatening sight within the game is a fleet of Scrin assault carriers and their accompanying fighters. Yet while the Scrin have some potent units and other advantages, such as the ability to collect endless tiberium without building silos, they require a lot of micromanagement and intimate knowledge of each unit and structure.
Regardless of your history with Kane and his cohorts, Command & Conquer 3: Tiberium Wars is one of the finest real-time strategy games in years. It's also a triumphant return to form for the series, because it's more than just a graphical update--it's an exciting, well-tuned experience with enough that's old and enough that's new to thrill old-timers and newcomers alike.
Suffice it to say, you should play this game, and expect to be playing it for a long time to come.

Going to recomend this because despite some big issues this game still manages to be enjoyable and memorable.
The Good:
Big Party Tactics:
8 per raid team squad action in RTS works better here than anywhere else I have seen. I found they got the right mix of chaos with planned action and the controls are simple and intuitive. Their are tons of different setups for each class and playing around with them is the highlight of the game. Micromanagment in battles is actually pretty minimal which is a rarity for RTS games in my experience.
Well-Balanced:
No explanation needed here.
Pixel Art: Done well IMO so plus there if that's your thing.
Fun: It just kinda is and if your on the fence you will likely get a feel for everything this game has to offer after playing it for an hour or so.
The big issues:
Too much loot: Yes, even for a loot em' up it's just far too much to handle. Inventory managment is a chore that seems to grow exponetially as you progress which could have been helped with some more decent sorting or autotrashing options. The sheer number of items you come across means that even when you do wind up with a legendary or artifact class item the joy of it's discovery starts to get lost in the shuffle of shuffling everything on everyone all the time.
Too few actived abilities: The ones that are here are well thought out and somewhat interesting but the novelty wears off by the time you have raided your thirty mission spamming the same activable abilities over and over. For as many options for different setups and passives (which are nice and definitely on the plus side) it's too bad they didn't extend the same to activables.
Like most RTS games micromanagment is a big part of this game and the inventory overload issue means that goes about 2x here.
It feels like the research portion of the game could have been fleshed out a little better. I could only recommend this game to somebody who knows *ABSOLUTELY* nothing about Hiragana or Japanese writing. This game can be extremely frustrating if you have prior knowledge; the more you know the more you will be annoyed.
Most of the impatience comes from RPGmaker, however, as this is bare-bones as RPGs come. This coupled with the aggravating UI (you have to scroll through an ever-growing list of all the Romaji syllables to make a selection) makes it more of a chore than it should be. I digress...
I haven't completed it yet, and I'm not certain if I will. As it is, this game is a great introduction to learning Hiragana. It is paced out well enough, and the lessons are simple to learn. I cannot fault the game for what it does, because it does it quite well. This game WILL make you remember the Hiragana characters, as promised, but in the most aggravating way imaginable.
An RPG where you fight enemy characters (literally) by matching them with the corresponding Romaji. Seems simple enough, but the rate of random encounters in this game is obscene. Areas that take 30sec to walk through can take up to 30 minutes because of all the battle sequences. After finishing an encounter, you cannot walk for even 10 seconds until the next one starts, which is infuriating. In a game depending on classic RPGmaker level design (ie. crude mazes), the player HAS to walk around somewhat unimpeded to complete the level. This is impossible in this game.
Since you won't fight more than a few characters in each battle, you will be seeing the same 5 syllables pop up in every zone (for example, the first zone consists of 30+ encounters with only 5 "S" characters). You only memorize a small chunk of Hiragana at a time, while completely ignoring those that were previously learned. If I did not already know my Hiragana, this would almost definitely lead me to forget the early lessons.
The small bits of vocabulary you learn are a nice addition, but is definitely not a focus or even really a selling point. Apparently you fight full words by the end levels, so I'm going to try and stick around until then.
TL;DR: This game will make you memorize Hiragana in the most annoying way possible, but it is effective. Only buy if you know *NOTHING* about Japanese writing.
P.S. you're better off googling the different alphabets and writing them out yourself, it's free and much simpler to remember.

I can't recommend this as it is clearly not for me. Ever wanted to learn Japanese and not go through boring classes for it? Well, this game doesn't fully replace a class, but it works just about as well, if not better.
Hiragana Battle is an indie RPG made to teach you the first part of Japanese: Hiragana, one of three character sets in Japanese. The game itself is your simple turn-based RPG with a leveling system and the plot isn't terribly rich, but it's entertaining enough to spend hours learning Japanese with.
In Hiragana Battle, you will learn all 46 characters of the Hiragana character set (and its dakuten and handakuten variants) and a bunch of words from yes/no to household items and a few simple phrases, along with their Romanized (Romaji) variants to make it easier to understand the pronounciation as an English speaker. The Hiragana character set is surprisingly easy to get a hold of, taking about 14 hours of gameplay to learn, however I still find myself going back through and still having to look at my notes (which I very much recommend you do, especially on paper and pencil), so the memorization definitely takes time. My best suggestion is to do a single or two chapters a day, then grind out for a good couple days until you don't need your notes to defeat all the enemies, and then move on. I made the mistake of going through and just jumping to my notes when I found myself stumped.
The game gave plentiful information to understand how the Hiragana set is written and pronounced, and gave many examples of words and a few phrases, but it didn't feel satisfying enough
because the game gives very minimal examples for conversation pieces, but it's permissible since its purpose is more-or-less get you hooked and researching afterwards.
tl;dr: I give it an 8.5 out of 10; It's a very great way to get into the Japanese Language and learn a bit of it, but it doesn't have enough content to fully replace what a class/your own research would do. I very excitedly await the release of Katakana War, and hopefully a sequel after that for Kanji. It and Hiragana Battle will be worth the $6.99 each. I almost wish I didn't get it on a Summer Sale Price so I could pay full-price for this.

Supercharged Robot VULKAISER is a game where you take on the role of a supercharged robot which is allegedly named Vulkaiser. Now that we've gotten the obvious out of the way...
Basically, you're in a mech suit, you fly around a screen, and you shoot lots of lasers, bullets, lightening, and a couple other things at a bunch of other mech suits and spaceships. It's a callback to games like Gradius, where the enemies come in specific waves, ending in a boss battle. Repeat the formula two or three times, and you have yourself an entire level. Repeat that formula a couple dozen times, and you have the game I'm currently reviewing.
This is not to suggest the game falls short of entertaining. I got it in a Humble Bundle with a dollar donation, so I can't really complain, but it's not often I find something I'll actually play again in the veritable bin of indie games available on humble bundle. This game shakes up combat by offering you an upgrade every so often, which will augment your current robot into something with better weapons, which is cool. Boss designs are pretty interesting, and the music is intense enough to help gameplay, and simple enough to not distract. Controls feel pretty good, and combat feels natural - well, natural if you're a supercharged robot vulkaiser. You could do a lot worse.

Generally the game is interesting, and provides interesting action and fun for a couple hours, worth IMO 5$.
The game seems largely complete, however feels quite like a beta. There are a couple semi-major bugs around the main campaign (useless messages repeating over each other at the junkyard race, rift meteors hitting though the station killing unsuspecting trading player), unexplained necessary functionality in the otherwise quite simple controls of the game (in order to equip ships and hacking devices, you need to load them into the mothership, who knew? Also, afterburner using shift, required for junkyard race. A better explanation for equiping ammo would be nice as well) And the massive lack of detail and content in non-campaign areas. These deserve a special mention since apart from several well made areas, others appear extremely rushed. Among others, there are the capital cities, being nothing but a bunch of big blocks, unuseable or empty merchants in others, and enemies instantly respawning out of mid air.
The game world is static and non-reacting, rather surprising for a game describing itself as open world. If you want to preserve a feeling of immersion, stick though the campaign. Otherwise, you will meet NPCs set as enemy, neutral or friendly for no reason what-so-ever, friendlies and neutrals being so much as having zero care while you demolish their entire fortress or capital city, and a certain villian still being sitting around despite being supposed to have been blown up during the campaign. As opposed to the game description of millions of sectors, there are only around 65 visitable locations, two-thirds of them worth mention.
Generally the action is solid and the difficulity is rather balanced, but despite the rather large variety of weapons, ammo and ships, you will probably stick to the default ship configuration from the start of the game. Buying ships is pretty much impossible, as the campaign itself will give you almost no money, while the only other way of profit is selling ores, which is an extremely slow and tedious progress, and you will spend most of the gain on scavanging fuel and oxygen. (Worth mentioning, however, is that in a certain non-campaign location which i forgot the name of, there is a building completely full of "Treasure" in cargo boxes, being expensive ores) You will most likely be able to upgrade your engine and armor, though. On the weapons and ammo side, there isnt really a reason to not stick with the rocket launcher and the basic missle for most of the game. The weapon has what appears to be the strongest DPS in the game, contary to displayed statistics, since the cannon is supposed to be able to have more than double the rocket DPS. Not to mention that about every ammo deposit will have basic rockets to more than restore your ammo pool, unlike about anything else in the game with the exception of the gatling gun basic ammo.
The game largely sticks to its promise of keeping the entire game world destructable, with a few noteable exeptions of massive station building blocks, or, wierdly enough, astroids. However, to destroy anything that is bigger than, say, barrels or doors, expect to spend anywhere between a dozen to a few hundred(!) of missles. (other weapons are simply not damaging enough to destroy in a reasonable time) It appears that some of these werent even tested, as, for example, what appears to be a futuristic house has the explosion radius of the nuke back from the beginning of the campaign, and small, almost invisible wire has a solid explosion and massive debris to boot.
The campaign itself is interesting, and has its fair share of experience, and the GPS is pretty much god's gift, as without it you wouldve been hopelessly lost inside the stations where its hard to tell rooms apart from each other, although the failure conditions are completely mishandled and could be made better. If you lose a mission objective, you lose control of your ship, while the rest of the game goes as if nothing happened. This includes losing the pirate base generator, not managing to escape a self destruct sequence (noteable is that the explosion doesnt actually happen, so you are left staring at a completely intact station!), mining in fort valiant, or losing the junkyard race (despite not supposed to have any meaningful objective other than "show off your ego to this random guy!"). The end of the campaign also leaves you in a very distasteful cliffhanger, with the protagonist ironically saying "So whats next?", for the non-existant sequel or expansion. The developers also saw fit to display the end of the campaign at the very beginning of the game, no more, no less. Why bother building suspension if the artifact is already known?
Of another thing thats worth a mention, is that the save points could be handled better. They save the moment you complete an objective. No more, no less. Even if you are one life bar away from death, and an enemy is aiming a missle at you. Good thing that the game keeps track of all save points made, though, so you can load from an earlier point from the menu.
If you buy the game, buy it expecting a FPS experience, as, sadly, the other aspects are not really developed. The FPS experience, however, is solid and is worth trying. The 3D, zero gravity combat is interesting is fun, and the weapons feel statisfying while the surroundings are often destructable and/or explosive and is nice to interact with.

I have long been a Command & Conquer fan, starting with Command & Conquer: Red Alert as one of the first PC games I experienced and have since loved to this day. I will side with many others in appreciation of what Command & Conquer 3 accomplished; a return to its roots from the brief transitional period of Generals and stupendous execution of it, at that.
Command & Conquer 3, as such, uses a far different method of base construction and economy as compared to traditional real-time strategy games; rather than workers, it relies on the construction yard as both the player's nerve center and primary construction unit. Buildings can be placed in control zones after they have been fully purchased, and are instantly constructed when placed. The player's economy functions through tiberium harvesters, which comb through a field of radioactive crystals rather than attaching themselves to a resource node. For 2007, even though it recalled much of older times in the RTS genre, it was quite a unique game.
Gameplay-wise, Command & Conquer 3 is a frantic game of hard counters. Anti-tank troops will rarely be able to take on rifle squads alone, and machine gun turrets will lose handily to main battle tanks. Units can vanish in the blink of an eye without warning, be it from high-potency artillery or sniper ambushes on isolated units. Economy plays a central role, as well; the player who establishes a powerful economy quickly and staunchly will often be the victor, as Command & Conquer games have never featured a supply cap or need for supply structures.
For some, this can be a headache. The leading role of economy, knowing troops will often die even with your keenest intervention, and the balancing act of fending off enemy counters in such a fast-paced environment leaves little room for the overly thorough in high-stakes games. Even a strong commander will find themselves in an unenviable position should they lose the economy war, as the frustration of losing harvesters on a stressed budget and watching one's veteran units dwindle with each skirmish can hardly be called a calming state of affairs. Some consider the workerless method of base construction to be backwards and that the over-reliance on economy to decide games is detrimental to the skill involved in playing the game.
In terms of storyline, Command & Conquer has always managed to captivate me. It may be nostalgia ballooning the series' writing and acting beyond what it should be, but the plot surrounding the intricate game of cat-and-mouse between GDI and Kane, the corruption of the planet by tiberium (most pointedly, the chilling depictions of red zones), and the live action cutscenes have all served to inspire me on many different levels. Command & Conquer 3's introduction of the Visitors and Kane's prophecy of their arrival have all served to bolster my apprecation of the storyline - C&C4 kept firmly out of mind.
While it is unfortunate that Frank Klepacki did not return to grant C&C3 a score similar to the stupendous soundtracks of Red Alert 2 and prior, Steve Jablonsky and Trevor Morris lived up to his quality - if not necessarily style - and brought quality music to the title. Voice acting is more a toss-up, however; while most units offer fitting and well-acted lines, some - most notably Nod's two early scouting vehicles - are overacted to the verge of ridiculousness. Acting, while somewhat overdone in some areas, is enjoyable and mostly believable, and Joseph Kucan's applaudable return as Kane once more can hardly go without notice.
Graphics and general sound quality are another toss-up, however. The SAGE engine - used originally for Generals in 2004 - was dated by 2007 standards, especially compared with the Essence engine used by Relic Entertainment in Company of Heroes a year prior. While effects and asset quality are undoubtedly good for their time, the SAGE engine often struggles to keep up, and some oddities can occur from certain situations. Notably, infantry cycling through "take cover" shouts on death and strangeness surrounding some explosion effects, such as the ion cannon strike. Audio, on the other hand, sports some noticeable stock sound effects, but is otherwise well-delivered and masterfully crafted for the various atmospheres in the game.
Overall, a dedicated real-time strategy gamer could easily find joy in Tiberium Wars, and a dedicated Command & Conquer follower would be mental to let it slip from their library. With mod support aplenty (if not necessarily as accessible as previous C&C titles) and an official map editor freely available, it is hard to say that minor slights could prevent this game from earning its price and thensome.

A game this sickly cute shouldn't be THIS good. Though I have played for only a couple of hours, this game is remarkable in pretty much every aspect. The controls and platforming are very smooth, every time I've messed up was my own fault and I've never felt like the game did some kind of bs. The gameplay mechanics are best described as if Kirby had hats instead of copying his enemies ability, where you get hats that have special abilities that help you proceed in the world. The music is extremely catchy and beautifully made and I would easily put it on the same level as Mario 64. The music will change dynamically depending on your location and what is happening, and is done pretty much perfectly. I will likely end up getting the soundtrack for the game as well.
The world design and exploration are bar none one of the best I've seen in awhile, with every corner to explore having some kind of collectable or reason to be going there. The humor in this game is strikingly refreshing and left me actually laughing out loud not just breathing in and out of my nose quickly per the usual jokes. Though I wouldn't want my dad seeing me play this, I would recommend and share this game to literally anyone, as the content is not offensive at all and is safe for kids as well. The humor has a very ageless feel to enjoy, that's both snappy & witty with a bit of edge without going too far.
tl;dr Did you enjoy platformers like Mario 64, Bomberman Hero, Kirby 64? Have you felt a hole in your heart where you've missed an amazing 3D platformer experience? Did you feel let down by recent attempts at original 3D platformers and want a quality one? Answered yes to any of these, get it. GET IT.

First things first, you must keep in mind that AGFPro IS NOT a complete one-stop game development tool where you can create a game from beginning to end using building blocks like Lego. You will need to delve into Unity 3D and learn some programming and other skills to enable your world to come alive and give birth to your creations and finally compile the game so people can download and play it. :-)
AGFPro is a great tool for aspiring game developers to get to grips with level design, terrain manipulation and world creation. The DLC will also enable you to create stand alone "games"with the Fantasy Side-Scroller (where you can create a 3D side scroll platformer with enemies to kill and chests to loot for gold) and the Zombie FPS Player DLC (where you can create a fully fledged First Person Shooter with your own interior corridor levels where you can run around and kill different types of zombies). These playable levels can be exported so your friends can play and enjoy it.
For those of us wanting to get our hands dirty with "proper" game development, we will need to use Unity 3D in conjunction with AGFPro. This means that you can create your open world (hight map/terrain) complete with towns, atmosphere/fog/elements, etc. and import that scene into Unity 3D so that you can add NPC's, lighting, game elements and other trigger events, etc.
I love this program as it is a great tool for testing out ideas and creating individual game elements in it. Also, it enables me to create the terrain in a real time 3D environment and I can test it out on the fly in the editor without needing to compile it.
Go ahead and get it. This will be a great addition to your tool set.

======== Pros/Cons ========
+ Great artwork
+ Loot-a-holic drops, 8 tiers (grey, dark green, light green, blue, purp, red, orange, and teal)
+ Nice skilltree, multi tiers, upgrading both characters and your ship.
+ Great rooms system on ships, has more potential later on.
+ Love having multiple units, each class has 3 play style options based on their class relic.
+ Ability to add difficulty to missions for better chance at loot drops.
+ There's a few rerferences to other games, which is a trip.
(Apparently there's a cube recipe for a cow level? I would love to see a wiki for unique recipes)
= Music is alright. Not blown away, but not hating it either. Chill, sorta ambient at times.
= Matter / Fuel become almost useless over time with high-tier Research Point upgrade.
= There's a nice number of planets to check out, but see my notes on level scaling.
- Major memory leaks / fps drops: I'm running a moderate+ system (i5 with a 1070 GPU)
I'll drop from 150 frames down to 20 over the course of one map. That needs to be addressed.
- No Auto Attack + Hold Commands don't work: I would make more use of tactical pauses, but it's just better to set a 2x4 basic team formation (Vanguard tanks up front, Marines 2nd, Healers 3rd, and Scout/Eng in the back) and just focus fire on one monster at a time. Your units will just sit there and eat damage if you don't do something about it. Keep a finger on Q, you'll be babysitting that key.
- Automatic level scaling: I love leveling to zone, and the bosses should reflect that progression as a milemarker.
Nothing feels better than grinding hard, swooping solid gear then smashing a boss into next week. (It should be a 15-25-35-45-55, Final 65+ kinda deal.) This way, If I want a hard battle, I can throw on the modifiers.
Instead, Give yourself 15+ mins (not kidding) to chip away at each boss and micromanage their timed minion summons.
Bosses aren't a challenge as much as they are obnoxius.
Every planet auto scales to you, so there's no benefit or need to travel far out to find the right zone.
- "Company Quests" are just cheap low-tier item / fuel / matter grabs. Take your pick of the three: Save prisoners, research rooms, collect random drops. Rinse. Repeat.
- They need to change the color on their final item tier. Top tier items blend in a little too easily. Try black/red/silver striped boxes or somethin' different.
- Multiplayer is a nice feature, but it needs a ton of work. I had some luck with playing LAN, but I have heard horror stories for those not playing locally.
- Endgame after the warp: I watched my brother play past the final boss, but... there's... nothing.
No endgame quest trigger, no special company quests, no unique planets. Did we miss something?
Why include it if there is nothing but a replay of the same game under the guise of an "alternative universe?"
Edit: I made it to the "alternative universe" to see it for myself.
... uhhh. Wut.
======= Final Verdict ========
70/100
The games an alright time sink for now, and with some much needed fixes, it could be worth 15+ bucks.

Tales of Zestiria is almost passable if you enjoy Tales games.   Awful if you just like RPGs.  I am usually a fan of Tales games however Zestiria leaves much to be desired.  It's actually the first in the series that I could not bring myself to complete.
The plot is cliche, none of the twists that you would expect out a Tales game were there at all.  There are no betrayals, no surprises, no complex moral issues; and how could there be?  Every single one of the characters is introduced as a flat anime cliche, and remains a flat anime cliche. The only interesting protagonist is unfortunately a temporary character.(mainly playable in paid DLC no less). The villains are equally as bad, there are less than half a dozen named villains I could even remember. The setting is rather bland and the world's lore works off corny premises that leave a lot to be desired.
The gameplay is where the game becomes truly cringeworthy.   If you insist on playing this game, please play with a friend.  (3 friends would be ideal, but for some reason this entry in the series only supports two players).  The AI does not  recognize the mechanics of the rock-paper-scissors system of gameplay, making it sometimes easier to simply set them to block and do nothing.  The battle system has gotten rid of the aerial combat Tales of Xillia, and combat is now ground based.
Progression is also non-linear.  Leveling up is essentially useless, skills and stats are strictly tied to equipment.  This allows you to customize your characters strengths as you see fit, however it ends up taking a long time to assess whether a piece of equipment is an upgrade or if your shiny new sword will actually make you weaker.  This ends up creating a long grind for the correct skills, and skill combos to maximize the strength of your characters.
Graphically this game is only a small improvement over the PS3 games.  Even though Some settings are larger and more detailed than in past games.  The game runs at 30fps, and is fairly optimized, but it seemed enemies on the map were sometimes rendered at an awkwardly lower rate for some reason.
Overall Tales of Zestiria takes far more steps back than it takes forward.   Of the Tales Games I have played it has by far been my least favorite, as such I wouldn't recommend it to anyone but the most die hard Tales Fans.

The Howler Review - Raymond KT
Following the general outline of the Lithuanian novel The Hour of the Wolf by Andrius Tapinas, the game is set in an alternate steampunk version of Vilnius, Lithuania. In order to observe the goings on around the city, Antanas Sadabras, the legate of Vilnius, takes to his hot air balloon. During his observations, Antanas discovers that rioters are planning an attack on the city and that they have released automatons throughout the airspace as part of their scheme. With his precious city in peril, it is up to Antanas to stop the rioters and return Vilnius to normalcy.
The story is simple, straightforward, and is presented to players through minimalist snippets of text just before you begin a mission. It's not extensive and it's not complex, but it gets the job done. That being said, I'm a sucker for a good story, and I would have loved a bit more insight into what exactly provoked these riots. In all honesty, though, this games isn't really about the story...
I thought the concept of the game was fun, simple. Get to one destination from another. All of the artwork was done the tried and true way: drawn by hand on paper. HAND DRAWN!!!
Overall, if you like platformers with highly sensitive controls, you will love The Howler. On the other hand, if you’re easily frustrated with games in this genre, you may want to spend the money on something less confounding…like a nice book about political intrigue!

While not a game-changer for the genre, Vulkaiser does enough things competently to be an appreciable scrolling shoot-'em-up. The first, definite eyecatcher is the delightful homage to mecha sentai anime of the 1970s that suffuses the whole thing, from the cheesy intro and theme song all the way down to little details like those yellow subtitles that should be familiar to anyone who's sat down to watch anime in the VHS days. This weakens a little in the actual game, which has some pleasantly goofy but otherwise very unimpressive spritework, including some enemies who emerge from the background, but barely signal their transition into the field of play by simply becoming lighter colored. The projectiles are the usual bullet-hell menagerie, without any particularly interesting patterns or designs. It's a definite low-res affair and not much to look at.
Gameplay uses the "charge while firing" mechanic seen in some games like Hellbound, where after firing for a while you fill up a meter (with accompanying audio cue) and can unleash a minor "super" attack. This is initially quite weak. However, the one small novelty is that, in lieu of powerups, you can choose to fuse with one of your four teammates, each giving you an additional secondary fire and upgrading your super attack to something more useful. Each one is meant to have its own situational niche and style, and they do a pretty good job of distinguishing them. As far as I can tell so far, you get your pick of any of the four to start with, but it seems like, thereafter, you can only choose to take or decline a single randomly chosen one at certain fixed points in the subsequent levels. It appears levels give you one pick at the beginning and another shortly before the boss. Functionally it's still a fixed-position powerup system, but it does at least add a little bit of choice in your playstyle and strategy.
All in all, though it's decent, I'm not strictly sure I could recommend this for shmup fans at large, but those with a fondness for chintzy, hot-blooded old mecha shows might find the style enough to propel this robot into their Steam libraries.

I can't stress enough how many things are wrong with this game. Don't get me wrong, it can be enjoyable, but it's worthless.
First of all, dying. You've got two possibilities. Either you let the game work on its defaults and be worthless and boring or you get utterly annoyed. By default everytime you die you respawn in the nearest booth. You loose some cash and that's all. This means that there's close to none penalty for dying. You just kill the remaining enemies and go on, there will be even more money later.
Now what if you turn that feature off? Well, first you need to know that you can. There's no info or tip about it, there's no telling the player in the tutorial part, that player can turn that off. You have to open the settings menu and find it on your own. Then disable it.
At this point let me remind you this game is using GFWL system, which is the worst kind of RDM I have ever seen in my life. All the files must be verified and synchronised with the cloud server, this means you cannot access your saves in offline mode, autosaves go there too, and worst of all, they have to load everytime you do something. You're in a menu? Three seconds of freeze so it can verify if you're logged in. Opening single player? Another three seconds of the same. Opening loading menu? Another 5 seconds of downloading your saves. Then you load the game and wait for it to load.
And that's the problem. When you die without respawn "feature" you do not get the last save loaded automatically, or loading screen opened. No - you get kicked out to the main menu. Getting through all the verifications, loading the saves and loading the selected save, everytime you die you loose 30-40 seconds of your life. Be in a tough moment of game and in 12 minutes you spend 9 loading the game and 3 trying to beat that hard part. I really cannot say how very bad that is.
What next? The difficulty.
When I said "hard part" before I meant "one of the three moments in the whole game IF you've chosen "hard" difficulty and turned respawns off". If you didn't there are no hard moments since you just go back there and kill whoever killed you. If anybody killed you. Unless you're on hard it's hard to get killed.
Whole game is generaly pointless, worthless and meaningless, because player is godmoded, spoiled kid that never gets punished for anything.
Speaking of anything - you can't change anything despite illusion of choice. You either save or kill little girls, harvesting power from them(gruesome, isn't it?), you get less of it if you save them, but the only reason to save them is so you can feel good about yourself getting a little nicer ending where instead of lying in hospital bed alone, you lie in hospital bed with some girls holding your mutated, ugly, old hand. Game took me 12 hours on hard with respawns off, it's not rewarding.
There's nice plot twist, though. But that's the only good side of it.

MinerWars 2081 is a 6DOF space shooter heavily inspired by Descent, but quite a bit more ambicious in scale. The game takes place in the remains of our solar system, which after a large scale space accident got reduced into an astroid belt. The large astroids, which have space stations build in and around them, form the levels in the game, but unlike Descent one is not restricted to the inside of those astroids, but can fly around in open space as well.
While the game does have ambitions to be open-world'ish, they are at the current stage of development extremely restricted. Jumping freely around between different areas in the solar system is possible via a mothership that acts as start and end point for each mission, but as the game doesn't provide any side quests, so it is pretty meaningless to visit areas outside of the main plotline, aside from a visit or two to mine some minerals. The trade system that the game has also feels mostly redundant at this point, as while buying and selling is possible, none of the minerals give any useful amount of money in return and the rest of the loot in the game is just ammunition and health packs which are better used for their intended purpose then sold. Money is also rather hard to come buy, so a lot of the additional gear stays unavailable. The way the stores are placed is also a little weird, as they most often are in the mid of a heated battle, making a quick shopping trip feel rather out of place.
The game also has a rather detailed damage model, instead of just shields, the game splits things up into player health, armor, oxygen, hull damage and fuel. But as with the trading, it doesn't impact the game a whole lot. Armor is by far the most important stat, while player health only becomes relevant in a tiny few situation where there is radiation in the environment. Fuel is a bit of an annoyance, as is it's easy to run out of it, without a clear indication on how to get more. As it turns out, the engine in your ship can not only consume the rare and expensive fuel packs, but also a specific mineral and that mineral can be mined. Doing a short mining trip can provide enough fuel for the rest of the game.
The way the inventory works in the game is also a little confusing, all the health and repair packs one collects stay in the inventory, but they can't be used manually, instead the game automatically consumes them when the healths goes below 100%. This means your actually hearth is the value shown in the HUD plus however many health packs you have, but as the game doesn't show how many health packs you have, so your total health isn't easily visible.
On the control side the game gives the option to use either keyboard and mouse or a joystick. Unlike most other modern games, MinerWars does not provide any preconfiguration for the Xbox360 gamepad, but Getting a decent manual mapping for the Xbox360 controller is possible, with the exception of the menu and trade systems, which have to still have be controlled with the mouse. Once the controller is mapped the game controls quite well and fluidly.
On the story side MinerWars is suprisingly good. The game has constant communication and mission objectives that frequently change over the course of the mission, not just simple key collection as one might have seen in the first Descent. The story also goes across the whole solar system visiting plenty of interesting places and factions. All the characters in your crew get quite well established and the whole things as a Firefly-like vibe to, it's essentially a really good space adventure story.
Overall I had a blast with this game. The game certainly still showing signs of not yet being fully finished, but all the core elements already work quite well. The game is essentially the Descent I always wanted and never got, as Descent always fell a little short in one area or another, MinerWars one-ups the whole thing in scale and wraps it up in a quite entertaining story. While the detailed damage model is not of much consequence to the gameplay itself, it still does a great job as enhancing your immersion, as having your systems fail and blacking out from lack of oxygen is just a more interesting way to go then simply exploding. Having the ability to just dig through an asteroid is also a neat little feature. My biggest issue with the game, other then the whole not-yet-finished part, is probably that the enemies could have been a little more varied, as you end up fighting the same ships for most of the game, with little variation in weapons or size, but given the varied mission design and the great story, I didn't mind that to much.
The game takes around 14 hours to finish. I recommend playing on Easy due to the rather bumpy balancing in spots, the game does right now not allow you to switch the difficulty mid-game. Checkpoints are however plenty in the game.

I cant really say much to this game, because I wasnt really able to play it.
While most of the other players never got behind the loading screen or the main screen, me and my Coop Partner were able to open a Coop Lobby. But starting into the first mission, it was mostly a total confusing mess:
The controls are strange and not very movement friendly. Most of the time you find yourself helpless rotating around, looking for the enemy shooting at you, never having the feeling of flying through space. The game is full of stuff, that seems to be really important, but is never explained to you. It seems that you need fuel, air and ammunition, also you can somehow get new weapons and equipment. Also in Coop you instantly respawn with 1% health, just to get killed again.
Last but not least: Disconnects, asyncron gameplay and bugs. It wasnt very easy to maintain a nice multiplayer round.
All in all, we never got to the end of the first chapter and deinstalled the game. I know, many of the problems were a player-side problem of understanding the game, but it is so frustrating and boring, that you simply dont have the mood to understand it.
Beside of that it lures you with an open world, that simply doesnt exist. Maybe it is somewhere in there, but we never found it.

Wow. So this game really filled a niche I didn't even know I needed filled (phrasing).
I love this game. It has hilarious callbacks and references to other geek culture things without being hamfisted about it, and a lot of the references are subtle enough that I barely caught them.
The gameplay is super tight, it has what I could call a couple of quirks (switching to a character to adjust a skill by using one of your F keys makes you lose control over the other chars in your party until you reselect them) but I am almost positive that it's just me being bad at the game, honestly. The inclusion of a tactical planning mode makes it much easier to juggle having a big roster in your landing party.
The graphics are super presh. The characters, even the bad guys, are pretty adorable, and it almost (ALMOST) makes me feel bad when I nuke them off the face of the planet we are landed on.
Multiplayer is a thing of beauty, a couple of friends played with me for the majority of my playtime thus far, and it has been an absolute delight having similarly like-minded folks trying to tactically plan our raids, to maximize loot while minimizing deaths. A couple of friends complained of sync issues, but it appears that these issues are a thing of the past, because I spent 6ish hours straight in multiplayer without a single hiccup.
I was honestly so pumped about playing the game that I was having reading comprehension issues, and couldn't figure out how to trade with people in multiplayer (it is literally the easiest thing, click people icon in bottom right, click person you want to trade with, hit trade, or, PRESS P), but luckily enough for me, Alex, the producer of the game, came into my Twitch stream and gave us tips and tricks (that I am sure I just didn't read in the first place lol) and helped us figure stuff out, while he was sitting at the airport. Hell of a team they have there, in my opinion
The music. OH. MY. GOD. The music. I sat in the bar on my ship for about 20 minutes just listening to the little ditties that my ship band would belt out. So incredibly well done. It's hard to explain the allure of the music, it's just so adorably silly, maybe? The in game sounds are really well done as well, when you hit a charged shot (don't actually know what the skill is called lol) and you hear that big pulse before it slams into an enemy and rips it to shred is a thing of excellence. The only audio issue I have is that in loading screens, the audio hangs and stutters for me (and a couple other folks I was talking to and playing with). If that is the only issue I am going to have with this game, well, let's just say that 7.8 hours on record (at the time of this review) is only going to go up and up.
I highly recommend this game to anybody who like tactical RPGs and party management, as well as loot hunting, and transmutation of items into better items (think Horadric Cube from Diablo 2).

Supercharged Robot Vulkaiser is a really fun game even though I'm not too big of side scrolling bullet genre. As a big mecha fan I really enjoyed the homages to the different super robots of the 70s with their bright colours and funny looking enemy designs. That being said the game itself is quite short but that doesn't stop it from being fun.
The game consists of four levels of difficulty and the option of playing the launch mode straight away or practice mode where you can access all six levels and get used to the level before trying it on the launch mode. An interesting feature with this game is that bullets are able to hit your hands and feet without you taking any damage, Vulkaiser's chest is your hitbox and as long as it doesn't hit an enemy blast you won't lose health.
You have the option to combine with four different types of support units or face the enemies alone with the base Vulkaiser and its rocket fists. Be careful though, if your support unit is destroyed during a stage it cannot be repaired. My personal favorite is the Lightning unit since it can clear mass swarms of enemies and is great for boss fights.
Some things that the game can add to make it better include:
-A pause button, something that can really help since you're forced to play the whole six levels in one go.
-An options menu, this is a big one since there's no guide to the control keys. Luckily I played the Satazius demo and learned the keys from that but if I went in blind, I'd be absolutely lost in terms of controls.
-Additional levels or the choice to choose levels after being defeated. Whilst the game is short it is a bit frustrating to hit the last boss and be forced back to the first level and go through everything again before getting back to the boss.
I'm a big mecha fan and if you enjoy side shooters and giant robots then this game is for you. It's short and sweet but something about it makes me want to keep shooting away at hordes of enemy robots and their retro design.

A good chunk of my early play time with Supercharged Robot Vulkaiser was spent with a grin on my face. As someone who’s watched his fair share of old Japanese cartoons, it really is a well observed little thing. From the slightly cheap looking splash screens, the pompy music, even the loading screens and level title cards, it’s chock full of character. Then there’s the game itself, you’re a giant red robot who can fire his fists like missiles and combine with his co-pilots like Power Rangers.
It’s not all just for colour either, which pilot you combine with affects your type of attack. Take Rocket Kaiser for example, combine with him and your shots will be accompanied by powerful missiles, with the charged weapon essentially being a huge bomb, great for taking down powerful enemies, but a spread of enemies could easily swarm you. In that case you’d be better off with Needle Kaiser, a wide shot type, but she’s weak both in terms of armour and damage dealt. Drill Kaiser is hugely powerful, but her range is tiny, meaning you’re putting yourself in danger every time you attack. Thunder Kaiser is something of a mix, his standard attack has decent range, his charge shot is powerful, but his bomb is feeble
Supercharged Robot Vulkaiser has a peculiar kind of difficulty, the most notable thing is that it must be beaten on a single credit, there’s no continues to be had. Playing on the easy difficulty I’ve raced to the end of the game, once not even really trying whilst capturing our First Play video. The step up to the next difficulty level though made me hit a wall I’ve struggled to get past. I’m not sure what it is that’s stopping me from getting better at the game, it could just be that I’m not the gamer I used to be. I do sometimes feel a bit blind to the incoming bullets, but no more than any other shooter, but I think it’s actually more to do with the shame of Vulkaiser. Your hitpoint is fairly small, still easy to hit, but only a tiny part of your giant mech, but because you’re essentially controlling a giant line whilst looking at the enemy, it’s very easy to drag it in to incoming fire.
Supercharged Robot Vulkaiser is a little sparse in terms of modes. There’s the story mode and ‘training’, which is just the main missions there for you to retry. I’m not sure Supercharged Robot Vulkaiser is the game to spend hours practising, learning patterns. The training mode does allow you to complete stages though, opening up the next one you couldn’t reach in a single run. It’s not a bad way to see the later levels on the harder difficulties, which at least helps keep things interesting. If you are chasing score then it does separate them by difficulty, and I think the scoring system works by rewarding you for destroying enemies as quickly as possible as they appear on screen, so maybe there is something to be said for spending the time learning patterns.
In terms of presentation, the game has no resolution options. As soon as you hit play though you’re presented with the option to go full screen, which may seem like a small thing, and does cause some problems on a 2 screen set up, as it merely changes your resolution to match the game’s. It’s welcome though, we’ve reviewed a couple of games in the past year or so that haven’t had that option. One of the drawbacks though, and this is kind of funny if you’re not playing seriously, is it means that when you unlock an achievement, or a friend signs in to Steam, you can’t see a third of the screen. So if you are planning a serious run at the game, maybe turn off notifications.
There’s no doubting Supercharged Robot Vulkaiser is fun, but a lot of that comes from its charm. It does a great job of harking back to old-school anime, both in tone and theme. I’m less sure the game itself rates as highly or holds up to repeated playthroughs. Which is a shame, I really like the mecha gimmick of combining with the other pilots, and their strengths and weaknesses do add a level of strategy to the game, it’s just a shame the level design doesn’t build on it, instead feeling more like a shooting gallery. Still, for the price it’s a fun bit of nostalgia, hard to dislike, and not something you’ll have seen too often

Hey all,
I have only played about an hour of this game and even then only the f2p content.
some observations i have are as follows
the premise is excellent along with the execution (in general)
the graphics and lore are beautiful
the heroes all seem relatively 3d; not graphically but in a storytelling manner
the cover system is clunky in that if i am close to cover, i may not want to magically stick to cover, i feel a system like that of tom clancy's the division works well in that it is on button press that you enter cover but you can still use cover without sticking to it. This allows for more freedom of movement meaning that silly situations like being melee'd to death just because you got sucked in to some cover don't happen as frequently.
The game as it stands from what i have seen from the mission statement seems to be a bit shallow. You have created a world with a plethora of opportunity in lore and story development. Why not capitalise on this? my suggestion would be to create a single player experience with the option of drop in multiplayer similar to borderlands. you have a world that needs exploring and the restrictive tunnelling does not do it justice. to expand a little more on the multiplayer aspect, as well as a drop in/out option for the raiders, why not have it like dark souls where the antagonist can invade at any point? in an open world situation (all be it with loading screens like borderlands) stalking your prey as an antagonist would be fun i think and then have an antagonist ability to essentially call down air support and a detatchment of soldiers making it a small mini-dungeon affair.
I see so much potential but i share the concern of many players, i have been biten by the indie bug, both in a positive way; banished, northgard, mechwarrior online, paragon, eden star, but also in a negative way; castle story, clockwork empires, paragon "insert other failed indie game here". as gamers we love to be taken to new places and see new people that the real world cannot come close to, we also like to stomp our foes into the dirt hard because doing so in real life tends to put you in gaol.
I guess what i am trying to say in a waffle kinda way is dont make the mistakes of others like paragon who made a really awesome game but then did the following:
did not listen to player base
lost focus/vision of end product changing too regularly and without proper testing
shallow gameplay mechanics that did not maintain interest in long run
lack of new content (no i dont mean new heroes, i mean new maps, game modes, stories)
i dont even mind its not f2p for the whole title, but if you can categorically state that its not going to be just the satan spawn of a bad telltale series and evolve then i wish you all the best and will be spending soon,

When you have a studio that can make a game with good production quality but you dont know what exactly your game wants to be...or maybe you do.. Maybe you want it to be a cash grab
Since alot of people praise the characters in this game and its setting it could be much more than this.
The similiar thing happened with Evolve 2 and Brink,except their quality was worse, either way they were so focused on their missions and 1v4 mode that they didnt even bother trying to experiment with normal pvp modes besides these.
While these missions might be interesting to some they get boring after few playthroughs. And now the players are being charged 10$ per each expansion which gets you 4 new missions... Which is very small amount of content. You can do whatever you want with your money but for me this seems very expensive. However this can be a good thing too if you want to play only certain missions, or just have a better taste of the game.
Even with these issues aside the base game is very mediocre, its super weird to run and move, the cover mehanic is kinda messed up you have one weakish weapon with very little ammo, one skill and overpowered meele. Also the maps are just extremely small instanced halls, but game uses alot of cutscenes to cover these up. Kinda reminds me of mgs.
If you are playing as antagonist you need to get 16 kills and after you do, you have 50 seconds to wipe whole team of 4 in order to beat them. If you dont, you gotta repeat the whole process. Fact that you can use anyone as Antagonist kinda ruins the story for me but at least it gives you option to chose which ever protagonist you want to counter.
I had alot of server issues too like taking 5 tries to connect and i litteraly conected at end of mission, and also while game runs decently on my pc the cutscenes made me lag abnormaly. These issues however are most likely only on my end...
The cover art is really beautiful and i thought its some game based on mgs, since one of characters looks like Raiden. I just expected alot more from it on every aspect.

I recommend this game for anynone who likes gritty and unforgiving WWII shooters where no ammo counter or crosshair is present (Unless you play action mode), the realism mode is where this game stands out. The free aim system is a big plus, and the detail is excellent right down to the animations and weapon models, which even have adjustable iron sights. The implementation of recoil, and the suppression system work very well to reduce the effectiveness of a pinned sniper and spray and prayer types.

This game is the compilation of a breach of trust by Davey Wreden. His "friend" Coda, who seemed more like someone he projected a friendship onto, made all of these games, and they were
. But let's get to why.
The Beginner's Guide is a walking simulator of a number of small projects made my Coda, as previously mentioned. They begin innocent enough, but quickly take an emotional turn. The one true fact of this game is that it is a betrayal. The creator of these projects made them to express himself and have a form of self-therapy, as many other artists do drawing or writing. These artists sketchbooks remain hidden and the writers notebooks remain tucked away as a matter of privacy, and the fact that Wreden is capitalizing on his friend's work is not just a breach of trust, it's plain piracy.
Do not support this game. It is a critique and self-appreciating adventure through a "friend" thinking they're a white knight without understanding the slightest bit of the person they are claiming to help.

For some reason, I remember looking at the trailers before this came out and saying "This looks like it has a lot of potential" and boy was I sure wrong. Depsite that though, I had no idea what to expect from this game before starting it. Something about looked promising enough for me to purchase it. After beating this game, I admit that I regret the decision.
From learning how the world was brought into such an awful, there are so many contradictions that come from the explanations. You would think if the world was destroyed by a giant solar flare, the odds of surviing would be impossible, especially to make a comeback with advanced technology. Also you wonder they all survived with limited resources.
The story was strange and confusing, with you really not understanding much about what's going on and the ongoing fighting between factions. You don't really know your faction or why you're there, only having the main goal of finding the alien artifact and whatnot.
I liked the idea that ships were a little customizable and there were quite a few that you could buy later on but it felt like there was really no scaling. Combat wasn't exactly the smoothest ever when you try to manuever with the AIs and the ship controls. Sometimes it was a pain to a hang of it and sometimes you might hit the wrong button, throwing off your flying and aiming. Speaking of AIs... they were such a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Though they do follow you around, they do so with the intent to do everything they can to get into your way, especially if you are trying to dig through asteroids with missels. As far as I can tell, they're just there with no reason and don't get targeted very much.
Since they are trying to advertise the game Space Engineers I'll throw in my thoughts on why you shouldn't get it. Like several sandbox games, you are gathering resources and building... except there is no survivalist aspects in the game. Besides the threat of you crashing your ship, there is no challenge in the game except those of building. Cool, you can build your own spaceship but that's all there is to it. It doesn't even deserve to call itself a survival game.

When I first bought this game I was hoping I could step off my ship... so if you're looking for that it's not here!
However, this game does bring a certain addiction with it. The gameplay is relatively simple, your ship is flown in a bigger ship that travels around a certain area of space which is controlled by different countries or factions. There is a storyline to follow and is a decent one at that. Like every game I play though I base its greatness largely on the game play. This game is about what you can expect from any first person space shooter game with a multitude of upgrades available (from armor, to weapons, to ammunition type, engines etc...). Adding the ability to dig through rock or mine adds a different paradigm to the game (... sort of. You can mine and then sell the rocks/element types). There is a different drill though if you press "m" that just rips through any asteroid in your way. This is not only pretty cool to mess with physical features of the map, but launching a few missiles also changes the shape or hole size in the asteroid.
Although I personally like playing it, for it to really stand out and be something else and differentiate itself from any other game I can't really say. It is definitely a fun game to play, and worth a buy if on sale. The amount of control you are able to have on how your ship moves/rotates/displaces itself is quite notable in this game. If you really like having control of your space craft, this is it! Beware though, some players may find this repetitive.
RATING : 7.1/10

This game was pretty entertaining, for a couple of hours. I mean, don't get me wrong, blasting the living meatchunks out of pigs is great, but that's all you do. For the entire game. It's so repetitive and mundane... Oh yeah, sure, there are bosses, but the same concepts -- Even the same animations and sound bytes -- are re-used.
Oh, and one more thing, spoilers ahead.
The thing that tipped me over the edge -- and I mean OVER the edge of edges -- was the final "boss." If you can even call it a boss. The final level that had such a massive build up was literally a group of harmless, mindless "friendly" pigs. When you kill all of them in a mess of bloody pig parts, like the game has taught you to do for about 6 hours, you're punished for it. Then guess what, your game restarts!
