Cheese style restraunt. The game is full of easter eggs that you probably won't notice untill you've played it a few times.
The Animatronics
Bonnie: A boy animatronic, Usally the first animatronic to move. However on night 3 Bonnie is extremely inactive, he moves at about 2AM unlike Chica who will move move at about 12AM (The hour you start on every night) after and on night 3. He will approach from the left door.
Chica: A girl animatronic, most active animatronic past night 3. Holds a cupcake in her hand. The cupcake is the same one that is on your desk. She will approach from the right door.
Freddy: It's everyones favourite! Do i really need to say what gender the animatronic is? It will approach from the right door. Unlike Bonnie and Chica, Freddy doesn't appear in your door lights, he just sneaks into your room so close the door when he's in the East Hall corner
Foxy: A boy animatronic, will run to the office once he's left Pirate Cove. Close the door when he is out of his curtain but hasn't left the camera.
Rooms
Show Stage: The place where all the animatronics (excluding Foxy) start. The camera for this area is CAM 1A.
Dining area: Let's Party! The place where parties are held and people eat. Bonnie, Freddy, And Chica enter this area on the way to The office. The camera for this area is CAM 1B.
Pirate Cove: Not much is known about Pirate cove. Foxy is behind the curtain. There is a sign that reads "Sorry Out Of Order" and the curtain is decorated with stars and there are also 2 lights at either side of the curtain. The camera for this area is CAM 1C
Backstage: There is something about this area that is unsettling. There's an Endoskeliton on the table and the room is full of masks aswell as heads for the animatronics. Bonnie is the only animatronic that goes in this area. The camera for this area is CAM 5.

Theoretically, while using this game, I am meant to be learning Japanese and having fun.
I am learning some Japanese. I am
having fun.
The lesson sets are fair educational material, with voice clips and tips on writing the hiragana, which are welcome enhancements. The music is fairly good. As a game, however, Hiragana Battle combines the worst missteps of the JRPG genre into a single frustrating experience. Gameplay is clunky and slow, made up of grindy battles in which every attack can take upwards of half a dozen key strokes. You can also use the mouse, but the game isn't well-geared to that either, and you have to click on the hiragana in the tiny menus instead where they loom large on the battle screen.
Drilling the Hiragana by selecting (or better, typing) matching English syllables is a fine thought for practicing them, but every element of the interface seems designed to take as long as possible to navigate and use. Or more likely, they were the default settings of a sort of JRPG-maker program that the devs didn't bother to find a way to improve, despite the fact that they cripple the experience by inserting pointless user-unfriendliness into everything.
Quests and story progression are not special, except that they also are laden with pointless, time-consuming delays and lazy design. Obstacles appear and disappear without explanation to railroad you through puzzles and the game takes up even more of your time with unskippable dialogue and cutscenes designed to show and tell you everything obvious so that you don't get a chance to explore anything on your own. For example, there is a quest to fix the broken bridge (of course) with three nearby logs. You will know where to find them without needing to explore because if you so much as approach the bridge, for the first, second, or twentieth time, your guide NPC will helpfully and vocally wish that you had some materials to fix it with, and you get to watch the camera slowly pan over to where the logs you need to go get are, and then slowly pan back. Then when you pick them up, you are treated to an identical dialogue pop-up congratulating you on finding each individual log, despite the fact that they are right next to one another.
There is no way to skip or quicken the repetitive animations, cutscenes and dialogue boxes that quickly become extremely tiresome. There is, however, a hotkey to quit to menu without confirmation and without saving, so you can lose all your session's progress with the press, even the accidental press, of a single button.
I would love to have games help me learn, but when my blood pressure is screaming because I am too frustrated by abysmal game design to focus on anything else, I don't learn very well. Google Slime Forest for a more user-friendly and less insulting, albeit also less pretty, guide to Japanese Hiragana and Katakana, available for
.

It took me about a month, but this game has succeeded in teaching me Hiragana. It has everything needed for learning it, and it's really well paced. It helped with learning the correct pronunciation of each character, as well as showing how to draw it, as well as showing slight variations on what we might see.
For the pacing of the game, each "chapter" would introduce about 5 new characters to remember. It would go one by one with pronunciation and how to draw the character. You really need a pencil & paper to copy it down. Once I had my next set of characters, I would save & quit, and spend a few days practicing and memorizing these characters. Once I had them memorized, I returned to the game to continue playing, where the game would use an RPG encounter system to practice what I had remembered, and I would do this without referencing my notes. This pacing worked perfectly for me.
In between, it would also show some common words, as well as some basic Hiragana grammar and special characters to know about. My notebook has 2 pages full of notes. One page for the 70 different characters, and another page for words that were taught.
It doesn't do much in teaching actual Japanese or overall grammar of Japanese, but learning how to read & write in Japanese is a very useful first step. All this is exactly as the product describes itself, and it has delivered on what it promised.

Zestiria is a very polished, interesting, and flushed out game. I recommend it for those who are new to JRPGs but I just cannot recommend this game for those who are mainly RPG / JRPG gamers.
There are a few reasons for this:
1. The storyline is too basic. I've been playing RPGs since around when Kingdom Hearts came out in 2002. I've experienced a lot of stories, and it takes a lot to make me interested or throw me off when I play RPGs now. So for those who maybe have a few RPGs completed, this game isn't going to really pull you in. I haven't finished the game, but I've been able to pickup, predict, and understand most of the main events before they have happened in the game, which kind of kills it for me.
2. The combat seems both too complex and too simple at the same time. On medium difficulty you'll be able to basically burn through any of the floor mobs without even really thinking. But when you get into a boss fight you will slightly struggle and find yourself needing to heal a lot and might even need to bring come characters back from KO.
But, overall I cannot say this is a bad game. The voice acting is there, the character interatctions are there, the world design is very good. Also, the animated cutscenes are great. I mean, this game does a lot of things right, but the overall plot is just so basic and predictible that I just cannot get into the game. I find myself playing the game for about 30 minutes and then putting it down. I'll eventually finish the game, and maybe later down the line there will be more interesting elements.
Was hoping this would suck me in like Dark Cloud 2 or FFX but it just doesn't. Still, I'll recommend it because it honestly isn't as bad as I'm making it out to be. It's just that the story is the most important thing in RPGs because it's what keeps you interested and playing - you play to get more of the story. But I just don't find myself wanting to play for long periods of time to get more of the story.

The current content is rather small compared to a 20€ or 30€ game, but the 10€ price tag fits correctly with the content offered which even has plenty of possibilities for replayability, from gathering more of the 3 currencies available to customize your Raider the way you want to play it, to playing the Antagonist mode, a mode where you must stop the normal 4 team of players from finishing the mission making it 4 v 1, the 1 having the backing of all the enemies on the map.

You can pause and all, you have a few powers to try to mitigate what is happening ; but it is like using a glass of water in a forest fire. The scale of what the players can do is ridiculously limited, shooting, and healing are for most automatic on timers things.
You imagine when yhou finally build a crew quarter having more squaddies will let you manage things more finely.
But no : having more squaddies means the game just drastically scales the game difficulty.
Everything is scaled in a geometric manner : resarch is the same.
This effectively negates any evolution in the players actions and gameplay and pretty much kills any sense of progress beyond the WOW loot colors your soldiers equip. A very poor evolution.
- The tactics aspect is just for show.
So, your engineer can deploy a turret. Which you will do over and over again.
The medics have a pain suppression ability and a heal both on a timer.
The whole thing is just crazyly underwhelming. The available player actions are more of a sideshow to the automatic heal/attacks of the squaddies. They are something to keep you busy while pretending there is some control over what is happening.
But this control is just too much a fringe thing. The 2d aspect of the game combined with the lack of control of the action just gives the illusion of control and turns frustrating when you discover this does not get any better while levelling up.
It really is too bad.
Some inspiration over the gameplay could have turned Pixel Privateers intop a must have.
But as it turns out, the gameplay choices made are just uninspired, leaving a semi automatic pilot loot management game (which there is WAAYYYY too much, seriously, another reason not to have too many recruits as it quicly turns hellishly tedious), with no true control from the player over the situation it randomly encounters.
You will still have a good time discovering stuff in the game.

A real shame that is.

Gameplay:
The Long Dark is a fun game. If you choose voyager or stalker modes (medium and hard), you're in for a fun and/or punishing depending on how hard you like it. On the downside, sometimes I find medium just a little bit too difficult (but it could jsut be me), but that could just be because I was playing it wrong. The Long Dark isn't an action game in the sense that you can just pound down enemies, you have to be smart. Pilgrim (easy) mode is great for exploring the latest update's worlds, but seems to almost only be fit for doing that, as animals will simply run away, making kind of frustrating to hunt wolves, who would normally run right into your line of fire.
Another thing I like about it is that Hinterland has thought about almost everything. If you survive a wolf attack, you could die of infection. If you pick up a can of pork and beans to save yourself from starvation, you could die of food poisoning. If you go inside a dam for shelter from the cold, you could get attacked by it's infamous resident wolf. It seems the only thing you can't die of is stabbing yourself.
Something that I don't like about it is that it can be boring. I almost wish there was something like a deck of cards, a harmonica, or a guitar or something to do when you're stuck inside a building to wait out a storm. Another thing I don't like (especially with new worlds) is the navigation. Environments can be dirosrienting, and so it would be nice if there was a compass or a map somewhere.
Graphics:
Some people might think that The Long Dark's painted textures aren't realistic, or a little ugly, and maybe they are, but Hinterland still has done a good job, and the fact that they are painted does create some more appreciation than if they had used smoother, more realistic textures.
Something that I think this game really needs is a character model, which I understand, has yet to be made, but for the time being, it's a little awkward and unauthentic to be playing as The Invisible Man.
When raiding houses, things like broken props, scattered toys in a children's room, and chipped wall paint do sometimes help tell a story of their own (one of destruction, or course), but a little housekeeping (go ahead, take the pun) to do would maybe be to create a variety in things like pictures (you see the same picture of the same girl in different houses) or in cars (truck, minivan, van?)
Sound:
First, I would like to cover the soundtrack. I haven't yet purchased the album, but the soundtrack itself is beautiful, haunting, and VERY atmospheric. I was a little surprised and a little dissapointed to see (or hear) that it's pretty much only being used for accents, which is really a hit or miss.
-At it's best, it creates an introspective atmosphere when walking through the wilderness, and gives a shocking/almost horrified feeling when walking into a forestry outlook where something clearly went wrong before you got there.
-At it's worse, it's absent. No, really, I think that it could play more often, either when a wolf is nearby, or something, because what it creates atmosphere when it plays, and it creates dullness when there's a 20 minute gap of silence.
The game's male character is voiced by David Hayter (Metal Gear Solid) and the game's female character is voiced by Jennifer Hale (Mass Effect). They both do a good job of making your character feel like a real, living, breathing person.... until you start digging around containers for a while. When doing this, you start to hear some repetition in phrases when you find something of some value in a container, and it starts to sound like a soundboard. This isn't something to start pulling out hair over, but still.

pricing is subjective, but some games need the base game plus 4+ extra DLC in order to 'enjoy proper', I avoid this more often than not.

Interesting aside, I love Soulsborn because progress happens everytime you play, even if it is minute.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The above mentioned list demonstrates my situation fairly clearly I hope, I need a game that I can play within my hectic life, a game with quality that doesn't demand 4 hours at a time minimum in order to feel like that game session was worth it.
Pixel Privateers fits this bill for me perfectly. It's playable in 8 hour bursts of for a quick 20 minute mission. So for my lifestyle and if you are in a similar situation to me, it's a candidate for Daddy's 45 minute breathing time until Saul, Underwood and Bojack come back...

As a game does it hold up??
I love the idea. It's a little bit of a few genres I am endeared wtih. I love the ability to name my squaddies. My kids love hearing the stories of their little pixels saving the group or wiping out the bad guys with that new flamethrower. The gameplay is fine, but I find that larger squads require a bit micro management that I am simply not good at. There is a quality of life issue I have; My squad won't attack unless I order them to.
I've had situations where I'm in a fight and my squad fights the boss, once the boss dies or explodes into a horde, I have to manually target the lesser enemies, which are small that feels like an extra step that isn't fun. The larger engagements are usually fine, but my squad not defending itself because I can't find the enemy or I'm looking up from my screen for real life issues. It's nothing major but is apparent.
The style and presentation are good, Tongue in cheek full of references and I must say, almost obligatory nowadays.
There is also alot of downtime between missions as you consider resources, fuel and weapon loadouts. I love it, each mission yields a surplus of items that you can sell for credits, which are used for ship upgrades, having more control on the loot you have via being abe to purchase from the shop or buying more squaddies. The other options are like the Kanai cube/Hordordic cube from Diablo to reroll 4 item types, rarity for different items or rarities and finally broken down into matter, which is used for teleporting your squad to missions and reviving the little buggers should you die on normal mode.
All in all, this game is fun, engaging and with its own flaws (That could be patched out easily.... please turn on auto fire!)

Banished runs very smooth. The graphic is beautiful considering the size of the game. The game mechanic is quite simple, you will understand most of the game by finishing the tutorial. The achievements for the game are very challenging to get. The events and accidents that happen throughout the game are realistic. The UI is simple and clear. The AI villagers are quite smart as well. For example, in winter farmers will become laborers rather than idling, and if there aren't enough resources to build a building, builders will become laborers to collect resources. The maps are randomly generated from map seeds, so when you start a new game, you will most likely to start with a new and different map. The name of your town can also be randomly generated as well.
Nevertheless, for a single-player game, Banished lacks of the Steam Cloud feature which is needed. The background music and ambient noises, lacks in variety. The game hasn't been updated for a long time. Haven't heard any news from the developers for a while.
In conclusion, Banished is a unique city-building strategy game, where the townspeople are your main resources. Even though there are some flaws, Banished is still a very fun and enjoyable game. I would really recommend this game.

This game is excellent in almost every aspect of a realt time survival sandbox.  Having tried most of the others, this is the one I keep coming back to.  It is atmospheric, realistic (as much as a game can be) and immersive, especially is the interface and view scale perfectly across multi-monitor displays.

I only have 2 criticisms: the constant 'tabbing' in order to see how you're doing is a distraction and a pain - especially if you're fleeing for a long time.  Some kind of optional UI that shows the basic information would be great, even if it was just the bars showing warmth, hunger etc across the bottom of the screen.
The second criticism is that there is no auto-run, so moving long distances involves pressing 'forward' for a long time.  It actually becomes quite uncomfortable after a while.
Overall, an excellent game.  Just need an end objective of some kind - reach 'sanctuary' or survive until day 60 to get rescued....would be very exciting to see the odd plane / helicopter overhead and rush to get the flares out of my backpack...

You play as Hat Kid, a young girl who needs to reclaim her time pieces that have been scattered across a new planet. Along the way you'll run into many wacky characters, such as the hyperactive Mustache Girl and the contract-giving Snatcher. All of the characters are colorful and have humorous dialogue, leaving for a memorable experience.
The game itself is a blast thanks to the fun levels and great gameplay. Each world has its own individual levels with a different scenario, similar to Mario 64 and Mario Sunshine. In each world are collectibles such as yarn to make new hats (each with their own abilities) as well as relics which can unlock time rifts (essentially the secret levels from Mario Sunshine). There are also other unlockables such as color schemes, music, etc. Collecting things is a blast and doesn't feel like a chore, and Hat Kid controls nicely thanks to the fluent controls and camera. In addition to all of this, 2 new worlds and co-op will be added to the game soon.
My complaints are minimal; the hookshot and camera didn't need to be equippable badges, and there are some minor technical issues. Nitpicks aside I had an amazing time with this game.
is the perfect example of a kickstarter game done right; it captures the spirit of classics such as Mario Sunshine and Wind Waker while also feeling fresh for the current generation of gaming. A must-have for all platformer fans.

This game has the privilege of being one of only a handful from my Steam library that I've actually asked to have permanently removed from my account by Steam support.
Cashing in on the nostalgia for classics like the Descent series (all of which are vastly superior to this dreadful "game"), Miner Wars 2081 is a broken mess.
Everything about the game is just "off" somehow.  The scale is really weird and difficult to describe.  Rather than feeling like you're flying around in a spaceship inside an enormous space station, it feels like you're driving a Micro Machine around someone's living room; nothing's got a sense of proportion or frame of reference and the design of the space station interiors seems designed to confuse, with little in the way of landmarks or anything that might actually make it look like it could be inhabited by actual people.
The combat mechanics are basic and the menu/inventory system is a nightmare to navigate, let alone understand.
The voice acting is pretty poor and what little I could glean of the story from the opening mission made no sense, being totally without context.  After the first mission ends you're dumped into a world/solar-system map with no idea where to go next or why.  Pretty much wherever you do decide to go, some people will autoamtically attack you, but it's not made clear why that's happening either, or if any of the ships are meant to be friendly.
Finally, the setting is so utterly absurd that it does nothing to help this sorry excuse for a game.  The idea that anything on/around Earth could survive its destruction by the Sun exploding is total nonsense.  That functioning societies could spring up from the debris and even start building new structures in a scant few years after an apocalyptic event is the metaphorical icing on this turd of a cake.
I cannot urge you strongly enough - do not buy this game under any circumstances.

A wondrous, adorable, sometimes extremely dark, love letter to the "Collect-a-thon" genre.
Every Chapter is distinct in both aesthetics and level structure, and almost every single level introduces a new mechanic, be it leading a parade, gathering evidence in a murder mystery, or hiding from a shadow monster.
This game brought me back to being 8 years old and playing Super Mario Sunshine for the first time in the best of ways, it instills a sense that this isn't just a series of platform challenges with a thematic skin laid over it; this is an actual location, where a cast of wildly diverse and quirky characters have their own lives, and you're just along for the ride that is their wacky world.
As for the platforming, it's some of the best I've experienced; I was repeatedly shocked by the fact that things just worked on my first attempt, and that's the best way to sum it up, it just WORKS! Even tightropes, which are infamously tricky to land on in 3D games, if you go for one you'll most likely make it.
This game is an instant classic that I'm bound to replay for years to come, but I won't have to wait that long with New Game+, 2 more Chapters, and Co-op all in development, plus an ever-growing Workshop.

Essentially the biggest failure as a whole with development software altogether is that it is an illusion. Most of the people jumping at experiences such as playstation home and even pc gaming as a whole are left with unknown angst filling their bladders and an insane artsy feel and inspiration akin to seeing someone's great art and fumbling around for paper to get good or at least try their hand at making this sort of thing a reality for them. And what do they find in their persuits? An empty field or empty environment with almost no content to use and forcing them into the depths of the internet to find another thousand or so mods to play with, essentially learning nothing in the process.
In my hollow opinion, Axis game factory attempts to bring the same experiences that made you even look for software to begin with, giving you some familiar modifiers and utilities to use and place together in a sims like format, while being open to other objects and allegedly even character models. So the same time you're wondering why minecraft is all blocks or why you can't do this sort of thing here is the sort of emotion that would bring you here. And with a cheap introductory fee, why not right?
Well, you are right, What this game does is bring you an experience that wont necessarily get you to become a designer, but still allow you to get that thought on paper and actually see it in motion and use it in the same effect. Switching around from running between walls and editing your landscape, it manages to still be a game while also being your playground as software that does not limit you. It takes absolutely no time to notice this if you've been running amok for software that doesnt leave you in your seat thanking yourself you are not on tuition, because you just failed. Though if you look around enough, it states you can use unity assets, and I think that requires the engine and its assets.
Unfortunately that is the only initial con I have with it is that it was not wholly stand alone, so until axis game factory emerges and either can or decides to take itself a bit literally, It is more of a tool engine. And looking at past comments, This engine appears to be more of an extremely fan friendly filter of engine and design, like some of the mmo character tools and landscape builders, and then ports itself onto real software, so you can be taken seriously, I guess? And while that is perfectly fantastic for those who just want a briliant assist to make an easy game, those who know nothing and have been embraced by axis game factory may have just been running on a boost panel into the same software models they thought they were escaping by getting this. But to be fair, I have not and probably will never touch unity 3d unless I need to use the assets that bad, or my map is seriously god tier and I need to get it out there. Though there is a tool to export a map and let people play in it. Not sure if it requires the software or not. I need to make something I'm ready to share first!
Personally, I can't speak on actually doing or getting any original works in here because... well it usually takes software that places you on an empty graph or mentions software that costs way too much for those who aren't seriously dedicated to either making money or content and it places you in a wall. You look up a tutorial of a model that looks great. How did they even get a model that good? texture baking what? What's maya? Oh god photoshop, Using actual skin as a texture, cutting it around as a map. Fantastic! Thanks for telling me what I need to do, and even if you know how or where to do it, Or actually know where and what programs can be easily substituted. You'll end up running in circles and in my case, periodically discouraged after downloading a dozen gb of resources and still not being able to get your model to import to a program with the colors intact. And even if you did, it's not even yours.
That being said, Axis game factory brings the experience to you as a game would, With premade assets and utilities you can make your own or even use in a final product. As a blunt point I'd like to say that it may be enough to get your feet wet, just know that you'll probably still have to hit that wall where you have everything you need on the table and you're looking at a program that is telling you yeah I can do everything you want to do. The only way I can describe this game is predatory. It's grossely misleading - class action lawsuit misleading. And I don't use that term lightly. They compare it to Descent with a fully destructable enviornment, but it's more like an amateur Unity project.
First off, you need fuel. Remember those old Nintendo games where you had to constantly pick up fuel to keep moving? The ones where  taking just a second longer to get the fuel meant losing the game? Well, imagine that in a 3d enviornment while you're being shot at and you have no clue where the fuel tanks are. Do you get into cover (yes, you have to take cover in your space fighter)? Then you just used fuel and probably can't reach the next tank. Do you rush to the next tank and fight from there? Then you'll get your oxygen system taken out and die.
The AI always knows where you are and has pixel perfect aiming, even when you're trying to shoot back at a target no bigger than a pixel. There are hardened turrets stationed everywhere.
So some stuff is destructable. Tunnel through it and flank them? Nope. That uses your fuel. You HAVE to take the shortest route possible or you run out of gas.
Even better, if you're fighting outside, there is a solar flare every 10 seconds or so. And yes, it will kill you. So you have to spend more fuel trying to hide in a meteor cave (how does this protect you from a SOLAR FLARE again?) or try to dash through a cluster of enemies which while tear you to pieces.
On the odd chance you do collect some resources, they're just used for a really basic crafting system.
Bottom line - stay away from this garbage and the developer. They also made Space Engineers, and I refuse to give them another dime until they fix this game.

*spoiler free*
It's interesting for what it is, don't get me wrong. I played the entire game in one sitting and was thoroughly entertained while doing so, not once thinking about stopping. My recommendation comes with a huge amount of qualification, though.
Obviously, this game is a walking simulator. I don't mean that in a bad way, there's nothing wrong with that, but there's no denying how unbearingly linear this game is. If you're looking for an experience like The Stanley Parable, where there are multiple endings, paths, and things to try when replaying, you won't find it here. It's pretty much just holding the W key and occasionally interacting with the environment in a predetermined way. I'd like to emphasize that there's nothing really wrong with this, but since it doesn't encourage replayability all that much you'll probably only play it for an hour and half or so and never pick it up again. For this reason, I'd recommend picking it up on a sale, $10 is a bit steep all things considered.
Now, everything beyond this point is technically a spoiler. I don't reveal any plot points or revelations, but some could argue this is a game that is best experienced without any prior knowledge about the story. If you have any doubts, don't read on. Read another review or play it yourself once it goes on sale.
The opening to this game explains the story between the narrator (the guy who made The Stanley Parable) and Coda, the man who made all the micro-games you'll be playing here. It's definitely interesting, and I think the narrator does a fantastic job presenting the game. While the game is extremely linear, I found myself engrossed none the less due in no small part to the fantastic narration and believable storytelling. What you're playing definitely looks, plays, and feels like something an amateur game developer could have made, and that really goes a long way in the grand scheme of the plot.
But here's the most crippling criticism I have about this game. It's very subjective. Insanely subjective, actually. But I feel I'm not alone here.
I didn't understand the story. Not in it's entirety, anyway.
I'm trying hard not to spoil too much here, but this game lost me around the last 30 minutes or so. I was picking up pieces here and there, but no matter how hard I examined the information being given to me, I still couldn't think of a coherent meaning behind it all. Perhaps that's the point, but I'd be lying if I said that it made the ending less satisfying because of it. That said, if The Beginner's Guide was created with a meaning behind it all, I appreciate that not everyone would understand it. In a lot of ways, the idea of not comprehending the whole picture goes very well with the narrative of this game, so I'd be lying if I said it wasn't fitting. But personally, I didn't get as much out of it as other people seem to. To me, it came off as a bit pretentious, often coming off like it's bigger than it really is. But perhaps I just don't get it. And that's okay.
Don't get me wrong, this is definitely a game worth picking up and experiencing at least once. Just wait until the price drops a bit or pick it up on sale, you'll be better off for it.

I've been dabbling with Unity for close to year and have tossed a lot of $$$ on the asset store - a significant percentage on terrain assets and tools.  Had I known about the capability of AGF, I could have saved a lot of money.  Simply put, this tool takes one of the biggest headaches out of Unity:  that of sculpting realistic-looking terrains.  I have spent countless hours on creating, deleting and re-creating outdoor environments in Unity.  AGF makes it easier than pie.  The asset base is not very big yet, but for me, that is not a problem.  I need AGF to build my base terrain on, sort out my vegetation, my lighting, better-looking fog effects, etc.  Once happy, I can import my scene into Unity and add the rest of my prefabs to it.
This tool is a timesaver and for someone who constantly nit-picks over silly stuff like 'that mountain just does not look right!', AGF helps a lot.  The developers are active in responding and assisting with issues and I really appreciate that.  I certainly look forward to seeing how this product further develops and recommend the investment for anyone looking for an edge in their terrain creation.

I used to love JRPGS back in the day.  Old Phantasy Star games, Chrono Trigger, Skies of Arcadia, Terranigma, Final Fantasys, Legend of the Dragoon, Secret of Mana etc – absolutely loved them.  I’ve always been looking for games that can recapture that wonderful sense of adventure and silly melodrama, but to be honest these days all I want is something better than Final Fantasy 13.  Tales definitely delivers that, although not an amazing game, it is a solid JRGP which I enjoyed for the 30 hours or so it took to complete it.
Tales got some love from me for its:
+Interesting character designs
+Insanely good music (especially the trial shrines)
+Fun, button mashy combat
+Whimsical yet funny dialogue and banter between the characters
However, it draws some flak for:
-Bland, ugly environments a PS2 would be ashamed of
-At times awful camera angles during the combat
-A cliché and quite boring ‘messiah needs the magic mcguffins to slay the ancient evil and save the world’ story
- needs a mod to run at 60fps (ok i'm being a bit of a princess here coz the ,mod was easy to install, but it is 2016, and there's NO WAY a game wit simple graphics like this shouldn't be ready to go at 60fps)
Like I said, not an amazing game but all round a good JRPG.  Doesn’t live up to the classics, and I dunno if I’d pick up another Tales game anytime soon (i'm not into anime and this is VERY anime), but I did enjoy my time with Zaevid and pals.

If you're interested in learning Japanese, but are scared of the monumental task ahead of you, this game is an excellent place to start. Slowly you'll have gorgeous little hiragana and vocab lessons, and side quests will open that give you more Japanese teaching as a reward. Banished runs very smooth. The graphic is beautiful considering the size of the game. The game mechanic is quite simple, you will understand most of the game by finishing the tutorial. The achievements for the game are very challenging to get. The events and accidents that happen throughout the game are realistic. The UI is simple and clear. The AI villagers are quite smart as well. For example, in winter farmers will become laborers rather than idling, and if there aren't enough resources to build a building, builders will become laborers to collect resources. The maps are randomly generated from map seeds, so when you start a new game, you will most likely to start with a new and different map. The name of your town can also be randomly generated as well.
Nevertheless, for a single-player game, Banished lacks of the Steam Cloud feature which is needed. The background music and ambient noises, lacks in variety. The game hasn't been updated for a long time. Haven't heard any news from the developers for a while.
In conclusion, Banished is a unique city-building strategy game, where the townspeople are your main resources. Even though there are some flaws, Banished is still a very fun and enjoyable game. I would really recommend this game.

tl;dr - Ever played a good game? This isn't like that.
Insta kill moves on a rock, paper, scissors system is not difficulty, It's annoying. This is the same gripe I have with many games, killing the player intantly is only cheap and never fun. The grappling mechanic kills the player on touch as a cutscene killmove removes you from play so you can only watch your face get bashed. If the the enemy was behind you then, well, too bad, instakill. You only get 8 lives that recharge after a few minutes of waiting. The name of the game is movement to avoid these cheapshots, but character movement is sluggish with a wind up time for running and if you play a heavy character then you will be grabbed from behind and therefore become a liability to the team.
The gameplay is pretty standard with nothing too innovative as far as been seen thus far. If you've ever played Mass Effect 3's and Andromeda's multiplayer this will feel like an old pair of shoes. Comfortable, enjoyable but do you need three pairs of shoes for that? To the games credit the stages are varied with a progression and story inbetween but unless you have some attachment to the characters it doesn't really matter.
I personally really like the character design, it was the only thing that made me want to try playing it. But unfortunately it does not take what other games have already built upon and refine it. It comes with the mistakes of the past and a few of it's own.
If you see a character you think is particularly cool then you better click faster than the other players because it's a first come first serve system. They don't want multiples of the same character running around, which does make sense if you want varied gameplay instead of the meta pervading player choice. However, if your connection isn't stellar you will get scraps every time. I support varied gameplay but playing the same character four times in a row makes me want to eat poison.
If Mass Effect's multiplayer, Battleborn and For Honor had a baby: This.
EDIT: Also the matchmaking is really slow. It takes a good while before a group is found. It only adds to the frustration to wait to play a game with wishy-washy mechanics.
EDIT 2: The player gets to use the insta-kill mechanics as well, but only when the game feels like it. Even when you have the drop on the enemy and time the move correctly against the RPS system, the game sometimes just doesn't follow through and your character stands next to the enemy. Which then opens you to a pummeling.

is a 3D platformer inspired by the N64/GC era of platforming, specifically Super Mario Sunshine. You play as Hat Kid, a young girl who needs to reclaim her time pieces that have been scattered across a new planet. Along the way you'll run into many wacky characters, such as the hyperactive Mustache Girl and the contract-giving Snatcher. All of the characters are colorful and have humorous dialogue, leaving for a memorable experience.
The game itself is a blast thanks to the fun levels and great gameplay. Each world has its own individual levels with a different scenario, similar to Mario 64 and Mario Sunshine. In each world are collectibles such as yarn to make new hats (each with their own abilities) as well as relics which can unlock time rifts (essentially the secret levels from Mario Sunshine). There are also other unlockables such as color schemes, music, etc. Collecting things is a blast and doesn't feel like a chore, and Hat Kid controls nicely thanks to the fluent controls and camera. In addition to all of this, 2 new worlds and co-op will be added to the game soon.
My complaints are minimal; the hookshot and camera didn't need to be equippable badges, and there are some minor technical issues. Nitpicks aside I had an amazing time with this game.
is the perfect example of a kickstarter game done right; it captures the spirit of classics such as Mario Sunshine and Wind Waker while also feeling fresh for the current generation of gaming. A must-have for all platformer fans.

Axis Game factory (AGF) is an unique piece of software. Let me start by telling you right off, that this IS NOT A GAME MAKING SOLUTION. With that said the software can be used in one of two ways.
1. Using the included assets or those from the DLC (Zombie and Side Scroller)  one can make mini games (more along the lines of levels) and share them with people that have AGF as well. This is a neat feature and is fun to mess around but you are limiting yourself with this option. Of course this would be great for those interested in making games and do not want to go through the hassle of coding. For example I have a buddy who loves the Walking dead show. He has no wish to be a game programmer but using the zombie DLC him and his son can create fun little stages.
2. AGF can be used as a landscaping tool (terrain modeler) where you can create your landscapes and export them to Unity as a starting framework for your game. Using this method you can even build the file as an executable in unity and send it to anyone, even to those who do not own AGF or Unity. Importing can be done between AGF and either Unity pro or the Unity free edition. NOTE AGF uses some higher level textures that are only available in Unity Pro; your levels will still load in Unity Free but some features may be downgraded. For example Unity Pro has better water shades and textures than Unity free. So if you build a map in AGF that uses the water (pro) it will be downgraded to the standard water textures if imported into Unity Free.
Should you buy premium or stick with pro
The big issue between AGF pro and premium is exporting out of unity into AGF. With AGF premium you get an asset kit that allows you to export asset packs out of unity into AGF. Unity free does not support the creation of Asset packages. So if you are using Unity free you will not need this but if you have pro you may find this useful. SIDE NOTE the development team is tring to find a way to get this to work in Unity Free
Should I buy the DLCs
As I already said the DLC add some fun little playthings. I could see someone who wants to mess with game development but either do not want to learn or have not had the time to learn coding. One thing that you may want to know is that some (few) of the assets are locked so they cannot be imported into unity. The only real one that comes to mind is the zombies; AGF does not own the redistributing rights to those so they cannot allow people to use them in their own game. This is not a really big deal, since they can be used for play testing and level design in AGF. Anyone who is thinking about selling their own zombie game would probably want to have original creations anyway
Final thoughts
AGF is a nice little tool, something people at all levels can mess around with. With more DLC on the way I doubt it will get old anytime soon. The big issue is how much you should buy just starting out? This is really one of where the buyer is at:
Just wanting to mess around: I say buy the pro (standard) version of AGF, and maybe a DLC or two and see what you think
Someone looking for a terrain editor: In this case it depends on the version of Unity you are using. As mentioned already if you are using Unity Free you really do not need the Unity to AGF exporter found in the premium edition.

A wondrous, adorable, sometimes extremely dark, love letter to the "Collect-a-thon" genre.
Every Chapter is distinct in both aesthetics and level structure, and almost every single level introduces a new mechanic, be it leading a parade, gathering evidence in a murder mystery, or hiding from a shadow monster.
This game brought me back to being 8 years old and playing Super Mario Sunshine for the first time in the best of ways, it instills a sense that this isn't just a series of platform challenges with a thematic skin laid over it; this is an actual location, where a cast of wildly diverse and quirky characters have their own lives, and you're just along for the ride that is their wacky world.
As for the platforming, it's some of the best I've experienced; I was repeatedly shocked by the fact that things just worked on my first attempt, and that's the best way to sum it up, it just WORKS! Even tightropes, which are infamously tricky to land on in 3D games, if you go for one you'll most likely make it.
This game is an instant classic that I'm bound to replay for years to come, but I won't have to wait that long with New Game+, 2 more Chapters, and Co-op all in development, plus an ever-growing Workshop.

I'm not entirely sure who this program is designed for. It's basically a very simplified version of Unity, which lets you edit maps by deforming the terrain, and adding a limited number of assets.
You can then "test" your map by playtesting the map using a variety of pre-build "games". After building a few maps in this program, I felt extremely limited as to what I was able to create, and there's not much creativity when the assets provided are a few basic houses, some rocks, and some walls...
Judging by the trailers, I'm assuming this was meant as a beginner tool for children to design their first "games", I personally thought it would be a fun way to design creative, and in-depth maps with a large number of provided assets, and then be able to design basic games to play with friends. Makes the Japanese language a lot less intimating and presents each new hiragana character with ease. The whole format is friendly and encorporates learning a new language in a game - which that itself makes learning and revising seem like less of a chore.
This game is also good for finding motivation to learn a new language due to the pace in which you learn new characters and words in hiragana. Within 30 minutes I managed to learn the vowels to a point I felt comfortable.
Despite tutorials and learning sessions the game offers "Hiragana Battles" these battles pit you against some Hiragana Warriors (Which literally look like Hiragana characters) - in order to damage these warriors you must answer the correct translation. I am really fond of this idea because repetition is the ultimate form of revision; so just by fighting these battles you are revising!
This game is definately worth the asking price, pick it up when it is or isn't on sale regardless you will still feel like you have invested your money correctly. If you are a newbie like myself; or quite involved in the language - you will enjoy this game.
NOTE: It is best to have a pencil and paper/notebook close when playing this game and to write down the Hiragana characters as you learn - the game even shows you an animation on where to start the pen strokes, how to tackle the pen strokes and also provides any key information on how to execute the character properly so you dont create any bad habits that self-tought students usually make.

Great game IMO. Been waiting for it for a while and I can't say it let me down.
+ Loot amount. Greed: Satiated
+ Item stat variety allows you to really customize your builds.
+ There's a Horadric Cube that lets you turn loot into loot.

Intially this game has caught my attention even before its launch, by proposing a nice and complex Colonial (kinda) Era town building game. The basic concept is simple, a group of "Banished" people is sent to a harsh land, where they just have to survive, isolated from the rest of the world.
De facto, this is what this game brought up to the table, it`s just a town building game, there`s nothing more than that, just chill and see those little people thrive and develop on that given piece of land.
If you played and liked games like The Settlers franchise or Anno games from Ubi, this is a must play game. It is not  very beginner friendly due to a lack of tutorial, however, its mechanics are not hard to learn either, since the goal, aswell, is simple, you just have to SURVIVE, later on, once you get used to it, you may start getting into the "fancy" part of the game.
If, after some hours, you get yourself tired of the game, you should definetly try mods like Colonial Charter and New Medieval Town, wich add a lot of content, like chains of production and a bunch of new and interesting buildings and interactions. It is not an exageration to say these mods make a whole new game.
It is worth to mention also mods wich may change Vanilla mechanics, if you find yourself annoyed with them, like Aging or how Quarries and Mines work in the game.

SUPERHOT is a game that is addicting and fun as time moves when you do. I will add a TL;DR at the end
SUPERHOT has an amazing game mechanic where when you move time moves making every single motion count. It’s a very fun game but had a short campaign mode. In the game you are given superhot.exe by a friend and are told to try it out, from the beginning it is just killing random red enemies as you control time and allow yourself be look like you came out of an action movie where you are a special agent or something along those lines. As you head further there is a plot and it darkens quickly. There are also little side games and such you can access if you are bored or listen to a game generated chatroom (because why join one yourself). The levels are fun and interesting with levels of difficulty trying to dodge enemies and bullets from all angles. The main storyline however feels short and beatable after a not so long period of time. However there is also an endless mode, mini games, and challenges.
So SUPERHOT’s graphics are pretty basic but with the type of gameplay it contains it feels as if you shatter glass figures when you destroy the red enemies adding a special kind of satisfaction. The sound is very useful for being able to tell if you are being shot from behind or anywhere and has saved me a few times. I love the polish song at the credits, did not even notice the the developers were polish untill I recognized some of the last names and the song.
+ Amazing gameplay mechanic
+ Replays of levels once beaten
+ Satisfyingly violent
+ Addictive
+ Other modes and mini games
+ Full controller support

Here are some suggestions I feel would improve the game
- Expansion to campaign/story
- Future ability to design levels
- More weapons

It’s a shame how short the main story is but an amazingly impressive title nonetheless. I cannot however judge this game as not being good enough for how long it's taken because I was not a part of that process like some were so I am just evaluating SUPERHOT for itself.

Short Version:
Give the Free Prolouge a try, you'll either like it or you wont. A mixed mechanics from multiple 3rd person shooters with added new/unique aspects. A breath of fresh air in my honest opinion when all shooters now are fps and or "mobas". Simple but effective character kits that get the job done, if you know how to play em but at the same time says this is this character and what they can do, but more then just run and gun.
Long Version:
they're are several things to point out about this game-
1) The free part of the game is the prolouge (as stated on the store page), not a demo, all items currency and other objects are retained and accesable after purchase of at least one campaign
2) This is is raiders of a broken planet not (insert game name here), so dont tell people to go play said game instead, you could compare this game to others of course, but fanboy/girling about a diffrent game is not helpful to reviewing and aiding in others possibly joining the game.
3) Both the prolouge and the first campaign are just part of the game are just part of the game there is more to come
4) Need to pay attention to mechanics on missions not everything is just kill with a gun, several missions have parts where you need to execute a certain mechanic such as collecting aleph via melee kills one certain enemies to activate an obeject, failing to do so could not only prolonge the match but cause an antagonist and or npc's the chance to overwhelm the party. also every character uses stamina a lil didfently so learn your character. another item to know is the ability to respawn is recharged after hitting 0 if you hold out for the npc to get more aleph so dont leave the match thinking you'll loose in mid game.
5) Melee is a rock paper scissors system: all players, antagonists, npcs bassically have it, if you learn it and practice it, like anything else you'll get good at it like anything else, it's not op just mechanics
Pros:
-Unique characters: all characters are a lil diffrent from each other tho take from basic pen a paper mechanics. all have assests and defects to add to a team.
-Multiple mission goals/mechanics: Not every match is just mow down the enemy. there are capture points, boss fights, escorts, overload the core/bomb, protect an object/person, and mechanics to work with em in each mission.
-Customization: Tho limited as of right now you can customize a characters kit or load out to slightly change their play style to better suit your's via in game currency. (side  note there are skins unlockable via real currancy as of the moment)
-Antagonist mode: Allows you to play against a party as the villian/enemy via the characters you have unlocked, gives a diffrent perspective on each mission, but is double edged. it both feels good to take down an enemy player amongts the npc hoards and boss battles, but can also be a challange if they are not only good but smart adding an extra level of difficulty to a level both new or old.
-Interesting story: Tho limited at the moment if you read, watch and pay attention to not only the ciniematics but the logs in the universe tab, it gives alot of insight to the lore of the game that is quit capatavating in my opinion.
-Style: Both serious and humorius. the art syle remind my a lil of a gorillaz like design for some of the characters which is nice. these are not your typicall front page models  with guns you find is most games and movies now a days, theyre rough n tough tryin to survive on a broken planet. the mix of scifi, mystic (tho only show breifly), and ancient tech is a nice blend upon the man made structures to the decaying lands and and abandoned ruins of this.
-In an out: can basically can just jump in play a few matches (depeding on que and completion time) and jump out
Cons
-Low pop (currently)/que times: dispite several other reviews matchmaking is "working" as of writing this review. in my experience it takes 3-17 min to get a match/team depending on the time of day, if solo, in a party, and the map, and antagonist que in too. but people do leave ques, lobby, mid match due to either being afk thinking they'll lose (both on antagonist and raiders side), disconnects and such. at the moment the fastest is the prolouge as its free and where most of the current pop will be, but latley ppl have been expanding to the the campain.
-Antagonist mode: tho i truly do enjoy this aspect of the game as it not only adds an extra level of difficulty for the raiders side depending on the player, if said player leaves it's an automatic win which is double edged, as with current pop ques may be long so if you dont "complete" the mission you dont progress even tho you won the mission due to the antagonist leaving. you'll also need to level up your antagonist rank to build certain if not all weapons as of writing this review.
-No co-op que. it'd be nice to just que up with your party wether its 2,3, or full with out having to match for the missing slots, or just to play with out the woory of an antagonist sometimes.
-short: tho the content is repeatable (an antagonists make each match a lil different), for me it as deffinetly left me wanting more, not only in story but in missions, to raid more.
-communication: no real ingame chat or speak currently implemented to communicate more detailed items, or just to chat. only a sytem of calls/shouts/signals and emotes.
mixed/misc items
controls: it takes a lil geting used to and seem a lil odd at first, but it does flow nicley once you get used to em, especially on a gamepad/controller in my opinion.
rewards: at the end of the mission u get 3-4 items every time win or lose. x amount of factions, x amount of character points, x amount of gold, and a blue print depending on how the party did. the thing is you have to choose 1, and if 1 or more players choose the the same item it's either split equally or if its the blue print it spins the bottle and who ever it lands on gets it. i both like an dislike this as it make it a lil realistic as its sayin this is what you all go split it amongs your selves, but can also cause the grind to lengthen.
Campaigns released seperetly: though the over all current purchase of all pipline season 2017 campains amount to 40$ or less if u only buy parts at 10$ per, the inital release of just the proluge and 1st campaign has left me wanting more, not later but now. but at the same time depending on reviews and feed back via this first campaign it could provide the developers a chance to tweek the upcomping portions in part instead of the entire game as a whole.
overall in my opinion it's a good game that has alot of potential, mixing alot of aspects of several other 3rd person shooters of the same genre while adding it's own mix, and i'd like to see where it goes.

I won't recommend it as it still has a fair number of problems to be considered as early access state.
- Low fps even in the main menu, low fps while in game. Making all low ends or mid ends computer unable to play smoothly and this cause problems to enjoy the game fully.
- High usage of memory even though a game like this shouldn't.
- Multiplayer is not stable, constantly out of sync even with good and stable internet.
- Multiple bugs such as falling through the elevator, unable to attack, target enemies or move, enemies constantly being teleported around like a ragdoll. (This problems mainly occured in multiplayer so it might be out of sync problems instead of game.)
- Even after the lastest patch v1.0.1, only rarely the crew will auto attack, otherwise they would just stand there being attacked and die like an idiot.
- Multiplayer should allow other players to view planets and market places information. Otherwise making viewing the map fairly useless except the host.
- Bugs even in single player such as unable to use elevator or opening doors, etc.
- There's this system where you will encounter enemies boarding your ship and you have to fight them off but it's so boring. The turrets and traps you put are just plain boring, only adding damage and thats all regardless what of you put. No point planning at all.
- Sometimes, tools are unable to be used when not put on auto-used.
- Characters falling through the fall and having a seizure teleporting up and down when falling off a elevator. (Likely a bug)
Alot of problems mainly happens in multiplayer. Fps is a huge problemsthough. Having to keep spamming right click to make sure your crew attack is also problem and really take a chunk of enjoyment away.
So far the planets only have a few background enviroments but with a number of different weapons which is nice but enemies not so much. Enemies either has gun or melee weapons or cyborgs. I only fought a few bosses but all of them is the same stupid thing. Another reason which should be early access, currently from my point of view, only allows for 15 - 20 hours of gameplay unless you planning on replaying the same content again and again or collecting better gear for your crew.
I enjoyed the game in the first few hours but after realising the problems it has with the game and multiplayer, i find it hard to continue on anymore. Low fps should be fixed for a game like this, minimum system requirement is not at all accurate at all. Multiplayer should be in early access or beta testing as there's constant problems with online play.
For now i can't really say i would recommend until most problems is fixed or patched. Looks like a fun concept but the co-op experience been awful so far.
TLDR: Buy it if you're planning on playing it alone and doesn't mind constantly playing it like an ARPG. Multiplayer has a number of problems which would take away the enjoyment. Get starbound if you're looking for a similar game.
UPDATE: I just realised that the gameplay is quite boring actually, the game has a element called RTS which makes you plan before making decisions and actions but so far it's worst than a ARPG. Constant spamming of right click, thats all. The more i think, the more flaws i find with the game. Honestly, even without the multiplayer problems, it should definitely be in early access.

Let me start this review by mentioning that I am a longtime player of FPS games and a veteran of both Stalingrad and Iwo Jima (I also fought at Ypres in 1917 as part of the British XVIII Corps, but that isn't important right now). That being said, I must say I find this video game (here on referred to as 'vidya gemez' or simply 'gemez') to be highly unrealistic and ultimately disappointing for a variety of reasons, many due to the purported 'realism' that the game advertises.
First of all, the weapons. I have never encountered such ridiculousness, except perhaps in the video game Mario 64 which I found also to be rather lacking (I mean, seriously Mario? Have you even been to a range?).  The primary problem with the weapons in this vidya gemez come down to problems with realism. I served as a weapons tester in the US Army from 1941-1953 (damn cowards kicked me out for smoking crack) and I can state with authority that the recoil system in the gemez is, for lack of a better word,  whack. I've fired the M2 Kugelringer many times at minorities trespassing on my property, and I can safely say that it does not have the huge amounts of recoil this vidya gemez applies. Nor does the gemez accurately simulate the sheer uselessness of 9mm in a self-defence setting. I have fired many 9mm machine gats (I spent 3 years as part of the Crips in the early 1990s) and I have witnessed first-hand the lack of damage it inflicts. In fact, I have actually seen 9mm heal people by cauterising the wounds. In this regard, the video game Killing Floor portrays the 9mm submachine gun perfectly.
However, these problems would be forgiven if it wasn't for the god-awful gameplay. I quickscoped and dolphin-dived my way across the Eastern Front during the war, yet this gemez does not allow for such historical gunplay? Furthermore, the cover system is just cray - I never took cover once during my time in the military, and I don't know of anybody who did. Trying to camp in cover was a quick way to get hardscoped or even kicked by a penal batallion. I once saw my entire squad kicked for camping, and my best friend was actually kicked due to admin abuse. I appreciate the admin abuse being simulated in the gemez, but I find the mechanics otherwise lacking. Speaking of mechanics; some of them are just terrible. One mechanic tried to charge me for indicator fluid and then wanted to charge for a tyre rotation on my brand new set of tyres - how can you allow this Tripwire? For shame.
As you can see, I am very disappointed with this game. It is not realistic and does not accurately reflect the war in any shape or form. For this reason, I'm giving it a 10/10.

Dungeon Defenders II is a tower defence/action-RPG hybrid, with a very heavy focus on co-op multiplayer, in which your fantasy archetype lays traps and wades into the fray themselves in the hope of defeating waves of marching monsters. Its ‘early access’ has been out on Steam Early Access for a short while now, and is proving rather popular. I gave it a very quick look to try and find out why.
Aka “ageing man plays game not really aimed at him.” Perhaps that should be an ongoing series? I can find a million of ‘em, I’m sure. Anyway: given I’m partial to tower defence, and to action RPG spin-offs like Orcs Must Die, I thought I’d take a look at Dungeon Defenders II. It’s doing well for itself on Steam despite being early access, so presumably was doing something right.
First thing to say is that I don’t think I’ve ever seen anything quite this slick and glossy with the phrase ‘pre-alpha’ stamped on it before. DD2 feels much further down the line than that, and is presented lavishly. I can’t tell you yet how much content the current build offers before petering out, but it’s certainly got its core up and running, I haven’t hit any bugs to speak of, the networking just works and there’s no shortage of players. It is bright, colourful, cartoonish and feels like it came from a huge studio: there is no doubt that a great deal of care has been poured into this.
On the other hand, what I’ve played so far is as shallow as a Hollyoaks cast member’s crayon drawing of a puddle. It may escalate to far greater tactical complexity some hours in, but so far it revolves around one thing: gimme gimme gimme.
Dungeon Defenders II is primarily a loot delivery system. Shiny things drop regularly during a match, chests appear at the end of it, unwanted items are frantically sold in the midst of battle or upgraded outside of it, and everything glitters and gleams and makes those Blizzardy ‘ooh! a trinket!’ sound effects. This is the operant conditioning chamber incarnate. Even the art style, falling somewhere between Warcraft and kids’ game, is risk-free and built from distractingly familiar parts; its evocation is cuddly safety and instant gratification. I found the ephemerality of it all to be oppressive.
Many people want that sweet, sweet loot, of course. I’m not saying that it’s a great evil, just that there wasn’t enough else for me to attach to, and I didn’t enjoy the extremely commercially-minded aesthetic.
Where I can imagine DD2 offering me something is in multiplayer at higher levels, as managing the rampaging swarm of personality-free goblinoids turns from perfunctory bashing and zapping and into desperate ‘oh God get over there!’ and ‘aaargh it’s trashed my lightning trap!’ and general panic/recrimination.
It’s Orcs Must Die 2 with far less invention in terms of trap types, placement and combination, but on the other hand it’s better at straight-up carnage. There’s less punishment for not having traps just so at every choke point, and more focus on smacking things down yourself, ideally in combination with others’ traps. Wade in, unleash hell, grit teeth as the enemies just keep on charging, come out of it all with some reward.
It grows more interesting the harder it gets, in other words. I can see why people are enjoying it – 15 minute adrenaline surges with a candy fountain at the end of it. You’ve got to really care about finding a hat that’s 2 better than another hat to connect with this game, and frankly there’s no shortage of people who do.
With a bolder look, and not these instantly-forgettable infantalised characters and chunky, squat constructions, I might have been amongst them. I quite like getting new hats. That the stuff I’ve claimed so far achieves nothing other than raising a number turns me off, though – I found nothing to show off, nothing to be proud of, nothing to drop my jaw, nothing other than licking at the salt block. Even the wacky fonts made me wince. Old man.
It really is impressively slick, though. Least Early Accessy Early Access game I’ve ever played, I think. On a technical level and even on a presentation level, it’s as solid as they come, but I won’t be going back. Then again, I am far too old for it. Don’t mind me.

I was very surprised by this short but sweet game, particularly considering how cheap it is. The premise of the game, to control a hot air balloon, is very simple, yet made interesting by the challenge of having to navigate often precarious routes. The game's controls are intuitive, as the only control over the balloon the player has is to increase its altitude, and to drop objects. The balloon's direction and speed are left to the whim of the wind, as the wind direction and speed alter according to altitude. By keeping both the premise and mechanics of the game simple and intuitive, yet introducing a new idea or challenge with each of 16 levels, the game kept me both intrigued and somewhat intellectually stimulated. Some aspects of the game I particularly enjoyed are the art style and music, and ability to use audio as a form of input instead of the mouse, which works very well. However, as with almost any game, there are a few aspects I would have liked to see imrpoved. Firstly, the inability to rebind controls, such as using the arrow keys instead of left click, the fact that the game doesn't scale with screen size, meaning there is a lot of unused black space around it, and the inability to move the camera independently from the balloon as I sometimes felt that my field of view was unnecessarily constrained. Yet, despite all of its flaws, I was left thouroughly satisfied by the game, and despite only taking up to an hour to complete, I would not expect any more for its price.

To make it clear Axis Game Factory is primarily a level editor and designer for Unity (and also made in unity) although the latest DLC does allow you to make sidescroller and zombie fps type games. An overlooked feature is that it also lends itself very easily to scenery and design for "serious" (non gaming) unity applications, and it's bristling with more useful features than you expect (machinima anyone?) and the developers have hinted at more new DLCs.
The developers tutorials are numerous and extensive, and very well presented, and their participation on the steam forums is supportive and helpful and very active.
If you have an interest, however casual, in level design or unity, this is a very worthwhile tool to have in your library just to play with or keep on the back burner to get started on levels for that game we all plan to make one day but will never get around to learning how to ;)  Its fun just to play around with.
It is easy to use, quite intuitive, and supplied with a very large library of excellent quality royalty free assets.  .  I used the demo for a long time before buying pro with the DLC in a Humble Bundle, and the features included are very extensive. For under $10 in a humble bundle deal this is unbelievable value for money, and at the regular steam price it is still very good value.
TL/DR  a superb quick-to-pick-up tool for beginners in level design for Unity, and pretty educational as well. Worth having.  Download the free demo, what have you got to lose!

Interactive linear story about a pretentious artsy terrible person.
The gameplay is absolutely linear, you need to do as the narrator says or you won't progress. You need to walk your way through more than a dozen game prototypes. There is no game, no exploration. You set the pacing, there is some interaction that makes you drive the story forward, but ultimately that has little influence on the game.
Now, that's not necessarily bad per se - a movie or a book are linear, and they can be good or bad. However, as you'll soon realize, the narrator talking to you is a pretentious jerk, and while I see the word "pretentious" abused a lot, it fits here: he pretends to an understanding he doesn't possess and can't communicate. So the game gives you about 15 chapters to realize that and then adds a bit of self-doubt to it at the end that doesn't exactly make him more sympathetic. So, if you ever wanted to experience a non-amusing story about an ar-se-hole, here's your chance.
Now I'm a real artsy type and absolutely not pretentious ;-) . My way to approach artwork is to let the author explain what they thought when they made it, and I can explain how this piece affects me, where it fits in the context of other pieces I've seen and the general world I live in, and what it makes me think. When I am talking about a game or art, I am talking about myself. The narrator in the game never quite gets to that point.
So, the audience for that game, the people who could profit from it, are pretentious jerks who don't know they are. Since I presume none of my friends reading this review fit this description, I don't recommend this game.
[Update: There's also a second audience: people who try to decode the body of games, find connections to each other and to The Stanley Parable, and try to come up with theories about what it all could mean. These guys go wild on the Steam forums atm, and I do know some friends of mine who probably would as well.]

Miner Wars 2081 is a 6DOF action-survival space-shooter simulation-game set in the year 2081, 10 years after the destruction of all planetary objects in the Solar System.
You operate an advanced mining ship in a fully destructible and open-world environment, which remains persistent as you complete missions or play online with others. Realism and survival are key aspects of gameplay. Inventory and the way you use resources such as fuel, ammunition, oxygen, ore, and weapons are important when surrounded by dozens of warring factions.

Tiberium Wars is a simple, yet very fun RTS game.  There are 3 factions to choose from, each of which are very well structured, yet still have their unique advantages and disadvantages.  This balances the gameplay beautifully.  Many RTS games have very complex gameplay mechanics, which often turns off newcomers of the genre.  The gameplay in Tiberium Wars is very easy to grasp and the customizable AI gives you a fun, comfortable learning curve, but there is a downside to this feature.  Tiberium Wars lacks any innovative RTS features and doesn’t bring anything new to the table. Fortunately, these imperfections are easily overlooked with its incredibly satisfying gameplay that deserves the attention of any RTS fan or gamers new to the genre.

I just don't understand the love for this game.
TL;DR: Low quality game but not the worst. Music is good.
It suffers from bad design and lack of polish in a worse way than Yooka did (presentation, camera, controls, boss fights) yet for some reason I don't see people talking about this because 'omg, hat kid is so cute.' Cute graphics do not a good game make. The whole thing feels janky and unfished. Story wise; very boring to me and poorly written. On top of this, there isn't really any challenge to this game, and I felt myself getting bored with it very early on. Sometimes the platforming works, sometimes it doesn't, leaving me very frustrated. Smooth platforming is incredibly vital to a 3D platformer as we should all know. Many, many parts of this game were an excersize in frustration.
It can also get confusing to find where to go next, especially in Subcon Forest and the sky world. At one point in the sky world, I used the hat to find my next time piece, and I went through all the trouble to get it (despite the fact that it looked like the exact route I used to find a previous piece) and after finally getting there, I find that it is indeed a time piece I had already gotten but blacked out. I had no idea that this game would send me to a piece I had already gotten as there was no clear indication. This just makes no sense to me because the "Finale" level for the world still isn't accessible and yet the game is sending me to collect time pieces I already have. I have no idea what to do at this point. This is an example of just bad design and confusion that is so pervasive in this game.
The boss fights were poorly designed as well, especially one which seemed straight up broken to me. It was the second fight in Mafia town, with the cook. There are certain points where you are meant to jump over his head and then press X to dive into it and hurt him. Most of the time this trigger just didn't work, and I ended up having to just touch his hat with my body and also take damage in the process. During the ball rolling phase, I was doing the right thing by climbing up the little crater to get to him and would still take random damage for seemingly no reason. The whole experience felt poorly designed and untested and served to be an incredibly frustrating experience. The other bosses in the game, while not quite as broken as this one, were not well designed either.
It wasn't all bad, however. There were some fun parts too. Some of the levels looked great, especially the sky world, but many of them (especially world one) felt cluttered and confusing. The game's music is its strongest point. Even if you decide not to play the game, it would be worth it just to give the soundtrack a listen. Really, it's very rare for games these days to have a soundtrack this good. The character design is pretty good overall as well. Some of the voice acting was good, but it was also painful to hear them read the many poorly worded lines.
Overall, I really do not recommend this game and didn't find it worth the frustration or the price tag. If you are a fan of old school platformers, I would recommend getting Yooka-Laylee instead because I found that game much more enjoyable. Very flawed as well, yes, but when it was fun it was a lot more fun than this game. To the general gaming public, I wouldn't recommend either of these games. Save your money for something with better quality.
