Five Nights at Freddy's is one of those rare occurences in the gaming industry where simplicity and mystery turn a title into one of the best games ever made. One could argue that jump-scares are cheap and lazy in scaring a gamer, but the way this game does jump-scares is remarkable. With the confusion and fear that lies in keeping the animatronics away from you, the game slowly builds a form of paranoia inside. The A.I. plays on that, too, with Bonnie & Chica constantly appearing and disappearing at your doors. Foxy adds to the stress by testing your frequency of watching cameras and Freddy makes it a nightmare as he makes a straight path to your door, never turning back. With these four animatronics, not to mention a hidden fifth one, out to murder you, the tension only rises with each night, leaving you fearing what is to come in the next night.
The most notable element in this game is the unique concept and story. On paper, Five Nights at Freddy's sounds like a lame idea for an indie game, trying desperately to be scary. Spending the night at a Chuck E. Cheese-esque restaurant? And the animatronics are out to get you? At first, one could pass it up as a horrible CreepyPasta story. However, with the freaky animatronics' designs combined with the terrifying storyline, Five Nights at Freddy's is a story I'll never forget, especially after the amount of time I've spent reading up on theories. My Fright Meter hit maximum after watching Game Theory's Five Nights at Freddy's theory.
Overall, this game deserves much praise. The unique storyline has made an impact on the Internet, leaving enough plot-holes to let fans speculate on what exactly happened at the fictional pizzeria. The simple gameplay is enough to strike fear into players, especially ones who are heavily invested. And at a price of $4.99? That is a very fair price and I look forward to Scott Cawthon's sequel coming in 2015.

SUPERHOT may just be one of the most fun games ever made! I have only had time to try out the first few levels which are pretty much tutorials, but holy crap is it awesome. There are lots of FPS puzzle games, but not like this. There isn't a puzzle in the level that you solve to move forward, the whole level is a puzzle and you're one of the pieces, so are all of the bullets and mobs. The time mechanic is great, it reminds me of an old game I used to play as a kid called "Robots" on Linux. You had a level which was a grid, nothing moves until you do, and the object of the game was to use the level to destroy the robots, as every time you move, they close in on you. SUPERHOT's a bit different as the mobs are closing in, but they are shooting at you which means that you have to dodge them, their bullets, and compesnate your aim so that your bullets find their mark too (since the mobs will try to dodge them). Obviously there's also the major difference of SUPERHOT being an FPS as well as having an awesome even if simple art style. An excellent job all around on this one!
The menu system and interaction is great too. When I saw the retro terminal interface I was immediately transported back to my early childhood where the command line was your only interface to the system.
Great job SUPERHOT Team!

The Long Dark is my favorite Early Access Game. I try not to buy too many, but this one appealed to me due to the survival sand box mode. I had many rough starts, but once I got a feel for my surroundings, I was able to start actually surviving... for a while. Eventually, you will die in sand box due to a limited amount of resources, but the challenge is to survive as long as possible. I played ten games and finally had a good enough start to survive for an extended amount of time - it was a challenge!
I will continue to check back with The Long Dark when they make updates, but I am most excited for the release of the Story Mode in the full game. I'm very satisfied with my purchase and look forward to continued developer updates!
PROS:
+ Remarkably stable! In over 45 hours of play, I can't think of a single crash or hiccup.
+ Well developed survival system that keeps you constantly wondering what risk to take next to get you to the next day... The calories burned when sleeping initially seems pretty harsh, but it is actually pretty realistic.
+ Streamlined survival system which is detailed enough to be challenging, but leaves out boring SIM-like issues like going to the bathroom, personal hygeine, etc.
+ Random seed keeps it fresh...
CONS:
+ Currently limited to two sand boxes, but the developers are expanding soon... I look forward to seeing how active the developers are.
I still think it is worth the price even with the two areas.

I'm always afraid alpha games are going to turn out like a bad home improvement project: unfinished, unpolished, and not worth a quarter of what you paid.  This game is not like that.  In its alpha state, it is worth twice the asking price.
This game has been updated and expanded twice since I bought it. The updates and expansions are more exciting than the next episopde of your favorite show, or the long awaited volume of a George RR Martin book.
This game provides the thrill of discovery. You discover new places, new items, new ways to not die. It is unforgiving for those that make dumb mistakes. I learned to never leave your "base" of choice unless you are stocked with food,  water, and a sleeping bag. A horrible storm that reduces visibility can leave you totally lost in your own front yard. For maximum torture and enjoyment, do not look up the maps of the zone you are in - map it yourself. Pushing yourself to expand your boundries and see what you can do is what makes the game so enjoyable..
The only disadvantage is once you survive 30 in-game days or more, living another day becomes a little ho-hum. By the time you've mastered that much of the game, the next expansion is likely only a few RL days away.
If you enjoy playing games that bring you to another time or place to burn a few hours during a snow day, buy this game.

In multi-player You can play as several diffrent roles, a few being: Commander, Squad Leader, Rifleman, etc., and all of these roles play a unique part in building a strong team. There is 1 Commander per team and this person's job is to manage and try to set up strategies that his whole team can agree on and execute with together, fire artilery, and other such things. Squad Leaders can act as moible spawn points for squad members, give commander marks to fire artilery on, use smoke grenades, and other things. Rifleman are the most common role, as the majority of the server's players will be rifleman. You have a bolt action rifle (as Americans in Rising Storm, it is possible you get the M1-Grand instead) and your job is to take the objective points and be supportive and coopertive of what your other team members ask you to do.

This is not a review. I only played the beta, therefore, this may be outdated. This serves only the purpose of informing new players, it's somewhat a small preview.
Weak theme, hindered gameplay, atrocious AI, bad CQC system that is forced on the player by being the only way to get more ammo (which is very scarce), faulty level design, auto-cover is badly implemented, enemies are sponges and have terrible spawn locations.
I didn't play the final version of the game, but there is a lot of work to be done here. The biggest problem is the decisions made by the team, they were not thought as whole functional concept. The game general design and the in-game sections are way too disconnected. The bad synergy between the gameplay mechanics (dynamics) is harming the game experience.
I must say that some cinematic value is found here, provided mostly by the humorous style of the characters, and there are some good moments with the FX. The graphics are not bad at all and the uninspired models of the protagonists are kind of compensated with the rest of the models. The UI, the sound, the physics and the animations are unnoteworthy.
It's strongly advisable to rethink how the game works and correct the mistakes, being the CQC system itself changed to better, mainly by adding fluidity or by excluding the need for using it to get more ammo and coming up with another advantage for using the system.
In the end, I am very disappointed with MercurySteam. I didn't expect a masterpiece, as this is not the genre they are accostumed with, but this is too much of a letdown, both conceptually and technically. I don't know about the writing, but I assume that it is generic and contextual.

The game is a pretty good descent clone. Plenty of claustraphobic space station dungeon crawls. The mining element is fun as well, not to mention you can blow holes in anything not manmade. The galaxy map and the ability to go where-ever when-ever is also pretty awesome. I think some people would be turned off by the voice acting, but I liked how campy it was. But there is a steep learning curve.
You need to keep oxygen and fuel in good supply, they will run out quicker than you'd think. I feel like modern space ships are better at storing/using oxygen. As for fuel, you can shut off your engine and just float around space to travel long distances so its not as much of a problem. Your starting machine gun becomes inefficient very quickly, which sucks because its the only gun you can find tons of ammo for. Your ship is also quite fragile and most enemies have hitscan machine guns. If you cant find cover or knock them around with missles, your ability to dodge their attacks depends mostly on the distance between you. Descent got it right by making the hitscan machine gun and the enemies that use it uncommon. To top off my list of complaints, raising money is hard. Maybe I didn't play long enough to find the stupid easy way of getting cash but a new ship costs millions and I was lucky if I had a hundred thousand on me.
I realize I have a lot of compliants, but I swear I enjoyed the game and would recommend it to anyone looking for a new descent-like experience.

I've played for a little under two hours but for the amount I have played I think I can give my opinion.
People complain about bugs and I've already witnessed one small, not glaring but small bug while playing. When approaching the beach in the beginning area walking into the water shoves you up into the air on an invisible platform. Nothing terribly special but it does show some signs of being unpolished. Beyond that the game is rather fun, kind of light-hearted if not seemingly a button-spamfest. The dodge-roll mechanic offers very little to the table, enemies when performing chain attacks still turn in your direction so trying to roll around to attack from the side is pretty much useless. So it's mostly run away when they perform a combo then rush in and spam the punch/kick buttons until you knock them down. Rinse, repeat. You're given "Shi" early on being a form of magic but it seems a little unimpressive so far. I'm still near the beginning so once I can unlock more Shi it may offer more strategy to combat. Speaking of combat, if you need to sneak by an enemy or just want to launch a surprise attack you can use Chado's rock summoning technique to hurl a stone to draw the enemy's attention, or hit an enemy with it and temporarily stun them. Aiming could be a bit easier admittedly but it's effective.
Visual-wise the game looks really good if you can look past some of the low polygons used on the 3D models. This definitely doesn't look next gen but it still looks quite beautiful. For an indie game a bit impressive even. One complaint I read was the voice acting, personally I like it. Combined with the comic panel cutscenes it adds for some very amusing moments that had me cracking a smile. All-in-all I would say this is definitely a game that's a must-have for anyone who enjoys action-RPGs with a light-hearted colorful approach. If you're unsure if you would like the game just wait for it to go on sale. I managed to pick it up for $12 at the time of writing this and I can say it is well worth the price.

An excellent tool for beginners and intermediate game-makers alike. Especially with the recent DLC's, this utility is a great piece of software that introduces the user to an easy-to-use 3D environment designer. The process isn't what I would call speedy, as adding detail takes quite a bit of time, but making a basic hall, platformer level, or exploration environment is doable in a few hours.
Tools are extensive and complete, and there is a huge variety of environment objects already designed and created. Accessing the latter is as simple as clicking "Load All" on the right side of your screen, and selecting a category to view and draw from.
My only gripe is that movement for the pre-programmed players is clunky -- movements last a little longer than the duration of the key-press or command, jumps are ridiculously huge, and the physics of the jumping is off (the ability to change the direction of your movement vector in midair to be specific).
I fully support this software, and I look forward to seeing it develop and get better and better over time. The developers are all invested in the project, and are engaged with the community answering questions, helping, encouraging, and really being fantastic.
Even if you posses no programming skills, this program is easy to use, and easy to master. Everyone should try it.

Game factory does not make games. It is a level / world design tool. A really good level / world design tool for Unity based games. You see everything in real time. You can play test your levels, run around and stuff, but its not a stand alone game game engine, just a level / world design tool. However, calling yourself Game Factory was slightly misleading, but whatever. On the forum, the developers hint at wanting to one day make it a stand alone game engine, but I'm not sure if its a hint or misleading. Since they call it Game Factory, I have to lean toward the potential of misleading here.
It is now a few months later and people are still asking if AGF is a game engine to make standalone games:
You can make some really great looking, lush environments. The tools are easy, robust and look fantastic. The video tutorials are great and explain a lot, even if they could get sped up a little for more advanced users.
The problem is there is nothing out of the ordinary from the default Unity 3D level editor. So if you're already developing for Unity, why not just use Unity? This is still a better editor to make levels and it will take you less time to make better levels.
The DLC packs offer a lot of variety. The FPS add on offers lots of great features, but there are already a lot of great FPS level editors out there. Game Factory FPS DLC expedites level creation with prefab rooms ala the Elder Scrolls editor. Instead of having to make every wall like Source, Unreal and even the Doom 3 editor. With all that said, the DLC is not free. It is just another add on to buy when Unreal 4 and Cryengine have plenty of free examples for every type of game. Plus they're cheaper and they are stand alone engines.
Game Factory is worth it if you're a level designer for Unity, but to the average kid expecting to make a big game, nope. Look at actual game makers, Unity, Cryengine and Unreal Engine. As for Unity, its simple enough to pick up and design for, so this is a great benefit.
I have respect for the developers and respect for the tool, but I'm just warning people. It's not what you think it is.

First off, "Fully Destructible" is a complete falsehood. This fact is important in highlighting the biggest problem with this software: the group that made it just doesn't care about their audience.
As quickly as possible, they try to force-feed you everything about the character you're playing and the situation your in. There's so much information that nothing stands out, so it isn't clear what the atmosphere is. Suddenly, you are driving a vehicle capable of movement in any direction and the controls aren't explained. Your character is inside a maze where nothing about the environment pops out to clue you in as to where you should go, and half the time the waypoint system lies to you (what did I expect, though, right?).
On top of all that, you are under attack, and to make a very difficult situation even worse, if your vehicle takes damage you might have a breach, which leaks out your oxygen unless you find a repair powerup (read: rare health kit), turning your screen dark as it slowly kills you.
The game is mercilessly convoluted and brutally unforgiving to it's player. At one point while trying to find the "exit", I found an opening and headed that direction to escape, only to realize as I was blasted to bits that the ship I saw outside was THE ENEMY, and after reloading realizing that I was supposed to come out of the doorway, then turn AWAY from the opening to see the doorway which was the intended direction.
I played with a friend and found one of the audio parts hilarious:
Evilsupervisor: "Did you exterminate them all?"
Evilsurbordinate : "Most of them. One or two miners escaped, but they have no idea what's going on".
How right they were, how right they were.
Save yourself the disappointment.

Hi
As a Unity 3D developer I have to point out the interface is incredibly frustrating to use.This application as designed specifically for unity and I find moving the viewport camera around clunky why not try to mimic unity's camera controls for developers who are already familair with moving the camera in unity when sculpting terrain the camera moves in the direction of the mouse click , making it very difficult to be precise.
The placement tool is more focussed on placing actual objects than prescision , and you have to select the ability to select a placed object , and even with the shortcut buttons (holding down ctrl and pressing space) it is very difficult to get the prescision with the mouse wheel for your rotation and scaling (but it might just be my very expensive mouse acting up.
The assets loaded on to the engine seem very repetitive and redundant, and it would have been nice if we had some texturing options for the various materials the object is composed of.
Here are my recommendations for making this much better for unity developers
1. The click and camera moving towards the mouse click thing has to go , it does not work well on any level of sculpting (for object placement if should be optional
2. Moving around the environment , please mimic unity's style everyone who wishes to use this software should get used to it
3. Objects placement , when placing castle objects you are not able to zoom back to the ground without goign into prefab design mode then going back to design mode,
4. Terrain sculpting, a limit to how high your current brush can sculpt would be nice , making a slightly elevated flat section is not as easy  (I might not have found the tool yet)
5 And this is probably where this software could pull the golden win , the ability to create prefabs from content packs fantacy / sci fi / vehicle , I like the idea of being able to create a building and then port it in various stages to my unity game.
For instance if i am able to build a level 1 building design it texture it and send it through to unity then go on to the second level for that specific building , or build diferent kinds of spaceships with powerfull texturing options like Spore for example
From the kickstarter campaign to the actual delivered product this is quite the let down in terms of what the vision was for this software
This is not a Game Factory (yet) but an advanced terrain prototyping tool prior to loading your project into unity and making it an actual game (using actual code, AI development) which i dont mind.
I know its easy to critisize and for the price measured against other unity assets i can certainly not complain
I am sure in the future we might see even greater things from this kit and taking all things into consideration I would recommend this kit for its terrain layout abilities and for what it might become

TL;DR: You cannot create your own gameplay. If you're completely new to game design, AGFPro is a nice starter package, but you'll have to learn to use something else to really create your own games.
If you're already familiar with using a game engine like Unity3D, you won't need AGFPro, but maybe you'll like it. I personally didn't.
When I first had a look into Axis Game Factory, I had a negative feeling about the whole thing. As I looked a little more into it recently, I found out that most of my problems were because of its presentation.
To start with this first: Like others stated already, the term "Game Factory" can be confusing. Unlinke Unity3D, the tool this tool was made with, you cannot create your own games with it.
What you CAN do is create Landscapes with a lot of ready-to-go assets. Buildings, textures for your terrain, extra shaders, everything there. The editor also comes with some features that may or may not make level design easier or faster than with Unity. When you're done, you either put one of the AGFPro Players into your level and play around a bit, or you import your level to Unity3D, where you can build a game upon what you designed. This feature was in beta while I tested it and crashed while importing.
But right here's another positive thing: The developer is constantly trying to improve this tool.
I personally couldn't really warm up to Axis Game Factory. I'm able to do pretty much I can do with it in Unity, and with that I don't need a second tool for level design. Also, the UI of AGFPro felt unintuitive to me, but that's subjective as well.
If you're able to use Unity or something alike, I don't recommend this tool, since I didn't see much use in the features that it adds to what Unity already gives you, or is available for Unity.
Maybe, for you, it's different, so you might want to take a look anyway.
Also, I do think that beginners with no experience with other tools can get a nice starter package here to have a first look into level design and if creating games could be something for them.
Just keep in mind that, to make your own game idea reality, you WILL have to learn to use another tool.

I just don't understand the love for this game.
TL;DR: Low quality game but not the worst. Music is good.
It suffers from bad design and lack of polish in a worse way than Yooka did (presentation, camera, controls, boss fights) yet for some reason I don't see people talking about this because 'omg, hat kid is so cute.' Cute graphics do not a good game make. The whole thing feels janky and unfished. Story wise; very boring to me and poorly written. On top of this, there isn't really any challenge to this game, and I felt myself getting bored with it very early on. Sometimes the platforming works, sometimes it doesn't, leaving me very frustrated. Smooth platforming is incredibly vital to a 3D platformer as we should all know. Many, many parts of this game were an excersize in frustration.
It can also get confusing to find where to go next, especially in Subcon Forest and the sky world. At one point in the sky world, I used the hat to find my next time piece, and I went through all the trouble to get it (despite the fact that it looked like the exact route I used to find a previous piece) and after finally getting there, I find that it is indeed a time piece I had already gotten but blacked out. I had no idea that this game would send me to a piece I had already gotten as there was no clear indication. This just makes no sense to me because the "Finale" level for the world still isn't accessible and yet the game is sending me to collect time pieces I already have. I have no idea what to do at this point. This is an example of just bad design and confusion that is so pervasive in this game.
The boss fights were poorly designed as well, especially one which seemed straight up broken to me. It was the second fight in Mafia town, with the cook. There are certain points where you are meant to jump over his head and then press X to dive into it and hurt him. Most of the time this trigger just didn't work, and I ended up having to just touch his hat with my body and also take damage in the process. During the ball rolling phase, I was doing the right thing by climbing up the little crater to get to him and would still take random damage for seemingly no reason. The whole experience felt poorly designed and untested and served to be an incredibly frustrating experience. The other bosses in the game, while not quite as broken as this one, were not well designed either.
It wasn't all bad, however. There were some fun parts too. Some of the levels looked great, especially the sky world, but many of them (especially world one) felt cluttered and confusing. The game's music is its strongest point. Even if you decide not to play the game, it would be worth it just to give the soundtrack a listen. Really, it's very rare for games these days to have a soundtrack this good. The character design is pretty good overall as well. Some of the voice acting was good, but it was also painful to hear them read the many poorly worded lines.
Overall, I really do not recommend this game and didn't find it worth the frustration or the price tag. If you are a fan of old school platformers, I would recommend getting Yooka-Laylee instead because I found that game much more enjoyable. Very flawed as well, yes, but when it was fun it was a lot more fun than this game. To the general gaming public, I wouldn't recommend either of these games. Save your money for something with better quality.

Tiberium Wars is in a lot of ways, the last hurrah of the C&C franchise. It is the last of the games to really stay true to the formula that made the series so successful but it was also the last of the series that failed to innovate and that is something that hurt it.
The great live action cutscenes make a return but instead of the wonderful b-movie quality of previous installments it is now little more than catwalk performances by semi-famous actors.
The gameplay is the same as in previous installments, although there has been some technical advancement you will immediately become comfortable with it. The poor unit AI and the lack of certain utility units common in other games does become frustrating rather quickly.
It is a good game if you liked the old C&C's in series but it is also a game that has become stagnant. A game that tries to innovate but fails every step of the way and although C&C will always hold a place in my heart, I am glad that the genre is advancing beyond it.

Indie games are everywhere these days. It seems like you can't escape them no matter how hard you try to hide. Sometimes, however, it's a lot better to play them than to run away screaming. Banished is one of those games.
You control a small group of people who have been banished from their homes and are now trying to make a living off of the land. Depending on what difficulty you start out on, the amount of resources available for you to build with at the start varies. An easy start means you have prebuilt houses and a lot of extra materials to expand with. A medium start requires you to build your own houses, and a hard start means that you have to gather a lot of resources before you can build the houses. The longer your people survive, the more babies they make. Food, as a result, becomes an issue really fast. If you're not careful, the delicate juggling act of this game can come crashing down on your head in the form of a food shortage. Make sure you have your priorities set, cause you'll never have enough civilians to handle all of the jobs in your village.
What makes this game really, really unique is the game over screen. Or, it's lack of one. I would highly reccommend getting this game simply for experiencing the haunting beauty that is the dead silence that comes over your village when everyone dies. There is no "Game Over" overlay that fades in, no sad music, nothing. Just the ambience of the wilderness. This indie game manages to make losing more haunting and memorable than any other game I have ever played.

I'm just going to get right down into it. The game is great, but not so great where I can enjoy it for hours upon hours on end. The gameplay gets rather repetative, the "story" is lackluster, and the loot mechanic... my God, don't even get me started. You spend almost 2-5k on an unidentified weapon in the blackmarket only to find something even better on the planet you were just prepping for. What the hell, I get that it's likely a mixture between a lot of games (Namely a Borderlands or Diablo loot mechanic feel), and that's not always a bad thing, but Pixel Privateers just doesn't feel... right.
However, this game isn't all bad. As above, I state it's great. And it is, I absolutely love the 'pixelated' genre some games go for. Pixel Privateers does it well, hell so did Pixel Piracy. The cute little banter your crew occasionally does is interesting, the Glorious is a mysterious... infection? that I want to find out more about. Even the random events that are triggered sometimes are awesome. Hell, met a guy named Thomas (Forgot last name) whose ship was attacked by the Glorious and he was a sole survivor. Now I got his ship and him as a member, pretty awesome RP element right there.
Another thing I don't like though, but this is a personal opinion so take it as a grain of salt I suppose, is that there's no immersive travel.
I remember back when I first got Pixel Piracy, I f**king loved how when you wanted to travel somewhere, the 'loading screen' would be you and your crew on a boat. Singing sea shanties?, talking, and better yet, the boarding of enemy ships. Pixel Privateers just doesn't have that, now it's you staring at a rather uninteresting map (similar to that of the before mentioned game) and maybe sometimes an event will trigger. Good or bad, regardless. It's just something that bugs me.
Final review? Just enough to warrant a recommendation. I really do like this game and hope to see more come of it.

Did you enjoy the frantic gunplay and cover-bouncing of hotline miami but were frustrated by not being able to plan your moves? Superhot's hook mechanic of time moving only when you move is not itself a new idea, but it's expertly applied here.
As time stops for you in between every shot, step and punch, your enemies have moved and every time you slow to plan your next move, you must reevaluate the scene over again. Allowing the player time to think in this kind of 'one and you're done' action setting is a golden idea, and the execution doesn't fall into the pitfall of 'bullet time' that many other games do. You have all the same faculties as your enemies, you can't move faster than them, and they'll predict your movements to shoot or flank to your predicted position, the advantage you have is planning time, while still giving you the feeling that your reactions are instantaneous and fluid.
Superhot has a nice balanced bite to it's difficulty as well- it isn't the manic 50% luck of hotline miami but it will still push you to be quick on the uptake as enemies are no slouches when it comes to trying to put you out.
The aesthetic of the game suits the mood- everything is colour-washed and minimalist, with an eerie, sometimes calm feeling throughout, much to a counterpoint of hotline miami's neon insanity.
Sound effects are crisp and defined, a shot from any weapons sounds and feels weighty, and all sound effects distort to the tune of your time-warping excellently.
Recommended for those who like their lethal action with a bit of brainwork involved.

Raiders of the Broken Planet is the latest game from MercurySteam (Castlevania: Lords of Shadow franchise, Metroid: Samus Returns) and is an adventure/third person shooter. The first 2 levels are also free, so you can try the game and (if you like it) buy the seperate campaigns for $9,99/€9,99 each or all of them for $39,99/€39,99.
Before each mission, you can choose a Raider to play as. Each one has different weapons and abilities. For example, Harec has a sniper rifle as his weapon and his ability lets him teleport somewhere and cloak himself there. Hans uses a machine gun and his ability is the jetpack. There are 5 of them that you can use in the prologue. Another one is released but you'll have to buy and finish the "Alien Myths" campaign.
The missions have objectives (DUH!) that you'll have to complete (No♥♥♥♥♥♥ bro). These include clearing the place, overloading things etc. You can do this Solo or with up to 4 players. I cannot speak for the 4-player part because I couldn't find any, but the Solo version gives you 3 extra lives. Once those lives run out, you'll have to survive until it is recharged. There's also the Antagonist mode that lets you attack the Raiders alongside the AI enemies. But most of the time, there are 4 Raiders against 1 Antagonist, so there's always a challenge there.
Controls-wise, I don't get some of the complaints about it. Personally, I found the controls responsive enough, didn't feel any clunkiness. The M&KB is pretty good, but some may prefer controllers.
As for the graphics, they are awesome. Like Castlevania: Lords of Shadow, MercurySteam did a great job.
In conclusion: If you like playing co-op games (hell, even if you enjoy playing solo) give this one a shot. The first 2 missions are free anyway, so you get the chance to see if this game is for you.
UPDATE: The founder's pack has apparently been removed. The price for seperate campaigns doesn't seem to have changed though. Also, the progression system is getting a complete overhaul. I didn't get any campaigns and there is little progress you can do in the first campaign so I sadly cannot comment on that.

One of the most underrated games out today.  This game has a steep learning curve, and it will take some real effort to learn and advance in.  It could take you a few days, maybe a few weeks, but once you do, you will be playing one of the greatest FPS games on the market today.

Honestly, I don't see how Raiders of the Broken Planet is worth anything near $40 from the presentation of the demo alone. Since demos are a representation of what to expect from the full package, it shall be judged based on the merits it has shown.
First and foremost, the graphical settings like motion blur cannot be turned off, as well as a few other settings. So you can't customize graphical settings to the preferences you may want. The game itself looks decent but the mechanics themselves are entirely different. Raiders has an awkward cover system. You can't run near a box without your character going into a cover mode and then getting shot to death. The lack of blind fire is sorely needed in a game that is about waves upon waves of enemies. This is needed because the enemy ai just rushes towards you like mobs of zombies. So you can't make quick time judgement shots, you have to slow down and aim in order for the shoot function to work. Additionally, the melee system is poorly implemented. It's just a quick time who hits the button first to win. Basically, a combo to death or one shot. I can't tell if the game is "difficult" or the AI is just poorly engineered. There is no point playing tactically in the sense of each character's role, just "stick together and go full on Rambo". Oh yea, there is no sprint mechanic.
Furthermore, there is no text chat function (I don't know about voice chat since I don't have a mic) to communicate with my teammates. Yea there is some bland warning system you can issue but it doesn't really get into anything specific. I'm not able to tell my teammates not to engage with an antagonist in CQC because they will most likely lose in that encounter. Not being able to coordinate with my team just leads to the antagonist and AI killing myself and another, while the other two are clueless that we're being demolished. Anyways, I don't have much to compain about the UI other than you'll just get used to it very quickly.
The bizarre presentation of Raiders is oddly "well", for the lack of a better word. While playing, I was surprised at the quality of the game itself. It was well crafted, obviously by professionals, but also felt very bland both mechanic and function of gameplay. The story premise is interesting enough, but I don't know about spending $40 for a game this lackluster.

The very first time I saw the trailer, Shiness came off as an RPG blend of  The Legend of Korra and Zelda. Here was this scrappy little monchichi who looked like he was Chris Pratt in chipmunk form. On top of that, from the trailer he seemed surrounded by a Guardians of the Galaxy-esque cast of characters with airships, magical beings, and a superbly colorful atmosphere.  Oh, oh, oh, and on top of THAT, it looked like the combat was arena fighter based! My heart fluttered. This is the type of game I could just lose myself in. So, that left me thinking, “The combat and story will make or break this game”, but I was wrong. While those parts have their share of ups and downs, the biggest problem I had with Shiness was something else entirely.
I wrote full review
, but it won't fit on Steam.  So, here is just the part about combat and half my final thoughts.
Don’t get me wrong, I enjoy the combat in Shiness. It rides a fine line of good aspects versus bad ones. On the good side, it does NOT go in the mold of Batman style combat. You cannot win by button mashing, at least not for long. If you parry, it must be a good solid parry right at the perfect moment. And if you block, you had better do it before the other guy comes at you. There are even battle perks for blocking or parrying at the exact moment you need to. The only problem is that I can’t always tell when I need to. Each baddie has some idiosyncratic attack method and it’s not obvious when to exactly parry or block. Too early, and it’s for naught. Too late, and you will be on the other side of a multi-punch combo that could literally drain you dead in seconds. My advice is to properly set up your party with Shi and Disciplines before getting anywhere close to combat. Even the very first monster hunting quest will nail your butt if you do not check on that. I’ve noticed some people feel that the parrying is too hard to handle, but keep in mind that if it was any easier it would be a button mashfest. I really feel it’s close to just right, but the actual enemy attacks need an adjustment to signal us to parry about 0.33 seconds earlier before it’s too late.
For those who have not played any fighters and come from a click-click RPG background, you may be overwhelmed. The combat is not to be taken lightly once you get outside the general plant-baddie areas. Batman veterans will have an easier time and I daresay Sleeping Dogs or Dragonball  vets will have no issues at all. All around you are endless respawning monsters to attack and level up with. In a way, it sort of resembles Zelda Breath of the Wild with baddies all over the place waiting to be beaten so their stuff can be snatched up, but only in the way a bagel with raspberries and cream cheese resembles a jelly donut. Some of these fights are minor, others are quite the challenge because more often than not you are getting tag-teamed by two or three of them at a time. What if you get hit with a combo that depletes more than half your health? Then, switch to another person in your party ASAP! They will regenerate while someone else fights. Just keep doing that over and over and you’ll be fine.
Now, combos can be assigned for certain elements – Earth, Water, Wind, Fire, Lightning, and so on. These are simple combos where you use LT+ a single button to fire some Shi, allowing players to Hadoken their way to victory. While incredibly simple compared to say Devil May Cry, the faster combos are decent with a lean towards people being able to pick up the combat more easily. You can’t just spam attack with it, though, because you’ll run out of Shi fast. It also is best if timed with the element flashing in the battle arena at the time. Some attacks don’t affect baddies one bit, so keep that in mind before trying to blast someone and use up all your Shi. Honestly, most battles will come down to how fast you can block or parry along with good old fashioned punches and kicks while spamming Shi when the screen flashes the right color.  Yes, the attacks are simplified, but the general structure of combat is just fine considering you cannot win everything unless you fight in a varied method.
The combat really comes into play with the bosses, and that’s when you had better get your block/dodge and parry down to an art. You will get schooled otherwise. To me, Shiness has a very competent, if imperfect combat system. Usually, the combat is horribly affected by…drumroll, please…..BAD CAMERA ANGLES. I’ve had an easier time balancing a marble on a bobblehead. For the love of all things rainbow-colored and poofy, please get that camera fixed. There is an option for AUTO-LOCK on the camera and if you play with that on or off, it still doesn’t really quite work correctly. Leave it off, and the camera is manually adjustable, yet now you have to move the camera along while battling it out. Leave it on, and it’s easier but if the camera gets stuck somewhere, under some grass for instance, then you will be unable to see anything whatsoever. I used two controllers to play this game, an Xbone controller and a Steam controller. The Xbone controller gave me the least issues but moved across the screen very slowly compared to the Steam controller, which had the right joystick/touchpad set to emulate a mouse. The Steam controller was like making my game magically more nimble, but then when I fought in battles the auto-lock camera would grab a terrible angle about 35% of the time, even in boss battles. I can reset with a right stick click, but it’s no fun to constantly reset the camera when I could be pressing an attack button instead. As I said, using an Xbone controller will have fewer issues, but I highly suggest trying the game with or without the auto-lock on and see what works for you.
Is Shiness worth spending your hard earned cash on?  In my opinion, if the game feels like something you can enjoy and you have the patience to work through the bad camera angles and bugs while patches come out later on,
.  This was a tough call for me because I had so many glitches, it was overwhelming.  But, I cannot ignore the incredible amount of hard work and love that is manifest in this game.  Yes, the story outside of the cutscenes is so-so, yet is unfolds nicely as you progress with good attention to detail, such as the Shiyawo Mountain level.  Yes, the menu is overly complex, but it functions well despite being maze-like.  Yes, the combat rides a razor thin line between difficult and easy to play, however, I don’t feel it is too tough for anyone with marginal experience with fighters.  What I want to remark most on is that the world is original, it’s uniquely Shiness.  Does it borrow from other games, why of course. Shiness offers what feels like a game made with heart and its own take on combat.  Is it entirely unique? Nah, but it’s unique enough that it’s not a cookie cutter of something else.  This is not some game thrown together without a soul, it’s an interesting game that gets better the more you play.  The only thing holding me back from a better rating is that the game bugs are much too frequent.   You are fighting the game along with the bugs, make no doubt about it.
I keep this one thing in mind, I love games where the combat involves your fists, even if I am generally mediocre at them. Do you prefer slashing or shooting?  Then, think twice.  Do you prefer Batman combat? Then don’t play Shiness.  What appeals to me is the same thing that appealed to me in the trailer.  I get to be a chipmunk Chris Pratt and kung-fu my way to glory with some members of the cast of Cats. Chado’s best friend, Poky, even fights with HIS BUTT.  My advice is to wait on patches and then buy discounted when it's working.

As a platformer fan cannot recommend this enough. Throwback to times when 3D platformers were good. Huge interesting levels with a unique artstyle and imaginative gameplay besides just collecting things. In a lot of places it's giving me a lot of Psychonauts vibes. It also runs super smooth, looks pretty as heck (and too damn cute :P) and it's fast and fluid to control. Overall just very refreshing and fun to play. Doesn't cease to run out of steam and amaze with all the new worlds it's thrown at me.
EDIT: Since I beat the game and I'm still playing it, thought this review deserved a re-write:
For a small indie team and a kickstarter game this is amazing. Best platformer I've played in a very long time, and it rekindled my interest in 3D platforming all over again, probably since Psychonauts.
Art direction and soundtrack are fantastic and the controls are very fluid, bouncy and never managed to annoy me through the course of the game. There's some learning curve to get used to the sliding and such but it feels rewarding to master.
I think the real highlights of the game are its creative worlds however, no world plays the same and you're really missing out if you only play through the first one. While the core gameplay stays the same, level design varies massively from open-ended, exploration focused levels with a single goal to more scripted puzzle-like interiors, mysterious forests to even horror sequences, or complete free roam in a massive mountain. For a super cutesy game there's quite a lot of dark humour in it as well, and the game never fails to make you smile. And the Hat Kid is just the best, I love her personality how she's just going around doing whatever she wants and doesn't even let such things as (spoiler?) losing her soul get in her way :P
You even get some choices in places which was surprising (I don't recall a platformer where I questioned 'if I did the right thing'), and you are free to progress the game in whatever pace you like. I was never bored and if I felt like switching to a different world, I could do so anytime.
I got a lot of Psychonauts vibes from the game in places and that's even intended with "memory vaults" at the end of certain time rifts unlocking additional backstory to the worlds and overall the level design felt similar, the time rifts might as well be mental worlds, not to mention the crow agents in various levels.
There's just something about the game that hooked me into playing it, and very few games have managed that. I wanted to 100% it immediately on my first playthrough and may even start a second just to see what I missed. It's just fun and refreshing to play for the heck of it and made with love, as games should be.
Workshop support for the game already looks solid and there's quite a few very nice user created levels. Hoping to possibly try editing some myself later.

Waited some time for a few patches before I decided to review.  Has it been 2 years already?
Well like most I was highly anticipating this game and was expecting that original DD feeling.  Did I get that?  ...Not exactly, but that is ok given games have to evolve in some way, even though it's not always based on our personal wants & needs.  At first I was excited and then somewhat disappointed and then hardly play anymore, but I come back time to time and it seems DDII can't grab me and keep me prisoner like the original still can.  I still recommend this because it has some changes coming, but replay-wise for now, not so much.  I still love the DD universe and appreciate all its parts, so hoping that flare to keep playing returns.
NOTE:  Some of the below are based on friends of friends opinions, but seem to be matching equally to random people I asked the same question.
PROS:
1. Familiar Music themes
2. Familiar map areas revamped
3. A little more hero customizations
4. Knight actually welds a shield without being an accessory
5. Graphics are well done frame to frame animations
6. Still maintains that unique hero feeling
7. Abilities are a bit different, but still enjoyable
8. Handling pets has changed
9. New Quest system is realistic & fun
10. Month-to-month quests for pets & other rewards is a nice addition
11. Still has that Boss Fight fun factor
12. Customizing inventory = Names, auto-loot categories, by class, etc and etc
13. Easy leveling
CONS:
1. Limited inventory compared to the original
2. You have to purchase inventory slots (Bags)
3. Towers to damage to creature formulas have changed
4. Huge limitations on gear upgrades compared to original DD
5. Handling pets has changed (placed as PRO and CON because it’s a huge argument to most in my circles and circles of circles)
6. Open tavern creates some negative feedback on the community as a whole and reporting system might as well not exist (can be avoided with solo tavern play or private + inviting friends); which leads to a very immature atmosphere
7.  Normal Mode difficulty does not feel like Normal mode, so difficulty to difficulty is not a realistic transition from one to the other.
Most arguable PROS & CONS:
Handling pets
Graphics
Abilities
Open Tavern with no control or monitoring
Difficulty
Easy leveling (easy to vets but to new players? ...compared to the original)
All-in-all I love that the DD community is still going in some way, but... (PERSONAL OPINIONS SECTION)
1. Did it grab me and dedicate me like the original?       No
2. Do I feel Trendy was able to make a worthy sequel?    Yes, but wanted that old rewarding feeling
3. Am I already finding myself anticipating the next Dungeon Defenders?    Yes
4. Will I still play DDII?    Yes, but not daily = a couple times a month
5. Am I not playing due to the unregulated chat?    No, but I see how the racist names and 24/7 bashing among people in the community can alienate many new players and some vets alike.

Did you enjoy the frantic gunplay and cover-bouncing of hotline miami but were frustrated by not being able to plan your moves? Superhot's hook mechanic of time moving only when you move is not itself a new idea, but it's expertly applied here.
As time stops for you in between every shot, step and punch, your enemies have moved and every time you slow to plan your next move, you must reevaluate the scene over again. Allowing the player time to think in this kind of 'one and you're done' action setting is a golden idea, and the execution doesn't fall into the pitfall of 'bullet time' that many other games do. You have all the same faculties as your enemies, you can't move faster than them, and they'll predict your movements to shoot or flank to your predicted position, the advantage you have is planning time, while still giving you the feeling that your reactions are instantaneous and fluid.
Superhot has a nice balanced bite to it's difficulty as well- it isn't the manic 50% luck of hotline miami but it will still push you to be quick on the uptake as enemies are no slouches when it comes to trying to put you out.
The aesthetic of the game suits the mood- everything is colour-washed and minimalist, with an eerie, sometimes calm feeling throughout, much to a counterpoint of hotline miami's neon insanity.
Sound effects are crisp and defined, a shot from any weapons sounds and feels weighty, and all sound effects distort to the tune of your time-warping excellently.
Recommended for those who like their lethal action with a bit of brainwork involved.

Spent about 9 hours in this game and i'm feeling pretty confident with my hiragana and enjoyed the game for what it is. The pacing of the game is excellent. The rate of which new hiragana is introduced was perfect for me And if you want to grind, it's also benifical for you to practice hiragana if you're struggling, but isn't required.
Story: Well, it's unique. I'm not going to say this is the greatest rpg story in history, but still a better story and makes more sense than FFI. Laughed a few times, got hopefull around the middle, and then the story went flat again. But it was enough to keep me to the end.
Characters: your party stays with the same 4 and gains no new party members. Considering the mechanics, more characters aren't really needed as your main four aren't really special.
Mechanics: sadly, theres a lot to be desired for an rpg. I went through the whole game using only one other move in combat other than the "attack" button, and it was the heal for grinding. hopefully in the next game, they can have some kind of magic system that does some kind of speed read or something. But the point of the game is to teach Hiragana and the game accomplishes that in a more entertaining way than writing out the characters repeatedly.
Quests/sidequests: main quest is stop the evil plan. Sidequest usually offer a better reward for going back to a place to grind for 5-10 minutes and can sometime work on your vocab which the main story doesn't focus on till the very very end.
Overall, I feel good about my hiragana and was entertained enough by the game that I would buy the sequel for Katakana when it comes out. Would recommend if you're looking to learn hiragana and want to have a reward and evidence of your improvement along the way.

Treat the Prologue as a demonstration of what the game has to offer.
About the Prologue:
It contains a tutorial and one mission, which is divided in three stages.
You can play either solo or matchmaking (p2p and cross-platform).
After successfully completing the mission for the first time you'll be allowed to play as the antagonist.
You have four raiders to choose from. (additional raiders available in other adventures)
Completing Solo matches allows you to earn gold (1500 per difficult level, once per level).
Completing Matchmaking matches allows you to earn any of the three currencies or a blueprint.
Currencies are Gold, Character Points and Faction Points. Mercury points is the premium currency.
Matchmaking matches provides a 4 player co-op experience and sometimes (usually) has a 5th player - the antagonist - who will play against the other four.
Additional information:
The Antagonist has a separate ranking (which is one of the pre-requisites for unlocking weapons).
Characters have loadouts, including one weapon, one active skill and a pool/deck of character and faction passive skills. Additional passive skills can be unlocked with character or faction points.
The game has interesting and unique mechanics which deserves a topic of its own.
The game offers a 3rd person over the shoulder shooting experience. Ammo is limited and can be replenished with melee. Melee is also an effective way of taking enemies down depending on your raider's class/build. Melee works on a rock-paper-scissors system (strike beats grapple beats dodge beats strike).
The game sometimes plays like a puzzle. You have to perform certain actions in order to progress while fighting constant waves of enemies (and the occasional antagonist). The same goes to bosses. Since you can only replenish ammo meleeing enemies, expect to find them throughout boss fights.
About the game:
A western-like space opera with a colorful cast, an expansive world and a myriad of references. You can easily identify character personalities based on tropes and set your expectations accordingly. Moreover, the story so far (1st DLC) has similarly been adept of such recognizable and enjoyable writing. Additional material is available at the developer's website, including four animated comics (one for each main character).
Most negative reviews so far have concentrated on what the "reviewers" thought the game should be instead of what it is, thus demonstrating a poor management of expectations, as well as poor critical thinking and acumen.
I have had a great experience so far and I am compelled to stick around and see more. If you're feeling uneasy about this game remember that 1) the prologue is free and 2) you can buy individual adventures very cheap.

Firstly, let's adress the elephant in the room. Superhot is not a two hour game as
people would have you believe, yes, the story is short, but I really believe the true game begins after the story, so I'm going to brush past it in this review and dive into the meat and bones of THE MOST INNOVATIVE SHOTER I'VE PLAYED IN YEARS.
At first glance, you'd be forgiven for wondering what makes SUPERHOT such an INNOVATIVE SHOOTER as it simply looks like a shooter with an incredibly basic art style, here's where things get interesting though, the game focuses around one central mechanic, time only moves when you move, well, not entirely, time moves very slowly when you're stood still, but you get the idea. Now you may be thinking to yourself, that sounds like it would be incredibly easy, you would be wrong, SUPERHOT actually plays less like an FPS and more like a puzzle game, you have to strategiecly plan every move on the spot and quickly react to the enemies coming at you from all sides. You can use a combination of guns, melee weapons and even throw objects or guns to stun your enemy, before plucking their gun from the air and shooting them with it. The game also includes the ability to switch into an enemy's body, however you do loose whichever weapon he is holding, if you're smart about it, you can throw a weapon, switch into that body and then
catch it again; the time stop mechanic really does let you pull of some excelently choreographed moves, which look awesome when you see them replayed in real-time.
So aside from the story, what else do you get out of SUPERHOT, well, quite a lot actually. First of all, my personal favourite is endless mode which drops you into a level and tests you to see how many enemies you can kill without dying. After beating enough enemies on a single level, you also unlock three aditional game types for the level, these test how many enemies you can kill in 60 in-game seconds, how many you can kill in 60 real-time seconds and how quickly you can kill 20 enemies in real-time. The fast paced nature of the game means that you'll be saying 'just one more go' for hours at a time.
Next up, we have challenge modes, there are a lot of these and require you to play through all of the story levels with various modifiers in place, things like using only a katana through the whole game or not being able to throw items but being able to insta-kill people with your fists. All of these change up the gameplay drastically and you often have to rethink your whole approach.
There are many secrets hidden throughout the game and each level contains one to find. These secrets are hidden in interesting, out of the way areas that can require you to leave what would normally be considered the boundaries of the maps, this is great as it really does feel like you're getting somewhere that you're not supposed to be. There's also plenty to be discovered by messing about in the main menu, including a lovely ASCII lumberjack game.
The art-style of SUPERHOT is indeed simple, but it works brilliantly, levels are completely white, enemies are red, so they stand out and objects and weapons are black so that you can easily spot what can and can't be used. This really allows you to react quickly to your situation and pull of some excellently choreographed maneuvers.
Unfortnately there's no way to save or even record a clean replay of any of your runs, which is a real shame, the only option is to upload a soundless low-quality clip to Killstagram and while the game offers a replay editor, it only allows you to select a specific part of the replay, no option to change camera angles or anything fancy, which is probably my main gripe with the game, after making something look so impressive and choreographed it's a real shame that there's no way to make a replay look more movie-like.
If you want a shooter that makes you think a little differently then, I would definately recommend SUPERHOT as it is THE MOST INNOVATIVE SHOOTER I'VE PLAYED IN YEARS.

EDIT (after the release or the second campaign): I kinda' promised myself to revisit this review after the release of the second campaign. However, after closely watching game-play clips of the new available missions, I concluded it's not worth another purchase. The conceptual flaws are exactly the same (small cramped mission areas with repetitive objectives). I don't know if the micro-transactions problem is still as I initially described it (so please doubt that part), but the rest of my initial review gloriously still stands (unfortunately). Also, I won't be revisiting it.
Initial review:
This review is based on also playing the first available campaign. Decided to put it also here 'cause this is where people end up first, upon finding out about the game.
The good:
- Cool art style and graphics. Also quite atmospheric, yet mostly in the cut-scenes and menus. It has a Wild West feeling, reminding me of Borderlands. The humor didn't rub off on it though.
- The single player experience is stable and free of bugs. Multiplayer has some issues, which I assume to be temporary.
- Cool looking characters and the cut-scenes give color to their personalities...albeit it's a tad the same color.
- Smooth controls and cover/movement system (at least in my own experience).
- Functional and somewhat engaging rock-paper-scissors melee combat system.
The bad:
- Shallow storytelling. There is a backstory and some lore, but it's only enough to explain the shape of the world and the context of the missions. There are cut-scenes at the beginning and the end of every mission, yet they're basically more focused on trying to give color to the characters. It is however slightly more than we usually get in multi-player focused games.
- Poor mission design. The missions are short and shaped as arenas, having you repeat various actions several times (example: kill some bad guys, fill a container, kill some more bad guys, fill another container, and so on).
- Poor environment design. I know, it doesn't feel like that in the clips, but you end up running and fighting around rocks most of the time.
- Too many customization options are locked behind multi-player gameplay. Hours of it, I'm assuming. Also, there's even game content locked behind the same feature. Lore, for example. You can READ most of it ONLY if you pay with in-game currency, the same kind you use for upgrades and even unlocking new characters. OK, you don't need to actually buy the lore with real cash, but it's a truly cheap and artificial maneuver to prolong your play time.
- The single-player (solo option) is not exactly optimized. You don't get AI team mates, so on higher difficulty you can't actually make it through the missions, unless you're really patient and lucky. Most of the AI feels an urge to shoot you point blank or break your neck with its bare hands, so you get swarmed easily. With nobody to watch your back and a high sensitivity to bullets and punches (on all characters) you're toast.
- Each campaign contains only 4 missions. Considering they are short, highly repetitive in terms of gameplay and taking place in really small arenas, I strongly doubt people will spend too much time playing this game.
- The characters' builds are not really interesting, nor engaging. Each protagonist has exactly one active skill, while rest are passive (AND locked behind repetitive gameplay and/or micro-transactions). The active skills themselves are...meh. In the heat of the fight I ended up not using any of them, on any character.
- If I am to judge the full game by this one campaign, I'd say it has little content. 4 campaigns, each composed of 4 short, cramped, horde mode missions with repetitive tasks.
The really bad:
- Outrageous "in your face" micro-transactions model. While it's not a "pay to win" game, almost every customization option is locked behind the shop. Also, the prices are quite steep. If you buy the whole game and a couple of pairs of underwear, you've paid the price of a triple A game. This is not a triple A game, nor it is going to be.
The disappointing:
- They give us these really cool characters and this amazing world, yet no option to explore and experience it. Not every game has to be an RPG, but this game's model is the simplest, cheapest and laziest multiplayer model on the market. It is sad to see such capable game designers bury their obvious talent and potential under the ugly choice of developing not a game, but a cheap themed amusement park.

I'm writing this review for Steam a bit after I had played the game, but I saw it was on sale and I felt the need to say something.
I tried very hard to overlook some glaring flaws I found in my playthrough of this game, but I simply cannot excuse some things due to the price. If you're going to sell a game for $30, it needs to be much better than this product as it is in its current form. So because it is the price it is, I'm going to judge it as a product like I would for anything at that level of expected quality.
I streamed this game. I'm sitting on the recordings of my playthrough but feel like honestly discarding them because it just wasn't a good time. I tried to find good things about this game, but instead I kept finding more things that were just done poorly or were broken. I wanted to like it. I didn't like it. I tried to pass off excuses -- like maybe the devs bit off more than they could chew for such an ambitious project-- but then I realized not only was I playing a $30 game, but I was also playing someones first game -- the later of which became painfully more obvious the more I played.
The game is buggy. It has weird glitches. If I recall correctly I fell through maps. Sometimes enemies would just teleport and kill me instantly from across the arena. It has awkward combat. The color system for drawing powers is really really poorly executed and makes encounters annoying and more difficult than they need to be. I really felt like it was trying to innovate in ways that were gimmicky, unneccesary, and just not fun in comparison to other games that stick to what works and as a result are way more fun. For your first game, I really need to stress, it's not wise to try and change what works. Maybe a sequel to this could attempt innovation on a 3D fighting game, but for the first one? Stick with what works. The combat isn't fun and can be just plain unfair at times. The way enemies join the battles even is weird, just spawning in without warning immedietely after the last one is taken care of. Other games of this type at least give you some warning, a notification, maybe even a short 2 second scene of the new opponent entering the field FROM THE OPPOSITE EDGE, not from the CENTER and sometimes ON TOP OF YOU and INSTANTLY delivering a ONE-HIT KO at times.
I found myself questioning the HUD of all things and felt that there are many times it doesnt give you ENOUGH information and other times it gives you WAY too much. The characters are incredibly hard to relate to as someone with no prior exposure to the series, and I found myself really disliking them by the time I was done because I have no idea what it's like to be them or what they're doing. It's very hard to insert yourself into the plot of a game that you just can't relate to. This game has that issue big time. I dont KNOW what it's like to be a short cat dude who can summon rocks for some reason, or a wolf/tiger/person man, or an overweight chipmunk with a magical wrench.
The game didn't help me understand these characters at all and just smacked me right into their shoes without any context. Poof. I am a cat guy who summons rocks. What's my motivation? I hear voices or something? Why? Also why can I summon rocks? What an oddly specific power to have. Surely THAT will be explained. No? Alright then. Oh and I know kung fu I guess too. Oh and I had an airship. Where did I get that? Who cares. I crashed it already. Time to summon rocks and put them on things while I kick stuff. I guess my fat friend is missing or something too. I have no emotional connection to him as a player, but the dead look on my characters face through his oversized emotionless eyes tells me this is someone very dear to him. Good enough for me.
Did I mention the giant eyes have almost no expression to them? It's really glaring. Usually you give a character big eyes when you want to draw attention to their facial expressions, to help the player connect to them emotionally in the moment of the game. It's important. Doesn't happen AT ALL in this game. I dont think your character even attempts to squint at maybe something important in the environment, like a switch, or a puzzle piece. I dont remember anything like even a slight turn of the head. Even N64 games did that. This is some pretty basic stuff nowadays, especially if you want to do Zelda style puzzles.
I commend the devs for making a game about a story they are passionate about. I commend them for trying to create a new way to play these games. You tried. You made a product. It KIND OF works. As a game it is functional at best. Fans of the series it is based on will probably love it. As someone who has no idea what Shiness even is even after playing through the game a bit and having a fan explain to me the source material, I still can't really latch onto anything. The game just assumes you already understand the complete lore of the series from the first moment, and gives you no easing in any of the bizarre fantastical concepts that are very core to the story.
Anyways, I got this for free from the devs to review. This game needs to be half the price it's asking for any of these flaws to be slightly more tolerable, but even then they're still glaring flaws.
I played Shiness for 2 hours. I had enough of it by that point. I had seen enough of it to know the game was pretty much not for me. I don't really know who this game is for besides fans of the series, and even then, if you have the ability to tell what a quality product is, you still might not like it.
Solutions?
Fix the bugs.
Make the game cheaper.
Dont bother changing the combat from the weird color system for this one because you might as well make a new game. For the next game? Don't do what you guys did here. Stick with what works. Look to games that have done this style of fighting and have been successful. Don't try to change that formula until you manage to pull it off right at least once.

The game throws a lot at you right from the start. Exposition, plot threads, several main characters, seemingly neverending tutorials. It's a cluttered beginning that does not know how to pace itself. It does get better though if you're willing to commit and become accustomed to the world & its mechanics.
So let's talk about Shiness' battle system. It's essentially a beat-em-up. You string together combos & special moves, block, dodge or interrupt enemy atttacks and pummel your foes till they drop. After initial trouble of understanding what the game expects from me i started to have more and more fun with the battle system. Timing is the key here, wait for openings in enemy attacks & counter attack. The only problem is that the controls don't feel responsive at all. I cannot even pull off the very first combo you learn reliably (press X+X+RT) it only works when the game feels like it. Usually you're best off spamming the parry button in regular encounters, mix in some distance magic projectiles and insta-waste bosses with the RB special combo.
Also pro tip: Don't take on tough enemies immmediately or you will see the game over screen quite a bit. Grinding is a necessity. And keep your pockets stacked with healing items.
Something i already spent most of my time playing on is sneaking up on critters in the wild to acquire ingredients. Seriously, i love it when a game let's me do stupidly immersive crap like that. There are some puzzles though i hestitate to even call them that. Pull a lever, touch a crystal, that's it. Not exactly brain teasers. Big personal plus for me is the fact that there's a map with a quest indicator, showing you where you need to go to progress to prevent getting lost and running around aimlessly.
As far as visuals go, the art direction is absolutely gorgeous. Easily its biggest point. While the anime-ish character design could be considered an acquired taste, the cell-shaded environements simply look beautiful.
Most of the cutscenes are dynamic comic panels, some may call that lazy but i'm digging the "franchime" comic style. Even the english voice acting is surprisingly decent. Only the cinematics are fully voiced though. In-game the characters keep their original french voice clips, though they don't actually speak french but some made up fantasy language...it's oddly inconsistent. Wish they had committed to one or the other. One very specific nitpick i have is that characters fidget around too much during in-game dialogue scenes, constantly making overexaggerated poses and spouting voice clips. It got on my nerves quickly.
Your mileage may vary but to me there was far too much fantasy babble. Every nation, tribe, monster and animal has a made-up fake sounding name. I barely managed to remember the main characters' names, much less the names of any of the places i've been too. And this feeds into a significant problem i have with Shiness. The characters. They're pretty lame. Not offensivly awful or anything but just kinda meh and forgettable. And that's a big issue with what is essentially trying to mimic story driven JRPGs.
Other objective negatives:
- As you are to expect from a 3D game collision can be wonky. I managed to get stuck in a wall within the first ten minutes after starting the game. Hit detection is a bit off, no way to judge jumping precisely, camera problems. The whole game evokes feelings of PS2 era levels of clunkyness.
- Yet
a game without auto-save. Groan. Is it really that hard to program auto-save into your game?! Thankfully the game is practically littered with save spots which begs the question why not make it possible to save directly via the menu...
- Game design 101: Don't EVER put the New Game button above the Continue button in the starting menu. I'm so fed up with accidently clicking the wrong button, goshdarnit.
Despite a troubling start & persistent technical issues, Shiness has been growing on me the more i played it. Frankly every time i see Kardamom or whatever his name is get stuck in mid-air doing what i can only describe as yoga poses, it puts a big stupid smile on my face. The cutscenes are so cheesy & ridiculous, the gameplay manages to be barely competent enough to be playable, everything about it feels so amteurish and yet i'm having a blast playing it. Shiness falls into a firm "so bad it's good" category for me.
I admittedly have a soft spot for B-grade games of this sort, games like Musashi Samurai Legend, Vexx or Opoona. If games like that are up your alley there's a chance you'll get a laugh out of Shiness as well. Definitely get it on sale though, it's not worth 30 full bucks.

Disclaimer: This is less a review and more a warning to people who prefer mouse and keyboard. I haven't played the game due to the issues surrounding the controls.
I backed this game on Kickstarter, and back then it was advertised as coming out on PC too. Since I've grown up playing games with mice and keyboards, I expected this game to support this input method. Well, it kind of does, but it's all set up in such a half-arsed way that it's barely acceptable for QWERTY users and unacceptable for anyone else.
The issues in detail:
Each key is mapped to a button on a standard XBox controller.
There's no in-game key rebinding. Even worse, rebinding in the ini file is almost unworkable because of the above issue. Say you want to rebind your jump key - this is what you'll find: "Bindings=(Name="SpaceBar",Command="xbox_A |OnRelease stop_xbox_A") There's more, but this is the important part. In order to really rebind your keys, you'll have to enter the game, find out which key does what, exit the game, reconfigure, then start up the game again and hope you didn't make any mistakes.
There's no mouse in the menus.
They know these issues are a problem for people who don't use QWERTY keyboards, because they brought out a patch that rebinds keys for AZERTY users (the users still don't get a say what the keys are rebound to, though). The rest of the world and any left-handed people who find it uncomfortable to use WASD controls are left out in the cold.
The worst thing about all this is that I got one response, telling me, basically, that all of this was intended. Their excuses are that the controls went through their publisher's QA, and that rebinding was possible in the ini files and that was good enough. No, it isn't. Thus my warning to anyone interested in this game or any other Ynnis Entertainment are going to publish in the future: Make absolutely sure that you're okay with shoddy programming and lousy customer support before you buy anything from them.
