As a platformer fan cannot recommend this enough. Throwback to times when 3D platformers were good. Huge interesting levels with a unique artstyle and imaginative gameplay besides just collecting things. In a lot of places it's giving me a lot of Psychonauts vibes. It also runs super smooth, looks pretty as heck (and too damn cute :P) and it's fast and fluid to control. Overall just very refreshing and fun to play. Doesn't cease to run out of steam and amaze with all the new worlds it's thrown at me.
EDIT: Since I beat the game and I'm still playing it, thought this review deserved a re-write:
For a small indie team and a kickstarter game this is amazing. Best platformer I've played in a very long time, and it rekindled my interest in 3D platforming all over again, probably since Psychonauts.
Art direction and soundtrack are fantastic and the controls are very fluid, bouncy and never managed to annoy me through the course of the game. There's some learning curve to get used to the sliding and such but it feels rewarding to master.
I think the real highlights of the game are its creative worlds however, no world plays the same and you're really missing out if you only play through the first one. While the core gameplay stays the same, level design varies massively from open-ended, exploration focused levels with a single goal to more scripted puzzle-like interiors, mysterious forests to even horror sequences, or complete free roam in a massive mountain. For a super cutesy game there's quite a lot of dark humour in it as well, and the game never fails to make you smile. And the Hat Kid is just the best, I love her personality how she's just going around doing whatever she wants and doesn't even let such things as (spoiler?) losing her soul get in her way :P
You even get some choices in places which was surprising (I don't recall a platformer where I questioned 'if I did the right thing'), and you are free to progress the game in whatever pace you like. I was never bored and if I felt like switching to a different world, I could do so anytime.
I got a lot of Psychonauts vibes from the game in places and that's even intended with "memory vaults" at the end of certain time rifts unlocking additional backstory to the worlds and overall the level design felt similar, the time rifts might as well be mental worlds, not to mention the crow agents in various levels.
There's just something about the game that hooked me into playing it, and very few games have managed that. I wanted to 100% it immediately on my first playthrough and may even start a second just to see what I missed. It's just fun and refreshing to play for the heck of it and made with love, as games should be.
Workshop support for the game already looks solid and there's quite a few very nice user created levels. Hoping to possibly try editing some myself later.

I've only played for about an hour or so, but I already ♥♥♥♥ing love this game. I will update my review when I finish the game, but I doubt my opinion will change much.
The controls are tight and responsive, and there are a TON of game mechanics here. So far in combat (which is designed like a  2D-3D fighting game), you have dodging, blocking, parrying, multiple attack types, spells, and spell charging. Then you get outside of combat (exploration) and you have jumping (with minor yet extremely satisfying platforming), a run button, and a ton of puzzle mechanics (block manipulation, telekenisis, and more).
This game has so many features outside of combat that weren't 100% necessary to add but they went ahead and did it anyway because you can tell they wanted to make a good game. Here are some examples: 1) the run button, 2) random wildlife everywhere that you can sneak up on and collect items from, 3) solid platforming... in an RPG of all genres :P, 4) surpising enemies for initial advantages, 5) puzzles that so-far are relatively quick and fun and don't overstay their welcome, 6) ratings after each battle based on performance and might even factor into item drops, and 7) quality menus [they took some notes from the Tales series] with mission briefings and notifications for like new items and such.
As an avid Devil May Cry, DMC, (and similar action games) player, and also an RPG enthusiast, this type of game is like a dream come true. Yes there are lots of action RPGs out there (Kingdom Hearts, Crisis Core, Final Fantasy 15, The Tales Franchise, etc.), but none of them really try to achieve fast-paced, balanced, responsive, and skill-based gameplay quite like this game does. Am I saying this game has as good of combat as say DMC? No, definitely not. But you can see and feel the effort, and it really pays off and succeeds more often than not. I can't wait to finish this game, and I really hope this game gives this developer the foundation to make a sequel, because given time to further develop the battle system (especially enemy AI), I honestly feel like this style of game could become my new favorite as well as take over the mainstream market.

So 7 or so hours into this game.  And I would have to say that this is not a very well developed game.
So instead of just bashing and complaining.  These are my pro's, cons and recommended changes in future installments (if Focus Home and Enigame plan to make this a franchise)
Note:  That theses are my own opinions about the game, and may not reflect your experience with it.
Also note that regardless of how i feel, I will be completing this game, and will be updating this review as i progress through the game.
Pros:
- Interesting world:  The world is very vibrant, live and gorgeous.  The use of light cell shading and with fantastical characters makes for a really breathtaking world.  The world design is quite thought out, and a mixture of pathed (Think Witcher 2) and open world (think Witcher 3) is blended nicely.
- Pros of Combat:  The use of dynamic, sem-skilled based action fast paced combat combined with a myraid of combos spells, and techniques can make combat quite fun, fast paced and enjoyable.  Albiet, you remember that you have combos, spells and techniques.
-  with 6 elements and 5 spells per element, makes for an interesting spell combinations since you can only bring into combat with you 4 equipped spells at a time.
-  Unique techniques for each of the party members.
-  Combat is a tag team match among 3 of the party members selected as your primary.  Which combined with different spells per primary, you can have a nice combinations of spells.
-  Back seated primaries arent beach warmers.  You can equip support spells to your party members, and based on set conditions set by the player will activate, like heals, status ailment cures, silencing enemies, etc.
- Final Fantasy Stylized items and equipment.  While you progress you constantly get better consumables, equipment, spells and techniques.
- Mastering.  This idea i like.  By mastering spells and techniques, you memorize them, and thus allows you to use them and newly acquired techniques.  And mastered techniques can be mastered further with more advanced versions of those techniques.
- Very generous save system.  The save system is very similar to Previous Final Fantasy installments, with designated save locations.  But they supply you with a plethora of save points, throughout the world.
Cons:
-  Lack of Exposition:  This may not be a con for everyone.  For me though, because i found the world interesting, i wish there was more exposition as to how to the world is.  When you enter it is like "Here is the world, a bunch of magical sky islands in a torrid void of swirling elemental energy.  Aaaannd Start."
-  The Characters.  I dont really care about the characters.  I understand that the characters are more for the pre-teen/teenager audience.  And by the design and character personalities that is definitely the target audience.  However, i just cant relate to their personalities.  More over, their motivations seems forced, contrived and derivative.  Some characters themselves seem annoyingly wannabe anime stereotypes.  "Fat scared nerdy kid, quick-ready to fight 'chosen one", misunderstood outlaw, Tsundere female characters, etc."  They seem very one dimensional and not much depth was put into their personality.
-  The story:  I just dont care. Now dont get me wrong, i love a good story.  Last of Us, Deus Ex. Final Fantasy 5,9,10, Chrono Trigger.  But i feel some elements of the story are very predictable.
-  The Cons of combat:
-  The Arean combat can get pretty wonky, and lost.  There is no target lock, as the fights are one-on-one tag team matches.  However, I feel this design choice limits the play. You will end up punching the air alot
-  While there is are there a large majority of spells there are only five real types just with different elements.  Buff/Heal, Single Target projectile, Aoe+ Defuff, Bigger Heal/Buff, Zone Attack.  Only thing that is changed up is the element.  The element dictates what the buff/defull are and the Zone attack layout and property (wind does a aoe knockback, earth does a straight line boulder thing, etc.).  Yes there are 30 spells, they seem rather limiting and mostly unoriginal to the next.
-  Techniques are boring.  While they are unique to the character, they are the same set of combinations across all the characters (kick+charge, punch punch+charge, punch kick+charge, and kick punch+charge.)  Now some may like this, and that is perfectly fine.  For me however, i like a bit of variety.
-  If you cant dodge a wrench you cant dodge death.  This game is unforgiving in terms of lack of dodging and parrying.  Normally i would have this in the pros as i love skill based defense and offense.  However, some enemies are absolutely ridiculous (even at low levels) and there are times where one missed dodge and you are stunned locked until that character's death.  There is a difference between being fairly unforgiving (for examples Dark Souls 3) and just plain unbalanced.  In Shiness, its more on the unbalanced side
-  Speaking off - Very unbalanced combat.  This game is like "Ok Billy time to take those training wheels off, and get in to that BMX Wold Championship Race. Leave the helmet here."  The combat difficulty skyrockets on normal enemies. Now this may feel this way to me because i just might be a crap player.
- Poorly Optimized - I run a pretty beastly computer playing this, and it lags, the audio quality is not all that great in the comic panel cutscenes, and overall a bit laggy.
-  Uninspired puzzles or annoying puzzles with no prior foreshadowing.  How let try to explain without spoiling anything.  There is a puzzle where you have to use Chad's poop boulders, and i spent over an hour trying to figure out this pretty simple looking puzzle, only to find that that the whole time, another character can use his Telekinesis to move the the poop boulder's that Chad laid out.  This was never explained, foreshadowed or expected.  Now. You could say "hey, why didn't you try to experiment earlier"  Because the telekinesis character just joined your party.  It is the first mission with him.  And Porky cant interact with your stuff, how was i to expect that.
-  Make sure you kill everything around you before triggering a cutscene.  Because if an enemy tries to engage combat when you do a pan out area view/cutscene, you end up in a deadlock and your game freezes (lost over an hour of progress just to that)
-  Chapter Level caps.  Yes, this game has level caps at each chapter.  While i dont personally have a problem with that, however, if i kill a the Chapter 1 end boss and i am already at max level for that chapter (lvl 20), i lose that Exp from the kill and from the mission.  Which is bullcrap in my opinion.
-  This is a personal con, When you equip new gear, your character looks the same.  I personally like to see my character grow and progress on a visual scale.  At level one hes wearing hobo clothes and level 100 wearing Full Plated, horned, spiked demon killing armor with a dragon head for a shield and the dong of god as his sword.
Recommendations:  (These are for me personally for my own tastes)
-   Add more than one enemy at a time, and add in target locking.  For me it would make combat more dangerous and more fairly unforgiving if i screw up.  I forget a dodge and how like 3 monsters repeatedly punch me in the junk.
-    A better variety of spells.  I mean the game pretty much steals its inventory system from Final Fantasy.  Why not the an improved version of their magic system too.
-    Be a bit less anime-ness.  Now there is alot of good anime out there, and a lot of good anime games out there.  But Shiness really hits it hard, that it wants to be a JRPG anime game, when it is clearly isn't.  I understand it is a style, but they mimiced that style very poorly.
-    Better Balancing and better progression based difficulty scaling

This is one of those games I'd like to give a score between "recommend" and "not recommend" because there are parts worth experiencing for sure.
Pros:
- Gorgeous world, nicely realized and fleshed out enough to fit the story.
- Good soundtrack, very fitting.
- Hand-drawn comic panels for cut scenes are beautifully drawn.
- The characters are well-enough animated and the voice acting is sufficient.
- Engaging enough story to keep my interest for 20 or so hours.
- Frequent save points (where you fully heal) are not only nice, they're an absolute necessity given the ridiculous difficulty of the battle system.
- Lots of really good secrets and encouraged exploration, especially as your "super power" (discussed below) are expanded.
Cons:
- Incredibly buggy. Many times I had to restart because I got into a situation during a battle that I couldn't hit the opponent and they couldn't hit me, so the battle would never end. I also fell through the ground once. Also, it really sucks to equip the discipline that "immunizes" its wearer "against poison" and still be poisoned in battle. Yay.
- The battles are BAD. The system is fighting-game like, which is a cool idea (one I've wanted to see for a while, which is why I backed it on Kickstarter), but who wants to play a fighting game where the enemy can trap you in a combo you can't escape and deplete your life bar? Super fun, right? This is especially true for the elite soldiers' spin move where, if you get caught in it, there's nothing you can do for about eight or nine hits...which kills almost any character not at full health. This single incredibly obnoxious move has made me restart at a save point more times than I remember. This is the primary reason the battle system does not genuinely feel like a fighting game to me.
- The controls are not responsive. There are animations that need to complete before new moves can be queued up during battle, which is impossible to judge because there is so much going on during battle. Also, the "block" button, which is CRITICAL, is so hard to judge the timing of and the window is so small that it's not particularly effective. I die so often it's ridiculous. Every "random" battle I end up having to heal with items after because so much damage is dealt to my characters.
- The camera is bad. Fully rotateable 3D worlds almost always have terrible cameras, but this one is worse because you need to be able to manipulate it during fights. Also, who wants to have to worry about the camera during a fight? Yes, there's an auto-aim (which, for smaller character models, essentially puts the camera in the ground), but I don't want to have to remove my buttons from the attack/magic controls to do that. Unless I'm stuck in an enemy combo, then I have all the time in the world. EDIT: Found the option to auto-focus the camera. Let's see if that fixes things. EDIT: It helps with some issues and makes other things worse, especially when fighting against large bosses.
- The enemies' AIs are too good at predicting your moves.
- The UI is clunky, and there's too much going on in the menu. Also, since each character gets to equip its own set of items to use during combat, unless you spend time memorizing the icons or simply set every character's items to be the same, it's very hard to remember what item is assigned to which directional button. Additionally, there were weird UI choices made (the animation for switching characters that adds extra unnecessary time to mundane tasks, the lack of a "best fit" option for equipment which forces you to re-optimize every few save points).
- There are a series of mechanics I found completely unnecessary. There's a good amount of incredibly easy platforming, along with sneaking, catching little animals to collect items, and the silly super powers that each of the characters has to solve puzzles were a waste of time. Just a bunch of feature bloat, in my opinion, but admittedly I do like more streamlined gaming experiences, even ones that last 15+ hours. EDIT: These grew on me by the end of the game.
- All the playable characters are male, which may limit the audience a bit. EDIT: This is no longer true as of about 85% of the way through the game, but by that point who cares?
I'm debating finishing the game at all. I have about three hours left, but the battles have become insane. I could probably grind for a few hours and make my stats as high as they need to be, but at this point I dislike the battle system so much I just can't do it. Changed from a bare recommendation to a not recommended. I just can't do it.
EDIT: I did end up finishing the game. Grinding helped a lot, as did spending the time to memorize the item icons. The cake items were key (I simply spammed Hyper moves for the two final fights). I changed my recommendation to "Yes" after completing it, but I recommend this only to hardcore JRPG fans who are looking for a decent story with unique fighting mechanics and a lighthearted cast of characters.

TL;DR: The Howler is a slow, extremely tedious game that will test your patience and relies on an art style that doesn't compliment nor is complimented by either the gameplay or the sound design, causing frustration (did I mention that you gotta wait for everything, even bringing the pause menu is slow) especially when using the gimmick, sound-based control feature.
The Howler is another gimmick "arty" indie game that hides its more than shallow and lackluster gameplay behind supposedly stunning art and visuals; which I normally have no problem with but in this case the graphics are far from gorgeous:
I presume it's supposed to fit into a certain art style given that (quote from the game's store page) "All art used in the Howler was meticulously created by classically-trained experienced painters." but this art style is not meant for games, it just doesn't work and looks like a scanned colored pencil piece of drawing. It has terrible affordance and does a very poor job at showing what element is going to pop the balloon and what is just part of the background.
Still going on the art: the sound design is dull and repetitive, as if they forgot to implement any sound and rushed it at the last minute.
I will however admit that the first time the balloon approaches the iron Wolf, and the jaw opens with a deep, metallic sound, it was pretty cool.
The gameplay, even though not the most important part in this kind of game, barely exists: it's roughly clicking and waiting with little challenge other than testing your patience.
The sound control gimmick (note that I'm consciously using the word gimmick rather than feature) is forgettable. It's not bad, but it's far from good. It's forgettable for the very reason that it has little to no gameplay to be applied on!
And regarding the level design, I'm hesitant whether it has been made by someone with little experience or someone simply lazy: it's over-simplistic and very repetitive.
As a conclusion I'd like to address some errors in the store page user-defined tags:
- Adventure: No. It's certainly not an Adventure game.
- Simulation: I can see why this tag, but it barely simulates anything.
- Strategy: Oh please, strategy? No. Strategy is term that defines long-term thinking and process. Even the word "tactical" would be more fitting here.
- Action: Ahah... If your definition of Action is: click-wait-click-wait-wait-wait-click... then yes, maybe.
- Shoot 'Em Up: Oh come on! Now that's just blatant lies.
- Sports: What the f...
- Puzzle: Nope. The Howler is very simplistic so no thinking requiered.
- Difficult: No. Tedious.
I give this game the rating of 15/100

This is not in any way, shape, or form intended to be a rage letter towards the developers. I fully understand that sometimes, we get the item or object we ordered and it isnt exactly what we expected. Sometimes it is a bug, glitch, or malfunction within the shipping. And I get this. But what I was blown away with from the provided performance WITHIN the software itself, was very rough and not a great experience.
My problems started right off the bat. In the game launcher, when you were suppose to select New Project, etc. the game-provided clicker was not corresponding correctly with your mouse's clicker. I had to put my mouse roughly an inch below the button to be able to click it.
Thinking this was a launcher induced problem, I decided to ignore it. After opening the application and getting into the full window with the settings, depth, brushes, etc. I continued to have more problems.
- The "Fullscreen" window, is not fullscreen. It is a window that does take up the FULL SCREEN, but can be clicked and dragged around your display. This was very hard to deal with when attempting to place the clicker (that as I said before, had to be put in a certain area to be able to click the given button) and accidentally grabbing the window itself.
- With the mouse clicker issue, I was not able to use the remaining two buttons on the bottom of the left side bar, because my real mouse (where I had to place it) was technically off of this "Fullscreen" window, so it wouldnt function with the game. Quite hard to explain, but I hope you get the point.
- The game seems to have a bit of drag, especially after placing down a certain tile of land or water, as it begins to slide in random direction as you attempt to guide the landpiece the opposite way.
- Several buttons within the side bars seemed to be unfunctional, even after being clicked by the real game clicker, so land was much more difficult to create.
Coming to believe there would have been many more bugs as I came around to playing, I unfortunately had only been interactive with the software for five minutes before deciding to quit using it as a whole.
I hope this review was a good guide to those who are thinking about purchasing the software. It really is your choice, because my product might have been especially bugged compared to others. As an analogy I used in the beginning of the review, it is like shipping. Once it comes to your door, it could have been hurt in the factory process, shipping process, or even handling process. So you never really know how the software performs for you as an individual, until you try it.
Thank you for reading the review.

the basic premise is this: You are random Jonny No-Face piloting a hot-air balloon, and you have to steer it from A to B, maybe dropping off a package every once in a while. you can only control upward motion, relying on air currents to steer you left and right through this steam-punk-esque balloon adventure. so to progress, you have to put your balloon in a specific air current, all the while dodging buildings, hazards and fighting your own flawed sense of timing.
the first few missions are rather easy, with them being simple tutorials to introduce you to mechanics. around level 5 is where the journey into keyboard-forcefully-lodged-in-monitor fury begins, as you have to continously thread the needle across this artistically-drawn cityscape.

AMAZING game,
As a developer, I find myself seeing the flaw in engines all too easily, but I love surivial type games, and every once in a while I come across something like this game.  No rules, no handholding tutorial levels, just you and the wolves from day one, awesome concept!  Also, its a great credit to the dev team that actions are intuitive enough not to require all that to learn how to play.
Cons:
The kind of things you find in alphas, some of the textures tear, and the shawdows can be a little funky.  The 2 test maps are getting a little old after almost 40 hours, but I get that this is an alpha and its a work in progress.  The wolf pathing and AI logic is a little rudimentary for now, they basically beeline for you at semi slow speed (no pack logic?)
Pros:
The atmosphere is like no other game I've played, you really feel a sense of solitude while playing.  Whoever did the stylized look and feel deserves commendation, just surreal enough to feel like a dream, excellent!  The weather effects are not only well done, but directly impact you, also very well done.  The music is subtle and haunting, and really adds to the atmosphere a great deal.
For anyone that is sick of Day-Z and is looking for an alternative, this is your game.  Not once, in the 40 hours or so I've played so far has the game crashed on me or had any fatal errors, a testament to how complete an "Alpha" we are dealing with here.  I LOVE the sandobx mode, please continue to grow it in scale!!  To me, this is almost better than the idea of the story that I suppose is coming in futures releases, I'm prefectly content exploring in the snow without the pressure of goals or checkpoints or any of that nonsense.  Also, what a GREAT way to test an engine and play balancing without committing to an arbitrary "on rails" type experience too early.
Maybe not for twich gamers, but if you are looking for a well paced survival experience you owe it to yourself to try this one (and for 20$, honestly its a steal).

Being the developers of Terraria, I given them a few chances with the games they developed but Pixel Piracy did not fit my taste very well. Pixel Privateers adventures very familiar toward that game, however, it brings about elements that effectively seperates itself from its predecessor, such as a faster-pace action, solid enemies that are easier to identify and attack, and other elements that makes players want to continue.
Pros:
The game give enough time for the player to become versed with the terms of the world.  Initially starting out to be a very easy runthrough of the game, the Tutorial is a very basic but extremely necessary component of the game, explaining detail that often would have been too complex for the player to grasp on their own. Additionally from the get-go, the game gives you enough crewmates to manage battles and task that is easy to grasp and understand at the onset. The loot-based perspective adds a lot to the game, as find a weapon that is quite stronger then the other previous weapons found is always satisfying to say the least. Moreso, players can chooose to clone a weapon at a percentage-success rate that will allow more than one of the crewmates to have access to those weapons, which allows the player to progress through the game without being farming the same level over again, a thorn with many loot-based games.
Secondly, the ability to change the difficulty at the whim of the players discression allows the player to decide how complex they want their battles to be; be warned, enemies found at the higher difficulties are enough to descimate the least-prepared players wandering at the difficulty level. I find that the amount of item drops are necessary for what the game is trying to achieve; as such, I have no complaints on that end.
Cons:
For the amount of time I spend with the playthough, gold seemed scarse until I was able to click on the the computer screen on the planets and ended up with $50,000 in my storage, with more comming as I continued to search. This amount seems to be a bit too much as I was able to buy as much as I please without limit, which it should not be THAT forgiving to acquire gold. Additionally, having my shield units sustain aggro with some of the monsters did not seems as effective as my units in the back were getting pelted by the monster that completely bypassed my shields.  As other players have suggested, the text is a bit too small, and sometimes certain explanation did not come accross clearly to me, which an explanation of how to access certain options or a help menu to go over some of the items covered in the tutorial would have been excellent.
Lastly, I would recommend this game as it is worth the purchase.

This game takes a bit to get the hang of it, but once you start figuring things out, it's so rewarding. There are a lot of resources to manage, there's plenty of things to take into consideration as far as keeping your people happy and healthy, and it's a mostly satisfying experience. The reason I say mostly statisfying is that there are some quirks that I find a little frustrating - people who are supposed to be working on building will ALL leave their job when you try to lay down road, and all trek the whole way over just to hit one square before slowly wandering back to their task. There's also a lot of time spent where they're not working which can be annoying when you need houses built and quickly. Overall, though, the game is a lot of fun and I like growing my settlement.

This is a free demo for a paid game, which is rare these days and should be praised for that fact alone.
This is also a high-production game with a relatively unique concept, which is also a very rare thing to see these days outside of the low-investment indie scene. Most AAA or even mid-range developers avoid such risks, so again the devs should be praised for their exploration and novelty, regardless of how the game turns out in the end.
As for the actual content of the game itself, I find that it shines in some aspects and fails miserably in others. But the game is definitely capable of becoming something really great if feedback is adressed and new conent added (which the game already includes a roadmap for built into the UI).
The game is basically Player vs Environment & Player. It plays like a co-op PvE shooter, but with the added challenge of an enemy player thrown into the mix. The enemy player gets rewarded the better they are at stopping you from your objective, while the co-op players get rewarded based on how far they make it into the mission and how fast they complete it.
Mechanically the game feels solid most of the time, but some mechanics such as the auto-cover system aren't as solid as they could be. While they clearly intended for auto-cover to streamline the experience, it often gets in the way and doesn't react the way you expect or need it to.
Visually the game looks great and seems to runs well on my machine, though I have a relatively high-end system.
Overall I'm intrigued and interested in seeing how this game develops, and with this being a free demo, I highly recommend checking it out yourself and seeing if it interests you as well.

A great game with a few flaws, I'll try to make like a midget and keep it short:
The Good - A very well thought out peaceful and "old school" city management simulator. There are options at the start of the game so you can make things easier or harder and it uses a seed generation system so you can play a different map every time (or find one you like and play it again at another time).
The Bad - The achievements are only obtainable if there are no mods installed / active, leaving the games "less desirable" parts as something you'll just have to deal with untill you've gotten all the achievements. (If they don't interest you then you can just install the mods from the steam workshop from the start.)
The Ugly - The games "less desirable parts" are relativley small, but unfortunatly have a knock-on effect that can get very annoying at later stages. The worst part is that there are fixes for them in the steam workshop but you can't use them without disabling achievements.
Ugly A - The games resosorce management system is bad, it's not awfull, but it makes things difficult at later stages. Anything that can be put in a stockpile will be put there (except for when it doesn't, it *might* go to a market). Anything that can be put in a market or storage barn flips a coin to decide which one it goes in (unless it gets put in one to be taken out and put into the other.... or goes somewhere else). Sometimes things need to be picked up to be put in *something* to be taken out to go to a market so it can be taken out by someone else to go to thier house.
Luckily this is all done automatically so you don't need to worry about enourmous command ques for everyone, but don't think they'll take the resorce to the *nearest* container, they'll seemingly pick one at random and there's no way of choosing what goes where. So the part of your city with most storage, food production and population might be the first area to starve, even if you have 10,000 food in storage (that's a extreme example, but the larger your city gets the less control you have over your own resorces).
Ugly B - People will use coal as winter fuel, which doesn't sound too bad, but there's a whole system made SPECIFICALY for winter fuel, it's called FIREWOOD. Foresters huts can infinetly plant / cut down trees, one of the uses for logs are firewood that people can use to heat thier house in the winter, there's even a specific window labaled "Fuel" that shows nothing other than your firewood stock. Coal can only be obtained from mines and trading.....
Mines are big, slow and cannot be removed once built, so once you've fully mined a mine that large area can NEVER be used for anything ever again. They can only be built in a mountain and they can also be used to mine iron (they SHARE the mine, so mining iron will deplete both iron and coal from that mine). Coal is needed to make the best tools in the game, you will need a constant supply at later stages taking up more and more unrecoverable areas. Trading for them is too unpredictable and is expensive, so coal is very valuable and firewood is easily available, at later stages a large city will take most / all of your coal every year leaving you without tools but an abundance of firewood.......
Ugly C - People don't seem to care about roads, once your city gets large they'll just walk next to the road or just wander off into the unknown when they could move MUCH quicker by sticking to the road. It doesn't sound like much but when you've got a lot of people (1000+) moving a long way you don't want people dragging thier *** when it comes to harvest and you need ALL of your food, not half of it and losing the other half to the winter because they insisted on walking through fields insted of roads.
That said, it's still a good game, good enough to warrant overlooking these flaws, the steam workshop has a fix for all of the ugly points and probably more. I haven't looked too far into it yet because I still have a few achiv's left to get, so I'm stuck with the ugly points that are VERY annoying at this stage, but I can't wait untill I have them all and can use the steam workshop.
Check gameplay footage on youtube and do some research on it before you buy it, but I'd say it's a pretty good city management game, worth it, definitly when it's on offer.

This is one of my favourite multiplayer FPS games that I have ever played and I highly recommend this to anyone looking for a semi-realistic WW2 shooter. I have to praise this game for it's gameplay, atmosphere and the community.
First and foremost comes the gameplay. I have to admit that I haven't played the first RO game. The gameplay is solid for an FPS and the controls are familiar to anyone. To be honest, I find it difficult to explain the gameplay considering RO2 fills a specific niche which makes it hard to find common comparisons. But, If you are used to playing twitch based shooters or arena types, that is where you have to change your mindset with the game. The most important thing to know is that this game rewards teamwork. The learning curve is a little bit higher than your average Call of Duty game however it does pay off in the end.
The atmosphere is what I enjoy the most about this game. Tripwire Interactive got things right on so many fronts that it's hard to explain to someone why RO2 is such a great game. The music is very well done and adds to the atmosphere when in game. At first I thought that it was silly to have music while playing, however the music is never invasive and manages to always feel "right". The in game sounds and the distances all feel correct and in the background you can always hear those faraway shots and falling arty. However those shots are actual players fighting it out. The sounds in general were well done. After the sounds comes the visuals. I will be honest that the visuals aren't CRYSIS tier worthy, however they pull off a very nice looking and well polished game regardless. The buildings all feel correct for it's time and they never feel too "clean" which helps capture the feeling that you are currently in the battlefield. All in all it's very good.
Finally, the community. I find that in games where friendly fire is available, there would always be that small group of people who would grief. I personally have never had that problem where a griefer or a group of them could ruin a game. Other people may disagree, however this is my own personal experience with the game. Another thing is that the community tends to be friendly to all players even new ones. Of course there would be that one person who wants to win and complains that new steam sale players are ruining "muh games", however, all in all everyones friendly and usually answers questions regarding gameplay help. One strange thing about the community however is how for some reason, once you join a side, you feel as if you belong to the team. Games such as Battlefield 3/4 or the CoD series had team modes, however what ended up happening is either multiple groups just doing their own thing or having one man army situations. With this game, of course there are people who do that, but everything feels more focused and together. The person in front of you running towards the objective while machine guns are cutting down your allies. You end up not caring for your supposed KD ratio but end up wanting to win it for the team.
TL;DR: Great sounds/music, pretty good visuals but combine with sounds well for atmosphere. Solid FPS gameplay. Great community. 9/10 breddy dam gud

My nostalgia and love for the genre aside, it's hard to contain just how happy I am to see 3D platformers starting to thrive again as indy games. After the noble but flawed effort of Yooka Laylee we have this, which was announced waaaaaaaaaaay back when Kickstarter was in full swing for reviving unloved genres.
A Hat in Time is an indy game that managed to mask its shortcuts with immense polish and loads of a loads of character. The initial level of Mafia Town doesn't really click, and it's clear (and known if you followed the development of the game at the start) that this was a very basic concept that stayed there. However, the platforming is fun and the controls are fantastic, so you press on. The next areas are a movie studio where you're caught between two rival producers trying to make very different movies, and a spooky forest where you'll encounter Tim Burton-esque ghosts and a genuinely tense and scary manor house. These sets of levels are a joy to play through and drip character from every surface. They provide the backdrop to some fantastic platforming setpieces and hilarious jokes that keep you invested. The boss fights are great too, with plenty of frantic split second jumps to keep your fingers flying.
The fourth area is a treat, and really shows what the developers can do in terms of creativity and artistic skill. I won't go into too much detail, but it's a beautiful open sky platforming bonanza.
All in all in spite of it's slightly short length and patchy areas here and there, the game is great time and not to be missed if you yearn for the days of simpler games with littlee objective beyond giving the player a fun challenge and some cosy times.

Having previously played Generals to death I was very excited when CNC3 came out.  It delivered better graphics and better netcode (the franchise's previous game "Generals" would crash every other time in multiuplayer) but the gameplay was a huge step backwards, with the only required tactics being to build tanks which could easily defeat defenses, infantry, air units and other tanks.  There was no need to build anything else and as a result the game became very simplistic and predictable.
The AI in CNC3 was also a step backwards from Generals.  It didn't attack with mixed units most of the time, and it rarely defended it's base at all.  When it did it often used just one type of defense, which of course makes for an easy attack.
Out of frustration, a friend and I worked on a mod with the help of the rest of the TALON Clan.  The TALON Mod made a lot of changes to the game that made it much more balanced, fun, challenging and enjoyable to play.  Look for it on ModDB.

I've only played about 45 minutes of this but so far, it's great at teaching. It's best to have a notepad/paper and a pen handy to write things down, the game will actually tell you to go do that if you don't have one there already. The game takes things slow and encourages good ways of putthing things into memory. It starts off simple, teaching you the vowels with their pronounciation, equivalent characters in English and character in Hiragana for each one. It lets you learn things and provides options to repeat stuff so you don't have to worry about missing things and if you note things down as it tells you to, you'll start to pick them up fairly quick.
I like how it teaches you how to read, speak and write Hiragana instead of just focusing on just one of those as a lot of other things seem to try and do. It also helps that it acknowledges learning another language is daunting and difficult so I feel I can trust in it more. It defintely helps with holding my attention.
Another thing I'm loving so far is that it's doing all of this within a traditional turn based RPG. So far it's fairly simple stuff for those elements but where it really stands out is that the enemies are Hiragana characters (potentially words and other stuff later on, I'm not far in) so that in addition to attacking, defending, support and item use, you have to actually understand the enemy in a very literal sense to damage them.
That really helps with learning as it gives you just enough pressure to keep your brain working and the things you're learning will start to fit into place as a side effect of playing. Instead of learning a bunch of stats and different elements or whatever enemies are weaker too, it's another language. The game is also just fun so far and both the characters and the story are quite charming. This isn't a game that's concent with boring the player.
It's not perfect as the dialogue text characters, the on screen characters and the how to draw/write animations for characters are all a little different to each other so it can get a little confusing when learning the correct way to write stuff but I guess that gets you used to different writing styles and it didn't get in the way much, I just wanted to make sure I was writing things down perfectly. That aside, I'm pleased with it so far and I would recommend looking into this if you are interested in learning Japanese.

In Outlast you play as a journalist who thinks it's a good idea to go and explore an apparently abandoned insane asylum. After you're in, you begin see to blood and bodies everywhere and discover that the asylum is not abondoned at all.
Ok, let's get something clear: Outlast it's not the best horror nor the scariest (i think that title still belongs to Amnesia), but it's a damn good one, one of the best you'll ever play.
Outlast plays like Amnesia and the Penumbra series, you're not given any weapons and you can't fight back. Instead you're given a camera, which you can use to see in the dark and record strange stuff (only when the game allows it). The camera it's not just a gimmick, it adds to the atmosphere in the game, giving it a very cinematic feel.
Great amosphere, something i really appreciate in horror games. Once you're forced to go into the dephts of the asylum it's when the game it's at it's best. Very sinister and grim. Also there's blood. LOTS AND LOTS of blood. Everywhere you go, there's always mutilated dead bodies and huge amounts of blood. In one part there's literally a fountain of blood. Don't get me wrong, i like my horror games bloody, but in Outlast it just gets ridiculous sometimes.
A great audio design can, sometimes, make a horror game. Outlast is no exception. Fantastic job here, so be sure to play with a good set of speakers or headphones! The voice acting and the music are also great.
Surprising how amazing the graphics are for an indie game. The asylum, the lightning and the textures are impressive. Some of the character models not so much. There's for example that huge s.o.b. that keeps hunting throughout the game, once you see him up close (wich is very early in the game), looks a little silly.
After all that praise, why isn't Outlast the ultimate horror game? Well, the game is very short, about 4 hours long, maybe a couple more of you get stuck or die a lot. But it's not just that, the game loses steam after a couple of hours. Sure, running and hiding away from enemies can still be thrilling, but stops being scary, specially after getting killed a couple times. Also there are the cheap jump scares, some more effective than others.
Outlast while far from being the best horror game you'll play, it's still worth playing.

It's a good, fun JRPG game. The story follow many typical elements characteristic of the Tale Of franchise, so it does feel a bit stale if you've played any of their other games, but the characters are what really make the story pop. Sorey & and his group of friends aren't necessarily the most unique in the industry, or even the series itself, but they struggle and interact and deal with hard decisions and consequences realistically and with great depth and emotion to them.
The gameplay itself is pretty standard - real time battles where you need to keep an eye on your health and magic levels while mashing buttons in certain combo orders to attack and dodge and so on. If you've played other Tale of games, particuarly Tales of Xillia, this will be pretty familiar to you. The weapon system is absoluely a hardache, though, and ridiculous to work with.
The music has some nice stand out arrangements, the usual "type" of music that Tale of has is there, and it's defnitely good and pleasant to listen to. But some of the best tracks are from Go Shiima, who adds much to the score with original and amazing songs.
The length of the game is about 40 to 60 ish hours, depending on how much time you devote to weapons, side quests (some of which become mandatory to progress the plot towards the end), and so on. It runs a bit on the short side as far as JRPGs go, but it's still a good game all round. It's by no means perfect, but if you like watching a great cast of characters interact and joke around and deal with extremely difficult situations, I'd recommend giving a go.

Matter being used to replicate items you have (Or revive/clone your crew). Found a really great armor you want to apply to all your toons? Sure, toss it in, spend some matter and now your crew can share that gear.
The strategy isn't super deep (AFAIK), and is more or less limited to "Melee front, snipers back and use your assault's abilities a lot" Sometimes you'll pause to use your melee's taunt to pull aggro or stealth your Sniper to sleep a distant threat. Overall, if you enjoy Dungeon romps set in space, with a 'heavy' emphasis on loot, humor and a good time. Get this.

By far the best Early Access game I've ever played. This game is gorgeous, and simply exploring the vast expanse of Canadian wilderness becomes a main driving point as every new cabin or site you discover is like some sort of picturesque painting. I've amassed a considerable screenshot collection, utilizing the handy HD Screenshot (Hud Disabled) hotkey. The beauty is enchanting, but also deadly--which is another great aspect of this game. No zombies or otherworldly threat. Just nature's bites--the cold and the wolves. Those damn wolves...
Surviving is a great challenge in either starting point, making each decision important since it is life or death with every hour that passes. A lot of games tout "Survival" as a selling point, but none have managed to really be an enjoyable experience to me until I played The Long Dark. I think the dev team have managed to strike a near-perfect balance of challenge and reward. Note that I've only played this on the standard diffuclty level--I've heard that the hardest difficulty adds more wolves... I'm confident they will change that and challenge the player some other way, as the wolves are notorious♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in this game. Like I mentioned, however, I think standard strikes a great balance and has been a lot of fun.
Be aware that there is currently no narrative story mode--Sandbox mode alone is worth the price during a sale. Throughout the play, you'll encounter hints as to what the story may be... I still haven't explored every last bit of the lands yet, and now they are going to double the size of the explorable terrain! So, I'll just leave off with that--I'm impressed with this game!!

A great game with a few flaws, I'll try to make like a midget and keep it short:
The Good - A very well thought out peaceful and "old school" city management simulator. There are options at the start of the game so you can make things easier or harder and it uses a seed generation system so you can play a different map every time (or find one you like and play it again at another time).
The Bad - The achievements are only obtainable if there are no mods installed / active, leaving the games "less desirable" parts as something you'll just have to deal with untill you've gotten all the achievements. (If they don't interest you then you can just install the mods from the steam workshop from the start.)
The Ugly - The games "less desirable parts" are relativley small, but unfortunatly have a knock-on effect that can get very annoying at later stages. The worst part is that there are fixes for them in the steam workshop but you can't use them without disabling achievements.
Ugly A - The games resosorce management system is bad, it's not awfull, but it makes things difficult at later stages. Anything that can be put in a stockpile will be put there (except for when it doesn't, it *might* go to a market). Anything that can be put in a market or storage barn flips a coin to decide which one it goes in (unless it gets put in one to be taken out and put into the other.... or goes somewhere else). Sometimes things need to be picked up to be put in *something* to be taken out to go to a market so it can be taken out by someone else to go to thier house.
Luckily this is all done automatically so you don't need to worry about enourmous command ques for everyone, but don't think they'll take the resorce to the *nearest* container, they'll seemingly pick one at random and there's no way of choosing what goes where. So the part of your city with most storage, food production and population might be the first area to starve, even if you have 10,000 food in storage (that's a extreme example, but the larger your city gets the less control you have over your own resorces).
Ugly B - People will use coal as winter fuel, which doesn't sound too bad, but there's a whole system made SPECIFICALY for winter fuel, it's called FIREWOOD. Foresters huts can infinetly plant / cut down trees, one of the uses for logs are firewood that people can use to heat thier house in the winter, there's even a specific window labaled "Fuel" that shows nothing other than your firewood stock. Coal can only be obtained from mines and trading.....
Mines are big, slow and cannot be removed once built, so once you've fully mined a mine that large area can NEVER be used for anything ever again. They can only be built in a mountain and they can also be used to mine iron (they SHARE the mine, so mining iron will deplete both iron and coal from that mine). Coal is needed to make the best tools in the game, you will need a constant supply at later stages taking up more and more unrecoverable areas. Trading for them is too unpredictable and is expensive, so coal is very valuable and firewood is easily available, at later stages a large city will take most / all of your coal every year leaving you without tools but an abundance of firewood.......
Ugly C - People don't seem to care about roads, once your city gets large they'll just walk next to the road or just wander off into the unknown when they could move MUCH quicker by sticking to the road. It doesn't sound like much but when you've got a lot of people (1000+) moving a long way you don't want people dragging thier *** when it comes to harvest and you need ALL of your food, not half of it and losing the other half to the winter because they insisted on walking through fields insted of roads.
That said, it's still a good game, good enough to warrant overlooking these flaws, the steam workshop has a fix for all of the ugly points and probably more. I haven't looked too far into it yet because I still have a few achiv's left to get, so I'm stuck with the ugly points that are VERY annoying at this stage, but I can't wait untill I have them all and can use the steam workshop.
Check gameplay footage on youtube and do some research on it before you buy it, but I'd say it's a pretty good city management game, worth it, definitly when it's on offer.

The Long Dark is a survival simulation game where the protagonist - Some random person that you'll never see a 3rd person shot of - is stranded in the worst place possible... Canada! As one of the coldest countries in the world, the Canadian Winter has just set in, and it's bound to be a long one. As your plane crashes in the northern Canadian wilderness, you must scavenge resources and clothing, kill or be killed, and eventually resort to eating a can of dog food to stay alive (If you make it that far).
The graphics, although unrealistic, are beautiful, and yield a great atmosphere that a Canadian like myself can really appreciate. The soundtrack is beautiful as well, and when a song starts randomly playing, your mood can change quite quickly.
Now, the way the game's sandbox mode works is that you spawn in either Mystery Lake or Coastal Highway, and must discover locations and collect whatever resources are there, and if you're encumbered, whichever are most valuable. A hunting knife or hatchet is an absolute necessity, you won't survive 10 days without one. A hunting rifle is also a bonus, especially when you get more than 2 rounds for it in the whole game... Yes, that happened in my first time making it past day 5. I survived to day 12.
Wolves will be your worst enemies after the bitter cold, the crippling hunger, and the painful thirst. Obviously, as a Canadian, I have never frozen to death (Though I've come quite close), but hunger is a real issue. As long as you have fire, you have water, and your sleeping bag will eliminate the possibility of dying from exhaustion. But the hunger... It seems that no matter how much food you have, it's never enough...
In my personal experience, wolves are the greatest killers, with hunger in second. I've not died from Cold, Exhaustion, or Thirst. Having just completed my 50-day run, I have a full appreciation for the sandbox mode of this game.
PROS
- Beautiful atmosphere and music
- Realistic stats (Need 8 hours of sleep, about 2 litres of water, and about 2000 calories a day)
- Moving around consumes calories, increasing the realism. Harvesting meat from animals also consumes calories, so you can't just hope to kill a deer while at 50 calories and expect to not starve.
- Infinite replayability (Literally infinite. Some gameplays can last upwards of 100 days.)
- Crafting
- Runs smoothly on poor PCs.
CONS
- Wolves attack at the slightest provocation (Reduced realism)
- Sometimes throwing a flare at a wolf will not scare it off (I'm assuming this is a bug. A very painful bug...)
- You can sometimes be stuck without a rifle or hatchet or knife, AKA you're screwed and should just restart.
- Mother Nature hates you (Throws storms at you when you're supposed to be harvesting meat because it's SUPPOSED to be warm out!)
* Yes, that above one is a joke, it does improve the realism of the game. Doesn't change that it still sucks. *
Overall, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who is patient and can think in outside the box, and plan ahead. For any who are having difficulties with the 50-day run, I stocked up on food, firewood, and water, and essentially hibernated from day 41 to day 50. As for making it to day 41 with that much excess food... you're on your own.

Between the fast-paced twitch shooting of Call of Duty and the (often ridiculously slow and boring) shooting of ArmA, there is a glorious sweet spot of well-paced action and satisfying realism. Rising Storm / Red Orchestra 2 is that sweet spot.
You almost always die in one shot, so every movement you make must be methodical.
You almost always kill in one shot, so being quick to take aim and fire accurately is a skill that must be honed. But even a miss will make your enemy flinch.
In Hardcore Mode, your kill notifications are delayed. Did you get him? Or did he make it behind that wall? The suspense and the satisfaction is unmatched.
This game is absolutely worth your time and money. It doesn't have the polish of some other titles -- the UI is a bit messy -- but once you are standing over the corpse of your first close-quarters hip-fire kill, pondering your luck and the tragic fate of so many soldiers, you'll be glad you tried the game and addicted to the rush of countless moments like it.

Let me start by saying this game is everything I had hoped it would be.
Since backing the Kickstarter when it first opened, I have been following the posts and updates, watching the game evolve to what it is now, and I must say, I am very satisfied with the results.
That being said, allow me to address one thing that has resulted in numerous negative reviews for this game: the bugs.  It's true, there ARE bugs present, many of them game-breaking.  HOWEVER, Enigami has been working tirelessly on providing a patch that addresses these, and this patch is already available to the Beta level Kickstarter backers, and will be available for everyone else within a week (the beta testers have to see if it fixed everything and didnt introduce new bugs first).  While I am not one of these backers, I have spoken with a couple of them, and they tell me that this patch so far HAS addressed all of the major bugs and most of the minor bugs!
So, if you are concerned about the other reports of bugs in the game and not sure whether you should buy it: absolutely get the game, but if you want a bug free experience, wait a few days for the patch to release.  You *can* begin playing before then, as the larger bugs do not show their ugly faces until slightly later, but if you are one of those people that speed through a game quickly you will likely encounter some of the major bugs before the patch drops.
On to other complaints:  the combat.  From what I have seen and read, aside from bugs almost all of the complaints stem from the combat, but there are as many praises on the combat system as their are complaints.  I am one of the people that actually likes the system as it is, with only one minor complaint, which I will get to in a moment.  One of the biggest complaints I have seen about the system is that people feel it is spammy.  Let me address this by saying you only get out of combat what you put in.  It is very easy to fall into a groove early in the game and stick with the first skills you learn, as they are fairly easy to spam, however the combat system has a lot of depth to it that you only gain by mastering more disciplines as you go in the game.  Combos and spells can be swapped out, making every character unique in their playstyle, and more suited to your tastes (in fact, I strongly recommend acquiring as many disciplines as possible early, and mastering the abilities - which are mastered through use - so that you have a variety of attacks available quickly).  Some monsters are immune to some types of damage, while others require different tactics to defeat (for instance, there is a monster in the starting forest that damages YOU if you attempt to deal melee damage to it, due to its spiny shell).  That being said, it is incredibly easy to miss or be dodged or parried on ANY attack - including Hyper Attacks (which basically is the character's ultimates), meaning you have to either time your attacks carefully, or get spammy with them.  Lazy people being lazy, most people just go with the spam option, hence the complaints.
My particular complaint on the combat is that often it progresses a touch too quickly, resulting in you getting hit with a combo of attacks that render you unable to act while being hit.  This includes item useage, and the potion equivalent in this game requires heavy use.  Expect to get hit, and frequently, but dont forgot that you can dodge, parry, and counter attack (in fact, there are boss fights that REQUIRE parrying to complete, as it is the only way to actually hit the boss).  There have been some occasions where an enemy will jump to the far side of the arena and start spamming spells at me, with just enough recoil from my character between each hit that I am unable to act before the next one hits, meaning I am forced to just watch while my character looses half of his HP before I am able to recover.
I have heard rumors that the upcoming patch addresses some of the combat concerns as well, but with nothing to confirm this I am going to continue to expect the same from combat after it drops.
Now on the the good things:
I absolutely LOVE the art style.  It is bright and colorful and I constantly find myself stopping to admire the scenery.
The music is also well composed, although the starting area music started to get on my nerves before I was through (it was just a touch too repetetive, and I spent way more time there exploring etc than I probably should have), but so far no other area song in the game has had the same problem.  The music is all beautiful and well suited to the visual style of every area I've encountered yet.
Side quests!  There are PLENTY of side quests available, although they are not readily apparent.  You need to talk to every npc in every area to find all of the side quests, with the only indication that a quest is available being an exclamation mark on one or more of the dialogue options once you are already talking to the person.  There are also bounty boards, which have been very enjoyable this far, but early in the game make sure you are paying attention to the level requirement before taking on the bounty - the first bounty I attempted at level 4, and I probably shouldnt have touched it until a bit later (The critter destroyed me my first few attempts).
The puzzles:  This game is VERY puzzle driven, and the majority of the puzzles are NOT explained, nor are hints provided usually.  However, they are typically intuitive once you have tinkered with them a bit (studying how the various parts of mechanical puzzles work to then understand how the overall puzzle works for instance).  Other puzzles require outside information to solve (I am referring to the infamous Princess Book Puzzle, which requires that you read the manga to solve, as there are no references in the game to the solution).
The voice acting is decently done, and the cutscenes are fantastic - both the cinematics and the comic book scenes (which I adore).
Critters - all throughout the game there are small animals (hedgehogs, squirrels, butterflies, etc) that are able to be captured for base loot.  This loot can be either sold for profit, or exchanged for good items and hard to get disciplines at merchants.  When you get near the critters, if they see you they run away, disappearing in a puff of smoke after a couple seconds of running.  You either need to sneak up on them, equip an item or discipline that renders your character invisible to a species of critter, or use one of your character's abilities, which allows you to steal loot from them from a small distance (which is different loot than the critters normal drops).  Much of this type of loot also drops in combat, so there are many ways to try to acquire the right items for trade-in at a merchant.
The story and characters:  So far, I have not advanced super far in the game, and have not had time for the plot to develop fully, but from what I have seen so far, the story is very well told.  I was hooked before I even got to the first boss.  The only thing I am unsure of is whether dialogue options actually change the outcome of events or not, but seeing how the rest of the game plays out I would guess that it doesnt matter which option you pick in most circumstances (although I can think of one that might make a difference early on, I don't know for sure as I have not replayed scenes to see how they change)  Character development proceeds at a natural pace that feels appropriate in most cases (there are a couple minor occasions early on where a character reacts to something in a way that is surprising of them, but if you have read the manga or once you advance in the game a bit it makes more sense).
THE VERDICT:
For being Enigami's first game, this game is very solid, with only the issues of bugs to ruin the experience, and this issue is rapidly being addressed.  I strongly recommend the game to any RPG lovers, as well as to people who enjoy adventure games.

A few people criticize the battle system and i really can not understand why. I played many Naruto, One Piece and Dragonball Games and i have to say i never had so much fun to fight since DBZ Budokai. Dont get me wrong - its nothing like these open area fighting systems like in Xenoverse 1 and 2 or even Tenkaichi. its basically just a small arena and thats what i like about it. Its simple but fun. You have a few different combos, 4 Combos combines with Hyper (something like Energy that is needed to make a "super" Move, many different Magic speels of different elements like Fire, Water, Light and Wind and a finishing move. You can swap beetween 3 Characters in a fight (Youll have 5 in your party in the end), you can block, dodge and parry.
You have to imagine it like the old Budokai Games where you actually had Combos to make a Kamehameha and not just press 1 or 2 Buttons (Cause the Hyper attacks feel like that). But the Magic speels are basically that (L2+ A, B, X or Y).
Even when i compare these Games now,  dont think it is like one of them. I wanted to point out that i like the old fighting systems of DBZ (Til Budokai 3) much more and this feels like it.
RPG elements are basic and simple. Youll get new clothes to make you stronger. Your party levels up after each fight equally (No matter who fights, everyone will gain EXP) and youll make your Combos Stronger.
Sometimes this game feels like a Adventure. You keep exploring new Areas and need to solve puzzles to open a Door etc. Its simple, easy and doesnt take to much time. The exploring part is actually very fun. The feeling when you finally get to the Place where you needed to go and needed 2-3 hours before to get there is amaizing. You feel rewarded to finally be there. You did so much to deserve to be there. Fighted against dozens of monsters, solved puzzles, walked through a Snowstorm, sabotaged a Bell to open up a underground path and more.
Bugs - im now at Chapter 3 (Last) and just had a single one (2D Cutscenes are like in slow motion (just Audio)). The Devs already said they look into it and want to fix it. Other than that, it is really polished in my expierence.
Overall this Game provides a very good expierence with basic elements good combined (Explore, Puzzle, Fight, Story). Nothing feels to short or to long. I admit, its not really something new but it does what it wants to do very good and i like it better than all the new DBZ, Naruto and One Piece games. Its cheap and you should definiatly get it to make sure we will get more Shiness Games!
Edit:
The End Boss is sadly nothing like the rest of the game. Fights feel fair and are fun til then. But i dont want to spoil anything, so thats all im saying.

My nostalgia and love for the genre aside, it's hard to contain just how happy I am to see 3D platformers starting to thrive again as indy games. After the noble but flawed effort of Yooka Laylee we have this, which was announced waaaaaaaaaaay back when Kickstarter was in full swing for reviving unloved genres.
A Hat in Time is an indy game that managed to mask its shortcuts with immense polish and loads of a loads of character. The initial level of Mafia Town doesn't really click, and it's clear (and known if you followed the development of the game at the start) that this was a very basic concept that stayed there. However, the platforming is fun and the controls are fantastic, so you press on. The next areas are a movie studio where you're caught between two rival producers trying to make very different movies, and a spooky forest where you'll encounter Tim Burton-esque ghosts and a genuinely tense and scary manor house. These sets of levels are a joy to play through and drip character from every surface. They provide the backdrop to some fantastic platforming setpieces and hilarious jokes that keep you invested. The boss fights are great too, with plenty of frantic split second jumps to keep your fingers flying.
The fourth area is a treat, and really shows what the developers can do in terms of creativity and artistic skill. I won't go into too much detail, but it's a beautiful open sky platforming bonanza.
All in all in spite of it's slightly short length and patchy areas here and there, the game is great time and not to be missed if you yearn for the days of simpler games with littlee objective beyond giving the player a fun challenge and some cosy times.

My second biggest issue with the game is the pacing. I think in my last 3-4 hours of the game that i've played has been nothing but nonstop combat. When the combat is the most unenjoyable part, this becomes a problem. I would've liked to see some more puzzles.
The third issue, while not really a big game changer, is the design of the menu UI. A good UI is one that doesn't make the user think while he navigates around it. I've never misclicked so many times on a menu UI as i did with this one. The reason is because you use like 10 inputs (RT, RB, LT, LB, D-pad, X, A) to navigate around it.
As of right now, i can't recommend this game until they polish the combat.

I dont think this game is terrible. In fact, theres a lot of strengths to the game; despite it being what I can only imagine as a first game in a multi-part series.
So lets go over those things and why I can't recommend it right now.
For starters, the graphics/artwork of  the game is rather...iffy at times, and absolutely amazing at other times. The artwork of the world around the characters is amazing, and really awesome to look at. The clouds in the background are all really well done, and the way the background looks makes it seems really awesome. Notice how I'm only saying the background? The characters themselves don't look too terrible, and the world around it doesn't seem that bad either, but they're really not that good either. So perhaps something for the devs (if they even read these things) would be just to work on the world art being similar to the background art? I dunno, it felt like the background was a different place altogether.
Nextly is the story/world itself. The story isn't terrible, not particularly interesting until about 2-3 hours into the game for me, then just interesting enough to keep me going. The ending to the game was far more interesting than most of the other story, but that could just be because some things felt like menial tasks and others felt really important but didn't do anything or took legit forever. The Snow Bloodor for the princess part took up a good portion of the game for me, and i think it was intended. For good reason 'cause to me that part was the most enjoyable and well done part for side stories and characters. As for the world, I think its pretty damn awesome, the different "shi" and the way everything is influenced by that is fun and interesting. The monsters and bosses of the world (excluding the final boss) were really well made and fun or mostly fun to fight against. There were a few clarity issues with a few of the later bosses, but I think those can be easily fixed, even if not in gameplay, there are cutscenes. King Meos was a pretty awesome boss to fight; and the giant worms made of Dark Shi (I forget their name.) look like they'd be a pain to fight but fun to fight too. Probably the only things I can think of that'd help would be to focus a bit more on characters and their interactions with each other; kinda seems strange when two people seem to not really trust each other are totally fine with each other three seconds later.
Combat! Oh boy. At first I enjoyed it, and learning the new combos made it more enjoyable, though using the combos themselves was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥for a while and actually still are outside the X, X+RB combo. It probably wasnt until about 4 or 5 hours in that the combat started to lose its charm. After completing the game I can safely say that the combat isn't really that fun to do. Maybe its that most mobs and the final boss in particular all have some form of Super Armor that lets them ignore your attacks while they attack you. Maybe its the fact that they all attack faster than your characters move and tend to spam magic (ranged combat in a super close range combat focus) like they have no physical strength. Maybe its that the final boss (in my cast at least) uses a relatively massive AoE skill that one shots everyone and it doesnt seem to have any particularly important cool down or build up. It was literally the only reason I had problems with her, everything else about the final boss was just pathetic. King Meos was a pretty well desgined boss, he had what seemed to be phases and the difficulty increased as I did more damage to him; even if he was an extremely easy boss even at the time. Oh and the camera! Yeah... I'd almost prefer a fixed camera to a mobile one if it would be this bad at times. Who knows though, maybe this is turly the best camera in combat given everything else.
For this I can only recommend or suggest to focus on the close range combat and combos and making them seem cool, strong, or tie together in ways that make players feel like they're using skill to fight, not spamming magic (or hitting her with Askel's Bommee (probably spelt wrong, eh) because it poisons and let the DoT kill her.) because the boss can one shot you if you're next to you. Or keep magic, and just make the physical side of things better or the combo-heavy fighting style more important. It'd help if the combat flowed better than just spamming X or A and then pressing Y when the mob also parries. No reason to block since they'll just pound on you, run away, or use magic that gives you a debuff that pretty much ends your life. Or breaks your guard and kills you immediately because the final boss's insta gib does this!
(can you tell I thought the final boss was just cheese?)
There's a lot wrong with the game, but it runs fine and if someone wants to really give it a shot, then all I can say is be prepared. The music is good, the backgrounds are pretty, and the story is at least interesting enough to keep me from tabbing away to adjust things in Clicker Heroes or looking at BS in discord. The combat is flawed and can be infuriating at times, enjoyable or just down right silly. The combat will take up about 80% of the games life, so with how bad it is it can be pretty turn offy.
Still though, looking forward to second if thats what they plan on doing.
*EDIT* They seemed to have fixed the camera problem I had. Though I had thought the camera problems weren't the biggest issue with the combat. Still its great they're fixing some things. Keep it up guys!

As a fan of retro turn-based-RPGs and of the japanese language I can really recommend this game. It is fun to play and you have the educational factor in there, which makes this game very compelling. I do believe that people find it cumbersome to remember all kana and especially the stroke order, but this game teaches you how to do it: left to right, top to bottom, just like the japanese kids learn it in elementary school. Hiragana are the first type of characters the japanese children learn, and you basically approach the language as they do.
If you ever plan to visit Japan, as I have done it multiple times in my life, this game at least gives you some basic vocabulary. You might not be getting that far with it, but this game is pretty much evoking curiosity in people, which is a splendid effect, as they might be getting more interested in japanese language and have a decent knowledge of Hiragana once they finish this game (I believe, I am not through it yet, but if the game keeps the lessons up in this manner, this will for sure be the case).
I bought this game during the steam sale, but (given that I pretty much like both characteristic features of the game) I would also have bought it at full price.
I wish there was an equivalent game for Katakana and Kanji, I would absolutely buy them within the fraction of a second.
Judging from the perspective that this is more or less an "educational" game, I would say I haven't seen a better one in a while.
Highly recommended!

I believe this game to be one of the first true interactive movies. It is not a game in the traditional sense, I wouldn't consider it a walking simulator and nor would I say this is an art installation. What it is, is a heartbraking, emotional letter to someone lost from someone in pain. It's painful at times to experience, and while it gives you a good look into these two individuals, it makes you look at yourself. Am I a good person? Am I truly alone? Am I hurting others in my pursuit of my own happiness and completeness? Don't buy this if you're looking for your standard shoot 'em up. Don't buy this if you're looking for an intense series of puzzles for you to solve. Buy this if you want to help these two broken people. Buy this if you want to take a good look at yourself and see if you too are broken. Buy this if you think you need help from someone else be it a friend, a doctor, a family member or a teddy bear. This isn't a game, it's a way of looking at your life.
