By far the best Early Access game I've ever played. This game is gorgeous, and simply exploring the vast expanse of Canadian wilderness becomes a main driving point as every new cabin or site you discover is like some sort of picturesque painting. I've amassed a considerable screenshot collection, utilizing the handy HD Screenshot (Hud Disabled) hotkey. The beauty is enchanting, but also deadly--which is another great aspect of this game. No zombies or otherworldly threat. Just nature's bites--the cold and the wolves. Those damn wolves...
Surviving is a great challenge in either starting point, making each decision important since it is life or death with every hour that passes. A lot of games tout "Survival" as a selling point, but none have managed to really be an enjoyable experience to me until I played The Long Dark. I think the dev team have managed to strike a near-perfect balance of challenge and reward. Note that I've only played this on the standard diffuclty level--I've heard that the hardest difficulty adds more wolves... I'm confident they will change that and challenge the player some other way, as the wolves are notorious♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in this game. Like I mentioned, however, I think standard strikes a great balance and has been a lot of fun.
Be aware that there is currently no narrative story mode--Sandbox mode alone is worth the price during a sale. Throughout the play, you'll encounter hints as to what the story may be... I've had a lot of fun with the minimalism of it all, and to see that sense of mystery last so long is impressive. I still haven't explored every last bit of the lands yet, and now they are going to double the size of the explorable terrain! So, I'll just leave off with that--I'm impressed with this game!!

Banished is a psychological thriller rather than a city builder.
The most intriguing part is to make a proper start and initially expand the city, which is not an easy task.
After this (approx. 10 years and hundreds of inhabitants) the game becomes little challenging unless you turn disasters on.

Although I've been enjoying the game and have already put in quite a few hours, there are some glaring issues. For the price, it's absolutely worth it if you like what you see in the videos (and I'm looking forward to trying out Co-op). My major issue with this game, however, is how much time I have to spend in the menu. I get that it's a Loot 'Em Up, but god damn, cool it on the loot please. Either that, or make it easier for me to compare and contrast certain items without having to go through each individual character and looking at their armor, helmet, and weapons for each new loot item.
Similarly, the giant red 'X' is really annoying for the characters that can't wear an item, as I can't even see what the item is. Perhaps make it smaller so that I can still compare the items and could then perhaps change out their other gear for that item in particular? In its current state, it's hard to tell armor from weapon from helmet with the 'X' the way it is.
Just making it easier to compare a given loot item to those which my characters are already wearing - without having to go through each item and character individually - would make this game ten times better. I enjoy the gameplay but keep having to take breaks since over half my time is spent in the menu system comparing each item of loot to each other item of loot. It's nuts.
Finally, having an easier way to access each character's special abilities (perhaps like a vertical collection of their activate-able abilities under each of their icons in the top left) would be fantastic. Scrolling through the characters in the middle of a battle is nigh impossible and I'm not trying to pause and play every millisecond just to get the abilities used. This, in tandem with an easier way to determine health bars (it gets confusing with 8 enemies and 8 of my own characters) would be great.
Love the game for what it is, looking forward to seeing the tweaks and changes you make, best of luck with sales!

The Long Dark is a survival simulation game where the protagonist - Some random person that you'll never see a 3rd person shot of - is stranded in the worst place possible... Canada! As one of the coldest countries in the world, the Canadian Winter has just set in, and it's bound to be a long one. As your plane crashes in the northern Canadian wilderness, you must scavenge resources and clothing, kill or be killed, and eventually resort to eating a can of dog food to stay alive (If you make it that far).
The graphics, although unrealistic, are beautiful, and yield a great atmosphere that a Canadian like myself can really appreciate. The soundtrack is beautiful as well, and when a song starts randomly playing, your mood can change quite quickly.
Now, the way the game's sandbox mode works is that you spawn in either Mystery Lake or Coastal Highway, and must discover locations and collect whatever resources are there, and if you're encumbered, whichever are most valuable. A hunting knife or hatchet is an absolute necessity, you won't survive 10 days without one. A hunting rifle is also a bonus, especially when you get more than 2 rounds for it in the whole game... Yes, that happened in my first time making it past day 5. I survived to day 12.
Wolves will be your worst enemies after the bitter cold, the crippling hunger, and the painful thirst. Obviously, as a Canadian, I have never frozen to death (Though I've come quite close), but hunger is a real issue. As long as you have fire, you have water, and your sleeping bag will eliminate the possibility of dying from exhaustion. But the hunger... It seems that no matter how much food you have, it's never enough...
In my personal experience, wolves are the greatest killers, with hunger in second. I've not died from Cold, Exhaustion, or Thirst. Having just completed my 50-day run, I have a full appreciation for the sandbox mode of this game.
PROS
- Beautiful atmosphere and music
- Realistic stats (Need 8 hours of sleep, about 2 litres of water, and about 2000 calories a day)
- Moving around consumes calories, increasing the realism. Harvesting meat from animals also consumes calories, so you can't just hope to kill a deer while at 50 calories and expect to not starve.
- Infinite replayability (Literally infinite. Some gameplays can last upwards of 100 days.)
- Crafting
- Runs smoothly on poor PCs.
CONS
- Wolves attack at the slightest provocation (Reduced realism)
- Sometimes throwing a flare at a wolf will not scare it off (I'm assuming this is a bug. A very painful bug...)
- You can sometimes be stuck without a rifle or hatchet or knife, AKA you're screwed and should just restart.
- Mother Nature hates you (Throws storms at you when you're supposed to be harvesting meat because it's SUPPOSED to be warm out!)
* Yes, that above one is a joke, it does improve the realism of the game. Doesn't change that it still sucks. *
Overall, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who is patient and can think in outside the box, and plan ahead. For any who are having difficulties with the 50-day run, I stocked up on food, firewood, and water, and essentially hibernated from day 41 to day 50. As for making it to day 41 with that much excess food... you're on your own.

Overview:
You control a privateer ship that does things in the galaxy, almost like XCOM. You can buy bigger ships, customize the rooms for different functions. Lay various traps and build defense points for when there are random invade events. There are five attributes that can affect character parameters (e.g. speed affects dodge and firerate) and these are fixed. Leveling up grants skill points to spend on these attributes. Classes arent fixed and can be switch anytime by equipping different "utility pieces". Given that you have matter, you can clone any character or equipment. The main flow of the game is regulated by missions, which you need to manually get from a menu, and navigate your ship in a galaxy mapped out in grids. Most of the game revolves around getting more loot and raising a more powerful squad so you can take on even stronger enemies.
Conclusion:
A good rpg that's set in a pixelated world. Get it if you have an appetite for some loot and farming. Bugs and annoyances are there, but given the cheap price and solid gameplay its easy to overlook them. However, if you are not a fan of farming/minmaxing, you will not enjoy this title and its better if you pass this one.
PROS:
1. Fairly big world - All the planets and missions left me in a state of exhaustion, and there's still a huge blacked out portion of the galaxy unexplored.
2. Tons and Tons of equipment and guns - There's a million ways to kit out your team and multiple paths to take even with the same class. The same vanguard could dish out pain or soak up damage depending on how you build him.
3. Quite aesthetically pleasing. The maps are pretty and looks detailed. I did find it becoming a tad repetitive as I come across the same tilesets though. Camera shake is conveniently an option that you can toggle on/off.
4. Customizable difficulty to determine how "tryhard" you want to play this game.
CONS:
1. Clunky menus - A stark contrast to the clean and well designed game map is the projector menus on your ship. If you have one artifact grade weapon and can't use the SELL ALL button, you'd have to spend an eternity clicking SELL for each piece of junk you want to sell. To compare weapons you have to hover over each of the 50 guns that just dropped from the last mission and check if something could replace old equipment.
2. Unergonomic squad controls - Each class had an active skill that you had to access through: Pausing the game, Look for him by scrolling through F1-F8, Look for skill in skillbar, Press correct button. Luckily you can minimize micro-management by putting passive abilities on all but a few of your squadmates. Do this to save your sanity.
3. Autosave and no way to undo a stupid mistake - To fly your ship and do missions you need Material and Fuel. If ever you run out of those two things at the same time your whole squad is dead/ your ship is in the middle of nowhere, its GGWP and straight out GAME OVER.
4. Music is a hit and miss. Most of the hours will be spent in listening to Bang Bang Bang Boom Boom Boom and watching explosions and bullets fly across the screen.
5. A not so inspiring story coupled with lack of variation with mission types. Sure when the squad sets foot on a new planet a different title appears (e.g. release all prisoneers, locate nerve cords...etc.), but it always ends with killing everything. Could really use a break like a plot twist or puzzle.

Between the fast-paced twitch shooting of Call of Duty and the (often ridiculously slow and boring) shooting of ArmA, there is a glorious sweet spot of well-paced action and satisfying realism. Rising Storm / Red Orchestra 2 is that sweet spot.
You almost always die in one shot, so every movement you make must be methodical.
You almost always kill in one shot, so being quick to take aim and fire accurately is a skill that must be honed. But even a miss will make your enemy flinch.
In Hardcore Mode, your kill notifications are delayed. Did you get him? Or did he make it behind that wall? The suspense and the satisfaction is unmatched.
This game is absolutely worth your time and money. It doesn't have the polish of some other titles -- the UI is a bit messy -- but once you are standing over the corpse of your first close-quarters hip-fire kill, pondering your luck and the tragic fate of so many soldiers, you'll be glad you tried the game and addicted to the rush of countless moments like it.

This game is tons of fun in the short amount of time I have played. I've read a few of the other reviews left here and I have to say most of them agree.
While the game is fun I only found a couple things that take away from the experience.
1. The amount of cash you earn is by far more than needed early game.
2. Stats aren't exactly clear in how they work/or what stats are better for what class.
3. No true tutorial.
4. There are a lot of menus, but it's just a matter of getting used to them.
Aside from those things this game is honestly great.
1. You get to shoot some mofos in the face
2. Some humor mixed in with a decent story line.
3. TONS of planets to visit
4. Difficulty directly influences drops and exp earned. (chosen before landing on a planet)
5. Tons of loot (I'm gonna go into this one a bit more here)
- A lot of people are saying there is too much loot. I beg to differ. Depending on how you're playing the game. Loot can be used for 3 things. 1) Upgrade character gear, 2) Sold for money, 3) Disintegrated for Matter    - Since matter is used for things like reviving characters and beaming down to planets it kind of balances itself. When converting gear into matter you get the weight of the gear back into matter. The heaviest items tend to be Heavy Armor (Weird huh?) So in order for me to revive 1 character (which costs around 50 matter atm) I sometimes need to disintegrate 30 items (Item weight can be anywhere from 0-30 from what I've seen so far) So yes. Tons of loot. Which I love.
6. 5 Classes each with different abilities
7. Skill trees for each class
8. Menus that make sense although there are a lot
9. Ships that can be customized (Not super in depth customization but I'm sure with enough feedback this could change)
10. You aren't always overpowered.
This list could go on but I'll leave it there. I'm currently at level 26. There were a couple times where  I felt I was overpowered even playing on harder difficulties but then a planet came along that royaly screwed me up. So yeah, I learned. Lol
It's a really enjoyable game for its current price I don't think it's a bad investment. If you're hesitant, just wait for a better sale. But for me, worth the money.

Welcome to Shiness: The Lightning Kingdom, a game with a slightly confusing plot, and with so much good content, it really is hard to find a thing I don’t like about it, save for the few that I’ve selected. But we’ll get around to that. The story of Shiness: TLK is one that is centered around Chado, an odd bear like creature that is following a Shiness – one of the primordial beings of Shi – whilst being accompanied by his friend Poky.
In RPG games, you level up by killing monsters for set amounts of XP. In Shiness, your stats level up with pre-determined values, but you can also learn moves that increase your stats by equipping Disciplines. The more you use the moves in combat, you'll earn experience towards that ability until you have learned it, allowing you to build and expand your combat repertoire.
While your current character is in battle, kicking and kung-fu'ing the crap out of everything that moves, your teammates are waiting on the sidelines of the arena. If you've set up your support commands, they can aid you in battle by healing you or negating negative status effects. Support commands can be found in treasure containers, awarded in challenges or given to you during the story. Once it is unlocked, it's available for every character to use.
During some cutscenes that look similar to the actual gameplay, the characters speak in english, while at other times during comic book/manga inspired cutscenes the characters will speak a foreign language with text bubbles to read. It's a weird style mixing them both like that but it works well enough to not feel like it could ruin someones experience. The voice acting was a little bit out of place and cheesy, with Chado's not clicking with me for some reason. Overall everything just sounds like the developers may not have agreed with one another's opinions so they "compromised." Graphically I loved the design of the world and characters. This is what I mentioned earlier in the review. There's never any cliche environments that when you walk through you absolutely know which biome it's meant to be. Each environment is unique yet encompasses enough diversity to surprise you of what you're seeing every other corner. The almost cartoon design behind it all makes it immediately project joy onto the player.
There is one major game-breaking bug, though, and I experienced it three or four times in my playthrough. Occasionally I'd have a character lose all of their health without being knocked out. Instead, they stayed standing but were unable to attack or be attacked. This would require a reset and some lost game time. Hopefully, this is something the developer will address quickly.
PROS:
+Great combat mechanics.
+Easy to use support system.
+Gorgeously presented.
+Great soundtrack that fit the games style and theme.
+Colorful presentation
+Simple to understand, hard to master action battle system
+Full Of Puzzle while exploring from place to place
Cons
-lacks of game time length for an RPG

-Game is well crafted but it offer nothing new.
-Mediocre Story
Neautral

Conclusion
those who love action RPGs from the 90s will find plenty to like in the game since Shiness is quite fun for the whole duration of the adventure, despite its predictable story, lackluster writing and somewhat wonky battle controls.
Many will find the length of the game to be 15-20 hours (more or less depending on your pace) but features a good amount of side quests and off the beaten path adventuring. The camera can be a huge pain, and the voice acting will most likely not be loved, nor hated. All in all, I thoroughly enjoyed my time spent in this strange world with strange characters and am looking forward to replaying it sometime in the near future. It tries to do a lot and for the most part successfully delivers.

Shiness: The Lightning Kingdom is a definetly a unique project that combines the Playstation 2 and Xbox nostalgia with earle 2000s shonen anime style in a now mostly forgotten fighting/RPG genre. What really stands out is the ambitiousness of the creators: with only Kickstarter funding, they aimed to create a solid adventure game with complex battle system, a strong story,  beautiful music, and even a unique language, created solely for this game. The game has been in development for years, and now, we can finally see if the game was worth the wait. And as for me, i don't regret waiting and reading all the time since 2015, when i first heard of the game. What really attracts me to this game is that is the product of fans, of someone who clearly loves and cherishes the memories of the old jRPGs and fantasy anime, and is inspired by them to create something similar, but unique and new - the highest form of inspiration. And as a fan of old games, it is always a pleasure to revive the memories of them, while also getting new experience. But for those who are not swayed by nostalgia, and also the younger audience, the game has a lot to offer, not leaning on nostalgia value alone. The visuals are pleasant and not straining the eye, the character design is simple yet attractive, the music is nice and blend into the whole athmosphere of the game. The action is one of the games most interesting feature. Unlike other games where the action is merely a exercise for your inex finger, the battle system in Shiness allows the characters to use  a vastly diverse set of tactics, using combos, healing object, magic attacks, hyper attacks and changing characters, each with their unique abilities and  combat styles, in battle.
Shiness is a incredible game, a indie game that is different from other indie games by its ambition. It aims higher than being just a homage to an era, it stands firmly on its two legs by having the quality and the scale of a game made by veteran professionals in the gaming industry and being made with love and dedication. I' enjoying it and would gladly recomend it to everyone.

I have decided to give a more indept review instead of my first one after playing for a longer time.
I would recommend buying it. 16 hours into the game and I have not encountered any game breaking bugs. Yes, the camera can be a problem sometimes, but the devs already told in a live stream that they are working hard to fix this problem.
Combat is something you have to get used to. Don't expect you can blindly jump into a fight and (hack/and/slash style) kill all enemies. Some enemies require different attacks, may it be melee or magic. You have to time your dodges and attacks.Switch between the two attack possibilities or even characters.
> Combat system can be a bit annoying if you try to block an attack from an enemy, fail and then receive a full on combo which you cannot block between blows.
> BUT, because of this I decided to play more save. If you notice that it is hard to melee attack a certain enemy, switch to magic and keep a save distance. And when the time is right, switch back to melee, hit the enemy a few times and roll out of combat.
Story is interesting so far. In the beginning of the game I was doubting whether it was worth playing. However, after the first areas the story takes of and it is amazing. I am really enjoying it. Don't want to give any spoilers :) Game has quirky humor and easter eggs, highly enjoyable.
Some areas might become a bit dull after spending a long time there, but just as I was starting to feel that way, I was transported to a different location.While some areas in game could have had something more in it (may it be trees, animals, people etc) it does not stop me from enjoying the game. Just walking through the game makes you feel that you are in a completely different world.
Graphics are clean, bright and colorful. While sometimes sprites disapear if you stand close to it and you turn the camera, this does not bother me. It is actually quit funny. And it only happens if you do the above mentioned thing.
Music is A+ and fits well with the areas you visit and the enemies you encounter. The music it not so noticable that you start to get annoyed by it. It just blends well with playing the game. They could not have done a better job.
While Shiness has some camera issues and dialogue mistakes (which are being worked on) this does not stop me from having a lot of fun playing the game. I have enjoyed every hour I spend in this game and will continue to do so till I finish the game.
For me Shiness is a 8.5/10 and I hope we will see a Shiness 2 in the near future. Maybe with multiplayer? :)

Even though there's still a lot more to A Hat in Time than I have played so far, I must admit, I have enjoyed it so far. True, it's not as big as, say, Super Mario Galaxy, but each of the current four chapters (and the final one, Time's End) feels unique just as the developers intended. Be it signing your soul away to open access to new Acts in Subcon Forest, fueling the feud between Grooves and the Conductor in Battle of the Birds, or even exploring the wide-open areas of Alpine Skyway's free-roaming level, each chapter beings something new to the table. And it has helpful tools for both casuals and speedrunners alike, including an in-game timer which shows both game time and indivual level times, auto-skipping cutscreens (Which is a bit bugged when it comes to getting the badge pins as of the current build) and the upcomming modding support currently being worked on. It's not a perfect game, though, with some lines of dialog which could be voiced not being voiced, but those are minor gripes for an otherwise amazing game.

I haven't put a great deal of time into this game, and I can tell there's some depth to it that I'd like to explore.  Unfortunately, I think in its current state I just don't see enough going on to motivate me to reach further and discover more. There's too much focus on the wrong challenges, which make you feel like your outcome will be the same no matter how you choose to play.
The survival elements stats in the game are well put together. Your survival menu displays your fatigue, coldness, hunger, thirst, overall condition, and these seem to be fairly balanced. You have a limited carrying capacity, which actually does come into play pretty quickly. I can sense there's a real threat from the elements and a challenge to be overcome in long-term survival. HOWEVER, you learn within the first couple hours that this feeling of fear that you may actually face a challenge in keeping warm and avoiding dehydration and starvation is completely and totally irrelevant because of WOLVES. I have played five sandbox games so far, and not once have I succumb to the brutal cold, or the scarcity of food, or the lack of potable water. Every single time, it's from wolves.
I think this game is currently struggling from having a very unclear idea of the conflict the player should be facing.
Is this a game about survival in an unforgiving natural environment, with the occasional threat of injury from wildlife?
Or is this a game about survival against wildlife in occasionally threatening natural environment?
The developers want to craft a realistic experience of survival, yet they argue that a "geomagnetic event" has had some kind of mystical effect on the wildlife, such that wolves are suddenly hyper aggressive against humans. I don't buy it. There's no realism to involved in magic wolves. It's disruptive to the core of what could be a good survival game.
Another frustrating aspect of the game is that certain critical items you will find in abundance, while others you may never find in a playthrough. For instance, I am able to quickly find dozens of matchbooks, which allow you to start fires (probably the most important survival skill, especially in cold weather), but I can turn over 5 or 6 cabins and find loads of canned goods but fail to find a can opener. Another example - I found a garage in my most recent play through. I dumped out three large tool cabinets and two work benches and found no tools, except for a pry bar laying on a shelf. Seriously, a garage without tools? The land is devoid of any other human life, and I don't really need the devs to explain why that is, but I have trouble buying into the realism that these people suddenly disappeared and took all their tools with them.
I just can't recommend anyone buying this game unless the developers make some adjustments to critical item rarity and the wolves' aggression. It is playable, but it just isn't enjoyable without these elements being properly balanced.

The Long Dark is a thought provoking exploration-based survival game.  You find yourself stranded in the northern Canadian wilderness with only the clothes on your back and a few meager supplies that will last you for a short time.  The game's intersting hunger meter (a calorie counter) provides you with an accurate measure of your character's craving for food that makes you feel more determined to actually try and endure the cold.  Speaking of cold, the weather varies from absolute blizzards that can get as cold as -55ºC to crystal clear sunny days where you're lucky enought to get a temperature that's right around the freezing mark.  Just like most people in real life, you need to have clothes warm enough to bear the freezing weather if you plan on making a trek outside for a long period of time;  that is, unless you'd rather slowly freeze to death.  As an additional way to combat the cold, you create campfires, light fireplaces, and even use kerosene lamps to warm you if you are getting too cold.  An ever growing issue in this game is your thirst.  Water can either be unsafe or potable.  Clean water can be found relatively easy as it is  prevalent in the world (Ex: drinking out of toilets).  Unsanitary water can be boiled over a fire or fireplace to clean and be made drinkable.  Soda can be found in most abandoned homes, they contain both calories and help quench your thirst.  Coffee and tea can be made as an additioinal source of liquids as well as containg special properties that make them slightly better than water.  If you're ever unable to find any of these and you have the materials needed to create a fire, you can melt snow into clean water.  Your fatigue is an important factor in determining your survival.  The longer you go without sleep and the more strenuous the activities you do are, the more lethargic and slow your character becomes.  This can be remedied by taking a nap.  If you're lucky enough to find a weapon you can defend yourself from the wolves which are your only real predator in the game.  Wolves are a surprisingly terrifying adversary in a game such as this.  Ammo for your rifle (which is the only firearm available this early in the game) is scarce and you are required to conserve and effiectively use your ammunitions for hunting deer or other smaller game or to protect yourselves against wolves.  Flares are also an effective recource to use in defending yourself from animals.  The Long Dark is overall a great survival game.  This review was written during the alpha and I'm sure there are many more features to come.  I'd easily give this game a 9/10.

I was looking forward to this game for many, many months following its announcement. The time I did spend playing Pixel Piracy, I really enjoyed it. So I thought, hey, the same sort of thing in space? Sounds great to me! Pixel Privateers is half of what Pixel Piracy was, while also being a lot more. In fact, Pixel Privateers is so much more than Pixel Piracy that it is actually bad for the game in my opinion.
Simply put, Pixel Privateers is basically Pixel Piracy in space with a 20x multiplier on the "what's going on" factor.
Pixel Privateers requires a massive amount of micromanagement due to the lack of any automation. Crew members do not attack anything automatically, requiring the player to right-click on every enemy to attack. Skills must be used manually, which is impractical for a few reasons.
I played Pixel Privateers only with my girlfriend, with four crew members each. This means a total of eight characters milling around, making it difficult to tell who is doing what and where at any given moment. Even when I had two crew members and she had three, it was difficult to sort through our crew members for our own characters. When in combat, it is especially difficult to see through the pixels flying. Next think we know, we're just sitting there doing nothing while being pummelled by enemies because we can't tell who is attacking what. With no auto-attack, this becomes frustrating and irritating quickly.
Because of the difficulty of telling what's going on or where our characters are, it can be difficult to select just one specific crew member to tell it to attack a specific target.
There are also some things that are left unexplained. In the science lab, there are icons for each class next to some of the tech (I don't remember what it's called). But then there are other strange icons which are not explained. Some look like guns, some look like toolboxes, some look like... I don't even know what... But none of these extra icons are explained.
The extensive tutorial is great, but it is a lot of reading. I personally can't stand long-winded tutorials. It probably took a half hour just for reading in the tutorial. The end of the tutorial was also confusing. I finished the advanced training, and the game told me I finished the tutorial. So when I clicked Main Menu to go back to the main menu to check out how the multiplayer works (more on that shortly), it told me I was leaving the tutorial and something else that I didn't quite get to read before I hit yes/ok. I loaded my save again to see if anything was lost, and I was greeted with a questionnaire similar to the one from Pixel Piracy. Everything was fine, but the message that popped up before I went back to the main menu lead me to believe I had lost all of my progress from the tutorial.
Now the multiplayer woes. The process of playing multiplayer is not very intuitive. It was not apparent (to me, anyway) that you had to be in-game (not at the main menu) for a friend to join you. There is no "host" button anywhere. My girlfriend and I spent a good 10 or 15 minutes trying to figure out why she couldn't join my game while I was playing.
It turns out, the "friends, invite only" online mode simply doesn't work. There is no way to invite a friend to play with you. Using the Steam overlay, or accessing the friends list from the main Steam interface, does not offer an "invite to game" option for friends, so the "invite only" mode is utterly pointless. Even if I set the online mode to the friends option that's not invite only, I don't have the option to invite a friend to the game until someone joins my game from the Multiplayer section of the main menu. Again, the invite function is utterly pointless as it doesn't exist until someone is in your game.
My girlfriend and I ultimately ended up requesting a refund for the game. I really wanted to enjoy this game, but I simply cannot. We spent the majority of our time with the game managing our inventories, selling/destroying items, training crew, messing about in the science lab, trying to figure out this that and the other thing... Basically everything except actually playing the game. Perhaps we'll check it out again in the future after it has had some updates and polish, but for now, our collective $24 could be spent better elsewhere.

The short version:
Why to buy:
It's a Tales of... game on PC.  If you're a fan that alone is a good reason to support the release.
It’s also a pretty solid port.
Feels like it is probably the best available version of the game -- my only regret is that I don't have a physical case to accompany the others in my collection.
Has both Japanese and English options for audio!
Why to skip:
Maybe not the best in the series.
The overall design is good but the battles are pretty meh due to how they are balanced.
Way too much gear optimization/crafting for my tastes.
The nitty-gritty:
So, this could be overly negative in how it is presented.  By the time I had reached the end of a 40 hour playthrough I was pretty tired of the mechanics and level design.  However, it still takes strides forward that I appreciate, it’s just that the implementation probably could have been better.
At the start, everything was great.. The areas were large and beautifully presented.  The battles seemed more or less on par with any other Tales game to date and everything was peachy.  None of the characters outright seemed to be overly annoying or just plain oddly presented (thanks Graces F).  The presentation or triggering for skits was a one of my favorite improvements - they now occur predictably at save points and Inns, making it relatively easy to know then to expect them.  It takes the stress out of those ‘Oh crap did I just miss one’ moments that sometimes occur in other Tales games.
However, as my playtime increased, I noticed that the dungeons stopped presenting new twists. .  Admittedly this is all a part of the fact that there are quite a few extra dungeons thrown in for good measure, but the overall quality seems to dip  after a certain point.  I should have just skipped what was unnecessary but a completionist bent made that difficult.
The combat system did not help with this either.  The overall approach to combat feels like it’s been simplified to the point of being trivial.  Magic does not have any actual cost - resulting in no items related to MP consumption even existing at all.  Even in the heat of battle it only takes a moment of blocking in order to recharge to full, so there is no point to being stingy on the heaviest hitting moves you have.
This resulted in the next problem, that in order to avoid spending time grinding needlessly you I spent most of the later part of the game just running from Point A to Point B, dodging monsters the best I could through lengthy, repetitive environments.  My enthusiasm then fizzed out, resulting in a need to just finish the game to be done with it.  The overworld areas are fairly nice and all, but it seems like it could have benefited from a more condensed approach to the design, or less backtracking.  This is somewhat managed by the teleportation mechanics but they tend to be finicky on how they function and will often bar you from using spots near to your objective (for scripting/trigger purposes I assume).  Perhaps at some point they will get to a system that clicks better, but I’d almost rather they just go back to overworld maps at this point, as they tended to help create a better sense of scope and vastness to the world.
That all being said, I still don’t regret the purchase.  It still holds a lot of the Tales characteristic charm and warmth via character interaction and development.  They also spent a considerable amount of time investing in the villain's backstory - more than I think any other Tales games has before.  While it still has an echo of the whole ‘Just cause,’ reasoning for ending the world, there is much more explanation into the ‘why’ of the villain's motives.  Tropes still ensue in excess, it still feels far more well-rounded than I would normally expect.
Also, while I am bothered by many of the finer aspects of combat there are also still plenty of moments in which the system clicks and just feels good.  It probably just suffers a bit from the scope of the game, resulting in the same problem I normally have with many open-world games - tons of content is great, but it can also be a pain when you have certain expectations regarding how extensive you want to be in searching every nook and cranny.  I would recommend approaching Zestria as either taking your sweet time throughout the playthrough, or by letting yourself skip side-quests to avoid exhaustion.

I bought this game without too much researching besides a few positive comments on another web board. And when I booted it up, I saw it immediately... the dreaded Cell Shading graphics. I've never been a fan of it in games... it's always made me feel as I was playing a cartoon. Unrealistic and colorful. Don't get me wrong Cell Shading is cool - I just really don't like it in games, where I prefer realistic 3D graphics from "art" styles.
So I actually closed it down without even starting up a game.
But the next day I decided to give it a go anyway, and boy... It didn't take 10 minutes in the world to completely forget my distaste of CS in games, the gameplay and overall feeling of the game sucks you in and spits out huddled survivor who is just desperately trying to find another can of dog food and not get eaten by the aggressive wild life.
The Long Dark is still Early Access - but you don't really think about it. It lacks content and world space for obvious reasons - but besides that it's as playing an advanced demo. I haven't encountered any game breaking bugs and I haven't had one single CTD. It feels very stable and polished for an EA title.
The thing that is really missing is an in-game map - I dont even need an I-Am-Here marker, I just want it since it breaks immersion to have to constantly flip to an Internet map to navigate. And for aesthetic reasons I wouldn't mind a window where I can see my characters equipment, equipped.
Bottom line, if you are looking for a game where finding a can of dog food can make you warm and fuzzy inside and a box of bullets is celebrated by dancing around the living room. Where you really fear for your in-game persona when getting caught out in a blizzard and where a safe house gives you a real feeling of being safe. Then this game is for you!

Pixel Privateers is no what I was expecting. Before I bought this game, I'll be honest, I was rescearching how to get a refund. But I was suprised just how well it delivered. I'm sorry if for this overly long review. But if you are wanting to know if this is your kind of game READ THIS REVIEW.
-Disclaimer-
My entire playthrough of the game is not finished. My point of view is also only from a Normal mode point of view may be different in Hardcore mode.
-First impressions-
I booted up the game and saw this beutiful screen. It was running pretty smooth. I'm even playing this game on a laptop that is so old, it want turn on without being plugged in. The tutorial was had some humor and went really well, though it could go a bit more indepth on the stats. The only problem was the menu screens. Everybody complains that it is way to much. I find that it is very well organised for something that could have been really bad. The problem with it, is the background stars. It lagged my computer to an unplayable fps. Luckily, you can turn off the stars, but it will take away the blue coloring along with it, leaving a boring black screen behind them. The desert planets are also extremely laggy. There is no option that can fix this. This also makes the surveying missions near impossible, but still luckily are.
-Gameplay-
The gameplay is very simple, but fun. You request some missions, go to a planet, kill the enemies, loot your surroundings, fisish the mission, and get your sweet reward. The planets are easy on a normal setting, but you can set a different difficulty at any point of going to that planet. The one time I changed a planets difficulty to 10% more enemy health, I was unable to beat it. I did change it back to normal mode, but this one room was impossible to get pass at my current point. Selecting your crew is easy. You can press q to select all, you can select a crew member's icon, or you can select them the same you way you would select a computer application. The abilities are useful but most of the most useful, take hit streaks. Hit steaks are easy to get but this causes the auto-tactical mode option, which tactical is where you can pause mid-game and plan what you are going to do next, to ultimatly become some what useless until 1-2 seconds into battle. Tactical mode is really useful but keep forgetting to use it, which can mean death, if death was a common threat. Tactical mode is also REALLY useful for items. When you need to set a trap for an enemy, use tactical mode. When you need to heal, use tactical mode.
-Mechanics for items and training-
Out side of battling, you have the menus. I will be honest, you may be looking at these for a while, but unlike everybody says, it is NOT as long as the gameplay on the planets are. This may be true in the begining of the game, but it can change after a few hours. The stats, training as it is called in the game, aren't explained in-game. If you hover over them with your mouse, it will become clear to you quickly. It is like video editing and some forms of computer programming. You can't make sense of it at first, but you will quickly. Items are the same way. You are given a lot of loot and you will be switching items a ton. I actually really liked this whole looking through the items thing for one reason. You have to plan who gets what. You can't give one guy the best gear and everybody else the hand-me-downs. You will have to think, which I love. When I saw that the game had weapon modifiers in its description, I was thinking Terraria modifiers. These are the same idea, but they don't feel like the are. I very rarely give them a second thought.
-Mechanics for crew-
Changing the subject to the crew, you have up to five. If you get six, the game makes you feel like a jerk, and FORCES you to disintegrate the extra passenger. This isn't Pixel Piracy, where it would make some since to do so. You are the good guys in this game. Anyway, If one of your crew happens to die in battle, to things could happen. 1: The rest of your team will die, which causes you leave the surface. This works 80% of the time for some reason, so you may have to press "esc" and go to the main menu. Don't worry, you want lose any progress. You will thin have to reconstruct crew, which uses matter. Matter is also a rescource that I saw somebody say was annoying and hard to come by. unless you are dying every ten seconds, you want be running out. 2: You some how survived and can retrive while still on planet. While you're not in combat, you can double click his Icon and he will be reconstructed with the price being only matter. To ubtain matter. get read of some usless items and/or choice it as a reward. You can clone a crew member but I would imagine that it isn't the most useful in Normal mode.
-Mechanics for your spaceship-
This is the shortest of the mechanics. You can extend and costumize your ship, but it isn't as I've grand as something like building it. I could be wrong though since I am yet to get to a ship dock. What can say about it though is that it will help you in the long run. Flying your ship is not like star wars anything like that. I have never played Pixel Piracy, but from what I have seen it, It may be similar to it, but more important and fleshed out. If the Pixel Piracy's traveling was bugged out, I can comfirm that Privateers, is not bugged and pretty interesting. Moving your spaceship will cost fuel. This fuel can only be obtained in market places for high prices low quantity or by choicing it as a reward. I have not had problems with fuel but you will have to keep a very close eye on it. I don't now what will happen if you run out, but there is a distress signal button to save your buns. I just have a feeling that it isn't the cheap.
-The conclusion-
This game is very well done and polished. I thought I saw a bug once in the game but even that wasn't true. I just didn't pay attention to my surroundings. It may lag with the stars and the desert planets may be worse when it comes to fps, but nothing else is bad. The gameplay pulls you in. The mechanics perfectly balanced. I would recommend this everybody who likes this type of game. Everyone except one. If you have a slow, laggy computer that doesn't play many games well, AVOID THIS GAME! The game is very good and you should give it a go but make sure you know your computer can handle it. Test it on your computer, and if it lags extremly badly on the lowest of setting, pull out a refund. The game is the most demanding game I have.
Re-Logic and Quadro Delta, if you are reading this, Thank you for making such an awesome game.
-Update-
I have finally gotten futher into ship mechanics. You can buy an new ship for high price... unless you have been saving the whole game, like I have. You can easily change the the rooms by clicking the green gear and selecting the room you want it to be. You must have a ship module to do so, which aren't the cheapest things in the world. You can also add in turrents/traps, but two conditions must be true.1: You have a ship turrent/trap. 2: You must have that room changed from default. It is simple as that.

Overall, I really like this game. I see a lot of people saying combat is busted, but I feel like they aren't putting in the time to figure out what is good when. Dodge before a combo so you can't be stunlocked, parry midcombo to prevent stunlocks, and only use block for lunging and/or teleporting attacks. Also when opponents start to get harder, character switching is essential. When opponents use magic, I simply walk out of the way of those, since they move fairly slow. The combat is different to get used to, but actually fairly easy once it's gotten down. Voice acting is meh, camera angles absolutely suck, and the occasional random invisible wall in the middle of a flat path. Other than those few downsides, the game is very good. To me, it feels as if it was a mix of Kingdom Hearts and Sly Cooper. The boss battles are very immersive and fun, beating those hard sections of the game are very rewarding, and the story is pretty good. The way they went for an almost retro type adventure game felt very good. I plan on speedrunning this game in the future because it has a good mix between action and adventure platforming. I couldn't recommend this game enough.
NEW EDIT:
While I did give it such a high appraisal earlier on, now that I have progressed further, I must warn everyone. DO NOT BUY THIS GAME YET. There are so many game breaking bugs right now. I am on one of the last mission in the game and I encountered a bug that will not allow me to progress. When looking into the discussions sessions of the games, I have been seeing complaints about people who have encountered many of these game breaking bugs where you can't progress. The only to fix this is by having a backup (I didn't have one because I wasn't expecting to find a game breaking bug) or to start a new save file. So basically if you encountered one of these bugs at the same moment that I did, you would be losing about 16.5 hours of gameplay. It really is a good game and I did enjoy it. Unfortunately, this kind of bug where you lose tens of hours of gameplay is completely unacceptable. Wait to buy this until there is an update. It is not worth the risk.

Limbo is a basic side scroller. The controls are easy enough to pick up, and the gameplay is interesting too. There were gravity puzzles, time puzzles, spider puzzles, spiders, lots of boxes, and spiders.

Limbo is the place that Christans believe is the "checkpoint" of sorts between death and heaven. Where especially young people are suspended for an extended amount of time.

One thing I didn't like was the ending. There wasn't really a twist, or a suprise ending, but it was dissatisfying. I'm sure that that's how it was meant to be, but they could have certainly teased more than THAT.

Seems good so far... About 4 to 5 hours in.
Combat is fun, at least I think so. Timing is critical and while it seems a tad clunky it actually works great. At first I was getting pounded but after mastering the parry mechanic and realizing the game rewards aggressive and pro-active play over reactionary play I've pretty much come full circle and now I'm kicking♥♥♥♥♥ Tips I'd suggest...
1. Don't over rely on blocking, you should very rarely be blocking in the first place, parrying is more beneficial and can set you up for a counter-attack, add to that that Blocking is suprisingly easy to break through and I'd say you should mostly steer clear of the block button except when using it do dodge roll. Blocking can have it's uses, but your 90% of the time you will be better served to parry or use one of the technique based counters.
2. Don't relent on the attack. I find most of the time I start to lose a battle is when I'm backing off to heal or power up my shi (This games "Mana" equivalent) Once you get a group together healing can happen automatically and if you think your enemy is gonna take five while you spend an eternity getting your♥♥♥♥♥♥together, healing up and powering up you have another thing coming. They will POUND you while your trying desperately to scarf fruit for a few extra hp... Your just better off staying on the attack. Occasionally you'll knock your enemy to the ground. That's when you go for a critical heal or power-up.
3. The game's combat is less about visuals cues and more about feeling out rythm. The enemy and your character will attack in a very identifiable and consistent rythm. Once you get that rythm down and have a feel for it you'll be able to parry enemies with extreme prejudice.
I'll update once I've got more time under my belt, but my initial impressions are very positive.

As an avid Nintendo fanboy I was both looking forward to and very skeptical of A Hat in Time, often advertised as a homage/tribute/throwback to Super Mario Sunshine (probably my favourite game of all time).
I never played the beta and/or watched content and I'm glad I didn't. From the moment I started playing until the moment I completed the final level I've had nothing but good ol' fun with this game.
All levels are different and clearly a lot of thought and passion went into creating them. And when I say "different", I really do mean many of the levels will make you think you stepped into a different game. Gameplay, Music, Enemies, Atmosphere. Gears for Breakfast nailed every aspect of the game.
A Hat in Time doesn't try to be anything except fun. But when it tries to be a scary game, it's scarier than most. When it tries to be "stealthy", the mechanics are more fun than most stealth games. And when the game tries to be funny, it's funnier than most.
Although the game isn't particularly long (it took me 10 hours to get to 100% completion), it's more than worth it. If the developers had priced the game at 60 dollars and I knew what I was buying, I would be more than happy to pay that amount.
Definitely one of my favourite games and probably one of the only games I'll bother getting the Steam achievements for.
Not a very constructive review, but I wanted to give this amazing game its due credit.

LIMBO is about as indie as an indie game can be, and that says alot since Braid used to be my example. It's got amazing art direction, the use of black and white and every shade of grey at first look makes the game seem bland, but in fact it breaths life into a game that constantly visualizes death and what you and everyone will do to survive.
Now LIMBO is simple enough you use your arrow keys and right control to do everything, up makes you jump even, so the game makes good use of varying puzzles and teaches them to you in the classic 'safe eniviroment' before letting you loose in the more deadly sides of things. If i had to say one thing about this game is it constantly challenges you to learn and adapt, the slightest error can cause death. But luckily the auto save is always close behind to kick you back in, the game has no lives system so you can retry all you want and generally if your looking for a short game to fill a sitting or something to play casually over a week this game would do you wonders.
But that being said it is not a light game, it's very serious in it's tone, your character often dies in gruesome ways only to see it happen again and again as you fail. But this serves one great purpose, to keep you going, see if you know anything about what limbo is, is that it is a space between earth and heaven or purgatory as it is more often called. Your in this space where all the horrors of life have invaded, everything is out to kill you even the world it's self, no colour, no freindly life, everything wants to kill you, but you persevere, for what? That is for me to know and for you to find out.
LIMBO shows amazing story telling through nothing but what happens in the game, no cut scenes, no words, just the game, even Braid needed books. Does this make LIMBO some Braid 2.0? No. LIMBO shows that small companies can tell an amazing story, better than even triple A companies and thier hundred man developement teams. But one thing i can say about LIMBO as a certain is that it is worth playing, help a little boy find what gives him the courage to carry on.

I've changed my mind: this game is a travesty. Maybe I've just gotten more bitter as I've grown older but honestly, if I think WORSE of a game the farther I get away from it then there's something wrong here.
There are two big things that kill this game: being compared to its predecessor, and death by a thousand cuts. There's so many niggling little problems (as well as a few big ones) that the whole of the experience gets dragged down. Which wouldn't be awful, except the previous game, for the most part, already got all of this right. Let's start with the big problems, and how Red Orchestra: Ostfront did it better:
Tanking is mind-numblingly boring in this game. It's just like tanking in every other arcade shooter. Actually no, it's worse, because tanking in this game is sluggish and unresponsive. Thing is, tanks are supposed to be sluggish and unresponsive, and this game's trying to capture that feeling, but you can't do that when you're the tank. It's not fun to play
something that's sluggish and unresponsive, you have to feel like you're
that slow and unresponsive thing, and this is where Ostfront got it right: in Red Orchestra 2, you
the tank. You control the turret with your mouse, you move back and forth with WASD (technically you're telling the AI where to go, but there's not enough of a disconnect for this to feel right), and you can't get out. You cannot leave the tank. You start inside the tank, you die inside the tank. In Ostfront, you can get out of the tank. You're a man. You're a soldier, you're a tank crewman behind the hydraulic turret controls of a machine. You feel at one with the tank because you and your tank are allowed to keep their individuality; you don't become devoured by the tank. Human players have to man every station in a tank in Ostfront. The driver drives, and the driver knows where to drive because his gunner, his man in the turret, pops out of the hatch and looks with his binoculars. The gunner has to rotate the turret and control elevation independently: A and D control turret rotation, while W and S control elevation. The turret feels like a
, not like a biological being. It's so much more satisfying to line up that shot with a perfect combination of windage and elevation to strike a weakpoint in the armor of your enemy with deadly accuracy, rather than just pointing and clicking like you were a sniper.
To be fair, this game only has two tanks, and the focus is no longer on combined arms, but only infantry combat. That'd be fine, if the infantry combat controlled any better. I'm not sure what feels more tanklike in RO2, playing a tank or playing a man. Red Orchestra 2's aiming and movement, the two most basic functions of a first person shooter: are completely wrong. Let's start with movement: it's simultaneously too fast and too sluggish. Let me explain: imagine your soldier was seperated into two halves: the top half, with the head, arms, and torso, and the second half, with the legs. Now, imagine that sticking out of the bottom of the torso and the top of the legs were two pins. Now, your soldier's top half and bottom half are not connected to eachother directly; connecting these two pins is a bar with two holes in it. In effect, your bottom half and top half are allowed to rotate and shift position independently of eachother. You run around but your view circles back and forth, without your head tilting. It feels gluey, like you're treading through waist deep tar, even when standing on concrete.
Ostfront on the other hand made you feel weighty in a good way: your dude felt coherent, yet you took time to gather a sprint from a standstill. It could be equated to wading through water but it only happens when you start sprinting. It really does take a bit of time to gather a sprint anyways, and to try to replicate that in a game will oftentimes feel strange. That's why a lot of games don't do it. Ostfront's the closest game that's gotten to making that feel right. RO2 was a step backwards in that regard.
That's just running, let's get to one of this game's most annoying unnecessary additions: prone blocking. My god, you can prone nowhere in this game. Going prone in Red Orchestra 2 is such an ordeal that oftentimes it can get you killed. Prone blocking, when done right, will at the most offer a mild inconvenience, and will discourage ridiculous camping. When done wrong, like in RO2, it will do its damndest to get you killed, every single time. First off: the ground has to be completely flat for you to prone. Second, you cannot scrunch up your feet to get closer to a wall, your dude is stiff as a board as you take up the entire outstretched length of your body proning. It just makes prone movement awkward, unintuitive, and annoying. Something that can save your life shouldn't be a chore to use. Speaking of which...
If you're not aware, a feature that carried over from Ostfront was resting: if you had a valid spot to rest your weapon, sway would be removed and you'd only have to worry about recoil and muzzle flip. This worked great in Ostfront, it was responsive, intuitive, and really helped bring an element of realism, utility, and uniqueness to the game. So of course they'd port over one of these core mechanics, right? Well, they did!
And they completely dropped the ball on it. Surface recognition for resting in RO2 is the most finnicky, unresponsive, unintuitive messes of a previously damn near perfect mechanic. In Red Orchestra: Ostfront, resting worked 100% of the time. In RO2, it works about 60% of the time. Even when it works, you don't feel rested, your gun still bumps all over the place, like the surface is greased and your soldier's arms are sliding all over it. This can make it especially challenging to use weapons with bipods. If you have a weapon with a bipod, I can offer you some tips: Forget about resting it on any surface not completely flat. Ten degrees of an angle? No go. A box just a bit too short? No go. Basically, if it's not the flat ground, and I mean
, it's a crapshoot if you'll be able to fire your weapon.
Also, you can press shift to zoom in. It's kind of neat, ARMA does it alright, it's supposed to simulate focus I guess. ARMA does it better though, and it makes more sense in a game like that, where you might want to look at something far away without necessarily raising your weapon. In RO2, this zoom comes from "holding your breath" which you can only do while aiming down your sights. It's extraneous but benign. Figured I'd quickly go by this little bit, it's not that bad honestly. Wasted development effort that could've gone into improving the movement, map design, sound design, historical accuracy, or many of the other myriad problems with this trainwreck of a game, but at least it's not harmful.

The combat system seems complex and fun at first, but as I'm getting further in I am starting to see big issues.  Namely, the responsiveness is not what it should be.  Going from a combo into a block or parry just flat out doesn't work sometimes, at least not without an intentional pause on your part between them.  Also, if you get caught up in an enemy's chain of attacks, no block or well-timed parry will do a thing to stop it.  You simple have to wait until the enemy is done, then proceed with your own flurry of attacks.  This is mainly in regards to mini-boss and boss battles, everything else is super easy to combo/parry or combo/roll your way through.  I've mostly stopped using magic unless the enemy is one of those that runs around a ton and I get tired of chasing it.  Otherwise, the magic attacks kind of feel useless.
What story? There's a ton of references to words prior to them ever being defined.  I don't really know what the big picture is...  You crash-land and are trying to make your way to the Lands of Life. There was a battle and political disputes that fractured the people of the world. I assume you work to piece it all back together.  Is that it?  I'm sure there is much more to come, so like I said, this is just based on what I have played so far.
I'll start off saying that I do not feel as negatively towards the game at this point.  To sum it up, it seems like they built the game from the middle onwards and then did the beginning once they were done.  The early game just doesn't feel right, but it DOES improve as you play further.  I would say level 20+ is where it starts to get good.  I hope the below update helps some of you as you make your decision to play.  I am now more interested in continuing my playthrough to see where the story unfolds and how well I can master the full spectrum of combat techniques.  I think that warrants a positive review, so I am now updating to reflect that.
Once you hit level 20 or so, and get to the area with the large field, it feels like the combat style changes.  Enemies seem to attack with more magic than earlier on, so using magic yourself becomes much more manageable and relevant.  Also, there is not much of a need to go from a combo into a block or parry as you already know the types of attacks the enemy will do, can run in with a combo, then back up and prepare for their next attack.  A HUGE help was the double dash move, this makes the world of a difference in the combat.  Now I am able to place some distance, launch a magic attack or two, run in with a combo, then jump back out to launch my Hyper move, and so on.  I only assume that as I become more proficient and practiced in the varying magic attacks that this will become even more fluid.
Now that I've played through quite a bit more, and talked to many NPCs, the story has been pieced together.  I understand more about the history and what my goals are throughout the game.  As mentioned in the comments below, the manga could be a prologue that is worth reading to fully understand where the story begins and what your role may turn out to be by the end. I am quite fond of hand done art in a video game. It reminds me of where graphic art truly began. The Howler is a very interesting game that utilizes hand done art in most, if not all, of its assets. Based on the book Hour of the Wolf, the game is set in an alternate steampunk version of Vilnius, Lithuania.
The Howler has a lot going for it. It is a physics game where you utilize wind current to move a hot air balloon to its destination. Don’t Touch The Zombies:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Imagine a gameshow where you have between four to five contestants in the arena; well, a maze really! Four of them would be formally known as Zombies, and one as a healthy human. The interesting point is that all zombies used to be human contestants before becoming undead. However, if they touch you they take your place and you become a zombie! So don’t touch the zombies!
Don’t Touch The Zombies is a casual action game where you swap between humans and zombies in several modes of play.
As you land on the menu page, you will have the option to play single player or multiplayer. By selecting the single player, you will have access to seven different modes of play. The adventure mode combines all modes in fourteen stages. The modes include Time Score, Time Killer, Score, Killer, Collector and Horde, across four maps: the warehouse, graveyard, rooftop and forest.
The gameplay is simple but fun. Depending on what mode you are playing, you will start playing either as a human or a zombie. Within the maze, several icons will pop up. Some will be in favour of the humans and others in favour of the zombies. Essentially, if you’re a human, you will be armed with a shotgun and a limited amount of ammunition. If you’re a Zombie, you’ll be able to fart or burp some sort of cloud which will slow down anybody who gets directly in its path. You’ll also be able to activate a speed-up boost which makes your zombie character run towards your opponent in a heartbeat every 10 seconds. Another interesting aspect is that you can play the game in the day or night. At this stage, it is very difficult to find a multiplayer game.
Graphically the game looks ok but I must admit that the audio is very funky especially at the end of a stage. In terms of controls, I strongly recommend playing with a gamepad instead of the mouse and keyboard. I think the game needs more content; not in terms of the modes, but I think in terms of maps - additional maps would make this game much better, in my opinion.
Positives:
~~~~~~~

-	Nice graphics
-	Several modes of play
-	Swap between humans and zombies
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No trading cards
-	Needs more maps
-	Hard to find a multiplayer game (beta)
This is a fun casual game swapping between humans and zombies. Definitely don’t touch the zombies.

Needless to say I haven't spent an exorbitant amount of time playing this game, but I thought that I'd share some of what I've experianced during my first playthrough.
First off, I'm a stickler for good graphics and was initially put off by the splotchy, water colored look of The Long Dark. Call me vain, but I that just what I tend to like. But I was pleasantly surprized by how well it works for this game. With my gaming PC down at the moment, I did my first playthrough on my regular laptop, with the graphics set a low for better performance. Even then, they wern't bad due to how the game is designed. Within two minutes of playing, I was no long conserned about how the graphics looked, but was more focused on staying alive.
The weather is cold and unpredictable, going from standstill wind to biting cold fronts with subzero wind chills. You're always on guard as to how much firewood you have scavanged and are forced to move through the in-game world to find other suplies, due to thirst, hunger, exposure, and fatigue. There is no stumbling onto a well stocked cashe and riding out the apocalypse in some bunker.
Food is a major concern as well, because you're constantly burning calories by moving around, gathering supplies, and just trying to stay warm. Finding a candy bar or a can of soda is like hitting the lottery. Without a high caloric intake, you won't be able to carry as many supplies or have the energy to move through the frozen wasteland. Often you'll come across some decent gear that you don't need, and will need to make a decision as to either take it, and deal with being encumbered, or leave it. Sometimes you might be able to break it down into a useful componet, but that takes time, and time costs you food, warmth, and daylight.
Daylight. You can see for miles during the day, but when the sun goes down, it's pitch black. You can't see your hand in front of your face. You need to find flares or a lantern, and it leaves you terrified when outdoors. Hearing random sounds in the woods, the not so distant call from a pack of wolves, or suffering the freezing, subzero temperature drops... you must find a place to hunker down well before sunset.
Something that struck me the most was the complete lack of people in the game. Starting off, I had the feeling that I'd probably see some NPC somewhere, sometime, but the longer I played, the more it sunk in: that I was truely alone. I figured that at somepoint I would come across someone that I could possibly trade with or talk with to figure out what happened in the world. If they were there, I couldn't find them (I know, probably might have something like that in the actual story mode, not the sandbox Alpha version). This caused me to be pretty excited when I thought I saw a person, and I had to carefully run down the side of mountain to get to them. Turned out that it was a person, or at least used to be. All I found was a frozen body not too far from a ditched car. Almost felt bad as I scavanged his corpse and stole his wool socks.
I thought that this added so much to the game and made it strangly unique. Similar games might not have NPC's but you can play online with people off your friends list, but here you're utterly and completly alone. Having to rely solely on yourself made this game in my opinion.
Eventually my adventure came to an end as I knelt shivering and tired by an old potbellied stove in a random ice-fishing hut, desperately trying to keep it lit, while a wolf stalked and howled just outside. Running out of fuel, freezing, hungry I made a mad dash across the ice to the shoreline fishing shacks as the sun started to rise, just to be knocked down and mauled by the wolf, who had so patiently circled my campsight all night. Dead by bloodloss from a wolf attack 20h 41m.
I was thoroughly impressed by this game and would love to see it fully developed with a complex story mode. There is so much potential and I would highly recommend this game to anyone who asks. For $20, I'll get more use out of this game than I would a large pizza lol. Here's to dieing in most horrible fashions imaginable and to the chance of living to see another day.

I’d been reviewing such good titles. Recently released titles such as Brute, Rocking Pilot and No Stick Shooter. These are all games that I spent several hours enjoying immensely. At some point, I knew that my luck would run out. You eventually must try and polish a turd. Unfortunately, Don’t Touch the Zombies was, for me, that turd.
Look, in all honesty, there’s nothing wrong with the product. It works as intended. It’s not a broken mess. It’s not a bug riddled mess and I’m certain that somewhere there is an audience for this game. Unfortunately, I am not that audience.
My Issues with the Game
There are never any players available for online multiplayer. My partner is not interested in playing video games and as such local multiplayer is out of the question. Therefore, the component of the game that I suspect would potentially bring some entertainment is a no-go for me.
None of the mini-games offer an enthralling experience for a single player. The one that I had the most fun playing felt like a poorly made up version of Pac-Man. The worst one had me running around aimlessly for thirty seconds trying to find the hunter so I could try and get my thirty seconds to win. I didn’t see a single opponent in that time and there was none on the map for me to try and hunt down. The next time I played I was awarded the role of the hunter and the opposing zombies were on opposite sides of the maps so avoiding them for 30 seconds was far too easy.
This is not the production values of an indie game that is priced fairly at $10. There are much better indie games on the market with a price a fraction of that. There is nothing within the game that would make me recommend it for anything more than a few dollars. This is 0indie bundle type quality where you add it to your Steam account and consider it a plus one. Either that or you gift it to a friend’s kid who's happy just having a game in their library but aren’t old enough to care about quality or lack thereof.
The game’s graphics are below average by today’s standards and the game isn’t attempting to be retro.
The highlight of the presentation, and arguably the entire game, is the limited soundtrack. However, it comes with one giant caveat. The soundtrack would be perfect for a party game or if I were leaving a club in Ibiza but it doesn't fit the zombie Vs hunters theme at all.
“This is the beginning; our game mode platform is very flexible so share with us the game modes you’d like to play” This quote from the game’s Steam store page makes me believe that the game should be in the Steam Early Access program and not fully released yet. It also makes me believe that the team are relatively young developers – age wise – that are making a game as their high school project. It’s hard to believe that this is their second published game following Debatazos, a Mexican politics mobile game.
Don’t Touch the Zombies feature Steam achievements and Steam stats. With regards to multiplayer it has online, local and apparently cross-platform multiplayer. It has partial controller support.
Unfortunately, there is no way that I can possibly recommend Don’t Touch the Zombies. I’m certain that the developers
mean well and have put undeniable effort into their game but it’s just not very good. I urge them to keep plying their trade and keep learning. Perhaps someday they’ll develop a good game for us to play.
Rating: 3/10

I am going to start by saying this, the game is fun, no denying that.
But, there are a few problems...
1. Too much loot. Each mission, I would have to change the entire gear of my 5 man team because I kept find better stuff.
That doesn't make much sense, why bother creating a market if you are almost certain to find new and more powerful stuff during a mission...
2. Too easy. I found out I could up the difficulty a notch, so I went and did that (added 10% ennemy HP), but I still managed to get through most mission or planet without a problems
3. Too much cash. This is, somehow, slightly related to the first point. After 12, maybe 15 planets top, I ended up with around 70K... I managed to buy easily a 7 room ship and my crew was only level 15... I have to blame the reward system for mission, they sincerely give way too much cash. I only went to sell my stuff once, and that was when I had the said 70K in hand.
4. Tutorial is lacking a bit. I believe the tutorial could be better, like to add how engineer can hack locked doors, something I learned on my own.
5. Repetitive bases. You will often see the same type of layout in a base on a planet. It took me 5 planets to discover that bases could have stairs
6. The stats when you level up. When you place your stats point after leveling up, it shows only the potential change AFTER you put the point in, not before. Also, if you place your last point in a stat, you wont be allowed to see what will be the change. This is a really minor thing.
The fun stuff
1. The story and it's caracters. The story is simple and yet I know there's a lot more in that game. More than only 2 hours of gameplay could allow me to see. The inhabitant of the universe are diverse and interesting.
2. The humour. There are some small joke here and there, to lighten up the fact that you are shooting the little hell out of critters and primitive ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Its neat.
3. The gameplay. The shooting/crew-based gameplay is well done.
4. The small detail. The equipment your crew wears change how they look, which is nice.
Overall, I would wait for you to buy the game, not until they update the game to address these issues...
But dont take my words for cash, I am a picky S.O.B.

Relaxing they said, good for anxiety they said... and it was, right up until I walked into the wrong one of those zoomy pipes. Tomb Raider and Mario 64 gave me a massive phobia of going underwater in video games because you never know wtf video game devs decided to put in there.
Being surrounded by ocean had been mildly triggering me my whole 10 minute session but I could power through that believing the game would always require me to avoid falling in and would probably respawn me on the last red thing I touched if I fell in.
So I approach this pipe, its bending down into the ocean - I'm immediately alarmed. However directly across a small gap the pipe bends back up out of the water..."oh okay, it just goes under the surface a bit and pops me up on that rock."
I prepare myself mentally to face my fear in a mild, controlled manner... a 1 second zip just under the surface safe in my glass tube... and I walk in.
I zoom around the bend expecting the second turn when I'm DUMPED OUT OF THE FILTY LYING TUBE INTO THE OPEN OCEAN! Suddenly I'm drowning in my chair!, I can feel the Shark from Tomb Raider, the thing from Mario and the god damn Kraken powering through the water to drag me into the blackness. This all happens in half a second that felt like a minute.
I start spasming and flailing madly at my keyboard, desperately trying to make it understand that my left hand violently smashing into as many keys at once as it can means "Alt + F4 plz plz plz".
I give up trying to pull off a complex combo like alt F4 and decide to just slam the escape button hoping this is one of those programs that can be closed that way. It's a pause screen, the game is still playing behind it, THE KRAKEN STILL COMETH.
After mashing the keyboard some more I hit the power button on my monitor so I could alt + F4 properly.
10/10 - the laugh I had at myself after all of this was worth the $1 easily.
