I specifically bought this game because I heard some people are upset about jontron having a voice in it. The fact that the developers are not spineless cowards, letting themselves being bullied by an overemotional minority of crybabies earns them my respect!
Now to the game itself:
I started playing it with absolutely no expectations whatsoever, but I knew that I enjoyed Rayman 2 and 3 in the past and A Hat in Time reminded me very much of these games as I watched the clips in the shop. After playing it for 20 minutes, I was immediately fond of the cute characters and the crazy setting and I soon found myself rushing through the levels.
Gameplay:
The gameplay of A Hat in Time is very smooth and I had almost no problems with it. I played through the whole game with an Xbox One controller, without experiencing any frustration, which was often the case with other jump and run titles. The only part in the game, where I had some problems, was with some platforming in the Great Windmill level. I tried to jump on a moving wall piece, where I slipped off and ended up reactivating a checkpoint way below me and I had to replay that whole part again. Other than that, I had absolutely no issues.
Like the title of the game suggests, you must use a variety of different hats to advance. These hats can then be upgraded by buying pins which give you unique powers. As you proceed through the game, you will get more hats and the game will get more complex.
Boss Battles:
There is combat in this game, but fighting against regular enemies, is smoothly combined with the rest of the gameplay so I won’t address this any further.
The real deal when it comes to combat though, are the Boss Battles in this game. When I encountered the first Boss, I was completely surprised. I wasn’t sure what to expect, but whatever I thought it would be, it was like 20 times better! THE MUSIC! THE FAST PACE! THE SETTING! This is where this game is shining the brightest.
I have 1 complaint about the last boss of the game though: The time slowing hat is kind of OP… I was using it throughout the whole boss fight and it ended up being way too easy. I’ll have to try it another time without the hat I guess.

Art & Music:
As I already hinted at in the Boss Battle part of this review, I absolutely love the Music! I am pretty sure that if you would remove the music from this game, it wouldn’t even be half as good. No matter where you go, you will always be followed by a catchy tune to hum along.
Then there is the colorful & warm art style, which gives the game a powerful atmosphere. I can’t really say much about it though, since I think everyone has his own taste when it comes to graphics 😊
Story:
The story is very simple: You are traveling home in your spaceship and are flying over a strange planet. An unfortunate event happens and you lose all your “fuel”, which you then have to regain in order to get home. On your way of regaining all your “fuel”, you will encounter a lot of funny, diverse and interesting characters that accompany you throughout numerous adventures.
Length/Content:
I took 13-14 hours to finish the game with 97%. For my taste, the length of this game is just right, as I rather replay the game a bunch of times instead of playing an eternity to finish it once. But I think this is up to debate, as some people would enjoy it to be a bit longer.
Conclusion:
Positives:
- MUSIC!
- Smooth Gameplay
- Boss Battles
- Gadgets & Customization
Negatives:
- Maybe the length for some people???
The game was more than worth it’s price and I will probably try to get myself some merch. I really hope that there will be a sequel to this game.

Personally, out of sheer coincidence or maybe I just was busy, I had never heard of Shiness until about a month ago. So when I approached Shiness I flew completely blind with no preconceptions or opinions. Everything I had gathered was from screenshots that looked incredible and reminded me of Dragon Quest and from a trailer that looked and sounded amazing.
I did a little bit of digging on the history of Shiness after having played it and I discovered quite a few things. For one, Shiness has been delayed a few times, much to the dismay of its backers. The game was due to release some time in 2015-16 but had been pushed back. This is also Enigami’s first developed game, and an extremely ambitious one at that. If you take in the amount of money vs quality that this game has achieved, it’s astonishing. They made an entire language up for this game and it even has a dictionary. The point is that Shiness’ development has been a bit of a mixed bag, with some good and some bad. Was all the wait worth it? I think so. Although I haven’t been waiting as long as others.
It was June 7th 2014 that Shiness was officially Kickstarted by 3,028 backers who pledged $139,865.
So here is an important disclaimer: I will not be putting any of the drama into consideration here in this review. I am judging this game solely based off of the merits of what I played, unaware of events or any promises beforehand. However, I will take core features and compare them to the original campaign promises.
With the amount of world building and unique style, Shiness reminds me of everything I loved about titles like Jade Empire and Fable.
Aside from a brief starting exposition cut scene, Shiness literally crashes you into the middle of its universe. The tones all feel familiar, but you definitely feel like there is a lore that you will learn as you play the game. There are times I felt thrown for a loop and a little lost. When I first heard the characters speak I had to stop and make sure that I didn’t click on the wrong dialogue option. That is when I realized there were no language options and that this was a made up language. This is amazing but does take a bit of getting used to. There is quite a bit of name dropping as well which I felt that a lore guide would’ve definitely helped with.
The story of Shiness is mostly in line with the standard RPG concept. You have six elements that live harmoniously and an evil version called Dark Shi. This is the macguffin of the game and gets things moving. There are three primary races: Waki which are cute cuddly teddy bears, the Shelk which look like furries on steroids, and finally Humans. Our protagonists name is Chado, a Waki who can speak to an elemental spirit named Shiness(Terra). This makes him an outcast from his own people. Adventure, go!
While I wouldn’t say that the story is forgettable in Shiness, I will say that it is your anime-esque typical affair, if you will. Shiness wears its inspiration on its sleeve. Taking from bits of DBZ, Naruto and other animes. This certainly isn’t a bad thing, but the story really requires minimal brain power to understand. The characters are cute, over the top and adventure seeking. That is the primary theme of Shiness; those looking for deeper plots and lore along the lines of Skyrim or Mass Effect aren’t going to find it here. It really depends on your personal preference. Sometimes you just want to enjoy something easy to chew.
Speaking of easy to chew, Shiness’ graphics have a wonderful sense of joy. The world is beautiful, bright, and brimming with magic. All of the villages, dungeons, and areas are lovingly crafted and you can spot details packed into every nook and cranny of the game. The first time you see Mantara you can’t help but be in awe at how imaginative and amazing it all looks. The graphics lend themselves perfectly to these types of moments.
The environmental design, by far, is the most appealing thing about the graphics in Shiness. The character models themselves aren’t as robust as I would’ve liked in comparison. This was obviously on the developers mind, as most often when heavy character expression is required, a cut scene takes charge with comic panels. These manga/comic moments are extremely well drawn and accomplish far more than the current character models ever could. I personally didn’t mind this style at all and felt it was a great way to get the story across. Keep in mind from a gaming development standpoint, one or two hundred thousand dollars isn’t much. Cutting corners in creative ways is impressive.
One thing to note is that Shiness is a very linear RPG compared to most these days. You won’t find an open world to explore but instead there are tight compact zones akin to an MMORPG. You can tackle side quests within these zones and markers are placed so that you never really get lost.  Zones are also level based so eventually you will just out level everything in the area if you find yourself grinding often.
Have you ever wanted to punch an anthropomorphic animal in the face or blast it with a fireball?
Then let’s talk about combat. No RPG would be successful without a great combat system. Shiness strikes a good blend between old and new. This is definitely where I draw comparisons to Jade Empire. Featuring exclusively one on one fights, you will seamlessly enter combat where you can use an assortment of combos, spells, and basic attacks to defeat enemies. Players who love the open world combat are going to be amazed how fast the game quickly transitions between exploration and combat.
There is no pause for loading or cute little screen dissolves. You punch that plant in the face and it’s go time! This switch happens so quickly that sometimes I was unprepared and the aforementioned plant blasted me in the face for half my health. Combat is a robust but simple system that doesn’t really take long to grasp. You have basic strikes, combos that you learn from disciplines(scrolls) and spells. Shiness took a page out of Final Fantasy IX’ book and lets you “Master” abilities from items. Once you master a combo or spell, that item can then be given to another party member.
Some combos are character exclusive but further enhanced versions of them are deeper in the game and add more effects and make combos stronger. The arena itself also plays an important role during combat. Depending on the color of the arena certain elemental spells will be enhanced or weakened. Then there is your characters “Hyper” which basically can be equated to a finishing move. Below your health bar is a meter that lets you combo break, deflect enemy attacks, and use hyper. This resource can only be built by taking damage or dishing it out, bringing everything back to slugging it out old fashioned style.
The combat system just works, and I mean it works really well. I have few complaints when it comes to combat. It’s fun, and definitely robust enough to my satisfaction. While I wouldn’t go as far to say it’s a true fighting game along the lines of Street Fighter or Mortal Kombat, it combines enough elements to keep things from getting boring.
There are some drawbacks though. For one, I hate the camera. When you enter combat there is no special arena it magically zips you away to. A circle appears around you and your foe at a fair distance. Most of the time this isn’t a problem. However, for some reason camera control is taken away from you and it becomes fixed in position behind your fighter. Natural terrain can become a hazard if you get stuck behind a tree and suddenly you can’t see anything. Additionally, for some reason the game will flip to the perspective of the enemy and this really makes it difficult to dodge or move.

The 1st 5 Hours Review, Will be updated later on.
Story
It feels like one of those 2000's era cartoons but better that everyone is not a goody two shoes save for the princess. I feel that the manga (included in pre-bought game) definately helps here. A plus that the audience target range is for ALL AGES. Some war is brewing around, a princess is escaping, two little runts who were flying on a ship and crashed...1 of them is what people think that the runt is cuckoo for talking to an invisible friend...
Animation,
It feels better watching it while I play, not so much when its the cutscenes. Its a mix of comic strips and 3D animations which is the worse of the 2. The comic strips are entertaining while the 3D is limited to a few expressions and its not centerized that it makes it cut out some parts of the face or body parts especially concerning the princess.
Music
Pleasant and fits the mood. I think I heard about 4 or 5 so far, and only 1 sticks with me.
Combat
If you are not used to fighting or action games, this might be harsh to JRPG players who are more used to turn based battles. Its dodging, parrying and defending is very dependant on crucial timing. The challenge is wonderful but you have to know what you're getting yourself into. Even early on, enemies know how to dodge, parry, run and defend just like you do.
The combos I've found so far has 3 inputs at best but it does look like it can be more complex?
Other than attacks and specials, there is also magic and depending on the character, they can learn it from disciplines. Of course the magic effectiveness depends on their elements.
Other actions on field
So far, I've found you can sneak and capture little animals like birds or even snails to get their items like fur or poop which is more expensive than the furs...You can sell it or barter the items to gain useful items like Disciplines (Skill Book) or Equipment.
So far it feels like 73/100 but this is just the 1st 5 hours...not even the prologue is even done at this point because I'm just getting used to combat for each character (everyone is different), leveling up and making sure I don't die. Get it if you want to challenge yourself.

The rest of the cast are underutilized and forgettable.  The NOD story is cliched with double crosses and predictable developments sadly.
Multiplayer is very fast paced and plenty of opportunities to be devious or brutal if you choose.
If you're into explosions, the game is for you.

SUPERHOT is a game where time moves only when you do. It is an action FPS/puzzler game that first started out as a prototype that a lot of people played a few years ago (and you can still play it to this day) and loved so much that the developers of SUPERHOT released a kickstarter for it, and now, this is that game.
And just like the original demo/prototype, it's damn awesome, and it takes what made the original prototype great and expands on it to prefection. The aesthetic, while simple, is quite pleasing, especially when you punch/hit/slice/shoot the red glass men and watch them shatter against the white background behind them. The videos on the store page do quite a good job of showing off what the game looks like, and in short, It makes you feel badass.
This is the game you want if you want to dodge bullets matrix style from a guy point blank, punch him, take his gun while he is reacting from the punch, blow his head off, shoot the guy next to him while still doging bullets, throw your gun at the next guy, pick up a katana, slice an oncomming bullet in half (yes you can do that and more, I'll put a few tips down below), cut the guy you threw the gun at  in half, and then throw the katana at the last guy behind you. All that, in just a couple of seconds.
It's just great, and in fact it is one of the few games that I have bought on day 1. Yes, I'm one of those (sensible and patient) people who buys games way after they've been released at 50 or 75% off.
Now with those such game mechanics, you might think this game is easy, but, at least in my experience, it's not. You're gonna die a lot, especially on the challenge modes which change up the gameplay rules and freshen up the experience, as bullets/melee weapons kill you in one hit. Or maybe its because I am too zealous when playing this game sometimes and forget to stand still and get shot in the back in the process a lot of the time. The game makes you think back to other shooters and what we take for granted these days in those games.
So it really saddens me to see a couple of "most helpful" reviews being negative, pointing out how short the campaign is (I beat it in about 2-3 hours), and thus saying that the game is not worth the asking price of 25 bucks (at the time of writing it is 10% off at $22.50). And I'm going to adress that. First off, this isn't a game that you play the campaign and put it down forever, and that's it. The campaign is not even HALF of the game. It might as well be the tutorial for the rest of the game, I'd even argue. As you can probably see from those negative reviews, they've only played 2-3 hours (the length of the campaign), then come here and post a negative review without bothering to try anything else that the game has to offer.
As I said, this isn't the game you play only for the campaign, this is the type of game you play for the core gameplay experience, and you won't get all of that core experience from the campaign alone, not by a long shot. After you beat the campaign, you unlock various endless and challenge modes. Endless modes are self explanatory, and within those endless modes there are variations such as time limits and stuff like that, and then there's challenges. Challenges put a spin on top of the core gameplay. There's modes to unlock from Katana only, to a "Ghost" mode where you can only hotswitch (possess enemies by teleporting into them) and one hit kill enemies with punches but can't pick up any weapons or objects. There is so much variety in these challenge and endless modes alone, you can get countless of hours into the game, to make it well worth the asking price.
I got 2-3 hours out of the game's campaign, but I have gotten a further 8 or so hours from the challenge modes alone, and I plan to put in even more hours into it.
There's even loads of secrets to find throughout the game if that's your type of thing. This game is packed full of content, it's just a shame that it presented itself with the campaign first, and people thought "is that it?" and then went on to spread negative reviews of it as a result.
But anyway, now that's out of the way, here's some actual criticism (sorta) that will hopefully be sorted out with time:

So there we have it. Buy this game if you like this sort of stuff or just vaguely like the idea, and it'll be a steal on sale. And like I said before, don't just play the campaign and drop it and then complain about it, because that's not the sort of game that this is and is not what all the game has to offer.

Current Patch:  1.0.0
Experience: got a squad of 8 to lv 50+
The Good:
-Loot explosions are great.
-Loot Donkies (like loot goblins from diablo.).
-Pixel art is wonderful.
-SFX and music hit the spot.
-Tactical mode feels like I'm playing a management game. (Dwarf Fortress/Rim world. This is a plus for me but maybe not for others.)
-Combat really shines on the big mobs/boss fights.
-Damage meter. This is the first ARPG-ish game I've played with a damage meter. This is very helpful and I love it.
The Bad:
-Managing 8 players without group hot-kets blows. It would be nice to assign hotkeys for multiple units so I can manage my tanks a bit better or mose my healers away without stopping my damage from dpsing.
-No auto attack. I know the devs made this intentional decision to have no auto attack but in all honesty it doesn't feel right. Clicking every single tiny mob is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ During boss fights or large mobs I always resort to tactial mode anyway. Having to click on every tiny mob cuts down on clear time though and it feels janky.
-Loot quantity and quality.
This game has tons of loot which you would think is good, right? Yes and No. I have played countless hours of diablo, grim dawn and Path of Exile (outside of steam).  While grim dawn drops a good chunk of useless loot there's less loot in that game than Pixel Privateers but it's more meaningful. In Pixel Privateers they have item find % as one of the stats from gear to acquire even more loot to offset the lack of quality loot. Path of exile did the same thing but they also had Item Quality % even though I think these types of stats are not very interesting they did serve their purpose to off set the bad drop rates of good loot. Diablo 3 vanilla had this same issue where you would not see an upgrade for hours or even days after max level. Pixel Privateers lacks the interesting loot affixes that ARPGs are known for; procs/auras/skills.
In Grim Dawn I might get a helm that can send my character into a berserking rage at the cost of taking more damage or have an item that can sometimes charge up in power before exploding later on.  The usual affixes I see on some of the gear in this game tends to be a % chance to maybe drop a healing item or spawn a drone ect. Nothing that really stands out or maybe I wasn't lucky enough to find said gear. There is a lot of time spent in menus but I'm used to these kind of games. Others may not like the down time though.
Bugs:
-F8 key will disable the UI and this happens to be a default keybind for selecting a unit. This could be unique to me though so I'm not so sure.
-Selecting a healing ability can sometimes make the attack command disappear and leaves your guys unable to attack until a restart of the game happens.
- 2560 x 1440 resolution makes the text so unbearably small that I need to whip out my old granny glasses to read it.
I love the game though. It has a strong theme.  If I had to sum it up this game is like Borderlands and a casual starcraft mod with a little diablo mixed in for good measure.

• For those who have not played this game:
This game is social commentary about 'mental health' and 'prison games', wrapped up in a walking simulator / interactive fiction.
• For those who have played this game:
It's a lesson of 'who is a person' and the importance of 'perspective'. Some days I feel like a Davey, other days I feel like Davey's idea of what is a Coda. Those are the two personalities we're introduced to in this work. 1. Davey. (the narrator) and 2. Davey's perception of 'who Coda is'.
Unfortunately we never get to meet the real Coda. So even though it's supposed to be a spotlight on Coda and what Coda thinks of himself... it's actually a spotlight on Davey and what Davey thinks about Coda. (And a rare glimpse into what Coda thinks of Davey.) Never once though do we actually get the pleasure of meeting Coda.
With that said, both probably have some mental issues ranging from 'slight', to 'better keep an eye out for that one'. (As for who is which... even that can be debated both ways.)
I will say this though... people who are, even slightly, 'creative', whether for fun or profit (maybe both) will be able to relate to the topics discussed in this project. Others... maybe not so much.
If Coda is real, I would love to chat with him. See his perspective on things... Really get to meet Coda for the first time.

Shiness: The Lightning Kingdom Review (Completed. Review was Under Updates from 19th-21st April, GMT +8)
If you have any questions, leave a comment below and I'll answer them. Have tech Issues? Lay them down and I'll do my best to help.
Imagine the Naruto like Combat system mix in with the Tales Combat System+reward based system and somehow has a feeling of classic Square Game setting (Not Square Enix, Square) and Zelda like feeling when it comes to the exploration + Interaction. That is what Shiness acts and feels like.
Rather than an RPG, its more of a JRPG because the cutscenes goes into a Manga Artstyle, the beautiful Environment is colourful and vibrant that it feels very alive. Although it can be quite eye induing pain if you are not used to it but you can tone it down but to tone it down to a proper quality, use 3rd party tools like SweetFX. There is many platform + puzzles when you start exploring and each main characters has their unique ability to solve them. Unique and interesting. The voice acting is actually quite decent for the characters. The music and ambience is strong. Some scenes has some odd flat dialog of expression though which becomes awkward.  There are reports of Audio desync but Developers acknowldge it and are working on a Fix.
5 Unique controllable characters each with their Strength and Weakness in Combat, Elemental and Environmental Interactive Abilities. One example would be Chado, a Waki race which looks Hamster like. His ability is summoning 2 Rocks which you can place and throw. It can be used for switches that needs to be hold down.
The combat system comes in a Form of Punch, Kicks, Spell casting, Guard, Dodge and Parry. There are combo system but the most interesting is the Shi/Elemental Arena when you engage combat. Combat is real time and the Elements of the Arena gives both Advantage and Disadvantage to the player and enemies. The only problem is the Camera. It always goes to the length of "This is the best Camera Angle" but it zooms in when you go to a corner of the arena and can be hard to navigate to see yourself and the enemies you are fighting with. Even the locked-on is kinda weird and difficult to use as you can't tell properly if you are actually locked-on or not. Developers has acknowledge this problem thankfully.
You also get to Craft equipments aka Barter once you have certain materials. You can collect materials from the Environment Wildlife like chasing Clams and Birds by sneaking up on them but also from Combat Rewards and Contracts. Be warn you might need to grind your level, Upgrade your equipment and change combat styles as the enemies might get tougher later on. Bewarn when doing Contract Side quest. The boss is not to be messed with when you are under leveled and geared.
Combat is 1v1, but you can swicth to your other 2 party members. While party members are not in combat, they do have support abilities you can equip them with certain parameters and condition. Like say Heal > Ally > 75% Below Health. There will be a cooldown.
The game is heavily Gamepad recommended and not for Keyboard Recommended. The gamepad I used is the Logitec F310 and I've experience no problems and no input delay. It's X-Input Recommended as there is no D-Input. Curiously there are some issues for those using Official Xbox Controllers but the Developers has acknowledge the Tech Problem and are working sorting that out.
PC Laptop users, if you experience FPS problem, you might want to switch the game to run on your NVIDIA/AMD GPU as the game defaults itself to use your CPU GPU. This is due to the fact that the game is not NVIDIA License. Despite that, with the CPU GPU I currently have, Intel HD Graphics 630 under the Kabylake i7-7700HQ, the game still runs very well because of the game engine. Performance is very stable although I did suffer some initial frame destabilization when I run on the NVIDIA (Running on a NVIDIA GTX 1060) only for a few minutes but after than, it becomes stable. I even tested the game slightly on an older PC of mine, it runs on i5-3210M + NVIDIA GT 640M and still it ran well though 30FPS. It supports 4k, it does support 1080p, two FPS Cap 30 & 60. Cutscenes ran on 30FPS oddly but the entire gameplay itself runs on 60FPS.
Overall: Game is Recommended but the Value is up to you to decide as according to the Steamdb, there seems to be price gap difference from my Region Asia to the US/EU Region.

My initial impressions:
-A semi-linear narrative story with 5 playable characters you meet along the way. Each character has its own unique attributes and you build them differently.
-The levels are reminiscent of n64 3d platformers. So they are semi-linear but you can go around looking for hidden items as well. Many of the level areas are very "open" so you will want to explore every nook and cranny, but you do move on linearly.
-There are 4 main elements that you manipulate like Avatar the Last airbender. Water can be used as a projectile, to heal yourself, barrier etc. Same for fire, earth, lightning. Initially you have no powers tho (but some characters start with one).
-RPG mechanics: Has the usual gamut of vitality, strength, magic, speed, etc. You upgrade them by playing and by getting loot from enemies. There is equipment and items, as per usual in RPGs. Each of your 5 characters seems to use different items.
For example, some scrolls give you water power. You must equip these to your particular character. So you are "building" your character Dark Souls-esque (although not even close to as complex as DS of course; you basically just use the items and skill points you are given. There's not that many of them)
-Combat is amazing. It's an RPG so you will see enemies in the distance and you can avoid them or engage them in battle. Unlike turn based RPGs where you sit there and queue moves, it's real-time and it's martial arts. It's kinda Sleeping Dogs or Batman Arkham style combat.
You get combos you must earn/learn and there's parry, dodge, block, kick, jump and then your magic (Shi) attacks and combos.
The arena you fight in is a circle. The only BAD thing is the camera so far. You can lock onto your enemy BEFORE you get in combat but once you get in combat, the lock on stops for some reason. You must keep pressing R3 to "center" the camera behind your character. If you dodge or run around the enemy, the camera stays in one place. So you can end up on left/right side or even in the background while the enemy is in the foreground.  I personally want the enemy to always be in the "center" as a pivot point while you can run around the enemy, like Dark souls. Right now, you must spam R3 to recenter the enemy in front of you.
It's really annoying right now and I hope they fix this

Here is a survival game that is actually about surviving and not about making weird random crap and shooting zombies. It's really cool!
It is also a very difficult game. After playing for a while you will start to find strategies though. The last update added different difficulty levels, so if you are overwhelmed then you can try an easier difficulty- however, I think that Stalker (Hard mode) is the most fun. It's extremely satisfying to beat the incredibly tough odds the game throws at you, especially when you are first starting out and have very few resources.
The game takes place in the northern canadian wilderness. The two biggest dangers in this game are cold and wolves. It is best to avoid the wolves, as they can and will kill you very, very quickly. You can also die from hunger, thirst, disease, and drowning.
You will need to go outside into a snowstorm to find food because you ran out. You will be unable to see in the snowstorm. While searching for a place to warm up and find food you will get jumped by wolves and die.
There is a gun, but it will not make the game any easier. First you have to find it (and I'm not gonna tell you where it is!), and even then you will be lucky to have even 4 or 5 bullets. Again, you are better off avoiding wolves entirely.
If you are looking for a difficult, realistic sandbox survival game, this is the most difficult and realistic one I know of! Eventually, you will run out of something, and you will die.
I think this game has turned me semi-masochistic... It's completely unfair- the weather is poor at the worst possible times, wolves start chasing me when I least expect it, I desperately need warmer clothing and all I can find is can openers  and tinder. It's so unfair, just like real life!
Hopefully the developers will not make it any easier ;^) My best so far is 36 days and counting on Stalker. Can you beat that?

Hi I'm Charles Loris.
I had it all on the racing circuit.
A red car.  Stickers.  Four tyres.  And even a guy to change them for me.
I still had to pump my own gas, but I was always a stickler for the simple things.
I raced in all the big races.  I did so many laps in the Indiana 500 that my race team found me six hours after the race rolling counter-clockwise around my own bath tab, yelling "Gotta clean fast!"
It was a crazy time.
Its amazing how it can all fall to pieces so fast.
I was sued for a cool half mill when in the headiness of being a young driver I called my sponsor Red Bull the taste of a new generation while drinking water from a diet coke can.
Some people would have gotten mad and blamed the man who put the drinks in my hand or my manager for hiring a fifteen year old to type my autocue lines, but I took it all in my stride.  I walked over fifteen press journalists and camera operators after slipping off the stage in a blur of flash photography and hurrying for the nearest stairs.  When the tv news completely ignored my embarrassing slip up and instead played the NASCAR prayer I knew my career was dead.
In my next race I took a wrong turn, took out four cars, and skewered a dart board right through the middle with a track side dummy I hit and sent flying into the nethers.
Rumors spread that I had been driving while drowsy and that news soon reached my manager.  I was out on the street.  Destitute with nothing, but a race car with no tyres and 13 rolls of sponsor stickers to keep me warm at night.
It was a tough time, but then I found this game.
And I was hooked.
I used a USB stick to get my now non-moving race car to run Windows OS and used my steering wheel for a controller.  Combinations of the buttons for opening my car trunk and hood were my a and b buttons for navigating menus.  At first my neighbours (mostly pigeons at this stage, don't ask) all told me I was mad.  But for the first time in years I had a real drive.
I sent my car hurtling over hills to take shortcuts.  I drove clockwise around an oval track.
I even used destruction derby as a way to get revenge on my racing enemies.
All this I did with a shouty glee.  When online mult-iplayer rolled around I had to get in on it.
I single handedly towed my tireless race car to a non-parking zone, where I knew I could get a free tow service closer to McDonalds wi-fi.
Sure I had to stay in my car permanently as a protest to prevent my not-so-mobile home from being crushed into a cube, but it was worth it.
I even got a new job snitching to police about local gangstas trying to use the car compactor to hide bodies and evidence, but I digress.
Oh the online racing!  How my heart did leap when I first saw online multi-player destruction debies and rolled around the outside counter-clockwise while the young-uns pummelled each others chassis with reckless abandon.  The destruction was joyous.  Until I realised the game let me re-spawn and I realised I had to enter the fray to score a point.  But still for the first time I felt like I really truly "got" this game that I loved.  And it turned out that the game understood me too.
Real life opponents asked me if they could drive backwards around oval tracks and I laughed heartily before allowing it.  Although I admit I have so far been too timid to drive backwards where others could see me.  I kept my secret joy for backwards racing to purer backwards versions of the tracks away from the prying eyes of the public.
So for now I have been living in my former race car in a wreckers yard a mere 15 feet from the local McDonalds for the past five months.  Every day I work hard on perfecting my laps and crashing strategies in this strange new life.  Occasionally I get on to the Steam forums and complain under my numerous aliases about the next update taking too long, but I guess that type of deviant behaviour comes too quickly to those who witness at least one murder and too numerous to count possum fights every week.
For now I must bid you adieu.  I look forward to seeing you on the racing tracks.
Keep watching the mirrors,
- Charles Loris

TL;DR: Great frantic squad-based shoot-'em up with tons of customization options, random items galore, awesome sprite artwork, a slight learning curve for the controls, some bugs, a fantastic bar complete with great in-house band, randomness galore, invasions, and it's even better online coop with friends(except the random prisoner quests that lag like crazy).
So.....
What is "A-move" or "attack move" that everyone is complaining about?  It's a queue-style command in other Real-Time Strategy games like Starcraft where players push a keybind(usually A) that puts their selected characters in Attack mode, and when the next move command is given, those characters will attack anything while moving to the target location.  It becomes tedious and extremely spammy spam, and yet you are forced to do this (in Starcraft 2) if you want to get better.
At first, I was like everyone else complaining: "Where's my A-move!?"  "Why are my units just standing there?"  And now after almost 20 hours of play, I'm actually glad there's no A-move or auto attack(aggressive mode)  It just makes it have a little bit of a learning curve, and I had to play around with the keybindings a few times until I felt comfortable controlling my squad.  Things get hectic quick, especially on Hardcore mode(perma death).  Also, there is a Tactical Mode(PAUSE - only in single player) for those that like to stop and issue commands.
If A-Move and/or auto-attack are added, please make them options, maybe in a Casual difficulty setting.  I don't want to be forced into having to play that way now that I've actually learned how to much better micro my squad members.  If you want to get better at this game, make every effort to SWITCH through and individually control your squad.  With practice, you will realize that your don't WANT your high crit squad member taking 1 of its only 2 shots from its rocket launcher on that mob that would have otherwise died to a small pistol shot and now has to spend another 5 seconds reloading, etc etc.  And A-move or auto-attack would take a lot of fun out of the frantic battles, since it would become just another typical strategy game in which you can just select ALL squad members, and A-move to victory.
So yeah, if you want a challenge, and don't mind putting in a little effort learning how to micro-manage better and more efficiently, this game will be extremely fun for you!  If you just want to Auto-Attack-Move or want your Squad to Automatically do everything for you, look elsewhere.

Wonderful in it's own special way, but bound to make some people disappointed. If you're looking for a fun game then don't bother, as it essentially lacks any game mechanics. It's quite short, meaning that the $10 asking price will not be worth it to many people. It also is very different from The Stanley Parable, and in fact it is very far from comedic, so fans of that might wind up disappointed as well.
It's a game that is difficult to explain without revealing some aspects of it and spoiling the whole thing, and it's best to go in totally blind. Blind faith is hard to sell, however, so if you're not willing to take a risk don't bother. It appeals to a niche audience that finds the medium of video games capible of being captivating and telling good stories without being a traditional "game," and this particular story heavily benifits from having some limited interactivity. If that sounds pretentious or uninteresting then stay far, far away. Others, however, might find something that resonates with them, as I and several others have.
It's an ambitious game, but it's also very small and personal. It finds a balance, and it's beautiful. It might even be the best "walking simulator" game to date, although that might not be fair because it's so different than any of those games that came before it.
In short, don't buy it unless you are fine with spending $10 on a story. It is, however, a damn fine story if you can buy into it.

I have really tried to like this game, but honestly it's tedious and artificially challenging. By that, I mean the AI is so erratic and illogical it's like watching an ant farm without a queen. Actually, that's an insult to ants. At least they get something done eventually. It really does feel more like watching the game than playing it, as well. Just because you tell your minions to do something, it hardly means they're going to do it in a timely manner. Unfortunately, as slow-paced as this game is, ♥♥♥♥ing winter is coming...and it is your greatest foe.
I just don't get this game. I've read strategies and guides about the mechanics to see what exactly I'm just not getting about this game, and as far as I can figure the problem is it is designed to be excessively slow and requires you to micromanage everything. The irony is the game is really basic in terms of what all you can do; it's just it doesn't let you do any of it in an efficient way. Gods forbid you try to build more than one building at a time--even using the priority tool--you can have the Great Wall of China sized stockpiles of supplies, an army of builders, and it will still take a year to build one motherlovin' house.
Of course, there are times everything goes smoothly, and you almost have fun. I played a game all the way to year 40, my city was doing well, I had ample supplies, and everyone was healthy and happy. I was building and growing steadily, planning ahead by expanding my infrastructure before the next wave of houses (which also work so illogically), and everything was great. Then two things happened: I realized I was not having much fun because there was almost nothing to do but expand with the same handful of buildings over and over, and also everyone starved to death.
Seriously, I had 15K food stockpiled, prebuilt more food-bearing structures for my new minions, then built a few houses which led to about a whopping 8 more population, and suddenly I found myself unable to keep up with the demand for food. I have no idea why. Those 8 people must have brought tapeworms, or were very well-disguised hippopotami of a hungry hungry disposition.
I suppose if you look at this game as a satirical statement on the futility (and stupidity) of mankind, you might find some passing interest in it. Otherwise, expect to spend of a lot of time playing out of spite just to figure out why you're not having any fun. I just feel like there's no need to keep going in this game because even if I have missed "the key" to making a successful city, there just isn't enough to do in this game to keep it interesting.
In short, this games feels like it should be great...but it's not.

For those looking for a bit more of a TL;DR: Hat in Time has been an interesting experience
I had forgotten how much heart and soul and polish could be put into a game, and how much joy you could experience playing one. And this game OOZES love. The attention to detail from little inclusions like visual changes in the eyes of a roomba from ^_^ to >_< while you stand on it to the chatty nooses in Subcon Forest that comment about how nice your neck looks today are the sorts of things most overworked game developers never get around to. They're either broke and headed for a deadline at Christmas or just tired of working on project bugs to get it out of Beta. But the designers and programmers didn't stop at "good enough", they went so far above and beyond that I am almost ashamed of my own game development projects.
Beyond that, the game runs on spirited, colorful imagination I haven't seen since the Paper Mario series. Hat Girl herself is utterly adorable to follow around on her adventures, her quiet but clever mannerisms make her an excellent foil to the explosive personalities she encounters. Dead Bird Studio and Subcon Forest both stand out in particular here, with the fun characters of DJ Grooves, the Conductor, and the Snatcher taking you out on crazy adventures from solving train murders with brown camera filters and classy jazz, to delivering stolen mail for an eccentric faustian devil who likes to "pretend to care" about his minions (have I mentioned how much I love the Snatcher? because <3 ). The soundtrack and the art style are phenomenal (no, really, the art of this game is GORGEOUS and ADORABLE! Every piece of art with Hat Girl puts a goofy grin on my face), and both are used well to complement the missions, giving different worlds distinct feelings.
I don't normally write reviews because I usually think buying a game and not returning it is enough approval. But A Hat in Time is different. I felt real childhood joy playing this game, a feeling I'd all but forgotten by, in the words of Yahtzee Crosshaw, "penetrating the caked on layers of doughy acceptance the game industry has been pelting me with over the years". It makes me want to give that love back by promoting this game as much as possible. So please, buy this game (full price, support those devs!) and see for yourself what true love looks like.

There is too many issues with this game right that just make it frustrating to play rather than enjoyable. Underneath all these glaring problems is a good game though.
1. Too much loot, you spend a while sorting out all of your loot after every mission. Only for it to become clustered again after the next mission. The time between missions is also too great because of all the stuff you have to do to sort your inventory out.
2. No auto attack. Your landing party will just stand there unless you tell it to attack. Once the enemy is dead they will just stand there once again until you tell them to attack the next enemy.
3. Tactical mode is nice. It is however the only way you can have all your crew use their special abilities before the fight is over. Using abilities is extremely tedious and unconventional when in the heat of a battle due to how difficult it is to actually get one of your crew members to use one. By which time the fight is over anyway. Tactical mode is also ruined by the fact that your crew members will not continue their attack on the enemy you have told them to use their ability on.
4. Loot progresses way too fast. They seem to double in stats every mission (not sure if this slows down later on though).
All these issues make the game a slog to play rather than a joy. Once they have been fixed  (such as easier crew selection during a fight) then it will be much better as the underlying game is great.
For now I cannot recommend this.

~DISCLAIMER~
I review this game as a seperate IP for it's franchise. I will not be comparing game on it's battle system, soundtracks or character comparison.
I have played a lot of Tales games, from Symphonia to Abyss to Grace to Vesperia to Xillia.
My favourite of them all is Abyss for it's introduction to TP system and good character development and best story.
The latest installment JRPG in the Tales of series. Tales of Zestiria is the first Tales of game to be released on PC. You play as a character called Sorey, a human raised by Seraphim. With his best friend and seraph Mikleo, he starts his adventure when he met a girl named Alisha. He soon becomes a Shepard to free malevolence with a goal to reunite humans and seraphim.
Pros :
+ First Tales of game to be released to PC
+ Combat is fluid.
+ Menu is really clean and understandable.
+ Fusion for a duplicate weapon to create the stronger equipment with attributes that helps during battles.
+ Skits and character interaction are hilarious and makes character believable.
+ Open world and on the fly type of battle encounters.
+ Soundtrack fits the environment and the locations.
+ English voice acting are actually great and believable, stays true to each characters personality.
+ No more TP for artes, the game uses SC and BG for artes, combos and  armatization to limits combo and removes endless combos.
+ Elements, weakness and status ailment matters during battle.
+ AP system is a good progressive battle assistant. Gives you more flexibility during battle as you go further.
+ Scenery in ruins, field and forest are beautiful and great to look at.
+ The option for dual language audio, Japanese and English.
+ 1080p.
Cons :
- 30 fps locked.
- Graphical problems can occur during battle and cutscene. Textures can stretch and cause artifacts problem. Lens distortion can be visible during cutscene.
- Story development is really slow. Interesting, but really slow.
- Character development can be shown a lot only at skits. Sorey, Rose and Edna's development focus on the story. While the others development are on skits.
- Skits are shown only at save points and point of interest.
- Targeting system is horrid during gameplay, button Tab to switch targets while the game pauses. It doesn't allow players to switch targets nearest easily or freely without pausing.
- Enemies have predictable moveset, causing sidestepping easy to master.
- Pulled an Abyss, removes vocal from opening.
- Not much graphical settings for PC.
- Party member's damage are shown on the UI, making it hard to know your attack dealt how much, causing less pleasure during combat.
- Quest pointers are sometimes confusing.
- Armatization are not balanced even with the element and weakness system.
- Main character is boring and easily predictable whereas the other characters are interesting.
Although this game is the latest installment of it's series, it failed to do justice to the series no matter how graphically improved it is to its game. It does not mean it is bad. It brings potential to a new Tales of games as it has introduced an open world system to the game. With the new battle system for the series, artes are less flashy than previous games. Sorey's character could have portrayed better with more meaning to it, but it falls flat due to the cliché 'friendship = power' plot that you can see from Kingdom Hearts, except much worst. He has the potential to be more interesting, but the others overshadow the protagonist in a more interesting character development on a standpoint.
This game may not be the best in it's series but it is still fun to play no matter how flawed it is. This game is still a good game, no matter how many cons. This game has it's charms to bring newcomers to the series. It is in my opinion a good game, the games price is worthy of it's gameplay. I recommend that it is a great game to start out in the series. Although I wouldn't recommend it as the previous release are console release, the graphical downgrade and different playstyle would hinder players. If you do own a console and don't mind graphical downgrade, you can get this as a start of a series and play previous games.
In the end, I am glad they finally start to reach out to PC gamers. For veterans, Symphonia has already been released  and hope for the best for Berseria.
PC gaming are lacking of JRPG as of late and this is a great addition.
Also, I would love if Edna would stop being an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to me every battle I am in. JK. Edna is the best character in the game.
I rate it 7.5/10.

"It's the most innovative shooter I've played in years!"
You've probably read that line a few times if you've read anything at all about SUPERHOT. And it would be correct. This game is legitimately one of the most innovative shooters that has been seen in years. With a minimalist design and a sneakily engaging story, SUPERHOT is the type of game that needs to come around more often. It challenges the "norms" and conventions that we've come to expect in modern video gaming. It gives the shooter genre a good solid twist and flip upside down and comes up with something special.
This game should be played by almost anyone who enjoys a shooter. The "time moves only when you move" mechanic is well implemented and creates a whole new way of approaching a shooter.
Pros:
+ Strong design.
+ Challenging.
+ Thought-provoking.
+ New modes unlock after completing the campaign.
+ Replay
Cons:
- MSRP (currently $24.99 at the time of this review, not counting release discount).
- Campaign length is saddeningly short. My playtime is at 3.3 hours for just the campaign - start to finish.
Overall I am very impressed with SUPERHOT. It lives up to the hype of innovation and is very engaging from the start. However, I do have a few gripes with it. Obviously, it's a fairly expensive game right out of the gate. While I respect the fact the developers put a lot of time (I've been following SUPERHOT for at least 1.5 years) into it and largely perfected the experience, it still feels high-priced for what it does provide.
There is a campaign which must be played before any of the other modes unlock, which include an Endless Mode (exactly what it means), "Challenges", and Speedruns. I am unaware at the moment if there are plans to expand the campaign levels or if there will be a level editor. I think this is exactly the type of game that would benefit greatly from that sort of addition. At the very least the Campaign is very engaging both in respect to the story (yep, there is one) and execution. Some of these levels make you feel like the ultimate badass as you cut through swathes of "red dudes". It's a lot of fun, but the length is very disappointing.
I definitely recommend this game with a few caveats. If you are a fan of shooters and want something new and different to play, this is right up your alley. If you're more of a casual gamer, I totally suggest you play it too, but you may want to wait a little while and get it down the line when its a little cheaper and perhaps will have more content or user-made content available. That said, this game is a wonderful step in a new direction and I applaud the developers for the work they've done here and no matter what you pay, you are likely to find enjoyment out of it.

If you are an aspiring comedian you should check out comedy quest. Comedy Quest is a video game about the life of a young aspiring comedian. You set out on a journey to become a stand up comedian and perform in front of crowds, you guide your character through creating comedy routines for him to perform in front of his audiences as he travels from city to city performing and growing as a professional comic. Comedy Quest is a 2017 favorite among game critics, pushing next-gen hardware to the limits with DirectX 9 compatibility, 8x nearest neighbor and 8x antialiasing graphic filters, 32-bit high definition textures (4k texture pack available via DLC). But all of this is nothing if your computer doesn't have a lot of memory, as Comedy Quest chews through a massive 20mb of RAM, and don't forget that a 60Hz monitor isn't usable as the game has a 40Hz FPS cap unless you play via a CRT, which then, and only then can you boost the FPS up to 85Hz, that's only if your computer has the horsepower to run this monster of a video game. The one downside of Comedy Quest is that it requires having a gtx 1070 as the minimum spec for the graphics card

Japanese to Survive delivers an exceptional introduction to those learning the language for the first time. The game provides a overview of Hiragana syllables, the fundamental writing system of Japanese grammar, with a number of vocabulary terms. Intermediate learners can brush up on old lessons while wishfully hoping on Katakana and Kanji DLC inclusions.
In the story, you play as a group of teenagers battling to retake their village from omnious "Hiragana warriors." The premise of a village being overthrown by Japanese syllables graciously teeters the line between cheesy educational writing and the script to a B+ anime. Writing aside, Japanese to Survive pairs its lessons with turn-based RPG battle sequences that ensure you are always reviewing material.
Overall, I highly suggest Japanese to Survive to any first-timers or anyone initially intimidated by a highly symbolic, Asian language. Each lesson is succinct in educating the player about the pronunciations, translations and writing strokes of each Hiragana character. The battles are a rewarding experience, knowing that you are applying the knowledge you just learned. I recommend having a pen and notebook ready alongside each playthrough.

I just don't get this game. I've read strategies and guides about the mechanics to see what exactly I'm just not getting about this game, and as far as I can figure the problem is it is designed to be excessively slow and requires you to micromanage everything. The irony is the game is really basic in terms of what all you can do; it's just it doesn't let you do any of it in an efficient way. Gods forbid you try to build more than one building at a time--even using the priority tool--you can have the Great Wall of China sized stockpiles of supplies, an army of builders, and it will still take a year to build one motherlovin' house.
Of course, there are times everything goes smoothly, and you almost have fun. I played a game all the way to year 40, my city was doing well, I had ample supplies, and everyone was healthy and happy. I was building and growing steadily, planning ahead by expanding my infrastructure before the next wave of houses (which also work so illogically), and everything was great. Then two things happened: I realized I was not having much fun because there was almost nothing to do but expand with the same handful of buildings over and over, and also everyone starved to death.
Seriously, I had 15K food stockpiled, prebuilt more food-bearing structures for my new minions, then built a few houses which led to about a whopping 8 more population, and suddenly I found myself unable to keep up with the demand for food. I have no idea why. Those 8 people must have brought tapeworms, or were very well-disguised hippopotami of a hungry hungry disposition.
I suppose if you look at this game as a satirical statement on the futility (and stupidity) of mankind, you might find some passing interest in it. Otherwise, expect to spend of a lot of time playing out of spite just to figure out why you're not having any fun. I just feel like there's no need to keep going in this game because even if I have missed "the key" to making a successful city, there just isn't enough to do in this game to keep it interesting.
In short, this games feels like it should be great...but it's not.

Pixel Privateers covers up its overly repetitive gameplay and basic dungeon crawling with annoying menus and a bad inventory management system. That is not to say the gameplay is not solid and the dungeon crawling is not entertaining. My main gripe here is - you will probably end up spending more time in the menus than actually dungeon crawling if you plan to fully loot a planet.
I don't believe the mass amount of collectible loot is the issue with Pixel Privateers. If anything, it is the poor filtering and all-categories inventory that causes conflicts and frustrations. With the amount of stats and comparing among different alternatives and strategies when loading out characters, it becomes an issue of having to take time and examine the loot and see if it is worth keeping. The problem? The game uses a poorly developed storage system to filter and juggle the insane amount of loot and loadout upgrades. To be frank, I never tend to stick to city builder games for very long. However Banished is a special exception.
Quite a while ago I discovered this game through GenerikB's spotlight. The game seemed so different from other city builders. Instead of visibly being able to see the balance of needs, you have to watch what happens to the town and figure it out from there. People are dying, they have low health, they are cold. Whatever the issue is, instead of simply looking at a graph - you have to check each of the steps. Is there enough leather? Enough variety of food? Are the deaths random or do they have a cause? Enough producers? Enough manufacturers?
This game is about fighting to stay alive and creating the simple basics it takes to create a township.  Banished's gameplay is balanced and user-friendly. At the very beginning there is a learning curve and the very first town is likely to die due to some oversite. However with time, frinding that balance becomes easier.
This is where I have a few problems with the game. The game itself is wonderful, but what keeps the gameplay going is the mods. Making modding very simple has added many more hours of gameplay to it. These mods make up for what the base game lacks. The base game is very limited, there are only so many different types of buildings and once you've mastered the ins and outs of the game, Finding the proper balance becomes too easy, and expanding  into a large town becomes dull. The character pathing needs to be improved, as that shouldn't have to be modded. Adding more variety and complexity to the games, and what keeps coming to mind is the Colonial Charter mod. It adds the opportunity to treade and create new items that would let the small town get more moddern items and luxeries. Each item has it's own purpose, and the step to create the final product requires time, space, and massive rescources. These final products end up in small numbers and sell for a high price, allowing the town to buy more expensive items that it's lacking. The base game lacks the "end game" entirely. All the fun is during the initial struggle to survive the first few winters- it needs more variety and substance for after the town becomes established.
For anyone who is considering buying the game, if you like rescource management games this is the game for you. It's well worth the money, and it will be a long time before you fully understand the working of the entire game. My complaints are coming from the point of someone who's put in 98 hours of their life into this game (and absolutely will continue to put more hours in) . All of my issues and problems arose once I became very expirenced with the game. If you end up loving the game as much as I do, adding mods won't be a problem. There is only a moddest number of mods out there, but each one seems to address individual problems. Some revamp the entire game, like the ones previosuly mentioned, and there are many small mods that change bits and peices that create the game to your personal taste.
Be prepaired for brutal beginnings, there will be death.

---
For those looking for a bit more of a TL;DR: Hat in Time has been an interesting experience
I had forgotten how much heart and soul and polish could be put into a game, and how much joy you could experience playing one. And this game OOZES love. The attention to detail from little inclusions like visual changes in the eyes of a roomba from ^_^ to >_< while you stand on it to the chatty nooses in Subcon Forest that comment about how nice your neck looks today are the sorts of things most overworked game developers never get around to. They're either broke and headed for a deadline at Christmas or just tired of working on project bugs to get it out of Beta. But the designers and programmers didn't stop at "good enough", they went so far above and beyond that I am almost ashamed of my own game development projects.
Beyond that, the game runs on spirited, colorful imagination I haven't seen since the Paper Mario series. Hat Girl herself is utterly adorable to follow around on her adventures, her quiet but clever mannerisms make her an excellent foil to the explosive personalities she encounters. Dead Bird Studio and Subcon Forest both stand out in particular here, with the fun characters of DJ Grooves, the Conductor, and the Snatcher taking you out on crazy adventures from solving train murders with brown camera filters and classy jazz, to delivering stolen mail for an eccentric faustian devil who likes to "pretend to care" about his minions (have I mentioned how much I love the Snatcher? because <3 ). The soundtrack and the art style are phenomenal (no, really, the art of this game is GORGEOUS and ADORABLE! Every piece of art with Hat Girl puts a goofy grin on my face), and both are used well to complement the missions, giving different worlds distinct feelings.
I don't normally write reviews because I usually think buying a game and not returning it is enough approval. But A Hat in Time is different. I felt real childhood joy playing this game, a feeling I'd all but forgotten by, in the words of Yahtzee Crosshaw, "penetrating the caked on layers of doughy acceptance the game industry has been pelting me with over the years". It makes me want to give that love back by promoting this game as much as possible. So please, buy this game (full price, support those devs!) and see for yourself what true love looks like.

I bought The Howler around Christmas time on sale- and to be honest it has sat in my games list untouched until now. It's been sat, waiting patiently, for a day where I have absolutely nothing else to do. Today was that day, and The Howler certainly helped me get through a hour or so until I went to get my Chinese takeaway.
The artwork, as others have said, is beautiful. Really really well done on that part :) But the main thing that grasped me about this game was the alternate controls- the ability to use your microphone to do all the controlling! None of my steam games have surprised me with a feature like this before- it made the game so much more fun! Others have said how boring and slow the game can be, but this feature brings your concentration to a whole new level.
THAT said- there were a few kinks to be worked out with the feature. At times it can be a little TOO sensitive- when a car drove past outside my balloon would fly away, or even on the Wolf cave level, the sound of the passage opening would be loud enough to also blow the balloon away... I have to complete that level using the mouse, which was a little disappointing.
One more point about problems while playing- your balloon CAN touch some objects/walls... but not all? And it's not obvious what will and what wont pop your balloon. This became quite frustrating in the more tightly spaced levels :/
All in all, really lovely little game, I'd recommend it to anyone for the unique controls input alone, especially as it's so cheap. REALLY wish this game had some achievements!!! Would play through the whole thing again for some achievements (Wink wink nudge nudge Mr Dev)- also it was nice getting 3/5 trading cards from drops :) That made the cute little badge nice and attainable too (Y)

I studied Japanese for 2 years in school and 4 years on my own, so I feel this game is a bit below my level, but I wanted a way to refresh on the basics and this game is okay, but also a bit flawed.
There is a lot of grinding in the game, it feels very RPG maker generic in terms of story and graphics, and the game tended to crash on me every hour or so, requiring constant saving or lost effort.
The battle mechanics are okay and help you memorize Japanese characters through rote practice in the RPG battle system, however it's noticably clunky, such as when you try to go down to get back tot he top of your menu, it is disabled and if you overattack an enemy, your next attacker will miss if he still attacked the same target.  Old school stuff that's frustrating.  Still, for an entry level Japanese game it gives you the entire alphabet, plenty of room to practice, and a few phrases and words to go with it.  The best part of the game is easily the last run, where you start using phrases instead of simple sounds to fight enemies.
I would recommend this game to fans of RPGs looking for entry level Japanese knowledge.  Could also be a good gateway for kids.  However, it is noticably clunky and crash prone.  Still, they advertised a sequel and I'd buy it, if only for the practice.  Give it a look.

I quite like city builders and especially if they're not always modern ones. This city builder is... well... I'd probably go as far as calling it "cute". :-)
I quite like the combination of survival city building and the fact, that it has trade as a major factor that could become a game changer at some stage during your many hours of growth and then sudden tragedy (the black death is lurking and suddenly all your blacksmiths died...!).
The learning curve I found quite hard, my first few games (I usually start playing standard game settings) I couldn't get my village to run without everyone dying either of starvation, cold or weird accidents (yes, tree can fall on your villagers). The graphics is neat and distinguishes - mainly because of the setting - quite from modern city builders which really gives it a good feel.
There are a few things I would have loved to see improved though.
- more buildings. It's quite interesting that despite all other city builders doing it differently, here all buildings are available from the start. However after some time it gets quite boring as you're basically building the same old all over the place. More variety would have been nice.
- resources. After a while, all my mountains were plastered with iron and coal mines. Once a mine has been stripped of coal, you can't just change to iron. If one resource has been stripped, the other resource has been stripped too. The counter basically counts for all resources together. Eventually, you will run out of resources. Keeping the map running is difficult then, because tools need iron, without iron mines you have to rely on the trade boats, eventually with bigger cities, the trade boat with tools won't come often enough.
- trade. Sometimes trade just doesn't make sense. I.e. some items could not be traded for certain other items. If that would be random I could understand (as in trader has requests too), but I remember trying each time and it was the same goods I wanted to trade-in that the trader didn't want. Rather odd.
- Stone quarries are quite big and once they've run out of stone, nothing can be done with them. So you'll also start plastering big massive holes into your area which then can't be used anymore at all. If at the beginning you put one of those stone quarries into the wrong spot that will block your expansion, then you basically screwed up your hole game.
But these problems are small compared to the fun I had with the game. Certainly something to be recommended. I hope at some stage it will get some expansions or DLCs or something to extend the content a bit. Multiplayer would be great - a feature often requested but rarely implemented. :-)

A Hat in Time is a game that is described on their main website as a 'cute-as-heck 3D platformer', and I think that's a fitting description. It was originally shown to the public on Kickstarter (as many indie games these days are), and it raised $296,360, destroying it's original goal. That was 4 years ago, and now the game is out, and it is truly something special.
As stated before, it's a 3D platformer: unlike Yooka-Laylee, which was clearly trying to replicate the magic of Banjo-Kazooie, A Hat in Time borrows the best elements of many 3D platformers from yester-year, and mashes them together to create a short but sweet adventure.
Firstly, there's movement. Hat Kid (the main protagonist) is a joy to control, and her moves are very simple: jump, double jump, a mid-air dive and the ability that your hat provides. There are a handful of hats to enjoy, and each offer a very useful ability. There wasn't a single hat that I didn't find useful.
The story is also very simple: your spaceship is flying by a planet, when one of the residents pops by, who destroys your ship and scattering the fuel (Time Pieces) across the world. It's pretty simple, but the characters all have charming personalities and voice acting that's actually pretty good (and you can turn it off if it's not your fancy).
The presentation is also top-notch: even when playing on the lowest settings (I have a pretty bad computer), the game looked great and sounded better. The soundtrack is exquisite also, and prefectly compliments each scenario.
The only problems are that the game can occasionally hiccup, I had a lot of technical issues (frame drops, clipping, etc.) and the game is pretty short (about 10 hours) but the game is so good I can really overlook all these things.
I really can't sing this game's praises enough: I loved it so much I went and got every achievement. Don't wait for a price drop or sale, go buy so we can have more amazing games from Gears for Breakfast.

Refunct is the debut Steam title from indie developer Dominique Grieshofer. It's been out for a couple of years, and I've had it in my library for a fair portion of that time, but I only just got around to playing it. I'm glad I did.
Refunct is rendered in full 3D and it looks very nice. From lovely sunlight-based lighting effects to wavy reflections on the surface of the water that covers Refunct's world, everything looks very nice.
The core game is about platforms and these are quite sharp and unreal - looking, with sharp edges and boxy shapes everywhere. The game is stylised, though -- it's not really supposed to resemble real terrain -- so this is fine and doesn't detract from the experience at all.
Colours are vibrant and effects are wonderful. While it lasts, Refunct looks simply lovely.
Refunct's sound effects are relatively minimal, but they do the job. There are no enemies or even inhabitants in Refunct's world, so don't expect voices, combat sounds, or any sort of interaction. But the sound effects do what they need to do. My only complaint would be that the sound of changing a platform's colour could be a little more intrusive, as a few times I missed it while trying to gain the 33% achievement.
Music is beautiful. Refunct's is a lovely ambient / chill-out sort of sound track which I really enjoy. It's well produced and I could listen to it for ages. Great job!
Refunct doesn't really have a story, at least as far as I can see. It's a first-person platformer with very light puzzle elements (the puzzles being limited to working out how and where to time your jumps to reach the next platform). Each platform on which you step becomes coloured differently, with the Store page suggesting that this is somehow restoring the world, but I'm not sure it's really relevant to the experience anyway.
You begin underwater and ascend to the surface, finding yourself on a small platform. You run to the next platform and it changes colour when you step on it. You continue moving to new platforms until you reach a glowing red beacon, which deactivates when you step on it, and then you notice more platforms -- and another beacon -- rising from the water. You continue running, jumping, climbing, and crouching across new platforms and deactivating new beacons until you reach the last one and the game ends.
There are no enemies, no death, and no time limit, apart from that set by the Achievements. The game is very short, and plays the same each time you play, so unless you're a an achievement hunter, speed runner, or are otherwise likely to get some sort of satisfaction from playing a short platform game over and over again, you should only expect an hour or less of actual content.
Refunct is extremely well made and only seems to have one goal: to be an interesting 'casual' 3D platform game. At that it excels.
Pros:
+ Lovely music
+ Very pretty graphics
+ Doesn't try to be something it's not
Cons:
- Very short
Refunct is an extremely short, but enjoyable, first-person platformer with light puzzle elements. It has beautiful music and lovely graphical effects, and is an experience that anyone who's even mildly interested can afford. If you're a speedrunner or achievement hunter then it holds extra appeal, but for me I'm happy giving up with that last achievement unsatisfied; there's no way I'll complete it in four minutes!

The Howler is a game of dexterity and timing in which you control a hot air balloon. Clicking the mouse (or making noise if you have a compatible microphone) makes the balloon go up. In each level, you need to manoeuvre the balloon through a parcours by making use of the wind. There are areas in which the wind blows the balloon forward and there are areas in which the wind blows the balloon back.
At first, this simple idea looks promising. The first few levels are fun. But soon, the real difficulty pops up: level after level, you need to manoeuvre the balloon through spikey things. And the balloon snaps on the slightest contact with spikey things, so it requires perfect timing. At that point, you realize the game is actually a lot like an unforgiving old-school platformer game. You know, a game that requires you to try and try again until you pretty much know the exact timing to get through each level. I'm sure a lot of people enjoy games like that, and they will enjoy The Howler for what it is, but I think it's only fair to warn other people about the nature of this game because it doesn't show from the description and the screenshots.
What you
tell from watching the screenshots, is that the artwork is very nice and pretty unique for an indie game like this. It's also a cheap game, especially when on sale, so if you're not sure whether to try it after reading this and some other reviews, I'd say give it a go. But because the Howler is not the sort of game I expected and because I simply didn't enjoy the game for what it turned out to be, I can't generally recommend this game so I feel obligated to click the 'thumbs down' button.

A delightful game with beautiful, hand drawn graphics & simple game play that whilst only mildly challenging is fun to play none the less.
There is no tutorial but adequate hints are provided in the first few levels and the game play is so simple the lack of a tutorial is not an issue.
The game is set in 2D with beautiful, hand drawn graphics. The game play is simple. You control a got air balloon that you must direct from one point to another, performing simple tasks like dropping off parcels along the way. The audio is restricted to sound effects which are fairly limited but effective.
The controls are simple, for vertical control you press the left mouse button to ignite the hot air and raise and stop pressing it to allow gravity to take over. For left and right control you must rely on the wind direction and speed which varies at different altitudes and is indicated by an arrow on the left hand side; the number of feathers in the quill indicating the strength. Thus you need to be at the correct altitude to move in the correct direction. The SPACE BAR is used to drop objects you are carrying and there is a pause button click able by the mouse.
You cannot pan around so you only see a screens worth of the level around the current location of the balloon. If you go too high, low, left or right and disappear off the edge of the level you die. Similarly if the balloon hits other objects you will usually die.
As you progress through levels additional obstacles like floating bombs are introduced. Fortunately these move in a predictable manner.
The only way to play is via a campaign of different screen levels you play in order (although once you have completed a level you can replay it at any time). The levels are pretty small (maybe twice the width of the monitor).
When you start a new level you are quickly shown what needs to be done by the camera panning about and short text messages appearing. You have a set time limit to complete the tasks.
This game play is short and the game can be easily be completed in 2-3 hours. Ignore my 17 hours game play - I left the game running in the start menu overnight by mistake.
