I got this game in pre-alpha as soon as it was released on steam since the first one was such a great game. When I got it, I immediatley saw that the second one had the potential to be even better. Vastly improved combat and lots of potential. As the game has developed it has not really tapped into the spirit of the first one. The maps make tower placement predictable, the upgrade systems are terrible (for bothe gear and hero), the heroes seemed all to similar without many unique elements, the tower options have been reduced, and the levels are very unchallenging. I still see the potential for this to surpass the orignal but I won't be holding my breath. Trendy would need to redo basically every single map because all but a couple are really boring, give every class an extra ability, do more to make sure every ability is unique, make it more of a tower defence game with rpg elements instead of an rpg game with tower defence elements, among many many changes.
*Edit*
I changed my review to recomended do to recent updates. The indoar/outdoar tavern was an excellent idea (inside the building is private outside is public) and many new and interesting shopkeepers have been added. The basework for even more RPG elements is their (gate to outside among other things) and could help solve the bland endgame problem. The new harbringer boss fight reminded me of DD1 in how interactive it was. The boss used various attacks and actually sucked you into a platformer type world that you had to escape. The map was still merely avergae (better than some of the other maps; I actually had to consider my tower placement and actually reconsidered at one point. It's not great but an improvment). The new class adds interesting strategy options and really revitalizes the game. You can buy him with real money or unlock him in-game. This should not be an in-game advantage but due to balance issues it is. Once these issues are fixed (which I'm sure they will be the character was just released) it will be more pay to explore more options than pay to win. The endgame still lacks a 'fun' element as it is still just re-doing the early game with higher stats on everything and the map design is, for the majority, still bland (DD1 maps are being added so that is changing) but overall this game is looking up. I wouldn't pay for it in its currewnt state but I definitley would pick it up for free and stick around to see if the devs keep on improving the game (instead of doing what they had been doing before). Overall with the past three (big) updates my mood about the game really changed - I'm now hopeful.
There have been some allegations about workplace misconduct from multiple Trendy higher ups but please don't let that stop you from getting the game. Your not 'helping' Trendy employees by boycotting the company and making it go bankrupt. On the plus side it looks like Trendy is improving their workplace standards.
Please stop complaining about Trendy sueing that company. A dev for that game violated a policy and they legitamately do have a reason to sue. I don't think Ark fans are going to buy tower defence games and I don't think DD2 fans are going to Ark so I don't really think It's about stopping competition.
I don't see why people are rating the company in the game review section. Please stop.
Overall the game is improving but a lot of my points before the edit still stand so I left them up.
*End Edit*
Please stop complaining about it now being free to play. Trendy had openly released when I bought it (and remeber I bought it as soon as it went on steam) that it was going to be free to play. They did do a data wipe but all the paid for content stayed so I don't see what the complaints over a screwed up busness model are. Trendy has been extremly open through the whole process.
Overall it is a pretty bland game, not without potential, but I cannot see the potential of the game being reached. The first one didn't really need much improving anyway so I'll just keep playing that one.

Short version: An otherwise very promising and fun game has largely been ruined by the developer's inability to deliver even basic updates at a reasonable pace.
Long version: As someone who has owned this game just about since it was released on Steam, this game is thoroughly unrecommendable. The developers originally tried to sell this game as being nearly finished, in fact if you don't believe me their preorder page still has a projected release date of spring 2014.

Take a look for yourself if you don't believe me:
Despite their claims, the game is still in pre-alpha one year later, and updates are coming further and further apart. We are still waiting in April for an update that was originally planned for January. One thing you realize once you start following this game is that updates NEVER come when the developer says they will. If you're lucky they will deliver a few weeks late. If you aren't then you're in the same state I am in right now.
On a positive note, this game will be fun for a while. Racing is challenging and rewarding so long as you don't encounter a troll or have the physics bug out on you. Both are relatively common occurrences though, so don't count on it. You could take care of trolls if hosts had better moderation tools, but they don't. 6 months after multiplayer was introduced and it is still absolutely bare-bones. You can't change tracks or car in lobby. You cannot set class limits on cars. You cannot set up a playlist for tracks. You can't fill empty slots with bots. You can't ban troublesome players for more than a few seconds. All of this was stuff we were supposed to have by now, but hasn't been implemented.
Tracks are well designed, but tiresome as the only multiplayer lobbies you are likely to find decent crowds in right now are oval and figure-8 racing. It is too easy to abuse the lack of moderation tools in multiplayer road courses. This might be fine if the single player AI were competent. In earlier iterations of the pre-alpha state the AI was actually tough. I'm not sure why they decided to make it so easy, you can practically win AI races in your sleep right now.
The physics in-game works ~95% of the time. Just don't touch a wall in a weird way. Even the slightest touch can suck you right in sometimes. Other times you bounce right off. Which will happen to you? Tough to say. I can't figure out when it sucks you in and when it won't.
I'll likely change this to a recommendation if the devs ever get back on track. The game really is fun until you get tired of turning left on the oval track in the dwindling multiplayer lobbies.

Counter-Strike confounds me. If my team lost to the other team, making my team lose all the gear we bought while letting the other team keep all of their gear just means that each subsequent round that they win, the odds are better stacked in the winning team's favor of winning again. One team can end up rocking the finest scoped weapons while the other has Counter-Strike's garbage guns because they're the best that they can afford.
If you're trying to make things interesting in a competition, you try to even the odds, not further stack them against the loser. This is why Left 4 Dead's AI Director sees one group of players doing well on a server and sends more hordes at them, and has less healing items and grenades sitting around, deliberately making it harder for them since they're doing so well. It could also see one group of players limping along, all wounded, out of healing items and low on ammo, and give them more healing items and grenads. It doesn't always work like that, of course, but that's what it's designed to do: try to even the odds to make for a fairer fight.
Counter-Strike does not like a fair fight. Nor does reality, but we're talking about a video game, here, where fairness is entirely within their power to distribute it, but they choose not to.

Have you ever played a game that you almost liked? Like, it was right on the cusp of making you say 'This is great!', but there are just too many niggling issues that make you wand to punch a hole through your monitor?
That's how I feel about Pixel Privateers.
Do not get me wrong, this is by no means a 'bad' game. There is plenty to like, but every positive point is marred by one or two little things that are insignificant on their own, but slowly add up. Let's go ahead and dig in...
1. Way too many menus. There's a menu for crew members. There's a member for leveling them up. There's a menu for 'research'. There's a menu for loot. There's a menu, for menus... I spent more time in the menus than I did playing the actual game.
2. Auto-Attack, what's that? As many have pointed out before, crewmembers do not attack automatically when an enemy is attacking them or other crewmates. I didn't realize this at first, so I ended up with this rather confusing situation where I was running around with an almost dead engineer as the rest of the team just stared at him, all the while some monster was trying to eat his face...
3. Clutter, clutter, everywhere. The idea of a looter is to collect loot, I know this. But, I feel, there is such a thing as too much loot, especially if it's boring. In my admittedly short time of playing, I didn't find a single interesting weapon or piece of armor... Nothing but slightly improved stats, and higher grade loot needs to be identified before you can use it, which means spending more time in menus. Oh, and any fuel that you pick up isn't automatically added to your tank, you are forced to convert it from a menu... And inventory space is extremely limited early on.
4. Matter and Fuel, the most boring, but important things ever. Both of these resources are extremely important, and for the time I played, my entire time was sitting there worrying if I had enough of both. Without fuel, you ain't going nowhere, and without matter, you can't do missions, clone dead troopers, nothin'... So, I spent of my game staring at menus, feeding these two resources the majority of my loot.
5. Trying to be tactical is a hassle. Each crewmember, depending on what kind of tool their wielding, has a small action bar with some useful abilities on it. These can be critical to mission success and survival, especially in difficult missions... So why do they make it so damned hard to use them? In order to use a skill, you must first select the appropriate crewmember with your mouse, then click on the skill. Doesn't sound too difficult, but in the thick of a fight it can damned near impossible to click on the correct tiny pixel outline to deploy the right ability.
If a few of these problems were fixed, I would have no problem recommending this game, but in its current state, I'd say give it a pass unless the premise really captures your interest.

We had a pretty good turn out on the Steam broadcast for this one, not to mention some lovely conversations with the viewers. Now, before we get into this, this title is very much in an “early access” and has only a small portion of the content that the full game will have. Eventually, this review will be updated and a final score will be given, but for now, we will be reviewing it as is. Let’s get going.
I – Story [~/10]
The Long Dark is a promising exploration and survival game from Hinterland Studio Inc. As I mentioned already, the game is in an alpha stage so there is no access to the story mode yet. I will therefore not be scoring it in this category at this time for this reason.
II – UI [8/10]
The user interface is pretty good overall, but it has it’s issues as well. The HUD can be changed between three settings. Normal, Debug, and Off. Normal and Debug feature a small, white reticle that you can use to find out what you’re aiming at currently, where as Off mode turns all HUD aspects off completely (as the name would suggest). Debug also adds a nifty coordinate tracker that let’s you know where you are on the map along with the name of the location.
The menus are well done for the most part, but, even with the sorting capabilities in the inventory menu, the inventory can become quickly tedious to navigate. This is especially true when you start to amass more and more items on various runs into the wild to resupply or whatnot.
As far as status effects go, the game will flash you some written warnings in either bottom corner and your character will make a comment to let you know what is happening in an offhanded manner.
III – Gameplay [9/10]
Gameplay is where TLD currently shines the brightest. When you think “survival game” you’re probably thinking of games like DayZ, 7 Days to Die, etc. You would be wrong in comparing them to TLD though. In this game, it is you against nature (and what seems like every damned wolf on the face of the planet). Honestly, in a market saturated with games that have you running from/killing one undead creature or another, it is refreshing to have the man vs nature scenario on the table.
For starters, this game has no tutorial (at least, not yet) and I truly hope that they keep it that way. It is a great experience to get dropped into a patch of snowy Canadian wilderness and be expected to figure it all out for yourself. If you don’t learn the ropes fast, you’re most likely going to be wolf bait in a matter of hours.
The greatest challenge you’ll face in TLD is yourself. Much like the character status set up from How to Survive, if you’re not keeping a sharp eye on your stats, you’re as good as dead. In the game you will have to constantly monitor your calorie count, hunger and thirst levels, your fatigue, and body temperature if you expect to last very long out there. It’s a delicate balance to stay in top form and maintaining that balance can be a punishing experience.
Combat (with wolves) can be unbelievably frustrating after your umpteenth time being mauled by wolves. Hand-to-hand combat is difficult as it is implemented through a “struggle system” of which, I was not fond in the least. You’re safest option is to pray that you find a rifle and some bullets and take out any wolves that you must encounter from afar. Aside from this, I have practically no other complaints about gameplay (aside from not being able to jump. Why can I not jump Hinterland?).
Also, permadeath. Did we mention the permadeath? No? Oh, well, now you know.
IV – Content [8/10]
Although it is in it’s early stages, and you can only access two areas of the game, TLD has a pleasantly large amount of content item-wise. As it stands now, the game boasts over 100 different pieces of equipment scattered throughout the landscape. You can find knives, hatchets, rifles, first aid goodies, clothing, a smattering of food, and more. A few solid runs into the game, you will probably have seen it all though. And that is okay at this point.
Wildlife in the game is severely limited. You’ll see some frozen corpses of less survival-savvy mortals, a suspicious amount of male deer, some unnamed blackbirds that sound like crows, rabbits, and enough wolves to last you several lifetimes. Most players are hoping to see this particular category expand within the next little while. Some of us would like to be horribly maimed and killed by something other than wolves to break up the maddening monotony.
V – Visual [9/10]
The artwork of TLD was initially what caught my eye about the game. It is hand-drawn and it is beautiful. It’s an incredibly stylistic world and I wouldn’t want it any other way. The landscape is nothing short of breathtaking.
Animal models could use some tweaking though, as most of them appear very stiff and unnatural when they move. It’s okay for the corpses to look stiff, mainly because they’re frozen…and corpses.
VI – Audio [10/10]
Music plays intermittently during TLD and it typically signifies something. Maybe you’ve discovered a new area or maybe you’ve just made it through another night. Whatever the case, the music is brief and brilliant and only works to improve the game experience.
Sound effects in the game are great. From drinking water to dying of dysentery, there is never a sound that makes you stop and say “Um, what?” Often you will find yourself saying “Um, no” when you hear a howling wolf answered by several other while stumbling back to your hideout in the growing dark though.
The voice acting is very well done up to this point and I’m excited to see where Hinterland takes it as far as the story goes.
VII – Overall [8.8/10]
Overall, I would very much recommend The Long Dark, as it is a wonderful addition to the survival family.

If you like loot, this game is a winner.
The basic gameplay loop is Request Missions (optional), go to planet/mission location, select you crew members and beam down onto a randomly generated 2d area and proceed to kill everything.
Each character has 4 slots to put things in.  A body armor slot, helmet slot, primary weapon slot and a utility/secondary weapon slot..  There are 5 classes and classes are determined by what item or weapon (Equipping 2 weapons makes you the Marine class) is in the offhand.  Classes are a Vanguard which acts as the tank, Marine which is DPS/Tank/Utility, Engineer which is utility or DPS (turrets are OP), Sniper which is DPS and some utility, and Medic which is heal.
Game has a huge variety of loot and each class has a couple different class items to choose from.  For example, for the Medic I've found a heal gun that shoots out a beam of healing.  A Heal drone, which has a little drone floating around doing AoE heals, and a Defibrillator which can resurrect members and also heal them (although it isn't automatic like the rest).
On top of all the classes, you also have access to a tech tree that you use to get more abilities and things.  It goes from Tier 1 up to Tier 7 and each tier has 6 categories you can pick for a 'major' ability and then 3-4 minor abilites in each category.
When you get ready to beam down to a planet you have 9 difficulty levels to choose from, ranging from Soothing (-5 elvl, loot quality -0.2) to Tribulating (+7elvl, loot quality +5).  I know this game has a NG+ mode so there may be even more.  Initially I was playing on Tormenting and it felt a bit easy but the first 3 missions are more of a tutorial and after them, it got challenging.  I had to make sure my Vanguard taunted and my healer dropped aggro.
Anyways, if you like loot games and the never-ending quest of getting loot to get better loot, this game is a winner.
It also supports up to 4 people in multiplayer, although I haven't tried it so can't comment on it.
I realize I basically just described the game but really, you're either a fan of loot games/ARPGS in which case you'll probably love this.  If you're not a fan, you probably won't like this.
In my case, I really love it and can see myself playing it for awhile.  Also the devs have been really responsive to any questions/concerns/tech issues (join the Quadro Delta discord).

Just Cause 2 is one of those games you don't want to put down. Where you want to explore every nook and cranny of its expansive world. Where you want to actually do sidequests because they are (gasp) fun. The gameplay is tight and responsive, and it's one of the best PC ports I've ever seen. I have a cheap Lenovo all-in-one from Best Buy, and it runs with minimal lag and pop-in.
You play as Agent Rico Rodriguez, whom--based solely on his quips and one-liners--I deduced he is the grown-up version of Carlos from The Magic School Bus. After a scandal involving Ms. Frizzle, a class full of children, and a secret drug ring, Carlos ran from the authorities away from home and changed his name. He lived on the streets, doing odd jobs and eventually ended up working for the CIA. He was sent to North Kor--ahem--Panau, where he is supposed to hunt down his old mentor from the original Just Cause.
This game plays like an action movie, with infinite avenues of approach to every challenge. If you want to take a base, you could:
A) Strap multiple plastic explosives to a truck and ram it through the front gate
B)Parachute in and steal their attack helicopter, then destroy the defenses
C)Do it the old-fashioned way wielding dual submachine guns and an unrealistic amount of grenades
D)All of the Above
Experimentation and dicking around are encouraged, and the primary goal of the game is to cause chaos. Do this by destroying government property and killing people. The parachute/grappling hook combo is one of the most fun ways to travel in any game, and it's all around a fun game. 8.5/10

I bought this on a whim because it is published by Re-Logic, the team that made Terraria. They've garnered enough goodwill from me to grab anything with their name attached to it. I'd never heard of the developer Quadro Delta but Re-Logic vouching for them was enough for me to take the risk sight unseen.
That said, I am absolutely loving the game right now. It's really scratching the itch that I've had for a loot-based game lately. It's a side scrolling, "dungeon" crawling, squad-based, loot grinder. You get up to 8 characters in a team, and run across the surfaces of worlds clearing out the baddies and grabbing piles of loot. At the start I thought there was a possibility that the combat would feel shallow, but as I've progressed through the game and unlocked more skills and tech, the difficulty has really picked up.
First, I love the contextual queues for using abilities popping up over squad members in trouble. Each character has around 5 abilities with a variety of effects. That seemed pretty overwhelming for how fast combat moves, but when characters hit low health or have certain status effects, the relevant abilities from all of the squad pop up as action buttons above that character. For example: Someone drops below 50% health, the medic's abilities, the mercenary's heal, and the scout's smoke bomb pop up as abilities to cast at that target. It really streamlines combat to the point that you don't have to frequently pause it and queue up abilities.
Second, the loot is incredibly varied. I have started to get a bit of loot fatigue. It is beneficial to pick up every single piece and disintegrate it for "matter" which is used for a variety of things, but there is just so much of it sometimes that it gets to be a bit much. I've started to only identify and manage purple-quality and higher loot. You also eventually find a combining cube (think Diablo 2 Heraldric Cube) that lets you do some re-rolling of items and stats.
Third, the worlds all seem varied enough for the 8 or so hours I've played so far. There have been a few occasions of things feeling a little same-y, but the random generation of NPCs and such has helped to diminish that. I've also stumbled across a few interactable elements that end up spawning waves of enemies and give great loot. That has been nice.
So far, what I have played feels like a full game. I get the feeling, though, that as I play I'm going to continue finding new elements and content that will add to the game. I've not had the opportunity to build or upgrade my ship yet. I've not had a boarding party show up while in flight. There are things I know I haven't encountered but already feel satisfied with the amount of content available.
If you enjoy looking through loot drops, min/maxing stats, squad combat, and mostly-funny dialogue, you should be happy with this. Especially considering the price of entry.

A Hat in Time is a game that is described on their main website as a 'cute-as-heck 3D platformer', and I think that's a fitting description. It was originally shown to the public on Kickstarter (as many indie games these days are), and it raised $296,360, destroying it's original goal. That was 4 years ago, and now the game is out, and it is truly something special.
As stated before, it's a 3D platformer: unlike Yooka-Laylee, which was clearly trying to replicate the magic of Banjo-Kazooie, A Hat in Time borrows the best elements of many 3D platformers from yester-year, and mashes them together to create a short but sweet adventure.
Firstly, there's movement. Hat Kid (the main protagonist) is a joy to control, and her moves are very simple: jump, double jump, a mid-air dive and the ability that your hat provides. There are a handful of hats to enjoy, and each offer a very useful ability. There wasn't a single hat that I didn't find useful.
The story is also very simple: your spaceship is flying by a planet, when one of the residents pops by, who destroys your ship and scattering the fuel (Time Pieces) across the world. It's pretty simple, but the characters all have charming personalities and voice acting that's actually pretty good (and you can turn it off if it's not your fancy).
The presentation is also top-notch: even when playing on the lowest settings (I have a pretty bad computer), the game looked great and sounded better. The soundtrack is exquisite also, and prefectly compliments each scenario.
The only problems are that the game can occasionally hiccup, I had a lot of technical issues (frame drops, clipping, etc.) and the game is pretty short (about 10 hours) but the game is so good I can really overlook all these things.

Before you continue reading or buy, read what the developers have to say in the Early Access Game notes.  Know what their plans are...
The standout feature of BFB is the executions.  Run up to an enemy and you can perform an execution, which there are several different styles.  Executions on humans seem to be the most polished while executions on animals can be performed they are broken.  The executions are gory and generally end up with the victim being torn from their limbs, showing their spines and other internals dangling out
Combat is not very inspiring, you are a giant mech trying to shoot tiny, fast moving, targets where pin point accuracy is required to hit your targets.  If this doesn't change then be prepared for a mediocre experience.  Having said that it's something that can be easily fixed by the dev's.  One option would be allow the projecticles to gravitate towards enemies (not homing missiles) allowing near misses to become hits, therefore slightly more forgiving on current pin point accuracy.
The first party of the game has you trundling around for around an hour or so through empty streets and building, before adding some K9's to kill, eventualy adding more intelligent, human, foe's.  All of which is interspersed by some puzzle mechanics that need to be overcome to continue on your journey.
A hacking mechanic is in game, which all you have to do is hold a key down to perform the hack.  Hack a terminal and you get a little mono rail journey towards a camera you can view and then hack another camera  until you can hack a switch that opens a door.  Very similar to Watch Dogs, though it needs more polish and copying Watch Dogs mechanic and style for hacking would be no bad thing.
Level designs are OK, though you will find yourself inside narrow buildings and outside in streets being lead down a corridor, with only one way to go.  Outside there is plenty colours as the Manchester streets are over grown with fooliage, while the inside of buildings are mostly barren and empty.  Though there is a nice night club building you visit briefly.
It took me around 90 minutes to complete what is currently available, the total play time for Episode One is guestimated to be 3hours.
If the Dev's are serious about their game then I would expect EA development time to continue towards the 12 month time to apply the polish needed to this game.
Early Access games are difficult to review.  Line up 10 EA games together and their current feature set and level of polish will differ significantly.  If you don't like to play games which contain bugs and expect all features to be present then I recommend you never buy an EA game.  On the flip side, if you like what you see and want to support the developers then go for it.

I got this game in pre-alpha as soon as it was released on steam since the first one was such a great game. When I got it, I immediatley saw that the second one had the potential to be even better. Vastly improved combat and lots of potential. As the game has developed it has not really tapped into the spirit of the first one. The maps make tower placement predictable, the upgrade systems are terrible (for bothe gear and hero), the heroes seemed all to similar without many unique elements, the tower options have been reduced, and the levels are very unchallenging. I still see the potential for this to surpass the orignal but I won't be holding my breath. Trendy would need to redo basically every single map because all but a couple are really boring, give every class an extra ability, do more to make sure every ability is unique, make it more of a tower defence game with rpg elements instead of an rpg game with tower defence elements, among many many changes.
*Edit*
I changed my review to recomended do to recent updates. The indoar/outdoar tavern was an excellent idea (inside the building is private outside is public) and many new and interesting shopkeepers have been added. The basework for even more RPG elements is their (gate to outside among other things) and could help solve the bland endgame problem. The new harbringer boss fight reminded me of DD1 in how interactive it was. The boss used various attacks and actually sucked you into a platformer type world that you had to escape. The map was still merely avergae (better than some of the other maps; I actually had to consider my tower placement and actually reconsidered at one point. It's not great but an improvment). The new class adds interesting strategy options and really revitalizes the game. You can buy him with real money or unlock him in-game. This should not be an in-game advantage but due to balance issues it is. Once these issues are fixed (which I'm sure they will be the character was just released) it will be more pay to explore more options than pay to win. The endgame still lacks a 'fun' element as it is still just re-doing the early game with higher stats on everything and the map design is, for the majority, still bland (DD1 maps are being added so that is changing) but overall this game is looking up. I wouldn't pay for it in its currewnt state but I definitley would pick it up for free and stick around to see if the devs keep on improving the game (instead of doing what they had been doing before). Overall with the past three (big) updates my mood about the game really changed - I'm now hopeful.
There have been some allegations about workplace misconduct from multiple Trendy higher ups but please don't let that stop you from getting the game. Your not 'helping' Trendy employees by boycotting the company and making it go bankrupt. On the plus side it looks like Trendy is improving their workplace standards.
Please stop complaining about Trendy sueing that company. A dev for that game violated a policy and they legitamately do have a reason to sue. I don't think Ark fans are going to buy tower defence games and I don't think DD2 fans are going to Ark so I don't really think It's about stopping competition.
I don't see why people are rating the company in the game review section. Please stop.
Overall the game is improving but a lot of my points before the edit still stand so I left them up.
*End Edit*
Please stop complaining about it now being free to play. Trendy had openly released when I bought it (and remeber I bought it as soon as it went on steam) that it was going to be free to play. They did do a data wipe but all the paid for content stayed so I don't see what the complaints over a screwed up busness model are. Trendy has been extremly open through the whole process.
Overall it is a pretty bland game, not without potential, but I cannot see the potential of the game being reached. The first one didn't really need much improving anyway so I'll just keep playing that one.

Let me preceed this review by saying
In fact, quite the contrary. This game got a lot of public exposure around 9 months ago when a very early build was available for purchase on BB's website. NerdCubed's vid sold me on this game. And for a while, it was fun to play the occasional race, or for me, play the figure eight track. I dunno why, but that track is sooo satisfying. Anyway, the reason most people are furious is lack of updates. This is the reason I recommend not purchasing
Allow me to explain:
This game is funded entirely off of BB. There is no pub like the Flatout games. When BB first gave the public this game, they expected maybe a small portion of the hardcore FlatOut crowd to be interested and back the game. For this reason, the game was somewhat small at first. However, many people bought in after seeing how much fun demolition derbys are and thus, BB realize the game in its then state was far too small. What BB did next was no small feat: over the course of a number of months, they completely remade the engine to allow for the ambitious game they are now developing. Support for 24 player multiplayer sounds like a minor update, but considering the damage models and realism of the game the net code had to be optimized and overhauled, as well as other key aspects of the engine. Inevitably, as happens in programming, methods affect methods, blah blah blah, and lots of things got messed up. The physics are really messed up, the cars handle like♥♥♥♥♥♥ and damage numbers are too high or low. What's currently happening (and why a stable update has yet to appear in recent months) is they are doing their best to revert everything back to the way it was in the original public release in this new engine.
Don't get me wrong: I'm as frustrated as the next NCG fan. I bought this game before it was even on steam. However, people need to understand that this is what happens with EA. BB has not abandoned this labor of love; in fact, quite the contrary. Weekly updates are pushed to the BB blog and the steam forums. Just be patient guys.
Also: If you saw videos of the game from way long ago and are craving some action, the game comes with their sneak peak 2.0 which contains the old engine and also an awesome playground to play on.
TL:DR- This game is going to be phenominal when BB is done with it, emphasis on
they're done with it. I can't recommend this game now because of the lack of updates. If you're a super mega fan of BB or Flatout or whatever, grab this on sale and play the sneak peak to your heart's content. Until then, wait for future updates.

The core concept of Comedy Quest is solid; the puzzle logic is good (I don't remember any where the solution seemed stupid after the fact) and the comedy is good for the most part.  The thing about the jokes is that a lot of them are intentionally eye-rollers; the idea is that when you "earn" a good joke by finding it in the environment (remember, at the end of the day this is a point-and-click adventure) it stands out among the others.  This means that the better (or, if we're being honest, simply more thorough) you are at canvassing the environment, the better the in-game jokes will be.
The one real complaint I have about the game isn't actually with the game itself, per se; it's the engine.  It's either trying
to recreate nostalgia that it fails to modernize, or it actually
an engine from an earlier time that hasn't matured.  It's functional, don't get me wrong, but after having played other point-and-clicks I guess I've been spoiled by vastly superior inventory management.  Also, there's an issue (I won't quite call it a bug, since it might just be an unfortunate coincidence) with hitting Shift-Tab to bring up the Steam overlay that causes the inventory display to go all wonky.*
At the end of the day, it's a fun little indie game if you remember what it is, what it's trying to achieve, and don't hold the low production values against it.  I quoted one of the jokes to my friend as I was playing the game: with a joke at least that good in a free game, it's certainly worth the price of admission (your time).
* Side note: if you hit this issue, I found that some combination of holding down Esc and clicking on the different action buttons (at the bottom of the inventory window) does seem to eventually unstick it.

Counter-Strike confounds me. If my team lost to the other team, making my team lose all the gear we bought while letting the other team keep all of their gear just means that each subsequent round that they win, the odds are better stacked in the winning team's favor of winning again. One team can end up rocking the finest scoped weapons while the other has Counter-Strike's garbage guns because they're the best that they can afford.
If you're trying to make things interesting in a competition, you try to even the odds, not further stack them against the loser. This is why Left 4 Dead's AI Director sees one group of players doing well on a server and sends more hordes at them, and has less healing items and grenades sitting around, deliberately making it harder for them since they're doing so well. It could also see one group of players limping along, all wounded, out of healing items and low on ammo, and give them more healing items and grenads. It doesn't always work like that, of course, but that's what it's designed to do: try to even the odds to make for a fairer fight.
Counter-Strike does not like a fair fight. Nor does reality, but we're talking about a video game, here, where fairness is entirely within their power to distribute it, but they choose not to.

When I bought this game i knew what to expect from various different sources such as Markiplier, PewDiePie or Yamimash. However; even though i thought i was going to be good at this game i found other wise, needless to say it made me jump out of my chair and find the nearest nuttella jar in a 50 km area.
!!BACKSTORY!! The game is set in somewhere around 1987 - 1995. You are a security guard who works at a restaurant known as Freddy Fazbear's Pizzaria. You have to work there for 5 normal nights in total with the addition of a 6th and 7th night (Nightmare and Custom). The animatronics: Freddy Fazbear, Bonnie the Bunny, Chica the Chicken and Foxy the Pirate Fox are going to hunt you down from 12:00 AM until 6:00 AM, this is something about their "servos" locking up.
!!GAMEPLAY!!
You're eternally bound to a security office, you have a camera, doors/door lights and the joys of the front wall of ugly-ness. The aim is to check that camera of yours all the while avoid getting yourself stuffed into a Freddy suit (It kinda hurts).
!!PROS!!
The game can be full of surprises be it the lore or anything else that you might find exciting in this game *winks*
FNAF requires some form of skill in order to be "Good" at with self set challenges such as 20/20/20/20 challenge for Night 7 or maybe its a type of permadeath type where if you die, you start over.
The jumpscares in the game are a great asset to the game's over all horror feel, after all; you cant have horror without jumpscares ;)
!!CONS!!
Five Nights at Freddy's can sometimes feel like it falls short in some aspects of gameplay, I mean that by the fact that it feels kind of repetitive when you find and use strategies.
Even though I complimented the jumpscares I have to say that they can get a bit bland after you learn the AI patterns or the charaters.
!!SUMMARY!!
Five Nights at Freddy's is one of the scariest games i've played in a long time, it truely rustled my jimmies. The game does in someway require a healthy level of paranoia accompanied by a high level of observance. If you dont pay enough attention then you will find yourself in a Freddy suit in no time at all. FNAF was a game that took the market by storm and had sold pleasingly in the first month of it's release. I only have one request: Please for the love of God put video/audio settings in the next game. Five Nights at Freddy's 2 HYPE.

I bought this game when it came out a few months ago and after reading through some of the reviews people have posted I wanted to mention a few things that no one seems to talk about (maybe someone did, I didn't read all the reviews).
First off I know this is an early access game and is subject to improvement, that being said it has been over a month since anything has been added/changed to the game. The last major "improvement" to the game was the addition of a new zone.
My problem with this game is that it is extremely limited in it's current state and it seems like the devs have drastically slowed down in their progress. In it's current state this game is worth about 5-10 hours of gameplay to most people. The problem is that after you find good clothing and a gun there truly is nothing left that this game offers. It turns into an endless cycle of forage wood -> melt snow for water -> kill a deer/wolf for food -> sleep. Sadly the only other thing there is to do is "explore" and loot, however the cabins and other buildings around both maps are quite generic. In the new map I exit out of the game after 30 minutes of running around and searching 30 drawers per house, because that's all there is to do.
I'm not saying this isn't a nice game, it has a lot of potential and for the first few hours it is quite fun but I wouldn't buy it if you're expecting to get a lot of hours of gameplay. You'd be better off going for one of the thousand generic zombie survival crafting games because although they all basically do the same god damn thing and 95% of them aren't finished games, there is still 10x more to do in them than in The Long Dark.
If the devs didn't quit on this game yet it can turn into something great, for now I would not recommend. Let the down votes begin, someone had to say it.

I picked up this game on a whim after reading a couple reviews and because I just felt the need for something different and new. 9 hours later of solid play, the only reason I put the game down after that first session was because I needed sleep.
The game has a variable pace, which is nice. What I mean by that is while you are on missions the pace can be kind of fast, but you can take little breaks between fights and you have the option to fight in real time or use a tactical pause to make combat a lot slower but more interesting than just run and gun. Then when you are off mission its basically turn based and you can slow down and take all the time you want. Which is a good thing because there is a LOT to do when not doing away missions. Researching loot and artifacts, spending that research on tech to enhance your ship or your team, going through all your loot to max your teams abilities, exploring the galaxy, browseing different markets on stations, the list goes on.
Class variance feels solid and the clases themselves have enough variance within them depending on what class equipment you have on that its almost like sub classes. Vanguard for example, the idea of the class is to tank and take damage and agro off the rest of the team. Depending on the equipment you have installed you can either be a power armor charger with a hard hitting melee weapon, or you can have different shield abilities and use ranged weapons... lots of options like this for all the classes so you really can built a team to be how ever you want. And classes are changable on the fly. The only thing that holds you back a little are the attributes on your characters. If you build someone as a high STR melee character, you could give them the Scout class (sniper) but it wouldnt really be efficient.
There is a ton more to this game, I couldnt go in to it all without writting a small book. The game is constantly giving me new and interesting things to play with. The current price of this game was well worth it since I am 9 hours in and still loving it.

Banished is a game about a group of people who were banished from their home (for an unknown reason) with just enough food and tools to start a new life in the wilderness.
In the game description, this is said to be a "city-building strategy game". Well, I think it is only 20% city-building. In my humble opinion, this is a "strategic survival of a town against nature". Things like collecting resources, building structures just the right way so your villagers can use the optimum route to their destination, planning village growth according to terrain, are what this game is all about. If you buy this game expecting a "city-building game", you will not like it. Actually half of the bad reviews are based on expectation of a "city-building game".
Game's complexity is fair. It does not have hundreds of buildings, tools etc. There is only one "tool" which villagers use to collect resources and build structures. There are also a handful of structures each with a different purpose, from producing fuel to keeping villagers happy. Its complexity comes from learning what works best how and with what.
Game does not have an end game goal. This may be a good thing or a bad thing depending on people's perspective. After you start a game and get the hang on basics, you put your own goal. For example mine was to grow to 600 citizens and got the achievement. It is not actually a sandbox game, but some people put some restrictions on themselves, like not building certain buildings. Some of these restrictions are also encouraged by achievements if you are into it.
Structures are very detailed, villagers are distinguishable, trees and nature look good enough.
Every villager has a status based on their hunger, clothing etc. and distance between their house and work place makes real difference.
Tutorial teaches the basics but doesn't give too much detail. For a survival game, learning optimum ways is part of the game.
My system is considered high end, but should work great on medium level systems because its recommended system requirements are currently considered very low end.
This is not necessarily a bad thing but it may make some people bored quickly.
Well, this game is about survival but classified as city-building strategy game. It makes expectations of new players different and most bad reviews are based on this.
I don't regret having this game and recommend it without a second thought. I hope developer (yes singular. afaik, it is developed by one person) considers making a sequel in the future.

Banished has become one of my favorite games, that I keep going back to again and again.  It's inherently a resource management and building game.  It has no warfare - you're soley focused on building and managing a small town.  The engine they have is fantastic...creating this realistic spiral when the resource balance is disrupted.  Food getting low?  Some families will hoard what is left. Workers who are hungry won't work as well, lowering productivity. (Which, if widespread enough, will eventually result in some of your population starving or freezing to death as less work = less reources snowballs.)  Preventing or correcting that spiral of doom is a lot of the fun - it's a delicate balance, because you have to manage labor as well as try to build protective surpluses.  Another bonus: the soundtrack is very pretty and relaxing, and the sounds from weather changes are realistic and keep the music from being repetitive.  It is easily one of the most fun sim games I've ever played!

Just Cause 2 is one of those games you don't want to put down. Where you want to explore every nook and cranny of its expansive world. Where you want to actually do sidequests because they are (gasp) fun. The gameplay is tight and responsive, and it's one of the best PC ports I've ever seen. I have a cheap Lenovo all-in-one from Best Buy, and it runs with minimal lag and pop-in.
You play as Agent Rico Rodriguez, whom--based solely on his quips and one-liners--I deduced he is the grown-up version of Carlos from The Magic School Bus. After a scandal involving Ms. Frizzle, a class full of children, and a secret drug ring, Carlos ran from the authorities away from home and changed his name. He lived on the streets, doing odd jobs and eventually ended up working for the CIA. He was sent to North Kor--ahem--Panau, where he is supposed to hunt down his old mentor from the original Just Cause.
This game plays like an action movie, with infinite avenues of approach to every challenge. If you want to take a base, you could:
A) Strap multiple plastic explosives to a truck and ram it through the front gate
B)Parachute in and steal their attack helicopter, then destroy the defenses
C)Do it the old-fashioned way wielding dual submachine guns and an unrealistic amount of grenades
D)All of the Above
Experimentation and dicking around are encouraged, and the primary goal of the game is to cause chaos. Do this by destroying government property and killing people. The parachute/grappling hook combo is one of the most fun ways to travel in any game, and it's all around a fun game. 8.5/10

A Hat in Time is a game that is described on their main website as a 'cute-as-heck 3D platformer', and I think that's a fitting description. It was originally shown to the public on Kickstarter (as many indie games these days are), and it raised $296,360, destroying it's original goal. That was 4 years ago, and now the game is out, and it is truly something special.
As stated before, it's a 3D platformer: unlike Yooka-Laylee, which was clearly trying to replicate the magic of Banjo-Kazooie, A Hat in Time borrows the best elements of many 3D platformers from yester-year, and mashes them together to create a short but sweet adventure.
Firstly, there's movement. Hat Kid (the main protagonist) is a joy to control, and her moves are very simple: jump, double jump, a mid-air dive and the ability that your hat provides. There are a handful of hats to enjoy, and each offer a very useful ability. There wasn't a single hat that I didn't find useful.
The story is also very simple: your spaceship is flying by a planet, when one of the residents pops by, who destroys your ship and scattering the fuel (Time Pieces) across the world. It's pretty simple, but the characters all have charming personalities and voice acting that's actually pretty good (and you can turn it off if it's not your fancy).
The presentation is also top-notch: even when playing on the lowest settings (I have a pretty bad computer), the game looked great and sounded better. The soundtrack is exquisite also, and prefectly compliments each scenario.
The only problems are that the game can occasionally hiccup, I had a lot of technical issues (frame drops, clipping, etc.) and the game is pretty short (about 10 hours) but the game is so good I can really overlook all these things.
I really can't sing this game's praises enough: I loved it so much I went and got every achievement. Don't wait for a price drop or sale, go buy so we can have more amazing games from Gears for Breakfast.

Once I looked past how uncomfortable the title Shepard made me, and learned to accept that I may be above the age of the target demographic and it shows in the writing, I had a lot of fun with the combat system in this game. Also worth noting that with the fan mod this game ran great at 1440p, 60fps.
The system in this game all feel over-engineered like they had people just adding systems on top of systems and you know what? I missed that.
I've spent a lot of time in this game trying to understand what makes it tick.
Basic attacks apply buffs,
Special attacks apply debuffs,
Enemies all have elemental weaknesses and resistances,
Physical/Magic resistances as well,
Equipment has modifiers which can be fused and combined and stacked with other modifiers,
Transformations,
A bunch of other minor details
There's a lot of poor writing and general design mistakes made within this game, but if you're willing to look past the flaws, you can have a lot of fun in Zestiria. I highly recommend the Japanese voices with subtitles and of course, the fan patch for better shadows and 60fps. The subtitles are likely directly from the localization so the main draw for Japanese audio is the much better sound leveling and line delivery.
I also recommend you brace yourself for internet memes if you have an aversion for those.

If you haven't already tried this masterpiece, what are you waiting for?
It has a great dystopian-nightmare-world setting, and a storyline that is engaging and contains many twists.  Much of this is revealed through audio recordings you find throughout the world.  But back to the setting -  you find yourself (via a plane crash in the middle of the ocean) in an underwater city built by an Ayn Rand disciple to escape the injustices of socialism.  Things didn't work out the way they were planned and things went horribly wrong.  The overwhelming freedom led to people wantonly mutating themselves and eventually killing each other.  Now all that are left are a bunch of gene-spliced freaks (called splicers in the game) that will kill you any chance they get.  Your job is to find the way out with the help of a mysterious man who communicates with you through radio transmissions.
The gameplay is top-notch.  It is not like mainstream FPS games in the sense that ammo is sparse, enemies are crafty/often surprise you, and running through the game world guns 'a blazin' is totally unrewarding and likely to get you killed.  There are the variety of weapons available, ranging from pistols to shotguns to rockets, but there are also special gene enhancements that give you powers that are basically supernatural.  Finding items, upgrades, and the way through each level can be challenging and add to the heightened tension that the game atmosphere so skillfully creates.
I'll let you discover the Little Sisters and Big Daddys for yourself.
Just buy this game if you like compelling story, FPS formats that are more cerebral than "twitchy", or video games in general.

Very easy to get into, and very basic.  This will teach you the Hiragana alphabet and some very, very basic Japanese quite quickly.

The game has a wonderful art style which is a combination of hand sketching and watercolor wash. The setting is steampunk and you play as a hotair balloon pilot. You have some control over the upward and downward motion of the balloon but you are at the mercy of the wind currents to move left and right. You will need to use momentum to navigate around obstacles, using the wind to your advantage and quickly changing elevation. The difficulty of the game ramps up quite quickly. On most levels (missions) you will be picking up and/or dropping parcels. There is a great deal of verticality in the game and often your destinations will be outside of your view. Each mission starts with a quick scan over the scene, but it will be up to you to remember where you need to go. You can control the game with your mouse and keyboard, but you can also control it with your voice. I tried this feature but found it less appealing than traditional controls. The game has a 4x3 aspect ratio and is locked at 30 FPS. I suspect this is due to it being available on iOS as well. Given how the level design works they would not have been able to simply expand the aspect ratio. This may be off-putting to some but the game can run in windowed mode so you won't notice any wasted space. In full screen you will have black bars on the sides. You cannot control the volume in the game, you'll have to rely on the system sound controls. This is probably another aspect of its iOS support.
Overall I enjoyed my time with the game so far and I will play more of it. If you like to be in complete control of your "character" you may not enjoy this title since a lot of the time the control is out of your hands.
If you'd like to see 20 minutes of my experience with the game check out my Twenty Minute Tryout video on YouTube...

I thought the combat and RPG mechanics would be terrible since it's an educational game; but the game is very solid. The lessons are at a reasonable size so you aren't overwhelmed and it gives you a few hints about the specific character you're learning. Don't forget to take as many notes as possible, it really helps. So far this game has been worth the purchase, a lot of love and work went into this game. If you're looking to learn Japanese you'll want to start with this game.

Banished is a lot like a medieval Sim City in several ways, though there's no real economy to speak of unless you download a mod like Colonial Charter (which now adds silver pfennings and gold guilders - the base game has no actual money). Development has been progressing pretty steadily, the game by and large runs well, though there is a bit of a learning curve in regards to positioning structures for proper supply rationing and which methods of gaining food work best in a given area.
All in all it's a very solid game, made even better by mods (CC is one of the best ones, but there are plenty of others if you don't want one that makes as many changes as CC does). The only thing I will say is that once you master the game's mechanics and build the structures you like, there's really not a lot to do anymore. There are occasional disasters like fires, diseases, crop infestations, etc (which can be turned off if you don't want them), but other than that there's really no end-game. It's just see how many citizens you can keep alive for how many years.
A combat mechanic would be nice, where you have to protect your town from raiders (it is styled after medieval times, after all, things weren't known for being peaceful back then), and even better would be making that mechanic optional for those who don't wish to be disturbed and like just watching their town grow. The parameters of the game are very customizable so I can't see "combat=optional" being too big of a problem.

Outlast puts you in first person control of a protagonist who must sneak past/run and hide from enemies rather than engage them (ala Amnesia). Armed only with a handcam, journalist Miles Upshur arrives at Mount Massive Asylum to investigate an anonymous whistleblower's tip that twisted things are afoot within its supposedly abandoned walls. It doesn't take long for him (and you) to realize that what lives within Mount Massive is far worse than anyone could have imagined. You must make your way through the asylum seeking escape, discovering and documenting more and more twisted truths (and resident psychopaths) as you progress. This is no shooter ladies and gents, Miles is an ordinary guy and you will literally spend the entirety of the game weaponless and unable to fight or defend. If your foes catch you, you're dead (esp on highest difficulty). Your only advantage is your handcam's night-vision mode that allows you to navigate Mount Massive's darkened halls and sneak around/past your NV-less enemies, but this mode requires batteries that are scattered about for you to collect. My advice: don't run out of batteries :)
Mount Massive Asylum's varied environments are relentlessly creepy, claustrophobic and DARK.
Excellent sound effects and an unnerving score strengthen the outstanding atmosphere.
Jump scares done right. Bring a change of underwear.
Great graphics thanks to Unreal Engine.
Tight, responsive controls.
Interesting dark storyline.
Lack of ability to fully customise graphics options within the in-game menu. Not a problem if you're familiar with tweaking Unreal Engine ini files, but would have been nice to have those options in the menu.
The game's enemies. Every one of them. I don't mean the graphics either, they're great. I mean these guys are UGLY. It's like uglytown, a total ug-fest.
Outlast is an intense experience that feeds the player a relentless diet of fear and dread from start to finish. It's a visceral and unflinchingly brutal game of cat and mouse where you play the mouse in an asylum full of insane cats. This is the first game in years to make me flinch, and did it more than once. If you're a fan of horror titles who feels that true fear has been missing in games of late, Outlast will pleasantly surprise you.

We had a pretty good turn out on the Steam broadcast for this one, not to mention some lovely conversations with the viewers. Now, before we get into this, this title is very much in an “early access” and has only a small portion of the content that the full game will have. Eventually, this review will be updated and a final score will be given, but for now, we will be reviewing it as is. Let’s get going.
I – Story [~/10]
The Long Dark is a promising exploration and survival game from Hinterland Studio Inc. As I mentioned already, the game is in an alpha stage so there is no access to the story mode yet. I will therefore not be scoring it in this category at this time for this reason.
II – UI [8/10]
The user interface is pretty good overall, but it has it’s issues as well. The HUD can be changed between three settings. Normal, Debug, and Off. Normal and Debug feature a small, white reticle that you can use to find out what you’re aiming at currently, where as Off mode turns all HUD aspects off completely (as the name would suggest). Debug also adds a nifty coordinate tracker that let’s you know where you are on the map along with the name of the location.
The menus are well done for the most part, but, even with the sorting capabilities in the inventory menu, the inventory can become quickly tedious to navigate. This is especially true when you start to amass more and more items on various runs into the wild to resupply or whatnot.
As far as status effects go, the game will flash you some written warnings in either bottom corner and your character will make a comment to let you know what is happening in an offhanded manner.
III – Gameplay [9/10]
Gameplay is where TLD currently shines the brightest. When you think “survival game” you’re probably thinking of games like DayZ, 7 Days to Die, etc. You would be wrong in comparing them to TLD though. In this game, it is you against nature (and what seems like every damned wolf on the face of the planet). Honestly, in a market saturated with games that have you running from/killing one undead creature or another, it is refreshing to have the man vs nature scenario on the table.
For starters, this game has no tutorial (at least, not yet) and I truly hope that they keep it that way. It is a great experience to get dropped into a patch of snowy Canadian wilderness and be expected to figure it all out for yourself. If you don’t learn the ropes fast, you’re most likely going to be wolf bait in a matter of hours.
The greatest challenge you’ll face in TLD is yourself. Much like the character status set up from How to Survive, if you’re not keeping a sharp eye on your stats, you’re as good as dead. In the game you will have to constantly monitor your calorie count, hunger and thirst levels, your fatigue, and body temperature if you expect to last very long out there. It’s a delicate balance to stay in top form and maintaining that balance can be a punishing experience.
Combat (with wolves) can be unbelievably frustrating after your umpteenth time being mauled by wolves. Hand-to-hand combat is difficult as it is implemented through a “struggle system” of which, I was not fond in the least. You’re safest option is to pray that you find a rifle and some bullets and take out any wolves that you must encounter from afar. Aside from this, I have practically no other complaints about gameplay (aside from not being able to jump. Why can I not jump Hinterland?).
Also, permadeath. Did we mention the permadeath? No? Oh, well, now you know.
IV – Content [8/10]
Although it is in it’s early stages, and you can only access two areas of the game, TLD has a pleasantly large amount of content item-wise. As it stands now, the game boasts over 100 different pieces of equipment scattered throughout the landscape. You can find knives, hatchets, rifles, first aid goodies, clothing, a smattering of food, and more. A few solid runs into the game, you will probably have seen it all though. And that is okay at this point.
Wildlife in the game is severely limited. You’ll see some frozen corpses of less survival-savvy mortals, a suspicious amount of male deer, some unnamed blackbirds that sound like crows, rabbits, and enough wolves to last you several lifetimes. Most players are hoping to see this particular category expand within the next little while. Some of us would like to be horribly maimed and killed by something other than wolves to break up the maddening monotony.
V – Visual [9/10]
The artwork of TLD was initially what caught my eye about the game. It is hand-drawn and it is beautiful. It’s an incredibly stylistic world and I wouldn’t want it any other way. The landscape is nothing short of breathtaking.
Animal models could use some tweaking though, as most of them appear very stiff and unnatural when they move. It’s okay for the corpses to look stiff, mainly because they’re frozen…and corpses.
VI – Audio [10/10]
Music plays intermittently during TLD and it typically signifies something. Maybe you’ve discovered a new area or maybe you’ve just made it through another night. Whatever the case, the music is brief and brilliant and only works to improve the game experience.
Sound effects in the game are great. From drinking water to dying of dysentery, there is never a sound that makes you stop and say “Um, what?” Often you will find yourself saying “Um, no” when you hear a howling wolf answered by several other while stumbling back to your hideout in the growing dark though.
The voice acting is very well done up to this point and I’m excited to see where Hinterland takes it as far as the story goes.
VII – Overall [8.8/10]
Overall, I would very much recommend The Long Dark, as it is a wonderful addition to the survival family.

I have a love/hate relationship with this game. Love is a strong word, but I love this game because the cinematic realism and the shear amount of reward when you succeed. Yet, I also hate this game; hate is a strong word too, but I hate this game because of the fact that I die constantly I have no idea where I was shot from and there is no forgiveness or reward for my death. This is not your typical miltary arcade COD clone. Simply put, this is war, war like you have never seen it before in any game. Red Orchestra 2 is a hyper realistic WW11 military shooter. Now if you cringe at the sound of HYPER REALISTIC, then stop reading this review right now because this game is not for you.
Now lets get down to the nitty gritty stuff.The gameplay... gameplay always comes first and this game almost nails. Aiming does not work like your typical FPS, you don't have crosshairs nor does your gun stay centered. The gun moves around the screen as if you are holding a real gun. That means noscoping DOES NOT WORK! When shooting you also have to compensate for bullet drop. This can be done one of two ways. First you can simply aim high which is a little bit less accurate. The second and far more efficient way to compensate for drop is to raise the sights on your gun to set the range. Other than those details gameplay works almost exactly the same way as any other FPS out there. I will admit though, the gameplay does not feel as flushed out as other AAA titles like COD or Battlefield. Gun models are very well designed and give a very decent amount of kick. The sounds for many of the guns were actually recorded by their real world counter parts giving an even greater feeling of immersion. The game also utilizes a cover system which is very interesing for an FPS; it can be quite finicky at times, but when it does work it can be quite useful. Combat is also much slower and far more meticulous than most FPS' out there. The reason for this is that, generally if you get shot once you die. You can't simply charge out into the battlefield and expect to be a one man army. This game takes time and teamwork. When the time is right you can charge in, but generally the turtle gets to the finish line before the hare. Its a very fresh and unique experience that is hard to find anywhere else.
Battles take place on very large wide open maps with many different ranges to shoot from. Some maps seem even excessivley large. They can be so large in fact that you can barely even see an enemy at the full range, they might look like ants on your screen. With big maps means lots, and I mean LOTS, of running. Maps are well designed, some with plenty of buildings with many open windows for shooting from while other maps are far more wide open with some shrubbery and low hills and a few building here and there; still, other maps have a good mix of both urban environments and wide open spaces. Typically most servers play territory mode which is the best mode for the large maps. In territory mode one team attacks while the other defends. The attacking team starts on one end with little breathing room for fighting. If the attacking team can push in and capture the first territory(s), the defending team will be pushed back to the next territory(s) giving the attacking team a lttle more breathing room. The attacking team wins by either capturing all territorys or by depleting the defending teams reinforcments. The defending team wins by either keeping the attacking team from capturing all territoys or depleting the attacking reinforcements. The defending team can also have a faster victory if they can hold one position for long enough a lockdown will occur, and when the lockdown time runs out the game ends. The game can also end when time runs out.
Graphically the game is very pretty. Character models are well done and the textures and shadows add a gritty feeling to the immersion. While playing you can almost feel the dirt on your skin. Colors tend to be dark browns, tans, reds, and greens. Even the snow maps have a feeling of darkness and despair in them. By no means is this game meant to look like some beautifully colorful piece of artwork. Its design choice really gives the game a darker feeling which contributes to its depiction of war which is not pretty.
Red Orchestra 2 is not for the faint of heart. If you are not fond of dying over and over again with very few kills between deaths and a much slower paced style of combat, then I suggest you don't play this game. For those of you who enjoy history, realism, big maps, and high risk high reward gameplay, then this is the game for you. By all means play it and have fun. The community could certainly use some more members! Now get out there and fight soldier!

If asked, Valve will tell you that Counter-Strike: Source originally began life as an experiment, designed to demonstrate how easy it is to port Half-Life modifications to the Source Engine. But it's easy to see how it's since established itself as Half-Life 2's chief multiplayer component; given that the majority of people who own the original Half-Life and still go online with it choose to play Counter-Strike, why waste time and resources trying to reinvent the multiplayer wheel when you can just polish an unbroken concept and re-release it as a pre-order bonus?
In the end, the idea turned out to be so good that Valve also decided to remake Day of Defeat, Team Fortress Classic, the original Half-Life single-player and more besides in its new Source Engine, not only attracting nostalgic fans back to retread fondly remembered paths, and gathering new blood to the shiny old flag, but saving the Seattle-based developer the trouble of designing an original multiplayer component to tack on the end of Half-Life 2 at the same time.
Having given ATI coupon holders, Condition Zero owners and LAN cafés the chance to try out a one-map beta version last month, Valve has now finally launched its Steam pre-purchase offers for Half-Life 2, and given fans who pre-order the game full access to a 'release version' of Counter-Strike: Source, featuring nine maps. Some argue that it's familiarity that fuels the success of unambitious sequels; in Valve's case, familiarity is just the kindling, and it's ignited pre-orders direct from the developer in a manner that's sure to have rival firms - including publishers - nursing furrowed brows of jealousy.
As long time veterans of the original Counter-Strike, we were some of the first in line. And having spent the past few days getting to grips with CS: Source, and reacquainting ourselves with hot headed bellowing - and, in particular, screams of "Stop running with the effing gun!" and "Defuse kit? DEFUSE KIT!" - we thought we'd let you know what you're up against; whether CS: Source is worth the trouble for fans of the original; whether it's good value as the multiplayer component of a £40 first-person shooter; and whether Valve's finally managed to give newcomers a way into the seemingly impenetrable world of Counter-Strike.
If we answered each of the last three questions in sequence, we could plot the resulting graph with a backslash. Yes, Counter-Strike: Source is "worth the trouble" for fans of the original - it's the game you remember and love, where a few minor shortfalls are offset by a resounding improvement in visual quality and a number of smaller, sensible alterations that subtly improve the experience. Secondly, maybe it's good value as the multiplayer component of a £40 FPS, but we'll deal with that in more detail later. And lastly, no, Valve's not managed to give newcomers a clearer way in.
For the completely uninitiated, CS: Source's problem is that it's too exclusive. It may be simple enough to get your head round quickly - Terrorists versus Counter-Terrorists with real-life weapons, one primary and one sidearm per player per round, bought along with grenades and suchlike before the round commences, you sit out the rest of the round when you're dead, and you can win by planting/defusing the bomb, protecting/rescuing the hostages, or killing off the other team - but it's a ♥♥♥♥♥ to master.
Valve had planned to include AI-controlled bots to help players practice their way into CS - an approach that almost worked with the much-maligned Condition Zero - but they're not in this build (something that's attracted particular criticism given that an illegal hacked version of the CS: Source beta has been circulating with the bots enabled). So, in the meantime, players are expected to pick up and learn the maps in hostile online environments, full of people (like this reviewer) who know how to kill them before they've worked out which gun to buy, or which way to turn to get from point A to point B, or even what they'll see when they do get to point B. Let alone the best map strategies, the right radio commands, the best way to handle each weapon, the best vantage points, and everything else that everybody else already knows.
Frankly, anybody coming to CS: Source afresh, hoping to pick up the multiplayer game all their friends rave about, is going to have their work just as cut out as ever, and may prefer to wait for Valve to activate the bots so they can practice and grasp the fundamentals - how the game works, which weapons to go for and why, the map layouts, and the best team strategies - offline, before heading online to start nailing down the subtleties, like the way crouching improves firing accuracy, how you move quicker with the knife drawn than a primary weapon, and what to expect from individual chokepoints in a live game.
For existing fans though, CS: Source ought to provide ideal fodder on those increasingly cold winter nights. In gameplay terms it's almost indistinguishable from its Half-Life-based predecessor. Two teams race towards chokepoints and try to achieve their objectives against the clock, taking advantage of the wide variety of weapons and tactics at their disposal, and the departed troops get to sit around and spectate as they do so, chatting about the action and sharing in the pervading mood of the encounter. It makes you laugh (particularly when it's one v. one and someone accidentally kills himself with a grenade or falling damage), and it makes you cry (particularly when people run with their bloody guns), but, given time to prove itself, it's also one of the most arresting FPS disciplines in existence.
Or, to make that a bit clearer, in gameplay terms the only practical differences can be run through in a couple of paragraphs. You can smash crates, computers and plenty of other destructible items littering each level. Glass, when hit by a bullet or knife, only falls away in a small radius around the point of impact, so it now takes another bullet or somebody jumping through the frosted effect of the cracked remnants to make it through completely. You can no longer penetrate two-foot walls with bullets, and a grenade going off on the other side of a wall will no longer hurt you anywhere near as much, but you can still send bullets through boxes, cupboard doors and the like. Water now splashes visually as well as audibly, giving the defending side on maps like Aztec a bit of an advantage in locating intrepid aggressors. And hostages are now capable of following you without getting stuck every five seconds, even if they still do so every once in a while.
And, of course, CS: Source adopts Half-Life 2's Havok-based physics code, meaning that barrels and limp bodies are now thrown around semi-convincingly by explosions (although they do seem to bounce a bit too much at the moment), adding to the spectacle. The gameplay benefits of this are, in practice, almost negligible (you'll be lucky to benefit from any extra cover as a result of it, in any case), but it certainly contributes to the increased believability of the whole thing.
But CS: Source makes no secret of its intentions - it was not envisaged as "Counter-Strike 2", and as a result it doesn't attempt to overhaul the dynamic, or even augment it in more than a few subtle ways. What it does aim to do though is make the game look like a first-person shooter ought to do in this day and age, and not like the five year-old game it really is. So far Valve's revisited, overhauled and released nine of the original game's maps.

Summary: I can't swallow the broken physics and without it there is no game.
Right:
Hot Air balloons can be controlled with a single "burn" input (one button), sending the hot-air balloon upwards. Think "Flappy Bird", not "Kerbal SPace Program".
Wrong:
The only thing that makes this a "game" (instead of a "follow the arrows" exercise) is that physics is twisted so that the balloon can gain momentum in one windstream, and when the balloon enters a different windstream, the balloon will briefly continue moving as though it were still in the first windstream. Neither Boyle, Bernoulli nor Newton would have approved this game-design decision. It's not how balloons work in air. And without this twist there is no game.
Wrong:
The player can hear the burn when the balloon is ordered to move upwards, suggesting a warm balloon filled with mostly Nitrogen and Carbon Dioxide. Yet the balloon detonates when it strikes an object, as thought the balloon were constructed of strike-anywhere matches and filled with hydrogen.
Wrong:
The balloon can go seemingly infinitely far off the map to the left, right, or bottom. But if it goes off the top of the map, it is "lost" and forces a restart. What, did it go into orbit? Doesn't the air on this planet get thinner with altitude?
Wrong:
No fuel meter, infinite burns are allowed. Fuel should have been the "game", and physics should have been real.
