There isn't any more praise I can give BioShock that it hasn't already received.  Story-driven games are my favorite and this one really delivers on the story.  The plasmid system in the game offers you many different ways to traverse through the world and gives you many reasons to play through the game again and again.  Being that it's heavily story-driven you'll probably need a couple of playthroughs to let it all soak in anyway.
The only complaints I have are the combat system and water and enemy death animations(which are clearly rendered at 30fps while the rest of the engine hums along merrily at 60fps), which are a little wonky and disappointing given the quality of the rest of the game's assets.  BioShock is a console game, first and foremost, as can be witnessed by the default control scheme, but this much can be easily corrected with a few settings adjustments so no real complaints there.
All in all, BioShock is a title I highly recommend for any gamer.

I got hooked into DD1 after playing the first mission. After I finished the game and modded the crap out of it, I played dungeon defenders eternity and fell in love with it all over again.
This sorry excuse for a dungeon defenders game is just that. A sorry excuse. The graphics may be 'nicer' (I personally prefer the look the old games had), and it may be less prone to awkward crashes, but damn. At the very least, DDE had some half/decent gameplay to go along with it.
Back to my point about being hooked at the first mission. I played through the tutorial level as the sorceror (which was my go to character considering how the summoner was yet to be implemented) and after putting up with the crappy enemy spawn times, the crappier enemy walking pace and the even crappier enemy damage (despite not having any armour at all), I uninstalled it and am glad it's no longer taking up space on my SSD. I did head back to the hub world, but got lost as to what I was doing. The UI was wonky and difficult to navigate, the new systems failed to improve the solid old ones and there was basically no point to having such a massive scale revamp.
It makes me even angrier that my favourite hero from DD1/DDE, The Summoner, had the one gimik that made his character interesting and different from the rest removed. In DD1/DDE, The Summoner had the ability to summon crystal versions of the enemies in place of towers. These crystal enemies has the ability to move and even chase enemies. Despite the AI for your minions being wonky and just plain broken at times, the gimik changed the flow of gameplay and allowed for such a dynamic sense of strategy. Suddenly, if my tower went down and I had no mana to replace it, I could choose to relocate some of my other minions to it's job. This was such a cool and different mechanic, and I loved it the instant I started using it.
NOW, The Summoner (as of the writing of this review) has had his best quality removed. All his towers function like towers and blockades, which is a huge let down and a shame. On top of that, he lost his other two great abilities which allowed easy surveying of the battlefield, namely his "Phase Shift Overlord" ability, which turned the classic 3rd/1st person perspective into a top-down look of the entire battlefield. He could even summon and move minions from this perspective, once again adding to the extra gameplay elements. But NOPE, Trendy thought it would be a good idea to remove the interesting mechanics they had set up in the previous games.
Trendy, get your act together. I'm happy that you're not actually charging anyone to trial what is essentially a shiny pile of garbage compared to your previous works, but seriously. What happen to the old magic, that made DD1/DDE so good?

This game is no longer a FPS. It is a World War 2 simulator.

Outlast puts you in first person control of a protagonist who must sneak past/run and hide from enemies rather than engage them (ala Amnesia). Armed only with a handcam, journalist Miles Upshur arrives at Mount Massive Asylum to investigate an anonymous whistleblower's tip that twisted things are afoot within its supposedly abandoned walls. It doesn't take long for him (and you) to realize that what lives within Mount Massive is far worse than anyone could have imagined. You must make your way through the asylum seeking escape, discovering and documenting more and more twisted truths (and resident psychopaths) as you progress. This is no shooter ladies and gents, Miles is an ordinary guy and you will literally spend the entirety of the game weaponless and unable to fight or defend. If your foes catch you, you're dead (esp on highest difficulty). Your only advantage is your handcam's night-vision mode that allows you to navigate Mount Massive's darkened halls and sneak around/past your NV-less enemies, but this mode requires batteries that are scattered about for you to collect. My advice: don't run out of batteries :)
Mount Massive Asylum's varied environments are relentlessly creepy, claustrophobic and DARK.
Excellent sound effects and an unnerving score strengthen the outstanding atmosphere.
Jump scares done right. Bring a change of underwear.
Great graphics thanks to Unreal Engine.
Tight, responsive controls.
Interesting dark storyline.
Lack of ability to fully customise graphics options within the in-game menu. Not a problem if you're familiar with tweaking Unreal Engine ini files, but would have been nice to have those options in the menu.
The game's enemies. Every one of them. I don't mean the graphics either, they're great. I mean these guys are UGLY. It's like uglytown, a total ug-fest.
Outlast is an intense experience that feeds the player a relentless diet of fear and dread from start to finish. It's a visceral and unflinchingly brutal game of cat and mouse where you play the mouse in an asylum full of insane cats. This is the first game in years to make me flinch, and did it more than once. If you're a fan of horror titles who feels that true fear has been missing in games of late, Outlast will pleasantly surprise you.

You take command of a rag-tag group of space mercs whose sole purpose in life is to explore wormholes, encounter aliens, and then blast those aliens into gooey bits so that you can collect loot and research materials.  Oh, and it's all presented in super stylish 2D art!  All in all, this game is worth the price of admission.  For the curious, take a look at this video which shows part of the tutorial and two planet-side missions:
Once I got past the initial premise and glossy presentation, I was pleasantly surprised to find a relatively deep simulation/RPG game that has you manage everything from your ship's fuel and "mass" (necessary to teleport your squad and to manufacture items through replication) to your crew's equipment, skills, and attributes.
The combat, as I mentioned above, is snappy and very pretty to watch, with particle effects going off in every direction.  The only downside is that your squadees don't seem to auto-target opponents, which requires a heavy amount amount of micromanagement during combat (and sometimes makes it difficult to multi-task).
The graphics, as you would expect, are 2D/sprite-based with flashy particle effects.  The worlds are beautiful, with lovingly crafted buildings and environments that are mysterious enough for me to want to know more (e.g., what the heck is those ominous ruins).
Overall, I really enjoy Pixel Privateers.  It's still unclear just how I'll fit into my gaming rotation--whether it'll be a staple that I sink endless hours into or whether it'll be something I play to unwind for a little bit--but it definitely won't go neglected!

Very early impressions ... looks like there's quite a bit of fun to be had here. I'm still feeling my way around, but what I've seen thus far seems polished. Though I'm still in the training wheels stage where the enemies are weak and resources are plentiful, I can see where the resource management decisions are going to be critical in short order, as will making sure each party member is kitted out with gear suited to each particular role in order to maximize efficiency. I like that the various roles, Vanguard, Sniper, Medic, Engineer and Marine can be switched between missions, meaning if you get stuck or find a particularly powerful bit of loot, you can switch things up. For the micro-inclined vets of RTS, there's a minor bit of that as well as you swap between party members during battle to implement the various special attacks, buffs and debuffs. The game features a playful, irreverent writing style that draws from pop culture (I've already encountered apparent nods to Star Wars and FTL). You can alter the difficulty by choosing whether party members who fall in combat can be cloned, though I don't know if they start over at base level or return with their gear and exp. All in all, I've enjoyed what I've seen, but I'll check back once I spend a little more time exploring the wormhole. My only gripe at this point, key bindings don't seem to be able to take advantage of mouse buttons beyond the traditional L, R and scroll wheel, but it's early days yet. Happy exploring travelers!
Update - About 17 hours in and while I still feel the game is fun and stand by the vast majority of my initial thoughts, I will say I'm disappointed that the game doesn't seem to have much depth beyond the initial charm. The pieces are there for a compelling experience. Unfortunately, the game showers you with so much loot and resources that it feels like it's impossible to fail. Those critical decisions - do I chance it with the fuel I have or try to clear another planet - simply don't happen because by a few hours in you have so much fuel, matter and cash piled up that gameplay seems to devolve into an exercise in finding slight upgrades for your gear and weapons. I hope they keep working on this, maybe incorporate a mode where resources are much more precious and hard earned. Like I said, I think the potential is there and I find the core gameplay enjoyable.

Compelling, thought-provoking stuff from the man behind The Stanley Parable. Unlike Wreden's last game, The Beginner's Guide is a short (~90 mins), linear experience which narrates the story of a game developer (and their shifting relationship with the narrator) as you play through each of their creations in turn.
It's a fascinating thing, which tackles topics including anxiety, depression, creative burnout, and more - all wrapped around the conflict between two people over the fundamentals of game design, and one's inability to comprehend the other (and struggle to deal with that inability).
The short playtime is worth noting - though I think a second playthrough might prove rather fascinating once the full story has been experienced - but as long as you are okay with that, The Beginner's Guide comes highly recommended by me. It will delight, confuse, astound, and leave you with a wealth of things to think about.

I could go on for hours about what this game does right. It captures the exact feel of the old great 3D platformers you grew up with (or maybe didn't, if you're a young'n). Its music is superb, sometimes almost choking me up on how good it is. The art style is charming, the sound design is lovely, the controls are airtight and an absolute joy to play, the humor had me genuinely laughing so many times, and Hat Kid is so precious that it ought to be criminal. I could go on and on, but it's easier to just say that A Hat in Time is simply fantastic.
It is however, unpolished. As much as I'd love to say the game is perfect, there are occasional bugs here and there that aren't exactly hard to replicate. Ledges that you feel like you really, REALLY should have reached from wall-running from what seemed like the "intended" jumping point (lookin' at you, Alpine Skyline), and invisible geometry sprinkled throughout. A certain bell in a certain dreamscape refused to activate as I relentlessly swung at it. A lot of characters that aren't Hat Kid or a Mafia goon are animated as though they belong in a bargain bin game, and ones that aren't simply don't have many animations to begin with.
That sounds like a lot of complaining compiled into that one paragraph, but only because I didn't subject you to 10 paragraphs singing the game's praise, which I could have easily done and I have to physically restrain myself from doing. Most problems that have any affect on gameplay are honestly minor, USUALLY don't end up with you falling in a pit, and only give brief "what the-? oh well" moments that you'll likely forget within half a second, and the complaints with character animations are just that. They don't hurt the game as a GAME, it's just something you notice and think "eh, that looks kinda janky, doesn't it?"
That said, some things like the invisible geometry (some of which is harder to avoid than to accidentally bump into) or Hat Kid just plummeting to her (non-gameplay affecting) death during a cutscene feel like things that just shouldn't be happening. They're problems I have no trouble replicating every single time, and have seen other people experiencing every single time in the same places, so it comes across as strange to me that such flaws would make it through development.
Despite the gears needing a little oil, A Hat in Time is still one of the best platformers to be made in recent memory. It honestly stands up to the classics in terms of gameplay, and may even surpass them in terms of technical gameplay, and definitely dwarfs them in terms of adorableness. I'd never tell anyone to not get this game due to the small issues. In the 12 hours I was messing around getting all 40 time pieces, and for all the extra hours I've spent just dorking around because it's genuinely fun enough just to play for FUN (what a concept!), I recall maybe two instances that I was honestly frustrated by those minor flaws. If updates in the future were to smooth out those bumps, then as a game, A Hat in Time would be very near perfect, held back only by some "meh" NPC animations.
Get this game. Its gameplay is fantastic, it has more heart than a blue whale, it's so cute that you'll question whether or not you ever had a single spit of testosterone in your body at all, and it may even move you to tears with how simply enjoyable the experience is.

There isn't any more praise I can give BioShock that it hasn't already received.  Story-driven games are my favorite and this one really delivers on the story.  The plasmid system in the game offers you many different ways to traverse through the world and gives you many reasons to play through the game again and again.  Being that it's heavily story-driven you'll probably need a couple of playthroughs to let it all soak in anyway.
The only complaints I have are the combat system and water and enemy death animations(which are clearly rendered at 30fps while the rest of the engine hums along merrily at 60fps), which are a little wonky and disappointing given the quality of the rest of the game's assets.  BioShock is a console game, first and foremost, as can be witnessed by the default control scheme, but this much can be easily corrected with a few settings adjustments so no real complaints there.
All in all, BioShock is a title I highly recommend for any gamer.

Very early impressions ... looks like there's quite a bit of fun to be had here. I'm still feeling my way around, but what I've seen thus far seems polished. Though I'm still in the training wheels stage where the enemies are weak and resources are plentiful, I can see where the resource management decisions are going to be critical in short order, as will making sure each party member is kitted out with gear suited to each particular role in order to maximize efficiency. I like that the various roles, Vanguard, Sniper, Medic, Engineer and Marine can be switched between missions, meaning if you get stuck or find a particularly powerful bit of loot, you can switch things up. For the micro-inclined vets of RTS, there's a minor bit of that as well as you swap between party members during battle to implement the various special attacks, buffs and debuffs. The game features a playful, irreverent writing style that draws from pop culture (I've already encountered apparent nods to Star Wars and FTL). You can alter the difficulty by choosing whether party members who fall in combat can be cloned, though I don't know if they start over at base level or return with their gear and exp. All in all, I've enjoyed what I've seen, but I'll check back once I spend a little more time exploring the wormhole. My only gripe at this point, key bindings don't seem to be able to take advantage of mouse buttons beyond the traditional L, R and scroll wheel, but it's early days yet. Happy exploring travelers!
Update - About 17 hours in and while I still feel the game is fun and stand by the vast majority of my initial thoughts, I will say I'm disappointed that the game doesn't seem to have much depth beyond the initial charm. The pieces are there for a compelling experience. Unfortunately, the game showers you with so much loot and resources that it feels like it's impossible to fail. Those critical decisions - do I chance it with the fuel I have or try to clear another planet - simply don't happen because by a few hours in you have so much fuel, matter and cash piled up that gameplay seems to devolve into an exercise in finding slight upgrades for your gear and weapons. I hope they keep working on this, maybe incorporate a mode where resources are much more precious and hard earned. Like I said, I think the potential is there and I find the core gameplay enjoyable.

SUPER! HOT! SUPER! HOT! You'll grow to love that sound.
You start the game. A Red Dude is suddenly in front of you, fists balled, hand drawn back. You melee quickly, knocking him back and down. A quick look left shows an assault rifle on the table, but another Red Dude is coming through the doorway just across ther room with a drawn pistol. You judge the distance, and race for the AR. As the weapon comes to rest in your hands, you hear Red Dude fire a shot. You come to a stop and turn towards the oncoming bullet.
Time suddenly slows to a crawl.
You take careful aim, pull the trigger, and fire three precise shots. As time again begins to flow forward, your first bullet impacts the oncoming pistol bullet, casuing them both to shatter and deflect. The other two shells go flying into the chest and upper arm of the last Red Dude, causing him to crumple to the floor.
SUPER! HOT! SUPER! HOT!

A fun loot-gathering game with a ton of options regarding party-comp and character customization. Two characters of the same class need not be the same stat/skill wise, and there are a ton of weapons to choose from (there are no class/weapon restrictions).
As an example, my medic uses hammers and gets bonus heals for every attack he does. He beats enemies in the face and heals while he does so.
Gameplay is interesting, albeit a bit uninvolved in the early game. Planets tend to be varied and there are a few different objectives that you may receive upon landing. Gameplay consists of the loop of:
Prepare party -> go to planet and get loot -> go to galaxy map -> prepare party -> repeat
It's simple, but it's addicting and the varied loot keeps me coming back for more. I recommend it if you're into games like Diablo, Path of Exile, Grim Dawn, etc.
My biggest gripe, aside from a lack of truly varied objectives, is that controlling five characters is tedious, thus leading me to leave most of them on auto while I control my tank and engineer.  I would like to see more viability for having fewer than five characters in a party (three would be my sweet spot between interesting gameplay/party comp and reasonable micro-management). The game does allow you to pause mid-combat to issue orders, which helps with this; think Baldur's Gate or Pillars of Eternity.
Overall, the game is quite fun and offers a really addicting loot-loop that I think will be enticing to many players.

Compelling, thought-provoking stuff from the man behind The Stanley Parable. Unlike Wreden's last game, The Beginner's Guide is a short (~90 mins), linear experience which narrates the story of a game developer (and their shifting relationship with the narrator) as you play through each of their creations in turn.
It's a fascinating thing, which tackles topics including anxiety, depression, creative burnout, and more - all wrapped around the conflict between two people over the fundamentals of game design, and one's inability to comprehend the other (and struggle to deal with that inability).
The short playtime is worth noting - though I think a second playthrough might prove rather fascinating once the full story has been experienced - but as long as you are okay with that, The Beginner's Guide comes highly recommended by me. It will delight, confuse, astound, and leave you with a wealth of things to think about.

"What are you going to play next?"
"Umm. Outlast I guess.  It's been in my backlog since summer. Supposed to be scary or something."
And there I went.  Oblivious to what I was getting into.  Honestly, I had only watched 2 minutes of vids online and a Conan O Brian review. Then came the game; immediately creepy. And it quickly moved on to scary and terrifying. The world seemed a bit Portal 2-ish, but the actual gameplay...was amazing.  Pacing, story, real HORROR, and tension like I had not really felt in a horror game.  Not that I have played a ton of horror titles, but I would put it on par with early Silent Hill games.
I won't go into the details.  Really, it would spoil it for you.  Honestly, very basic.  You are a reporter checking out the weird stuff happening at the aslyum.  And then you walk in into an evil Wonderland complete with menacing large evil killers and a nutso with no pants.
Speaking of that, tweedle-nude and tweedle-nuder didn't get me once.  I was kinda proud of that.
You can't fire a gun or use a weapon.  The only defense is running, hiding, ducking, and having your heart up in your throat as Chris Walrider walks by you...aw! He found me!  AwHHHHHH!! RUNNNN!!!
Of all the games I have played this year, this has to be one of the best made in totality.  The length is just right.  Cues and progression move at an exact rhythm that does not allow you to slow your scare down. The jumpscares are there, but are by no means the meat of the game.  There are no useless time wasting missions.  Everything has a reason and the most annoying mission in the game
is perhaps one of the most terrifying when you do not know what will happen next at all.  Normal difficulty is not impossible and not once did I get stuck on geometry.  A few things are not apparent - that much is true.  Granted, if they were, the game would not be hard enough.  It's just right.  Really.  It's absolutely just right.  Kudos to the dev team.
At one point I told my buddy I was really wasn't super scared anymore by about the middle of the game.  BUT.  I could not play for more than an hour or so or my heart would not slow down enough for me to sleep well.  Too much tension.  Then he said "Isn't that what terrifying means?"
He was right.  Even when the horrific graphics no longer phased me, it was the sheer tension of the game that kept me in it's grip.  That is amazing, and impressed me more than many AAA titles I've played in the past.

First things first:
If you saw that this game was made by the same creator of The Stanley Parable, thinking you'll get another wild and absurd game like that one, DO NOT BUY THIS ONE.
The Beginner's Guide, instead, is actually a heartfelt and emotional trip through the works of a talented and bright abstract video game artist. Overfull with visual wonder, interpretation and pure creativity. The actual experience is not in the game itself but the backstory of the relationship between the narrator and a close friend who made originally made this collection of small games over the course of 2009-2011.
I won't say too much about it, since the experience is all in the history of these two people, but I will say that the collection of work is magnificent, some of the most visually stunning abstract video game art I've seen.
But just like The Stanley Parable, The Beginner's Guide does not follow the rules of video games and instead sets out to make it's own experience without pandering to a mainstream crowd.
With that said, this game is not meant for average gamers. There are no objectives or anything of the sort to be had, it's just a tribute to a friend. Which is I think the main downpoint, if you're making this for a friend, why are you charging $10? For a total length of an hour and a half, I can't see any justification. It's not like a museum gallery with a hefty entrance fee, it's a tribute.
Well, I don't have all the facts. So I'll just say this: If you're interested in video games as an art form, a means of expression or just a creative outlet, then The Beginner's Guide would probably be right up your alley. Otherwise, you'd be best off moving along.

A Hat in Time was a bit different from what I expected gameplay wise, I though it would be more open world (or open area) but instead was more akin to mario 64 of various areas with selectable missions that slightly change the area's layout. The goal also being similar to mario games in that you're looking for timepieces that are essentially stars (with 40 in the game). There are 4 "worlds" though some are less of areas and more like linear levels. Even the world that is labeled "freeroam" is one of the most linear areas. Each area also comes with bonus "rift" levels where you find the rift in the world and try to complete the level. As for gameplay, you have a rediculous range of motion and can get from one place to a fairly far away place without touching the ground. You have a double jump, a mario 64 style dive/cancel, a homing attack, short vertical wall run and wall jump, as well as a "wind waker" grapple (and crawl) along with other utilities. The only thing is that with such a wide range of movement and the game being a 3D platformer, you're expected to make full use out of it which (along with the less then perfect camera) can sometime make it difficult to figure out which way you're expected to go (a few times, your best way to counter this is just not to underestimate the jumps you can make). The camera could definately use some work and if I had one peice of advice to give, it would be to turn off "camera assist" otherwise, once it starts turning on its own, you'll be forced to match it's movement with your jump angle which got me killed more times than I can count before checking to see if I could turn it off. It can also be a little hard to determine depth which can make certain jumps difficult. That all being said, once you grasp all the movement mechanics, the levels are fun and interesting with little puzzles here and there and some really interesting platforming mechanics with new things being introduced at a good pace.
Outside of the mechanical aspects, the game advertises as being cute as heck but heck doesn't even begin to describe the level of cuteness in the game. Similar to how you might this of "Nintendo polish", this game has little bits and peices to add to the cuteness to the character and the world. There were too many moments to count where the game just made me feel happy. The story it also very entertaining and funny (albiet a bit weird towards the end) and there are many levels that do different and neat things. The only thing is that the same levels after played, won't have the same effect after being experienced the first time thought that in no way means they won't still be fun, just not the same. This game is aimed squarely at a generation of gamers that grew up with anthropomorphic duos and critically important shiny gold things. And boy howdy, does it deliver. I've been pining for a proper 3D platformer for years now, and, indeed, have wondered why it hasn't happened yet. But it's finally, *finally* here.
For those who don't really understand the collectathon genre, it's not really about the collecting. Mario 64 wasn't a game about collecting stars. What made it great (aside from being a novelty at the time due to pioneering several mechanics and concepts still used today) is losing yourself exploring the levels and slowly chewing through the game as you unlock things. The old adage holds true; it's about the journey, not the destination. Banjo-Kazooie expanded on this by adding lovable characters (eekum bokum), a real story, and a bunch more stuff to collect to unlock abilities, making you feel more powerful as you progress. A Hat in Time is a mashup of this, with a modern flare.
In short, 10/10 would hug Hat Kid again.

Life as air-balloon pilot is tough.  You aren't afforded any of those nifty steering doo-dads.  All you have to guide you is the wind.  Playing The Howler is all about learning to become one with the wind as you soar around this pastel world.  Its a simple concept for a game but it comes together quite well.  Its a short but sweet ride that should keep you entertained for just over an hour.
The controls are super simple.  All you can do is increase the heat to ascend or subsequently release the hot air to descend.  By controlling the elevation you will pass through different zones of air blowing the wind this way and that way.  Certain currents will be stronger than other and you must be careful of the potential momentum of the stronger winds.  By straddling these currents you can proceed to your destination or pick up goods required for the different objectives.
Many levels will simply have to going for one spot to another.  Other levels may have you pick up and deliver a package.  Later in the game you'll be given bombs you can drop.  Use these to destroy obstacles in your path or take out the enemy's bridge.  Just be careful not to be too close to your bombs as you can easily be sent floating off screen and into the abyss.
One of the coolest parts of the game is the hand drawn art.  The backgrounds are gorgeous and rich with detail.  They distinguish themselves nicely from the sharp,clean, lines of the objects in the foreground.  There isn't much to the sound design.  There isn't any music while playing which could be justified to help you concentrate.  Usually all you hear is balloon's propane kicking in as you turn on the heat to ascend.  That being said the automatons and cars really stick out in the levels they're present.
There really isn't much else to say.  This is a really simple game, one that doesn't take long to finish.  That isn't necessary a bad thing considering the low price point.  Not to mention there really isn't many other games like it.  The unique art style might make it worth considering if you're on edge.  As long as you're not expecting anything too fancy there is fun to be had playing The Howler.

However, it also involves a mechanic for combining colors into a single stream and then separating that stream back into its original colors. This is heavily involved in the levels. I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys puzzles, especially minimalist ones, as that is exactly what the game provides.

I've just finished this 'learning' game (don't know how to call it) recently and would like to give a little review of it.
This game is the first RPG game that I mostly willing to buy, a game for learning Japanese. When I was searching some random games on Steam and saw this special game. It is hard for me to find a way to start and here it is, a game for the beginner to learn Japanese characters and vocabs. However, I can't fully recommend this game for everyone to play because it is not easy to learn-and-remember in this game, even I take lots of notes and keep practicing on writing the characters. It is a method for me (maybe including anyone) to 'Learn' Hiragana but not 'Remember' Hiragana. Maybe it is just me having some learning problems, but seriously, the game's battle system is quite boring that you focus on defeating the enemies and get money to buy stuffs, then go to the next area and do the same thing. The aim still is still finishing the game and have a happy ending after a while I may forget all I have learnt and wasted several hours. I don't mean that playing this game is wasting time but it is not a choice to keep learning Japanese. Like I said, it is a good start for learning Japanese language but if you have already had a bit or more knowledge of this language, this game may not perform effectively.
Let me sum up this long freakin' review:
Pro:
- a choice for someone who would like to learn Japanese but don't know where to start
- suitable for someone who like playing RPG games
- educative
- feel fun to learn Japanese name of the daily stuffs
Con:
- quite boring battle system
- not easy to focus on learn-and-remember the Japanese characters
- some of the stuffs in game are useless or unable to use (spoiler alert!)
All above are just my unprofessional review and give a big support to the developer if you enjoy this game like I do :)

In the end, the entire game is repeating the same thing over and over while surrounded by differently colored pixels... No strategy, planning, or even thought required. I suppose it can be called a game, since all the pieces are there. However last time I checked, games required the interest of the players, which this title very much did not.

Blood and Bacon is a Nex-Generation survival/shooter game that pits you against swarms of undead boars which have seemingly overrun a strange and remote farm. You, a mysterious stranger must assist a Farmer... tormented by the evil he has unwittingly unleashed upon this land, surviving round after round hordes of blood thirsty swine. You can feel the pain and anguish the Farmer feels as he pleads with you to help cleanse his farm from the armies of boars that gather upon his barns doorsteps daily... as they grow ever so stronger each day. You will be moved to tears as hear him pitifully try to be optimistic in this hell... cracking jokes to keep your spirits going as he hangs there, slowly bleeding to death in agonizing pain from a pitchfork pierced deep within his gut.
The stunning graphics make it all look almost real as I've never seen a game looked quite this gorgeous, the attention to detail the developers gave is incredible to say the least. The voice acting is phenominal and is deserving of an Oscar as I felt a connection with the farmer... I empathized his struggle and knew exaclty what he was feeling... regret for his sins... the feeling of hanging onto whatever sliver of optimism you can in a dark and seemingly hopeless hell in which he is living in. The futility of struggle as every time you conquer an army of hell spawn, the next day brings upon an even greater obstacle than the last, but you must tread on... for the Farmer...
The story is filled with action, drama, and mystery as you must battle your way forward... day and night to uncover the truth of what happened here... slaughtering tens of thousands of swine by your hand, for you shall become death incarnate...

Blood and Bacon is by far the greatest game I have ever played. The game's steep price may cause some gamer-gators to stray away from the game, but trust me, it is WORTH every single penny. Well, this is not the case with Blood and Bacon. It's unique setting of some kind of rural area makes for an amazing experience. It is like I'm ACTUALLY THERE, and that is not something I can say for 'brown gun warfare'. Another aspect I love in the game is the quirkiness, and the sense of a deeper lore. The game has such a ♥♥♥♥ing AMAZING sense of humor. The farmer is very likeable, and I give my infinite praise to whoever the voice actor. I won't spoil anything, but if you find some really well hidden easter eggs, you're going to be scratching your head trying to figure out the developer's clues and secrets. The soundtrack to this game is groundbreaking. Yes, it's a bit primitive, but that's what I love about it. It KNOWS what it wants to be, and isn't some awful, confused instrumental! Sure, you may have heard it somewhere, but if it ain't broke, don't fix it! The weapons are so well balanced, and the pigs are challenging, yet fair. (Unlike Left 4 Dead 2, Valve's very awful spiritual predeccesor.) I give Blood and Bacon a perfect 10 / 10.

End of 2017 Update:
Wintermute: After much time spent in Survival, I finally played through the first two episodes of story mode.  10/10: I was quite skeptical of story mode, to be honest. I thought it would be lame and detract from the unparalleled survival mode experience. Well, the opposite is true. Wintermute is very fun.  Highlights:
1. It's arcade-like compared to Survival, but it works! Regenerating ammo, forced paths, and unavoidable animal fights sacrifce realism for gameplay, but it is fun!
2. There are very few NPCs, and that's nice. Too many games have 100s of NPCs that get lost, having single digit NPCs makes each important. I suggest stressing the importance of "Trust" more.
3. Realism is sacrificed too much when fighting the Old Bear. "Stand in until you see the white of his eyes!"? Really? No one has ever survived being mauled 5 times by a bear - not even the Revenant. Actual strat is to find unclimable terrain and snipe.
4. Keep it up!
SURVIVAL:
I like most of the updates. Major thoughts:
1. Your "odds computer" is broken. I missed 10 times in a row on 75% fire - maybe I'm the lottery loser, but more likely you need to fix your randomization algorithm.
2. Water system still kills believability. How about "containers" mechanic... Also, why do I still get food poisoning form pristine melted snow yet toilet water is like Evion?
3. Is the wolf-bait mechanic realistic? I kill them like fish in a barrel.
4. Caloric store makes no sense. we need "fat" or "reserve" or whatever. You  should feast on meat to stock up, and then be able to survive for WEEKS without food.  I suggest "Fat Reserve" mechanic.
5. Suggest to replace "Cabin Fever" with "Sanity" bar. "Fun" or "Interesting" activivities add to sanity. Sitting inside or getting attacked etc reduce. The most fun some people have is doing something intersting indoors (making a bearskin coat, eg).
6. 3 animal coats, and not hat? Please, let's make a hat from animal skin! Also, melee weapon?
Faithful Cartographer Update:
Fantastic Sandbox Update! Oh how I love this this game.  Almost 365 days in on Interloper and here are my thoughts on the latest version:
Pro:
1. I can finally pick up rabbits! The rock-throwing mechanic is great, though I lose a little piece of soul every time a snap Mr. Fuzzy's neck - survival of the fittest... And the quartering command is a great way to appease (silence) those asking to pick up deer.
2. "Scent" is a good mechanic. Still needs to be tweaked. Why don't animals like my pile of 20kg of rotting meat, but the second I pick it up, a million wolves descend upon me like Wargs in LOR?
3. Mapping is interesting, but tedious.  It's not advantageous in Interloper and is an end-game activity. Also, It would be greatly improved if you marked the map with an X or crosshair in the exact spots in which you mapped.
4. Deer flee much better making deer-flushing more realistic and harder.
Cons: (mostly things that still need work as opposed to problems with FC itself)
1. The water system needs an overhaul.  Where do I get all these containers? How am I gathering so much snow in all locations? Why do I need almost a liter of water every time I wake up? To quote Seinfeld, "it's not like I was running a marathon, I'm just lying there." Why doesn't my water freeze? I don't know the answer, just that this is the one thing still killing the realism.
2. Torches and Flares are basically useless for wolf-scaring now. And baiting and then popping Fluffy in the head with an arrow is too easy.
3. More melee! Rocks were a great start, but I want to stab a deer if I get close enough! How about a spear too?
4. We need regenerating flora just like fauna.  Unless this game truly is an homage to the Existentialist philosophers and we are to inevitably wear away to nothing at the hands of an indifferent, decaying world. If not, let's have some birch saplings and rosehips regrow!

It was on my 7th city that I finally felt as though I'd mastered the game. In "hard mode", starting with four families with the clothes on their backs, hours and hours and hours later, I finally expanded to ~1000 people. Mini villages all over the large map, with little markets as their centerpiece. Each had their own school, church, blacksmith, hospital, woodcutter, tailor and the like. I had four trading posts well stocked, in case of any emergency, multiple deliveries could be made. The food was well stocked (~100k at any given point in the seasons). My people were healthy, happy, clothed, educated.
Along comes a pack of 143 nomads. One Hundred and Forty Three Nomads(!!!!) in this lovely little single file line to add to the gene pool and grow my population to numbers unseen! I'm squealing with joy, even taking a picture with my cell phone to send to my roommate! Now, I'd had my fair share of nomads, and knew what to expect (generally a plague of some sort) but my food was high, my herbs were stocked and the labor is always welcome.
Patient Zero had scarlet fever, then proceeded to walk through every single citizen she possibly could on her way to the hospital, infecting each one. 20 infected, then 40, then 140, then the yellow scroll of death began on the information window. It was unstoppable, for you see, when a family dies, another family splits and moves into the vacant lot, and they don't bring their own firewood or food or ANYTHING, and then I didn't have enough to work my 276 fields, and couldn't get wood farmed to cut for fires and when I looked at the line graph, my population had halved and continued to fall. Oh, the humanity!
If I could suggest one thing, it is this:
Always save before you accept the nomads.
10/10, would welcome nomads again with open arms.

Five Nights at Freddy's is a refreshing take on the survival horror genre.  You work the night shift at a children's pizza restaurant akin to a Chuck-E-Cheese; however, that is where the similarities stop.  Fazbear's Pizza has a shady past, and a few "malfunctioning" animatronics seeking your inadvertent death.  You have to survive the nights with only your cameras, doors, lights, and quick click reactions.  Don't be too hasty or your limited supply of power will run out!
There are three unique aspects that make this a must play--the simple design/gameplay mechanics (you are stuck in a room--no escape just survival), sinister environment (camera features and sounds play with your sanity), and the constant suspense (you see them coming closer and CLOSER).
On the other hand, the jumpscares get tiresome and the gameplay repetitive, but that doesn't overpower the great aspects of the game.  I'm looking forward to the next installment.

BIoShock isn't really notable for its gameplay, which is pretty standard FPS fare (though seeing the physical effect a plasmid has on the environment and the NPCs is neat). No, what makes this game a masterpiece is environment, its attention to detail, and how it carefully weaves in the narrative. Before going further, I will say this: I like Tales games.  So from my perspective, a bad Tales game is still a decent game overall.  If you've played all the other Tales games, then play this one, and it'll scratch that jrpg itch.
While the combat and visuals are the best they've ever been, and the world is as expansive and full as ever, it did not strike me as a good Tales game.  The story was just too bland and straightforward.  I played all the way to the last boss, ran into the slightest roadblock of difficulty, then just dropped it.  I didn't even remotely care to know what happens.
Spoilers ahead, but ones you should know ahead of time:
I started on my journey like this: become the Shepherd, get stronger shepherd powers, purify hellions, kill Lord of Calamity.  After over 40 hours of waiting for the big twist, I: became the Shepherd, got stronger shepherd powers, purified hellions, killing Lord of Calamity.  Where's the twist?  Where's the part where seraphim are farming humans for Shepards or something?  Where's the part where a big dumb cycle of world-ending shenanigans gets revealed?  There's just nothing.  I understand the value in this kind of straightforward story, but the convoluted twist-filled story is what Tales games are known for.  It's so out-of-place here.
Decent gameplay, empty story.  Worth a play for Tales fans, but don't expect much.

A beautifully challenging set of puzzles. I especially like the graded scoring system. If you just want to spend a few minutes, you can look at the hint and complete the puzzle fairly quickly. More challenging is to get the gold bonus (usually a different method to the hint so you can work it out for yourself). Finally, for the ultimate challenge, try to beat or equal the online rating, which really tests your knowledge of the subtle nuances of the game, especially since the original game has been around for a year on a different platform than the PC version which was my first encounter with Terraform, so people have had time to come up with good ideas for high-scoring solutions. Some planets are so well designed, they have a great number of different solution methods, with some red herrings (like tools you don't need which mislead you and some obvious methods suggested by terrain which end up failing for a subtle reason). Okay, not EVERY planet is a work of art (some of the planets introducing asteroids are a bit perfunctory in comparison to the great depth of most levels) but a pretty large number are. I have not managed (yet!) to equal the online rating on quite a few of the puzzles, but any time I equal or beat it gives a real glow of satisfaction. Lateral thinking is needed for some of the best scores, and you need to keep an open mind and avoid making too many assumptions, so it's a real brain workout.
The only quibble I have is that the online ratings don't seem to be completely stable (the game allows me to upload a lower online rating than the original sometimes, which I now try to avoid doing) but hopefully that will be fixed soon.

I love epic AAA titles that take three full work-weeks to complete just as much as the next guy; but sometimes I also enjoy those short and simple games that are easy to digest after a long day.
is a great example of the latter. It has simple, straightforward mechanics with a pleasing, intimate art style. It is short and gratifyingly challenging without being too frustrating. And there is also an optional
which can be used to add a little dash of flavor to the experience.
The game is comprised of a small amount of short levels. Most of them won’t take long to beat. The puzzles involve simple two-dimensional movement which requires timing and precision. It is all very simplistic. But if you want to try out something a little different, you can enable
which will allow you to use your voice (via humming, whistling, or blowing into the microphone) to control the game. It’s kind of fun at first, but some of the harder levels require a lot of precision and it can be real difficult in
The hand-drawn artwork is also very nice.  It is a pleasing mix of intimate, curious, and casual. It isn’t the most refined or aweing art, but it is unique and full of character, and it fits the game well.
The last thing I’ll mention is that it is very short. To me, short games are great because I love variety and hate leaving things unfinished; but I know some people may have a problem with it, so be aware. Also, I generally try to not discuss price in my reviews, because everyone values a dollar differently depending on their lifestyle. But in this case I do want to say that I feel like the developers have priced this game reasonably considering its length. And so, like I suggested earlier: it is a nice, little game for those times you want something lightweight and intuitive. If that sounds like something you would be interested in, I would recommend you give
some consideration.

This... is not... Flatout.
The developer pitched this as a spiritual successor to Flatout but their vision of the franchise is very different than mine. As a diehard Flatout 2/UC fan I HIGHLY recommend this game... but don't go looking for FO staples such as ragdolls, mini games, nitro, or tracks with tons of stuff to smash into. What you should look for is a very deep and nuanced physical racing experience.
What Wreckfest does so brilliantly is the same thing that both FO1 and 2 did well: Deep semi-realistic driving that's easy to pick up and play but hard to master. Even at this early stage it is clear the finished product will be a finely tuned machine. Unlike most arcade racers you'll need to master the brake as much as you'll need to understand throttle control. You can feel the bumps and subtleties in the track. You can feel your car falling apart as it takes hits. And when you make contact with another car you can feel the heavy beasts smashing into each other. But as it currently stands the game is nearly undrivable on a 360 controller. There simply isn't any feedback telling you when you're about to lose control and when you DO lose control pretty much the only way to fix it is to come to a near stop (before you go calling me a noob I'm a top 1%er in Forza using a controller ;) ). At this point in development the cars are too difficult to drive to be arcade and not realistic enough to be a simulator. But as a huge physics update is due any week now all signs point up. I fully expect this games handling to land somewhere between GRID and Forza and avoid terrible handling games like The Crew or any of the Need for Speeds.
Now lets talk about the biggest draw of this game: The crashing. Just... wow. This physics engine puts GTA IVs to shame. Every little bump will leave a realistic dent in your car. Someone tapped your bumper? You'll see that bump the rest of the race but you'll drive on fine. Get t-boned at a crossing? Not only will you be feeling that in the handling for the rest of the race but wow does the damage look good and behave as you'd expect. It's also not yet where it needs to be though. Currently as your cockpit takes damage your driver will warp and bend and twist as well. Also cars can inexplicably take crippling damage very quickly. They also don't yet have a solution to bent hoods blocking the drivers view. But damn is it awesome watching twisted metal and broken glass fly everywhere!
Racing against AI is... frustrating. Currently player to AI car interactions are very one sided. If you happen to be where the AI wants to be you'll get shoved out of the way easily. If you want to bully an AI driver good luck, they're boulders. Unfortunately this makes Wreckfest, a game about crashing, the kind of game where you want to avoid contact at all costs. It's not all bad though. Watching the AI in front of you is very entertaining. Some are very good drivers and some are not. The carnage at corners is absolutely spectacular with 24 cars battling it out at once.
It's a completely different story online though. In player vs player collisions the cars behave exactly as you'd expect making contact a legit strategy. Lobbies are for up to 24 players and can get absolutely crazy. I don't play too much online so it's unfair for me to really judge it right now but as I understand it the MP is currently VERY bare bones.
The tracks in the game do what they intend to do. This is a game about banger racing and that's the exact theme you get with the tracks. They're short, they're dirty and they're the types of tracks you could see this sport happening on in real life. For me unfortunately this means the tracks are very boring for the most part. I feel like they've limited themselves too much by grounding the tracks in reality. Gone are the races through the canals, the mall and cities from FO2/UC and in there place are trees dirt and sand on wide and empty tracks. There are physics objects on the tracks to smash into and brake but they're all either barriers or out side the track very much unlike FO2/UC. That said I absolutely love the tried and true tarmac ovals and figure 8s. The 8 even has a jump crossing :D Also, despite the fact that I find the tracks to be mediocre for the most part that really isn't a bad thing. The layouts allow for plenty of brutal and physical racing which makes the otherwise boring tracks not matter at all. You're simply having too much fun driving and crashing to care. Currently there is a very small selection of tracks.
The cars also fit the banger racing theme perfectly. They're all the exact kind of muscle/broken down beaters you'd expect to see at your average derby. This does limit the variety of cars the game will ship with though. Don't expect to see anything new and DEFINITELY don't expect to see any exotic cars. Bugbear hasn't confirmed or denied if there will be trucks or busses in the game but the last I heard they didn't even have any refrence material for such vehicles. To me that makes it seem like there won't be trucks but that's nothing but a guess. There are currently only 5 cars but many more are planned. Not a huge amount but substantially more than we currently have.
The derbies are probably the best I've played in any game. That said, derbies aren't my thing and I haven't invested more than a few hours into them. As with racing the best strategy for winning at the moment is to avoid contact at all costs. Let the AI destroy themselves and prey on the weak. Not something you want in a game about wrecking. But the collisions are simply spectacular. It is so much fun just hitting other cars I could care less if I win or lose :P
As for game modes there currently is no career at all but one is planned for both online and offline. No idea how it's going to work. So basically you can either do single races/derbies on or offline. I know team derbies are planned but am not sure about other modes. I know that there will NOT be any mini games like in previous FOs.
The graphics are amazing. They're not the benchmark of racing games but they absolutely hold their own. The cars are beautiful, the scenery is lush and I have no issues with any of the textures. The crowd in the stands is flat and in a low speed game like this that kinda stands out unlike in Forza but it really isn't a big deal. Lighting is spectacular though it's highly unlikely we're going to get night races. Getting this game to 60 frames on max graphics will require a proper gaming rig. I have an AMD 8.0GHz 8 core and a GTX 760 with 8 gigs of ram and while the game mostly stays above 30 it will frequently dip much lower. Minimizing all the graphics setting results in a HUGE FPS boost so 2-3 year old rigs SHOULD be okay. That's what Bugbear is targeting at least.
This is a Early Access done right... nearly. Bugbear is a really great developer. They have a solid history of fairly bug free and very fun games that run on a wide range of systems. They're doing a pretty good job of keeping people at the official forum informed though until recently the info has been very disorganized. I know Bugbear needs to do a better job with communication and so do they. I really don't know why they don't post updates on Steam. That said these guys really do listen. They read EVERY post on the official forums and are very open to taking criticism and tweaking the game based on feedback. Many small features are working their way into the game because of community suggestions. These guys are new to EA but they are passionate about their project.

2. For the writing segments to use only one image of the character, or to have both images side by side and to have the drawn image stay on the screen until a button press. My video version.
Outlast is a Psychological Survival horror game developed and published by Red Barrel Games for the PC and in Q1 2014 for PS4. Red Barrels was founded by people who were involved in previous works such as Prince of Persia and Assassins Creed.
So how did this talent go to use within Outlast…
The player plays as a character called Miles Upshur, a freelance journalist, who received a tip about Mount Massive Asylum, the psychiatric hospital within Outlast, however it wasn’t stated what the tip-off consisted of or why he of all people got this tip-off.
Upon entering the halls of the Asylum you quickly realise that something has gone horribly wrong, with dead bodies scattered throughout the main hall and blood up and down the walls….
Miles has to figure out what when wrong within the Asylum.
Outlast is by far one of the best looking indie horror games on the market as of 2013, with its detailed environments and horrifying character models adds to the element of horror,   keeping in mind this is still an indie horror game. Not only are the graphics just impressive to look at but the shadows and lighting are also well presented which furthers the element of surprise.
With the inclusion of bloody footprints after walking in a blood pool got me really excited because that type of detail isn’t exactly seen in many games these days so it was a nice added bonus.
Although the game is mostly in the darkness you can clearly see were Red Barrel Games shines.
The game politely gives the player the use of a video camera which you can use to see in dark places or simply use the cameras night vision to help navigate the environment easier. However using the camera or nightvision drains the batteries extremely fast for some reason. Its ok though batteries are scattered throughout the world.
When Miles gets injured the game uses a health regeneration system so just stick to cover or hide for a while and you will be fine.
Miles is a defenceless human who can’t do anything but run away or hide from the enemies but that’s not to say the game has its scary moments mind you. Apart from some scripted events which cause miles to nudge enemies away from him the only means of escape is through the fear of death.
Miles can do all the normal game attributes like climbing ladders and vaulting over ledges but presents a fluid motion between both the running animation and vaulting mechanics which provide a satisfying feel when you evade your enemy successfully.
You as the player are also able to hide inside lockers, under beds or tables. Using any of these hiding methods still doesn’t mean you are safe as some enemies will search every room and under or inside objects to find you.
However there are a few sections within the game were you can exploit a crawl mechanic (in between 2 shelves) to easily evade enemies which made these areas feel a lot safer. Alongside the exploit came the mission objectives that require you to turn on generators which felt like the pace of the game had hit a stop while I fiddle with this meaningless objective.
Within Outlast every sound is extremely versatile in determining whether you will stay alive or be run down by a psychotic inmate that roams the halls. The music also plays a part in if you will get scared or not at the scripted jump scares within the game which I assure you there aren’t that many of..
All I can say about the soundtrack is that it’s beautiful to listen to, I found myself not even paying much attention to the environment sometimes were I would just simply be listening to the soundtrack and then get the♥♥♥♥♥♥scared out of me because I would get butt♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by an inmate..
Outlast past my expectations with flying colours however there were a few nit-picky moments were the game bogged down with the generator missions and exploiting the shelves made the experience dull.
If you could only go through the shelves once then if you tried to back track the enemy would break through the shelves to reach you then I could understand but since it could be easily exploited to the point where the enemy would just roam off and then you could come out and past them, I found quite annoying.
Being unable to defend myself game mentality of horror games these days seems to be the only way that horror seems viable yet if there were more enemies in one area and I could pack a wrench then I’d still be frightened but still be having fun.
With that being said the overall presentation of the game with the horror elements and story behind it.
Outlast gets a 7.5/1

The following review is for Red Orchestra 2 and Rising Storm. (both included when buying Rising Storm)
Red Orchestra 2 and its stand-alone expansion Rising Storm are World War II military First-person shooters with an emphasis on solid gameplay mechanics and gritty authenticity. While the two differ in gameplay, both are grounded in realism without being marred by unnecessary clunkiness. Both were developed by Tripwire Interactive, the studio that is probably best known for Killing Floor and the original Red Orchestra game. Much like Killing Floor, these games shine most in the way that they feature what are quite possibly the best shooting mechanics that you will find in any video game.
These games are by no means "dead" as some doom-and-gloom internet posters would have you beleive. Despite featuring a complex set of controls and being fairly unforgiving about deaths in multiplayer, the games do a great job of expressing that the multiplayer expirience is hard but fair. Perceptivness, tactical forsight, and team communication are always heavily rewarding for players willing to go the extra mile.
Much of the early criticism for Red Orchestra 2 by popular review sources and Metacritic mainly focus on the game's rough state at launch rather than the game you will be playing today. RO2 and RS have been greatly improved with the help of official patches and updates and even moreso with the help of the player community that is the backbone of the series.
Rising Storm offers a new and different expirience to that of Red Orchestra 2. While still featuring the original game's brutality and satisfying gun mechanics, rising storm features more asymetrical gameplay that is more rooted in fast-paced action than the base game. This stand-alone expansion is great for both veterans looking for something fun and different as well as new players that felt intimidated by the heavily punishing nature of RO2's multiplayer. Upon purchasing Rising Storm players will recieve a copy of Red Orchestra 2 if they do not already own it. Red Orchestra 2 owners will be able to play a limited version of Rising Storm and will also recieve a discount when buying the expansion.
These games are great for anyone looking for a First-Person shooter with solid gameplay mechanics. Red Orchestra 2 and Rising storm offer a great experience that rivals and even surpasses those offered by AAA FPS titles.*
*The games are to be appreciated on their own merits rather than to be used to boost one's own ego for not being part of the Call of Duty or Battlefield audience.

A Hat in Time was a bit different from what I expected gameplay wise, I though it would be more open world (or open area) but instead was more akin to mario 64 of various areas with selectable missions that slightly change the area's layout. The goal also being similar to mario games in that you're looking for timepieces that are essentially stars (with 40 in the game). There are 4 "worlds" though some are less of areas and more like linear levels. Even the world that is labeled "freeroam" is one of the most linear areas. Each area also comes with bonus "rift" levels where you find the rift in the world and try to complete the level. As for gameplay, you have a rediculous range of motion and can get from one place to a fairly far away place without touching the ground. You have a double jump, a mario 64 style dive/cancel, a homing attack, short vertical wall run and wall jump, as well as a "wind waker" grapple (and crawl) along with other utilities. The only thing is that with such a wide range of movement and the game being a 3D platformer, you're expected to make full use out of it which (along with the less then perfect camera) can sometime make it difficult to figure out which way you're expected to go (a few times, your best way to counter this is just not to underestimate the jumps you can make). The camera could definately use some work and if I had one peice of advice to give, it would be to turn off "camera assist" otherwise, once it starts turning on its own, you'll be forced to match it's movement with your jump angle which got me killed more times than I can count before checking to see if I could turn it off. It can also be a little hard to determine depth which can make certain jumps difficult. That all being said, once you grasp all the movement mechanics, the levels are fun and interesting with little puzzles here and there and some really interesting platforming mechanics with new things being introduced at a good pace.
Outside of the mechanical aspects, the game advertises as being cute as heck but heck doesn't even begin to describe the level of cuteness in the game. Similar to how you might this of "Nintendo polish", this game has little bits and peices to add to the cuteness to the character and the world. There were too many moments to count where the game just made me feel happy. The story it also very entertaining and funny (albiet a bit weird towards the end) and there are many levels that do different and neat things. The only thing is that the same levels after played, won't have the same effect after being experienced the first time thought that in no way means they won't still be fun, just not the same. Boss battles are also fun and interesting and can also be played over and over without losing their touch. The graphics are beautiful making exploring and looking for collectables just an overall enjoyable experience. The soundtrack is amazing and enhances the experience even more. I was sitting on the title screen like "I want to hit A but Ill just wait for the title music to finish it's loop". The area music perfectly suits the setting and the boss themes are epic and so fun to listen to. There are also a number of customization items that you can unlock with said collectables. If I were to recomend it to anybody, I would recomend it to anyone who likes fun, cute things, or is horribly depressed and needs some happiness in their life.

This game is aimed squarely at a generation of gamers that grew up with anthropomorphic duos and critically important shiny gold things. And boy howdy, does it deliver. I've been pining for a proper 3D platformer for years now, and, indeed, have wondered why it hasn't happened yet. But it's finally, *finally* here.
For those who don't really understand the collectathon genre, it's not really about the collecting. Mario 64 wasn't a game about collecting stars. What made it great (aside from being a novelty at the time due to pioneering several mechanics and concepts still used today) is losing yourself exploring the levels and slowly chewing through the game as you unlock things. The old adage holds true; it's about the journey, not the destination. Banjo-Kazooie expanded on this by adding lovable characters (eekum bokum), a real story, and a bunch more stuff to collect to unlock abilities, making you feel more powerful as you progress. A Hat in Time is a mashup of this, with a modern flare.
In short, 10/10 would hug Hat Kid again.

Along comes a pack of 143 nomads. One Hundred and Forty Three Nomads(!!!!) in this lovely little single file line to add to the gene pool and grow my population to numbers unseen! Fantastic game thus far. I was concerned about playing it until the story was assembled and the game was polished but the sandbox as it stands is highly playable. The long dark is a survival game that does not rely of zombies but puts the player in a terrain that requires scavenging. If you're lucky and skilled enough (every playthrough has variations to it and spawning is set at restart) you should be able to eventually depend on the wildlife for food and clothing.
Mindfulness to weather is one of the best contributions to gameplay thus far. I've squirrelled away days worth of food, water, and wood at a base with a fireplace only to step into a snow storm and get lost in the mountains. Gusts of wind and omenous clouds tell me to stay inside and work on repairing tools, patching clothing, and boiling more potable water for the next day's search.
Everyone will have their own strategy but regardless it is largely contingent upon what you have available. If you find a rifle and some rounds then hunting will be your best option. If you have flares, then stalking deer you can run into wolves could mean a free meal. If the wolf scares from the flare you've got food, warm clothing, and materials for trapping. This is not a gratuitously violent game. Tangles with wolves are no easy scenarios and has been the cause of restarts more than anything. Even when roaming with a rifle, every round counts and may mean the difference weeks down the road.
As an addition to this review I want to say these past months have seen a lot of development in the game. Three new maps, more streamlined HUD, harvestable herbs and fungi for food and medicine, new items to find and craft, new animals. With every addition, bugs are smoothed out before I find them and the dev team is on their ish.
The story mode hasn't even been put out yet but the sandbox feels like its own game as it is. I've had a lot of luck with Early Access choices, this is one of the shining examples of a game worth supporting.

Original review:
It seems "not recommended" reviews get downvoted to hell but I'll try my best to explain ASAP.
Early Access review as of early January 2015:
TLD has a very outstanding art style, reminiscent of Telltale's Walking Dead games, and is largely a PVE scavenging game. There's unfortunately very little motivation to go very far as it is. There's very little crafting, no building, and you're not so much 'lost in the wild' as you are just moving from house to house with some stuff in between, scavenging.
I realize it's in alpha and there's more to come...but at the moment there isn't much there. However...what IS there is very good, the art style, UI, the world and levels, the mechanics behind the survival aspects like hunger and warmth, etc. There just isn't too much level interaction, creativity, and a lot of just waiting around. Lots of waiting. You don't actually gather wood, you wait. Cooking food? Wait. Sleeping, crafting, scavenging.. is all waiting.
"Not recommended" is NOT the same thing as "this is a bad game" or "I don't like it." It's just at this particular moment, I wouldn't say there's enough in there to really get it. Will edit my review as time goes on and mechanics change. I like what there is so far, and it looks promising.

I woke up in the middle of a blizzard, freezing and disoriented I looked around me, only able to see a few feet ahead in any direction. As I started walking forward I questioned myself, did I choose the right direction? All around me are trees and snow, wind and doubt, in the distance I see a shape taking form, a sign and guard rails. As I get closer I see the remnants of a road winding up a hill on my left, the wind is getting stronger and I can tell im moving slower, im taking a gamble there is shelter at the top of this hill. As I clear the top of the hill I see an outpost, 30 – 50 feet in the air atop a winding red staircase.
Struggling to make it to the top of the stair I fall through the outpost’s door and into one small cramped abandoned rangers post. Rifle on the table, 5 shells on the floor, some kindling by the stove and an energy bar. I lit a small fire in the stove, but without proper clothing I never really warmed up. Taking some snow from outside I melted it on the stove, but before I could get it to boil the fire went out. I ate the energy bar and grabbed the rifle, made my way back into the howling wind, down the stairs and started descending down the hill.
Im starting to freeze to death, no food, no shelter, no heat, it doesn’t look good. I follow the road heading away from the outpost atop the hill, the wind starts to die down and I can see further into the distance now. Round a small hill to my left and see a building in the distance built into a mountain, ive lost track of the road, lost under the snow, I head to the building. Under the snow I see something red, I get closer and see it is a dead fox, half eaten, mostly frozen. I have no tools, nothing to cut the meat, I have to abandon the carcass and pray there is food in the building up ahead.
I open the giant metal door, this is a hydroelectric dam, empty and abandoned, dark and silent.  My body is going into shock, I have no food, no water, no way of building a fire. My only hope is to find a furnace and pray there is wood nearby to burn. As I walk into the main room coming through the front door I can see hulking machinery, up ahead, file cabinets to my right, and stairs going down to my left. It reminds me of something out of a horror movie, pitch black with only light from a small window, something is lighting up the stairs, beckoning me. Im dying, I can hear the wind outside starting to pick back up, I head down the stairs in a last ditch effort to find heat, to find what the light is coming from below. I take 3 steps and see a shadow at the bottom of the stairs, it’s a wolf, and it guarding something, meat… I pull out my rifle and before I can take aim the wolf lunges at me, I cant fight back, im too weak. I die on the floor of the building.

Alright, so first of all, i will be comparing this to "Tales of Vesperia (360 Version)" quite alot since thats the first Tales game i played and its known as one of the best tales games, So prepare to die, Eggbear!
Tales of Zestiria.
Where to begin....
The story is pretty good, its a bit generic with the whole "Chosen one" saving the world from "Evil" concept, but overall it was quite good.
The main character isn't as good as Yuri Lowell from Vesperia, but i still quite liked Sorey (I just hate how his name is pronounced, i expected it to be Sorei, its So-Ray..
Graphics were pretty good, the artstyle was nice, the animated cutscenes (not the ones that are In-Engine) were beautiful like they always are, i will say however, Vesperia's artstyle was a bit nicer, felt warmer, Cities had a distinct feel to them....
Gameplay includes lots of mashing buttons (Its best to not randomly mash tho, good to learn what all the skills do and when to use them so you can quickly mash out a 4 hit combo that the enemy is weak to) and also alot of talking to people or just watching a scene.
I was surprised how much death was in this game compared to Vesperia, in Vesperia its implied that you do kill every monster and most humanoid enemies aswell, but you don't really see them die, get stabbed, cut or bleed, They would usually just fade away, where as in this game i did see alot more of that wich was a bit diffrent than what i was used to in a Tales game.
Game length: An average playthrough takes between 40-60 hours, can take more if you farm alot, I did most sidequests on my first playthrough, as far as i know i missed one or two, i also skipped the EX-Dungeon as i didn't wanna spend 5 hours at 6 AM running around with LV 70 Enemies.
Characters: The main characters and notable characters you encounter throughout the game are well designed, pretty well voiceacted (though Mikleo in the first 4th of the game is a bit hilarious) and they all have a good chemistry between eachother, i dont like the whole Alisha issue however and that did sour me a bit on the character on a whole.... so i made her wear a goofy moustache and large goofy glasses.
-Main Character is pretty generic, he however loves archeology, so thats cool.
-Mikleo (Meebo) is pretty simmilar to Sorey, but he's alot funnier as he gets annoyed easily
-Pun-Master Lailah... She likes Puns... i dont...
-Edna, Rita without any emotion, and lacks tidal wave spamming.
-Dezel, obessed with revenge, has shark teeth (must be annoying to keep that sharp)
-Zaveid, Exactly what i'd imagine a young Raven to act like. (I know Zaveid is not young, he looks young however)
-Alisha, I WAS ROBBED OF MY SPEAR USER!!!!!!
-Rose, You'd think a human with knives would be better than a Dog with a knife... she's not.

Combat: I am very used to the Vesperia system, where aslong as you learnt a very easy system, you could combo almost any move into another forever and just keep doing damage forever aslong as you had enough MP (MP? forgot what Vesperia used) aswell as the overlimit system. Zestiria's combat system is extremely annoying at first, it will take you some time to learn it, you get punished if you try to just mash random attacks, it wont work well unless you play on Simple.
Equipment System: So this section would normally not exist, its an RPG, it has items and stuff, what did you expect?
Well..... Zestiria screws with equipment quite alot...
In Vesperia, if you ever entered a new area there was a high chance that a new item you found was an instant upgrade or sidegrade, where as in Zestiria.... gear has its default stats... and randomised skills on the items, and an annoying system to combine skills.
If you're the kind of person that loves to read guides and look at spreadsheets and charts just to become the most powerful... you will love this system... I didnt, I would have liked the Vesperia system of "This item is the best, its always the best" and not "Hey... go farm 1000 items just to START making the ultimate weapon, then do it again for all your characters"
Conclusion: Zestiria is a great 50-70 hour game that can possibly turn into a 400 + hours game depending on how much farming and how many ng+'s you wanna do.

Amazing!
Before I get into detail, I want to view this game from two different angles and review them seperately.
Learning:
This just blew me away! Within 10 hours of gaming split across two days I was able to master all the hiragana and learn some basic vocabulary. I spoke some japanese phrases beforehand but never bothered learning how to write so this was totally new to me.
I found the lessons to be very well paced and never felt over- nor underwhelmed.
Gaming:
Likely made with some version of the RPG Maker, so adjust your expectations accordingly.
I always liked the RPG Maker games so this was totally fine to me.
The graphics are nicely done and quite fitting. Sound and music are your typical 8-bit retro RPG sounds, so don't expect an amazing OST.
The story, while absolutely sufficient for this kind of game, is the only weak point. A very very basic RPG story that tries to take two interesting turns, but those are easily predictable. For this kind of game I don't see this as a bad thing though because you can easily take a break and absorb what you've learned without wondering all day how the story will continue. If the story was too good you might end up rushing to the finish in one session (which is totally possible) and end up with way too much to learn.
Overall I can only recommend this game to anyone who wants to learn hiragana and I'll definitely buy the Katakana sequel.
