Pixal Privateers. I love the Pixel Artstyle thus far, the way things glow and the User Interface is stunning. Great inventory mechanics and looting options. Can't wait to play more, I'll update this review in a week or so. Thus far I recommend it! This is what happens when devs get the time they need to develop a game before releasing a pre-alpha. More of the "when it's ready" mentality. Very polished!
--------------------------------------------------
[Update 1]
About 10 hours in and still stand by what I said. Thus far The inventory, mass, and fuel systems are very polished. and the missions you go on just don't seem to get stale. There's always something on the planet that makes you smile or think about how you want to proceed.
The Loot:
At first glance I was going to say that I "think the loot style to be like Diablo" - however, I find it much more accurate to say that the loot in this game is far more similar to games like Borderlands with random properties, damage types, common, uncommon, rare, Legendary, Ancient - It's great! And the time-intervals in which you find Legendary or Ancient weapons is very well spaced out, it doesn't make you ever feel "OP" by dropping tons, but just enough to keep you above the edge at most times.
The loot mechanics and style in this game has varying *damage types* (just like in borderlands), ranges, cooldown rate, reload time, magazine size, and even a physical 'weight' attribute which gives incentive for light-armor style classes to throw a few spare points into Strength(increasing that Privateer's carry capacity) for the purpose of carrying perhaps heavier gear or 2-handed weapons.
----- That ends Update 1 -----
I'll try and give a more in depth review in regards to "Quality of Life" aspects of the game in my next update. I'm still recommending this game highly especially with the gracious price tag of $15. :)

Wow. I thought I Was going to hate this game, and I can really understand why some will. This is not everyone's cup of tea. First thing first, I came in to this with no expectations, And no research on it, SO i was suprised with it. Also  I only played with a full group of dedicated friends, And Im certain this enhances the experience as we discover and discuss everything togheter, And we bring crew members that we build to support eachother and make nice combos.
First let's talk about the good things.
- Combat looks visually nice, Everything has this bit graphic to it but still you can clearly see what is what and there's an interesting artwork and visual layout on planets and ships so far.
- Customisation, There's a ton of weapons outfits that looks nice and feel nice to use. You can make some interesting characters. You can't change body appearence but you can rename them. yet there armor covers most of them so it don't matter.
- The story, Wow.. It's so simple but somehow it keept me interested, As It's all random generated on where things happen it feelt nice whenever we found a base belonging to one of the antagonist and small dialogues broke out where we could vote on our responses as a group. There's also a pause of 10 sec in each part in the dialogues so if someone tries to skip it you still get 10-15 sec to finish reading it. It jumps only when everyone skips it.
- Gear, Holy crap there's allot of them, weapons armors, tech. Allot to find and use.
- Random encounters and Cameos. Damm we fought a race based on SLENDER MAN!! WTf? Awesome but wtf?
-Cameos, As a Sci-FI fan you will see Star trek, Star wars, Stargate and many other cameos return for you to laugh at.
They are more but Thos are things that stood out to me.
Bad stuff?
- It get's repedetiv quick and sometime you can go through many planets without anything interesting happening and all you do is kill enemies. I can see that becoming boring.
- Combat, It's well It's ok but theres only 5 classes with 3 abillities each and as a 4 player group we got 2 characters each. thats 6 abillities. Sure there are talents, Stats, Special gear with active functions and Tech to develop that give you more to do but in terms of tactic there's not much but SHOOT ( Click on ) Everything until it's dead.
- Story, It has it's weak part and can come off as pretty poor and obvious at some points.
-  It takes it self a bit to unserious, I guess some will love that but It breaks immersion more then i would like.
Verdict: Recommended = I think this is a good game so far, My opinion may change as i dig deeper in to it. But I can see many people with a good group of friends enjoying this. It's very casual to play. It keept me going so far. I fear it may get repedetiv and that you won't advance with such interest to keep one coming back for more. But so far It has not had that problem. This will not be a game for everyone And If your planning to go Solo I would not myself, As that would get boring quick. But hey.. Try yourself. 2 hours is more then enough to get a feel of the game and the price tag is not so high.

After the disappointing sequel to Amnesia, it was time to play a game that lives up to the genre Horror/Survival. Luckily there was Halloween sale on Steam and this game was put in the basket.
The game in a nutshell: you are a reporter with a hand camera as a deadly weapon. You want to investigate an asylum where supposedly experiments were performed on the nut jobs locked in there. Getting in is a piece of cake, but getting out, that's what the whole game is about.
The macabre atmosphere is overwhelming at start. You continuously look through the lens of you camera, because it is equipped with night vision. This green/black tones add to the darkness of your environment, making it easy to poop your pants whenever a freak comes dangling from the sealing or start chasing you in a hall way. But in the end, this scary stuff also loses its effect if you are being chased around for the umpteenth time and all you want is the chase to be over and continue.
Nonetheless, a great addition to the Horror/Survival genre and let's hope the Outlast 2, which is currently in the making, continues along this path.
Edit: just finished the Whistleblower DLC. Nice addition to the game, but nothing special. Look at it as a Blue Shift to Outlast.

Outlast is a Psychological Survival horror game developed and published by Red Barrel Games for the PC and in Q1 2014 for PS4. Red Barrels was founded by people who were involved in previous works such as Prince of Persia and Assassins Creed.
So how did this talent go to use within Outlast…
The player plays as a character called Miles Upshur, a freelance journalist, who received a tip about Mount Massive Asylum, the psychiatric hospital within Outlast, however it wasn’t stated what the tip-off consisted of or why he of all people got this tip-off.
Upon entering the halls of the Asylum you quickly realise that something has gone horribly wrong, with dead bodies scattered throughout the main hall and blood up and down the walls….
Miles has to figure out what when wrong within the Asylum.
Outlast is by far one of the best looking indie horror games on the market as of 2013, with its detailed environments and horrifying character models adds to the element of horror,   keeping in mind this is still an indie horror game. Not only are the graphics just impressive to look at but the shadows and lighting are also well presented which furthers the element of surprise.
With the inclusion of bloody footprints after walking in a blood pool got me really excited because that type of detail isn’t exactly seen in many games these days so it was a nice added bonus.
Although the game is mostly in the darkness you can clearly see were Red Barrel Games shines.
The game politely gives the player the use of a video camera which you can use to see in dark places or simply use the cameras night vision to help navigate the environment easier. However using the camera or nightvision drains the batteries extremely fast for some reason. Its ok though batteries are scattered throughout the world.
When Miles gets injured the game uses a health regeneration system so just stick to cover or hide for a while and you will be fine.
Miles is a defenceless human who can’t do anything but run away or hide from the enemies but that’s not to say the game has its scary moments mind you. Apart from some scripted events which cause miles to nudge enemies away from him the only means of escape is through the fear of death.
Miles can do all the normal game attributes like climbing ladders and vaulting over ledges but presents a fluid motion between both the running animation and vaulting mechanics which provide a satisfying feel when you evade your enemy successfully.
You as the player are also able to hide inside lockers, under beds or tables. Using any of these hiding methods still doesn’t mean you are safe as some enemies will search every room and under or inside objects to find you.
However there are a few sections within the game were you can exploit a crawl mechanic (in between 2 shelves) to easily evade enemies which made these areas feel a lot safer. Alongside the exploit came the mission objectives that require you to turn on generators which felt like the pace of the game had hit a stop while I fiddle with this meaningless objective.
Within Outlast every sound is extremely versatile in determining whether you will stay alive or be run down by a psychotic inmate that roams the halls. The music also plays a part in if you will get scared or not at the scripted jump scares within the game which I assure you there aren’t that many of..
All I can say about the soundtrack is that it’s beautiful to listen to, I found myself not even paying much attention to the environment sometimes were I would just simply be listening to the soundtrack and then get the♥♥♥♥♥♥scared out of me because I would get butt♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by an inmate..
Outlast past my expectations with flying colours however there were a few nit-picky moments were the game bogged down with the generator missions and exploiting the shelves made the experience dull.
If you could only go through the shelves once then if you tried to back track the enemy would break through the shelves to reach you then I could understand but since it could be easily exploited to the point where the enemy would just roam off and then you could come out and past them, I found quite annoying.
Being unable to defend myself game mentality of horror games these days seems to be the only way that horror seems viable yet if there were more enemies in one area and I could pack a wrench then I’d still be frightened but still be having fun.
With that being said the overall presentation of the game with the horror elements and story behind it.
Outlast gets a 7.5/1

Melee-focused action games have spent years enacting the fantasy of engaging in armed combat, fortunately sparing us the hours of rigorous training and resolve it takes to actually do so in real life. But Pixel Privateers, Ubisoft's third-person weapon-based arena combat game, is different from other melee-focused action games, like Dark Souls or Dynasty Warriors. Its combat system is simple on the surface, but executing its more advanced tactics requires a patient mind, as well as an understanding of its deliberate pacing. There are not many games quite like For Honor; it's an incredibly entertaining fighter that's satisfying both in single and multiplayer, even despite the narrative flaws of its story mode.
Its fantasy medieval world is populated by three of history's most iconic warrior classes: knights, vikings, and samurai. Regardless of which faction you choose to play as, Pixel Privateers challenges you to restrain yourself and uphold self-control in the face of strenuous conflict. The elegance of its combat is at times awe-inspiring, easily pulling you into the euphoric highs of a well-deserved victory, where your patience was maintained and your reflexes were on point.
I recommend this game.

I've been back and forth on this review. Throughout the day, and through running arguments with fans of the game, I have come to ask "Was I wrong about SuperHot? Did I simply not appreciate its genius? Have I been letting a bad experience partially related to mobile hardware ruin my opinion of an otherwise sound game?"
The answer is no.
The reason I cannot reccomend superhot is simple. It is a lazy product, especially at its base pricetag of 25 dollars.
- Combat is one dimensional. Your arsenal consists of 3 samey guns and a melee attack, to be used on one basic enemy type, using two AI scripts. All guns shoot slow bullets with overlarge hitboxes that kill enemies wherever they hit them. Combat itself just boils down "click on the nearest enemy." There's no strategy, risk/reward, or anything else, because the only thing that makes enemies remotely dangerous is proximity.
- The presentation is bland and empty. While visually functional, which is extremely important and should be lauded, there was zero meaningful artistic effort put into this game. Yes, the polygon men shatter and ragdoll nicely, but what does this mean to the narrative, the world? Nothing. The story as well is a vapid copypasta of late 90's cyber-angst so lazy I quit 60% of the way through the game and just looked it up on wikipedia. I was still disappointed.
- The playtesting was lackluster. Bullet on bullet collissions, a cool idea on paper, happen so often they become a frustration. I didn't even play a full hour and had it happen to me 5 times. It happened so often that I started to hate it happening, and that's too often. If enemies were actively shooting my bullets down, I might credit it as some modicum of AI intelligence, but no, all were just stupid accidents resulting from center-of-mass shots on enemies that were shooting back. But if this is bad, then level hitboxing is even worse. I had a bullet disappear in midair because it hit an invisible corner, and it was a perfect shot too. You're telling me they spent two and a half years on barely 150 minutes worth of content and couldn't polish the collision?
Really, at the end of the day, it doesn't feel like SuperHotTeam even tried when they made this game. Two and a half years ago, SuperHot was a proof-of-concept demo being debuted at 7 day FPS Challenge. Today, it is still a proof-of-concept demo that now goes for 25 dollars. Maybe when they decide to make an actual game it'll be worth it, but for now take your money and go buy a game from a developer who cares.

Here's what I'll say: I beat this game under two hours. Meaning, if I so chose I could get my ten dollars back and be left with this game's experience.
But I won't.
This game managed to invoke a profound sense of loneliness, and somehow let me relate to Coda without ever knowing a single thing about them, except for their work.
If a game can make me feel sincere empathy towards a character that I never knew for sure was fictional or not then that means there was a powerful delivery somewhere in there.
So, simply put, this is a 10 dollar art piece. If you like art, buy this game. Unlikely you'll regret it.
If that's something you don't care for, move along. Or maybe try it still, you never know.
After all, it can be beaten in less than two hours. Up to you to decide if it was worth it or not.

End of 2017 Update:
Wintermute: After much time spent in Survival, I finally played through the first two episodes of story mode.  10/10: I was quite skeptical of story mode, to be honest. I thought it would be lame and detract from the unparalleled survival mode experience. Well, the opposite is true. Wintermute is very fun.  Highlights:
1. It's arcade-like compared to Survival, but it works! Regenerating ammo, forced paths, and unavoidable animal fights sacrifce realism for gameplay, but it is fun!
2. There are very few NPCs, and that's nice. Too many games have 100s of NPCs that get lost, having single digit NPCs makes each important. I suggest stressing the importance of "Trust" more.
3. Realism is sacrificed too much when fighting the Old Bear. "Stand in until you see the white of his eyes!"? Really? No one has ever survived being mauled 5 times by a bear - not even the Revenant. Actual strat is to find unclimable terrain and snipe.
4. Keep it up!
SURVIVAL:
I like most of the updates. Major thoughts:
1. Your "odds computer" is broken. I missed 10 times in a row on 75% fire - maybe I'm the lottery loser, but more likely you need to fix your randomization algorithm.
2. Water system still kills believability. How about "containers" mechanic... Also, why do I still get food poisoning form pristine melted snow yet toilet water is like Evion?
3. Is the wolf-bait mechanic realistic? I kill them like fish in a barrel.
4. Caloric store makes no sense. we need "fat" or "reserve" or whatever. You  should feast on meat to stock up, and then be able to survive for WEEKS without food.  I suggest "Fat Reserve" mechanic.
5. Suggest to replace "Cabin Fever" with "Sanity" bar. "Fun" or "Interesting" activivities add to sanity. Sitting inside or getting attacked etc reduce. The most fun some people have is doing something intersting indoors (making a bearskin coat, eg).
6. 3 animal coats, and not hat? Please, let's make a hat from animal skin! Also, melee weapon?
Faithful Cartographer Update:
Fantastic Sandbox Update! Oh how I love this this game.  Almost 365 days in on Interloper and here are my thoughts on the latest version:
Pro:
1. I can finally pick up rabbits! The rock-throwing mechanic is great, though I lose a little piece of soul every time a snap Mr. Fuzzy's neck - survival of the fittest... And the quartering command is a great way to appease (silence) those asking to pick up deer.
2. "Scent" is a good mechanic. Still needs to be tweaked. Why don't animals like my pile of 20kg of rotting meat, but the second I pick it up, a million wolves descend upon me like Wargs in LOR?
3. Mapping is interesting, but tedious.  It's not advantageous in Interloper and is an end-game activity. Also, It would be greatly improved if you marked the map with an X or crosshair in the exact spots in which you mapped.

Fantastic game thus far. I was concerned about playing it until the story was assembled and the game was polished but the sandbox as it stands is highly playable. The long dark is a survival game that does not rely of zombies but puts the player in a terrain that requires scavenging. If you're lucky and skilled enough (every playthrough has variations to it and spawning is set at restart) you should be able to eventually depend on the wildlife for food and clothing.
Mindfulness to weather is one of the best contributions to gameplay thus far. I've squirrelled away days worth of food, water, and wood at a base with a fireplace only to step into a snow storm and get lost in the mountains. Gusts of wind and omenous clouds tell me to stay inside and work on repairing tools, patching clothing, and boiling more potable water for the next day's search.
Everyone will have their own strategy but regardless it is largely contingent upon what you have available. If you find a rifle and some rounds then hunting will be your best option. If you have flares, then stalking deer you can run into wolves could mean a free meal. If the wolf scares from the flare you've got food, warm clothing, and materials for trapping. This is not a gratuitously violent game. Tangles with wolves are no easy scenarios and has been the cause of restarts more than anything. Even when roaming with a rifle, every round counts and may mean the difference weeks down the road.
As an addition to this review I want to say these past months have seen a lot of development in the game. Three new maps, more streamlined HUD, harvestable herbs and fungi for food and medicine, new items to find and craft, new animals. With every addition, bugs are smoothed out before I find them and the dev team is on their ish.
The story mode hasn't even been put out yet but the sandbox feels like its own game as it is. I've had a lot of luck with Early Access choices, this is one of the shining examples of a game worth supporting.

It is with a heavy heart that I must downvote this game. However, I feel a little backstory is important in order to justify this opinion, so I'll give you the whole story. TL;DR at the end.
Dungeon Defenders was possibly one of my top games of all time. I bought it off of Humble Bundle, so for 7 bucks I got hundreds of dollars worth of game for 7 bucks, which is what got me hooked. IMO it was a flawless tower defence game with shooter mechanics that was all too new to me. I played this game almost religiously with my brothers, and we had such an amazing time. Sure, the game had some pretty interesting bugs, but it was always ok with me because it felt so rewarding to FINALLY finish that really high level mission on hard, or to FINALLY complete that challenge and get some sweet loot.
I was following the pre-alpha of dungeon defenders 2, back when the game was going to be a MOBA. That cracked me up and disappointed me because I wanted an actual sequel to Dungeon Defenders, and this wasn't really that. Eventually Trendy scrapped the idea and went back to making an actual sequel and I couldn't have been more excited. Everything was going smoothly, until suddenly Dungeon Defenders Eternity came out.
I had no knowledge of this whatsoever, so I was pleased when I read the description. I was thinking to myself "cool they fixed some of the bugs and reworked it a bit. I'll spend the money on it." but what I got was a disaster. Forced online interractions, slow loading times, few possible private connections, a terrible server, a redone inventory system that to this day makes so sense to me (if it ain't broke don't break it, right???) and the game just felt like a total flop to me. It was OK, because I had hopes for DD2. I was hoping it would still be a true sequel to 1.
But it just wasn't. They literally released Eternity without telling anyone, and then took what DD2 WAS going to be, and just changed it based off of Eternity. I didn't know a single person who was pleased with DD:E and suddenly DD2 was changed to match it. The game feels so riddled with microtransactions, doesn't let me use multiple characters I want to use unless I BUY THEM (my favorite thing in 1 was using a wide variety of towers and testing what works, and leveling characters based off of the playstyle I enjoyed.) Tower numbers were reduced, hero abilities had a seperate mana bar (still doesn't make much sense to me) and the game just didn't have the same fun feel that 1 did so well. I've tried again and again to come back and play this game, but through all the unplayable bugs, like the fact that I have to practically uninstall steam every time I want to update the game because they STILL haven't fixed the family sharing issue that makes the game unplayable.
TL;DR: This game is not DD1, so don't expect something like it. I don't think original fans such as myself will be pleased, and it would take an overhaul to make it worth in my eyes.

Brilliant or Pretentious?
"This game is unlike any I have ever played". An over-used, hyperbolic statement that frequently appears in headlines and reviews for games that innovate in some meaningful way. We all roll our eyes when we read it being used yet again... however, I simply cannot think of any other way to describe this game.
• Publisher: Everything Unlimited Ltd.
• Developer: Everything Unlimited Ltd.
• Platforms: PC (Reviewed)
_________________________________
I never played The Stanley Parable. Not because I wasn't interested, or because I didn't have time, but because I... just didn't play it. I realize now that was a huge mistake, and I missed out on a game I would have likely adored (it's on my wish list now!). However, I thankfully did not miss the boat for The Beginner's Guide. This time, I wasn't late to the party, and I have to say, from the feedback the game has gotten, I gather that this is a far more interesting party. This is not to say Davey Wreden's "The Beginner's Guide" is a better game than The Stanley Parable, but a much more interesting one; primarily because of the conversations it has started.
Understand that what I can write here is very limited. To tell you about the game, it's premise, and story would be to spoil the entire experience. Instead, I want to tell you the impact the game had on me.
I started out genuinely intrigued. The game begins on a very fun note, almost like you're hanging out with a friend as he makes a game. Towards the middle of the hour and a half experience, the game almost got a tear out of me. It touched me on a very emotional level, and had me deeply invested. Then towards the end, I became worried, and ultimately angry. I thought about writing a review right then and there, but to do that I feel, would have colored the review in an unfair way; so I decided to wait until the end of the day.
I'm ultimately glad I did. I realize that what angered me initially actually impressed and satisfied me in the end. This is a game I immediately wanted to share with my friends; to see how they'd react. I even thought about having my parent (who does not enjoy games) have a go at it. It's a game that makes you think, feel, and reflect; when's the last time any AAA, or even an indie game made you do that? Journey was the last game that resonated with me in such a way, but in The Beginner's Guide, the emotional impact is more explicit.
The Beginner's Guide is a very philosophical experience. One that tackles heavy topics like "What makes us motivated to do the things we do? How do our actions influence other's actions? Why do we not pursue our dreams like we know we should?". It's heavy stuff for sure, and it pushes the boundaries of what games can do, and the kinds of stories they can tell.
Conclusion:
When I was in the middle of the game, I was prepared to give this title my "Game of the Year" award. Yes; even beating out MGSV, Bloodborne, and Arkham Knight. Upon completing it, I've chilled the hell out about it, and even after my initial anger, I still consider it a contender. Some people have reviewed the game calling it pretentious, self-indulgent trash, while others have praised it for obliterating the lines between games and art (it made Jim Sterling write an emotional biography about his childhood for Christ's sake!).
I think both of those sentiments have some merit. It's a game you'll likely come away either loving or hating. I did both myself, and that's ultimately a part of why I like it so much in hindsight. I'm a guy who typically avoids "Walking Simulators" and I can say with certainty, I've never been on the edge of my seat like I was playing this in ANY shooter or action game. What Mr. Wreden has done here is infinitely intriguing to me, and I hope he continues to challenge us like this. It's not your typical game, and that's what makes it so special.

First the bad news:
If you're looking for a traditional JRPG, there are far better alternatives out there in terms of story, gameplay and animation quality. Both input methods (keyboard and controller) are cumbersome and there's no option to rebind any buttons or keys. The battles are highly repetitive and you'll need some old school notebook (the paper kind) and a pen in order to really get something out of it.
Sounds like a lot of negative points right? So why do i still recommend this?
Because this game delivers what it advertises. It's teaching you a pretty complex language in a fun way, by going step by step and repeating the important parts often enough to keep them in your head. You're not only taught the writing system Hiragana along with the pronunciation of the characters but also basic conversational skills, important words and a bit of japanese culture. And the rudimentary RPG style is an additional motivation to keep going. "Just five more battles until i can afford that new sword" means that you voluntarily repeat a lesson 5 times more. And no matter what "wholesome" or "natural" approaches to language learning might say, practice is what makes you perfect.
Keep in mind though that this will only teach you one of the three writing systems. If you really want to learn japanese, this can only be complimentary to real language lessons (online or in class).

A game that is just simply a fun sandbox to mess around in.  A true sandbox, if you will.
A huge improvement from the original Just Cause in pretty much every department.  This is a game all about explosions and messing with physics (through the use of the grappling hook/tether), in a beautiful and huge island-world.
If what you are looking for in this game is a good story, with good acting, and meaningful quests then forget it.  It is just as I said above: explosions and physics.
The game can be quite repetitive.  If you played games with similar "zone capturing" mechanics--games such as Red Faction Guerilla and FarCry 3--and you found that particular part of the game to be a chore and ultimately boring, then it would probably be the case that you would not like Just Cause 2, since the meat of the game involves you capturing settlements (and there are many, many settlements to capture).
Despite it's repetitiveness, however, I still found the game fun, in the same way that I found Red Faction Guerilla and FarCry 3 to be fun.  It isn't necessarily the "zone capturing" that is fun, but actually the freedom that the game lends you to be creative in the way you choose to capture those zones.  You can be straightfoward and effecient by using your arsenal of guns, or you could be silly and use your grapple and objects.  The game just gives you a great sense of freedom to be creative and experiment with silly tactics, and that is what I feel is it's greatest strength.
(... and it is also very pretty)

I've been back and forth on this review. Throughout the day, and through running arguments with fans of the game, I have come to ask "Was I wrong about SuperHot? Did I simply not appreciate its genius? Have I been letting a bad experience partially related to mobile hardware ruin my opinion of an otherwise sound game?"
The answer is no.
The reason I cannot reccomend superhot is simple. It is a lazy product, especially at its base pricetag of 25 dollars.
- Combat is one dimensional. Your arsenal consists of 3 samey guns and a melee attack, to be used on one basic enemy type, using two AI scripts. All guns shoot slow bullets with overlarge hitboxes that kill enemies wherever they hit them. Combat itself just boils down "click on the nearest enemy." There's no strategy, risk/reward, or anything else, because the only thing that makes enemies remotely dangerous is proximity.
- The presentation is bland and empty. While visually functional, which is extremely important and should be lauded, there was zero meaningful artistic effort put into this game. Yes, the polygon men shatter and ragdoll nicely, but what does this mean to the narrative, the world? Nothing. The story as well is a vapid copypasta of late 90's cyber-angst so lazy I quit 60% of the way through the game and just looked it up on wikipedia. I was still disappointed.
- The playtesting was lackluster. Bullet on bullet collissions, a cool idea on paper, happen so often they become a frustration. I didn't even play a full hour and had it happen to me 5 times. It happened so often that I started to hate it happening, and that's too often. If enemies were actively shooting my bullets down, I might credit it as some modicum of AI intelligence, but no, all were just stupid accidents resulting from center-of-mass shots on enemies that were shooting back. But if this is bad, then level hitboxing is even worse. I had a bullet disappear in midair because it hit an invisible corner, and it was a perfect shot too. You're telling me they spent two and a half years on barely 150 minutes worth of content and couldn't polish the collision?
Really, at the end of the day, it doesn't feel like SuperHotTeam even tried when they made this game. Two and a half years ago, SuperHot was a proof-of-concept demo being debuted at 7 day FPS Challenge. Today, it is still a proof-of-concept demo that now goes for 25 dollars. Maybe when they decide to make an actual game it'll be worth it, but for now take your money and go buy a game from a developer who cares.

Darkness Within 2: The Dark Lineage is a disappointment. Not just in the sense that it’s not as good as Darkness Within 1: In Pursuit Of Loath Nolder, but also in that it actively squanders the potential of the first game, and is mechanically inferior.

The biggest change is that DW2 is a 3D exploration game rather than a point and click game. The player has full control over protagonist Howard Loreid. He can freely walk, run, jump, crouch, and manipulate certain movable objects. That all sounds fine and dandy, but it’s apparent quite early into the game how little these changes add to the experience. Howard can explore locations freely, but the locations themselves often feel as small as, or smaller than the areas of the 1st game, only you can interact with them now. You mostly deal in closed spaces and isolated rooms. The village you arrive at early in the game is little more than a small town square with few enterable locations, all quite short and insignificant. There are some larger areas you gain access to later on, but you are either unable to fully explore them, or it is monotonous and pointless to do so. This isn’t helped by the fact that the Howard’s “running” speed feels like walking, his walking speed feels like crawling, and if you have run toggled on, it toggles off anytime you enter a separately loaded area. I am no point and click purist, I’ve probably played less than 10 games of the genre, but DW2’s decision to go 3D feels fully unnecessary and detrimental. I don’t know if it was an attempt to reach wider audience, or perhaps achieve greater immersion. If it was the latter, then it was an absolute failure because…
Jumping is a buggy mess. I thought I was just incredibly unlucky when I fell through the floor 30 minutes into the game, but then it just kept happening again, again, and again. Step 1: start walking into any wall/door/obstacle. Step 2: Jump. Step 3: Continue holding down the walk button. Repeat a few times if necessary. Congrats, you are now able to clip through about 95% of the game. This clipping almost exclusively ends in you falling out of the map, into oblivion. There are a few instances where it can give you access to rooms prior to when you’re meant to access them, but this never provides any advantage. Even if we set aside how utterly broken jumping is, I don’t think you’re actually
to jump at all in the game? There are a few points where it might be more convenient to do so rather than moving some furniture out of the way, but all in all, jumping is wholly bugged and superfluous. Crouching is slightly less buggy and slightly more useful, but not by much. You can clip through some walls by walking into them while crouching, but it’s not as ubiquitous as with jumping. Some clues/objects can only be found/examined while crouching, which I guess is moderately realistic, but crouching to find a clue never made me go “Yep, this makes abandoning the point and click genre worth it”. Object manipulation is similarly useless. Howard must occasionally move something out of the way in a room, but most of the time the objects serve no purpose and only get in the way. It’s also pretty ridiculous how having to drag a chair out of the way is slow and tedious, but said chair can be sent flying across the room if you jump into it at a certain angle.

The more puzzly parts of DW2 are mostly intact. There’s plenty of material to read, but there’s generally less clue underlining and thought combining than the first game. Puzzles are still frequent, but they never intrigued me as much as they did in DW1.
You might think that the game having larger focus on exploration would bring you into contact with more people, but that is not the case. There are 5 NPCs you can talk to throughout the game, all hideous, rubbery, quasi-human, and donning yaoi hands. The conversations are nothing but exposition, and when you have multiple dialogue options, you’re expected to exhaust them in the order they’re presented, or else there’s a good chance they won’t make sense. There are a handful of background/bystander NPCs in the town, but they only serve to make you feel more alone. They don’t even have any canned dialogue responses. You can shine a flashlight at and jump on a sleeping train station hobo without consequences. Most of DW1’s conversations took place over the phone, and human interactions were rare. Though where the world of DW1 felt isolated, the world DW2 feels empty.
Aiming for more immersion may have been attempted with good intentions, but those intentions are all for nothing when you’re falling through the map every 5 minutes, exploring sparse locations, and talking to lifeless NPCs.
Criticism of DW2’s story is more vague, because DW2’s story
more vague. DW1’s story wasn’t exactly crystal clear, but DW2 is even guiltier of obfuscating the truth (that’s assuming there is one). I am no stranger to how Lovecraftian stuff works—it would be silly to expect every detail and mystery to be completely explained. Yet the story of DW2 feels so… unfulfilling? Part of the problem is how disconnected it feels from DW1. None of the locations from DW1 are revisited, most references to it are just in passing, and for spending DW1 “In Pursuit Of Loath Nolder”, Loath Nolder has a noticeably small role in the 2nd game. Whereas DW1 was a game of deduction and getting to the bottom of things, in DW2 it feels like you’re just doing various tasks because you’re told to. There’s the supposed threat of people coming after you and such, but overall the story feels without a purpose. As the title “The Dark Lineage” indicates, this game is primarily about Howard’s connection to these conspiracies and plots. Yet Howard comes off as having less of a personality than the first game. Between the two games, he seems to have completely gotten over his potential insanity (aside from an occasional outburst), which in turn makes things a lot less interesting. Likewise, the nightmare sequences induced by Howard’s madness are almost entirely absent too. For no good reason, and only serving to make things less interesting. Howard has zero personality in NPC conversations; he just asks what he needs to know. He comes out of his shell a little more in the 2nd half of the game when he’s brought into direct confrontation with his past, but ultimately it’s not enough to salvage his character.
The dissatisfaction with the story that doesn’t come from the game’s relationship to DW1, comes from the game’s conclusion. Everything that comes after
basically feels like a non sequitur to the rest of the game. Yes, I know it’s supposed to be Lovecraftian and weird, but it comes off as dull, rushed, and nebulous, even taking into account the multiple endings. It is unfulfilling to the story of DW1, and what had been set up in DW2 up to that point. Then there’s some frustratingly unresolved plot points, like
, or how halfway through the game
??? There’s Lovecraftian storytelling, and then there’s bad storytelling.
Even if you really enjoyed DW1, I would recommend staying away from this game. Your questions aren’t going to be answered, and you’ll leave disappointed and frustrated. The only thing I can say that’s of truly equal quality between the two games are their excellent soundtracks. The game’s waxy NPCs and loose understanding of walls may come off as unintentionally Lovecraftian, but overall this game is a thing that should not be.

"Darkness Within 2: The Dark Lineage (Director's Cut Edition)" brings us back to Howard Loreid after the events of the previous installment. While Darkness Within 1 was narratively set up as a flashback to show Loreid's descent into madness, Darkness Within 2 shows events afterwards. Ditching the point and click to a free roam horror game inspired by Lovecraft's works. While it is not necessary to play Darkness Within 1 (recounting those events early on), it certainly makes you see the ending.
Unlike the first, Darkness Within 2 doesn't suffer as much from pacing. Not requiring you to go back and forth to read documents as much (in fact, you're not really required to except in one or two instances). Instead it encourages you to speak with residents of Arkhamend to gain information to progress. It also brings free roam exploration as the focus while puzzles are used to get to important items for the ending. Darkness Within 2 seems to want to engage the player more into the character, and it helps with these changes. It also has an quick save system when pressing 'F5' which is highly appreciated.
However, with these changes, there are problems. The voice acting, while some are good, most is flat. There is no difference between the voice used for monologues than when you are actually speaking to someone (at least with the previous game, the voice actor used a hushed tone to distingush between the two). There is no difference between inner monologue than speaking  Some areas have areas where you can fall through the floor. While some are behind areas blocked off, there was one towards the end after a puzzle. Along with this, I do suggest if there will be invisible walls, have them to where the player can't jump over most of them. While subtitles are translated to english, at the end it is not.
It also needs to be said that this version has objects moved and some puzzles added (this is not the first version of the game), so there is only a german walkthrough that tells you where those objects are located and how to solve the new puzzles. Darkness Within 2 also gives too much information, not leaving the player to question whether these events truely happened or not.
While Darkness Within 2 can be frusturating, it is worth playing.
Overall:
+ pacing is improved
+ sound effects realistic
+ more immersion
+ quick save system
+/- difference between this and other version can cause confusion while looking for a walkthrough
+/- objects or hotspot can be too small to see
- flat voice acting
- bug where you can fall through the map

Five Nights at Freddy's is an Indie point-and-click horror game that literally bombed the Steam Store on its very first month of purchase and is infamously known as a fresh breath of games that play along the themes of tension, paranoia and sudden fear. It is also most known amongst fans of the game that famous Youtubers such as Markiplier and PewDiePie who have made the sales of this game boost even higher than usual indie game sales. As a small synopsis related to this game, you'll be waddling through Freddy's game of don't-hide-but-seek, right to the very perilous end.
With only little power reserved for poor old Mike Schmidt in the Security Guard's Office of Freddy Fazbear's Pizza, a family restaurant complex, you'll be struggling to stay alive and out of danger on your six hour shift of work, starting from 12 AM to 6 AM for five days straight, hence the title of the game. With every night progressively getting worse in both psychological fear and paranoia. The repulsive animatronics that run alive during the night become much more unpredictable, with unexpected jump scares that will leave your heart to skip a beat and without a doubt, make you want to rage quit the game as quickly as possible. You will be having to deal with Freddy and his fearsome buddies, Bonnie the Bunny, Chica the Chicken and Foxy the Pirate Fox. Rather cute names, yet really ugly faces indeed.
Inspired by the beloved restaurant, Chuck E. Cheese, now, the deepest nightmares of those kids have come to life as these animatronics in game don't want to sing you no birthday song or throw you a party. They simply plan to crush your body into a mascot costume, completely mashing, fracturing and probably suffocating you in the process. Pretty gruesome way to die, no?
What makes this game very intriguing is the community's efforts on theorizing the deeper meanings of the game's overall plot and context. Ranging from how the phone guy is the actual killer, to Foxy being a good animatronic rather than a bad one. This is all deeming down and shredding away the structure of the story that makes us think in our own perception. And I love the community's reasons for that as it takes devotion and well-thought ingenuity to piece together the mysteries that still lingers on, even to this day.
The game honestly doesn't become as scary as you may think. If you have been playing for hours upon end, it becomes somewhat highly addictive in a sense. Not to spoil anything about the game, but after the main five nights, you have an optional 6th night and even after that, you can proceed to the insane 20/20/20/20 difficulty mode, where you're doomed from the very start. Unless you can manage to live through it that is.
This game actively toys around with your mind, as you will mindlessly switch the lights on and shut the doors in the much more frightening and perilous nights ahead. Things begin to get real hectic as odd noises protrude from various locations in the restaurant, from the animatronics humming, to random musical tune, to loud footsteps and of course, the demonic laughter. You never know if Bonnie and Chica are ganging up on you or even worse, if you can't turn the lights on or shut the doors, knowing you're doomed with an eventual jumpscare at the end. Even Foxy begins to act creepy, since he's the biggest reserved essence of paranoia for me; you never know his patterns directly and you're left shook up if or when you witness his hasteful, creepy run down the hall, leaving you only little precious seconds to slam the emergency door down, or else you'll be greeted with an expected jumpscare and a game over.
Definitely recommend this game, and the time I recommend to play this game perfectly fits at midnight, all alone in the dark. I bloody dare you and if you have completed this game, congratulations! Move onto the even more scarier sequels that wait up ahead, brave soul. It's about to get a whole lot more nightmarish.

An excellent sequel to one of the best Lovecraftian adventure games ever.  I highly recommend this game and its predecessor.
But, to be completely fair, it's not quite as good as the story it finishes.   This slight drop in quality is simply a result of it showing the player too much.  Arguably, the secret to nailing a proper Lovecraftian vibe is to keep all the important things endlessly in the shadows.  This game breaks that rule, and takes you right to the center of everything.
Still, that's a very minor sin here, especially since the story had to go SOMEWHERE.
(Eccentric side note: the game looks amazing on a 3D monitor once you turn off a few of the new graphics settings.)
All in all, I highly recommend this game unless you haven't played the first one yet.  But if that's the case, I just recommend the first one even harder.

tl;dr A Hat in Time is a flawed first outting for an indie platformer that makes up for its numerous small deficits with a boatload of character, heart, nostalgia, and most importantly, fun.
A Hat in Time is short but sweet and can be completed 100% with all achievements in about fifteen hours. That said, that fifteen hours manages to encompass most if not all of the positive aspects of the collectathon games of yore without any of the bloat or filler that those games could often be bogged down by. This game most closely resembles games like Mario 64 and Mario Sunshine in that each level typically houses 8-10 Hourglass Pieces that you can obtain, while unlocking new levels requires that you hit a certain threshold before they're unlocked.
The platforming and movement feel incredibly crisp, mixing double jumping, a dash, and wall climbing to create easily controlled speediness that meshes well with the design of the environments. Three of the four worlds are fairly open in design and afford areas that are large enough to explore but not large enough to illicit boredom or undue traveling times. Time Rifts, which are self-contained levels that can be found throughout the worlds, provide some of the most engaging platforming challenges in the game while showing off some really great linear level design that provides a break from exploration.
The music is phenomenal and ranges from cheery tunes for exploration, frantic melodies for more intense moments, and especially memorable boss music that brings the action of each world to a satisfying and energetic climax. The voice acting does just enough to set the tone of the game. Hat Kid doesn't talk much, but her face is occasionally quite expressive during cutscenes. A Hat in Time chooses its voiced characters well, though, and really hammers in a lot of character for the fairly small amount of voiceover work.
Overall, A Hat in Time has a metric ton of character, but it's riddled with small issues that could potentially inhibit the experience:
-- Unlike Mario games, each chapter in a world is tied to a specific hourglass. The level typically changes in some way to encompass this, but A Hat in Time is lacking the free roam feeling of exploration and the excitement of finding secrets that older collectathons are famous for because hourglasses can't be find by exploration.
-- Most of the platforming surprises or secrets outside of Time Rifts either afford you thread for creating hats or coins for getting music remixes and cosmetic changes, so the sense of accomplishment from roaming an area can quickly dwindle.
-- Hats afford special abilities, but only two feel like they have any real impact on the game or platforming. Even then, their impact is fairly minimal. There's not a lot of back tracking or using hats to unlock secrets. As a counter-point, this does make the game feel more focused and less bloated by filler despite lacking the joy of discovering new ways to use hats.
-- I encountered several collision issues throughout the game, particularly when it came to rounded objects. The game's way of fixing these issues is to teleport you to your last safe spot, which can be jarring.
-- The last third of the game feels rushed and the main antagonist feels underbaked.
These might seem like a lot of negatives for a game, but these were things that I felt compelled to nitpick after my stellar experience. I can't stress enough how much fun this game was to play through despite its flaws and length; I haven't been this enthralled by a collectathon since the N64 era. A Hat in Time captures all the best aspects of those games without falling into the pitfall of being iterative or boring, allowing you to spend just enough time with its characters and worlds before pushing you onto the next experience. While there are issues with the polish, none of those problems threatened to ruin my enchantment with A Hat in Time while I was playing. The sheer amount of heart this game has is incredible, and I was enthralled throughout.
A final important note is that the developers are planning on releasing two new FREE DLC worlds in the future. A modding toolkit will also be readily available to players in due time. It's very clear that the devs have a strong commitment to community, and that means a lot for the game's longevity. It's a great thing to see from a group of folks in the modding community who put out their first game with Kickstarter.

Two hours in and Im having a blast! Fun little space adventure loot-em-up. Quirky style. So far, I love what Ive seen. Little oddball games like this are a real joy to me.

At its price range - Id say the game is well worth every penny.
Update: Since the lack of auto-attack seems to be the one main flag people are rallying negatively behind: auto-attack would be weird in this. Since exploring a planet is a very simple thing at its core (IE: literally all you do is move, attack and interact) - having auto-attack just wouldnt make any sense - it would be like having auto-attack in Diablo or Torchlight.
This game, while having some controls similiar to an RTS, is still more of an ARPG - and auto-attack, I think, doesnt belong here any more than it does in any other ARPG title.

* You can play normal mode or hardcore mode (your whole crew dies = your save file is done)
* You can choose your own difficulty in each planet, each one determines the loot quality you'll get.
* 5 classes (Vanguard, Marine, Engineer, Scout and Medic) and you can have 1-8 crew members in your squad both for SP and MP.
* Each class has their own abilities and also equipable tools which give you different extra abilities for each class.
* 9 loot tiers (poor, common, uncommon, exceptional, rare, epic, artifact, legendary, ultimate).
* Huge pool of modifiers meaning that your armor, weapons and tools can have some crazy stats added to them.
* Many different planet types. Each planet is unique with randomly generated "dungeons"/rooms you have to clear.
* Tons of different/unique enemies from each faction.
* The universe is finite with around 300-400 planets in it,
* Click to attack a single enemy, you can control one by one your crew members or all of them as squad, you can also pause the action in single player.
* The game scales everything to you, you will have a different experience fighting at level 1 than at level 10 or 20 for example.
* You can buy new ships and add modules to them which give you extra perks (for example your ship can carry more crew members).
I hope this huge wall of text helped you decide if that's the game for you or not.

Unfortunately, DW2 takes a step down in quality compared to its predecessor -- this, I suspect, is largely due to the switch away from Scratches-esque point-and-click style to a fully 3d engine.  Everything just looks and feels a little wonky (and occasionally buggy).  Worst of all, the world is too soft around the edges and lacking in detail compared to DW1... I just didn't feel as immersed in the environments despite the increased freedom to explore.  This lack of visual subtlety seemingly leads to a similar lack of subtlely in the story and characters (e.g. in DW1, Howard is understandably shocked by every strange thing that occurs; in DW2, Howard is carrying
).  And while the inclusion of more characters in the world was ambitious, the more prominently featured conversation system is clumsy at best and occasionally broken.
DW2 does do one thing more effectively than the first outing:  the flow of the game and its puzzles seemed much smoother and more intuitive... I never felt stuck simply because I had no idea what Howard was supposed to be trying to do (as sometimes happened to me in DW1).
If you played and enjoyed Darkness Within 1, I can recommend Darkness Within 2 simply by virtue of the resolution it (sort of) provides to the storyline and the healthy dose of Lovecraftiness.  If you haven't played or didn't enjoy DW1, however, you should consider avoiding DW2.

Having played the pretty decent first Darkness Within, I came in expecting good things from the second one. I was unfortunately disappointed. I don't mind that the graphics aren't impressive, since it's an old game and it does get the story across just fine, but the story is the biggest problem. It's full of Lovecraftian horror cliches, loose plot threads, bad story pacing and hardly makes use of the previous game's story or events at all.
I get the feeling that the game really wanted to be a classic Lovecraft-style horror tale set in the 1930s, but kept forgetting it's established in 2011. The first time we see an indication of a modern day environment is when we see a box of discarded VHS tapes in the bookstore, but it ends up being the only one. Howard has misplaced his cellphone sometime between the two games, and the newest-model phone we see is a broken 60s variant. There's not one television in sight, let alone a computer. Even the few (nonfunctional) light switches we see are early 20th century. The only car we see (and actually get to use) is a 30s style fordor that belonged to Howard's grandfather - gone is the small but modern car from the first game. Every NPC talks like they stepped out of a turn-of-the-century novel, fear of "strangers" is rampant, everyone talks about curses and "rites" even though in the next breath they insist they don't actually believe any of that, oh no, but let me tell you in detail and purple prose about all these curses anyway. And who writes diary entries that come with cliffhangers for events that will take place weeks or months later!?
Almost all of the referred-to NPCs from the previous game are killed off somewhere behind the stage before the game even begins. We never find out what became of Howard's police friend, Arthur. We spend a good quarter of the game making a mysterious machine work at the bottom of an abandoned building, but besides one scrawled note, we get no results or consequences from it. We don't know who the robbers' employer was, nor do we know what was in the sewer. I understand that part of horror is fear of the unknown, but that's no excuse for sloppy storytelling!
This game does have superior sound design, and the full 3d environment is more comfortable to play in than the Myst-like static backgrounds, compared to the previous game. But as a whole, DW: In Pursuit of Loath Nolder is much better than this one.

This is a really good game and it's clear the developer knows how to make this sort of game. It's like a much better version of Masters of Olympus in terms of managing food (farming crops, animals etc / production resources). However, I played this game solidly for a lot of hours in the first 24 hours but after I had planted everything and built all the buildings there didn't seem like a whole lot more to do / aim for. Therefore, although I'd definitely recommend this game, I'd also suggest that it needs to have more to aim towards once you manage to survive the first 20 winters.
Here are some simple suggestions:
1) Resources: Increase the range of harvest -> modify -> consume options available. For example... harvest wheat -> grind to flour -> bakery bakes bread and cakes. Or... harvest grapes -> make into wine or harvest milk -> dairy makes cheese etc.
2) Buildings: Create more buildings to build in the town. For example, town centre where all the villagers gather, light a big fire, eat food, dance to music, and drink in the evenings. Or what about a shipyard to build large ships to sell? Would create new trades in the game too (e.g. rope, sails).
3) Technology: Although it's nice that the game is quite specific about the technological age the villagers live in, it would be good to have some sort of tech tree to work along (perhaps requiring scholars). Not suggesting tractors and combined harvesters, but different irrigation / fertilisers, house improvements, farming and mining tools / techniques, or even new crafts.
4) Disasters & Events: I only played it on normal difficulty but the disasters didn't seem very disastrous! Perhaps there could be things like an especially cold/long winter or a very nasty plague. Similarly though, there could be good events too such as a bumper crop, a farmer winning a prize for growing the biggest pumpkin... Just some thoughts...
5) Houses: It would be good if houses could be extended for different types of people (e.g. better houses attract wealthier or more skilled nomads / make wealthier more skilled settlers happy). For example, underfloor heating (the Romans had this after all), a third floor, wider, longer, or other things. This idea could even be expanded to build castles for a monarch or something.
Anyway, these are reasonably simple suggestions that would improve the game's longevity and give players something to aim for beyond what's already there. I know some of this can be done with mods too. Don't get me wrong, this is a very good game with a great deal of potential... not least the graphics which IMO are spot on in terms of appearance and performance. The fact that I've bothered to write a review at all and make suggestions shows just how much I have valued my experience of this game so far... because I was a teenager the last time I cared enough about a game to do so!

Takes what Amensia focused on, adds horrific gore, additional suspense, and a shocking story. Plays very much like a found footage film. You'll never feel safe in Mount Massive Asylum. Just when you get comfortable, the story will take a turn for the worst.
Visually the game is impressive. It's not so much in the overall sense of graphics, but the attention to detail is excellent. No gore in this game looks the same. Everything helps to build a sense of dread in the environment in Outlast.
The audio is excellent. Whether it be the murmuring of harassed patients or the fear soaked hyperventilation of the main character, Outlast uses the sound to its most horrific benefit.
The gameplay is great. The designers definitely know how horror game players think and react. Jump scares play on your predictability and level design forces the player into uncomfortable situations of being exposed. If that weren't the worst of it, the maze like structure of the asylum turns on the player when they're forced to flee from an enemy into unexplored areas. Just when you think you have this game down, they change it up on you.
If you love horror titles, don't think; just get this game.

I'm not usually one for horror games, but since I was gifted this by my friend (thanks, by the way) I had to try it out. This'll probably get buried amongst the awful 'joke' reviews, but here goes...
Basically, you are the night watch at Chuck E. Cheese's from Hell. The animatronic robots (Bonnie, Chica, fan favourite Foxy, and the titular Freddy) move around the premises at night, trying to get into your security office and stuff you into one of their suits, which would be alright had they not been full of mechanical gears, wires and crossbars.
However, you can 'deter' (you can never really fight them back, which adds a lot to the horror factor) them by using your security doors to shut them out. This drains power from your limited power supply though, so use them wisely.
In gameplay, you check the cameras to find where Freddy and the gang are, which also uses power. There are 2 blindspots outside your door which you use lights to check too.
For the actual horror factor... Well, just look at my playtime. This game is rightfully named one of the scariest games this year, and there's lots of hidden backstory to tell the story of the pizzeria.  There's the paranoia of the animatronics moving around and not knowing where they are until you find them, and the fear of getting a jumpscare when pulling down your camera tablet. This game gives you a constant feeling of dread, and that works out well for it.
Overall, while there are lots of logic holes (why the guard keep coming back every night, for instance), this game is a terrifying and maybe even fun, if you're into this sorta stuff.
I recommend this, but don't expect to see me playing it again anytime soon!

I was surprised there weren't more reviews for Steamalot so I decided to write this in support of this small game. This game is quite fun despite being a phone port. Gameplay is simple square grid turn based strategy, which can be difficult at times though never overwhelmingly so. There are a few things I would like to point out that I don't think have been said already:
1) Deck sizes are 20 cards which seems to limit some of the possibilities for customization (though it probably also keeps the levels from going on for too long)
2) Card packs are purchased with coins that are won from battles or won from completing certain battles. You can buy more expensive packs with guaranteed rarer cards, but I found that just buying the cheapest pack with 5 random cards provided enough uncommon and rare cards to be a better purchase, especially since the extra common cards can be sold for coins or used to level other cards.
3) The developers have posted all the card creation combinations on their website. If you want to create cards, check out the list there. The combinations would otherwise be too difficult and time-consuming to figure out on your own.
4) Leveling cards is not necessary to beat the game on normal mode. Leveling more than a few cards to their max seems like it would take too much level grinding for coins unless you want to sacrifice some of your uncommon and rare cards that you only have a single copy of. Only recommended for completionists and extreme PvP players.
Overall, Steamalot is a fun, short strategy game that can be played in small bursts. I'm already hoping for a sequel.

I think I've played enough to give my opinion on this game.  I like it.  I don't want to stop playing, I got that "just one more turn!" bug.
Quick note before I go further, this is a PC port of a phone game, so if you are biased against phone games you might want to keep that in mind.  However, I think there's a free version out there you could try to see if you like the gameplay.  And if you want to complain about having to pay for something that is free in a different format, I'd like to remind you that on Steam this game has trading cards which you can sell to make back some of your money.  And the price isn't bad, $5 seems right.  If you have issues about price, then wait for a sale.
This game is a tactical turn-based card game.  You have a deck of cards with fighter charcters (and animals), weapons and armor, and other items that affect buffs and debuffs.  There is a main story but there's also online PVP.  So far I've only been playing the story against the AI.
In this game you lose if your commander gets killed, so guard him (or her) carefully.  It's like the king in chess.  Checkmate and it's game over.  You can choose who the commander is when you start each level.
Characters have various levels of attack strength, movement range, etc.  Some can only attack in four directions (up, down, left, righ) while others can attack diagonally also.  Some have to be right next to the enemy to attack, others can be one space away to attack with a bow.  You can equip armor and weapons if you get those cards drawn.  At the start of the game you get 5 cards and one card each turn.  It's random so you never know what you're going to get.  Part of the difficulty is that some of the characters are better with specific weapons (the archer gets a bonus for using a bow) but if you didn't get the right cards you might have to give your archer a sword or else wait and hope you get the bow card.
There are also animals that fight for you.  You start with pigs (sow).  They can't equip anything, except if you get the collar card later on.  I just got another animal or creature but haven't gotten to use it yet.
As you can see from the screenshots the gameplay takes place on a grid.  The colors represent where your characters can move.  There are barriers that you have to move around, though remember some characters can attack diagonally and what seems to be a solid line of mountains actually might have a gap.
You get money (gold) after each level.  Use that to buy card packs to get more cards.  There is also crafting to level up your cards.  I haven't experimented much with that yet because I haven't gotten many extra cards yet.
Graphics look kind of old school.  If you don't like that sort of look, then you can decide from the screenshots.  I personally don't care what a game looks like if the gameplay is good.
I can't think of anything else to say right now.  I might update this review later on as I play more of the game.

This game looked stupid. And then the first video - BARF! super cheesy. But a reference to Card Hunter (dig it) caught my eye, so against my better judgement I gave the game a proper look. The game "sounded" solid, and the second video seemed to like it, so I honestly don't know why, but i bought it.
I'm shocked. Halfway thru the campaign and my impression is that It's good. It doesn't appear to have the same depth or polish as Card Hunter, but it's a worthy comparison. For me it captures the same engaging strategy thinking in ~15 minute chunks without being punishing or tedious.
Pro's:
Price - It's well worth $4
UI - Easy to grasp and efficient. Adding extensive mouse-over text would take it from good to excellent.
Tutorial - Sparse but effective. The "pass" mechanic (npi) seemed gimmicky at first, but now I see at as important to the flavor of this game.
Quality - The writing and card descriptions are sharp. No major bugs. Only one crash and it even told me why (failed to adjust resolution) and crashed gracefully.
Gameplay - It's deep enough to not be casual, and simple enough to not be hardcore. I'm fine with the amount of  RNG so far.
PvP - Haven't tried it yet, but if anyone else is playing, i look forward to it.
Cons:
Marketing: The first impression (before buying) was so bad that I'm afraid not many others will buy it.
Graphics: I'm not a fan of the overall appearance. It doesn't detract from gameplay, but I find it amateurish. Reminds me of Dungeons of Dredmore which I also liked despite disliking the visuals.
Card Hunter fans should enjoy this, it's better than it looks,

Change can be scary. Familiarity breeds comfort, and nowhere is this notion of familiarity greater than in our memories. Nostalgia is a powerful sentiment that has the potential to inspire or to hold back. Jonas Kaerlev, the creator of A Hat in Time, understands this keenly. He and his team at Gears for Breakfast hearken back to an older, beloved generation of games while developing their own sense of identity and fun. A Hat in Time doesn’t reinvent the wheel; it turns it into a brightly colored, well-designed, cute-as-heck unicycle.
Gears for Breakfast has done a fantastic job of revisiting an old genre with a new, fresh perspective. Featuring tight controls, a whimsically colorful universe and characters, and a gorgeous soundtrack, 'A Hat in Time' hits all the right notes to become an instant classic. Despite the content being on the shorter side for the moment, future updates will add more to an already great game. For collect-a-thon veterans and platformer newbies alike, there’s something for everyone to enjoy in this heckin’ cute adventure.

If you've ever wanted to make a video game, but have no idea how to do it or where to even start, I might provide a bread crumb for you.
RPG Maker VX Ace is one of the best programs for beginners to use. The base has been made for you; all you have to do is fill it in. You can craft enormous stories and make the game as large as you want. You can craft maps up to any size (though, be aware that it will suck the very will to live from your poor computer, depending on the size), you can fashion heroes and villians to your whim, and you can create a landscape no one has seen. Quite honestly, the possibilities are endless. As long as you have access to YouTube, providing you with a plethora of tutorials to choose from, and a steaming imagination, you'll enjoy this program immensely. Of course, it is no masterpiece, and I might have embellished myself a bit too much by saying that you could do anything on this program, if you have the knowledge, you can work around the kinks, and create a truly brilliant game.
Pros:
- Vast amount of items. Many items are pre-made for you, so you don't need to stress about creating thousands of different potions or poisons.
- You don't have to program that much. Many events have already been written in code for you, and the developers have created a menu that will allow you to customize events such as combat, dialogue, animations, and so on.
- If you're not an artist, you don't need to fear. The avatars are premade and well drawn, and there's plenty of DLC to purchase if you don't like the original avatars. (Though, personally, I go on an RPG Maker VX Ace website where  people allow others to download their art for free.)
- It's a good base if you want to go big. Not only does this expand your experience, but it encourages you to stretch out your stories to the maximum. They can be 60 hours long if you wish, and even if you might not like the pre-made items, you can use them as a placeholder until you begin to delve deeper and customize it yourself.
- You don't need to be locked into boundaries. Being an artist myself, I'm more enticed to create the characters, the world, and the events myself. The game allows you do do that, importing your own drawings of maps and people inside of the game. You can even create your own sprites if you wish.
Cons:
- The price. Never would I advise beginners to buy a program that is more than $30. I was lucky and came across it randomly during a Steam sell. I purchased it for ten dollars. If you're patient, you can find that its price can drop down that low and snatch it before the sale ends.
- Your first words will be, "What do I even do?" It's a vast program. If any of you have opened Photoshop, it's practically the same thing. It will take time to get familiar with it, and take even longer to master it. I've used it for several months for a school project, placing over sixty hours into creating it. The game demo itself was only three minutes long.
- It takes time and dedication. If you're not interested in this, not only with the price not be worth it, but you'll drop it by the second day. You need to be dedicated if you want to purchase this.
- At first, it will feel overwhelming, and then it will feel constraining. There is only so much to do with pre-made characters. You'll eventually get bored looking at the same faces. If you want something truly unique, you'll need to find an artist to help you out, or be an artist yourself.
- Even with the programming done for you, you'll often find that you'll need to work in the nitty gritty in order for events to work. They lag out. You might forget one single line, and then every piece of that even will ruin the rest of the game. You'll forget to turn the event off. You'll spend hours working on a problem that you didn't even know could happen. It's frustrating at times, and you mind leave the project for days, even months.
Nevertheless, it's still one of the most solid programs I've used. Mind you, it's actually the only game-making programs that I've used, but it's been quite usefull to me. I jump on and off again, and I can't say that I'm completely passionate about the projects that I work on, but for the sale that I got on it, and for the end result, it was beauty indeed.

I don't often write reviews for games, but here I go. First, I love the slow-motion feature, particularly because time's not truly "stopped" when you're not moving.
Second, I love the fact that there are a LOT of references to some obscure movies, like Oldboy. The game is, in large part, a number of different set pieces from various action movies that you play out in bullet-time. Is it fun? Oh yeah. So much fun. I love the feeling of satisfaction I get from solving the "puzzle" of how to move around the levels and in what order to kill the red dudes. I also love that you can cut bullets with a katana. And the fact that you can beat an entire level by throwing bottles at guys (it takes a while). Oh, also wanted to mention the fact that you can save your runs so that when you do pull off that perfect action movie combo, you can record it and put it up on Killstagram! :D
You might be questioning the price, but from what I've seen, they plan to be very active as developers, and release content in a lot of small packages, rather than just nickel-and-dime you with DLC every couple months. So, if you enjoy FPS and the ability to fight in slow motion,  I'd say the whole thing is definitely worth the money. I suppose one way to put it is... if you're in it to just beat a game, nah, you're better off waiting for a sale. But if you're wanting to be creative with your kills and gameplay, and want to be a part of something bigger than yourself, it's very worth it.

Me and some of my friends play horror games during school at lunch sometimes. My friends really wanted me to buy this so we can play it. I thought the game was over hyped and didn't see what was scary about it. After playing I found out its rather scary. The gameplay is simple yet it works perfectly. Just sit in a room, watch the cameras, close the doors, flicker the lights and wait for your night to end. Watching the animatronics is very creepy as one second they'll all be there and the next "ooh, wheres Bunny gone?" and you'll find her right down the hall from where you are. The little hallucinations that happen to you can be very scary as well. The pre-rendered graphics are pretty cool and Freddy and the rest of the animatronics models look really neat. Now onto the not so great stuff. From what I've played and how I've been playing, the power seems to not last very long. I can get rather scared at times so maybe its from me just looking at the cameras too much. The jumpscares can be predictable and if you've seen some one else beat the game there isn't really any reason to buy it. Its nothing groundbreaking and the game is a little over hyped.
Made it to night 6. I have now worked out how to save more power. The animatronics move a lot more and it can be rather frightening. I'm not as scared of the jumpscares as I was when they firsted happend, mainly because if you listen you can hear them behind the cameras. Also, night 6 is tough. Like really tough. The animatronics move more often and you ALWAYS have to make sure Foxy hasn't moved, because if he comes running you'll have only a few seconds to close the door before you hear what the fox really says as he shoves you inside a suit. I used to get bullied by my friend because I was scared of the jumpscares. I'm not scared now though so HAH, suck it Felix. *ahem* anyway, Five Nights at Freddy's is an excellent (a little over hyped) indie horror game that I highly recomend you get. I think the game would possibly be better on a WiiU or with a tablet hooked up to your computer to be used a the camera monitor. It would make the experince more immersive in my opinion.
So yeah, if you've seen your favorite youtuber complete the game don't bother getting it. Its just not as fun.
But yeah, I like this game and can't wait for FNaF 2 to be realeased.
