So completely enigmatic it's almost maddening, LIMBO tosses you into a hazy black and white world as a silhouetted little boy with two distinguishable white eyes. The ultimate beauty of this puzzle-solving/adventure-platformer is that everying is a mystery: You haven't a clue where you are, who you are, what you're doing, and why. This UNKNOWING is exactly what makes this game wonderful; no overly complicated plot, no names to learn, NOTHING. Leave this experience entirely up to what you make of it, relativity at it's best.
Moving away from the story; we are given very few abilites as the kid. The player can jump, and grab or "interact" with objects that appear within the level, having to do so to overcome various deadly obstacles/traps/creatures/and even more dark silhouetted people (or so we believe, creatures and people within the world of LIMBO are also black silhouettes).
The wonderful delivery of this game also comes in another form: the lack of tutorials. As you progress through levels, you're given no hints in-game to determine how to go about avoiding dangerous situations. Allow me to be more clear: YOU WILL DIE. This game teaches players through sheer gameplay, allowing for the first time in a long long while for the player to learn on their own and discover solutions for themselves, often resulting in the player dying a very grizzly death (accented with blood squirts, and again silhouetted blood and gore), but ultimately learning from the experience and passing it.
Everything about this game is dark and cryptic, and without the presence of in game pop-ups or tutorials the player feels accomplished with surpassing a difficult puzzle or obstacle. Give LIMBO a try, it will enthrall and delight you, giving you a playing experience like you've never encountered before.

I'm awake and more alert and I STILL don't understand what Indigo Prophecy was about! First it was about supernatural rituals and crime-drama, but then they started talking about aliens and Evil AIs species which came literally right out of nowhere and then our main protagonist is suddenly able to fly and fight like he's in a low-budget Matrix film!
I am really alarmed by the speed at which he gets over the deaths of others and immediately gets involved with someone whom he knew personally for all of ten minutes before deciding "Hey! Let's shag!".
Why is the game even CALLED Indigo Prophecy? I know it's named after the Indigo Child, but what does that even mean!? What does Indigo have to do with anything? What does a bluish color have to do with anything? Pretty sure they picked a name just to make it sound cool when it was really nonsense even by video game standards!
On top of that, I really hated how they made you tap color-coded buttons to move instead of, say, just giving you the ability to kick the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of someone like in a fighting game. Even simple things like TALKING required a trial like Guitar Hero-style button mashing on hard mode most of the time!
And the exposition...Jesus Christ, no. Half of the game was just color-coded button mashing and frustrating movement controls (imagine Silent Hill only ten times worse) and the other half was really rushed exposition drops that suddenly explain away half of the game....except for the possibly omnipotent AI villain who just came out of nowhere!
For its time, Indigo Prophecy was probably considered revolutionary as one of the first few cinematic games, but for our point in time, it's just absolute trash. It's a good concept spoiled by its glaring flaws and mediocrity.

This game is open world gaming at its best.
I have spend over 200 hours playing this game on PC and over 250 hours on the Playstation 3. The game is extremely beautiful for the time of release. Even when playing this game today I don't have the feeling that I am playing an old/ugly game.
The Pro's:
The world is build up pretty nicely. There are different regions with different types of vehicles and camouflages. When you are in the desert your clothing actually collect sand and up in the mountains you get white of the snow.
Grappling around the world feels nice and fast, and switching between freefalling, tethering and the parachute feels fast and action-movie like.
The vertical freedom in this game is absolutely insane. Flying high above the ground and freefalling for over 10 minutes is just part of the game and causes no issues with the game at all.
Exploding stuff feels satisfying, however not everything that you might want to destroy, can be destroyed.
The police is actually smart. They will follow you everywhere, even if you take your vehicle offroad. Helicopters and planes try and will kill you, and taking them over makes you stronger, yet still you can be taken down by the soldiers on the ground.
The Con's:
Some places on the map show a lot more glitches compared to others, mainly when tethering with your grappling hook.
Cars don't handle that well compared to other popular open world games, some feel like boats, others like tuned motorbikes.
The story is short and doesn't really catch you in any way. You just play through it because it gives you another oppertunity to blow stuff up, but that's really it.
You cannot complete this game 100%. Due to a last minute change in the map, about .7% of the games collectibles got lost.
Summary:
You should totally buy this game. It is cheap, fun and addictive for at least a few months. Even if the singleplayer gets boring you can always install the multiplayer mod and play with hundreds of other Just Cause 2 fans. Even though the game cannot be completed for 100% and the story lacks content, this game features a very beautiful and big map, in which you can explode almost anything you can think of (yes, even trees). There is a wide arsenal of vehicles and weapons to choose from and navigating through the map feels not slow at all (walking from one side to another will take you about 3 to 4 hours though).
9.5/10

I'm not really enjoying this so-called "Art Appreciation" pack. So far, the first two games just show artistic promise while having actual gameplay about as bad as trying to walk with tent poles for legs.
The Howler (odd enough name, as the actual Howler is only in the first level), revolves around a city being thrust into madness... oh, you can't tell? The level design doesn't imply that? Yeah, see that's the big issue with games that rely on cutscenes or text to simply TELL you what's going on and not backing it up. It's like getting ready for a dinner party, and your friend tells you, "Hey! Get ready! This is really high society. Act your best!" And when you get in, dressed in your tuxedo, the place is actually a hillbilly hoedown. The world of The Howler feels very empty and lifeless, rather than tense and on the brink of destruction, like the so-called "story" would imply.
I have some humongous problems with the gameplay (very similarly to Gravilon), being that momentum is NOT a good mechanic for a video game. It's simply too much of a semi-controllable variable that makes beating levels feel more like you got lucky rather than actually feeling like you accomplished and learned something. So many of these levels are agonizingly hard because of how semi-predictable the movement of your hot air balloon is.
The world is designed just fine. I have no issues with it, visually. It certainly looks a lot more vivid than Gravilon, but again the design makes a lot of obstacles much harder than they are. Such as building up momentum to get over a fair-sized chimney proved to be a right pain in my a** after attempting the level about 15 times.
If you like momentum games, and a decent challenge, The Howler will shortly satiate your starvation. But as for people looking for actual "art"... I suggest you look over by Dear Esther or Elegy for a Dead World. There's very little art around here.

It's unlikely that you'll actually get anything done using this.
However...
It offers hundreds of hours of messing around with a system that truly can allow someone to get into some basic game development. Looking at lines of code and figuring out how to manipulate the engine to your will is actually pretty fun.
-IN DEPTH BELOW-
Starting off, the engine is actually pretty intuitive. Once you figure out how to use events and whatnot you will easily be able to make some sub-par but interesting rpg ideas and games. Nothing significant is likely to come from any of your time using it, but it is very easy to use and figure out.
There is a lot of music automatically placed in the engine. Most of it is the kind of music that you acknowledge it exists, but doesn't really fit the settings of the games I've tried to create. Sure, the tracks add some livelyness to the scene you make, but none of the music is going to really add much to your game.
Now here's one of the main problems with the engine: Movies and pictures.
You can display a video or a picture in the middle of events. However, because you have to activate a movie with an event, using a video for the start menu is difficult, requiring programming that is hard to learn because the ruby script is garbage. (movies use weird file types, too. I require online converters any time I want to use anything I've made.)
Pictures are easier to put on the title screen, but are not intuitive at ALL to putting in the game. If you want to say, put a picture of the goblin you just decapitated in an event, you have to know exactly how the engine displays pictures in order to place it how you want it to.
Overall, not a bad engine, but some things require tricks and long scripts in order to force the system to work how you want it to. If you can get around that, maybe you can make something worthwhile, but you will want to put in your own music and probably do something about those base character sprites because they are fairly lacking.

Of all of the "Early Access" games I have had the fortune to play, this is by far the most polished.  The developers seem to be very involved with the community as well.
Now for the actual review:
A survival game without zombies or other players hunting you down?  Impossible, you might think.  Some might also think, screw that, where is the real threat?  From nurishment to wolves, the biggest threat is the weather.  Shelter is a commodity, offering temporary reprieve from the frozen world outdoors.  God help you if you have to spend a couple nights outside.  I loaded up my makeshift fire with plenty of wood, only to awaken after a couple hours in the midst of violent winds.  Needless to say, my fire had been extinguished, and I spent the remainder of the night inside a ruined boxcar.  As morning broke, I was nearly dead from the cold, but I managed to find an outpost with plenty of supplies and a furnace.  Besides having to share the haven with the corpse of its former tenant, I was quickly able to thaw out, boil some drinkable water, and cook up something to eat.  I have probably a day or two worth of food, and will inevitably have to venture back out shortly to aquire more wood to keep that furnace running.  I dread my next trek, but in the best of ways.  Very few games immerse me in such a way as The Long Dark has managed, and it is merely in Early Access!
The few complaints I have with the game look like they will be hashed out long before the game's official release.  And those complaints are very, very minor (as of writing this, the only thing that comes to mind is the rate at which your clothing wears down).  The developers are constantly asking for feedback, and have been quick to work out balancing issues.
I have been burned by most other Early Access games, to the point that I was considering never buying one again.  I am so glad that I did some research on this game and saw exactly what it has to offer, right now, aside from the coming additions that it promises to offer.  Do some research, like I did.  Check Youtube for some gameplay.  Read up in the forums.  Anyone on the fence about this game should take a hatchet to that fence.  You're going to need all the firewood you can carry once you decide to brave the cold... ;)

Change can be scary. Familiarity breeds comfort, and nowhere is this notion of familiarity greater than in our memories. Nostalgia is a powerful sentiment that has the potential to inspire or to hold back. Jonas Kaerlev, the creator of A Hat in Time, understands this keenly. He and his team at Gears for Breakfast hearken back to an older, beloved generation of games while developing their own sense of identity and fun. A Hat in Time doesn’t reinvent the wheel; it turns it into a brightly colored, well-designed, cute-as-heck unicycle.
Gears for Breakfast has done a fantastic job of revisiting an old genre with a new, fresh perspective. Featuring tight controls, a whimsically colorful universe and characters, and a gorgeous soundtrack, 'A Hat in Time' hits all the right notes to become an instant classic. Despite the content being on the shorter side for the moment, future updates will add more to an already great game. For collect-a-thon veterans and platformer newbies alike, there’s something for everyone to enjoy in this heckin’ cute adventure.

I don't often write reviews for games, but here I go. First, I love the slow-motion feature, particularly because time's not truly "stopped" when you're not moving.
Second, I love the fact that there are a LOT of references to some obscure movies, like Oldboy. The game is, in large part, a number of different set pieces from various action movies that you play out in bullet-time. Is it fun? Oh yeah. So much fun. I love the feeling of satisfaction I get from solving the "puzzle" of how to move around the levels and in what order to kill the red dudes. I also love that you can cut bullets with a katana. And the fact that you can beat an entire level by throwing bottles at guys (it takes a while). Oh, also wanted to mention the fact that you can save your runs so that when you do pull off that perfect action movie combo, you can record it and put it up on Killstagram! :D
You might be questioning the price, but from what I've seen, they plan to be very active as developers, and release content in a lot of small packages, rather than just nickel-and-dime you with DLC every couple months. So, if you enjoy FPS and the ability to fight in slow motion,  I'd say the whole thing is definitely worth the money. I suppose one way to put it is... if you're in it to just beat a game, nah, you're better off waiting for a sale. But if you're wanting to be creative with your kills and gameplay, and want to be a part of something bigger than yourself, it's very worth it.

I'm addicted to this game, playing at least two runs per day in the midst of playing other games.  Note this is a review of the ALPHA version, so my opinon may change as the game changes en route to release.
The Long Dark forces you to try to survive in the frozen north where there is limited food and there are wolves that attack on sight.  If you honor the spirit of the game and play without maps (posted by folks who made them), this is a very difficult game.  Even after many runs, you can find yourself in an area without any idea which direction would be best.
Typical game 1:  Start in woods area with nothing in sight but more woods, with a blizzard raging around you.  You note that you are freezing, but have no food so you can't just grab some wood, hunker down, and start a campfire.  Your choice is to try to get warm and starve to death, or keep moving in hopes you will stumble across a cabin or other shelter.  Typical outcome -- you freeze to death.
Typical game 2:  Start where you can see cabins, ice fishing huts, or where you know the general area.  Head for shelter, search and find some food and drink, maybe some more clothing, perhaps even a tool.  Step outside the cabin heading for the next one, take ten steps and "Bam!" -- a wolf attacks you.  You're dead.  Again.
After a few runs like these two typical ones, you discover how to watch for and avoid wolves (mostly -- can't always succeed), you know enough of the general layout of the map to find enough sustenance to last several days.  Then you find the dam, enter, and Fluffy kills you.
Note that there is no saving and restoring available to get around being killed.  The game saves when you enter a cabin and when you start a campfire, so you can quit the game from the menu and come back the that point.  But once you restart the game, the save is gone.
Can this be frustrating?  Oh, yes.  But you develop the urge to play, to get the thrill of finding a new location, of finding a can of peanut butter just before starving.  It's a real rush to succeed just a little bit in this game.  Some folks don't like the wolves or dying so much -- these are the same people who save and reload their way through a game and then brag about how easy winning was.
The atmosphere given by the graphics and sound really add to the game.  You can hear the weather and see the fog and snow just as if it were real.  Not state of the art graphics to be sure, but IMHO the graphics add to the flavor of the game.
The Long Dark is a 10/10 even in its current stage of developmen.

SuperHot a great little game that'll take you 2-3 hours to beat the main campaign. While I recommend it, if you're not sure you'll love this game already I'd wait for a sale. It's absolutely worth $15, but $25 may be a bit much if you don't have much cash to spend.
While it's true that the campaign is 2-3 hours long, the truth is that it's more of a tutorial. After you beat the story, plenty of new challenge modes unlock for you to play. While I'd prefer they be unlocked from the beginning, this means that, if you enjoy the base gameplay gimmick enough, this game has PLENTY of content to justify its initial asking price. Just because it isn't narrative-focused or considered part of the campaign doesn't mean that it isn't worthwhile content. If you enjoy the time-stopping gameplay of SuperHot, you will find a lot of content here.
As for the story, it really isn't anything special. It really does come off as pretentious (if you've played Pony Island, it really gives off that same exact vibe), and frankly I was just waiting for the sections of story to be over so I can go back to playing. It serves as a good preamble for the hours I plan on investing into the challenges and endless mode. A lot of people seem rather irate that the game doesn't have many weapons to play with, and while more would have been appreciated, the weapons we do have serve themselves well. They all have a learning curve to use, and they all work well enough to keep things fresh.
If I did have one suggestion for the devs, it would be to enable the game for modding support or provide a level editor. I can see glorious fan-made levels being made here, and it would be a shame to see that potential squandered. It would also help people swallow the $25 asking price.
The gameplay is tricky, super satisfying, and rewarding to master. It really does feel like playing a scene in The Matrix. It's a super unique gimmick that I'd love to see expanded in a sequel. As for right now, though, SuperHot still remains a game I recommend, if only to experience what people claim to be the most innovative FPS ever.

For a city-building strategy game it sure adds a lot of features that I enjoyed. Just enough features to let creativity flow. It's nothing like Cities: Skylines but it does add enough for you to build a large enough settlement. The whole premise to the game is that you are controlling people who have been banished from their homes in medieval-like ages. You control what they build, and ultimately their fate.
Because it is based in earlier ages the seasons take a huge toll on population of you are not prepared. There is generally a set path to follow if you would like to survive the longest but that strategy is for you to figure out and after becoming sufficient enough, your town is entirely under your control. You can trade whatever you'd like and depending on what you build, can ultimately control the population of your town. Or, continue expanding.
It would be nice if we could upgrade to larger building or ages but the features they have in the game allow for a good amount of difficulty that will leave you losing the game with 0 population if you do not know what to do or do not manage your town effectively. I would have loved to eventually build a large castle with walls around the city center and farms surrounding the walls eventually, but we can't do that. We're limited to 2 types of homes and 1 type of everything else.
For $20 it is a great buy if you enjoy city building. Otherwise, I would suggest Cities: Skylines for a more modern city building game like Sim City with more features and more stable.

The gameplay is simple,you have a camera monitor that you can use to switch between security cameras in the place,you can close/open the electrical doors in your office to keep the animatronics from coming in,and lights to see if they're outside the room.
All of these different things at your disposal are important in their own way for protecting yourself from the animatronics and surviving each night.
In addition to the 5 nights in the game,there's an additional 6th Night,and even a 7th Night,where you can customize the AI to make it easy as heck or as hard as The Impossible Game.
The atmosphere is REALLY well done,and it gives you a feeling of tension,panic,and anticipation,which is really effective in scaring you.
The music is pretty cool,tho the game mostly relies on ambiance and atmosphere.
Overall,while this game is pretty simple,it's one of those games that while simple,can still scare the crap out of you.

I bought this game because I really liked the Stanley Parable. However, while there are some similarities between The Beginner's Guide and The Stanley Parable, I think the qualities that made the Stanley Parable so enjoyable are lacking here.
First of all, The Beginner's Guide is not a game. It is more of an interactive commentary, in which the narrator guides you through different landscapes (in the form of short, unfinished "games" created by a developer) while analyzing the meaning of each game. You are forced to progress in a linear fashion and cannot make any choices, other than minimal dialog choices which have no efffect on the plot progression.
In the Stanley Parable, there is replay value in the form of making different choices. In this game, there is not. In addition, I completed The Beginner's Guide from start to finish in under 2 hours of game time.
While The Beginner's Guide is unique and interesting in its own right, I would classify it more as a piece of art rather than a game. It's entertaining while it lasts, and will certainly make you think. Also, I'm assuming it's a work of fiction. I won't spoil the story for you but I have to say that the ending left me in an odd mood. If it's a true story, I'm not sure how I feel about it. I think the developer left it open to give it more of an emotional effect on the player.
That being said, if you like interactive stories, I think you will enjoy this. But treat it like a cerebral movie rather than a game. And if you're concerned about getting you're money's worth, just remember that you're paying $10 for an hour or so of entertainment with no replay value.

This game peaks before the half-way point. After that the scares get more lazy until they just stop happening and the game makes it rain batteries. Then the stealth mechanics and atmosphere are left to hold up the second half.
To avoid spoilers I'm just going to say the world is very immersive. The game throws small bits of lore at you, each one making the plot a more tangled mess until you resign yourself to understanding what's going on. This  adds to the game because horror thrives on the unknown.
Unfortunately fatigue of the unknown sets in after the game stops being able to really make the player feel in danger. I had watched at least three play-throughs of the game and it's DLC before I even owned the game. Even with vague memories of the game it still startled me a lot; squeaking, screaming, cringing, gasping, covering my face, bumping my arms on my desk... its a fun game.

In short: ToZ is a dull slog story-wise but its combat is a real joy, and I'd happily recommend the game to anyone who can stomach a JRPG story for the sake of some of the most engaging JRPG combat out there.
***
ToZ's story is half-baked and full of missed opportunities, even compared to the low standards set by some other Tales games. The game's writers seem to want you to think about the moral greyness of the Shepherd's duty, but the central characters' moral dilemmas are rarely presented in a way that seems convincing or thought-provoking.  Some of ToZ's strongest early story beats (like those involving Sorey's ambivalent relations with normal humans) drop out after a few hours, never to return. The plot twists are predictable yet drawn-out, and your playable characters have histories and motivations that are barely touched on over the course of your journey before being wrapped up abruptly dozens of hours down the road--or, in some cases, without fanfare in optional sidequests. Most cast members have interesting personalities and show good chemistry in optional dialogues ("skits"), but this chemistry rarely shows in the main quest. The one consistent shining point in this game's story and characterization for me was the bond between Sorey and Mikleo--I'm a sucker for bromance.
Visually, this game is pretty good, particularly if you install the fan patch to break the FPS cap.  (Definitely do this!)  Each town with its attached field zones has a different look, and as you go about your Shepherding duties, these areas' appearances will sometimes change a little as you work to make things better.  I thought that was a nice little reward for moving ahead in the story or engaging with the optional content.  Dungeons are a mixed bag at best: Sorey wants to explore ruins around the world, but spends most of his time running back and forth between a few towns with large open fields, and the ancient ruins that you do explore are generally dull winding corridors with slightly different tile-sets.  The four elemental dungeons are the exception to this complaint: all of them have slightly more varied layouts, fun gimmicks and puzzles (yes, even the water one!), and music that's so good you'll want to leave the game running just to have the themes on in the background.  Please, JRPG developers, keep hiring Go Shiina for your soundtracks!
The lack of creativity in most of the other dungeon designs sticks out, though, because the game will often require you to back-track through areas for story purposes. Fast travel is unlocked early, but the game commits the terrible sin of frequently locking most of your fast travel points so as to push you toward the next cutscene.  ToZ is more open-world than other Tales series entries, but many areas in the early- to mid-game are blocked off by broken bridges, groups of soldiers, and other contrivances, preventing you from exploring beyond the strict limitations set by the story.  The end result is a world that should be about the "zest" of exploration, but which feels sadly small and limited.
The game's non-combat mechanics are obtuse, and the developers made the bizarre decision to hide critical tutorials behind missable signs and conversations scattered around the world. The best thing that can be said about the equipment fusion system is that you don't need to understand it as long as you're upgrading your gear regularly and fusing things when you can.
The only downside to the game's combat is the terrible camera, which is fine in fields but not built for dungeon corridors.  In confined spaces, it frequently gets stuck in corners or jitters around wildly as you and your enemies move. At least the developers had the sense to put most boss battles in large arenas where there are few opportunities for the camera to wonk out.
Here's the thing, though: camera issues aside, the battle system is *incredibly* fun, and since this is a JRPG, you will spend 90% of your time fighting things, so 90% of this game is an absolute joy to play.  The Tales series has always been known for its active, combo-based battle systems, and ToZ draws on aspects of previous entries while throwing some new ideas into the mix.  You have a basic four-hit combo; as you play and level up, you'll learn more skills that can be chained together with different combinations of face and directional buttons (assuming that you're playing with a controller).  Defending and dodging are key as usual, especially as your attacks rely on a meter that depletes as you attack and recharges as you stand still or defend.
The biggest change is that ToZ allows some of your characters to fuse with others.  "Armatization" gives you access to new and stronger attacks and abilities in this fused form, but it also reduces the number of characters on the field to as few as two. This may not be appealing to you if you enjoy the series's multiplayer aspects, but I think it's good fun and it gives the game a different rhythm. This mechanic also encourages some strategic thinking, as your combined forms lend you new attack types and stat bonuses, but also tend to be slower and come with elemental weaknesses. (Plus, reducing the number of possible targets for an enemy can be risky.) I loved cranking up the game's difficulty and using the fuse-and-separate and attack-and-defend mechanics to rapidly heal up without opening a menu, efficiently defeat enemies, raise item drop rates, and earn that sweet sweet Grade.  This is the first Tales game that I've ever bothered to play on a higher difficulty.

Was very impressed with the game. Not a bad price at all. It seems goofy at first fighting Hiragana characters, but I began to realize quickly that I was actually recognizing the different hiragana from memory.

Firstly, let me say that I am a huge fan of the Tales series and that I follow the games mainly for their story. So if you are like me and don't care about the other aspects of the game as much, prepare to be disappointed.
The story of ToZ is lacklustre at best. It is not memorable at all and far too short. About 50h into the game I encountered an overlong and obnoxius cutscene and I thought: okay, maybe now they will reveal an unexpected plot twist that will make the second half of the game awsome. But nope, after that it was straight to final dungeon. Keep in mind that I play games like this slowly; exploring every corner, listening to every conversation, doubling back in dungeons to make sure I didn't miss any chests, not running from battlles...Even in Tales of Synphonia 2, which was pretty much made just to ride on the popularity of the original ToS, I clocked in at over 120h with my playstyle. In ToZ I was out of things to do by 60.
And don't even get me started on the characters. They are probably the weakest part of the game. In practically every Tales game there is at least one bland character and sometimes it's even the main pair (looking at you, Emil and Marta), but in this game the whole party is like that. Practically everyone can be summed up in just a couple of words: Sorey the dumb hero, Mikleo the
tagalong, Alisha the responsible little princess, Lailah the goofy lady with a secret, Rose the pure uncorruptable assassin, Edna the snarky, Dezel the mopy guy with a secret, and let's not forget Zaveid the shirtless. The secrets, if you can even call them that, are spoiled heavily and have almost no ambiguity surrounding them. The friendship between Mikleo and Sorey is handled badly too. It's too forced. The scenes where they are teasing each other are far too childlish. I get that it's supposed to convey brotherly love, but that doesn't mean they have to act like 6-year-olds.
The villians aren't any better honestly. A cazy fox dude who's evil because he's crazy, a goth loli obsessed with nihilism and a big bad bosskitty, who spends most of the game waiting for the hero to come kill him
. There is one cheap tearjerker moment
, but that is the only part when the game comes somewhat alive.
As for the other aspects: the world feels smaller than in other games, possibly because of the lack of overworld map and the checkpoint teleporttion. Looking for the vistas was kinda fun. Graphics are about the same as any other Tales game, so nothing ground-breaking. Battles are a bit boring and I found myself switching to autocombat freqently. The item combining system is confusing at start and badly explained and the lord of the land perks are frustrating, as getting them means sacrificing items you could combine.
Overall I can't really recommend this game. I got to the final boss, beat the first form, saw the cutscene, started fighting the final form and realized two things: the game had been suprisingly short and I was bored. So I quit, reloaded a save and went faffing about for another 20h. Trying to see if combining high level gear will cause a miracle and make it more interesting (spoiler: it didn't).

Video Review:
Japan produces some pretty cool stuff. Some of the best games of the last few decades have been either first released in Japan or exclusively released in Japan. A lot of the times, nice folks who know the Japanese language will translate Japanese games so that we can enjoy them to their fullest. However, that may take a while, if it ever happens at all. Besides, self-reliance is an underrated thing. Now, if you’re a chowderhead like me, then you only know one language, and that’s ‘murcan. But what if you want to broaden your horizons? You could take a Japanese course at school. But only if your school offers it, and if it’s a college course, you may be spending quite a bit of money on the course and books. You could buy Rosetta Stone, but that could cost you up to $200. I don’t know about you, but I’m not a great learner in the normal classroom setting. I’ve tried games before like My Japanese Coach, but I was bored and frustrated soon after starting. I’ve always wanted to learn Japanese, but have never found a way that works for me.
And now this is starting to sound like an infomercial, and as much as I love me some infomercials, I purchased Learn Japanese to Survive: Hiragana Battle from the Steam store on a whim the day it launched. I didn’t even know this was a thing until the day I bought it, but I saw the $7 price tag and good early reviews and figured I’d give Japanese one last shot. It’s been one of the best decisions I’ve made.
Hiragana Battle is an educational game. It teaches the player Hiragana, one of the 3 forms of the Japanese language, in the wrapper of a traditional JRPG. Misaki, your Japanese instructor, gives you lessons. You’ll then set out to the world map and fight Hiragana characters by selecting the matching sound they represent.
The story, which isn’t of much importance, goes like this: Noboru, a strange, unkempt man, is summoning Hiragana characters into the real world in hopes of taking over the land. It’s up to you and your friends to fight off the Hiragana Warriors and seal the gates before Noboru gains too much leverage and conquers Japan and all around it. But of course, you don’t know any Japanese at all, so you have hit the books before you’re able to save the world.
Hiragana Battle is made using the RPG Maker engine, an engine I quite like. And the game looks very good, for that sort of style. It does have an aura of being generic, mainly because this is how most of the games made with the RPG Maker engine look, but it’s well-done nonetheless. I never looked at anything in the game and said, “Oh, that’s just ugly.” It’s a good looking game, even if it isn’t the most impressive looking game.
The lessons are nice. Calming music plays in the background as you’re told about each Hiragana character. Unfortunately, you are going to have to break out a notebook and do some old school learning, as Misaki will ask you to practice writing each character. Even though this is by far the least fun part of the game, it's actually very beneficial as you'll more than likely need to recall back to earlier sets of characters later in the game. And although you have the option to revisit an earlier lesson with Misaki, it's a lot easier to be able to flip through a notebook. Throughout my 15-hour playthrough I took several pages of notes which gave me a much needed crutch.
You see, Hiragana Battle doesn't do a great job of mixing up all of the characters throughout the game. You'll go hours and hours without seeing some of the earlier characters and if you don't have a great memory, like myself, then you're going to have to look back in your notebook to see which character is which. There are many characters that look nearly identical with the only difference being the stroke of a final line.
Which brings me to my next qualm with the game: the confusing font. Most of the time, we see Japanese characters typed out. Whether that be on a website or in a game, you usually see the same font. Hiragana Battle includes this font in the game in their menus, but when Misaki teaches you how to write the characters, and when the characters show up in battle, they’re a more stylized version. Often times, they look different than what we read as normal Japanese font, and this can also make things very confusing for beginners. However, it does teach you to recognize the characters in different fonts, so it can be a good thing.
I was able to triumph over all of that and push forward, and soon after, I started recognizing Hiragana characters on Twitter from all the Japanese wrestling posts I see and from the man himself, Mother/Earthbound creator Shigesato Itoi. And I kept going forward. And then I started recognizing Japanese words, and that excitement continued to push me through to the end of the game. One of the more interesting things that Hiragana Battle does is, towards the end of the game, it’ll start listing items, weapons, and armor in Japanese only, so you’ll have to be able to read the word in Japanese to understand what you’re buying. There was a side-quest where some dude in Japan really wanted a Manga issue, and I had to go down to the convenience store, look at their items that were only listed in Japanese, and then read and buy the correct item to give him. The feeling I got when I read “manga” in Japanese was euphoric. It was a sign the game was truly working.
Along with the main quest, you’ll have side-quests. Most of these are fetch quests, but all of them teach you new vocabulary. You can also acquire special points from these side quests to help boost the levels of your party members.
Every RPG element about this game is pretty standard and basic. You’re not going to see any new functions. You fight enemies to earn money, you spend that money on better weapons and armor, you level up to get stronger, and you save after every battle. If all of your party members die in Hiragana Battle, it’ll reload to your last save, so make sure that you’re saving every few minutes.
Hiragana Battle isn’t a perfect game by any means. It has issues both on the RPG side and on the teaching side. I would have like to have seen some form of mnemonic teaching in the game, aka helping the player remember by relating the character to something else, like a kangaroo for ru or a pig tail for su. But then again, maybe it’s best to leave that up to the player.
Even with its flaws, Hiragana Battle is well worth the $7 asking price. $7 will teach you all the characters in the Hiragana set, plus grammar and punctuation, vocabulary, and even some common phrases. And it’ll do it in a way that keeps you engaged. It’s about time someone used the grind of RPG’s for an educational purpose. I’m sure it’s been done before, but learning the Japanese language through a traditional JRPG is just about the best combination you can come up with.
The developers, Sleepy Duck Educational Games, have plans for a sequel that will teach the next phase of the Japanese language, which they plan to call Katakana War. It’s good to know that you can invest in Hiragana Battle and be able to continue forth at some point in the same style. I will definitely be buying Katakana War, and if you’re interested in learning Japanese, I highly recommend you pick up Hiragana Battle.

The Howler, a game where you can scream as loud as your heart desires, and to this day, the only game (which I have played) where actually screaming of rage, can help you pass a level.
Graphics - Wow, just wow, every single thing here is hand drawn. Only by the sheer amount of detail, you know that those guys who did this, really poured their hearts into it. And once again for the painters wow. 9/10
Music - Deep and mysterious, it just adds to the whole aesthetic to the game, which itself is deep and mysterious. 7/10
Story - Couldn't quite understand the story, because it is mostly given to you by little chunks of story, at the start of every level. That is probably done to not spoil the book it is based of off/on, yes you heard right, a book. ''Hour of the Wolf'' by Andrius B. Tapinas. (Now I don't know, if I can post links which are not directly connected to steam, I may be mistaken) You can find the book on Amazon, for a pretty cheap price I might add. (The score is based on playing only the GAME, it may change when I get and read the book.) 5/10
Content - A few levels, but as you progress through the game, more and more mechanics are unlocked, which make every single new level, something new to be experienced. 7/10
Controls - Done by the mouse or your own voice, or any sound that you make, be that bashing your head on the desk (don't do that) or by breaking every single bone in your body (or that). Press and hold to go up, let go to go down or scream to go up, don't scream to go down. Just by having the option of using sound as a way to control the game, it gets an easy 8/10.
Gameplay - Simple, but effective. Also well paced, but I do warn you, some levels need a little bit more thinking to get through. Remember, if what you are doing does not work, try and think of a solution, rather than raging. After losing my RPG Maker VX software and all it's files due to my harddrive getting burned to a crisp, I decided to try RPG Maker VX Ace assuming that it was an improved version of VX. Sadly I'm not too impressed with what is available in VX ace.
For starters the RTP tilesets feel kinda lacking from VX, I don't have the talent to create my own assets and I just want to use this software for fun but man do the tilesets feel so limiting now. One thing that annoys me is that world map tiles and dungeon/town tiles are separated. This is annoying because I liked to mess around with differrent tiles from each side to give the map design more flavor. Plus a lot of the tiles from VX are missing too, the new tiles don't replace them sadly.
I do like the character generator though, I think it's a great idea as it allows you to essntially make a character of your own rather than a pre-set look which makes things more thematic. Other than that though it is mostly the same as VX and since VX already had compatability with 3rd party character gen tools, I don't reccommend this due to its limitations.
If you're making serious games then I don't really think it matters either way since you'll be using your own assets/scripts anyways and both use the same event system so it's still just as simple as VX. I do think that £52.99 is a steep price though. If you are going to get this I reccommend getting it on a sale, don't buy it for full price it just isn't worth your money.

Despite the ambitious plot and unusually intelligent character design, the story arc is sometimes hindered by poor pacing and lengthy, albeit well animated, cutscenes that lend themselves to some dull exposition. That said, the way the game approaches contemporary issues of race and equality with fun and engaging mechanics, as well as an upbeat soundtrack helps to propel the game's message without the typical heavy-handedness of modern arthouse/socially aware games. The use of skilltrees is one of the most interesting apects of the game. Investing in perks is an unforgiving and extremly punishing mechanic to an unattentive play, which I saw on my first playthrough. This was annoying originally, but I find it quite nicely fits in with the game's themes of choice and regret. Overall the somewhat clumsy handling of a potentially enticing plot is quickly made up for by really solid gameplay and heavily polished controls.

My negativity for this game is simply because I'm not a fan of this niche, and not for the quality of the product. I saw Rising Storm advertised within Killing Floor, but paid it no mind until I saw it as part of a Humble Indie Bundle. Seeing it got me nostalgic for the first Call of Duty (yes, I know this is not an arcadey shooter). Got it dirt cheap and gave it an install. I knew nothing of it's connection to Red Orchestra. From what I can tell there seems to be a lot quality here - the maps look GREAT on highest settings and there is so much detail in them that make them feel almost like real places. Sound effects and the risk of getting shot from god knows where makes this a deeply immersive WW2 shooter experience. However, I'm just not a fan of realistic shooters, and this game takes "realistic shooter fetish" to the highest degree, and what's worse, is with the few servers available, it seems like the player community is only interested in the "Realistic" game type. There's only multiplayer, though I found a way to play with bots on a beta version - but there is no honor/xp system that way. I saw video of a player doing Banzai rushes with the Japanese team - and they are just awesome.
In all honesty though, I found no major quality or content issues from the teeny amount of time I decided to bear with this game, and if not recommending this hurts the game's success, then I apologize to the developers and the community, I'm only stating from my personal opinion that it isn't my type of game and playing this help solidify my gaming preferences. Anybody remotely interested in a multiplayer only, realistic WW2 shooter simulation that plays somewhat similarly to Battlefield should get this game immediately, unless your system can't run it. I will personally only play it for the Steam Trading cards and MAYBE with friends, but I doubt the latter.

The Long Dark is a very simple yet challenging game. Keep fed, warm and hydrated and you will continue to live. It sounds easy, but they have done an excellent job of keeping it very challenging. Everything in the long dark is a trade off, you cut some logs that makes you tired, you sleep that makes you thirsty and hungry, you melt some snow into water and you get hungrier still, you eat and then eventually you run out of logs to cook water and food and the whole process starts again. The harsh winter weather keeps you form doing too much at a time, you will find yourself going inside to warm up after just about every small task until you get good clothing.
Usually in The Long Dark there isn't too much sleeping just for the sake of passing time though it does happen, though most the time you sleep to bipass a storm or nightfall since its pitch black at night. Your first instinct is to stockpile food and water since you can put things in cabinets and containers, and that does work pretty good. But eventually you use up all the resources in the area and will have to leave your collection behind to survive. So there really is no 100% perfect plan.
Guess you will have to try and see for yourself :p
I recommend The Long Dark!

I don’t even know how to describe this game, it starts out pretty strong as this multiple character story crime drama with some interesting ways to experience things. For example, in the first chapter my character had blood on himself and I accidentally sat in a chair, during the next chapter I was actually able to get a blood sample from that chair as a detective. That alone is something I’ve never really seen in a game before, that sort of experience however was never used again and even worse the story of an interesting crime investigation thriller turns into this weird matrix / conspiracy / cult story. (YOUR CHARACTER LITERALLY PULLS A HELECOPTER DOWN AT ONE POINT!) The game is also full of QTE’s , it’s not even a here and there thing , it’s a main gameplay mechanic. I bought this game because I really liked the Stanley Parable. However, while there are some similarities between The Beginner's Guide and The Stanley Parable, I think the qualities that made the Stanley Parable so enjoyable are lacking here.
First of all, The Beginner's Guide is not a game. It is more of an interactive commentary, in which the narrator guides you through different landscapes (in the form of short, unfinished "games" created by a developer) while analyzing the meaning of each game. You are forced to progress in a linear fashion and cannot make any choices, other than minimal dialog choices which have no efffect on the plot progression.
In the Stanley Parable, there is replay value in the form of making different choices. In this game, there is not. In addition, I completed The Beginner's Guide from start to finish in under 2 hours of game time.
While The Beginner's Guide is unique and interesting in its own right, I would classify it more as a piece of art rather than a game. It's entertaining while it lasts, and will certainly make you think. Also, I'm assuming it's a work of fiction. I won't spoil the story for you but I have to say that the ending left me in an odd mood. If it's a true story, I'm not sure how I feel about it. I think the developer left it open to give it more of an emotional effect on the player.
That being said, if you like interactive stories, I think you will enjoy this. But treat it like a cerebral movie rather than a game. And if you're concerned about getting you're money's worth, just remember that you're paying $10 for an hour or so of entertainment with no replay value.

Looming about aimlessly and adhering to scripted entry point A, then direction B does not a realistic adventure make.
The enemy for some odd unexplained reason can either,
A. Smell you (in the dark)
B. Hear you (in the dark)
C. see yo- oh wait, that's clearly impossible, it's pitch black! how is this possible?

Very interesting title in the mould of Settlers from BlueByte way back in the day. The only issue I have with this game is the fact that people are starving despite a surplus of food due to stupid AI.  They wander off into forests whilst starving instead of going to the storage barn or market and pick up food.  At some point they usually try to pick up food then promptly keel over on the way home to eat it.  They become ex-villagers but if you have a cemetery you get a nice headstone for them...
Great concept, very peaceful and even tranquil gameplay to be had if you don't zip forward the time using the options to do so but be aware of the idiotic AI which can kill off a half dozen inhabitants of your village in a short space of time through the starvation mechanics.
The graphics are pretty enough but rather basic and in saying that everything is represented as it should be and as you expect a medieval village to look.  The music is quite atmospheric and non-intrusive so you can concentrate on the task at hand without being assaulted by a cacophony of noise parading as music.
I have stopped playing this game after a relatively short period of time simply due to losing so many valuable assets from starvation.  If this is fixed by the developers then I would give it more play-time but as it stands it's pointless when so many avoidable deaths keep happening which can cripple an early settlement.  I recommend this game in the hope that these issues are addressed as if they are then this could be a cracking title to delve into.

This is a mixed bag, but I'll go on and say "Not recommended as a Tales Game"
Story: It's okay. It's definetly not bad. But it's also definetly nothing special. There's certain elements of the story that feel too much like padding (IRIS GEMS) but in general it's not
Gameplay: If you're new to the Tales Of series, you can jump in and learn the battle system without much difficulty... If you've played any Tales game before (Specifialy Graces, for example) you're not gonna enjoy this much.
Another aspect of gameplay that destroys this game is the equipment skill system: It's too relevant yet not very well explained, especially for the bonus chart on the top right: You'd better own multiple pieces of the same kind only to try and get the bonuses you want
Characters: This is the most mixed part, some of the party members are really well-written and enjoyable, namely Edna, Lailah, Alisha (DLC Required lmao) Dezel and
. But then there's Sorey, who's practically the dumbest person on the continent with a few obsessions (Namely, ruins and Mikleo), Mikleo, who's pretty much the Butt that everyone pokes fun at (Sometimes including Sorey) and has pretty much just one motivation (Again, Sorey) and Rose, a "Pure hearted" assassin with ridiculous idealism that somehow never conflicts with the... Y'know, assassin part. (Also, the Alisha DLC Story makes Rose a complete ♥♥♥♥♥)
EDIT: Adding my thoughts on the villains: First you got Generic Crazy Dude Lunarre, who's... There, I guess, he eats someone, then hungers, and that's his story. There's Symmone, who... Does... Edgy nihilist things? And Heldalf, who
The real problem with him is his actions as lord of calamity, not his backstory: While Sorey and Co. are doing the elemental shrine trials (AKA More dragging the plot out), what is he doing?
In conclusion: the game's ok, but that's it: It's ok. Tales games usually have very good stories and/or a very fun battle system, this one falls too much into the point of "Standard" to be good on the two points that matter. Plus some gimmicks (Equipment skills, Iris Gems, etc) just otherwise make the experience less enjoyable than what It should be.

I won't write about the features of the game, you can find that in other reviews. What I will write about is some tips to save yourself time and effort.
1. If you want to play the game, READ THE TUTORIALS first. There are so many things different in this game than others so be prepared.
2. Prepare to be frustrated the first few games. You are going to die a lot and may only kill 1-2 kills. This is normal until you get used to the flow of the game.
3. This game has team killing enabled, and it will not show you names of others at every moment. With 32vs32 battles things can get confusing, as you will have to shoot primarily based on the uniform the other player is wearing so learn which ones which.
4. This isn't a solo game. You will hear others organizing the attack. Follow their lead so you can win. Going solo will get you killed, and you will waste your team's reinforcements. By participating with your team and squad, you will be an asset even if you die a billion times. That being said, you don't need to actively socialize. You can keep quiet if you wish just so long as you focus on team playing.
100% recommended.

I don't play many shooters anymore, I found that they had started to feel pretty identical, and the gameplay was too shallow, and most posssessed horrid communities (I'd really rather not have some kid yelling "♥♥♥♥♥♥" into the mic, not cool dude). Red Orchestra is different. The gameplay actually requires you to think, take cover, and play intelligently, and the assault/defense gameplay encourages close co-operation and teamwork. A match on a full server is one of the most intense shooter experiences out there. Bullets whiz by your head, artillery explodes around you and you're desperately clinging to a little piece of cover firing shots off at advancing Germans/Russians, you watch as the guy in your squad next to you gets shot in the face as he moves to advance, but then that friendly tank moves into view blasting away the infantry ahead allowing you to charge forward with a hurrah. Capturing a well defended point feels like an actual accomplishment. Plus, the community is friendly and I've yet to have someone yell ♥♥♥♥♥♥ at me over the mic.

*SPOILERS*
Despite the ambitious plot and unusually intelligent character design, the story arc is sometimes hindered by poor pacing and lengthy, albeit well animated, cutscenes that lend themselves to some dull exposition. That said, the way the game approaches contemporary issues of race and equality with fun and engaging mechanics, as well as an upbeat soundtrack helps to propel the game's message without the typical heavy-handedness of modern arthouse/socially aware games. The use of skilltrees is one of the most interesting apects of the game. Investing in perks is an unforgiving and extremly punishing mechanic to an unattentive play, which I saw on my first playthrough. This was annoying originally, but I find it quite nicely fits in with the game's themes of choice and regret. Overall the somewhat clumsy handling of a potentially enticing plot is quickly made up for by really solid gameplay and heavily polished controls.

A hat in time is a cute 3D platformer, and ive been told it is an homage to old Nintendo 64 platformers like Super mario 64, ive never really played many collect-a-thons and certainly not any of the older ones but i'll admit this game has got me hooked.
I'll start with the many pros this game has and then list a couple of nitpicks i have with the game.
Pros:
- Cute graphics.
- Fun and well constructed levels and worlds.
- Amazing and catchy soundtrack.
- Workshop support A.K.A endless hours of community made levels and mods.
- It's incredibly fun to just swing around aimlessly in the world and get lost.
- Collectibles actually matter, you collect hourglasses to ofcourse progress in the story but aside from that you collect yarn to make new hats A.K.A abilities and rift tokens to unlock new cosmetics.
- A Kickstarter project that was actually not a massive dissapointment A+
Now i don't really have many "cons" to list but i have atleast a few things i would have liked to see in the game.
- A new game+ mode where you carry all your items from your safe file over to a new game, maybe even add some exclusive NG+ items to be collected (To be fair it is listed as a stretch goal on their kickstarter so a NG+ will most likely be added at some point.)
- Free roam for all worlds, There is one particular world where you start out with just wandering around with no clear goal, id have liked this as a feature for all the worlds especially the first and third. Now i can easily just pick any act in a chapter and just not do the goal but it feels sorta awkward, it's hard to explain, in any case maybe just add it when you 100% a certain world?
- Restart mission button, this one is really low on the agenda and it's more of a luxury i wish was there when i was chasing certain achievements so it's not really that big a deal, could be nice for speedrunners? if they are only speedrunning a certain level or practicing speedrunning certain levels maybe?
TL;DR
game is great with minor nitpicks, this is a cute 3D platformer that will give you hours of fun if you're into these sorts of things.

SUPERHOT is an awesome mix of a first person shooter with puzzle-like elements. This game is unforgiving with every wrong move but when you succeed and finally complete a level its extremely satisfying. It also includes a replay feature where you can save and upload all of your replays after completing a mission to their website
which seems to currently be in the beta stages.
The story is also fairly unique and the way they execute it is quite genius for the type of game it is (for example, the game will tell you to leave, and glitch out forcing you to exit the game). The game plays tricks on your mind as you navigate through the world not knowing whats next. It feels like you're playing virual reality while stuck in the matrix. Time moves when you do allowing you to plot your next move but if you move in the wrong direction or waste too much time, youre dead and have to start the level over again.
SUPERHOT is really different from any other game I have ever played and has plenty of replay value with its Endless Modes and Challenges. I highly recommend this game, although the price tag is fairly steep I would suggest looking for it cheaper elseware.

I have been searching for a good survival game for a couple weeks now, when I told my husband about my quest. He mentioned this game, I watched the trailer, and purchased.
I have to say, this is one of the BEST survival games I have played, and it is only in the Alpha stages, that is saying a lot.
I like to play on 'easy mode', no wildlife attacking me. I want to be able to explore the world that the developers have worked so hard to create, learn my stuff, and I will eventually graduate to the harder modes.
Although this, from what I have experienced so far, is not a scary game- I can't help but constantly have that eery feeling of complete alone-ness in this game. The sounds alone have made my heart sink- people screaming, people walking...just creepy. I came across a corpse earlier and darn near had a heart attack haha. The controls are easy to learn, and this is just a flat out survival game.

Well, where to start? The world is beautiful to look at. The map is huge, with aspects of land, air, and sea. Your character can run around, fly airplanes, fly helicopters, drive cars, drive boats, drive garbage trucks, drive motorcycles, drive regular trucks, drive sports cars, etc. There is so much stuff in the game.
The actual game part is mediocre with layers of annoying. Cut scenes would have been better off omitted. Story and voice overs would have been better off omitted. The vibe of the game is mediocre action movie I guess?
The camera is where annoying begins. Trying to point it in the right direction and keep it there is impossible. Getting -any- heat in the game throws on another blanket of annoying. Enemies crawl out of your backside and reign bullets down on your character with the bang of powerful lightning striking the ground from last year's biggest thunderstorm.
If that doesn't wipe your character from the face of the island the trifecta of fully loaded enemy helicopters that can shoot the wick off a candle at a thousand meters while flying upside down certainly will. The enemies keep respawning relentlessly as if popping fresh out of a clone machine folded up in your back pocket. Unlike most mediocre action movies, your character will die often in this one. And this is with the game set at normal difficulty mode, maybe easy mode would have been a better idea.
Driving vehicles in the game is like trying to maneuver a whale down a molasses filled creek in the backyard, with input lag while looking through a pinhole camera that is anchored by a balloon in a tornado. Many of the land vehicles have just enough power to propel them along only if the ground is flat, if there happens to be a small incline, backwards is the new forwards.
This game is about blowing stuff up to take over areas of interest. But to take over areas of interest you also have to find boxes scattered all over that occassionally flicker. This is unfortunate and makes taking over these points all about hide and seek. After an hour of hunting for the last box, then finding it tucked away in what looks like a garden shed made out of scrap metal, can't help but feel like the game is trolling its players time.
Not sure why I played for as long as I did. Maybe because I kept thinking that if only the island could be taken out of this game, then merged with: driving mechanics of a good driving game, flying mechanics of a good flying game, the camera from a good camera based game, story from a good story driven game...then there would be something amazing here. But that isn't this, and I'm tired of playing hide and seek with a thunderous bullet-firing cloud over my head the entire time. Not recommended.

I'm writing this review only after 40 minutes of play but I plan to play much longer! If you have ever played a game created through RPGMaker than you already know everything you need to play this game.
But you want to know if you can actually learn Japanese?
So far, I've been able to learn sounds and recognize how those sounds look if written on paper. While that doesn't seem helpful, it is a huge asset. Things get a bit trickier when "Dakuten" are introduced, making sounds you can easily remember into completely different sounds.
The game is slow paced so that you can take your time. There is no rush. Pencil/Pen and Paper is a MUST. This way you can take your lessons with you on the go, and as a helpful guide in case you forget. You can also access every lesson from your inventory after you complete the lesson and quiz. Fighting the words helps with the visual but they don't make the sounds in order to help you memorize how to pronounce the sound even when you choose the correct sound translation.
Overall, an amazing experience thus far.

Welcome to the horrid world between Death & Shadow. LIMBO.  You play as a small unnamed boy who first finds himself waking in the middle of a dark and gloomy forest.  In this 2 D scroller you’ll traverse what appears to be a dead forest and a ruined ancient city. Along the way you’ll encounter some people, small animals and deadly Monster type enemies that will either try to kill you or control you. If this doesn’t finish you off the elaborate death puzzles will. The game is played in Black and White and is lite by various lighting sources. There are some achievements to discover and you’ll soon be captivated by the angst of one small boy in search of his kid Sister. You can finish this game in about 4 to 6 hours and it does have it’s replay value as you’ll probably miss some awards the first time around. If you have an appetite for Morbid darkness, this will add some flavor to your diet.

I like the idea of a game engine that is flexible enough to make any sort of game (within a limited genre) and yet easy enough for anyone to use.  RPG Maker attempts this, and it's a lot of fun, but I'm not sure if it suceeds enough to justify actually using it for a real game.
(There are a few great games made with RPG Maker, but that only proves it is possible, it doesn't prove it is easy or that they wouldn't have been as good or better had they chosen a different engine.)
RPG Maker VX Ace is more than just a game engine.  It includes enough assets that the runtime is basically a complete topdown pixel art fantasy RPG. A very, very generic one.
It is written in Ruby.  (In never versions they replaced Ruby with JavaScript.)  But it comes with a level editor that is advanced enough to create games without modify any of the Ruby code.  (Indeed, using the Ruby API directly is documented but officially unsupported.)
The best feature is also the worst feature: that it comes with a bunch of assets and you can buy many more all in the same style.  It's good because it enables you to make a 'game' very quickly - you are just editing levels of someone else's game, in effect.  It's bad because it means most RPG Maker games all look exactly the same and are thus not very marketable.
So, would I use it?
For programmers, the event system visual programming offers very little appeal. It's just a set of macros that you select from a list rather than typing.  It's no faster than proper coding in an IDE and it is obviously limited.  It's advantage is that it can supposedly be used by non-programmers (and I'm not entirely convinced that is true).  Programmers are of course free to use the Ruby API directly, but if you know enough to do that you may as well use one of the free Ruby game engines or write your own.  I think the main use of Ruby is for programmers to publish scripts that can then be copy pasted into projects by non-programmers.  This can extend the engine's functionality greatly for them, but I suspect at a cost of quality and ease.
If you are not an artist, or you don't have time to create artwork (e.g. gamejam, prototype) the provided assets are very useful.  But then if you do use them your game looks like everybody else's.
The combat system too is going to be a reskinned Final Fantasy combat.  (Unless you replace it with a different Ruby script, but then if you want that must customisation why are you using RPG Maker and not GameMaker, Godot, etc.  This is basically a Final Fantasy game with advanced level editor remember.)  That might not be a problem - most of the successful RPG Maker games don't include any combat at all.  So then your game is basically Interative Fiction or Visual Novel.  But then why don't you use something free and designed for that like RenPy or Twine...?
I guess the main usecase for RPG Maker is if you are an artist and you do want to produce games with your own artwork but you can't/won't learn programming.  I find it difficult to recommend though.  Even doing art yourself, you still need to invest a lot of time to make a game.  10x or 100x more than you would using the default assets.  If you're investing that much already it seems that hiring someone else to program a better engine for you would be a relatively minor investment, and you would probably end up with a higher quality product at the end.
So conclusion: Valid for making hobby projects for fun using default assets (and without needing to involve a programmer if you don't want to). Valid for educational use, maybe?  Valid for artist to make a prototype of their artwork intending to replace it with better engine later.  Probably the wrong engine for anything else, but that's never stopped anybody before.
I might try checking out the older and newer versions, which are all still popular, because I suspect the balance between ease and complexity is different in each.

People don't remember this game, and that's sad.
This game is the pinnacle of 1990s PC FPS. The best game to use the fabulous Quake II engine.
A game that stirred controversy, and actually had content to back that up. This isn't some edgy just to be edgy title, the controversial content adds to the environment and the story. It's a story about a strangely steampunk dystopian 1940s-1950s setting. You'll get your fill of art deco in this game.
At its core, the game is about revenge. Revenge on the Kingpin and his liutenants, people like Nikki Blanco, who had you beaten and left for dead.
Profanity is generously offered by the NPCs, and you can respond negatively (swear at) or positively to characters through simple keypresses. Sometimes you can hire and command NPCs, as you sometimes need their specific skills. NPCs are voice acted, and your character is as well.
Money is a thing. You loot it or find it, and it allows you to hire NPCs, buy items, ammo, and upgrades.
The AI is BRUTAL. It's not unfair, but the AI is pretty devious in combat. . They notice if you are brandishing a weapon, they take cover, they shoot to kill, and they don't screw around (unless they glitch). They miss, but not much. Hard, but fair.
Soundtrack by none other than Cypress Hill! The soundtrack is fantastic, but don't let it distract you from the awesome ambient sound work that's in this game.
Overall, I think this is the best FPS of the 1990s, and it paved the way for FPS / RPG crossover games that came afterward. The controversy coused by the drug use and profanity was compunded by the fact that this was the first FPS released after the Columbine school shooting caused many major retailers to refuse to stock the game. Electronics Boutique was one of the only places you could get it, and that's a shame because this game would be put on a pedastal next to QUAKE II and UT99 as one of the best 90's shooters, but so many people missed out on it.
TL;DR: This is the best shooter of the 1900s. 11/10. Buy this.

Stylish as all hell and plays like a puzzle game with guns due to its core mechanic. Is it worth $25? I'm compelled to say no, but only as a general recommendation. Most people probably won't get $25 out of the game, but some people definitely will.
I put a lot of hours into just the proof of concept they put out forever ago, which speaks to the replayability inherent in its design: while linear overall, the spaces you're given to work in have a lot of nooks and crannies and there are often many ways to approach a level. Since you're navigating these small spaces in fractions of realtime, even the smallest bits of cover can become huge boons to you and the smallest bits of bare corridor can become deathtraps.
In this full version, there are a now bevy of modifiers and cheats that you can add in while replaying levels to spice things up, a score attack/survival mode and other nifty little extras to keep you coming back. If you're the type of person who enjoys exploiting novel mechanics, experimenting and seeing how far you can push your luck, it may be a $25 game. For people interested in the concept but not of the type to replay things over and over, I'd say $10 is the sweet spot.
Also, go play the free prototype on their website if you're unsure about the game. (Requires the Unity web plugin, so if you use Chrome, you'll have to switch to something else to play, as they cut NPAPI support a while back.) The core gameplay is almost indistinguishable from the final product and it's a hell of a lot of fun. I'm tempted to say you'll want to give these guys money just to encourage them to keep developing new concepts into the future.

I'm addicted to this game, playing at least two runs per day in the midst of playing other games.  Note this is a review of the ALPHA version, so my opinon may change as the game changes en route to release.
The Long Dark forces you to try to survive in the frozen north where there is limited food and there are wolves that attack on sight.  If you honor the spirit of the game and play without maps (posted by folks who made them), this is a very difficult game.  Even after many runs, you can find yourself in an area without any idea which direction would be best.
Typical game 1:  Start in woods area with nothing in sight but more woods, with a blizzard raging around you.  You note that you are freezing, but have no food so you can't just grab some wood, hunker down, and start a campfire.  Your choice is to try to get warm and starve to death, or keep moving in hopes you will stumble across a cabin or other shelter.  Typical outcome -- you freeze to death.
Typical game 2:  Start where you can see cabins, ice fishing huts, or where you know the general area.  Head for shelter, search and find some food and drink, maybe some more clothing, perhaps even a tool.  Step outside the cabin heading for the next one, take ten steps and "Bam!" -- a wolf attacks you.  You're dead.  Again.
After a few runs like these two typical ones, you discover how to watch for and avoid wolves (mostly -- can't always succeed), you know enough of the general layout of the map to find enough sustenance to last several days.  Then you find the dam, enter, and Fluffy kills you.
Note that there is no saving and restoring available to get around being killed.  The game saves when you enter a cabin and when you start a campfire, so you can quit the game from the menu and come back the that point.  But once you restart the game, the save is gone.
Can this be frustrating?  Oh, yes.  But you develop the urge to play, to get the thrill of finding a new location, of finding a can of peanut butter just before starving.  It's a real rush to succeed just a little bit in this game.  Some folks don't like the wolves or dying so much -- these are the same people who save and reload their way through a game and then brag about how easy winning was.
The atmosphere given by the graphics and sound really add to the game.  You can hear the weather and see the fog and snow just as if it were real.  Not state of the art graphics to be sure, but IMHO the graphics add to the flavor of the game.
The Long Dark is a 10/10 even in its current stage of developmen.

What I ininitally thought was an entertaining gimick has really matured into a great blend of innovative gameplay and interesting story from its first demo days. I love the interface the game is presented with and the overall style of the gameplay itself. The story mode is short, but in reality is the few hours-long tutorial for the endless modes and challenges that unlock upon completion. That's where the real game begins.
As far as the story mode goes, it's actually quite interesting and engaging for a game that I was expecting to be just about slicing red dudes with katanas and matrix-style bullet dodges. It's just thought-provoking enough to provide a layer of abstract substance on a game that would otherwise be just fine if it was pure action and no story. Icing on the cake, if you will.
The post singleplayer features range between endless survival modes and extra challenges on top of the single player levels. The endless mode is incredibly fun and the variations on it, including limits of in-game time or limits on real-world time are also very interesting from a puzzle perspective.
SUPERHOT is a great game. Some might think that the game is too short to warrant a higher than $20 pricetag, but that's not where the core of the gameplay is. I can see myself spending so many more hours on the endless and challenge modes than the singleplayer campaign. It's worth every second and every penny.

After the initial hype of this game blew over, I sought about seeing what might lay behind the initial glitz and face-cam jumpscares of the typical YouTube Let'sPlayers out there. What I found was, quite evidently, a labour of love by creator Scott Cawthon.
Aside from the kudos toward him for creating the game by his lonesome, it's evident that he's taken much effort to make the game as 'low-fi' as possible. The engine, Multimedia Fusion has been largely untouched since the mid-90s; upon ripping apart the game's files, you'll find all the graphics in the game are encoded in the original CompuServ GIF format - aptly debuting in 1987 (coinciding with the game's entirely ambiguous 'Bite of '87' of which you are informed of the first night); the sound is encoded in earlier versions of FruityLoops (even so far as to be from FLS1.1 - which has been largely unavailable outside of DOS discs from 1997), and even the infamous 'SCREEEE' sound when the animatronics pounce on you is, as far as I am aware, pulled from a public service announcement from the late-80s regarding child safety in the kitchen. Beyond the technical achievements (or rather, deliberate /under/achievements) of the game, the story is told outside of typical explained means, allowing the user to rely on breadcrumbs, theory and superstition - even going so far as to backmask portions of Paramahansa Yogananda's 'Autobiography of a Yogi' into the game's garbled ambience.
Cawthon's done as much as possible to set the game's mood, and while its threats reside nigh-entirely in recyclable (and eventually predictable) jumpscares, the atmosphere, sense of isolation, memorable characters, and easily-grasped,  simple mechanics serve a purpose to make this a refreshing and, in a way, quite charming survival-horror game - of which I'm glad to hear will be sequelised.
