Easily one of the best horror games I've played in recent memory, and the DLC is equally well done--a feat not many games can boast. I played this with my roommates when we were freshman in college and it bonded us for life in our shared terror and outrageously girlish shrieks; we still go back and play it some nights just for fear-fun and for nolstalgia.
+Solid graphics, even for its age
+Cramp, suffocating environments with oppressive levels of darkness and an excellent, if not a bit cliched, setting
+Protagonists that you genuinely feel bad for having to go through all this♥♥♥♥♥♥
+Some really interesting characters, antagonist-wise; they really stole the show for me
+Highly recommended DLC, which wraps up some questions presented in the main game
+Not overly reliant on cheaper jumpscares to get the fear done
+Excellent use of spooky audio
-Game's plot is not really all that strong, sort of loses its way in the third act...still interesting, though, and there's plenty for you if you're the type that's painstaking about reading notes
-Wish some of the antagonists had a little more screentime or got used more often...the Twins in particular, who you'll be introduced to fairly early on
-Low enemy variety, but that didn't really bother me too much
-Maybe don't play it right before bed
Overall, my complaints are minor at worst and nitpicky at best. I can wholeheartedly recommend this game and it's DLC to you, especially for the price. If you're on the fence about Outlast/Whistleblower vs. Outlast 2 and you haven't played either and just want to buy one, I'd recommend Outlast and, perhaps, its DLC if you have a little extra to spare; there's a lot of great bundle deals on PC and on PS4 as well if you're interested in picking them up for a very affordable price. There's no big story continuity aside from a single note between Outlast and Outlast 2 so I don't recommend the first one over the second one for that reason; rather, I think, personally, that Outlast 1 does and understands horror a bit better than its sequel, and I think the plot and characters are more fleshed out and interesting as well. If you're in the market for a good horror game, I'd definitely recommend you give Outlast a shot.

I've played most of the "Tales of" games and although Zestiria is better than a few of them, it suffers from the same issues all the other games have: the script is written by little kids. The characters are always one dimensional, unrelatable and contrived. The dialogue is full of cliches and is often mind-numbingly empty. The overall plot is another run-of-the-mill "You're special, now save the world" storylines. These games would be so much better if they were written for an adult audience.
Another issue is the battle system. I'm still getting tutorials on how to fight battles after six hours of game time. I'm serious. The battle system feels overly convoluted for no real reason. You're simply hammering the same buttons over and over but the game introduces new mechanics after every battle. The combat is no different than any other Tales games, but for whatever reason, they had to make up a bunch of complex meta-mechanics that aren't even needed. Simple would have been preferred because combat is already chaotic enough.

This was an interesting game.  Much of the game is dark purposely making you use the character's camera which has a night vision setting. So half of the game if not more is seen in this greenish dark picture where you can't see more than 8-10 feet ahead of yourself.  There's also an annoying grainy setting that stays throughout the whole game that I tried unsuccessfully to remove.  Overall though, it's an impressive effort for an indie game.  The sound is the star of the game.  Combined with the legitimately tense and errie setting it's a powerful facet of the game.  Many of the cues of when to move and react come from the sound and the developers made good use of it.  When the game first starts you don't really know what to expect and the gameplay seems fairly unique.  As the game goes on, the scaryness and tenseness of the game dimishes as you realize how easy it is to manipulate the mechanics of the game and how easy it is to avoid death even when being caught multiple times by a character.  It's disappointing and the simplicity of the gameplay starts to show.
It's a single player only game with no other features to play with after the game's over and it's a pretty short game.  It's hard to say the game is ever fun at any point because it's the type of game that tries to make you a nervous wreck 100% of the time.  It is a good change of pace from most of the other games out and a unique experience worth playing through at least once.
Single Player Play Time - 5-6 hours

The Howler is a beautiful but whisper-thin sort of puzzle game that'll provide you with about an hour of entertainment. You pilot a balloon through a very nicely handpainted 2D representation of Vilnius, Lithuania, done up all steampunk-like. You press the mouse button to provide thrust which carries the balloon higher—steering is left up to the winds which're denoted on the side of the screen. Using those winds you steer around, over, and under obstacles and enemies to reach your goal, which always consists of picking up and/or dropping off items before plopping down on a landing pad elsewhere in the level.
That's really it. Lunar Lander with some extra physics. There's a story attached involving impending riots and your efforts to stave them off supposedly taken from or relating in some way to the Lithuanian novel
, but like the rest of the game it's pretty insubstantial.
There's also an option to use your PC's microphone to control the balloon with your voice, which I didn't use at all. One, it feels like a bit of a gimmick which I don't consider to be either innovative or even essential to gameplay. If the voice commands were integrated into the experience in some way that made them inseperable—or even more effective than just clicking the mouse—I might take the concept seriously, but it seems more like the developer asking you to handicap yourself to make its game seem deeper than it really is. You can play Snake with a Dance Dance Revolution pad, but that doesn't make it innovative, it's still just Snake. Two, I have roommates.
All that said the levels are well designed—occasionally cunningly so—and it is very well presented with lovely artwork and music, giving the game a cohesive style that kept me relatively engrossed for the 58 minutes it lasted.

A Hat in Time progresses similiar to Mario64 and - I hear, Mario Sunshine. The game is separated into chapters, which are further separated into different acts. You can do them in the order you want and return to them at any time, assuming you have enough stars - I mean, timepieces to unlock them.
The game has huge worlds that are filled to the brim with content and collectibles, the soundtrack adjusts according to the area you are in to set the mood, the visuals are excellent and the gameplay is what I really enjoy in this game.
It's a cute-as-heck 3D Platformer and the way the camera and your character move in the game are excellent. The controls are tight and the character handles well, you can make long jumps and flips from the tiniest branch of a tree to the next with no trouble. You almost have too much movement as you can skip most of the puzzles and long platforming sections with no upgrades or abilities, just the basic jumping and diving abilities.
A Hat in Time shows what a kickstarter project can be when done right.

DISCLAIMER: I REVIEWED THIS GAME WHILE IT WAS IN EARLY ACCESS (it still is), SO THE GAME ISN'T FINISHED YET. There's something about The Long Dark that makes me love it. I don't know if it's the graphics, the gameplay mechanics, or even the survival experience of it all. The graphics have a calm feeling to them, and they're beautiful. When you die, you have to restart the entire game, which is great. You can be a boy or a girl, and you get to pick one of two maps. There are three different survival experiences you can choose from. One is based on survival, and the other is based on exploration. The third option is a mix of the two. You will get eaten by wolves a lot, but that just makes it more fun. This game is true survival in the Canadian wilderness. If you drink unpurified water (yes, you can drink toilet water in the game) then you can get sick. You can also get sick from raw meat, or getting bitten by a wolf. Then, you have to have the right supplies such as bandages and pain killers. The game has a nice crafting element in it as well, which adds to the survival experience. If you're buying this game thinking you'll get something like Rust or Minecraft, you're wrong. This is a unique game, and I can't think of a single other game like it. This is one of my favorite games ever, and I highly reccomend it.

Let me say one thing just to clear things up: I'm a huge horror fan, but at the same time, I hate scary things. Outlast, though, is one horror game that has made me more of a horror fan than ever before. Outlast is a game that puts you in the shoes of journalist Miles Upshur, and your job is to go into Mount Massive Asylum and collect evidence of the illegal activity that the Murkoff Corporation is secretly performing. Easy, right?
. You instead discover that the insane inmates of the asylum are loose, and ready to kill. This game has unique jumpscares for all kinds of horror fans, an amazing soundtrack with noises you thought some instruments would never make, immersive atmosphere and sound effects, and brilliant voice acting and narratives (by that I mean the notes that Miles can write). The graphics are also the best I've ever seen in a horror game. A little too good, actually. If you've seen any screenshots with any of the game's blood and gore in it, you'll know what I mean. The nightvision feature in the game just serves to make the game even more terrifying, as when it is active, any eyes you see (whether they're attatched or not) seem to glow in the dark, and sometimes that's all you can see of an enemy when you're trying to sneak past it. I would give the entire game a rating of 9.9/10. It has everything you want in a horror game (not literally), and then some. Needless to say, Outlast is a game that drags you into the hell that it wants to show you, and doesn't want you to leave.

What I ininitally thought was an entertaining gimick has really matured into a great blend of innovative gameplay and interesting story from its first demo days. I love the interface the game is presented with and the overall style of the gameplay itself. The story mode is short, but in reality is the few hours-long tutorial for the endless modes and challenges that unlock upon completion. That's where the real game begins.
As far as the story mode goes, it's actually quite interesting and engaging for a game that I was expecting to be just about slicing red dudes with katanas and matrix-style bullet dodges. It's just thought-provoking enough to provide a layer of abstract substance on a game that would otherwise be just fine if it was pure action and no story. Icing on the cake, if you will.
The post singleplayer features range between endless survival modes and extra challenges on top of the single player levels. The endless mode is incredibly fun and the variations on it, including limits of in-game time or limits on real-world time are also very interesting from a puzzle perspective.
SUPERHOT is a great game. Some might think that the game is too short to warrant a higher than $20 pricetag, but that's not where the core of the gameplay is. I can see myself spending so many more hours on the endless and challenge modes than the singleplayer campaign. It's worth every second and every penny.

Let me start off by saying - I am nowhere near finished. 16 hours in, I can still see tons of conflicts to be resolved, and have accidentally wandered into many maps that I wasn't supposed to yet(and subsequently got wrecked by the mobs there). However, I wanted to convince any potential buyers out there that this game is absolutely worth the price, even if not on sale. Some things I'd like to point out to potential buyers include the combat system, as it's different from any other RPG I've ever played(coming from games like final fantasy, withthis being my first tales of game). You can have up to four people in battle, and you actively control one character, whereas the rest of them are automatically controlled by a computer. I suppose the easiest way to describe it would be an "open-world combat" in an encounter battle. The game is not too hard, with adjustable difficulty. However, without doing some grinding, it can be hard to clear some boss battles. Finally, the storyline is very anime(speaking of which, there's now a great anime based on this game that's currently airing!), so it's good for fans of that. Be warned though, the game feels like it has a very slow start, at least to me. The game will very quickly suck you in though!

Pros:

+Character animations are really good.
+Lots of Exploration and optional content.
+Likeable main characters(Though they have cliche personalities.)
+Your team's AI is good at supporting you.
+Good humor(Both between character converstaions and item/monster descriptions.)
+Wide range of enemy variations(apart from some of model and palette swaps), especially for equipments.)
+Awesome and memorable soundtracks.
+Attachments have physics.
+Little fun skits for nearly everything.
Cons:
-I said that AI is good at supporting you right? Well...thats the most that they can do. In fact they are so selfless, they don't even care about themselves most of the time which they often get KO'd and that is not really good when you want to achieve a good grade or win the battle.
-The only bug?? I've encountered is that sometimes in game menus(like shops or equipment screen etc.) the confirm button doesn't work.
-The skits that can be easily missed if you don't really know how to get them and there are lots of skits in the game.
-The combat can be frustrating sometimes. One of the reasons is that most of the enemies move fast as you. When you are alone with horde of enemies and low at hp, you need to get away and heal yourself right?.....Oooh boy, good luck with that, since you will need it.
-The ending of Alisha's DLC story....like wtf was that ending?? Even the achievement you get from it makes fun of the ending. It was a good troll 8/8.
Mixed:
+/-The battle system is confusing and hard to keep up sometimes, but its not extremely hard.
+/-The endboss was kinda lackluster but eh, I enjoyed it anyway and it was cool so I'm forgiving it.
Sooooooo......would I recommend playing this game?

Hey and welcome to my review for Banished! I hope you enjoy reading this and it teaches you something about the game that you may want to know before purchasing or playing!
Summary:
Banished is a fun almost RTS city building survival game.
Depending on what difficulty you choose, you start with a few people and maybe some houses and different supplies.
From that point, your main goal is balance. You don't want to expand too fast or else you'll have too many people to feed and not enough space, but you dont want to not expand at all, and see your small village soon die off.
Starting by gathering materials, you want to balance out your laborers into different jobs to do things such as: fishing, tree cutting, educating, herb collecting, trading and many more.
All of these jobs factor into your villages happiness and wellfare and the expansion of your village.
So to start, Banished is very unique in the way that it is more about being a stable community, rather than a huge empire that controls everything.
Pros:
Randomly generated maps
Lots of ways to start
Weather
Good looking graphics
Workshop support
Lots of different buildings
Good Soundtrack
Replayable!
Cons:
Sometimes resources (mostly stone) can be hard to acquire and you can be without stone for quite a while, which leads me to my next con:
Merchant are way too far and wide, im aware that you can build more trading posts for more, but when youve ran out of materials and you have to relay on merchants for things like stone, its almost impossible.
Alot of waiting, which can be helped by speeding up time, but still alot of waiting.
All in all I would reccomend this game for anyone who wants a game that they can play for an hour or two at a time and have great fun with it!

I nominate this game Kingpin;
Let me tell you something about this game first…it was released in a time when PC gaming was faced with the likes of Unreal, Quake, Duke Nukem...I would beg borrow and steal to afford games, it usually resulted in me buying them, downloading a new .EXE file and taking the game back to game for a refund..…
but I will admit when I first encountered this game on a website that allowed one to steal without buying it first… (a bit like the torrents of today) it was one of the first games I actually paid money for and kept because It deserved it!
Because back in the day it was a benchmark in PC gaming. It was one of the first games to feature amazingly skinned graphics (especially using 2 voodoo 2 cards in SLI mode to get an impressive 1024x768 graphics!!), the story line was very interesting...it allowed the control of NPC body guards… the sort you could direct what to do and actually set them upon a junkie that needs a crowbar over the head…
The sounds and music are awesome, so awesome in fact the game got banned in many countries for its obscene profanity that it featured and I have to mention, the game has guns & blood / gore. everything a man needed all those years ago.
It was also one of the first; first person shooters i actually enjoying playing online, it was released about the time of unreal and I found this game so addictive I splurged out on a ISDN connection for a better ping… to get an edge over my American friends that all had t1 connections e.t.c. which was about a weeks wages in rental costs from British Telecom…
See games like unreal / quake and the likes never took my fancy because I have a problem being inside a sci fi story… but this game was different… it took me into the hood with homies and gangsters and all that stuff you see on SKY 1 cops..… it was an epic adventure… so epic I bought It again in 2016….
While its practically impossible to get a server full nowadays back in its day the servers where bouncing with hordes of players. With that i met a great community of players all those years ago… the game also got me to found a clan, I even learned html to code a website / forum for my henchies… (a time before you could go online an rent / buy a pre coded version)
it came with a gamespy client. We used to jump into unreal chat and give all those players a real hard slagging off for loving another crap sci fi game with no soul…
Unfortunately i have lost contact with all my old {THUGS NOW}. but who knows or remembers {ThUg Pioneer?} ... well if you do.... hit me up im sure you have all aged well!!
While I will admit playing the game now in 2016 doesn’t have the same feel of "wow this game is impressive" with its awesome graphics… i do find it touches my heart and soul with all the memories the game gave me…
but I will say the story line and ingame control still rivals a lot of games today, and for the cost of a few beers its worthy of any game collection.
Long live Kingpin!

While Red Orchestra 2 had the potential to become a real 'game changer' in the area of realistic and tactical shooters, several important shortcomings and at least one disastrous multiplayer decision ended up sabotaging the game's sincere efforts at carving out its own niche in the era of increasingly generic Call of Duty and Battlefield titles.
Those shortcomings include clumsy (and often glitched) controls (eg. cover system that 'sticks' a player to a wall), map errors (eg. Barishka map traps tanks in a lag cycle), imbalanced weapons (eg. overpowered machine guns and 'spray and pray' autos) and very dated graphics.
Its fatal flaw, however, was Tripwire Interactive's decision to allow third party server managers to control the multiplayer experence of this game.  From absurd game changing manipulation (eg. changing the number of tickets) to abusive moderators (eg. 2fjgclan is one the noted offenders in this regard as they often brag about the number of RO2 owners they have banned from their servers), Tripwire Interactive has let many parties who are not associated with RO2 to essentially ruin (or otherwise block) the multiplayer experience for owners of the game.

"Review RPG Maker VX Ace!" a friend told me today.
"Why?" I asked. "It's not a game."
"Because I'll plow your♥♥♥♥♥like a white plantation owner with a timeshare if you don't."
Okay okay, put that jackhammer away, I'll do it! Sheesh, relationships are tricky.
RPG Maker VX Ace... I'm not really sure what to say about it. It has a lot more features than RPG Maker 2000, which is the only one I can claim any familiarity with. In theory you can rewrite parts of the game engine to change the battle system to whatever you want, and I am sure you can make games other than RPGs with it (though why you would want to when Game Maker Studio is available I can only speculate). I feel the included resources are a little derpy-looking but there are too few of them to make a full game by themselves anyway. There seems to be less community support than the venerable RM2K, with many people claiming "ohoho u dnt need tilesets cuz u can do a parallalax backgrnd lol" ignoring the fact that a lot of people CAN'T ♥♥♥♥ING DRAW. So if you want to make a quick and dirty RPG to laugh about with your friends I don't feel like this is the one for you. A serious game should probably be assembled in the aforementioned Game Maker Studio, and a less serious game can benefit from something with less demanding art asset requirements like RPG Maker 2000.
But then, I'm a grouchy old man so who cares about my opinion...

A complete mess of a game. 11 hours wasted.
The first third of the game is a detective with a really, really great opening. It's very interesting and mysterious. The voice acting is okay, and the characters are likable and interesting.
There's this alternating mechanic where you're playing as the guy who unwillingly committed a murder, and then you're playing as the detectives investigating him. It makes you want to keep playing. The best part is when the detectives and the main guy's paths intervene.
The second third gets sillier. I'm not a big fan of the Matrix movies, but it can be pretty much summed up as what Reloaded was to the original. More of the same, but dumber, sillier, and less interesting this time around.
There are some good parts where the detectives start making connections to the protagonist, and some neat horror elements, but other than that, there's not much new here. The mystery goes away as some nonsense Illuminati plot is revealed and the hero gets Matrix-like superhero powers. There's also some nonsense about the character having been involved in some supernatural incident in his childhood.
The last third is the worst part of the game. This part is completely divorced from the suspenseful detective thriller that the game introduced itself as. Characters' personalities get demolished. They were likable at the beginning, but not incredibly unique. This time, they're not likable, and they're even less unique.
The superpowers get crazier. The main character is a zombie now. The female lead, originally a strong woman, now falls in love with the frozen zombie, completely breaking her character, and they have awkward sex in a train car. The most likable lead, the black guy, disappears.
The plot is revealed to actually be a bunch of cobbled together, crappy, unfinished conspiracy theories thrown in. The Aztec clan is fighting with the AI Robot clan to obtain an indigo child who knows the truth of the world. Tie that in with some Mayan apocalypse nonsense. Then everything is resolved magically.
To top it all of, the "remaster" is about as barebones as you can get. There have been many cases of remasters being released recently where the only difference is that they run better, have hi-res support, some updated textures (while others are ignored), and have some better effects. Other than high-res support and a few improved textures, I really didn't see any improvement here.
The controls suck. The PC controls are horrible, so you pretty much have to use a controller. I used an Xbox 360 wired controller, and while it worked much better than the standard PC controls, there were still some issues, especially with the movement and the quick-time events.
33% a good detective thriller, 33% silly explanations for what actually happened, 33% Matrix Illuminati nonsense. 100% a waste of time.

The remaster of this cult classic holds up as well as a bottle of spoiled wine: it gets the buzz on, but makes you cringe most of the way through. While offering a gripping story with real cinematic qualities and innovative mechanics ahead of its time, it is mired by outdated visuals (even remastered), QTEs and a slew of other issues, both minor and major. Still kinda fun to play, but hard to whole-heartedly recommend to anyone but a die-hard fan. As one of them, I sure hope this is not the definite edition.
I first played the original around its release in early 2006 and I still have a box with it somewhere, but as much as I enjoyed the interactive storytelling, I didn’t finish it then, discouraged by the ridiculously frequent and difficult QTEs. After many years, however, I decided to give the remaster of this cult classic a second chance.
(+) one of the best openings in the history of video games kicks off an instantly gripping story with parallel and intersecting plots that pit the fugitive Lucas Kane against the NYPD investigators Carla Valenti and Tyler Miles (the three POW characters) in a protracted, forty-odd-chapter game of cat(s) and mouse with many twists and turns along the way
(+) some parallel plotlines let you choose an order in which to follow the protagonists’ specific chapters, a few even let you switch back and forth between the protagonists in a single chapter with each of them given different tasks to accomplish
(+) the main cast is properly fleshed out through their interactions with secondary characters and their everyday environments, offering the player a chance to actively participate in their mundane professional duties or a peek into their personal routines and private musings
(+) solid voice acting by professionals, but suffers from the wooden writing occasionally
(+) mechanically ahead of its time due to its timed dialogues and illusion of choice (akin to Telltale games’ formula), emotional state meter (typical of today’s horror survival games), QTEs (a staple of the modern action adventure), multi-frame shots (reminiscent of
TV series), cinematic camera angles and extensive use of motion capture, all integral parts of an “interactive drama experience”, to quote the buzzword frequently invoked by the developers
(+) a wide mix of gameplay mechanics: item interactions, timed dialogue selections, QTEs (of a colour-coded Simon Says or alternate-button-mashing variety), timed interactive sequences, stealth sections; often combined within a single chapter
(+) a tutorial is included and highly recommended to learn the ropes and understand the mechanics
(+) atmospheric music by Angelo Badalamenti, a regular collaborator of David Lynch, and the late Normand Corbeil, a composer for the subsequent Quantic Dream’s PlayStation exclusives, Heavy Rain and Beyond: Two Souls
(+) extra content preserved from the original in the form of movies (low-resolution making-of videos or in-engine clips), soundtrack, concept art and replayable action sequences, most of which can be easily unlocked by spending bonus points gathered by collecting bonus cards during a playthrough or awarded automatically upon every game completion
(+) the textures remastered in HD by Aspyr advance the visuals somewhat, making them look a little less outdated (the early PS3 era quality)
(+) the original and the remastered textures can be switched back and forth at the press of a button
(+) supports higher resolutions and widescreen aspect ratio, but the screen is still letterboxed with black mattes above and below to imitate a movie
(+) restores the original title and vision by including the nude scenes previously cut from the censored North American version (curtesy of GTA: San Andreas’ hot coffee controversy)
(+) playable with a mouse and keyboard (but somewhat inconvenient)
(+) adds partial support for a handful of controllers, though an Xbox gamepad is highly preferable
(−) the story has a brilliant set-up but progressively runs out of steam with a noticeable tonal shift around the halfway mark
, as if the developers couldn’t decide what movie genre they want to imitate and ended up aping several, turning the last act into a messy mashup of overly ambitious and hardly compatible ideas
(−) David Cage’s inconsistent writing: rarely brilliant, mostly passable, truly pretentious or overly expository at times, but his creative ideas are enough to keep you entertained at the very least
(−) a ridiculous amount of QTEs that can be so frantic and frustrating (even on Easy difficulty) as to at least distract from, if not obscure altogether the often drawn-out, over-the-top action sequences on screen
(−) the touted “interactive drama experience” is constantly undermined by typical gaming, immersion-breaking elements such as the collectible cards and talismans, on-screen prompts, or the above mentioned QTEs, emotional state meter and life indicator
(−) the stealth segments, as in many games with no proper stealth mechanics, are an unnecessary drag
(−) the mo-cap doesn’t really lend itself to the 2005 character models and animations, which makes the action sequences look floaty like
and
at their worst
(−) a distinct lack of modern quality-of-life features: the checkpoints are few and far between, which makes repeating some long action sequences over and over a real chore; unskippable cutscenes and dialogues are equally annoying if you want or need to repeat a whole chapter
(−) the remaster upgrades the textures, but the difference is not that noticeable, to be honest: I had to switch back and forth between them a few times to be sure which were which
(−) the original meshes are retained, making the models look as blocky as before
(−) the switch between the original and the updated graphics is not at all seamless, revealing the messy inner workings whenever you push the button
(−) the restored nude scenes feel pointless, and as awkward and robotic as ever
(−) no developers’ commentary, which is a unique selling point for many remasters
(−) keyboard and mouse controls are inconvenient at best as they sometimes require switching one hand between the keyboard and the mouse, especially in the sections involving both action sequences and dialogue

I was one of those kids who was afraid of the animatronics at Chuck E. Cheese's, so naturally this game creeps me the heck out.  Since this is a horror game, that means mission accomplished.
What makes the game work is that it's a "damned if you do, damned if you don't" scenario.  You NEED to keep an eye on the security cameras or else 2 of the enemies will get you, but you also NEED to stop looking at the cameras and check the hallways right outside your doorways or else the other 2 will get you.  There's no way to do both at once; you're always vulnerable to something if you're not precise with your actions, and if a single robot animal gets into your room a single time, you're dead.
The game does get slightly repetitive once you get a good pattern going, but in a way it adds to the atmosphere.  In-game the protagonist has to survive for 6 hours each night.  Imagine being stuck in a run-down restaurant for 6 hours a night, 5 nights a week, with killer robots out to get you, with no way to fight them off (You'd actually be fired for damaging the robots!), and limited power to keep them out of your one safe zone.  You don't have time to come up with a crazy involved plan for showing your boss the characters are dangerous, you need to do find the most efficient way possible of staying alive, as a single misstep means a quite literal game over.
The scariest, most terrifying, or simply creepiest horror games are built upon atmosphere, and this game's got lots of it.

Hi guys,
This is not a typical review, but it might give a very important hint to someone who is new to The Long Dark, supposed one wants to have the most possible fun and challenge when playing a game and I think this should be the claim in every game, isn't it.
Please excuse my style of writing in English. It is not my native language but I wanted to do this "review" in English as I think it is important for everybody who is new to TLD.
I supported TLD and bought it because I think the guys from Hinterland deserve it and I am really looking forward of getting much more out of this game.
OK, I suppose you are interested in TLD or even played already a first round and tried your first steps.
Now, start by asking yourself, "What do I expect from this game...?"
It's obvious, TLD is a different kind of computer game. It has nothing to do with the common shooter type, hunting for enemies and zombies or similar kind of more or less realistic wild west style of games. And yes - the graphics are average compared to what is possible today. And to make it even worse, TLD is a single player game in times when in the gaming industry the economic success is mainly coming from games, which are programmed to be multiplayer or even MMOGs. I mean we have all seen complex games like BF and alike and know what's in fact possible. Sure I know that Hinterland as a small company is in no way comparable to DICE or the other big game producers, but at the end of the day, it's the  game user who decides what to play for a similar price.
So you might ask yourself, what's the use of spending time in TLD?
Well, TLD is in the alpha phase with only two playable maps so far and there are still a couple of bugs. But important as this all may appear, it's not if you know how to handle it and why you want to play this game. TLD is different, it's an indie type of game with the flavor of an exploration and survival simulation.
You are a pilot and a victim of an airplane crash somewhere in the northern Canadian wilderness. You don't have much with you, nothing to eat or to drink, no weapon and especially no compass or gps or something what tells you, where you are. The only thing you know is, that you are in a huge forest. Your task in the game is to survive as long as it's possible. Why all the people you will find around are dead but not the animals is unknown. Maybe the storyline will bring this up one day and may even bring you back to the civilization, but for now just accept it, it's a fact in TLD and increases the suspense. So far, so good.
Now, there are several ways how to succeed in this disquieting situation. I will not go deeper into this, as there are a couple of fine guides out there from some committed community members and there is no use for me to invent the wheel twice. Please refer to these guides, they are important for a new player in TLD and really help a lot.
But you will also find some guides here and there which offer maps of the TLD landscape.
And here it comes,
my most PRECIOUS HINT:

By all means, DON'T USE MAPS in The Long Dark or you will spoil yourself the most interesting part of this game. The idea of TLD is NOT to check a map, running to these known spots, finding all the stuff you need to survive, and at the end (hahaha)  complaining that the game is "easy, crap and boring".
If we are really using maps to walk around and to find all the hidden secrets - I mean don't let's be ridiculous, that's kindergarten and as I said, not the idea of the game - why playing it then when there are others around?
Try to stay honest to yourself, just stay the brave adventurer who crashed in a plane and play your role. Find yourself lying in the snow underneath or near a rock after spawning, not knowing where you are and where to go. Be bold and decide the direction where to go next and you will be fine after a while. Maybe you find the sun in the sky if the weather is favorable enough to allow it, this gives you at least a certain idea about the time of day. Never walk into the night or in a storm! Learn how to prepare food and drink.
Just allow yourself the suspense of being lost in the wilderness, lost in the cold and really try to find your way through the game. After a couple of sandbox trials you will know better and find your path anyway, since the playable maps are still small. Beware of wolves, stay away or surpass them, they are really dangerous and can end the round in seconds. At this point there is even something of a simulation in the game. Just feel the situation, feel the idea of this game and it will be YOUR game.
This is the little secret for me and those who love The Long Dark
You will soon see, it's not rocket science to find the first cabin or even a house and it is much more fun to play this unusual game as is instead of just looking into an offered community map, only to see that the next house is just around the next hill. These guys from Hinterland are still developing TLD but offered us the sensation to already being part of it.
So, my advice is, if you really want to have most out of TLD, don't use maps - ahh - by the way, our pilot doesn't have maps neither, they all burned down in the crash :-)
He is smart enough to find his way alone, will you also do it?

This is an early stage review of only the sandbox.
Now, I love a good survival game, I love the concept of managing your resources,
and making educated choices based on your condition.
And this game does exactly that, it's putting you in a harsh environment to fend for yourself.
With each step you take you pray for an easy weather, some food and that you'll find and a shelter.
On a personal note,  I love the outdoors, and take a intrest in survival (though my surrounding is more of a desert),
so I find this game much to my liking.
My expirence so far:
I entered the game in a forrest clearring, already freezing and hungry, in a middle of a storm.
I've found a ruined cabin and stayed there untill the storm have passed.
I knew I need to find a good base and a good supply of food so I ventured out to seek such place.
I came across a railroad, and thinking that I might stumble on some buildings on it's path, I followed it to the east.
I found a cabin by a lake and have made my homebase there. found a steady supply of food from fishing and hunting near by, while saving all the canned food for later. From that base I'd scout around to find more supplies and craft better suited gear. I was in luck, others weren't as lucky.
It was a simple few hours, but I enjoyed it all.
Some pros to the game:
1. Immersive harsh environment.
2. The cartoonish style makes everything look beautiful.
3. Great crafting system.
4. Easy to use and understand UI.
5. Wildlife and its reaction to you and your actions was great, I really feared meeting with a wolf at first.
6. Immersive cues of your condition.
7. Great atmosphere.
Some things which I didn't like or find missing, and would love if the devs will consider it:
1. Weather clues. When I travel or backpack, I always look for the shape of the clouds or a sign to bad weather, so I'll know to seek a shelter, make camp or to get to a high ground to avoid a flood. The game has no warnings, snow and blizzards hit without you having any way to predict it.
2. The terrain. The game has no logical terrain flow, it has cells that don't match topographically. In the real world, the terrain has a flow, there are ridges with high points, there are slopes that conjure a basin that flows and drains to some direction. It's a basic rule in navigation to follow the water and where it flows, to understand the terrain and your position. I wish the level design would be arranged like that, though I still enjoyed it, it only bugged me because it's easier for me to navigate like that.
3. A map and a journal. The idea of not having a map in a survival game, I would prefer a map that I can draw myself in game (I actually drew a simple map in a notebook while playing the game), also it bugged me that the camp office didn't have a map of the surroundings. And I know there is a journal that records your discoveries, but I would love to edit my own enteries. In a combination with a map and journal you can mark best hunting spots, best places for traps and snares, stashes and possible shelters to expand your exploration area whilist keeping a safehouse. In my opinion it will greatly infuse and improve the immersive roleplaying.
4. Other survivors. Now this is something I'm not completly sure about, but I think there should be others in the game. It should be rare to encounter someone else, but the idea that you would compete on resources with others or maybe joining up and sharing, really calls to me. Though the feeling of loneliness adds to this game's survival aspect, I think that adding that element will add to the challenge. I think that NPCs are a better choice or maybe up to 5 players on a huge map.
Finale notes:
All in all I enjoyed this game very much. If you're into survival you should buy it even without the story mode just for the snadbox. You'll love it.

Why I love Five Nights at Freddy’s 1
Now like many of you I was a skeptic for this game. I thought: Surely this game isn’t that scary. So I bought the first game.
I click new game and was greeted with the following message from phone guy.
I thought oh how nice. At least this guy’s friendly.
“
At this point it started to get ominous. I thought: “What do you MEAN death?!”

It was at this point I fell in love with the animatronics and I even felt bad for them.
At this point I got the chills. I froze with fear.

This calmed me down a bit. I thought “Oh well that doesn’t sound too bad.”

And with this the fear was back. “WHAT?!” I screamed.
“But hey! First day should be a breeze, I’ll chat with you tomorrow, uhh, check those cameras, and remember to close the doors only if absolutely necessary. Gotta conserve power. Alright. Goodnight.”
And with this the gameplay started. One of the first things I noticed was that I can’t move. That was truly terrifying. At least in other horror games you can run away from the things trying to kill you.
I checked the cameras as I was supposed to. Everything was fine until 3 am. That’s when it really got ominous. One was missing. So the guy wasn’t crazy after all. I wasn’t really paying attention to him, though I did listen so I was lost.
I figured it out but at four a.m. I experienced my first jumpscare: Bonnie.
He was the first one to kill me and because of that I fell in love with him.
My second jumpscare was Freddy. Freddy was just meh for me. He was just a big teddy bear for me.
Next was Foxy. Oh man Foxy. I froze when I heard him bag on the door, and when he screamed bloody murder at me, I jumped back what felt like teen feet.
I never did get Chica or Golden Freddy though.

as a huge fan of the series who started with tales of phantasia on an emulator, it pains me to say this:
tales of zestiria tells a very cheesy tale, which is suprising, given most of the other tales-games really explored difficult themes, even if the way they did it aren't everyones cup of tea. here we have a good vs bad-story, that is eager to show grey-areas in a not very subtle way.
the characters are very likeable, but i lost interest in them when the main plot started to get stranger and stranger over the course of the game. and strange it got. whenever there's something impressive happening the next awkward scene is just around the corner. dramatic events happen out of nowhere and are explained poorly, while obvious things are explained to an extend, that you start to question them, waiting for some foundation-changing revelation. but sadly: there is none. this is good and this is bad. but remember, bad people can still be good and good ones can still be bad. that zesteria's storie's depth.
gameplay-wise we have a very cool battle-system with rock-paper-scissors-mechanics and a super-sayajin-mode. BUT we also have:
huge open areas that are a pain to walk through (unless you invested 20 hours of grinding in the ability to sprint). the places zestiria lets you discover are nice to look at but in the end they feel empty due to their size. nearly every dungeon looks the same and what i find the most irritating: because there are no really memorable set-pieces and no exciting stories, there is no build up. visiting the next huge area does not come with the typical awe, that this kind of game - for me - is about.
the real dealbreaker however, is a convoluted, unmotivating skill- and equipment-system that makes you grind for hours in order to get identical equipemnt to fuse together. i don't even want to explain this mess. the result that comes out of it, however, is the following: lack of noticable character-progression.
quite harsh, i know. and it's not like this is the worst game ever. it's a very average role-playing game missing the essence, that i like about those. and it's an extremely dissapointing tales-game. but it depends on what you want out of those games. i would not recommend it, unless you have no way of getting your hands on any other tales of. exept tempest of course :)

The best way to describe this game is… reaching for depth and maturity, but not quite making it. There’s a lot going on, but very little is used or explained, explored or expressed to anything resembling true potential. It builds a large world, but only uses a chunk of it. It gives us a taste of side characters and stories we’d like to hear or know more about, but nothing is ever done with them.
As to the main characters, they’re not as endearing as in earlier installments. They identify more with hard anime stereotypes than anything else, some of which flies in the face of their given role. Sadly, worst of all is the main character, Sorey. His insufferable whimpering in the face of conflict becomes tiresome quickly, and never stops.
Really, it’s a game that fails to take enough chances, doesn’t go big enough, or deep enough, and wastes a lot of time with setup it doesn’t fully realize. While Tales of Symphonia set up a quest and system to save the world, it then continued on to completely subvert and even upend the entire idea. This...? This builds its box and then stays there until the end.
What about the gameplay itself? The battle system is alright for the most part, but it isn’t enough to hold the game up on its own. Items have too many abilities and synergies and convolutions, and none of that complexity manages to hide the fact that little of it is fun. Lackluster and really uninteresting, much of the game feels like a geology lesson in terms of the itemization, which is far too systematic to really feel rewarding.
Yes, the graphics are… okay, the voice acting is good, the music is great, but the story and the game system itself just really don’t work.

I never cared for the 30 fps cap or for how Bamco insisted that the game freeze if anyone watched you play by steam broadcast. Progressing through to the end of the game only brought my opinion of this title even lower.
Small golden flakes of quality decorate an otherwise bland experience. Remember collecting the triforce pieces in the Wind Waker? (Miyamoto apologized for that aspect of the game being padded filler.) You'll be doing a sidequest very similar to that in this game.

Combat is a grindy chore and I constantly feel helplessly under leveled. Apparently I'm supposed to be level 85 for figing the Dark Turtlez secret boss but by the time I got to him I was just at level 50.
They replaced the world map with a huge open world loaded with....pretty much nothing. I found myself hard pressed to engage with the plot, constantly checking the objective node to find out where to go. Annoyingly the destination hints are sometimes cryptic, requiring you to use the internet lest you spin your wheels in the mud.
Combat seemed absolutely badass at first but quickly became a crutch for the enemies to consistently use one shot attacks that wipe your stupid AI buddies. ❥ Disclaimer: This is my opinion and others may not share the same views as me.
►Disclaimer 2: This game is for hiragana only. Do not expect to speak Japanese after this.
❥ Played: 7 hours
►Currently located: Ghoul Ruins
----------------------------------------
I have had a positive experience with this game.  I currently have worked and lived in Japan for about a year now, and have had trouble learning the language. This being said, I have been exposed to the everyday Japanese language, and I can say this is a good starting place for people who like to play games and want to learn Japanese. Below is a list of pros and cons I have found within the game so far.
-------------------------------------
✱Pros:✱
---------------------------------------
❤ 1.)  The order the lesson is presented to you.
Details: I really like the order they present the material(s) to you, and I think it is one of the best styles I have seen for a beginner learner.
❤  2.) Defeating the "hiragana."
Details: Although, this might be a minus for some, I like it. You have to constantly kill the same hiragana, but there is enough of a mix, that it does not get boring to me. Repetition is key to learning a new language.
❤ 3.) The side quests
Details: The side quests are optional but give you the option to expand your vocabulary. I really like how they just don't focus on the hiragana alone. This and visuals are sometimes shown through out the side quests, which help! I have also learned a little culture from it, like types of food and drinks in Japan.
❤ 4.) The "lessons"
Details: The lessons have a listening and writing part, which I really enjoyed. If you actually read what Misaki says, it gives you a lot of good tips! I highly recommend not skipping through it. The quizzes are nice. They don't grade you, just check your comprehension and do not let you go to the next question until you select the correct choice. (Although the monsters are not as forgiving. haha)
❤  5.) The humor
Details: As you start in the game, the humor is quite funny. *At least to me*. (SPOILER: Leon's story about the pumpkins. The snowman in the town and the dog in snowleaf village, etc.)
❤ 6.)  "Bonus point crystal"
Details: As you do side quests, you get bonus points which you can turn into the "bonus crystal" next to Misaki that you can exchange for levels.
❤ 7.) Option to review with Misaki
Detail: I like the option to review when you want to!
---------------------------------------------------
✱Cons:✱
---------------------------------------------------
✘ 1.) The story
Details: The story is a bit ridiculous and it is sometimes hard to take the game seriously, but if you remember you are here to learn the language versus playing a game, a lot of this cons can be overlooked.
✘ 2.) The interface
Details: There is some features I think that can be added to help the game be a little more smoother for the learner. One  is as you progress and learn more hiragana, the list obviously gets bigger. However, as it gets bigger no arrow/scroll is shown, so as a beginner you are searching through the big list of hiragana and not realizing there are more choices. I got stuck for a good 5 minutes the first time this issue arose. I could not find the choice, so I thought I had remembered incorrectly. Load and behold, I scrolled down on my mouse because I became frustrated and the list scrolled down and there were more choices! This seems so obvious now, but it might be a similar problem to someone else. In addition, I think the hiragana should have an hp box. It is a bit annoying not knowing how many more hits I have to do before I should pick the next pair. (For example: I might pick answer "ko" for the hiragana "こ" for ALL my players, and than the hiragana dies...and the player still attacks with the answer "ko" to the next mob...even though it is "か". I found this to be VERY annoying.) However, one you are in the area a bit, you start realizing how many hits the hiragana needs before it dies.
✘ 3.) Too easy to "escape"
Details: For me, I like a little strategy in a game. So this might not be a con for some. Whenever you click the option to "escape" you always do. There is no real struggle. So I could go through a dungeon without practicing any hiragana. (You need to for money and exp though.)
----------------------------------------------
✱Other suggestions to the game that I feel are not critical but would help the game.✱
---------------------------------------------
1.) ❥ Customization
Details: It is a bit boring to not see the characters change at all as you give them new equipment or items. I wish I could name the main character too.
2.) ❥ More variety earlier
Details: As I have progressed through the game, I did see change; however it is a bit of a too slow of a pace in my opinion.
3.) ❥ Features to include:
Details: Things that I think that should be added but not necessary. I wish as they attacked there was sound effects. For example when you answer "e", it would be nice if the character pronounced the hiragana. This gives repetition and makes it easier for the listener to remember how it is pronounced. There should be a feature where you can turn it off too, for the people who think it would be too annoying. Secondly, when you are getting exp, it will show a bar and +number of exp earned, but there is no numbers on the bar. It is not too annoying, and it might be cleaner for some gamers, but I like seeing the numbers. Maybe you can include a feature to add or remove numbers to both exp bars and hp/mp bars. Thirdly, when going to the inn to rest, it does not show you how much money you have. Although it is very cheap (only 10¥ and you should have it), it still seems weird not to see it. I would feel differently if it was free.  Lastly, I think when you save the game it should say where you are located. The only way I can tell the difference between the files is by the hours I have played.
4.) ❥ More side quests + order they appear
Details: When the side quests are first introduced they all appear at once! I am an eager learner, so I tackled them all at once, hoping more would come as the game progressed. So far...NOPE. I think the pacing of the appearance of them should be fixed. The learned might either get overwhelmed or bored due to no new variety.
5.) ❥ Stealing the little boy's  life savings from the vase
Details:  I just think it is a sad feature, that maybe we should have the option to give it back.
6.) ❥ Starting a new game (Option to skip dialogue or repeat it)
Details: Although you can mash the "esc" key; It would be nice to skip, as a return player.
7.) ❥  Double checking (Are you sure you want to quit?)
Details: The game doesn't ask if you want to save or if you are sure you would like to quit, when clicking the "x". Same with selling things, it just sells it.
8.) ❥ BOSS fights
Details: I think it should be a BIGGER hiragana that changes as you hit it. This would be a bit of a variety OR you should introduce kanji!!  It can review the vocabulary we already learned....like "犬" (いぬ) [dog].  How to attack: the boss comes in and it shows the kanji + hiragana + english. After the monster gets to 75% the hiragana disappears, Than the english at 50%. I think it would be fun and challenging!
9.) ❥ In game notepad
Details: Just a suggestion, but not needed.
10.) ❥ Equipment tutorial.
Details: It is a bit confusing. I self-taught myself but it is a bit frustrating not having a bit of a guide.
-------------------------
► Additional remarks:
-------------------------
✿ Great for the "gamer" learner!
✿ The game is just $6.99 (at present), why not give it a shot? It is far cheaper than other options out there.
✿ Remember to save your game a lot!

Holy crap. I've long been an anime fan and have been interested in learning Japanese for some time, but have never worked up the momentum to start learning. While the plot and dialogue are straightforward in the extreme, the mechanics of the game are solid and really help with retaining the knowledge. I've only played up to the first boss and completed the first two lessons, but I'm guessing the structure of the game won't change much. While the type of random encounters often derided in classic JRPGs is there, it is essential in helping you memorise the letters, meaning that if you need to revise a certain set because your memory is rusty, just go back to the area where that set is found and wander around.
You will need a pen and paper so you can learn to write all the characters and keep notes if you wish, but other than that all you need is a curious mind and the suspension of disbelief.
Well done Sleepy Duck Games! I look forward completing this game and to similar titles when this is successful.

Onto my first game review here on Steam.
For an early access game still in Alpha stage, this game has provided me with countless hours of F U N already! The insane wrecks and carnage I have had with others in multiplayer have provided me and others with some great laughs. I can only imagine that Wreckfest will continue to get better and better with more content and options placed into the game.
If competitive racing or smash-em-up derbies sound fun to you and you do not mind an early state game (and content), buy Wreckfest.
UPDATE 7/19/2015 -- I'm certainly glad I bought it and it appears that playability time (as far as engine/body damage goes) has been improved upon which gives the player a fair amount of time again to participate in events.
I purchased NCG: Wreckfest to enjoy the insanity, crashing, unpredictability, high octane FUN that goes along with banger racing and derbies.
I am currently unsure of my feelings about the handling, physics, steering and other things right now in Wreckfest. They seem to be in a state of flux and changing often so it's difficult for me to really state how I feel about them. I do feel that, overall, the cars feel and drive a fair bit slower than they did in the old build (Build #6) and I do miss the fast top speeds and insane crashes you could cause with that.
I am very glad they added the Camera Intensity (shake) Slider though, so I can turn the impact shaking off completely as I REALLY disliked that feature.
EDIT -- Apparently, this option will be included in a patch soon and I certainly appreciate that this option will be added. Thanks!
Onto my thoughts on an option in the player network settings --
This setting allows the player to drag a slider left and right so they can balance out (FPS and server accuracy) in multiplayer sessions. While this setting does help out, it can be frustrating to dig it out of the menu and change the slider during online sessions and races, to compensate for different server pings, maximum players, etc. Perhaps this slider is a temporary placeholder for now?
I'll update my review accordingly, depending on what later patches and builds do to the game and we'll go from there -- At it's current state, I CAN recommend Wreckfest!

After being introduced to Super Meat Boy by a friend and also finding out that EarthWorm Jim had been ported to XBox, I got on a little bit of a platformer kick. I stumbled across this gem while browsing the Steam Store and the screenshots caught my attention; minimalistic, slightly out of focus, greyscale, simple, yet enticing. I figured it was worth dropping $5 to give it a shot.
I was not disappointed. The puzzles were (at times) very challenging, but not indecipherable. I admit that I needed help with some of them but I figured out most on my own; getting the timing right is key on the majority of these.
I was quite struck by the environment. Eerie and playful (you ARE a kid running through this world), and frightfully gory at times (you die in very graphic ways; electrical plates, saws, walls/ceilings/etc of spikes) but the gore is somewhat implied as everything is in shades of grey.
A rather short game (I finished it over 3 evenings after work; maybe 6 hours total) but found it thoroughly enjoyable. A little more storyline about WHY you are doing what you are doing would have been nice but again, that is something you sort of pick up on as you move through the different areas of this shadowy world (I won't spoil it but apparently you are a young boy looking for his sister after some "event"). Just a very interesting concept and definitely original in it's presentation.
A great game. I'm interested to see what the developer comes up with next.

RPG Maker VX ace is probably my favorite version of the "modern" RPG maker applications. It's not too simplified, and it still has many of the core features as the older iterations of the program. It's nice to be able to make sprite sheets and character graphics of any size, however, one of my big complaints is how compicated it is to make a new tileset when compared to how it's done for 2000/2003.
I'm also a bit bothered by the fact that you can't make different sized tilesets/change the tile size, while you're able to do it without any problems for the character sets. This, in my opinion, is one of the biggest flaws with the map editor in this version, and up (I can't say much for RPG maker XP, as I've rarely used it).
The scripting system first introduced in XP is still available, and it's been expanded upon. I have no clue how to code in RGSS3, but I've managed to at least make simple modifications to certain scripts. This software also now allows for users to have loop points in their MP3/OGG files by adding a special ID3 tag specifying the sample to loop at; this is a very welcome addition.
Overall, if you're gonna buy any 2 versions of RPG maker, I'd reccomend getting 2003 first, followed by VX.

I bought Kingpin on a whim and I honestly can't believe how good it is! It plays and feels quite allot like half-life which is less of a  coincidence than you might think as it too uses a similarly highly modified Quake2 engine. The whole game has a really good feel to it; gritty and grimy as you battle the mean streets. The characters are engaging, the levels are amazingly well designed, even had Cyprus Hill do the music and voice the characters! A nice variety of real weapons and the enemies have good variety too with good AI and path finding. It's a very unique game with allot of intuitive features, I especially like the recruiting thugs to follow you around in your own little protection racket! It took me 12 hours to get through on hard, it's a very decent size game and I honestly loved every minute of it. It's quite challenging from the start. but persevere and you will be rewarded with a great play through. Amazing it's from 1999! Real hidden gem of a game! I can't actually find anything to criticize, other than there's no sequel! 10/10.

DISCLAIMER: I REVIEWED THIS GAME WHILE IT WAS IN EARLY ACCESS (it still is), SO THE GAME ISN'T FINISHED YET. There's something about The Long Dark that makes me love it. I don't know if it's the graphics, the gameplay mechanics, or even the survival experience of it all. The graphics have a calm feeling to them, and they're beautiful. When you die, you have to restart the entire game, which is great. You can be a boy or a girl, and you get to pick one of two maps. There are three different survival experiences you can choose from. One is based on survival, and the other is based on exploration. The third option is a mix of the two. You will get eaten by wolves a lot, but that just makes it more fun. This game is true survival in the Canadian wilderness. If you drink unpurified water (yes, you can drink toilet water in the game) then you can get sick. You can also get sick from raw meat, or getting bitten by a wolf. Then, you have to have the right supplies such as bandages and pain killers. The game has a nice crafting element in it as well, which adds to the survival experience. If you're buying this game thinking you'll get something like Rust or Minecraft, you're wrong. This is a unique game, and I can't think of a single other game like it. This is one of my favorite games ever, and I highly reccomend it.

I never cared for the 30 fps cap or for how Bamco insisted that the game freeze if anyone watched you play by steam broadcast. Progressing through to the end of the game only brought my opinion of this title even lower.
Small golden flakes of quality decorate an otherwise bland experience. Remember collecting the triforce pieces in the Wind Waker? (Miyamoto apologized for that aspect of the game being padded filler.) You'll be doing a sidequest very similar to that in this game.
With the exception of the 4 elemental dungeons, the remaining two dozen dungeons are all bland copy paste branching hallways on mutliple floors. Combat is a grindy chore and I constantly feel helplessly under leveled. Apparently I'm supposed to be level 85 for figing the Dark Turtlez secret boss but by the time I got to him I was just at level 50.
They replaced the world map with a huge open world loaded with....pretty much nothing. I found myself hard pressed to engage with the plot, constantly checking the objective node to find out where to go. Annoyingly the destination hints are sometimes cryptic, requiring you to use the internet lest you spin your wheels in the mud.
Combat seemed absolutely badass at first but quickly became a crutch for the enemies to consistently use one shot attacks that wipe your stupid AI buddies. The human player can dodge the slow, telegraphed attacks, but it's less likely your AI buddies will. As a crutch, your allies (essentially) respawn thanks to the unique battle mechanics.
If you love to grind then this is the game for you, but it's completely not worth the effort. The characters are a little bland, but I love seeing them bounce off the only good personality (Edna). I even managed to laugh during a couple of the game's numerous cutscenes.
Combat and journeying feel like a tedious min-maxing chore and simply aren't worth the effort to see the plot unfold.
Tales of Symphonia is a vastly superior game in nearly every regard. It's sad to see this sequel regress so far.

I've heard this is considered the "spiritual successor" to the original Amnesia (that I loved) but I have to say I am disappointed.
Note: I have played a couple of hours in offline mode, that's why steam says I have only played 12 mins or so.
Outlast in my opinion does a fairly poor job at giving you that sense of "atmosphere". Sound assets are fairly average (nothing compared to the original Amnesia), enemies are kinda thrown at you from the early beginning and most of the scares you'll get are the classic, cheap, jump scares -.-
What made Amnesia special to me was the fact that it was incredibly atmospheric: amazingly real sound assets for the most part, but also the fact that enemies were very rare in the first place and even when you had an encounter with one of them, you rarely had the chance to look at them in detail. Enemies were often far away from you and most rooms were fairly shady or dark. I think I had a close up encounter with an enemy only 3 or 4 times in the whole game, maybe less.
All this made Amnesia effectively very scary because of its atmosphere. Also
. EVER.
I also don't like how this game manages the concept of "dark" (obviously a key element in horror games). In Outlast you have a camera with a night mode that can be toggled. Night mode consumes batteries, which is a rare resource that has to be managed. The problem lies in the fact that dark in this game is as black as it can get, you can't see a damn thing without the night mode toggled. This means that if you run out of batteries you basically can't progress in the game because you have no clue if you are going somewhere or if you are just walking against a wall. Not to mention that in the dark enemies often spawn in front of you without any sound warning whatsoever. This is a dumb unnecessary mechanic in my honest opinion.
Amnesia managed to do it way better. In the dark your eyes progressively (this took some seconds) adapted to the lighting in the area, allowing you to always see some meters ahead of your position. This not only gets rid of the "I can't progress because I have no batteries" mechanic, but it is also a perfect addition to the horror aspect of the game. "I can barely see" is way scarier that "I can't see at all" (if you are blind you don't see it coming, you just hear some sounds and that's it).
I'd also like to add the fact that the lighting system is poorly done: transition from light to full black dark is way too abrupt and happens too close to the lighting source. Judge it yourself:
even though Outlast is still fairly well put together (you will find a lot of positive reviews), I can't recommend it to anybody.
If you haven't played "Amnesia: The Dark Descent", then I suggest you turn around and play that game instead of buying this one.
On the other hand, if you have already experienced what Amnesia has to offer, then I honestly think you'll be disappointed by Outlast unless you don't mind getting a worse experience.

Free from spoilers ( well maybe a little bit on the first point from negative side, but i think it is not really a spoiler ). Well, this is the seventh Tales of series that I played. I think the first two positive point is relevant to most of Tales of series, because it is always their strong points.
(+)
1. As expected from Tales of series, character skits and interaction are fun and worth of your time, not to mention their VA is also pretty good.
2. Battle system is addicting once you get the grab of it.
3. Graphic is pretty good and suit the series
4. Most of the soundtrack is great, IMO one of the best from Tales of series

(-)
1. Storyline is (too) generic. You can easily predict the storyline, and the plot twist is also a bit predictable. If you are new for Tales of series and wanted the good storyline, then i recommend to try Tales of Symphonia first.
2. Battle camera in a closed space is so f***ing annoying
3. Keymap when using keyboard when playing is messed up every f***ing time when there is a random rumor popped out around OR any your party's member chat popped out
4. AI is stupid, and it will be clearer at the mid-late game, where the boss can one hit your uncontrolled character with easy-to-dodge attack but the AI just willing to get hit for lulz. Not to mention they are sucks in armatization mode ( AI be like: "Well I'll de-armatize for lulz" )
5. Battle system is confusing at first time and too deep for no reason. ( I ignored about half of the tips from the monolith )
6. MC is too generic goody two-shoes type --> "I want to save the world no matter what", not to mention half of your party's member is lack of character development
7. Late game armatization seraphic arte is too broken. Spam your Ancient Nova and it will rekt a final boss in Chaos mode too easy, and with a proper combination skills, can even rekt powered up final boss in hard mode relatively easy. Spam your Crystal Tower for stagger-lock your early mob then Earthshaker, Calamity Flare, and Maelstorm to stagger-lock your mid-late phase mob. ez.
8. Some item skills is too OP, you can literally finish most of the boss fight ( even in highest difficulty ) in several second.
I'll rate this 7/10. Storyline is a bit meh( Well, this is not new for Tales of series ), with a generic MC lead. Also a keymap bug and closed space in battle camera is really annoying. But I think battle system and skits make up some of it. Recommended, but you better grab this when there is a sale, and I recommend you Symphonia over Zestiria

This game is exactly what the "about this game" section says. "It lasts about an hour and a half and has no traditional mechanics, no goals or objectives. Instead, it tells the story of a person struggling to deal with something they do not understand."
It is not Stanley Parable 2. It's a very separate but similarly emotionally powerful experience, though somewhat opposite in the direction it takes your moods. It's more of an interactive movie. After being introduced to Super Meat Boy by a friend and also finding out that EarthWorm Jim had been ported to XBox, I got on a little bit of a platformer kick. I stumbled across this gem while browsing the Steam Store and the screenshots caught my attention; minimalistic, slightly out of focus, greyscale, simple, yet enticing. I figured it was worth dropping $5 to give it a shot.
I was not disappointed. The puzzles were (at times) very challenging, but not indecipherable. I admit that I needed help with some of them but I figured out most on my own; getting the timing right is key on the majority of these.
I was quite struck by the environment. Eerie and playful (you ARE a kid running through this world), and frightfully gory at times (you die in very graphic ways; electrical plates, saws, walls/ceilings/etc of spikes) but the gore is somewhat implied as everything is in shades of grey.
A rather short game (I finished it over 3 evenings after work; maybe 6 hours total) but found it thoroughly enjoyable. A little more storyline about WHY you are doing what you are doing would have been nice but again, that is something you sort of pick up on as you move through the different areas of this shadowy world (I won't spoil it but apparently you are a young boy looking for his sister after some "event"). Just a very interesting concept and definitely original in it's presentation.
A great game. I'm interested to see what the developer comes up with next.

First off, I'm already fluent with Hiragana. I learned the writing system back in my first year of Japanese with Morihara Sensei. That being said, when I saw this...I had to stop and take a double take. I stared at it for awhile. Thought to myself, "RPG to learn Hiragana? Battling Hiragana? Seriously?" And for 7$, I thought it would be a fun little refresher. I'm only into the third set, beyond the k's and their ten-ten's, but even without going any further, I am going to stop and make this a recommendation.
I love RPG's. I adore them. I love Japanese, and I've adored learning the language. This is the cutest darn little game and already I've had the most fun I've had in learning the language - as fun as Sensei's classes were. You're adventurers on a quest to stop a Japanese mage and his Hiragana warriors. You use the correct english translations to damage and defeat them. This will even show you the proper order of character strokes. You get INN's to sleep in, places to explore, treasure, money, equipment - like legit adventuring.
If you have any interest in learning the language, get this. Just do it. :)

Kingpin is a very 90's game. It's a game very in-line with the "screw the censors let's have violence and swearing" mindset from around the same time that gave us games like Doom and Postal. Unfortunately this backfired for the game since it released around the same time as the Columbine shootings. Which gained it a great deal of controversy and seemingly didn't improve the sales of the game.
The premise of the game is you are a criminal who is beaten by several thugs in an alley. You pick up a lead pipe and decide to get revenge on the criminal organization that runs the city. The storyline is extremely minimalistic and there isn't much to get attatched to. The main protagonist isn't particularly well fleshed out and the motivations of the characters are never elaborated upon.
This gets into the brunt of my complaints with the game. The game feels like it lacks focus. The game starts out as a semi-stealth game before you get any good weapons or upgrades. Once you get access to a few decent weapons it turns into a straight up run and gun shooter. There's a mechanic where you can talk to NPCs in the world and even enemies if you put your weapon away. But it feels a little half baked since you typically trigger their aggro by accident and have to quickload. The writing of the characters was also pretty terrible. With enemies yelling "♥♥♥♥ER" frequently as soon as you're spotted.
However, I can see why Kingpin got a cult-like following after release. The game takes place in a 1930's styled dystopian city. All of the characters resemble 1940's mobster charicatures and you eventually gain access to a tommy gun. However, all of the dialogue is very 90s, and you see more modern inventions like monorails and helicopters. It has this strangely surreal vibe to it that reminds me of similar games like Manhunt although I don't know if it was intentional or not. It also has wonderfully good AI for the time that actually follows you through vents and up ladders. The game also does have this unique sense of progression. Where you start out the game waking up in the gutter and progressively become more powerful and influential. Lastly there are a lot of clear influences from films like the Big Lebowski and Pulp Fiction. With the antagonist of the game being a clear parody of Marcellus Wallace from the latter.
I wouldn't say Kingpin is a bad game but you have to go into it being aware it's a very mediocre one. I only recommend this game to people who are overly curious about old first person shooters who are willing to accept the game for it's very rough edges.
