Hi guys,
This is not a typical review, but it might give a very important hint to someone who is new to The Long Dark, supposed one wants to have the most possible fun and challenge when playing a game and I think this should be the claim in every game, isn't it.
Please excuse my style of writing in English. It is not my native language but I wanted to do this "review" in English as I think it is important for everybody who is new to TLD.
I supported TLD and bought it because I think the guys from Hinterland deserve it and I am really looking forward of getting much more out of this game.
OK, I suppose you are interested in TLD or even played already a first round and tried your first steps.
Now, start by asking yourself, "What do I expect from this game...?"
It's obvious, TLD is a different kind of computer game. It has nothing to do with the common shooter type, hunting for enemies and zombies or similar kind of more or less realistic wild west style of games. And yes - the graphics are average compared to what is possible today. And to make it even worse, TLD is a single player game in times when in the gaming industry the economic success is mainly coming from games, which are programmed to be multiplayer or even MMOGs. I mean we have all seen complex games like BF and alike and know what's in fact possible. Sure I know that Hinterland as a small company is in no way comparable to DICE or the other big game producers, but at the end of the day, it's the  game user who decides what to play for a similar price.
So you might ask yourself, what's the use of spending time in TLD?
Well, TLD is in the alpha phase with only two playable maps so far and there are still a couple of bugs. But important as this all may appear, it's not if you know how to handle it and why you want to play this game. TLD is different, it's an indie type of game with the flavor of an exploration and survival simulation.
You are a pilot and a victim of an airplane crash somewhere in the northern Canadian wilderness. You don't have much with you, nothing to eat or to drink, no weapon and especially no compass or gps or something what tells you, where you are. The only thing you know is, that you are in a huge forest. Your task in the game is to survive as long as it's possible. Why all the people you will find around are dead but not the animals is unknown. Maybe the storyline will bring this up one day and may even bring you back to the civilization, but for now just accept it, it's a fact in TLD and increases the suspense. So far, so good.
Now, there are several ways how to succeed in this disquieting situation. I will not go deeper into this, as there are a couple of fine guides out there from some committed community members and there is no use for me to invent the wheel twice. Please refer to these guides, they are important for a new player in TLD and really help a lot.
But you will also find some guides here and there which offer maps of the TLD landscape.
And here it comes,
my most PRECIOUS HINT:

By all means, DON'T USE MAPS in The Long Dark or you will spoil yourself the most interesting part of this game. The idea of TLD is NOT to check a map, running to these known spots, finding all the stuff you need to survive, and at the end (hahaha)  complaining that the game is "easy, crap and boring".
If we are really using maps to walk around and to find all the hidden secrets - I mean don't let's be ridiculous, that's kindergarten and as I said, not the idea of the game - why playing it then when there are others around?
Try to stay honest to yourself, just stay the brave adventurer who crashed in a plane and play your role. Find yourself lying in the snow underneath or near a rock after spawning, not knowing where you are and where to go. Be bold and decide the direction where to go next and you will be fine after a while. Maybe you find the sun in the sky if the weather is favorable enough to allow it, this gives you at least a certain idea about the time of day. Never walk into the night or in a storm! Learn how to prepare food and drink.
Just allow yourself the suspense of being lost in the wilderness, lost in the cold and really try to find your way through the game. After a couple of sandbox trials you will know better and find your path anyway, since the playable maps are still small. Beware of wolves, stay away or surpass them, they are really dangerous and can end the round in seconds. At this point there is even something of a simulation in the game. Just feel the situation, feel the idea of this game and it will be YOUR game.
This is the little secret for me and those who love The Long Dark
You will soon see, it's not rocket science to find the first cabin or even a house and it is much more fun to play this unusual game as is instead of just looking into an offered community map, only to see that the next house is just around the next hill. These guys from Hinterland are still developing TLD but offered us the sensation to already being part of it.
So, my advice is, if you really want to have most out of TLD, don't use maps - ahh - by the way, our pilot doesn't have maps neither, they all burned down in the crash :-)
He is smart enough to find his way alone, will you also do it?

This is an early stage review of only the sandbox.
Now, I love a good survival game, I love the concept of managing your resources,
and making educated choices based on your condition.
And this game does exactly that, it's putting you in a harsh environment to fend for yourself.
With each step you take you pray for an easy weather, some food and that you'll find and a shelter.
On a personal note,  I love the outdoors, and take a intrest in survival (though my surrounding is more of a desert),
so I find this game much to my liking.
My expirence so far:
I entered the game in a forrest clearring, already freezing and hungry, in a middle of a storm.
I've found a ruined cabin and stayed there untill the storm have passed.
I knew I need to find a good base and a good supply of food so I ventured out to seek such place.
I came across a railroad, and thinking that I might stumble on some buildings on it's path, I followed it to the east.
I found a cabin by a lake and have made my homebase there. found a steady supply of food from fishing and hunting near by, while saving all the canned food for later. From that base I'd scout around to find more supplies and craft better suited gear. I was in luck, others weren't as lucky.
It was a simple few hours, but I enjoyed it all.
Some pros to the game:
1. Immersive harsh environment.
2. The cartoonish style makes everything look beautiful.
3. Great crafting system.
4. Easy to use and understand UI.
5. Wildlife and its reaction to you and your actions was great, I really feared meeting with a wolf at first.
6. Immersive cues of your condition.
7. Great atmosphere.
Some things which I didn't like or find missing, and would love if the devs will consider it:
1. Weather clues. When I travel or backpack, I always look for the shape of the clouds or a sign to bad weather, so I'll know to seek a shelter, make camp or to get to a high ground to avoid a flood. The game has no warnings, snow and blizzards hit without you having any way to predict it.
2. The terrain. The game has no logical terrain flow, it has cells that don't match topographically. In the real world, the terrain has a flow, there are ridges with high points, there are slopes that conjure a basin that flows and drains to some direction. It's a basic rule in navigation to follow the water and where it flows, to understand the terrain and your position. I wish the level design would be arranged like that, though I still enjoyed it, it only bugged me because it's easier for me to navigate like that.
3. A map and a journal. The idea of not having a map in a survival game, I would prefer a map that I can draw myself in game (I actually drew a simple map in a notebook while playing the game), also it bugged me that the camp office didn't have a map of the surroundings. And I know there is a journal that records your discoveries, but I would love to edit my own enteries. In a combination with a map and journal you can mark best hunting spots, best places for traps and snares, stashes and possible shelters to expand your exploration area whilist keeping a safehouse. In my opinion it will greatly infuse and improve the immersive roleplaying.
4. Other survivors. Now this is something I'm not completly sure about, but I think there should be others in the game. It should be rare to encounter someone else, but the idea that you would compete on resources with others or maybe joining up and sharing, really calls to me. Though the feeling of loneliness adds to this game's survival aspect, I think that adding that element will add to the challenge. I think that NPCs are a better choice or maybe up to 5 players on a huge map.
Finale notes:
All in all I enjoyed this game very much. If you're into survival you should buy it even without the story mode just for the snadbox. You'll love it.

The premise of this game is bonkers, even by Tales standards.  You play Sorey, a young man who grew up since infanthood in Elysium, the land of the Seraphim, who are a race of spiritual beings who can inhabit many forms.  As the game is starting, he finally gets to strike out into the human world, to fulfill his dream of being an adventurer who explores ruins.  Ridiculously soon after setting out, he discovers that he is The Shepherd, a person who forms pacts with Seraphim and fights against malevolence.
Normal humans don't generally see Seraphim unless they have a high spiritual resonance, but they often feel their influence.  Some seraphim act as stewards over particular regions of the world, and these regions are called their Domain.  During the time of the game, human-seraphim relations are at something of a low point, but it is revealed that during other periods in history, humans and seraphim lived side by side.
Malevolence is a kind of amorphous negative influence that can become so powerful, being influenced by emotions and actions and situations, that it can turn people and other animals into monsters known as hellions.  The Shepherd's job is ultimately to rid the world of malevolence, and finding out the ultimate means of doing so is part of the Shepherd's journey, a journey that has been taken many times in the past.
Sorey, as the Shepherd, is accompanied by a number of seraphim with whom he has made a kind of pact early in the game.  These seraphim represent the four elements of water, fire, earth, and wind, and each of whom Sorey can fuse with in order to increase his combat power.  He is joined for most of his adventure by another human companion who can also fuse with Sorey's seraphim companions.  Otherwise, most other humans are unaware of the seraphim's existence, leading to some comical situations when Sorey is speaking with them in public.
The game has switched to an over-the-shoulder, free moving third person camera for all travel.  There is also no overland map, world exploration is done in the same mode as city exploration.  Skits (short, optional, often comical dialogues between party members) return in absurd abundance, all of them fully voiced in both English and Japanese.  But you might find, as I did, that you run into an issue of quality in all that quantity, not least of which because the localization is truly nonsense at times, and the English voice acting is pretty lackluster and seems to have lacked good direction.
But who cares about any of that?  Tales games are, at their core, about the battle system.  This battle system is very different from those in the past.  Your party will consist of up to two humans: yourself and eventually a human companion.  Each human can have one of the four seraphim set who will appear as a normal party member in combat, using skills and spells, aiding the player and attacking the enemy.
During combat, Sorey (and/or his human companion) can perform an action known as "Armatization" which will fuse that character with their currently summoned seraph, restoring some amount of health, boosting their attack and imbuing it with the seraph's element.
It's an incredibly complex system I won't bother to try to run down for you here, but suffice to say that careful chaining of combos can lead to huge damage for skillful players.  However, most of the combat system is obscured by how it's related to you, which is mostly in text.  Monuments scattered around the game world provide you with knowledge about the various mechanics of the game, including the combat system, but your best bet would be to look for a guide on the internet if you are truly interested in becoming proficient.
This is the place where the game really fell down for me.  I'm usually a big fan of the larger-than-life weirdos in Tales games, but I'm not interested in any of these characters.  You have a Lydia, a cool loner, an airhead, and a naif.  Lailah, and everyone's reaction to her, is the only endearing point from the seraphim side.  Your eventual human companion is also pretty neat, but everyone else is kind of boring, and for the most part the villains have no substance, and you kill many of them as soon as you know they exist.  For all the abundance of dialogue and plot stuff, it seems a waste with a game that has so little to offer as far as interesting characters.
I originally wrote a one sentence condemnation of this game, appalled as I was by the characters introduced in it.  After pushing through and engaging fully with the combat system, though, I'm prepared to recommend it based on that alone.  I think the plot might be a sarcastic parody of a classic Tales plot, which makes it a little easier to handle.  But ultimately, you should play it because you want some of that sweet battle system goodness, and a game that recognizes when you do cool stuff like take no damage or kill the last enemy with a special move.

The concept behind this game is simple; You kill red guys, and time only moves when you do. Actually, time still moves very slowly when you stay still, but whatever. There are very few weapons in the game, but it doesn't feel like any more need to be added. Each weapon has it's own role: pistols are slow but reliable, rifles are dangerous to use, but powerful (they fire multiple bullets per trigger pull, and time speeds up while firing), shotguns act as you would expect, and melee weapons are good for hitting things with. This simplicity of design permeates SUPERHOT; the game never tries to do more than it needs to, and this works to its benefit. The simple acting of shooting things feels incredibly good. You can shoot bullets out of the air with other bullets, and if the shrapnel is close enough to an enemy, they will be stunned and drop their weapon. That is pretty damn cool.
You wouldn't notice it at first glance, but as you play through the game, you will quickly realize that it's actually a series of real-time puzzles, in a similar vein to Hotline Miami. The game requires you to make quick decisions and pay close attention to your environment, especially sound. In later levels, you will probably need to play multiple times to figure out the best way to deal with a situation.
I only have two real issues with the gameplay. Sometimes it can be hard to discern whether a bullet is going to hit you or not, which is especially frustrating knowing that you can only take one hit. And the game has punch and pick-up bound to the same key. Sometimes you will go to grab a weapon out of the air, only to find you clicked a few pixels to the left, punch an enemy, and die because you wasted a few precious seconds. The second problem doesn't come up very often, but it is very frustrating when it does. The reason these problems are so annoying is that they are the only problems I noticed; if they weren't present, the gameplay would be perfect, as far as I'm concerned.
There isn't a lot to say about the visuals in SUPERHOT, its very minimalist. If you've seen one screenshot of the game, you pretty much know whether you like the look or not.
The music isn't really worth mentioning either, as it doesn't stand out too much, so I'll just breeze past that.The menus in SUPERHOT are presented in the form of a DOS-esque interface. There are plenty of interesting things to find, and little hidden jokes; I think I spent the first 30 minutes of playtime just exploring the menu.
I thought the story was a little predictable, but it was interesting enough for what it was. I can't talk too much about it without spoiling, however, so I'll just leave it there.
The game automatically records your playthrough of every level for later viewing. This seems like a cool idea at first, but I felt the execution was a bit lacking. Although the game looks fine in slow motion, it doesn't feel quite right in real time. And the game constantly chants and covers half the screen with the words SUPER-HOT, seemingly to distract from the weird looking animations and general lack of any other audio. You can disable this by pressing 7 on the Numpad, which is useful, but makes the lack of polish on the replays painfully obvious.
SUPERHOT's story is fairly short, but it has and endless mode, and several challenge modes to complete. If you're the sort of player that is concerned about longevity, they've got you covered.
Although the game has a lot of flaws, I'd still recommend it to almost anyone. The only real issue might be the pricetag but, after playing, I don't feel that its acutally that far off the mark. It's such a unique experience-and the core gameplay is almost perfect-, that it still managed to impress me.

9.5/10 - Why such a high score for a game this simple? Because there is little to find wrong with it. Seriously. Sure, it might be on the short side, clocking in at just a couple 2 or 3 hours. But that is about it. For what it is, it is wonderful. In Limbo, you play the role of a boy, who is for the purpose of this game, nameless. You will pretty much go from left to right the entire game, with very little need to backtrack, and when you do, not very far. You will run through a macabre-like setting, that changes atmosphere as you progress the various settings. You will see a few people, but not many. You will see very few enemies period. The game just seems like you are in some hopeless kind of setting. and that is the whole point of Limbo.
The gameplay is a mix of platforming, and environmental puzzles, seamlessly mixed together, without need for an inclined difficulty as you progress. Instead, it chooses to go for a more relaxed increase, and keep you focused instead on the atmosphere, rather than difficult situations. However, when die, is it ever satisfying! As grim as that sounds, it is indeed. Limbo has some wonderfully sadistic and amusing deaths for our young nameless protagonist. The animations for each are wonderfully extecuted, as the young boy is well...executed, so to speak.
Visuals are entirely black and white, on purpose. But you do get wonderful shades of everything with the lack of color, and a nice film grain to really set the tone for the eerie environments you will find yourself pushing through. The audio is mostly ambient, with really no traditional music to speak of. Instead, it goes for acoustamatic music to set the tone. Everything basically has a purpose to pull you into the game.
As for story, it is entirely left up to interpretation. But once you get to the ending, you will find yourself either scratching your head, or thinking up one of many possible explanations on what really happened. Either way, Limbo will leave you satisfied.
Simply put: BUY THIS GAME!

EARLY ACCESS REVIEW:
An excellent idea for a game and so far works great, a lot of what is missing should be added in future updates.
PROS:
- Very detailed survival system
- Acceptable to drink from a toilet
- Can automatically retrieve things like wood for you rather than manually
- Art style is gorgeous, feels similar to Telltale Games art style but with a full 3D environment.
- The 2 maps so far are pretty big and plenty to explore
- For an early access game its nice and stable, I get more crashes on a lot of AAA released titles
CONS:
- Poorly optimized. R9 280X and I'm forced to use low settings for smooth experience, although only lighting looks different at low settings
- Limited content. Only 2 sandbox maps and no story yet, of course this should be improved easily and the sooner the better.
- Thirst seems to be a little quick, as well as hunger for that matter. A human would be able to survive for a day easily without health deteriorating but in this game I start to lose health after a 12 hour nap
- That leads me on to another thing, it can become rather easy at some points in the game where you can simply sleep 12 hours, drink and eat, and then repeat. That can be done for a few days at least with an inventory full of food and water, there is no reward for exploring.
- There is limited amounts of different things to find, finding 10 cans of peaches in one house can be a bit boring, so there definitely needs to be more variation in each location and more unique items. Houses also only have a few different layouts and gets repetitive looking through the same model each time, it would be great if these had some randomisation to the designs of them, even something as little as furniture positioning. Perhaps I'm just being picky here I don't know.
- Ability to carry is a little low, encumbered at 30kg is too small I feel but perhaps my suggestion below would help with this
Features I want in story mode or just in general
- More player progression - strength, speed, ability to go longer without food, quicker at searching
- Side quests - Perhaps some cool unique items to find just as an additional thing, perhaps some achievements for doing so for those that like collecting achievements.
- Changing environment other than weather, perhaps changing amount of snow, even melted ice on the ice occasionally?
- Co-op, because this could be great fun playing with a friend with just the two of you as survivors.
- Other co-op game modes could be where 2-4 players are placed in the map all far apart and can survive together when they find each other, or fight against each other for survival. This I think would need to be random lobbies rather than with friends as communication outside of game could ruin it.
Overall the start of what is going to be an awesome game on release, keep up the awesome work devs!

Easy enough...except that these steps are required for every attack, and for each of the attacking characters in your party.  By the second or third battle, you know the correct characters instantly, but have to navigate the same tedious menus for each character in your party repeatedly.  Despite a lot of potential here, It's simply not fun.

The problem with a game like this is that the "RPG" part is just intrusive on the learning part.
For example, once I figure out what a character represents in battle, it's just tedious and doesn't help learning to repeatedly hit him. They should consistently morph or do something slightly cleverer.
Aside from that, wasting your time with clunky JRPG mechanics from the 80s while you're trying to learn is annoying.
The concept is cute, but just focus on making it exclusively a learning game next time. Nobody who's up for learning a writing system needs to be entertained by junky JRPG mechanics like a child.
Longer edit:
I can't go too in-depth as I've only put about 40 minutes into the game before I dropped it.
The battle system is very simplistic - you slap the Hiragana character icons repeatedly with their corresponding english sound and use typical video games skills that have nothing to do with language learning like heal skills.
It's simply a missed opportunity. The battle system hasn't got any depth, there's no reason the Hiragana characters shouldn't just die in one hit to their corresponding sound and/or replace themselves with others, and all the video-gamey stuff is very detracting from the actual learning.
Beyond slapping characters around there doesn't seem to be anything more, for example an integrated drawing tool to recognize that you can draw the characters.
What I learned in 40 minutes of playing this I could have learned in a youtube video of 5 minutes. And it shouldn't necessarily be that way. Yes, I get that it's a game, but it's a learning tool first. Nobody's gonna get into this game thinking "hmmm I crave a real good JRPG right now", it's purely for the learning in an enjoyable way - it is neither a good learning tool nor enjoyable.
Seems like this review is garnering a lot of traction. I say judge for yourselves, and refund it like I did if you don't like it. But let me tell you as someone who speaks multiple languages fluently - this is a very poor learning tool, even for something as basic as this. (And for that matter it is not a good JRPG either, it's silly and simplistic)

The concept behind this game is simple; You kill red guys, and time only moves when you do. Actually, time still moves very slowly when you stay still, but whatever. There are very few weapons in the game, but it doesn't feel like any more need to be added. Each weapon has it's own role: pistols are slow but reliable, rifles are dangerous to use, but powerful (they fire multiple bullets per trigger pull, and time speeds up while firing), shotguns act as you would expect, and melee weapons are good for hitting things with. This simplicity of design permeates SUPERHOT; the game never tries to do more than it needs to, and this works to its benefit. The simple acting of shooting things feels incredibly good. You can shoot bullets out of the air with other bullets, and if the shrapnel is close enough to an enemy, they will be stunned and drop their weapon. That is pretty damn cool.
You wouldn't notice it at first glance, but as you play through the game, you will quickly realize that it's actually a series of real-time puzzles, in a similar vein to Hotline Miami. The game requires you to make quick decisions and pay close attention to your environment, especially sound. In later levels, you will probably need to play multiple times to figure out the best way to deal with a situation.
I only have two real issues with the gameplay. Sometimes it can be hard to discern whether a bullet is going to hit you or not, which is especially frustrating knowing that you can only take one hit. And the game has punch and pick-up bound to the same key. Sometimes you will go to grab a weapon out of the air, only to find you clicked a few pixels to the left, punch an enemy, and die because you wasted a few precious seconds. The second problem doesn't come up very often, but it is very frustrating when it does. The reason these problems are so annoying is that they are the only problems I noticed; if they weren't present, the gameplay would be perfect, as far as I'm concerned.
There isn't a lot to say about the visuals in SUPERHOT, its very minimalist. If you've seen one screenshot of the game, you pretty much know whether you like the look or not.
The music isn't really worth mentioning either, as it doesn't stand out too much, so I'll just breeze past that.The menus in SUPERHOT are presented in the form of a DOS-esque interface. There are plenty of interesting things to find, and little hidden jokes; I think I spent the first 30 minutes of playtime just exploring the menu.
I thought the story was a little predictable, but it was interesting enough for what it was. I can't talk too much about it without spoiling, however, so I'll just leave it there.
The game automatically records your playthrough of every level for later viewing. This seems like a cool idea at first, but I felt the execution was a bit lacking. Although the game looks fine in slow motion, it doesn't feel quite right in real time. And the game constantly chants and covers half the screen with the words SUPER-HOT, seemingly to distract from the weird looking animations and general lack of any other audio. You can disable this by pressing 7 on the Numpad, which is useful, but makes the lack of polish on the replays painfully obvious.
SUPERHOT's story is fairly short, but it has and endless mode, and several challenge modes to complete. If you're the sort of player that is concerned about longevity, they've got you covered.
Although the game has a lot of flaws, I'd still recommend it to almost anyone. The only real issue might be the pricetag but, after playing, I don't feel that its acutally that far off the mark. It's such a unique experience-and the core gameplay is almost perfect-, that it still managed to impress me.

Brilliant thing. The game looks great, sounds great, plays great. There's nothing else like it. It's like a combination of strategetic turn-based shooter, and twitch shooter. You can take a moment, calculate your next move while everything moves around you super-slowly, and then once you do finally make your move, you need to be precise and deliberate, because when things do move, they move super fast, and it's very easy to make one misstep.
The possibilities are endless. You can slice bullets out of the air, you can pass your gun to an enemy, possess that enemy, and then catch the gun you passed to yourself, and so many other amazing tricks that make you feel so, so good when you pull them off successfully. And when you beat a level, you see a replay in real-time and see all of your awesome tricks come to life like the best action scenes from your favorite action films.
People are criticizing the game for the short story mode. It's two hours, very interesting, but only two hours. However, this game is much more than the two hours of its story mode. Endless modes, dozens of challenges, dozens of modes, so on and so forth. I've got four hours in this game so far, and I am nowhere near done with it. Love it to pieces. I'm just taking a break now to hopefully remind people that some games, like this one, have the majority of their content outside of the story mode. If you love score attack, time attack, and/or generally improving your ability, this is right up your alley and you'll have hours and hours of incredible fun.
Pick it up. Not only is it extremely unique, but it's also extremely good. Worth every penny. Just as good as it gets.

[maybe mild spoilers ahead, nothing serious tho]
This is like horror-gameplay back to the roots, mixed with modern elements. You are a reporter and got a message to investigate and unveil illegal medical experiments in the local asylum. So, at night you sneak in there, with your masterplan to film the story of the century, to become famous etc. etc. ... But of course everything is going to hell as soon you reach the point of no return, what did you expect, right? ;)
Some of the psychotic and sociopathic inhabitants broke their chains and are running freely around the building and now you have to hide and escape insane murderers and hell yes, some of them are indeed looking damn ugly like someone failed even more than one plastic surgery on them.
Only armed with your videocamera (with a nightvision mode) to capture this story, you are trying to get the hell out of there, where you are alone with the probably most dangerous beasts of mankind, who got not much more left than the voices in their heads.
You have to sneak and hide or run and escape on your way out and are going to uncover by finding many clues, what actually happened there.
What I dislike are some of the most obvious jump-scares. I mean these are made as quick and in-your-face that it would even use to shock me if a cute and fluffy pet would jump in my face as this instead. That's a bit exaggerated. Sometimes it destroyed the creepy atmosphere to me a bit, by reminding me that this jumpscare looks like scripted to scare the shiznit out of me. But there are only a few like this. But beware, there are indeed quite a bunch of jumpscares to catch you! ;)
As a horror-fanboy, I highly recommend playing it to any other horror-fan, the gameplay is actually pretty simple and the feeling of being desperately lost and in deadly danger is everywhere around.
Yes, the game got some images of heavy violence.
Get it only if you dare! ;)

I want to recommend this game but I can't in good faith.
City builder's are one of my favorite genres of games and Banished had the potential to become one of the best but it failed to execute in the long run. Future updates could make this game great.
Before the core game its self is discussed, I really need to voice my dissatisfaction with the mods available on the steam workshop and that process. The game needs significant modding to make some elements palatable in the long run and the workshop provided this; that is, it provided this until most of the important mods were pulled automatically updating my version of the game to no longer include them making many save games unplayable.
There is not enough content in this game and play from game to game is too identical with little possibility of variation unlike other city builders where specialization and different city design choices abound. The lack of building choices is crippling for re-playability; the lack of environmental differences is also dull.
This game is supposed to be a 'survival game' but after reaching about 200 citizens survival is effectively guaranteed which leaves you only to the city building aspect which is somewhat of a let down.
The AI is terrible and the citizens will often make very poor management decisions. This has been improved since release but is still substandard.
This game is very impressive for one person to have made, but it needs work before I could endorse spending $20 on it. The game may be worth picking up while on sale.

The game itself is good, I recommend it if you like Tales or JRPGs, or even fast-paced fights. It's not my favorite Tales game but I did really enjoy it.
Mostly comparing to Tales of Xillia/2 as those were the last games in the series:
- Battles: The battle system has a little bit of a learning curve but it's nice in the sense that you can play it simple or get more complicated with combos/taking advantage of weaknesses/switching characters on-the-fly. Feels like a nice combination of Graces of Xillia - it's fast paced but not obscure and impossible to take advantage of.
- World map: Navigating the world is much better than Xillia/2 and the world feels a lot less empty. Revisiting places is easy with save point travel, thank god for that - if you do have to backtrack, you can quickly warp through dungeons/maps.
- Story: It's kind of meh as far as Tales games go but at least not as ridiculous/rushed as Tales of Xillia/2. It feels more Tales-ey than Xillia/2 in the kind of plot events/plot twists - ridiculous plot twists even for a JRPG that somehow manage to keep you hooked anyway.
- Characters: Tales is not really known for its characters but more for character interactions, and continues that with this game. Tales of the Abyss was the only Tales game with character development and interesting characters as well as interactions.
- Music: Average Tales. Joint between Motoi Sakuraba and Go Shina. I don't like it as much as Xillia/2. The Shiina stuff is good; the Motoi Sakuraba stuff is bland bland bland generic Sakuraba.
- Graphics: Clearly not meant to be a triple A game with realistic graphics, but it does its job well of portaying an anime-style world. Sometimes large areas will have repetitive textures. Characters are expressive.
The port itself is a good port. It seems to be well optimized with no slowdowns. I'm sure controller is the recommended input but it has really well-done keyboard+mouse controls; not only in battle but also navigating menus is a breeze. I have played the PC version entirely with kb+m and enjoy it more than controller.

I never got the chance to play Kingpin when it was first released (mostly because the computer I had at the time was unable to run it) so it fell off my radar for years -- until now that is. I saw that it was on sale for 5$ and after reading the onslaught of positive reviews from other steam users, I decided to give it a go. I went into this game knowing it was dated, and perhaps a bit overpriced - but after reading the countless reviews saying it was a great game, with great voice acting, superb A.I. and had an awesome soundtrack - I was sold.
After beating Kingpin (which took a mere 5 hours) I came to the bitter realization that all these positive reviews were written by people nostalgic about this game and had played Kingpin when it was initially released. I'm sure this WAS an amazing game when it first came out -- but now it's not.
The graphics are playable, the A.I. is good and very advanced for the time it was released. Those are about the only positive things that I can say about Kingpin. The sountrack is literally the same 2 songs which can be heard playing thoughout the duration of the game over and over and over and over and over again. The storyline is atrocious, it gives the players little reason as to why our protagonist was left for dead at the beginning of the game, or why Marsellus Wallace (from Pulp Fiction) is the Kingpin and wants to kill him. There was a small selection of firearms, all of which were weak and barely did any damage to enemies. The difficulty of Kingpin ridiculous to say the least - there are 5 levels, ranging from Easy to Realistic. I tried Normal to begin with and after 10 deaths within the first 10 minutes of the game, decided to drop down to easy. The voice acting was bad, they didn't even match the characters they were for (with the exception of the Kingpin).
For me, the most negative aspect of Kingpin was the amount of foul language - it just wasn't used appropriately. I'm sure it was a shock factor back in the day, but it was used and abused to the point of tedium throughout Kingpin where it just becomes annoying to hear.
Kingpin was not worth the time or the money that I spent on it. I would suggest Postal 2 over Kingpin to anyone looking for a game that is similar to Kingpin, but far superior in every aspect.
I hope this review was helpful.

'I'm gonna bury those two ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.'
Kingpin opens with a cutscene in which the player character utters the above line after rising up from a beating with a swollen face. It tells a simple tale of revenge, or rather, -taking a cue from the Cypress Hill album that the game borrows tracks from- a tale of going from 'Rags to Riches'. You'll be going from town to town -taking down small-time mob bosses along the way- until you confront the current Kingpin to exact your revenge and usurp his throne. As for the journey, right from the first moment it becomes apparent that it will be a raw, brutal, harsh and above all else, very messy one (and unashamedly so).
Even though it is gritty, Xatrix's underdog may very well be the most aesthetically pleasing game to date utilizing the idTech2 engine. Where the other games that are based on the same technology are quick to betray their Quake II origins, Kingpin has a style and feel of its own thanks to the developers' meticulous work on the visual side of their creation. Beautifully textured and elegantly lighted, every single map therein has a life-like scale and quality to it. Though the meshes themselves are not more than a handful, the stylized characters also benefit from the top-notch 2D art, offering a great variety due to the three-way skinning that Xatrix coded in. The sound design is also of high standard; from the footstep sounds to the voiceovers of the NPCs, everything fits perfectly to the fictional world the developers try to portray. Simply put, the game oozes with atmosphere. The fact that this is the one and only shooter of the period that feels better without background music should alone be enough of a testament for the said quality.
But make no mistake, even within its era's boundries, Kingpin is a hard and unforgiving game. Rather than going Quake, it expects you to play in its own terms, that is, to traverse carefully and try to get the upper hand on your enemies. If you do not comply to that, don't expect your experience to be any different than a novice's in the midst of an old-school deathmatch wherein all the other players are seasoned enough to navigate the map perfectly and are capable of ripping you to shreds in a matter of seconds. Play it as intended though and you'll quickly discover that Kingpin is one of the most visceral and satisfying shooter experiences of the 90s.
Xatrix adds a few touches of their own to the engine to spice it up and expand its functionality. The most prominent are  the ability of robbing the downed of their bucks which you use to buy weapons and stuff from specialized shops known as 'Pawn-o-matic's or hiring goons (two max) to back you up, alongside interacting with NPCs through the use of positive and negative conversation commands. But the most pleasing of it all is surely the impeccable pathfinding of the NPCs, especially the ones to be hired to fight alongside you: they run, jump and crouch their way through every single obstacle without a hitch to keep up with you. In fact, I spent two-thirds of my seven-hour trek with two on my side and there was only a single time where they needed extra care on my part. I was constantly surprised by the fact that they were able to traverse the map from one side to the other without an additional command to find me, as if they were not computer but human-controlled.
I believe Kingpin is one of the better shooters of the late 90s. It doesn't reinvent the genre like Half-Life did. Instead, just like its engine-brethren SiN, Daikatana and Soldier of Fortune, it aims for a more classical approach. Its strength lies not in its ingenuity, but in its solid design sensibilities. It has an overarching theme that is full of style and backed up by a ghetto tale told through cutscenes, offers a highly visceral yet never offending combat experience on top and builds up on an already solid engine without introducing any bugs or breaking it. I only wish that it had a longer campaign or an expansion pack of sorts. If it had been kept, the slightly non-linear feel of the first episode would have been welcome too.
Recommended for fans of old-school. Don't forget to answer the phone.

So, to be completely honest this is one of the best games I have played taking in to consideration it is still beta. If this is the foundation of the game, then we can expect something truly good. But at this point it shows its great potential but does not guarantee that it will be executed greatly at the end. Let me explain a bit.
The experiences you get gather trough playing this game can be so intense that you wish to share them over a camp fire, cloaked in wolf skin, with a claw scar over your face looking deeply in the dancing flames. Game has the full potential to bring a realistic and intense survival when you have to tryly fight the great outdoors in order to survive. For example, I was so desperate for food once I got the flare ignited and was running after a wolf chasing a deer just to fight with the wolf after it hunted, and get some meat. Or experienced a slow walk, completely exhausted, while night was falling mixed with snow, praying for a house where I could sleep safely and then saw a lodging camp in the distance. Or fishing on ice while wolves are howling outside, together with wind, and red stove was the only light in the dark...
Now combine this with great realism of real life problems such as how the holes in your underpants influence the speed with which your back side is freezing in the snow storm. You will do more quality checks and sewing that you ever did with your clothes, and even the manliest male will chose his shoes with a level of concentration a high fashion woman has. Everything from how sharp is your knife to what type is your firewood will be important and that just sucks you in the game like a vacuum of space!
On the other hand, the story can be far from anything you would wish to share ever. And not because you died because of your own mistake, but because there is a shine of true black hole in the game mechanic that pulls all the fun out instantly. And one of the evident problems is that it is not a survival in the wild, it a survival between the two houses that still have some canned food in them. Only after my fourth session and after about 25 days in the wild did I managed to get the rifle, and only then I could get enough meat to survive from hunting. Snares are just Christmas decorations for the field, and fishing often results in a big fish that has a same nutrition value of a guppy. Occasionally (for me only once) you can manage to get a big fat fish that can save you from starvation, and you are starving as you are fishing for so long. And even if you get your food and your nice clothes, you might just die from boredom, as when you accomplish those two there is nothing to do... Explore? Chance is, by the time you get your food and clothes, there is nothing more to explore. There will be a time when you will just go outside to poke wolves for any type of entertainment. But lets remember this is just a beginning and more fun stuff will come, I hope so.
So, if somewhere in the future there is more to just that food and clothes border, and if you can actually live out of the wild, instead on your can opener, this will truly be amazing game.

Please note, I played this game primarily with the "Rags 2 Riches" mod as it fixes how much of a slog the game becomes in the second half.
The game's bread and butter is shooting criminals in the face. The formula for the game is you go in an area, visit the bar, talk to some people who can get you access to a part of the map, maybe recruit someone. You go to the newly available area, murder basically everyone and loot bodies, then   after doing whatever you need to do after, you go to the second part of the map, murder everyone, fight a guy with incredibly high health, then you move to the next level. Repeat. Each level has its variation on how this actually plays out but when you play you can easily see the formula. There are 7 levels, amounting to around 9 hours of gameplay, more if you play the base game. In the base game, your weapons are pathetic and are quite ineffective as the enemies have absurd amounts of health. You rely on the 1 or 2 goons you can typically get in all but 1 level of the game, and place them on corners, then you bait the enemies to the ambush point and they get smoked. Charging in all willy nilly is going to get you murdered, because the enemies have perfect accuracy and incredibly high health. In the Rags 2 Riches mod, you can still do this and on some parts its very helpful, but its much easier to just charge in gung ho with your crew and try to take on the bad guys.
Besides slowly increasing your body count with your crew, you'll be doing a few other things in the gameplay. You can Visit a shop called the "Pawn-O-Matic", despite not being automatic, is a store where you can buy armor, health, weapons, ammo, and mods that wear out over time without Rags 2 Riches. You can also talk to random people on the street, a select few will tell you stuff that can be incredibly helpful, others may do stuff for you for money, most will just tell you "Another freekin' night and no ♥♥♥♥♥." You can also visit the bar, found in all chapters but 1, where most of the helpful npc's reside, and where the recruitable goons usually are. You can also go exploring which can net you even more surplus cash to spend at the Pawn-O-Matic, ammo, armor, and health. Theres not a whole lot to be done outside of the main shooting bits of the game.
The plot sucks but its all you need. Some guy named Nikki had his shmucks beat the snot out of you in a back alley for unknown reasons, and you vow to get revenge and go around either a city or multiple cities, its not very clear, ravaging gang after gang. The Kingpin is like "yo kill this guy". Excuse me, he's more like "you ♥♥♥♥in ♥♥♥♥s better ♥♥♥♥in kill this ♥♥♥♥in ♥♥♥♥ or ill ♥♥♥♥in ♥♥♥♥ your ♥♥♥♥in ♥♥♥♥ up you ♥♥♥♥in ♥♥♥♥s." Seriously, this game has a lot of swearing, and violence. The dialogue is great, almost every line in the game has a cuss in it, and the main voice actor did a great job of making the lines memorable. Seriously, the line "♥♥♥♥ YOU ♥♥♥♥" that enemies sometimes yell when you alert them has been burned into my mind for 3 years now.
Easily the best part of the game is the atmosphere. The graphics, music, voice acting, and design of the world all are great. Forget I said music, the CD Music setting didn't work for me on the steam version, not surprised, and theres like 3 songs that loop on the radios you find in the game, albiet I do actually like one of the songs that loops. The lack of music helps create this forboding and tense and sorta creepy atmosphere. You could just be walking in this silent apartment building or run down area, and you have no idea where the enemies are hiding, while the ambient noises of cars in the background and a tin can dropping let you know that you're not alone, but you're not welcome either. The graphics don't help, which is a great thing. Almost every enemy you face is either some tattoo'd up thug looking for a fight, or some guy with a messed up face and demented smile, usually with some strange uniform to go along with it. The more regular looking people in the game are broad shoulder'd and taller than you, and the other model for the male characters is a short fat guy, it adds to the surreal feeling the game gives you.
The short version, the gameplay is a frustrating grind and eventually is hard just for the sake of being hard about 6 hours in, with Rags 2 Riches this is more or less remedied, still challenging though. Don't expect a gangster Deus Ex or anything, just a unique shooter with a nice setting. The plot is nothing special, but the atmosphere is incredible.
I say give this game definiately give this game a go with the Rags 2 Riches mod, I wouldn't say theres too much replayability in doing the whole game over again, but I would definately play the first level or 2 over and over.

Gameplay: What amazes me most about this game, is its ability to suck you in emotionally, and just get lost in its hypnotic struggle against the odds. Utilizing only 2 buttons and a direction pad, this game's allure doesn't come from its mechanics, but the puzzles you have to solve. Each puzzle is slightly unique, never making you feel as though you're repeating the same thing over and over.
Visuals: This game is beautifully crafted with only white, black, and all the gray's in between. Despite such a restriction, this game can portray both ugliness and beauty, the natural and the artificial, evil and virtuous. And by depraving the game of color, it highlights grace. Grace of death. Grace of sin. Grace of life. Grace of good.
Audio: When you play this game, make sure you're in an environment where you can hear clearly. No distractions. The ambient music adds a layer of depth that is unmatched in any other platformer I've played. When you sit down and put on your headphones, you're in LIMBO. You're there with the boy through every step, jump, and fall that he experiences.
Replayability*: My first run through got me about 7 hours, but this isn't a game you play when you're bored. This is a game you play when you're calm, and alone. I often find myself on rainy nights, when everyone around me is asleep, picking up this game. This isn't a "play everyday game." This is a "play when you want to feel again game." This game isn't a compliment to your library. This game is a compliment to your soul.
Point where I'd say you have to buy it: Now.
*This varies A LOT from person to person, so only rely on this category from me if you've agreed with my other reviews' replayability sections.

So after 1,971 hours playtime I guess this would be the right time to give my thoughts about the software. RPG maker isn't strictly speaking a game in itself, but it's a decent tool for allowing you to create your own game. What's really notable about it is how easy it is to pick up for people who are unfamiliar with programming and have never made a game before. At the same time it is also powerful and versatile enough to be used even by experts. As the name implies, RPG maker is mostly for making Role-playing games. Simple 2D JRPGs with random encounters can be made without the use of any scripts, but with the help of scripts even more advanced mechanics and battle systems can be added to one's games. RPG maker already comes with a lot of resources to help with game-making - music, sprites, battler art, and so on, but it allows the user to import custom resources as well. VX Ace is the newest of the RPG makers on PC and it is the most advanced, giving more versatility than the ones before, as well as adding some new features as well, such as a character creator. It can be up to a lot of debate whether it does everything better than previous RPG makers or not, for example RPG maker XP's mapping system is considered better by many people due to the use of multiple layers, but on the other hand, VX Ace allows some parts of the scenery and other decorations to be used as events, which can be utilised to make some stunning cutscenes, such as things appearing out of the ground on a whim, or changing colour or shape, and so on.
The games can be made of any length and size and can be eventually sent to other people to be played, and overall RPG maker is a good starting point for anyone who's considered even for a minute to make their own game. In addition to what the program already has, there's also a whole community out there, with artists, musicians and script-designers making their own custom resources for others to use in their games. When one thinks about it, there aren't many limits to what can be done in RPG maker. It takes some effort to figure out how to make it work, but well worth it. Having a blast with this. Good learning tool for kids too. Visuals are old skool, but its easy enough to add your own content to the graphics files.

is a fun retro platformer but where is the saving feature and controller support? I mean we talking about 4-8 hour game here because the last level will take hours of practice. It kinda reminds me Castlevania games because you attack with a chain whip and use it to swing across gaps. Movement is rather sluggish which is probably intentional retro design. Overall it has enough variety and the gameplay is enjoyable.
When you kill enemies you will collect their souls as currency. I am pretty sure it is a Dark Souls reference although the game does not follow that format very deeply. There are several very important upgrades so the soul collecting is a vital part of the game. The importance of currency makes it fun to look for hidden chests and grind enemies.Also, it has some Metroid inspired exploration. Not like a labyrinth or anything. You will unlock better mobility tools overtime which will allow you to enter new areas that were out of your reach. So it encourages some backtracking. Although I felt that game needed a map in few places.
It has a reasonable difficulty progression until you get to the last stage. The difficulty spike went like 500% above the previous one. I never complain about the difficulty but that level is ****** miserable. Visually I really enjoyed it. Hitting things feels satisfying because of the sound and visual effects.Pixel art, music, and cutscenes were decent. For the low price, it has enough different themes and even some cool boss fights.
It is hard to defend a platformer where you can't save or use a controller. Hopefully, those two things will be addressed. It has a lot going for it in terms of nostalgic design and above average gameplay mechanics. That last level though...WTF

I remember that a long time ago i wanted this game so bad that i made a subscription to a videogame magazine just because they gifted this game as a present for that subscription. I received that game, launched and thought "wow, that's amazing".
It was one of the first examples of an adventure/action game where you can decide what's gonna happen next. It's all a matter of choices. You can be bad, you can be good and everything changes. For example, you could be sleeping alone if you don't say the right words to Tiffany, or maybe if you're smart enough you could be "sleeping" with her.
Here's the plot. A young man kills an old man in a diner's bathroom without even knowing how and why. He just remember that moment as a nightmare where he couldn't do anything but stare at his body moving and using his knife to kill that man. What happened? He has to find out the truth, also because the more he goes on, the more he gains special powers and abilities. A strong drama filled with side stories and characters. You can play as the main character, and as the 2 policeman, Tyler and Carla. Make choices, change the story, see the 3 different endings.
Good graphics (remember is a 2005 game), updated textures in this remastered versions and epic soundtrack by Angelo Badalamenti (creator of some of the best videogame and movies soundtracks).
Now the bad things: first, the second part of the game is more action than adventure. It remembers the old quick time event games, funny at first, but annoying and frustrating later. Second, controls are not so responsive. During this quick time action events the game asks you to press 2 buttons at the same time, but sometimes even if you press them, the game doesn't recognize it and make you fail the sequence.
Pros:
+ Good graphics
+ Nice facial expressions
+ Epic soundtrack
+ Really inspired plot based on your choices
+ 3 different endings
+ Charismatic characters
+ Good replayability
+ Linux support
Cons:
- Too much quick time action events in the second part of the game
- Controls not so responsive
I recommend this game without a doubt!!!

Kingpin: Life of Crime is really interesting, what starts off as a tough as nails, slow paced, atmospheric first person experience which hates you quickly turns into an all out guns blazing fast paced action game that hates you even more. This is far tougher than the average 90's FPS game and will require luck, strategy and a skillfull approach to progress through it's big, open, levels.
The gameplay is varied, you can approach combat situations in different ways, going slowly and picking off enemies one by one or go in guns blazing like a typical FPS game from the 90's but don't expect to live for too long that way, the best approach is to use a mixture of the two.
The level design is somewhat reminscent of Quake 2's with non-linear layouts and multi-levelled structures that overlook area's of the map you're soon to visit or have already, mixed with some Half-Life's design choices. The levels are extremely well thought out and designed with not only looks but gameplay in mind and similar to that of Quake and Doom require you to look around for keys or items needed to progress and does not hold your hand and pull you through the map. The combat situations are often tough and leave you to overcome disadvantages which adds to the difficulty in a good way.
The AI is insane, the enemy will shoot you with almost instant, deadly accuracy as soon as you poke your nose around a corner which will frustrate a lot of people but I was able to overcome this by outsmarting the enemy in many ways such as luring them around corners and into your commandable gang members line of sight who will then mow the enemies down with the same ferocity the enemy AI shows towards to you which is really fun to watch. The AI is far from perfect, but in my opinion is WAY better and more interesting than what we see in modern shooters today, instead of artificially/dumbly taking cover behind barrels,walls and other forms of cover which makes them sitting ducks and actually easier to pick off, will run around, retreat then hide somewhere on the map, jump down from higher levels, climb ladders and attempt to out maneuver you which sometimes works to their success.
The visuals are amazing and take full advantange of the Quake 2 engine, with great lighting effects and detailed environments, there is literally nothing wrong with them but 50$ says this gets the bland, soulless HD remake along the line. The sound effects and voice acting are good, the weapons sound deadly and the AI has tons of classic lines, many including the 'f' word multiple times.
Overall this game really impressed me through-out, took around 8-9 hours of tough gameplay to complete, I wasn't able to finish this as a child due to it's crushing learning curve but if you stick around you'll experience a time when gaming was at it's peak but BE WARNED, a lot of patience is required!

I just finished The Beginner's Guide, a PC game available on Steam, made by the developers behind The Stanley Parable. As a traditional game, it makes no effort to hide that its ideas and implementations are unpolished. That's the point, actually, as the game is a walkthrough of one developer's unfinished, unreleased games, narrated by another developer who was their friend.
In truth, this is the kind of game that defies a traditional review. The single best, concise description I've read so far was little more than a stream of confused, but deeply emotionally affected, consciousness. But I also like and agree with what Rock Paper Shotgun had to say, that where Stanley Parable is about sarcastic detachment and subversion, The Beginner's Guide is about intimacy, and... to say any more would only spoil it.
Recommended.

I will try to make my review and advice as ambiguous as possible for anyone interested in playing this game without being spoiled.
First of all, I would recommend that you don't watch the trailer. Don't read anything about this game. You probably shouldn't even be on the reviews. I'm not sure how the game would translate if you already know the main idea, but I can promise you that performing a blind playthrough is supremely impactful, and I'd highly advise doing so.
I, like many others, bought the game without hesitation after a more than delightful experience with The Stanley Parable. My biggest regret with TSP was exposing myself to the game's unique concept before playing, so I didn't want to make the same mistake twice.
I went into The Beginner's Guide expecting it to be another quirky, time passing videogame that would challenge standard ideas and mechanics. And while it did certainly "challenge" ideas, I can't say I was prepared for what this game presented. Throughout the entirety of the playthrough I felt a lingering discomfort, though I made the mistake of allowing the story to define for me where that discomfort lay.
TBG has left me so overwhelmed with thoughts and emotions that I almost feel empty. So diluted with contradicting feelings, with no single thought other than "perception" standing out in my head. I'm conflicted, having to choose between starting over, and mulling over. On one hand, I can replay the game, figure out where *I* as the player and audience went wrong in my thoughts, and maybe, knowing what I know now, can find and appreciate aspects of the game I originally and incorrectly perceived as something else, something horrible. On the other hand, I'm having trouble coming to terms with some of the major points, as it would mean me coming to terms with my own issues abruptly and over a godamn videogame. I'm sitting here after my first playthrough, still unable to decide whether I feel deceived or enlightened by its core message. Instead of dissecting this feeling, however, I can't help but think of how the game's core ideas have been presented in my life. When I was a victim of such occurences. When I was the perpetrator. What I did right and what I did wrong. How my creations have reflected on others in society, and when others' creations impacted me. No matter who you are, I feel like there is so much to be gained from this story, and much to learn from the key moments of the plot.
All in all, TBG is an emotionally taxing experience, and the more you can relate, the harder it becomes. I found myself understanding things about me that I once could never pinpoint. I've cried over games before, sure, but usually it's for the fictional characters one is forced to fall in love with over the course of events. So I have to say, I didn't expect to end this playthrough emotional about myself and my actions. In A Hat in Time, you take control of an adorable protagonist simply named "Hat Kid." Hat Kid is stopped at a fairly unusual world as her fuel for her space ship, the Time Pieces, are taken from her. Hat Kid will have to jump and sprint her way across the planet to retrieve all of her Time Pieces, meeting a lot of whimsical characters along the way.

If you've ever played literally any 3D Mario game, get this. You will be far from disappointed.

A Hat In Time is a fantastic platformer.  I never thought that any platformer would dethrone Voodoo Vince as my favorite, but after fourteen years it has happened.  A Hat In Time is a wonderfully cute game where no planets are the same.  You can be riding a train for one act, and the next one you are leading a marching band in a parade.  If I had to describe A Hat In Time, I would say it is a combination of Super Mario Sunshine, Mario Galaxy, and Banjo Kazooie.  The game takes what makes those three great and leaves out all that doesn't.  The soundtrack is so wonderful that I felt that I had to go and purchase it so I can listen to it while I play other games.  The upbeat nature of all the characters and music is enough to get anybody hooked.  At the time of writing this review, I only have eight hours and I have beat the story.  I usually consider story length to decide if a game is worth it, but in this case I judged the game's value off of fun factor.  I am currently working on hitting 100 percent, and I am having a fantastic time fooling around in the acts as I do so.
If I had to give this game a score, it would be a 10/10.  I absolutely love platformers, and this game has all the characteristics of a fantastic one.  The soundtrack, the characters, and the comedy all come together wonderfully.  For me, this has absolute potential to be my game of the year.
Edit : I have now gotten 100 percent completion, but not all the achievements.  I'm very excited for the community to start creating things for this game.

I am having trouble enjoying this game anymore, even though I want to.
Pros:
You can get fun outfits without having to pay real money for them.
You can get some of the highest lvl pets without having to pay real money for them.
There is no pay to win aspect in this game.
With those pros you would think that this game would be a great mmo tower defense, but the cons make you loath the process you have to undergo in order to even attempt the nightmare difficulty playthroughs. DD2 stops being a game of strategy long before you reach even the hard or insane difficulty levels preceding the nightmare ones.
Cons:
Grind, Grind, Grind goes the player. Item drops are arbitrary. What I mean by this is that the high lvl gear that drops as you solo a difficult map, will hardly ever be gear you actually want for ANY of your characters.
What adds insult to injury is the carnival ticket mechanic. During every map playthrough, carnival ticket's drop, and for every 10 tickets that drop, you can spin the carnival wheel for the chance of getting Legendary gear of your current avg item lvl. This is the only way to dependably get good gear, because Legendary gear is the best in the game. So, even if it is not perfect for your build you may still be able to use it. To use the wheel in this way requires that you equip terrible tier gear that have high item lvls. This way you increase your avg item level before you spin the wheel.
If you do not have tickets, you can use 2500 in game currency to spin the wheel. So, you end up farming maps for gold, then spinning the wheel until you get better gear, finally playing the same old maps at a higher difficulty setting, and then restarting the process all over again to advance to the next difficulty setting.
Therefore, this game is more than just a grind fest, but also a redundant waste of time with no true reward for effort expended.

"There are no zombies -- only you, the cold, and all the threats Mother Nature can muster. " - meaning will you by any chance find that can of pork and beans...
***WARNING might contain spoilers***
So, to be completely honest this is one of the best games I have played taking in to consideration it is still beta. If this is the foundation of the game, then we can expect something truly good. But at this point it shows its great potential but does not guarantee that it will be executed greatly at the end. Let me explain a bit.
The experiences you get gather trough playing this game can be so intense that you wish to share them over a camp fire, cloaked in wolf skin, with a claw scar over your face looking deeply in the dancing flames. Game has the full potential to bring a realistic and intense survival when you have to tryly fight the great outdoors in order to survive. For example, I was so desperate for food once I got the flare ignited and was running after a wolf chasing a deer just to fight with the wolf after it hunted, and get some meat. Or experienced a slow walk, completely exhausted, while night was falling mixed with snow, praying for a house where I could sleep safely and then saw a lodging camp in the distance. Or fishing on ice while wolves are howling outside, together with wind, and red stove was the only light in the dark...
Now combine this with great realism of real life problems such as how the holes in your underpants influence the speed with which your back side is freezing in the snow storm. You will do more quality checks and sewing that you ever did with your clothes, and even the manliest male will chose his shoes with a level of concentration a high fashion woman has. Everything from how sharp is your knife to what type is your firewood will be important and that just sucks you in the game like a vacuum of space!
On the other hand, the story can be far from anything you would wish to share ever. And not because you died because of your own mistake, but because there is a shine of true black hole in the game mechanic that pulls all the fun out instantly. And one of the evident problems is that it is not a survival in the wild, it a survival between the two houses that still have some canned food in them. Only after my fourth session and after about 25 days in the wild did I managed to get the rifle, and only then I could get enough meat to survive from hunting. Snares are just Christmas decorations for the field, and fishing often results in a big fish that has a same nutrition value of a guppy. Occasionally (for me only once) you can manage to get a big fat fish that can save you from starvation, and you are starving as you are fishing for so long. And even if you get your food and your nice clothes, you might just die from boredom, as when you accomplish those two there is nothing to do... Explore? Chance is, by the time you get your food and clothes, there is nothing more to explore. There will be a time when you will just go outside to poke wolves for any type of entertainment. But lets remember this is just a beginning and more fun stuff will come, I hope so.
So, if somewhere in the future there is more to just that food and clothes border, and if you can actually live out of the wild, instead on your can opener, this will truly be amazing game.
